Muhammad ibn al-Hasan (may God be pleased with him) narrated to us, he said: al-Hasan ibn Matil al-Daqqaq narrated to us, he said: Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn Abi al-Khattab narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from al-Mufaddal ibn Umar, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about passionate love (al-'ishq), so he said: Hearts that became empty of the remembrance of God, so God made them taste the love of other than Him.

By this chain of narration, he said: Al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) said: Whoever's two days are equal is at a loss; whoever's latter day is the worse of the two is cursed; whoever does not recognize improvement in himself is closer to decline; and whoever is closer to decline, then death is better for him than life.

Muhammad ibn Musa ibn al-Mutawakkil (may God be pleased with him) narrated to us. He said: Ali ibn al-Husayn al-Sa'd Abadi narrated to us. He said: Ahmad ibn Abi Abdillah al-Barqi narrated to us. He said: Ali ibn Muhammad al-Qasani narrated to us, from Sulayman ibn Dawud al-Munqari, from Hammad ibn Isa, from al-Sadiq Ja'far ibn Muhammad (peace be upon him) who said: Among that which Luqman advised his son Natan is that he said to him: O my son! Let that with which you arm yourself against your enemy, so as to overcome him, be kind treatment and voicing your acceptance of him. Do not confront him with avoidance, lest what is in your soul becomes apparent to him and he prepares against you. O my son! Fear God with such a fear that if you were to come to Him with the goodness of the two heavyweights (humans and jinn), you would still fear that God would punish you. And hope in God with such a hope that if you were to come to Him with the sins of the two heavyweights, you would still hope that God would forgive you. O my son! I have carried boulders, iron, and every heavy load, but I have not carried anything heavier than an evil neighbour. And I have tasted every bitterness, but I have not tasted anything more bitter than poverty.

My father (may God be pleased with him) narrated to us, he said: Al-Husayn ibn Musa narrated to us from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar - and al-Husayn did not memorize the chain of narration - he said: Luqman said to his son: O my son! Take one thousand friends for yourself, for one thousand is too few; and do not take even one enemy, for one is too many. Then Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) said: Increase in brethren as much as you can, for they are pillars and supporters when their help is sought. One thousand close friends and companions is not many, but indeed one enemy is too many.

7 - Our father (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated to us, he said: Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated to us, he said: al-Haytham ibn Abi Masruq an-Nahdi narrated to us, from his father, he said: Yazid ibn Makhlad an-Naysaburi narrated to me, he said: someone who heard al-Sadiq Jaʿfar ibn Muhammad (peace be upon them both) narrated to me He said: Friendship has conditions, so whoever does not have those conditions in him, do not attribute to him the perfection of friendship, and whoever does not have anything of those conditions in him, do not attribute to him any part of friendship. The first of them: that his inner self and his outward be one and the same for you. And the second: that he sees your adornment as his adornment, and your disgrace as his disgrace. And the third: that neither wealth nor authority changes him toward you. And the fourth: that he does not withhold from you anything that is within his ability. And the fifth: that he does not abandon you in times of calamities.

Al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) said to one of his companions: Whoever among your brethren becomes angry with you three times, and yet does not say anything evil about you, then take him for yourself as a friend.
Al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) said: Do not place complete trust in your brother, for indeed the fall caused by over-reliance can never be recovered from.

Al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) said to one of his companions: Do not reveal to your friend any of your secrets except what would cause you no harm if your enemy were to learn of it, for indeed a friend may become an enemy one day.

Al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) said: My father narrated to me from my grandfather (peace be upon both of them) that the Commander of the Faithful (blessings of God upon him) said: Who can guarantee you one day a brother who is completely [without flaw]? And which of men is without blemish?

Muhammad ibn Ali Majiluwayh (may God have mercy on him) narrated to us. He said: My uncle Muhammad ibn Abi al-Qasim narrated to me. He said: Muhammad ibn Ali al-Kufi al-Qurashi narrated to me. He said: Muhammad ibn Sinan narrated to me from al-Mufaddal ibn Umar, from al-Sadiq Ja'far ibn Muhammad (peace be upon him), who said: Whoever fasts three days at the end of Sha'ban and connects them with the month of Ramadan, Allah shall record for him the fasting of two consecutive months.

'Ali b. Ahmad b. Musa al-Daqqaq (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated to us. He said: Muhammad b. Abi 'Abdillah al-Kufi al-Asadi narrated to us. He said: Muhammad b. Ismail al-Barmaki narrated to me from Ja'far b. Ahmad al-Kufi al-Bazzaz. He said: Ismail b. 'Abd al-Khaliq narrated to us from al-Sadiq Ja'far b. Muhammad (peace be upon them both), that he said: Fasting Sha'ban and the month of Ramadan is repentance (forgiveness) from Allah, even from forbidden blood.

Al-Husayn ibn Ibrahim ibn Ahmad ibn Hisham al-Mu'addib (may God have mercy upon him) narrated to us. He said: Muhammad ibn Ja'far al-Asadi al-Kufi narrated to us. He said: Musa ibn Imran al-Nakha'i narrated to me from his uncle al-Husayn ibn Yazid al-Nawfali, from Ali ibn Abi Hamza, from his father, from al-Sadiq Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, from his forefathers, from Ali (peace be upon them all). He said: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said: When the Day of Resurrection comes, you will be brought — O Ali — on a she-camel of light. Upon your head will be a crown with four pillars, and upon each pillar will be three inscriptions: 'There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, Ali is the Friend of Allah.' You will be given the keys to Paradise. Then a seat known as the 'Seat of Honour' will be placed for you, and you will sit upon it. Then the former and latter peoples will be gathered before you on one plain. You will direct your Shi'a to Paradise and your enemies to the Fire, for you are the Divider of Paradise and the Divider of the Fire. He who aligns with you is triumphant, and he who opposes you has lost. On that Day, you will be the trustee of God and the clear Proof of God.

The venerable Shaykh Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn Musa ibn Babawayh al-Qummi (may God be pleased with him) narrated to us. He said: Muhammad ibn Musa ibn al-Mutawakkil (may God be pleased with him) narrated to us. He said: Ali ibn al-Husayn al-Sa'd Abadi narrated to us, from Ahmad ibn Abi Abdillah al-Barqi, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr al-Bazanti, from Abu al-Hasan al-Mosuli, from Abu Abdillah al-Sadiq (peace be upon him), who said: A rabbi from the rabbis came to the Commander of the Faithful, and said: O Commander of the Faithful, when did your Lord come into existence? He said to him: May your mother mourn you! And when did He not exist that it could be said 'when did He exist'?! My Lord existed before the before, without a before, and He will exist after the after, without an after. There is no limit and no termination to His eternity. All limits are severed from Him, so He is the ultimate end of every end.

My father (may God be pleased with him) narrated to us, he said: Ahmad ibn Idris narrated to us, he said: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya ibn Imran al-Ash'ari narrated to us, from Ahmad ibn Abi Abdillah, from Ali ibn Ja'far al-Jawhari, from Ibrahim ibn Abdillah al-Kufi, from Abu Sa'id Aqisa, who said: Al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Abi Talib (peace be upon him) was asked about intellect, so he said: It is suppressing grief and dealing gently with enemies.

Ali ibn Ahmad ibn Abdullah ibn Ahmad ibn Abi Abdillah al-Barqi narrated to us, from his father, from his grandfather, from Umar ibn Uthman, from Abu Jamila al-Mufaddal ibn Salih, from Said ibn Turayf, from al-Asbagh ibn Nubata, from Ali ibn Abi Talib (peace be upon him), who said: Gabriel descended upon Adam (peace be upon them both) and said: O Adam, I have been commanded to give you the choice of one of three things, so choose one and leave the other two. Adam said to him: And what are the three, O Gabriel? He said: Intellect, modesty, and religion. Adam said: I have chosen intellect. So Gabriel said to modesty and religion: Depart and leave him. They both said: O Gabriel, we have been commanded to be with intellect wherever it goes. He said: As you wish. Then he ascended.

4 - My father (may God be pleased with him) narrated to us. He said: Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Attar narrated to us. He said: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya ibn Imran al-Ash'ari narrated to us, from al-Hasan ibn Ali al-Kufi, from al-Abbas ibn Amer, from Ahmad ibn Rizq al-Ghamshani, from Yahya ibn Abi al-Ala', from Jabir, from Abu Ja'far al-Baqir (peace be upon him), who said: A servant remained in the Fire for seventy autumns, and each autumn is seventy years. He said: Then he asked God, Mighty and Majestic: "By the right of Muhammad and his Ahl al-Bayt, why have You not shown mercy to me?" He said: So God, Exalted is His Majesty, revealed to Gabriel: "Descend to My servant and remove him." He said: "O Lord, how can I descend into the Fire?" He said: "I have commanded it to be cool and peaceful for you." He said: "O Lord, I do not know where he is." So He, Mighty and Majestic, said: "He is in a pit in Sijjin." He said: So he descended into the Fire and found him chained upon his face, and took him out. Then He, Mighty and Majestic, said: "O My servant, how long were you calling upon Me in the Fire?" He said: "I cannot count it, O my Lord." He said: "By My glory! Had you not asked Me by it, I would have prolonged your torment in the Fire. But I have decreed upon Myself that no servant shall ask Me by the right of Muhammad and his Ahl al-Bayt except that I will forgive him for what was between Me and him. And I have forgiven you today."

My father (may God be pleased with him) narrated to us, he said: Ali ibn Ibrahim ibn Hashim narrated to us from his father Ibrahim ibn Hashim, he said: Ibrahim ibn Raja' al-Jahdari narrated to me, he said: Waki' ibn al-Jarrah narrated to us from Sharik ibn Abdullah, from Abdullah ibn Muhammad ibn Aqil, from Jabir ibn Abdullah al-Ansari, who said: The Messenger of God (may God bless him and his family) said: Whoever prefers anyone from my companions over Ali has indeed disbelieved.

My father (may God be pleased with him) narrated to us, he said: Ali ibn Ibrahim ibn Hashim narrated to us, from his father, from Ibrahim ibn Raja, he said: Hammad ibn Zayd narrated to us, from Aban, from Ibn Abbas -- or from Aban ibn Thabit, from Anas ibn Malik -- he said: The Messenger of God (may God bless him and his family) said: Whoever shows enmity toward Ali has waged war against God, and whoever doubts in Ali is a disbeliever.

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan (may God be pleased with him) narrated to us. He said: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar narrated to us from Ali ibn Muhammad al-Qasani, from Sulayman ibn Dawud al-Minqari, from Yahya ibn Sa'id, from Abu Abdillah al-Sadiq, from his father (peace be upon them both). Regarding the saying of God, Blessed and Exalted: "And they ask you: Is it true? Say: Yes, by my Lord, indeed it is true" [10:53]. He said: The people of Mecca ask you - O Muhammad - about Ali ibn Abi Talib (peace be upon him): Is he an Imam? "Say: Yes, by my Lord, indeed it is true."

8 - My father (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated to us. He said: Sa'd b. 'Abdullah narrated to us. He said: Ahmad b. Muhammad b. 'Isa narrated to us from Musa b. al-Qasim al-Bajali from Ja'far b. Muhammad b. Sama'a from 'Abdullah b. Muskan from al-Hakam b. al-Salt from Abi Ja'far Muhammad b. 'Ali from his forefathers (peace be upon them). He said: The Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and his family) said: Take hold of the belt of this bald man — meaning 'Ali — for indeed he is the Great Truthful One (al-Siddiq al-Akbar), and he is the Distinguisher (al-Faruq) who distinguishes between truth and falsehood. Whoever loves him, Allah guides him; whoever hates him, Allah hates him; and whoever opposes him, Allah destroys him. From him are the two clans of my nation — al-Hasan and al-Husayn — and they are my two sons. From al-Husayn are the Imams of Guidance; Allah has granted them my knowledge and my understanding. So align yourselves with them and do not take a confidant from besides them, lest the wrath of your Lord come upon you. And whoever upon whom the wrath of his Lord comes has indeed fallen. And the life of this world is nothing but the enjoyment of vanity (1).

1 - The eminent Shaykh Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn ibn 'Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn Musa ibn Babawayh al-Qummi (may God be pleased with him) narrated to us. He said: Muhammad ibn Musa ibn al-Mutawakkil (may God have mercy on him) narrated to us. He said: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated to us. He said: Abu Muhammad al-Qasim ibn al-'Ala' narrated to us from 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Muslim. He said: In the days of 'Ali ibn Musa al-Rida (peace be upon him), we were in Marv. We gathered in its central mosque on a Friday at the beginning of our arrival. The people discussed the matter of the Imamate, and they mentioned the multitude of differences regarding it. So I entered upon my master al-Rida (peace be upon him) and informed him of what the people had delved into. He smiled (peace be upon him), then said: O 'Abd al-'Aziz! The people are ignorant, and they are deceived regarding their religions. Indeed, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, did not cause His Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) to pass away until He perfected the religion for him and revealed the Quran to him, in which there is elucidation for everything. In it, the lawful, the forbidden, the limits, and the rulings were made clear, as well as all of what the people need, completely. He said, Mighty and Majestic: 'We have neglected nothing in the Book' [6:38]. And He revealed at the Farewell Pilgrimage, at the end of his (peace be upon him and his family) life: 'This day I have perfected your religion for you, and I have completed My favour unto you, and I have chosen for you Islam as a religion' [5:3]. And the matter of the Imamate is from the completion of the religion, and he (peace be upon him and his family) did not pass away until he clarified to his community the landmarks of their religion, clarified their paths for them, left them on the way toward truth, and established 'Ali (peace be upon him) as their scholar and Imam. He did not leave anything that the community would need except that he clarified it. So whoever alleges that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, did not perfect His religion has rejected the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and whoever rejects the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is a disbeliever. Do they even know the significance of the Imamate and its station in the community, so as to dare give their opinions regarding it? Indeed, the Imamate is of a more majestic station and greater affai

May Allah bless Muhammad the Chosen One, Ali the one He is pleased with, Fatima the Radiant, and the Chosen Imams from her descendants, the Goodly Family of Ya Sin, the Righteous, and grant them much peace.

I was informed by the Sheikh Abu ʿAbd Allah Muhammad ibn Muhammad ibn al-Nuʿman, may God have mercy on him, who said: I was informed by Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn al-Walid, from his father, from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar; and Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn ʿIsa and al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan ibn Aban; from al-Husayn ibn Saʿid, from Ibn Abi ʿUmayr, from Abu Ayyub, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu ʿAbd Allah (peace be upon him): that he was asked about water in which animals urinate, dogs lap, and from which a person in a state of major ritual impurity (junub) bathes. He said: If the water is the measure of a kurr, nothing renders it impure.

And by this isnad, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Hammad ibn 'Isa, from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, from Abu 'Abd Allah (peace be upon him), he said: If the water is the measure of a kurr, nothing can make it impure.

And the Sheikh (may God have mercy on him) informed me, from Abu al-Qasim Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Qulawayh, from Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, from Safwan, and from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father, from Hammad ibn Isa — all of them from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, who said: I heard Abu Abd Allah (peace be upon him) saying: 'When the water reaches the measure of a kurr, nothing renders it impure.'

As for what Muhammad b. Ya'qub narrated from 'Ali b. Ibrahim, from his father, from Muhammad b. Abi 'Umayr and Muhammad b. Isma'il from al-Fadl b. Shadhan — all of them from Hammad b. 'Isa, from Hariz, from Zurara, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him): He said: When the water is more than a rawiya, nothing shall make it impure — whether something decomposes in it or does not decompose in it — unless a smell comes upon it that overpowers the smell of the water. This does not contradict what we have previously presented of narrations, because he said 'when the water is more than a rawiya,' making clear that it carries no impurity only when it exceeds the rawiya; and it is not excluded that what is meant by that excess is the amount by which the kurr is completed.

As for what Muhammad ibn Ya'qub has narrated — from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Abdullah ibn al-Mughirah, from some of our companions, from Abu Abdillah (AS) — he said: 'The kurr of water is approximately like this jar of mine,' and he pointed to a jar from those jars that are found in Medina. So it is not impossible that the jar holds the measure of a kurr of water, and this is not far-fetched.

As for what Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub narrated from al-Abbas, from Abdullah ibn al-Mughira, from some of his companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): He said: When water reaches the measure of two qullas, nothing makes it impure. And two qullas are two jars. The first issue with this narration is that it is mursal. It is also possible that it was issued under taqiyya, for it is the position of many of the 'amma [Sunni scholars]. And even if we accept it, it is possible that the interpretation is what we mentioned in the preceding narration — namely, that the measure of two qullas equals the measure of a kurr, since that is not objectionable, for qulla in the [Arabic] language is the large jar. And on this basis, there is no contradiction between the narrations.

As for what Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb narrated from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn, from ʿAlī ibn Ḥadīd, from Ḥammād ibn ʿĪsā, from Ḥarīz, from Zurārah, from Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام, he said: I said to him: A waterskin containing water—if a dead mouse, rat, or sparrow falls into it? He said: If it decomposes in it, then do not drink from its water and do not perform wudu (ablution) from it. But if it is not decomposed, then drink from it and perform wudu (ablution), and cast away the carcass when you remove it fresh. The same applies to the jar, the large water vessel, the waterskin, and similar containers of water. He said: And Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام said: If the water is more than a rāwiyah, nothing that decomposes in it or does not decompose renders it impure, unless an odor comes to it that overpowers the smell of the water. So this report may be understood such that his statement, “a rāwiyah of water,” refers to when its amount is a kurr; for when it is like that, nothing that falls into it renders it impure. And his statement, “if it decomposes in it, then do not drink and do not perform wudu (ablution),” is understood as referring to when one of the qualities of the water changes. The same applies to the jar, the large water vessel, and the waterskin. No one may say that the jar, the large water vessel, the waterskin, and the rāwiyah cannot contain a kurr of water, because the report does not say that a single jar has that ruling; rather, it mentioned them with the definite article, and that indicates generality according to many of the people of language. If that possibility exists, then it does not conflict with the reports we have presented earlier.

As for what al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from 'Uthman ibn 'Isa, from Sama'a ibn Mihran, from Abu Basir: He said: I asked him about a kurr of water I passed during travel, in which a donkey, a mule, or a person had urinated. He said: 'Do not perform wudu from it, and do not drink from it.' The correct approach to this narration is to interpret it as applicable when one of the water's characteristics has changed — either its taste, its colour, or its smell. As for when that is absent [i.e., none of the properties have changed], there is no harm in using it, in accordance with the preceding narrations. And what points to this meaning is...

Informed me thereof the Sheikh — may Allah have mercy on him — from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, from his father, from Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah, from Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from Yasin al-Darir, from Hariz ibn 'Abd Allah, from Abu Basir, from Abu 'Abd Allah (AS): that he was asked about stagnant water (al-mā' al-naqī') in which animals urinate. He said: If the water has changed, do not perform wudu from it; but if their urine has not changed it, then perform wudu from it. Likewise blood, when it flows into water, and its similars.

And by this chain, from Sa'd ibn 'Abdillah, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from al-'Abbas ibn Ma'ruf, from Hammad ibn 'Isa, from Ibrahim ibn 'Amr al-Yamani, from Abu Khalid al-Qammat, that he heard Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) speaking about water that a man passes by, which is a stagnant pool containing a dead animal and carrion. Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: If the water's smell or taste has changed, do not drink from it and do not perform wudu from it. And if its smell and taste have not changed, drink and perform wudu.

As for what al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Muhammad ibn Isma'il ibn Bazi', he said: I wrote to the one who was asked about a ghedir (pool) in which rainwater collects and from which water is also drawn from a well — a person performs istinja in it from urine or excrement, or the junub (one in a state of major ritual impurity) performs ghusl in it. What is its minimum hadd (threshold) below which [its use] is not permissible? He wrote back: 'Do not perform wudu from the like of this except out of necessity.' This report is interpreted as indicating a type of juristic disapproval (karaha), because were it not so, the water of the ghedir would either be less than a kurr — in which case it becomes najis and its use is not permissible under any circumstance, and the obligation would be tayammum — or the intended amount would be more than a kurr, in which case it does not carry impurity and is not restricted to cases of necessity. The correct interpretation of this narration is karaha, because in the presence of waters whose purity is certain (mutayaqqan), it is not appropriate to use these waters; they are to be used only when [pure] water is entirely unavailable.

Abu al-Husayn ibn Abi Jiyd al-Qummi informed me from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn al-Walid, from al-Saffar, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad and al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan ibn Aban, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Ibn Sinan, from Ibn Muskan, from Abu Basir, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him). He said: I asked him about the person in a state of janaba who places a rakwa or a tawr and inserts his finger into it. He said: If his hand was unclean (ritually impure), let him pour it out; and if no impurity had touched it, let him perform ghusl from it. This is from what God, Exalted be He, said: 'He has not placed upon you any hardship in the religion.' (Quran 22:78)

And by this chain of narration, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from his brother al-Hasan, from Zur'ah, from Sama'ah ibn Mihran, from Abu 'Abd Allah (peace be upon him), who said: When a man is in a state of janabah and inserts his hand into a vessel, there is no harm — if no semen has touched his hand.

And the Sheikh, may God have mercy on him, informed me from Abu al-Qasim Ja'far b. Muhammad, from Muhammad b. Ya'qub, from Muhammad b. Yahya, from Ahmad b. Muhammad, from 'Uthman b. 'Isa, from Sama'a, who said: I asked Abu 'Abd Allah (peace be upon him) about a water jar in which a beetle was found dead. He said: Throw it out and perform wudu from it [the water]. And if it was a scorpion, then pour out the water and perform wudu from other water. And [I also asked] about a man who has two vessels containing water, into one of which an impurity fell and he does not know which one it is, and he has no other water available. He said: He should pour both out and perform tayammum.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from al-'Amarki, from Ali ibn Ja'far, from his brother Musa ibn Ja'far (peace be upon him). He said: I asked him about a chicken, a pigeon, and birds similar to them that tread on excrement and then enter water from which wudu is to be performed for salat. He said: No, except if the water is abundant — a measure of a kurr of water.

As for what al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from 'Ali ibn Abi Hamza — he said: I asked Abu 'Abd Allah (peace be upon him) about still water in which there is a carcass: is it proper to perform istinja' from it? So he replied: Perform wudu from the other side, and do not perform wudu from the side of the carcass.
From him, from 'Uthman ibn 'Isa, from Sama'ah. He said: I asked him about a man who comes upon a dead animal in the water. Then he said: He performs wudu from the side where the dead animal is not.

And from him, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from Aban, from Zakkar ibn Farqad, from Uthman ibn Ziyad — he said: I said to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him): I am on a journey and come to stagnant water while my hands are dirty, then I submerge them in the water. He said: There is no harm.

Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from al-Ala ibn al-Fudayl — He said: I asked Abu Abdillah (عليه السلام) about pools in which urination occurs. He said: 'There is no harm, if the color of the water overcomes the color of the urine.'

Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn Abī Naṣr, from Ṣafwān ibn Mihrān al-Jammāl, who said: I asked Abū ʿAbdillāh (peace be upon him) about the pools between Mecca and Medina — to which wild beasts come, in which dogs lap water, from which donkeys drink, and in which the junub bathes. Can wudu be performed from them? He said: How much water is there? I said: Up to half the shin, or up to the knee. He said: Perform wudu from it.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Fadala ibn Ayyub, from al-Husayn ibn 'Uthman, from Sama'a ibn Mihran, from Abu Basir: He said: I said to Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him): We travel, and we may encounter a rain puddle near a village in which there is human excrement; a child urinates in it, and a riding animal urinates and defecates in it. He said: If something stirs in your heart about it, then do this — meaning: part the water with your hand, then perform wudu — for religion is not restrictive; indeed Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: «He has not placed upon you in the religion any hardship.» (al-Hajj 22:78) The correct interpretation of all these narrations is to understand them as referring to water exceeding one kurr; for in that case it does not become impure by what falls into it, unless one of its properties changes, as we have previously established. As for what these narrations contain regarding the command to perform wudu from the side where there is no carcass, or to part the water, this is to be understood as recommended (mustahab) and as a precautionary measure — for the soul finds repulsive touching water adjacent to a carcass, even though its ruling is the ruling of pure water. What indicates this is what we previously cited from the narrations: the threshold of water that is not made impure by anything is water whose volume reaches one kurr; when it falls below that, it becomes impure by what is in it. And what further clarifies this is...

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from 'Uthman ibn 'Isa, from Sa'id al-A'raj, he said: I asked Abu 'Abd Allah (peace be upon him) about a jar that holds one hundred ratls — an uqiyyah of blood falls into it: may I drink from it and perform wudu? He said: No.

As for what Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb narrated, from Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad al-ʿAlawī, from al-ʿAmrakī, from ʿAlī ibn Jaʿfar, from his brother Mūsā (peace be upon him): He said: I asked him about a man who had a nosebleed and then blew his nose, so that the blood became small pieces and fell into his vessel. Is it permissible to perform wudu from it? He said: If there is nothing visible in the water, there is no objection. But if there is something clearly apparent, then wudu shall not be performed from it. The appropriate interpretation of this report is to understand it as follows: when that blood is like the head of a needle — imperceptible and undetectable — then such an amount is pardoned.

The Sheikh (may God have mercy on him) informed me, from Abū al-Qāsim Ja'far ibn Muḥammad, from Muḥammad ibn Ya'qūb, from 'Alī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from Ibn Abī 'Umayr, from some of our companions, from Abū 'Abd Allāh (peace be upon him) who said: "Do not fumigate the shroud [with incense]."

And by this chain of narration — from Muhammad b. Ya'qub, from a group of our companions, from Ahmad b. Muhammad al-Kufi, from Ibn Jumhur, from his father, from Muhammad b. Sinan, from al-Mufaddal b. 'Umar — he said: and narrated to us 'Abd Allah b. 'Abd al-Rahman, from Hariz, from Muhammad b. Muslim, from Abu 'Abd Allah (peace be upon him) — He said: Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) said: 'Do not incense the shrouds, and do not anoint your deceased with perfume except camphor, for the deceased is in the status of one in a state of ihram.'

And by this chain of narrators, from ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from al-Nawfalī, from al-Sakūnī, from Abū ʿAbd Allāh (peace be upon him), he said: The Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) prohibited that a funeral procession be followed by a censer.
Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from Ibn Abi Hamza, who said: Abu Ja'far (عليه السلام) said: 'Do not bring fire near your dead' — meaning the incense fumigation (al-dukhna).

As for what Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Bint Ilyas, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): He said: There is no harm in fumigating the shroud of the deceased, and it is recommended for the Muslim person to fumigate his clothes when he is able to.

And what Ghiyath ibn Ibrahim narrated from Abu 'Abd Allah (AS) from his father (AS): that he used to fumigate the deceased with oud wood containing musk; and sometimes he would place hanut on the bier, and sometimes he would not; and he disliked that the deceased be followed by the incense burner. The correct interpretation of these two reports is to take them as a form of taqiyya, because they are in conformity with the schools of the (Sunni) majority.

Al-Husayn ibn 'Ubayd Allah informed me, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Yahya, from his father, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan ibn 'Ali, from 'Amr ibn Sa'id, from Musaddiq ibn Sadaqa, from 'Ammar ibn Musa, from Abu 'Abd Allah (peace be upon him): He said: The kafan (burial shroud) should be a burd (striped cloth). If it cannot be a burd, then make it all cotton. If you cannot find a cotton turban ('imama), then make the turban of sabiri (fine woven cloth).

Muhammad ibn Yahya from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Hashim from Abu Khadija from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) He said: Linen was for the Children of Israel — they would shroud [their dead] with it — while cotton is for the community of Muhammad (may Allah's blessings be upon him and his family). So this report does not contradict [what has been previously established].

What Sahl ibn Ziyad narrated from Muhammad ibn ʿAmr ibn Saʿid, from Yunus ibn Yaʿqub, from Abu al-Hasan al-Awwal (peace be upon him): He said: I heard him say: "I shrouded my father in two shatawi garments in which he used to enter the state of ihram, and in a shirt from his shirts, and in a turban that had belonged to ʿAli ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon him), and in a burd which I had purchased for forty dinars — had it been valued today, it would be worth four hundred dinars." Because the [correct] interpretation of this report is [that it pertains to] a circumstance in which cotton cannot be obtained; moreover, it is a narration of an action, and it is possible that this was specific to them (peace be upon them). He did not say therein 'you ought to do the same.' And when this is not [stated] in it, following it is not obligatory.

As for what Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated from Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from Muhammad ibn Sa'id, from Isma'il ibn Abi Ziyad, from Ja'far, from his father, from his forefathers, from 'Ali (peace be upon him): he said: the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'How excellent a shroud (kafan) is the hullah, and how excellent a sacrificial animal (udhiyyah) is the horned ram.' The proper interpretation of this report is that we should take it as a type of taqiyyah, because it agrees with the doctrines of the 'amma (Sunnis). The report we cited previously is consistent with the narrations we presented in the commentary on the washing of the deceased (ghusl al-mayyit) in our major book.

As for what Muhammad b. Ahmad b. Yahya reported from Muhammad b. 'Isa from al-Hasan b. Rashid — He said: I asked him about garments made in Basra in the style of Yemeni qasab, from raw silk and cotton: is it proper that the dead be shrouded in them? He said: If the cotton is more than the raw silk, there is no objection. [al-Tusi:] This does not contradict what we have previously stated, for we only forbid garments in which salat is not permissible — even though pure cotton is preferable. This narration is interpreted as indicating permissibility, not preference. And what further indicates that linen is makruh is in addition to what has already been stated.
What Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Ya'qub ibn Yazid, from a group of our companions, from Abu Abd Allah (peace be upon him): He said: The deceased should not be shrouded in linen.

Al-Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) informed me, from Abu al-Qasim Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from 'Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abu 'Abd Allah (peace be upon him): He said: When you intend to apply hanut to the deceased, go to the camphor and wipe with it the places of prostration on his body, all his joints, his head, his beard, and upon his chest from the hanut. And he said: The hanut is the same for men and women. He said: And I dislike that [the body] be followed by a censer.

'Ali ibn Muhammad, from Ayyub ibn Nuh, from Ibn Muskan, from al-Kahili and Husayn ibn al-Mukhtar, from Abu 'Abd Allah (peace be upon him), who said: Camphor is placed on the deceased at the places of prostration, and upon the labbah (throat-pit), and the soles of both feet, and the place of the sandal strap on the feet, and upon both knees, and both palms, and the forehead, and the labbah.
And Fadala narrated from Aban, from ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Abi ʿAbdillah, who said: he said: 'Do not place hanoot in the ears of the deceased.'

As for what 'Ali ibn al-Husayn reported from Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn 'Ali, from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Salt, from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from 'Abd Allah ibn Sinan — who said: I said to Abu 'Abd Allah (AS): 'How should I apply the hanoot (camphor)?' He said: 'Place it on his mouth, his ear openings (masami'), and the marks of prostration — on his face, his hands, and his knees.' The [correct] interpretation of this narration is that we should take his saying 'fi masami'ihi' (in his ear openings) to mean 'upon' — for prepositions can substitute for one another. Allah the Exalted said: «And I shall surely crucify you upon the trunks of the palm trees» — by which He meant 'upon the trunks of the palm trees.' We have done this [interpretation] so as to accord with the earlier narrations and to be consistent with what we presented in the commentary on enshrouding (takfin) the deceased in our major book [al-Mabsut], so as not to contradict it.

As for what was narrated by 'Ali ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Khalid, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Hammad, from Hariz, from Zurara, from Abu Ja'far and Abu 'Abd Allah (peace be upon them both): He said: When you have dried the deceased, proceed to the camphor and rub it on the marks of prostration and all of his joints; and place in his mouth, his ears, his head, and his beard some hanut, as well as upon his chest and his private parts. And he said: The hanut for a man and a woman is the same. The ruling on this matter is also identical to what we stated in the first hadith.

Al-Husayn ibn 'Ubayd Allah informed me, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Yahya, from his father, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah al-Misma'i, from Isma'il ibn Bashshar al-Wasiti, from Sayf ibn 'Amira, from Abu Bakr al-Hadrami, from Abu 'Abd Allah (peace be upon him): He said: «Do not descend into the grave while wearing a turban, nor a cap, nor a ridāʾ, nor footwear; and unbutton your buttons.» He (the narrator) said: I asked: «What about leather socks (khuff)?» He said: «There is no problem with leather socks at a time of necessity and taqiyya; and let him strive in that matter to the utmost of his ability.»

As for what was narrated by Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya from Ya'qub ibn Yazid from Ibrahim ibn 'Uqbah from Muhammad ibn Isma'il ibn Bazi': He said: I saw Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) enter the grave without undoing his buttons. The interpretation of this report is the lifting of the prohibition upon whoever does not undo his buttons, because doing so is among the recommended acts (masnnunat) and not among the obligatory acts (wajibat).

The Sheikh, may God have mercy on him, informed me, from Abu Ja'far Muhammad b. Ali, from his father, from Muhammad b. Yahya, from Muhammad b. Ahmad b. Yahya, from Musa b. Ja'far, from Ali b. Sa'id, from Ubaydallah b. al-Dahqan, from Abu Khalid, he said: 'Wash all the dead — the drowned one, the one devoured by a wild beast, and everything else — except what was killed between the two battle lines. If there was still a breath of life in him, he shall be given ghusl; otherwise, no.'

From him, from Sa'id ibn Abdillah, from Harun ibn Muslim, from Musaddiq ibn Sadaqa, from Ammar, from Ja'far (AS), from his father (AS): That Ali (peace be upon him) did not perform the ritual washing (ghusl) for Ammar ibn Yasir, nor for Hashim ibn Utba al-Mirqal, buried them both in their garments, and did not perform the funeral prayer over them. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan (may Allah have mercy on him) said: The narrator's statement 'and did not perform the prayer over them' is an error (wahm) on the part of the narrator, because the funeral prayer does not lapse for the deceased under any circumstance whatsoever — as is indicated by [what follows].

What Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from 'Ali ibn al-Hakam, from al-Husayn ibn 'Uthman, from Ibn Muskan, from Aban ibn Taghlib: He said: I asked Abu 'Abd Allah (peace be upon him) about the one who is killed in the path of Allah — is he to be washed, shrouded, embalmed with hanut, and prayed over? He said: He is buried just as he is, in his clothes — unless he had a breath of life remaining and then died, in which case he is washed, shrouded, and embalmed with hanut. Verily the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) prayed over Hamza and shrouded him, because he had been stripped [of his garments].

And by this chain, from Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from Ḥammād, from Ḥarīz, from Ismāʿīl ibn Jābir and Zurāra, from Abū Jaʿfar (peace be upon him): He said: I asked him: 'How do you see it — is the martyr buried with his blood?' He said: 'Yes, in his clothes, with his blood; he is not washed (ghusl) and he is not embalmed (hanut), and he is buried as he is.'

And by this chain of narration, from Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Humayd ibn Ziyad, from al-Hasan ibn Muhammad, from more than one [narrator], from Aban, from Abi Maryam, who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) say: The shahid (martyr) — if there is still a breath of life (ramaq) in him, he is given ghusl, shrouded (kafan), embalmed (hanut), and the salat is performed over him; and if there is no breath of life in him, he is buried in his garments.

As for what Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated — from Abu Ja'far, from Abu al-Jawza', from al-Husayn ibn 'Ulwan, from 'Amr ibn Khalid, from Zayd ibn 'Ali, from his father, from his forefathers, from 'Ali (peace be upon him): he said: The Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him and his family) said: 'If the martyr dies on that same day or the next day, bury him in his garments. But if he lingers for several days until his wounds change in condition, he shall be given the ritual bath (ghusl).' This is a report that conforms to the Sunni position; we do not act upon it. For we have demonstrated that if the slain person did not die on the battlefield, his ghusl is obligatory — whether [his wounds] changed in condition or not. The practice must follow this ruling. It also conforms to what we have mentioned in our major book [al-Mabsut], where we treated the matter exhaustively.

Al-Sheikh (may God have mercy on him) informed me, from Abu al-Qasim Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Humayd ibn Ziyad, from more than one person, from Aban, from a man, from Abu Abd Allah (peace be upon him): that he said, regarding a man who dies with a group at sea — he said: 'He is to be washed (ghusl), shrouded (kafn), the funeral prayer performed over him, weighted down, and cast into the sea.'

And by this same chain, from Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb, from a group of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyād, who relates it marfūʿ from Abī ʿAbd Allāh (peace be upon him): He said: 'When a man dies on a ship and it is not possible to [reach] the shore, he said: he is to be shrouded and embalmed with ḥanūṭ in a garment, the funeral prayer is to be performed over him, and he is to be cast into the water.'

And from him, from Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Ali, from his father, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Khalid al-Barqi, from Abu al-Bakhtari Wahb ibn Wahb al-Qurashi, from Abu Abdillah (عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ): He said: The Commander of the Faithful (عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ) said: When a deceased person dies at sea, he is to be washed (ghusl), shrouded, embalmed with hanut, and the funeral prayer (salat) is to be performed over him. Then a stone is tied to his feet and he is cast into the sea.

As for what Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Safwan, from 'Abd Allah ibn Muskan, from Ayyub ibn al-Hurr, who said: Abu 'Abd Allah (peace be upon him) was asked about a man who died while he was on a ship at sea: what should be done with him? He said: 'He is to be placed in a clay jar (khābiya), its mouth sealed, and cast into the water.' The correct interpretation of this narration is that it should be understood as a type of recommended (mustahabb) practice when one has the ability to do so, and the earlier narrations as applying to cases where this is not feasible, thereby lifting the prohibition.

The Sheikh (may God have mercy on him) informed me, from Abu al-Qasim Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from 'Ali, from his father, from Ibn Faddal, from 'Ali ibn 'Uqba, from Musa ibn Ukayl, from al-'Ala' ibn Siabah, from Abu 'Abd Allah (AS): He said: You begin carrying the bier from the right side, then pass along it from behind to the other side, then continue until you return to the front — such is the rotation of the millstone.

'Ali, from his father, from more than one [narrator], from Yunus, from 'Ali ibn Yaqtin, from Abi al-Hasan Musa (peace be upon him) — he said: I heard him say: The sunnah for carrying the funeral bier is that you face the side of the bier with your right flank, then grip the left [side] with your right palm, then proceed along it to the fourth side that is near your left [side].

Abu Ali al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, from Ali ibn Hadid, from Sayf ibn Amira, from Amr ibn Shimr, from Jabir, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him): He said: The sunnah is to carry the bier from its four sides; whatever carrying is done beyond that is voluntary (tatauwwu').

As for what ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn narrated from ʿAlī ibn Mūsā, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from al-Ḥusayn — He said: I wrote to him asking him about the bier of the deceased when it is carried: does it have a [particular] side from among its four sides that should be started with in the carrying, or is whatever is easiest for the man [sufficient], so he may carry from whichever side he wishes? So he (the Imam) wrote back: 'From whichever [side] he wishes.' The correct interpretation of this narration is that it lifts the prohibition on carrying the funeral bier from any of its sides, because what we have previously mentioned [of the specific method] is of the sunnah (recommended), not the obligatory.

The Sheikh (may God have mercy on him) informed me, from Abu Ja'far ibn Ali, from his father, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn Abi al-Khattab, from Ali ibn Asbat, from Ali ibn Ja'far, He said: I asked Abu al-Hasan Musa (peace be upon him) about building upon a grave and sitting upon it — is it permissible? He said: It is not permissible to build upon it, nor to sit [upon it], nor to plaster it with gypsum, nor to coat it with clay.

As for what Sahl ibn Ziyad narrated from Ibn Mahbub, from Yunus ibn Ya'qub, who said: When Abu al-Hasan Musa (peace be upon him) was returning from Baghdad and proceeding to Medina, a daughter of his died at Fayd. He buried her and ordered some of his mawali to plaster her grave, to write her name on a tablet, and to place it in the grave. The correct interpretation of this narration is that it lifts the prohibition against doing that and constitutes a form of dispensation (rukhsa), because the first narration was delivered in the context of dislike (karaha/makruh), not prohibition (hazr).

Al-Husayn ibn 'Ubayd Allah reported to me, from a group of our companions, from Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from 'Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father, and Muhammad ibn Isma'il from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan—all of them—from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Hisham ibn al-Hakam: He said: I saw Musa ibn Ja'far (peace be upon him) offering condolences (ta'ziyah) before the burial and after it.

As for what Ibn Abi Umayr narrated from some of his companions from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), he said: Condolences (ta'ziya) to the bereaved family [are given] after the burial. The proper approach to this narration is to interpret it as indicating merit and recommendation (istihbab).

Al-Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Abū Jaʿfar Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn, from his father and Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan, from Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā, from Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā, from Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā, from Yūnus ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, who said: Ismāʿīl ibn Saʿd al-Ashʿarī al-Qummī narrated to me, saying: I said to al-Riḍā عليه السلام: How many rakʿahs is the salat (prayer)? He said: Fifty-one rakʿahs.

And from him, from Abu al-Qasim Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Ibn Udhayna, from Fudayl ibn Yasar, from Abu Abd Allah (peace be upon him): He said: The obligatory and supererogatory prayers are fifty-one rak'ahs. Among them are two rak'ahs after the 'atama [night prayer] performed sitting, which count as one rak'ah while standing. The obligatory [prayers] among them are seventeen rak'ahs, and the supererogatory [prayers] are thirty-four rak'ahs.

And by this chain of narration, from al-Fudayl ibn Yasar, al-Fadl ibn Abd al-Malik, and Bukayr — they said: We heard Abu Abd Allah (peace be upon him) say: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) used to perform voluntary (supererogatory) prayers equal to twice the obligatory prayers, and fast voluntarily equal to twice the obligatory fast.

And by this same chain of narration, from Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Muhammad ibn Isma'il ibn Bazi', from Hanan ibn Sadir, who said: 'Amr ibn Hurayth asked Abu 'Abd Allah (peace be upon him) — while I was sitting [present] — and said to him: 'Inform me, may I be your ransom, about the salat of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family).' He said: 'The Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) used to pray: eight rak'ats of the zawal; four of al-ula (Dhuhr); eight after it; four of 'Asr; three of Maghrib; four after Maghrib; four of 'Isha al-Akhira; eight of the night prayer (salat al-layl); three of witr; two rak'ats of fajr [nawafil]; and the morning prayer (salat al-ghadata), two rak'ats.' I said: 'May I be your ransom — if I am able to perform more than this, will Allah punish me for the abundance of prayer?' So he said: 'No, but one is punished for abandoning the sunnah.'

As for what Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn 'Isa narrated from al-Hasan ibn 'Ali ibn Bint Ilyas, from 'Abdullah ibn Sinan, who said: I heard Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) say: 'Do not pray less than forty-four.' He said: And I saw him praying four rak'at after al-'atamah. There is no prohibition in this report against what exceeds forty-four; rather, he (peace be upon him) prohibited only that it be reduced below it. And there is nothing preventing him from encouraging these forty-four due to their being emphasized, while encouraging what is beyond them through another hadith. We have previously presented hadiths that encompass that.

As for what Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa has narrated from Yahya ibn Habib: He said: I asked al-Ridha (AS) about the most excellent means by which servants draw near to God, Mighty and Majestic, through salat. He said: Forty-six rak'ahs — its obligatory and supererogatory [prayers]. I said: This is the narration of Zurara. He said: Do you see anyone who was more forthright in proclaiming the truth than him? This report likewise contains no negation of prayers beyond these. Rather, the questioner asked about the most excellent means of drawing near [to God], and [the Imam] mentioned these forty-six and singled them out for specific mention because the prayers that exceed them are inferior to them in merit. What indicates what we have stated — that he intended only to emphasize the merit of these forty-six rak'ahs — [continues in the following text]

What al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Ḥammād ibn ʿĪsā, from Shuʿayb, from Abū Baṣīr, who said: I asked Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about supererogatory prayer in the night and the day. He said: What is recommended not to be reduced from it is eight rakʿahs at the sun’s decline, two rakʿahs after ẓuhr, two rakʿahs before ʿaṣr, two rakʿahs after maghrib, two rakʿahs before al-ʿatamah, and in the pre-dawn time eight rakʿahs; then he performs witr, and the witr is three separate rakʿahs; then two rakʿahs before salat al-fajr. And the most beloved time of salat al-layl to them is the latter part of the night. So it is clarified in this report that these forty-six rakʿahs are among what is recommended not to fall short of, and that what is besides them does not share with them in this recommendation. As for the reports other than these two reports that imply a reduction from fifty rakʿahs, their basis in all of them is Zurārah, even if they are repeated with different chains. We have fully covered what relates to this chapter in Kitāb Tahdhīb al-Aḥkām and clarified the aspect of it there, so whoever wishes to examine all of them should refer to it.

The Shaykh, may God have mercy on him, informed me from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan ibn Aban, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: The salat during travel is two rak'ahs; there is nothing before them nor after them, except Maghrib which is three.

As for what al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Muhammad ibn Abi 'Umayr from Muhammad ibn Ishaq ibn 'Ammar, he said: I asked Abu 'Abd Allah (peace be upon him) about a woman who was with us on a journey, and she was performing the Maghrib salat — going and returning — as two rak'ahs. He said: There is no make-up upon her. This does not contradict the first narration, because this is an anomalous (shadhdh) narration. And it is from the well-known, agreed-upon matters in which there is no doubt that the Maghrib salat during travel is not shortened (qasr), and that whoever shortens it is obligated to make it up. Therefore this narration is abandoned by consensus (ijma').

He informed me: al-Husayn ibn 'Ubayd Allah, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Yahya, from his father, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from al-'Amraki, from 'Ali ibn Ja'far, from his brother Musa (peace be upon him). He said: I asked him about the skink (lizard), the snake, and the gecko that falls into water but does not die — can wudu be performed from it for salat? He said: There is no harm in it.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn Abi al-Khattab and al-Hasan ibn Musa al-Khashshab, both together, from Yazid ibn Ishaq, from Harun ibn Hamza al-Ghanawi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): He said: I asked him about the mouse, the scorpion, and similar creatures that fall into water and come out alive — can one drink from that water and perform wudu from it? He said: It [the water] is poured out three times, and a small amount and a large amount are of the same ruling, then one may drink from it and perform wudu from it — except for the gecko (wazagh), for nothing it falls into may be benefited from. Al-Shaykh Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn al-Hasan (may Allah have mercy on him) said: What this report contains regarding the ruling on the gecko and the command to pour away what it falls into is interpreted as a type of legal dislikedness (karahah), based on the indication of the preceding report, and contradiction between reports is not permissible.

As for what Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Muhammad ibn Isa al-Yaqtini, from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from Umar ibn Shimr, from Jabir, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him): He said: A man came to him and said: "A mouse has fallen into a jar containing ghee or oil. What do you think about eating it?" Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said to him: "Do not eat it." The man said to him: "The mouse is too insignificant to me to abandon my food on its account." He said: Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said to him: "You have not shown disrespect to the mouse; rather, you have shown disrespect to your religion. Verily, Allah has forbidden the dead from every thing." This does not contradict the first report, because the meaning of this report is that when the mouse dies in it, using it is not permitted. But if it exits alive, the ruling is what the first report contained, as the following indicates.

What was narrated by Ali ibn Ja'far from his brother Musa ibn Ja'far (peace be upon him) — he said: I asked him about a mouse that fell into a jar of oil and was removed before it died — can we sell it to a Muslim? He said: Yes, and you may anoint yourself with it, and this does not contradict what...

It was narrated by Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Ibrahim ibn Hashim, from al-Nawfali, from al-Sakuni, from Ja'far, from his father, that Ali (peace be upon him) was asked about a pot that had been set to cook, and lo, there was a mouse in the pot. He said: "Its broth is to be poured out, the meat washed, and it is to be eaten." For the meaning of this report is: when it [the mouse] dies in it [the pot], discarding the pot's contents becomes obligatory.

As for what Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from Wuhayb ibn Hafs from Abu Basir — He said: I asked him about a snake that entered a large clay water jar (hubb) containing water and then exited from it. He said: If he finds other water, let him pour it out. The correct interpretation of this is that it should be understood as a type of dislikedness (karahah), given the availability of water whose purity is certain. For this reason he commanded him to pour it out only if he finds other water. If it were ritually impure (najis), it would be obligatory to pour it out under all circumstances.

Al-Shaykh, may God have mercy on him, narrated to me from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub and 'Ali ibn al-Hakam — both together — from Abu Yahya al-Hannat, who said: I asked Abu 'Abd Allah (peace be upon him) about the supererogatory prayer (nafila) during the daytime while traveling. He said: 'O my dear son, if the nafila were valid during travel, the obligatory prayer (farida) would have been complete.'

And by this chain of transmission, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from 'Ali ibn Ahmad ibn Ashyam, from Safwan ibn Yahya, who said: I asked al-Rida (peace be upon him) about performing voluntary prayer (tatatawwu') during the day while I was traveling. He said: No. But you may make up the night prayer during the day while you are traveling. I said: May I be your ransom — [what about] the daytime prayers that I perform at home; may I make them up during the day while traveling? He said: As for me, I do not make them up.

As for what al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Muhammad ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar: He said: I asked Abu 'Abd Allah (peace be upon him): 'Can I make up the daytime salat at night during travel?' He said to him: 'Yes.' Isma'il ibn Jabir said: 'Can I make up the daytime salat at night during travel?' He said: 'No.' He (Isma'il) said: 'But you said yes!' He (the Imam) said: 'That one is capable, and you are not capable.'

And what al-Hasan ibn Mahbub narrated from Hanan ibn Sadir from Sadir, who said: Abu 'Abd Allah (peace be upon him) said: My father used to make up (qada') the daytime nawafil at night while traveling, and he would not complete the obligatory prayer [in full]. Regarding these two reports, [the interpretation lies in] one of two things: one of them is that it should be understood as [indicating the] lifting of hardship (haraj) for one who prays at night what he missed during the day, even if that is not recommended (mustahabb). This is indicated by...

What al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated, from Fadala, from al-Husayn, from Ibn Muskan, from 'Umar ibn Hanzala: He said: I said to Abu 'Abd Allah (peace be upon him): 'May I be made your ransom! I asked you about making up (qada') the daytime salat at night while traveling, and you said: Do not make it up. And our companions asked you, and you said: Make them up.' He said to me: 'Shall I then tell them: Do not pray? For I am reluctant to tell them: Do not pray. By God, that [obligation] is not upon them.' The other interpretation is that both reports were directed at one who had missed the nawafil salat while in residence (hadar), such that their time had entered upon him before he departed and he had not performed them — so it was incumbent upon him to make them up thereafter. [A subsequent narration] indicates this.

What Ahmad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Faddal narrated from Amr ibn Sa'id, from Musaddiq ibn Sadaqa, from Ammar ibn Musa, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him). He said: He was asked about a man who, when the sun declines while he is at home, then departs on a journey. He said: He begins with the zawal prayer and prays it, then prays al-ula (the zuhr) shortened to two rak'ahs, because he departed from his home before the time of al-ula arrived. And he was asked: What if he departs after the time of al-ula has arrived? He said: He prays al-ula as four rak'ahs, then after it he prays the nawafil of eight rak'ahs, because he departed from his home after the time of al-ula had arrived. Then when the time of asr arrives, he prays asr with a shortening — and it is two rak'ahs — because he departed on the journey before the time of asr arrived.

Al-Husayn ibn ʿUbayd Allah informed me, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Yahya, from his father, from Muhammad ibn ʿAli ibn Mahbub, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn, from al-Hasan, from Zurʿa, from Samaʿa, who said: I asked him about the traveler: how much does he shorten the salat? He said: During a day's journey — and that is two barids, which are eight farsakhs. And whoever travels must shorten the salat and break his fast, except if he is a man accompanying an unjust ruler, or he has gone out for hunting, or he has gone to a village of his own that is a day's journey away while he sleeps [each night returning] to his family — he does not shorten [the prayer] and does not break his fast.

And the Sheikh, may God have mercy on him, informed me, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from al-Saffar, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Abdullah ibn Yahya al-Kahili, who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) speaking regarding taqsir (shortening of prayer) in salat. He said: A barid within a barid [equals] twenty-four miles.

Ahmad ibn 'Abdun narrated to me, from 'Ali ibn Muhammad ibn al-Zubayr, from 'Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Faddal, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Najran, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from 'Is ibn al-Qasim, from Abu 'Abd Allah (peace be upon him) who said regarding taqsir (shortening of prayer): its limit is twenty-four miles.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from al-Nadr, from 'Asim ibn Humayd, from Abu Basir, who said: I asked Abu 'Abd Allah (peace be upon him): 'At what [distance] does a man shorten [his prayer]?' He said: 'At the whiteness of a day (bayadh yawm), or two barid.'

As for what Ali ibn Ibrahim narrated from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Jamil, from Zurara, from Abu Ja'far (AS): he said: The shortening [of prayer] is at [the distance of] a barid, and a barid is four farsakhs.

And from him, from his father, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Ayyūb, who said: I said to Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام: What is the minimum distance at which the traveler shortens? He said: A barīd. So there is no contradiction between these two reports and the first two reports, because the proper way to understand them is that when the traveler intends to return on the same day, shortening becomes obligatory for him over four farsakhs, and that which indicates this is:

What Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allāh narrated, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Faḍāla, from Mu'āwiya ibn Wahb, who said: I asked Abī 'Abd Allāh (peace be upon him): "What is the minimum [distance] at which prayer is shortened?" He replied: "A barīd going and a barīd returning." [Al-Ṭūsī:] With the qualification that what I say regarding this is: shortening is obligatory when the distance is eight farsakhs, and when it is four farsakhs one has the choice — if he wishes he may complete [the prayer] and if he wishes he may shorten it. And that which indicates this — I mean the permissibility of shortening at four farsakhs [is as follows]...

What Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Muhammad ibn Abi 'Umayr, from 'Abdullah ibn Bukayr — He said: I asked Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) about al-Qadisiyyah — [when] I travel out to it, should I complete [the prayer] or shorten? He said: How far is it? I said: It is as you have seen. He said: Shorten.

Sa'd from Ahmad, from al-Husayn, from Fadala, from Hammad ibn ʿUthman, from Abu Usama Zayd al-Shahham, who said: I heard Abu ʿAbdillah (peace be upon him) say: "A man shortens the salat on a journey of twelve miles."

From him, from Abū Jaʿfar, from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Faḍḍāl, from Muʿāwiyah ibn ʿAmmār, who said: I said to Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام: In what distance do I shorten the salat (prayer)? He said: In one barīd. Do you not see that the people of Makkah, when they go out to ʿArafah, shortening is incumbent upon them?

From him, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn Abi al-Khattab, from Ja'far ibn Bashir, from Hammad ibn 'Uthman, from Muhammad ibn al-Nu'man, from Isma'il ibn al-Fadl, who said: I asked Abu 'Abd Allah (peace be upon him) about the taqsir. He said: [It is obligatory] at four farsakhs.

From him, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Mu'awiya ibn Hukaym, from Abu Malik al-Hadrami, from Abu al-Jarud — He said: I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him): 'At what [distance] is the taqsir?' He replied: 'At a barid.'

From him, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Mu'awiya ibn Hukaym, from Sulayman ibn Muhammad al-Khath'ami, from Ishaq ibn Ammar. He said: I asked Abu Abd Allah (peace be upon him): 'At what [distance] is the shortening [of prayer]?' He said: 'At a barid. Woe to them! As if they had not performed hajj with the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) and [they] shortened [prayers].'

From him, from Abu Ja'far, from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Yaqtin, from his brother al-Husayn, from his father Ali ibn Yaqtin, who said: I asked Abu al-Hasan al-Awwal (peace be upon him) about a man who sets out on a journey, and it is [a distance of] one day's travel. He said: Shortening [of prayer] (qasr) is obligatory upon him if it is a journey of one day, even if he travels around for his work.

As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from Ibn Abī Naṣr, from Abū al-Ḥasan al-Riḍā عليه السلام, he said: I asked him about a man who intends travel: at what distance does he shorten? He said: in three burud. So this report conforms with the ʿāmmah, and we do not act upon it.

As for what Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb narrated from Aḥmad, from al-Ḥasan ibn Maḥbūb, from Abū Jamīlah, from Abū Baṣīr, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: There is no harm for the traveler to perform the prayer in full during travel of two days’ journey. This report also accords with the generality, and we do not act upon it, because that in which shortening is obligatory is the measure that we mentioned, whether it is a journey of two days or less or more. And it is possible that the report is to be understood as applying to one who travels in two days less than the amount in which shortening is obligatory; then, in that case, completing the prayer becomes obligatory upon him. And that which clarifies what we have mentioned is:

What Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub narrated from Ya'qub ibn Yazid, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Abu Ayyub, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): He said: I asked him about the taqsir (shortening of prayer). He then said: [It is] for two barids or the whiteness of a day.

As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā narrated from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Khalaf, from Yaḥyā ibn Hāshim, from Abū Hārūn al-ʿAbdī, from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, who said: When the Prophet صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم traveled one farsakh, he shortened the salat (prayer).

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar narrated from Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from 'Amr ibn Sa'id, who said: Ja'far ibn Muhammad wrote to him, asking him about travel and in what amount qasr prayer becomes due. So he wrote in his own handwriting—and I recognize it: Amir al-Mu'minin عليه السلام, when he travelled and went out on a journey, would shorten in one farsakh. Then the following year he repeated the question to him, so he wrote back to him: in ten days. Thus, the sound way of understanding these two reports, including his statement, "he shortened in one farsakh," and other reports of the same kind, is that when the distance reaches the limit at which qasr becomes obligatory or more, then if the traveler travels for a day or more, or a farsakh, or less than that, or more, qasr becomes obligatory upon him, because the total distance has reached the limit in which qasr is obligatory. The consideration is not the amount a person travels at one time; rather, the consideration is the intended distance, even if he does not travel it in a single stretch. So this interpretation is not contradicted.

What Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā narrated from Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī, from ʿAmr ibn Saʿīd, from Muṣaddiq ibn Ṣadaqah, from ʿAmmār ibn Mūsā, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who goes out for some need and travels five farsakhs or six farsakhs, then comes to a village and stays there, then departs from it and travels five farsakhs or six farsakhs—this does not qualify—and then he stays in that place. He said: He is not considered a traveler until he travels eight farsakhs from his home or village, so he should perform the salat in full. For this narration is restricted to one who left his home without the intention of travel, then the journey continues with him until he becomes a traveler without intent; in that case, completing the salat is incumbent upon him. Even if the distance exceeds that for which, had he intended it, shortening would have been obligatory upon him, completion is only binding on him because he did not intend a journey whose amount reaches that in which shortening becomes obligatory. And that which supports this interpretation is...

What al-Saffar narrated from Ibrahim ibn Hashim, from a man, from Safwan, who said: I asked al-Rida عليه السلام about a man who left Baghdad wanting to catch up with another man at the distance of one mile, and he continued following him until he reached al-Nahrawan, which is four farsakhs from Baghdad. Should he break his fast if he wants to return, and shorten? He said: He should neither shorten nor break his fast, because he left his home not intending a journey of eight farsakhs. Rather, he only went out intending to catch his companion on part of the road, but the travel continued with him until the place that he reached. But if he had left his home intending al-Nahrawan, going and returning, then he would have had to intend from the night a journey and breaking the fast. If he entered the morning without intending travel, then it appeared to him after morning to travel, he would shorten, but he would not break his fast on that day.

And that which Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated from Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan ibn Faḍḍāl, from ʿAmr ibn Saʿīd al-Madāʾinī, from Muṣaddaq ibn Ṣadaqah, from ʿAmmār ibn Mūsā al-Sābāṭī, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbd Allah عليه السلام about a man who goes out for some need of his, while not intending travel, then continues in that and the going on keeps extending for him until it reaches eight farsakhs. How should he act regarding his salat? He said: He shortens, and he does not perform the salat in full until he returns to his home. So the correct way of understanding it is that shortening becomes obligatory for him after he has covered eight farsakhs, until he returns to his home, because he has become a traveler even if he did not intend that at the outset. The first narration only indicated the obligation of performing in full during the period of his going the amount that we mentioned, and the two are not contradictory according to this interpretation.

Al-Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from al-Saffar, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Sulayman ibn Hafs al-Marwazi, who said: The Faqih, peace be upon him, said: Shortening in salat is at two barids, or one barid going and returning. A barid is six miles, and that is two farsakhs. Shortening applies in four farsakhs. So when a man leaves his home intending twelve miles, and that is four farsakhs, then he reaches two farsakhs while intending to return, or [to continue] another two farsakhs, he shortens. But if he turns back from what he had intended upon reaching two farsakhs and wishes to stay, then full salat is upon him. And if he had shortened and then turned back from his intention, he repeats the salat.

As for what Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn Abī Naṣr, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Mūsā, from Zurārah, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbd Allah عليه السلام about a man who goes out on a journey intending it, then the time enters for him while he has gone out from the village by two farsakhs, so they prayed and departed. Then one of them turned aside for some need, and it was not decreed for him to continue the departure. What should he do regarding the prayer that he had prayed as two rakʿahs? He عليه السلام said: His prayer is complete, and he does not repeat. Thus, the correct way of understanding this report is one of two things: one of them is that if the time had passed, repetition was not required of him; rather, repetition is only binding upon him so long as the time remains. The second is that even if it was not decreed for him to continue the departure, he had not turned back from the intention of travel, and whenever that is so, repetition is not required of him; rather, shortening remains binding upon him up to thirty days, as we have explained in the major book.

Al-Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Abū al-Qāsim Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from his father, from Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allāh, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from Faḍālah, from Abān ibn ʿUthmān, from Ismāʿīl ibn al-Faḍl, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام about a man who travels from one land to another, and he only stops at his villages and his estate. He said: When you arrive at your villages and your estate, then perform the salat (prayer) in full; but when you are in other than your land, then shorten it.

Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Mahbub, from Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from 'Imran ibn Muhammad, who said: I said to Abi Ja'far al-Thani عليه السلام: May I be made your ransom, I have an estate at a distance of fifteen miles, five farsakhs. So at times I go out to it and stay there for three days, or five days, or seven days. Should I perform the salat in full or shorten it? He said: Shorten on the road, and perform it in full at the estate.

From him, from ʿAlī ibn Isḥāq ibn Saʿd, from Mūsā ibn al-Khazraj, who said: I said to Abū al-Ḥasan عليه السلام: I go out to my two estates, and from my home to them is twelve farsakhs. Should I perform the salat (prayer) in full or shorten it? He said: Perform it in full.

From him, from Muḥammad ibn Sahl, from his father, who said: I asked Abā al-Ḥasan عليه السلام about a man traveling to his estate, at a distance of two or three barīds, while his route passes by the estates of his paternal cousins: should he shorten the salat (prayer) and break the fast, or should he complete it and fast? He said: He should not shorten, nor should he break the fast.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Faddal, from Amr ibn Sa'id al-Mada'ini, from Musaddaq ibn Sadaqah, from Ammar ibn Musa, from Abu Abdillah عليه السلام, concerning: A man goes out on his journey and passes by a village belonging to him or a house, then stays in it. He said: he should complete the salat (prayer), even if he does not have in it except a single palm tree, and he should not shorten; and let him observe sawm (fasting) if the fast comes upon him while he is in it. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: What these reports contain of the command to perform fully in a person’s estate admits of several possibilities. Among them is that full prayer only becomes binding on him when he resolves to stay for ten days, and that which indicates this is what...

Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah narrated it from Ibrahim ibn Hashim, from Isma'il ibn Mirrar, from Yunus ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from 'Abd Allah ibn Sinan, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: Whoever comes to an estate, then does not intend to stay for ten days, he shortens the salat (prayer). But if he intends to stay for ten days, he performs the salat (prayer) in full.

From him, from Ibrahim, from al-Barqi, from Sulayman ibn Ja'far al-Ja'fari, from Musa ibn Hamzah ibn Bazi', who said: I said to Abī al-Ḥasan عليه السلام: May I be made your ransom, I have an estate short of Baghdad. I set out from al-Kufah intending Baghdad, and I stay in that estate. Should I shorten or complete? He said: If you do not intend to stay for ten days, then shorten. And the second possibility is that the reports are to be understood as applying to one who passes by a residence of his that he had made his homeland for six months or more; at that point, completing the prayer becomes obligatory upon him. That is indicated by what follows.

It was narrated by Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from Ibn Abī Naṣr, from Ḥammād ibn ʿUthmān, from ʿAlī ibn Yaqṭīn, who said: I said to Abū al-Ḥasan al-Awwal عليه السلام: A man adopts a dwelling, then passes by it; should he perform in full or shorten? He said: Every dwelling that you do not reside in as a homeland is not a dwelling for you, and it is not for you to perform in full therein.

From him, from Ayyūb ibn Nūḥ, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Ḥammād ibn ʿUthmān, from Abū ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, concerning: A man travels and passes by a dwelling of his on the way. Should he perform the salat in full or shorten it? He said: He shortens it. That is only [treated as full-residence prayer] for the dwelling which he has adopted as a watan.

From him, from Ayyūb, from Ṣafwān ibn Yaḥyā, from Saʿd ibn Abī Khalaf, who said: ʿAlī ibn Yaqṭīn asked Abā al-Ḥasan al-Awwal عليه السلام about a house belonging to a man in a town, or an estate, by which he passes. He said: If it is among what he had already lived in, he should perform the salat there in full; and if it is among what he had not lived in, then he should shorten.

From him, from Ayyūb, from Abī Ṭālib, from Ibn Abī Naṣr, from Ḥammād ibn ʿUthmān, from ʿAlī ibn Yaqṭīn, who said: I said to Abī al-Ḥasan al-Awwal عليه السلام: I have estates and dwellings between one village and two villages, at a farsakh, two farsakhs, and three. So he said: Every dwelling among your dwellings that you do not take as a place of residence, then shortened prayer is upon you in it.

From him, from Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā, from Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan, from Muḥammad ibn Ismāʿīl ibn Bazīʿ, from Abū al-Ḥasan عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who shortens in his estate. He said: There is no problem so long as he has not intended to stay for ten days, unless he has a residence there which he takes as a homeland. I said: What is residence-settlement? He said: That he has a residence there in which he stays for six months; then when that is so, he performs in full there whenever he enters it.

As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Bukayr, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Ḥajjāj, who said: I said to Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام: A man has estates, some of them near to one another, and he goes out and circulates among them—should he perform the prayer in full or shorten it? He said: He should perform it in full. So there is nothing in this report that contradicts what we have stated earlier, because it does not mention the distance he travels therein.
