If that is not mentioned in it, it remains possible that what is meant is when the estate is near to him; in that case, shortening does not become obligatory upon him.

As for what Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb narrated from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan and others, from Sahl ibn Ziyād, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn Abī Naṣr, who said: I asked al-Riḍā عليه السلام about a man who goes out to his estate and stays for one day, two days, or three: should he shorten or complete? He said: He completes the salat (prayer) whenever he comes to an estate among his estates. The explanation regarding this report is the same as what we have already presented concerning the earlier reports.

Al-Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan ibn Aban, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Fadalah, from Aban ibn 'Uthman, from al-Fadl ibn 'Abd al-Malik, who said: I asked Aba 'Abdillah عليه السلام about a traveler who stays with some of his family for a day or a night. He said: He shortens the salat (prayer).

As for what Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā narrated from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from Dāwūd ibn al-Ḥuṣayn, from Faḍl al-Baqbāq, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a traveler who stays with some of his family for a day, or a night, or three; he said: I do not like that he should shorten the salat (prayer). So the proper understanding of this narration is that it indicates a kind of recommendation, according to what is explicitly stated in it.

The Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from his father, from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan al-Ṣaffār, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Mughīrah, from Ismāʿīl ibn Abī Ziyād, from Jaʿfar, from his father عليه السلام, who said: Seven do not shorten the salat: the tax collector who moves about in his tax collection; the amir who moves about within his governorship; the merchant who travels in his trade from market to market; the shepherd; the Bedouin who seeks places of rainfall and where trees grow; the man who seeks game, intending by it worldly amusement; and the fighter who cuts off the road.

Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā, from Abī al-Miʿzā, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, from one of the two of them عليهما السلام, who said: There is no shortening upon the sailors during their travel, nor upon the muleteers, nor upon the camel-drivers.

Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from Ḥammād ibn ʿĪsā, from Ḥarīz, from Zurārah, who said: Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام said: There are four upon whom full prayer may become obligatory, whether they are in travel or in residence: the mukārī, the karī, the shepherd, and the ishtiqān, because it is their work.

ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā, from Yūnus, from Isḥāq ibn ʿAmmār, who said: I asked him about the sailors and the Bedouins: is there shortened prayer upon them? He said: No; their homes are with them.

As for what Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Saʿid, from Faḍālah, from al-ʿAlāʾ ibn Razīn, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from one of the two of them عليهما السلام, who said: The muleteer and the camel-driver, when travel presses on them in earnest, then they should shorten.

From him, from Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥusayn, from Faḍālah, from Abān ibn ʿUthmān, from al-Faḍl ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about the muleteers who travel back and forth, and he said: When they press on seriously in travel, then they should shorten. The proper way of understanding these two reports is what Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb al-Kulaynī, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned. He said: This is to be understood as referring to one who treats the two stopping places as one stopping place, so he shortens on the road and performs in full at the stopping place. And that which clarifies what we have mentioned...

What Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from ʿImrān ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿImrān al-Ashʿarī, from some of our companions, raising it to Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said: The camel-driver and the muleteer, when the travel presses on earnestly with them, should perform qasr between the two stopping places, and they should perform the prayer in full at the stopping place.

As for what Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated from Muhammad ibn Khalid al-Tayalisi, from Sayf ibn ʿAmirah, from Ishaq ibn ʿAmmar, who said: I asked Aba Ibrahim عليه السلام about those who hire out riding animals and travel back and forth every day: is shortened prayer obligatory upon them when they are in travel? He said: Yes.

From him, from Abī Jaʿfar, from his father, and Muḥammad ibn Khālid al-Barqī, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Mughīrah, from Isḥāq ibn ʿAmmār, from Abī Ibrāhīm عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about the muleteers who hire out riding animals, traveling about every few days; whenever some work comes to them, they go out. So he said: shortening is upon them when they travel.

From him, from ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Mughirah, from Muhammad ibn Jazzak, who said: I wrote to Abū al-Ḥasan al-Thālith عليه السلام that I have camels, and I have keepers over them, and I do not go out with them except on the road to Mecca due to my desire for hajj, or rarely to some places. So what is obligatory upon me, when I go out with them, to do? Is shortening in salat and fasting during travel obligatory upon me, or completion? So he عليه السلام wrote: If you do not remain constantly with them, and you do not go out with them on every journey except to Mecca, then shortening and breaking the fast are upon you. Thus, the correct interpretation regarding these reports is that completion is only obligatory upon such people when their stay is five days or less. But if it is more than that, then their ruling is the ruling of the rest of the people: the obligation of shortening upon them and breaking the fast. This indicates that.

What Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated from Ibrahim ibn Hashim, from Ismaʿil ibn Marrar, from Yunus ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman, from ʿAbd Allah ibn Sinan, from Abu ʿAbd Allah عليه السلام, who said: The mukārī, if he does not remain settled in his residence except for five days or less, shortens in his travel by day, completes the night prayer, and the fast of the month of Ramadan is incumbent upon him. But if he has a stay in the town to which he goes for ten days or more, he shortens during his travel and breaks the fast.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Ibrahim ibn Hashim, from Isma'il ibn Marrar, from Yunus ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from one of his men, who said: I asked him about the limit concerning the mukārī who fasts and performs full prayer. He said: Any mukārī who stays in his home or in the town that he enters for less than ten days, fasting and full prayer are always obligatory upon him. But if his stay in his home or in the town that he enters is more than ten days, then shortening the prayer and breaking the fast apply to him.

Al-Saffar narrated from al-Hasan ibn 'Ali, from Ahmad ibn Hilal, from Abi Sa'id al-Khurasani, who said: Two men entered upon Abi al-Hasan al-Rida عليه السلام in Khurasan and asked him about shortening the prayer. He said to one of them: Shortening has become obligatory upon you, because you intended me. And he said to the other: Completing the prayer in full has become obligatory upon you, because you intended the ruler.

As for what was narrated by Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb, from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn, from al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿUthmān, from Ismāʿīl ibn Jābir, who said: I sought permission from Abū ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام while we were fasting in Ramaḍān, to go and meet Walīd at al-Aʿwaṣ. So he said: Meet him and break your fast. So the proper understanding of this report is that it pertains to a state of taqiyyah and fear, not to a state of choice.

Al-Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Abū al-Qāsim Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb, from a number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyād, from ʿAlī ibn Asbāṭ, from Ibn Bukayr, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about a man who goes hunting for one day, two days, or three: does he shorten the salat (prayer)? He said: No, unless a man is escorting his brother in religion, for hunting is a vain journey in which the salat (prayer) is not shortened. And he said: He shortens when he escorts his brother.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Faddal, from Ibn Bukayr, from Ubayd ibn Zurarah, who said: I asked Aba Abdillah عليه السلام about a man who goes out for hunting: should he shorten or complete? He said: He should complete, because it is not travel in truth.

Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Mahbub narrated from al-Hasan ibn 'Ali ibn Mahbub, from al-Hasan ibn 'Ali, from 'Abbas ibn 'Amir, from Aban ibn 'Uthman, from Zurarah, from Abi Ja'far عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about one who goes out from his family with falcons, hawks, and dogs, taking recreation for one night, two nights, or three: does he shorten his salat (prayer), or does he not shorten? So he عليه السلام said: He has only gone out in amusement, so he does not shorten.

As for what Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb narrated from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn, from Ṣafwān, from ʿAbdullāh, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about a man who goes hunting. He said: If he moves around within his area, then he should not shorten; but if he goes beyond the distance, then let him shorten.

From him, from al-‘Abbās ibn Ma‘rūf, from al-Ḥasan ibn Maḥbūb, from some of our companions, from Abī Baṣīr, from Abī ‘Abdillāh عليه السلام, who said: The one engaged in hunting is not subject to qaṣr for three days; then when he goes beyond the three, it becomes binding upon him. So the proper way of reconciling these two reports is that whoever hunts for his own sustenance and the sustenance of his dependents, qaṣr is binding upon him; and whoever hunts for amusement and wantonness, qaṣr is not permissible for him, according to what we have explained. And that which indicates this is...

What Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā narrated from ʿImrān ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿImrān al-Qummī, from some of our companions, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: I said: A man goes out hunting for the distance of one day or two days; should he shorten or complete? He said: If he goes out for his own sustenance and the sustenance of his dependents, then let him shorten. But if he goes out seeking excess, then no, and no honor.

As for what Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā narrated from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad al-Sayyārī, from some of the people of al-ʿAskar, he said: A report was issued from Abī al-Ḥasan عليه السلام that the one engaged in hunting shortens the prayer so long as he remains on the main road; then if he turns away from the road, he performs it in full; and if he returns to it, he shortens. So this is a weak report, and its narrator is al-Sayyārī. Abū Jaʿfar Ibn Bābawayh, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his Fihrist when he mentioned Kitāb al-Nawādir: he excluded from it what al-Sayyārī narrated, and he said: I do not act upon it, nor do I give fatwa by it, due to its weakness. That whose ruling is such cannot be used to oppose the reports we have presented earlier. Even if it were conceded, it would be possible that its meaning is that whoever is on the main road not for the purpose of hunting must shorten; then if he turns away from it toward hunting, he must perform in full. If, however, while being on the main road his intent was hunting, then the ruling would not differ regarding the obligation of performing in full upon him if his hunting was for diversion, and shortening if his hunting was in pursuit of sustenance.

Al-Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from al-Saffar, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Hammad, from Hariz, from Zurarah, from Abu Ja'far عليه السلام, who said: I said to him: What do you think about one who arrives in a town—until when should he be shortening, and when should he complete? He said: When you enter a land and are certain that you will stay there for ten days, then perform the salat in full. But if you do not know how long you will stay there, saying, “Tomorrow I will leave, or the day after tomorrow,” then shorten during the period between your arrival and the passing of one month; then when a month is complete for you, perform the salat in full, even if you wish to leave that very hour.

Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Mahbub narrated from 'Abd al-Samad ibn Muhammad, from Hanan, from his father, from Abu Ja'far عليه السلام, who said: If you enter a town and say, “Today I will leave,” or “Tomorrow I will leave,” then you remain for a full month, then perform fully.

ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm narrated from his father, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Abī Ayyūb, who said: Muḥammad ibn Muslim asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, while I was listening, about the traveler: if he resolves within himself to stay for ten days, he said: then let him complete the salat (prayer). But if he does not know how long he will stay, whether a day or more, then let him count thirty days, and then let him complete; even if he has stayed one day or one salat (prayer). Then Muḥammad ibn Muslim said to him: It has reached me that you said five. He said: I did say that. Abū Ayyūb said: Then I said, May I be made your ransom, can it be less than five? He said: No. Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan, may Allah have mercy on him, said: What this report contains of the instruction to complete for one who intends to stay five days admits of two possibilities: one of them is that it is to be understood as recommendation, and the second is that it is specific to one who is in Makkah or al-Madīnah; and that which indicates this is:

What Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb narrated from ʿAlī ibn al-Sindī, from Ḥammād ibn ʿĪsā, from Ḥarīz, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, who said: I asked him about a traveler who arrives in a land. He said: If he resolves within himself to stay ten days, then let him perform in full. But if he says, “Today I will leave,” or, “Tomorrow I will leave,” while not knowing, then let him shorten between that time and one month. Then if a month passes, let him perform in full. And he does not perform in full in less than ten days except in Makkah and al-Madīnah; and if he stays in Makkah and al-Madīnah for five days, then let him perform in full.

Al-Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Abū al-Qāsim Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from his father, from Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allāh, from Abū Jaʿfar, from al-Ḥasan ibn Maḥbūb, from Abū Wallād al-Ḥannāṭ, who said: I said to Abū ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام: I had intended, when I entered al-Madīnah, to stay there for ten days and thus perform the salat in full. Then it occurred to me after that to change my plan, so what do you think for me: should I perform in full or shorten? He said: If, after entering al-Madīnah, you performed there one obligatory salat in full, then it is not for you to shorten until you leave it. But if, when you entered it, you had intended completeness, yet you did not perform in it even one obligatory salat in full before it occurred to you not to stay, then in that state you have the choice: if you wish, intend a stay of ten days and perform in full; and if you do not intend the stay, then shorten for the period up to one month. Then when a month has passed for you, perform the salat in full.

As for what Saʿd narrated from Abū Jaʿfar, from Muḥammad ibn Khālid al-Barqī, from Ḥamzah ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Jaʿfarī, who said: When I departed from Minā, I intended to stay in Makkah, so I performed the salat in full. Then news came to me from home, and I found no alternative but to go to the home. I did not know whether I should perform in full or shorten, while Abū al-Ḥasan عليه السلام was at that time in Makkah, so I came to him and related the story to him. He said: Return to shortening. The proper understanding of this report is that he only instructed him to return to shortening because he had not yet performed any of the obligatory salawat. So when his intention changed, his duty became shortening, according to what was explained in the first report. The questioner's statement, 'and I had been performing in full,' is to be understood as referring to supererogatory prayers rather than obligatory ones, because what is considered here is that he must have performed one obligatory prayer in full; at that point it becomes obligatory for him to continue performing in full for the rest of his stay, as was clarified in the first report.

Al-Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Abu al-Qasim Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah, from Abu Ja'far, from 'Ali ibn Hadid and al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Hammad ibn 'Isa, from Hariz, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I asked Aba 'Abd Allah عليه السلام about a man who is returning from his journey, and the time of salat has entered while he is still on the road. He said: He should pray two rak'ahs. And if he sets out on his journey and the time of salat has entered, then he should pray four.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad, from al-Hasan ibn 'Ali al-Washsha', who said: I heard al-Rida عليه السلام saying: When the sun passes the meridian while you are in the town and you intend to travel, then perform it in full; but when you depart after noon, then shorten the 'Asr prayer.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Ibn Faddal, from Dawud ibn Farqad, from Bashir al-Nabbal, who said: I went out with Abu Abdillah عليه السلام until we came to Masjid al-Shajarah. Then Abu Abdillah عليه السلام said to me: O Nabbal. I said: At your service. He said: It is not obligatory upon anyone from the people of this camp to pray four rak'ahs except me and you, because the time of the prayer entered before we set out.

As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Ṣafwān, from Ismāʿīl ibn Jābir, he said: I said to Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام: The time of salat enters upon me while I am traveling, so should I not pray until I enter upon my family? He said: Pray and complete the salat. I said: Then the time of salat enters upon me while I am among my family and I intend to travel, so should I not pray until I go out? He said: Then pray and shorten, for if you do not do so, you have opposed the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم. So this does not conflict with the reports we presented earlier, because the way to reconcile them is that whoever returns from his travel while enough time remains for him to complete his salat, completion is required of him; but if he fears missing the time, shortening is required of him. Likewise, whoever sets out on a journey and fears that the time will expire shortens; but if there is sufficient time for him, he completes. And that which indicates this is:

What Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Ja'far ibn Bashir, from Hammad ibn 'Uthman, from Ishaq ibn 'Ammar, who said: I heard Aba al-Hasan عليه السلام saying concerning a man who returns from his journey at the time of salat: he said, if he does not fear the passing of the time, then let him perform it complete; but if he fears the exit of the time, then let him shorten.

From him, from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn, from al-Ḥakam ibn Miskīn, from a man, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, concerning: A man arrives from his journey at the time of salat (prayer). He said: if he does not fear the time passing, then let him complete; and if he fears the time passing, then let him shorten. And it is possible that completing is directed toward one upon whom the time entered while he was a traveler, then he entered upon his family, by way of recommendation and not obligation or mandatory requirement—this indicates that.

What Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā narrated from Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd, from Sayf ibn ʿUmayrah, from Manṣūr ibn Ḥāzim, who said: I heard Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام say: If a man is on a journey and the time for salat enters before he reaches his family, then he continues traveling until he enters upon his family, then if he wishes he may shorten, and if he wishes he may complete; and if he completes, that is more beloved to me.

Al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿUbayd Allāh informed me, from a number of our companions, from Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb, from Aḥmad ibn Idrīs, from Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā, from Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī, from ʿAmr ibn Saʿīd, from Muṣaddaq ibn Ṣadaqah, from ʿAmmār al-Sābāṭī, from Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said: He was asked about water from which pigeons drink, and he said: Everything whose flesh is eaten—wudu (ablution) may be performed from its leftover water, and it may be drunk. And about water from which a hawk, falcon, or eagle drinks, he said: From whatever birds drink, wudu (ablution) may be performed, unless you see blood in its beak. If you see blood in its beak, then do not perform wudu (ablution) from it, nor drink from it. And he was asked about water from which a chicken has drunk, and he said: If there is filth in its beak, then do not drink from it and do not perform wudu (ablution) from it. But if you do not know that there is filth in its beak, then perform wudu (ablution) from it and drink. And this report is general regarding the permissibility of the leftover water of everything whose flesh is eaten among the rest of the animals, and that whatever flesh is not eaten, the use of its leftover water is not permissible. We have also explained in our book Tahdhīb al-Aḥkām what relates to that, and there we presented the reports fully. What this report includes of the permissibility of the leftover water of birds whose flesh is not eaten, such as the hawk and falcon, when their beaks are free of blood, is specified as an exception from among those whose flesh is not eaten regarding the permissibility of using their leftover water.

And likewise, what Isḥāq ibn ʿAmmār narrated from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, that Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام used to say: There is no بأس in the leftover of a mouse when it has drunk from a vessel: that one may drink from it and perform wudu (ablution) from it. The reason in this is that it is specified, apart from those whose flesh is not eaten, because it is not possible to guard oneself from the mouse and that is burdensome upon the human being; so its leftover was excused on account of that.

The Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Abū al-Qāsim Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from his father, from Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allāh, from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn, from Ṣafwān ibn Yaḥyā, from ʿĪṣ ibn al-Qāsim, from Abū ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who prayed while he was traveling, and he completed the prayer. He said: If it is still within the time, then let him repeat it; but if the time has already passed, then no.

As for what Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from 'Ali ibn al-Nu'man, from Suwayd al-Qalla', from Abi Ayyub, from Abi Basir, who said: I asked him about a man who forgets and thus prays four rak'ahs while traveling. He said: If he remembers on that very day, then let him repeat it; and if he does not remember until that day passes, then there is no repetition upon him. So what this report contains of the command to repeat after the expiration of the time within that day is to be understood as a form of recommendation. And what the first report contains of making it up so long as one remains within the time is upon obligation and requirement, and there is no contradiction between them in any way.

Al-Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar, from Abd Allah ibn Amir, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Najran, from Abd Allah ibn Sinan, from Abu Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about shortening the prayer. He said: When you are in the place where you do not hear the adhan, then shorten; and when you return from your journey, it is likewise.

As for what al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Safwan, from Ishaq ibn 'Ammar, from Abi Ibrahim عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who is traveling, then arrives and enters the houses of Makkah: should he perform the salat in full, or should he remain shortening it until he enters upon his family? He said: Rather, he should remain shortening it until he enters upon his family.

From him, from Ṣafwān ibn Yaḥyā, from ʿĪṣ ibn al-Qāsim, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: The traveler continues shortening until he enters his house. So there is no contradiction between these two reports and the first report, because his statement, “The traveler continues shortening until he enters his family or his house,” corresponds to what he mentioned in the first report: that when the adhān becomes hidden from him, he shortens. This is by understanding the limit of his entering to his family as the disappearance of the adhān from him. And his statement, “then he enters the houses of Makkah,” may be understood to mean what is near Makkah, even if it is in a place where one there does not hear the adhān, because among the conditions of the adhān is not extreme loudness such that one outside the town at a distance would hear it. In this way, there is no contradiction between the reports.

Al-Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Abū al-Qāsim Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from his father, from Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allāh, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from Muḥammad ibn Ismāʿīl ibn Bazīʿ, from Thaʿlabah ibn Maymūn, from Ḥammād ibn ʿUthmān, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī ʿAbd Allāh, from Abū ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said: No one prays the obligatory prayer upon a riding animal except a sick person; he is to be turned toward the qiblah, and Sūrat al-Fātiḥah suffices him, and in the obligatory prayer he places his face upon whatever he is able of something, and in the supererogatory prayer he gestures with a gesture.

As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from ʿAlī ibn Aḥmad ibn Ashyam, from Manṣūr ibn Ḥāzim, who said: Aḥmad ibn al-Nuʿmān asked and said: “May I perform salat (prayer) in my litter while I am ill?” He said: “As for the supererogatory prayer, yes; but as for the obligatory prayer, no.” And Aḥmad mentioned the severity of his pain, so he said: “I had been severely ill, and when the time of salat (prayer) came, I would order them to make me stand, and I would be carried on my bedding and set down, and I would perform salat (prayer), then I would be carried on my bedding and placed in my litter.” So this narration is to be understood as referring to a kind of recommendation, or to a condition in which one is able to be lowered to the ground. Salat (prayer) in the litter is only permissible when one is unable to get down, in a manner indicated by that.

What Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā narrated from Aḥmad ibn Hilāl, from Yūnus ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Sinān, who said: I said to Abū ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام: May a man perform any part of the obligatory prayer while riding? He said: No, except in a case of necessity.

Al-Husayn ibn 'Ubayd Allah informed me, from a number of our companions, from Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Salamah ibn al-Khattab, from Yahya ibn Ibrahim ibn Abi al-Bilad, from Abi Basir, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: Whoever performs salat (prayer) outside the time, then there is no salat (prayer) for him.

As for what Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā narrated from his father, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Ḥammād ibn ʿUthmān, from ʿUbayd Allāh al-Ḥalabī, from Abū ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said: If you perform some prayer during travel at other than its time, then it does not harm. The correct understanding of this report is that this refers to one who prays outside the time, meaning after the time has passed, so it does not harm him because he is making it up. But before the entry of the time, it is not permissible, whether he is a traveler or resident.

Al-Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Abū al-Qāsim Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb, from ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā, from Yūnus ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Sinān, who said: I heard Abā ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام saying: For every salat (prayer) there are two times, and the first of the time is the more excellent of them. And it is not for anyone to make the latter of the two times his time, except in a case of excuse, without illness.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Fadalah ibn Ayyub, from Mu'awiyah ibn 'Ammar or Ibn Wahb, who said: Abu 'Abdillah عليه السلام said: For every salat (prayer) there are two times, and the beginning of the time is the better of the two.

As for what was narrated by Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb, from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn, from Jaʿfar ibn Bashīr, from Udaym ibn al-Ḥurr, who said: I heard Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام saying: Indeed, Jabrāʾīl عليه السلام instructed the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم regarding all the salats, and he assigned for every salat two times, except al-maghrib, for he assigned to it one single time.

ʿAlī ibn Mahziyār, from Ḥammād ibn ʿĪsā, from Ḥarīz, from Zayd al-Shaḥḥām, who said: I asked Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about the time of Maghrib, and he said: Jibrāʾīl عليه السلام came to the Prophet صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم for every salat (prayer) with two times, except the salat (prayer) of Maghrib, for indeed its time is one, and its time is its becoming obligatory. So there is no contradiction between these two reports and the first two reports, because the way to reconcile them is that the time of Maghrib is restricted: there is not, between its beginning and its end, the same breadth as there is between the beginning of the time and its end in the rest of the prayers, as we shall clarify later. He did not mean that it has one single time such that it is not permissible for it to be advanced or delayed. And no one may say, in reconciling these reports, that Maghrib prayer is singled out from among the rest of the prayers, and say that every prayer has two times except Maghrib, because here there are detailed reports, which we have cited in our larger book, that include mention of Maghrib prayer and that it has two times, an earlier and a later one. Perhaps we may mention some of them later, if something arises that requires that. And when the matter is as such, this interpretation is not possible, and nothing besides what we have said is admissible.

Al-Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from al-Saffar, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from Ibrahim al-Karkhi, who said: I asked Abu al-Hasan Musa عليه السلام, “When does the time of Zuhr enter?” He said, “When the sun declines.” I said, “When does its time go out?” He said, “After four feet have passed from its decline. Indeed, the beginning of the time of Zuhr is narrow.” I said, “Then when does the time of Asr enter?” He said, “Indeed, the end of the time of Zuhr is the beginning of the time of Asr.” I said, “Then when does the time of Asr go out?” He said, “The time of Asr is until the sun sets, and that is due to an excuse; otherwise it is neglect.” So I said to him, “If a man were to pray Zuhr after four feet have passed from the sun’s decline, would he, in your view, be one who has not properly performed it?” He said, “If he did that deliberately in order to oppose the sunnah and the appointed time, it would not be accepted from him—just as if a man were to delay Asr until near sunset deliberately, without an excuse, it would not be accepted from him. Indeed, the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم appointed times for the obligatory prayers and set limits for them in a sunnah for the people. So whoever turns away from a binding sunnah among his sunnahs is like one who turns away from the obligations of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.”
Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Mahbub, from al-'Ubaydi, from Sulayman ibn Ja'far, said: The Faqih, peace be upon him, said: The end of the time of the 'asr prayer is six and a half feet.

Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Sama'ah, from Ibn Muskan, from Sulayman ibn Khalid, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: The 'Asr prayer is at two cubits, so whoever leaves it until it reaches six feet, then that is the one who is neglectful.

From him, from Ja'far, from Muthannā, from Manṣūr ibn Ḥāzim, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: Pray the ʿAṣr prayer at four feet. Al-Muthannā said: Abū Baṣīr said to me: Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام said to me: Pray the ʿAṣr prayer on Friday at six feet.

From him, from Husayn ibn Hashim, from Ibn Muskan, from Abi Basir, who said: Abu Abdillah عليه السلام said to me: Indeed, the one bereft of his family and wealth is the one who neglects the salat of al-'Asr. I said: What is al-mawtur? He said: He will have neither family nor wealth in Paradise. I said: And what is neglecting it? He said: He leaves it until it turns yellow and sets.

Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah, from Ya'qub ibn Yazid, from al-Hasan ibn 'Ali al-Washsha', from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Abi al-Hasan عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about the time of Zuhr and 'Asr, so he said: The time of Zuhr is when the sun declines until the shadow goes to one qamah, and the time of 'Asr is from one and a half qamahs until two qamahs.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from 'Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from Yunus, from Yazid ibn Khalifah, who said: I said to Abu 'Abdillah عليه السلام: Indeed, 'Umar ibn Hanzalah came to us from you regarding a time. So Abu 'Abdillah عليه السلام said: Then he does not lie against us. So I said: He mentioned that you say that the first time of a salat (prayer) which Allah, Exalted is He, made obligatory upon His Prophet صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم is the noon prayer. And it is the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: “Establish the salat (prayer) at the declining of the sun.” So when the sun passes the meridian, nothing prevents you except your supererogatory prayer. Then you remain within the time until the shadow becomes one stature, and that is the end of the time. So when the shadow becomes one stature, the time of the afternoon prayer enters, and you remain within the time of the afternoon prayer until the shadow becomes two statures, and that is the evening. He said: He spoke the truth.

As for what Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb narrated from Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Faḍḍāl, from ʿAlī ibn Yaʿqūb al-Hāshimī, from Marwān ibn Muslim, from ʿUbayd ibn Zurārah, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: The salat (prayer) is not missed for one who intends the salat (prayer): the daytime salat (prayer) is not missed until the sun sets, nor the nighttime salat (prayer) until dawn rises, nor the fajr salat (prayer) until the sun rises.

Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from al-Qasim ibn 'Urwah, from 'Ubayd ibn Zurarah, who said: I asked Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام about the time of zuhr and 'asr. He said: When the sun declines, the time for zuhr and 'asr both enters together, except that this one is before that one. Then you remain within the time of both of them together until the sun sets.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Fadalah ibn Ayyub, from Musa ibn Bakr, from Zurarah, who said: Abu Ja'far عليه السلام said: The most beloved time to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is its earliest part, when the time of the salat (prayer) begins. So perform the obligatory prayer; and if you do not do so, then you remain within the time of the two of them until the sun sets.

Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn ʿIsa and Musa ibn Jaʿfar, from Abi Jaʿfar, from Abi Talib ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Salt, from al-Hasan ibn ʿAli ibn Faddal, from Dawud ibn Abi Yazid—and he is Dawud ibn Farqad—from some of our companions, from Abi ʿAbd Allah عليه السلام, who said: When the sun passes the zenith, the time of Zuhr has entered, until there passes the amount of time in which a person praying can perform four rakʿahs. When that has passed, then the time of Zuhr and ʿAsr has entered, until there remains before sunset the amount of time in which a person praying can perform four rakʿahs. When that amount remains, then the time of Zuhr has ended, and the time of ʿAsr remains until the sun sets.

Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from 'Abd Allah ibn Muhammad al-Hajjal, from Tha'labah ibn Maymun, from Ma'mar ibn Yahya, who said: I heard Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام saying: The time of the ʿasr prayer is until sunset.

Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn Abī Naṣr, from al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Yazīd, from ʿUbayd ibn Zurārah, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, concerning: His, Exalted is He, saying: “Establish the salat (prayer) at the decline of the sun until the darkness of the night.” He said: Allah, Exalted is He, has made four salats obligatory, the beginning of whose time is from the decline of the sun until midnight. Among them are two salats whose initial time is from the time of the sun’s decline until sunset, except that this one is before that one. So the proper way to reconcile these reports is that we interpret them as referring to one who has excuses and ailments with which he is unable to perform the salat at the beginning of the time. Abū al-Ḥasan عليه السلام clarified that in the narration of Ibrāhīm al-Karkhī from him when he said: “That is due to an excuse, and it is neglect.” We have also previously stated that it is not permissible to treat the end of the two times as a time except due to an excuse, and that further clarifies it.

What Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā narrated from Ismāʿīl ibn Sahl, from Ḥammād, from Ribʿī, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: Indeed, we sometimes bring forward and sometimes delay, and it is not as is said: whoever misses the time of the salat (prayer) has perished. Rather, the concession applies to the forgetful, the sick, the severely weakened, the traveler, and the sleeper regarding delaying it.

The Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Abū al-Qāsim Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from his father, from Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allāh, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā, from ʿAlī ibn Ḥadīd and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Najrān, from Ḥammād ibn ʿĪsā, from Ḥarīz ibn ʿAbd Allāh, from Zurārah, from Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said: The Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم used to perform the two rakʿahs of ṣubḥ—and that is al-fajr—when the dawn had spread across the horizon and had become well illuminated.
Ali ibn Ibrahim narrated from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yunus, from Yazid ibn Khalifah, from Abu Abdillah عليه السلام, who said: The time of fajr is from when it appears until it becomes bright.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Fadalah, from al-'Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I said to Abī 'Abdillah عليه السلام: A man performed the fajr prayer when dawn had risen? He said: There is no harm in it.

Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from Faḍālah, from al-ʿAlāʾ, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, who said: I said to Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام: “A man performed the fajr salat when dawn had risen.” So he said: “There is no harm in it.”

Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā narrated from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from al-Ḥuṣayn ibn Abī al-Ḥuṣayn, who said: I wrote to Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام: May I be made your ransom, your followers have differed regarding the salat (prayer) of al-fajr. Some of them pray when the first dawn rises, extending upward in the sky, while some of them pray when it spreads across the lower horizon and becomes clear. I do not know which of the two times is better so that I may pray in it. So if you see fit, O my master—may Allah make me your ransom—to teach me the better of the two times, and to specify for me what I should do when there is moonlight and the dawn does not become clear until it reddens and morning comes, and what I should do with the moon, and what the limit of that is in travel and residence, then do so, if Allah wills. So he wrote in his own hand: Al-fajr, may Allah have mercy on you, is the white thread, and it is not the whiteness rising upward. Do not pray, whether in travel or residence, until you clearly discern it—may Allah have mercy on you—for Allah has not left His creation in doubt concerning this. For He said: “Eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread at dawn.” So the white thread is the dawn by which eating and drinking become forbidden in sawm (fasting), and likewise it is that which makes salat (prayer) obligatory.

Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn Abī Naṣr, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Sālim, from Isḥāq ibn ʿAmmār, who said: I said to Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام: Inform me about the best of the times for salat al-fajr. He said: At the rising of the fajr. Indeed Allah says: “Indeed, the Qur'an of fajr is ever witnessed.” Meaning salat al-fajr: the angels of the night and the angels of the day witness it. So when the servant performs salat al-subh at the rising of the fajr, it is recorded for him twice: the angels of the night record it and the angels of the day record it.

Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Mahbub, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from al-Husayn, from Fadalah, from Hisham ibn Hudhayl, from Abi al-Hasan al-Madi عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about the time of salat al-fajr, and he said: when the dawn spreads across the horizon, so that you see it like the river of Sura'.

ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from ʿAlī ibn ʿAṭiyyah, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: Ṣubḥ is that which, when I see it, spreads across the horizon as though it were the whiteness of the river of Sūrāʾ.

As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā narrated from ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Mughīrah, from Mūsā ibn Bakr, from Zurārah, from Abī Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said: The time of Salat al-Ghadah is from the rising of dawn until the rising of the sun.

And among what Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn Abi al-Khattab and ʿAbd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn ʿIsa, from ʿAmr ibn ʿUthman, from Abi Jamilah al-Mufaḍḍal ibn Salih, from Saʿd ibn Tarif, from al-Aṣbagh ibn Nubatah, who said: Amir al-Muʾminin عليه السلام said: Whoever catches one rakʿah of the morning prayer before the rising of the sun has indeed caught the morning prayer in full. Thus, the proper way regarding these two reports is that we interpret them as applying to one who has excuses and one who has a necessary need that prevents him from salat (prayer) at the beginning of the time, according to what we have already set forth regarding other prayers; this indicates that.

What Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah narrated from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan ibn 'Ali ibn Faddal, from 'Amr ibn Sa'id, from Musaddiq ibn Sadaqah, from 'Ammar al-Sabati, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, concerning: About a man whose eyes overcame him with sleep, or some matter hindered him, from performing the obligatory prayer of dawn between the time dawn rises and the sun rises—and that is specifically regarding the obligatory prayer. If he has prayed one rak'ah of the morning prayer and then the sun rises, then let him complete it, and his prayer is valid.

And Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb narrated from ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Ḥammād, from al-Ḥalabī, from Abū ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said: The time of Fajr is when the dawn breaks until the morning light spreads over the sky. It is not proper to delay that intentionally, but it is still a time for one who was occupied, or forgot, or slept.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from al-Nadr, from 'Asim ibn Humayd, from Abi Basir al-Makfuf, who said: I asked Aba 'Abdillah عليه السلام about the fasting person: when does food become forbidden for him? He said: When the dawn is like the white Qibtiyyah cloth. I said: Then when does the salat (prayer) become permissible? He said: When it is like that. So I said: Am I not within a time, from that hour until the sun rises? He said: No, we only count that as the prayer of children. Then he said: A man was not considered praiseworthy if he were to perform salat (prayer) in the mosque and then return and wake his family and children.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from al-Nadr and Fadalah, from Ibn Sinan, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: For every salat there are two times, and the first of the two times is the more excellent of them. The time of Salat al-Fajr is when the dawn breaks until the morning light spreads over the sky, and it is not proper to delay that deliberately; rather, that is the time of one who was occupied, or forgot, or was heedless, or slept. And the time of al-Maghrib is when the sun becomes concealed until the stars become intermingled; so it is not for anyone to make the latter of the two times his time except due to an excuse or an ailment.

Al-Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Abū Muḥammad al-Ḥasan ibn Ḥamzah al-ʿAlawī, may Allah have mercy on him, from ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Ibn Udhaynah, from a number [of narrators], that they heard Abā Jaʿfar عليه السلام say: Amīr al-Muʾminīn عليه السلام would not perform prayer during the daytime until the sun had passed the meridian, nor during the night after he had performed the ʿIshāʾ prayer until the middle of the night.

Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Mahbub, from 'Ali ibn al-Sindi, from Muhammad ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Jamil ibn Darrāj, from Zurārah, from Abu Ja'far عليه السلام, who said: Amir al-Mu'minin عليه السلام would not perform any prayer from the night, after he had prayed al-'atamah, until the middle of the night; and he would not perform any prayer from the day until the sun had passed the zenith.

As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā narrated from ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥakam, from Abī Ayyūb, from Ismāʿīl ibn Jābir, who said: I said to Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام: I am occupied. He said: Then do as we do: pray six rakʿahs when the sun is in a position like its position for the ʿaṣr prayer, meaning at the greater rise of the forenoon, and count them as part of the prayers from zawāl.

And from him, from ʿAmmār ibn al-Mubārak, from Ẓarīf ibn Nāṣiḥ, from al-Qāsim ibn al-Walīd al-Ghassānī, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: I said to him, ‘May I be made your ransom, the daytime salat of the nawafil—how many is it?’ He said, ‘Sixteen. Whichever hours of the day you wish to perform them, you may perform them, except that if you perform them at their proper times, that is more excellent.’

From him, from ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥakam, from some of his companions, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: He said to me: The prayer of the day is sixteen rakʿahs; whichever part of the day you wish—if you wish, in its beginning; and if you wish, in its middle; and if you wish, in its end.

From him, from ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥakam, from Sayf ibn ʿUmayrah, from ʿAbd al-Aʿlā, who said: I asked Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about the supererogatory prayers of the day, He said: Sixteen rakʿahs, whenever you have the energy. Indeed, ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn عليه السلام had hours in the day in which he would perform salat; when an estate or the ruler occupied him, he would make them up. The supererogatory prayer is only like a gift: whenever it is brought, it is accepted.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Ibrahim ibn Hashim, from ʿAmr ibn ʿUthman, from Muhammad ibn ʿUdhafir, who said: Abu ʿAbdillah عليه السلام said: The supererogatory salat is like a gift; whenever it is brought, it is accepted. So perform of it whatever you wish earlier, and delay of it whatever you wish. So the proper way regarding these reports is that we understand them as a kind of concession for one who knows that if he does not perform them earlier, he will become occupied from them and will not be able to make them up; this is indicated by that.

What al-Ḥusayn ibn Muḥammad narrated from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀmir, from ʿAlī ibn Mahziyār, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from Ḥammād ibn ʿĪsā, from Yazīd ibn Ḍamrah al-Laythī, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, who said: I asked Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام about a man who will be occupied at the time of zawāl: may he perform it earlier from the beginning of the day? He said: Yes, if he knows that he will be occupied, then he may perform it earlier in the early part of the whole day.

Al-Husayn ibn ʿUbayd Allah informed me, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Yahya, from his father, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan ibn ʿAli ibn Faddal, from ʿAmr ibn Saʿid, from Musaddiq ibn Sadaqah, from ʿAmmar al-Sabati, from Abu ʿAbd Allah عليه السلام, who said: He was asked about the beetle, the fly, the locust, the ant, and the like of that, dying in a well, oil, ghee, and similar things. He said: Everything that has no blood, there is no harm in it.

And with this chain of transmission, from Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā, from Abū Jaʿfar, from his father, from Ḥafṣ ibn Ghiyāth, from Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad عليه السلام, who said: Nothing spoils the water except that which has flowing blood.

Al-Shaykh Abu 'Abd Allah informed me, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan ibn Aban, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Ibn Sinan, from Ibn Muskan, who said: Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام said: Everything that falls into the well which has no blood, such as scorpions, beetles, and the like, then there is no harm.

As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from ʿUthmān ibn ʿĪsā, from Samāʿah, from Abī Baṣīr, from Abī Jaʿfar عليه السلام, he said: I asked him about the beetle that falls into the water: may wudu (ablution) be performed from it? He said: Yes, there is no harm in it. I said: Then what about the scorpion? He said: Pour it out. So the proper way regarding this report, in what relates to the command to pour out that in which the scorpion has fallen, is that we carry it upon recommendation rather than prohibition and obligation.

As for what was narrated by Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd, from Yūnus ibn Yaʿqūb, from Minhāl, who said: I said to Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام: “A scorpion is taken out of the well dead?” He said: “Draw out ten buckets.” He said: I said: “And other than it from among carcasses?” He said: “All carcasses are alike, except a carcass that has become putrid. So if it is a carcass that has become putrid, then draw from it one hundred buckets; and if the smell overcomes it after one hundred buckets, then drain it all out.” So the appropriate understanding concerning this report as well is that it indicates a kind of recommendation, not obligation.

The Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from his father, from al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Ḥasan ibn Abān, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from ʿUmar ibn Udhaynah, from Fuḍayl, from one of the two of them عليهما السلام. That the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم used to perform thirteen rakʿahs after the night had reached its midpoint.

From him, from Safwan, from Ibn Bukayr, from ʿAbd al-Hamid al-Ta'i, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu ʿAbd Allah عليه السلام, who said: I heard him saying: When the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم had performed the later night prayer, he would retire to his bed and would not perform any of the supererogatory prayers except after the middle of the night, neither in the month of Ramadan nor in other than it.

As for what ʿAbd Allah ibn Muskan narrated from Layth al-Muradi, he said: I asked Aba ʿAbd Allah عليه السلام about salat in the summer, during the short nights—salat al-layl in the first part of the night. He said: Yes, excellent is what you considered, and excellent is what you did. So this report bears two possibilities: one of them is that it is a concession for the traveler, and the second is that it is a concession for one upon whom standing in the latter part of the night is difficult and who is not able to make it up. Then it is permissible for him in that case to advance it to the first part of the night. This is indicated by that.

What Ḥammād ibn ʿĪsā narrated from Muʿāwiyah ibn Wahb, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: I said to him: A man from your followers, from among their righteous ones, complained to me about what he suffers from sleep. He said: I intend to rise for salat of the night, but sleep overcomes me until morning comes. Sometimes I make up my prayer for a whole consecutive month or two months, bearing its burden. He said: Coolness of the eye for him, by Allah. He said: And he did not grant him permission to perform the prayer in the first part of the night, and he said: Making it up during the day is better. I said: Among our women are virgin girls who love good and its people, and are eager for the prayer, but sleep overcomes them until morning. Sometimes they make it up, and sometimes they become too weak to make it up, while they are stronger for it in the first part of the night. So he granted them permission to perform the prayer in the first part of the night if they became weak and neglected the make-up.

From him, from Muḥammad ibn Sinān, from Ibn Muskān, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, who said: I asked him about a man who does not wake up at the end of the night until those ten and fifteen have passed: is it more beloved to you that he perform it at the beginning of the night, or that he make it up? He said: No, rather making it up is more beloved to me. I dislike that this be adopted as a habit. And Zurārah used to say: How can he make up a prayer whose time has not yet entered? Its time is only after the middle of the night. As for that which indicates the permissibility of that for the traveler...

What al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Muḥammad ibn Sinān, from Ibn Muskān, from al-Ḥalabī, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about performing Salat al-Layl and al-Witr at the beginning of the night while traveling, if I feared the cold or there was an illness. He said: There is no harm; I do so when I fear that.

From him, from al-Naḍr, from Mūsā ibn Bukayr, from ʿAlī ibn Saʿīd, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about Salat al-Layl and al-Witr during travel, in the early part of the night, when one is not able to perform it in its latter part. He said: Yes.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from al-Hajjal, from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Walid al-Kindi, from Isma'il ibn Jabir or 'Abd Allah ibn Sinan, who said: I said to Abī 'Abd Allah عليه السلام: Indeed, I rise in the latter part of the night and fear the coming of dawn. So he said: Recite al-Hamd and hasten, hasten.

From him, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Muḥammad, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀmir, from ʿAlī ibn Mahziyār, from Faḍālah ibn Ayyūb, from al-Qāsim ibn Burayd, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, from Abī Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who rises at the end of the night while fearing that dawn may suddenly overtake him: should he begin with al-Witr, or should he perform the prayer in its proper order so that al-Witr is the last of it? He said: Rather, he should begin with al-Witr. And he said: I used to do that.
Al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from Faḍālah, from Ḥammād, from Ismāʿīl ibn Jābir, who said: I said to Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, “Should I perform the witr after dawn has risen?” He said, “No.”

As for what Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Barqi, from al-Marzuban ibn ʿImran, from ʿUmar ibn Yazid, who said: I said to Abī ʿAbd Allah عليه السلام: I get up when dawn has already risen. If I begin with the fajr prayer, I perform it at the beginning of its time; but if I begin with salat al-layl and the witr, I perform the fajr prayer in the time of those ones. He said: Begin with salat al-layl and the witr, but do not make that a habit.

From him, from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn, from ʿAmmār ibn al-Mubārak, from Muḥammad ibn ʿUdhāfir, from Isḥāq ibn ʿAmmār, who said: I said to Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام: I rise when dawn has already come, and I have not performed Ṣalāt al-Layl. He said: Perform Ṣalāt al-Layl, and perform the witr, and perform the two rakʿahs of dawn. So these two reports were transmitted as a concession regarding the permissibility of delaying Ṣalāt al-Ghadāt from the beginning of its time, because that is permissible in cases of excuses, as we have mentioned before; and among the excuses is making up Ṣalāt al-Layl. However, what we mentioned earlier is more excellent, and that which also indicates this concession is:

From what al-Saffar narrated from Ya'qub ibn Yazid, from 'Amr ibn 'Uthman and Muhammad ibn 'Umar ibn Yazid, from Muhammad ibn 'Udhafir, from 'Umar ibn Yazid, from Abi 'Abdillah عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about Salat al-Layl and al-Witr after the rise of dawn. He said: Pray it after dawn, so long as it remains within a time in which you would pray the morning prayer at the end of its time, and do not intentionally do that every night. And he said: Perform the Witr also after you finish it.

Al-Husayn ibn 'Ubayd Allah informed me, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from his father, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from 'Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Abu al-Fadl al-Nahwi, from Abu Ja'far al-Ahwal Muhammad ibn Nu'man, who said: Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام said: If you have prayed four rak'ahs of salat al-layl before the rising of dawn, then complete the prayer whether dawn rises or it has not risen.

As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Muḥammad ibn Sinān, from Ibn Miskān, from Yaʿqūb al-Bazzāz, who said: I said to him: I rise shortly before dawn and pray four rakʿahs, then I fear that dawn may break. Should I begin with the witr, or complete the rakʿahs? He said: No, rather perform the witr and delay the rakʿahs until you make them up in the early part of the day. So the proper way regarding this narration is that we interpret it as referring to what is more virtuous, because what is more virtuous is that one perform the obligatory prayer at the beginning of its time, and the first narration is a concession, as we explained before this.

The Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Abū al-Qāsim Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb, from ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Zurārah, who said: I said to Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام: The two rakʿahs that are before al-ghadāh, where is their place? He said: Before the rising of al-fajr; for when al-fajr rises, the time of al-ghadāh has entered.

From him, from ʿAlī ibn Muḥammad, from Sahl ibn Ziyād, from ʿAlī ibn Mahziyār, who said: I read in a man’s letter to Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام: Are the two rakʿahs before salat al-fajr part of salat al-layl, or are they part of the prayer of the day? And at what time should I perform them? So he wrote in his own handwriting: Insert them into salat al-layl as an insertion.
Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn Abī Naṣr, who said: I asked al-Riḍā عليه السلام about the two rakʿahs of dawn, and he said: Insert them within the salat of the night.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from al-Hasan, from Zur'ah, from Ibn Muskan, from Abi Basir, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: I said, “Are the two rak'ahs of dawn part of salat al-layl?” He said, “Yes.”

And from him, from al-Naḍr, from Hishām ibn Sālim, from Zurārah, from Abī Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about the two rakʿahs of fajr: before fajr or after fajr? He said: Before fajr. Indeed, they are part of salat al-layl, making salat al-layl thirteen rakʿahs. Do you wish to make an analogy? If you had something due from the month of Ramadan, would you perform a voluntary act when the time of the obligatory duty had entered? Then begin with the obligatory duty.

From him, from al-Naḍr, from Hishām, from Sulaymān ibn Khālid, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about the two rakʿahs before al-fajr. He said: You perform them when the morning begins to brighten; indeed, they are before the morning prayer.

From him, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Makhlad ibn Hamzah ibn Bayd, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I asked Abu Ja'far عليه السلام about the earliest time of the two rak'ahs of al-Fajr, and he said: the remaining sixth of the night.

Sa'd narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, who said: I said to Abu al-Hasan عليه السلام: "The two rak'ahs of fajr—should I perform them before fajr or after fajr?" He said: "Abu Ja'far عليه السلام said: 'Join them onto the night prayer, and perform them before fajr.'"

As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Faḍālah, from Ḥammād ibn ʿUthmān, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, who said: I heard Abā Jaʿfar عليه السلام say: Pray the two rakʿahs of al-fajr before al-fajr, after it, and at its time.

From him, from Safwan, from al-'Ala', from Ibn Abi Ya'fur; and Muhammad ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Muhammad ibn Humran, from Ibn Abi Ya'fur, who said: I asked Aba 'Abdillah عليه السلام about the two rak'ahs of al-fajr: when should I perform them? He said: Before al-fajr, with it, and after it.
And from him, from Muḥammad ibn Sinān, from Ibn Muskān, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, from Abī Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said: Pray them with the dawn, before it, and after it.

Ibn Muskan, from Ya‘qub ibn Salim al-Bazzaz, who said: Abu ‘Abd Allah عليه السلام said: Pray them after al-Fajr. And recite in them, in the first [rak‘ah]: “Say: O disbelievers.” and in the second: “Say: He is Allah, One.”

From him, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from ʿUmar ibn Udhaynah, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about the two rakʿahs of fajr, and he said: Pray them before fajr, with fajr, and after fajr.

From him, from Ṣafwān, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Ḥajjāj, who said: Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام said: Pray them both after dawn rises. The proper way of understanding these reports is one of two possibilities. One of them is that this is a concession for one who prays the two rakʿahs at the beginning of dawn as a precaution, so that the time of the obligatory prayer may become clear with certainty. This is indicated by that.

What al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Muḥammad ibn Sinān, from Ibn Miskān, from Isḥāq ibn ʿAmmār, from one who informed him, from him, peace be upon him, who said: Pray the two rakʿahs during the time between where you are and when the light comes level with your head; then when it is after that, begin with the Fajr prayer.

From him, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Abi al-'Ala', who said: I said to Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام: A man rises when it has already become light at the time of the morning prayer? He said: Then let him perform the two rak'ahs that are before al-ghadah, then let him perform al-ghadah. And the other possibility is that it is to be understood as carried upon a kind of taqiyyah, because that is the doctrine of most of the 'ammah, and none agrees with us on it except a small number. And that which indicates this is...

What Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā narrated from ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥakam, from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ḥamzah, from Abī Baṣīr, who said: I said to Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, “When should I perform the two rakʿahs of fajr?” He said: He said to me, “After the rising of fajr.” I said to him, “Indeed Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام instructed me to perform them before the rising of fajr.” He said, “O Abā Muḥammad, indeed the Shiʿah came to my father seeking right guidance, so he gave them fatwa with the bitter truth; and they came to me in a state of doubt, so I gave them fatwa in accordance with taqiyyah.”

As for what Ibn Abī ʿUmayr narrated from Ḥammād ibn ʿUthmān, he said: Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام said to me: Sometimes I pray the two rakʿahs while it is still night upon me; then if I rise and dawn has not yet broken, I repeat them.

And what Ṣafwān narrated from Ibn Bukayr, from Zurārah, who said: I heard Abā Jaʿfar عليه السلام saying: Indeed, I perform Salat al-Layl, and I finish my prayer, and I perform the two rakʿahs; then I sleep for as long as Allah wills before dawn rises. Then if I awaken at dawn, I repeat them. So the correct way regarding these two reports is that we interpret them as referring to one who performs the two rakʿahs before the first dawn. It is recommended for him to repeat them so long as the second dawn has not yet risen, and that is not obligatory.

Al-Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan ibn Aban, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from 'Umar ibn Udhaynah, from Zurarah, from Abu Ja'far عليه السلام, that he was asked about a man who prayed without taharah, or forgot prayers and did not perform them, or slept through them, so he said: He should make it up when he remembers it, at whatever hour he remembers it, by night or by day. If the time of a salat enters and he has not completed what he had missed, then he should make up so long as he does not fear that the time of this present salat will pass; and this one has more right to its time, so he should perform it. Then when he has completed it, he should perform what he had missed from what has passed, and he should not perform even a single rak'ah of supererogatory prayer until he has completed making up the entire obligatory prayer.

Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Ya'qub ibn Shu'ayb, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: He said: I asked him about a man who sleeps through the morning prayer until the sun rises: should he pray when he wakes up, or should he wait until the sun has spread? He said: He should pray when he wakes up. I said: Should he perform the witr, or pray two rak'ahs? He said: Rather, he should begin with the obligatory prayer.

As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Faḍālah, from Ḥusayn ibn ʿUthmān, from Samāʿah, from Abī Baṣīr, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who slept through the salat (prayer) until the sun rose. He said: He should perform the two rakʿahs, then perform the morning salat (prayer).

From him, from al-Naḍr ibn Suwayd, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Sinān, from Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said: I heard him saying: Indeed, the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم slept, and his eyes overcame him, and he did not awaken until the heat of the sun troubled him. Then he awoke and performed two rakʿahs, then he performed the morning prayer, and he said: “O Bilāl, what is with you?” Bilāl said: “The One who caused you to sleep caused me to sleep, O Messenger of Allah.” He said: And he disliked remaining there, and said: “You slept in the valley of a shaytan.” So the proper way regarding these two reports is that we understand them as applying to one who intends to lead a people in prayer and is waiting for their gathering; in that case, it is permissible for him to begin with the two rakʿahs of nafilah, as the Prophet صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم did. But if he is alone, then that is not permissible for him in any situation.

The Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Abū al-Qāsim Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb, from a number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyād, from Muḥammad ibn Sinān, from Ibn Muskān, from Abū Baṣīr, who said: I asked him about a man who forgot the ẓuhr until the time of ʿaṣr entered. He said: He begins with the ẓuhr. Likewise with the prayers, one begins with the one that was forgotten, unless you fear that the time of the prayer will go out; then you begin with the one whose time you are presently in, then make up the one you forgot.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from al-Qasim ibn 'Urwah, from 'Ubayd ibn Zurarah, from his father, from Abi Ja'far عليه السلام, who said: If a salat (prayer) has passed you by and you remember it at the time of another, then if you know that, were you to perform the one that has passed you by, you would still be within the time of the other, then begin with the one that has passed you by. For Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: “Establish the salat (prayer) for My remembrance.” And if you know that, if you perform the one that has passed you by, the one after it would also pass you by, then begin with the one whose time you are in, and make up the other.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Ibn Sinan, from Ibn Muskan, from al-Halabi, who said: I asked him about a man who forgot to perform the first prayer until he had performed the 'Asr prayer. He said: Let him treat the prayer he performed as the first one, then let him begin the 'Asr prayer anew. He said: I said: What if he forgot both the first prayer and the 'Asr prayer together, then remembered that at sunset? He said: If he is still within a time in which he does not fear missing either of them, then let him perform Zuhr and then perform 'Asr. But if he fears that it will pass him by, then let him begin with 'Asr and not delay it so that it passes him by and both would then have been missed together. Rather, he should perform 'Asr within what remains of its time, then perform the first prayer immediately after it.

From him, from Faḍālah, from Ibn Muskān, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: If a man sleeps or forgets to perform the maghrib and the later ʿishaʾ prayer, then if he wakes before fajr with enough time to perform both of them, he should perform them both. But if he fears that one of them will escape him, then he should begin with the later ʿishaʾ. And if he wakes after fajr, then he should begin and perform the ṣubḥ prayer, then maghrib, then ʿishaʾ before sunrise.

From him, from Ḥammād, from Shuʿayb, from Abū Baṣīr, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: If a man sleeps and does not perform salat al-maghrib and al-ʿishāʾ al-ākhirah, or he forgets, then when he awakens before al-fajr with enough time to perform them both, he should perform them both. But if he fears that one of them will escape him, then he should begin with al-ʿishāʾ al-ākhirah. And if he awakens after al-fajr, then he should begin by performing al-fajr, then al-maghrib, then al-ʿishāʾ al-ākhirah before sunrise. But if he fears that the sun will rise and one of the two salats will escape him, then he should perform al-maghrib and leave al-ʿishāʾ al-ākhirah until the sun rises and its rays go away, then let him perform it.

As for what Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated from Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Faḍḍāl, from ʿAmr ibn Saʿīd al-Madāʾinī, from Muṣaddaq ibn Ṣadaqah, from ʿAmmār al-Sābāṭī, from Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who misses the Maghrib prayer until the time of ʿIshāʾ arrives. He said: If the time of ʿIshāʾ has arrived and he remembers that he owes the Maghrib prayer, then if he wishes he may begin with Maghrib, and if he wishes he may begin with ʿIshāʾ, then pray Maghrib after it. So this is an anomalous report, contrary to all the reports, because practice is based on what we have stated previously: that when the time is ample, one should begin with the missed prayer, and when the time is constrained, one begins with the current prayer. There is no time here in which a person is truly given a choice. It is possible that this report may be understood as indicating permissibility, while the earlier reports indicate merit and recommendation.

As for what Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb narrated from al-ʿAbbās, from Ismāʿīl ibn Hammām, from Abī al-Ḥasan عليه السلام, that he said: Regarding a man who delays the ẓuhr until the time of the ʿaṣr enters, then he begins with the ʿaṣr and then performs the ẓuhr. So the correct understanding of this report is that when the time of the ʿaṣr has become restricted, he begins with it and then performs the ẓuhr, according to what we have explained in detail.

As for what Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb narrated, from ʿAlī ibn Khālid, from Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Faḍḍāl, from ʿAmr ibn Saʿīd al-Madāʾinī, from Muṣaddaq ibn Ṣadaqah, from ʿAmmār al-Sābāṭī, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who sleeps through the fajr until the sun rises while he is on a journey—what should he do? Is it permissible for him to make it up during the day? He said: He should not make up, during the day, either a nafilah prayer or an obligatory prayer; it is not permissible for him, nor is it established for him. Rather, he should delay it and then make it up at night. So this is an anomalous report, which is not to be used in opposition to the reports that we have presented earlier, along with their accordance with the apparent meaning of the Book and the consensus of the Ummah.

Al-Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Abū al-Qāsim Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from his father, from Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allāh, from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn ibn Abī al-Khaṭṭāb, from Muḥammad ibn Bazīʿ al-ʿAdawī, from Abū al-Ḥasan ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAwn al-Shāmī, who said: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Yaʿfūr narrated to me from Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام concerning making up Salat al-Layl and al-Witr when a man misses them: should he make them up after Salat al-Fajr and after al-ʿAṣr? He said: There is no harm in that.

From him, from Musa ibn Ja'far, from Abi Ja'far, from Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Jabbar, from Maymun, from Muhammad ibn Farah, who said: I wrote to al-'Abd al-Salih عليه السلام asking him about certain مسائل, so he wrote back to me: Pray, after al-'Asr, whatever you wish of the nawafil, and pray, after al-Ghadah, whatever you wish of the nawafil.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn Umar al-Zayyat, from Jamil ibn Darrāj, who said: I asked Abā al-Ḥasan al-Awwal عليه السلام about making up salat al-layl after fajr until sunrise. He said: Yes, and after al-'asr until the night; for it is among the hidden secrets of the family of Muhammad.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from 'Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Sayf ibn 'Umayrah, from Sulayman ibn Harun, who said: I asked Abu al-Hasan عليه السلام about making up the prayer after al-'Asr. He said: Then make it up whenever you wish.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Fadalah ibn Ayyub, from Al-Husayn ibn Abi al-'Ala', from Abi 'Abdillah عليه السلام, who said: Make up the prayer of the day at whatever hour you wish, from the night or the day; all of that is the same.

From him, from Faḍālah, from ʿAbd Allah ibn Miskān, from Ibn Abī Yaʿfūr, who said: I heard Abā ʿAbd Allah عليه السلام say: The daytime prayer may be made up at whatever hour you wish, during the night or the day.
Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from 'Ali ibn Sayf, from Hassan ibn Mihran, who said: I asked Aba 'Abdillah عليه السلام about making up the supererogatory prayers. He said: Between sunrise and its setting.

As for what al-Tatari narrated from Muhammad ibn Abi Hamzah and Ali ibn Ribat, from Ibn Muskan, from Muhammad al-Halabi, from Abi Abdillah عليه السلام, who said: There is no salat after al-fajr until the sun rises, for the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم said: Indeed, the sun rises between the two horns of al-shaytan and sets between the two horns of al-shaytan. And he said: There is no salat after al-'asr until you perform al-maghrib.

From him, from Muḥammad ibn Miskīn, from Muʿāwiyah ibn ʿAmmār, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: There is no salat after al-ʿAṣr until you perform al-Maghrib, and there is no salat after al-Fajr until the sun rises. The proper way to understand these reports and others similar to them is one of two things: either that they are to be understood as taqiyyah, because they agree with the doctrines of the ʿāmmah; or that they are to be understood as indicating the dislikedness of beginning the nawāfil in these two times, even if that is not prohibited, because a concession has been narrated regarding the permissibility of beginning the nawāfil in these two times.

A group of our shaykhs said to me, from Abū al-Ḥusayn Muḥammad ibn Jaʿfar al-Asadī; and there came to him, among what came of the answers to his questions, from Muḥammad ibn ʿUthmān al-ʿAmrī, may Allah have mercy on him. As for what you asked about regarding salat (prayer) at the rising of the sun and at its setting: if it is as people say, that the sun rises between the two horns of al-Shayṭān and sets between the two horns of al-Shayṭān, then the nose of al-Shayṭān is not humbled by anything better than salat (prayer). So perform it, and humble the nose of al-Shayṭān. And that which indicates this detail that we have mentioned.

What Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā narrated from Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā, from Abū al-Ḥasan ʿAlī ibn Bilāl, who said: I wrote to him concerning making up the supererogatory prayer from the rising of dawn until the rising of the sun, and from after al-ʿAṣr until the sun sets. So he wrote: That is not permissible except for the one who is making it up; as for someone other than him, then no.

As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from Saʿd ibn Ismāʿīl, from his father Ismāʿīl ibn ʿĪsā, who said: I asked al-Riḍā عليه السلام about a man who performs the first prayer, then performs a supererogatory prayer, and the time of ʿaṣr comes upon him before he finishes his nāfilah: should he delay ʿaṣr until after his nāfilah, or perform the nāfilah after ʿaṣr, or postpone it until he performs it at the end of its time? He said: He should perform ʿaṣr and make up his nāfilah on another day. The correct way of understanding this report is that if he were to pray at the end of its time, he would have approached the setting of the sun, and that is a time in which prayer is disliked, as we have explained. This too is to be understood in accordance with what we mentioned regarding recommendation.

As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from al-Barqī, from Saʿd ibn Saʿd, from Abī al-Ḥasan al-Riḍā عليه السلام, he said: I asked him about a man who is in his house praying, while he thinks that night still remains upon him. Then another person enters through the door and says: 'Morning has come upon you.' Should he pray the witr or not, or should he repeat anything from the night prayer? He said: 'He repeats it if he performed it in the morning.' The meaning in this report is that he only made repetition obligatory upon him if he performed it in the morning, because once morning begins, the time of the obligatory prayer has become constrained, so it is not permissible for him to perform a supererogatory prayer. Thus, if he performed it, it would be upon him to repeat it, because he performed it outside its proper time, as we have explained; that clarifies it.

What Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥakam, from Sayf ibn ʿUmayrah, from Abū Bakr al-Ḥaḍramī, from Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad عليه السلام, who said: When the time for an obligatory salat (prayer) begins, then there is no supererogatory prayer. As for the manner of making up missed prayers, we have devoted a separate chapter to it immediately after this chapter.

ʿAlī ibn Mahziyār, from al-Ḥasan, from al-Naḍr, from Hishām ibn Sālim and Faḍālah, from Abān, all together from Sulaymān ibn Khālid, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about making up the witr after ẓuhr. He said: Make it up as witr always, just as it was missed. I said: Two witrs in one night? He said: Yes. Is not one of them a make-up?

From him, from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī, from ʿAlī ibn al-Nuʿmān and Muḥammad ibn Sinān and Faḍālah, from al-Ḥusayn, all together from Ibn Miskān, from Sulaymān ibn Khālid, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, concerning making up the witr; so he said: Make it up as witr, always.

From him, from al-Hasan, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Jamil ibn Darrāj, from Zurārah, from Abū Ja‘far عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about the witr that a man misses. He said: He should make up one witr always.
From him, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Mughīrah, who said: I asked Abā Ibrāhīm عليه السلام about a man who misses the witr. He said: He makes it up as witr, always.
