From him, from al-Ḥasan, from Faḍālah, from Ḥammād ibn ʿUthmān, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: I said: I reach the morning having missed the witr until the night; how should I make it up? He said: Like for like.

As for what was narrated by ʿAlī ibn Mahzīyār, from al-Ḥasan, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from ʿUmar ibn Udhaynah, from Zurārah, from al-Fuḍayl, who said: I heard Abā Jaʿfar عليه السلام say: He makes it up during the day, so long as the sun has not passed the zenith, as witr; then when the sun has passed the zenith, then two by two.

From him, from al-Hasan, from Fadalah, from Husayn ibn 'Uthman, from Sama'ah, from Abi Basir, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: The witr is three rak'ahs until the sun passes the meridian; then when it has passed, it is four rak'ahs.

From him, from al-Hasan, from Muhammad ibn Ziyad, from Kurdawayh al-Hamadani, who said: I asked Aba al-Hasan عليه السلام about making up the witr, and he said: Whatever is after zawal, then it is shaf‘, two rak‘ahs by two rak‘ahs. The correct approach regarding these reports is one of two possibilities. One of them is that we interpret them as referring to one who wants to make up the witr while sitting; in that case, it is appropriate that he pray two rak‘ahs in place of each rak‘ah, by way of what is more virtuous, though if he were to pray one rak‘ah in place of each rak‘ah while sitting, there would be nothing against him. What indicates that is: 6 — What al-Husayn ibn Sa‘id narrated from ‘Abd Allah ibn Bahr, from Hariz, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I asked Aba ‘Abd Allah عليه السلام about a man who becomes lazy or weak and so performs the supererogatory prayer sitting. He said: He doubles it, making two rak‘ahs count for one rak‘ah.

From him, from Faḍālah, from Ḥusayn, from Ibn Muskān, from al-Ḥasan ibn Ziyād al-Ṣayqal, who said: Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام said to me: When a man performs salat sitting while he is able to stand, then let him make it double. And that which indicates that it is permissible for him to make it up as witr, even if he makes it up after al-ẓuhr.

What Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Yaqṭīn, from his brother al-Ḥusayn, from ʿAlī ibn Yaqṭīn, who said: I asked Abā al-Ḥasan عليه السلام about a man who misses the witr during the night. He said: He should make it up as witr whenever he remembers, even if the sun has passed the meridian. And the second explanation regarding the previous reports is that it is directed toward one who is negligent regarding salat and deliberately abandons it, by way of sternness against him; that indicates this.

What was narrated by ʿAlī ibn Mahzīyār, from al-Ḥasan, from Ḥammād ibn ʿĪsā, from Ḥarīz, from Zurārah, who said: If you miss the witr of your night, then whenever you make it up on the following day before midday, you make it up as witr; and whenever you make it up at night, you make it up as witr; and whenever you make it up in the daytime after that day, you make it up as an even-numbered prayer, adding another rakʿah to it so that it becomes even. He said: I said to him, 'And why was it made even?' He said: 'As a punishment for his neglect of the witr.' As for that which indicates that when he prays sitting, it is permissible for him to perform one rakʿah by one rakʿah.

What al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad, from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ḥamzah, from Abī Baṣīr, from Abī Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said: I said to him: We discuss and say that whoever performs salat (prayer) while sitting without an illness, his salat is counted as two rakʿahs for one rakʿah, and two sajdahs for one sajdah. So he said: It is not like that; it is complete for you.

Al-Husayn ibn ʿUbayd Allah informed me, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Muhammad ibn ʿAli ibn Mahbub, from al-ʿAbbas, from ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Mughirah, from Ismaʿil ibn ʿAbbad, from Khirash, from some of our companions, from Abu ʿAbd Allah عليه السلام, who said: I said to him, “May I be made your ransom, these opponents against us say: when the sky is overcast upon us or it becomes dark over us, and we cannot recognize the sky, then we and you are equal in ijtihad.” So he said, “It is not as they say. When that happens, then let him perform salat toward four directions.”
Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Isma'il ibn 'Abbad, from Khirash, from some of our companions. The like of it.

As for what Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb narrated from Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from Ḥammād, from Ḥarīz, from Zurārah, who said: Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام said: Seeking one’s best judgment is always sufficient when it is not known where the direction of the qiblah is.

And from him, from Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā, from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn, from ʿUthmān ibn ʿĪsā, from Samāʿah, who said: I asked him about salat (prayer) at night and during the day when the sun, the moon, and the stars cannot be seen. He said: Exercise your judgment, and deliberately face the qiblah to the best of your ability.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from al-Hasan, from Zur'ah, from Sama'ah, who said: I asked him about salat (prayer) by night and day when neither the sun nor the moon nor the stars can be seen. He said: You exert your judgment and deliberately face the qiblah to the best of your ability. Thus, the proper way regarding these reports is that we understand them as applying to a state of necessity in which a person is unable to perform salat (prayer) toward four directions. In that case, informed estimation suffices for him; but if he is able, then he must perform salat (prayer) toward four directions.

ʿAlī ibn Mahziyār, from Faḍālah ibn Ayyūb, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī ʿAbdillāh, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: If you perform salat (prayer) while facing other than the qiblah, and it becomes clear to you that you performed salat (prayer) while facing other than the qiblah, and you are still within the time, then repeat it. But if the time has passed, then do not repeat it.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Hisham ibn Salim, from Sulayman ibn Khalid, who said: I said to Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام: A man is in an open barren land on a cloudy day, so he performs salat (prayer) facing other than the qiblah, then the sky clears and he comes to know that he had performed salat (prayer) facing other than the qiblah. What should he do? He said: If he is still within the time, then let him repeat his salat (prayer); but if the time has passed, then his ijtihad is sufficient for him.
Ali ibn al-Hasan al-Tatari, from Muhammad ibn Abi Hamzah, from Abd Allah ibn Muskan, from Sulayman ibn Khalid, from Abi Abd Allah عليه السلام. The like of it.

Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Mahbub, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Ya'qub ibn Yaqtin, who said: I asked Aba al-Hasan Musa عليه السلام about a man who prayed on a cloudy day facing other than the qiblah, then the sun rose while he was still within the time. Should he repeat the salat (prayer) if he had prayed facing other than the qiblah? And if he had sought the qiblah to the best of his effort, would his salat (prayer) suffice him? He said: He repeats whatever is still within its time; but when the time has passed, then there is no repetition upon him.

From him, from Aḥmad, from al-Ḥusayn, from Faḍālah, from Abān, from Zurārah, from Abī Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said: If you have prayed facing other than the qiblah, and it becomes clear to you before morning that you prayed facing other than the qiblah, then repeat your salat.

From him, from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn, from al-Ḥajjāl, from Thaʿlabah, from Muʿāwiyah ibn ʿAmmār, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: I said: A man rises from the salat (prayer), then after he has finished he looks and sees that he had deviated from the qiblah to the right or the left. He said: His salat (prayer) has passed as valid, and what lies between the east and the west is qiblah.

From him, from Aḥmad, from his father, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Mughīrah, from al-Qāsim ibn al-Walīd, who said: I asked him about a man for whom it became clear, while he was in the salat (prayer), that he was facing other than the qiblah. He said: He should turn to face it when that is established. But if he has already finished it, then he does not repeat it.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, said: I wrote to al-'Abd al-Salih عليه السلام: A man prays on a cloudy day in an open land, and he does not know the qiblah, so he prays. Then, when he finishes his salat, the sun appears to him, and he realizes that he had prayed toward other than the qiblah. Should his salat be counted, or should he repeat it? So he wrote: He should repeat it so long as the time has not passed him. Does he not know that Allah, Exalted is He, says—and His word is the truth—: “So wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah.”

As for what al-Tatari narrated from Muhammad ibn Ziyad, from Hammad, from Amr ibn Yahya, he said: I asked Aba Abdillah عليه السلام about a man who performed salat facing other than the qiblah, then the qiblah became clear to him while he had already entered the time of another salat. He said: He repeats it before performing this one whose time has entered.

From him, from Muḥammad ibn Ziyād, from Maʿmar ibn Yaḥyā, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about a man who had prayed toward other than the qiblah, then the qiblah became clear to him while the time of another salat had entered. He said: He should perform that prayer before he performs this one whose time has entered, unless he fears missing the one whose time has entered. So the proper way regarding these two reports is that we carry them upon the case that he had prayed facing directly away from the qiblah, for then repeating the salat is obligatory upon him whether the time remains or has expired. That is indicated by the following.

What Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb narrated from Aḥmad ibn Idrīs, from Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā, from Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Faḍḍāl, from ʿAmr ibn Saʿīd, from Muṣaddiq ibn Ṣadaqah, from ʿAmmār al-Sābāṭī, from Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, concerning: Regarding a man who prayed toward other than the qiblah, then realizes while he is in the salat, before he has finished his salat. He said: If he was facing within what is between the east and the west, then he should turn his face toward the qiblah when he realizes. But if he was facing toward the back of the qiblah, then he should break off, then turn his face toward the qiblah, then begin the salat.

My shaykh Abu 'Abd Allah informed me, from Abu al-Qasim Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Qulawayh, from his father, from Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah, from al-Hasan ibn 'Ali, from Ahmad ibn Hilal, from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from 'Abd Allah ibn Sinan, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: There is no problem in performing wudu (ablution) with used water. And he said: the water with which a garment is washed, or with which a man performs ghusl from janabah, it is not permissible that wudu be performed from it, and similar things to it. But as for the water with which a man performs wudu, so he washes his face and his hand in a clean vessel, then there is no problem for another person to take it and perform wudu with it.

As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Ibn Sinān, from Ibn Muskān, who said: A trustworthy companion of mine narrated to me that he asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about a man who comes upon a small amount of water on the road and wishes to perform ghusl, while he has no vessel with him, and the water is in a hollow; if he performs ghusl with it, the water from his washing returns into the water. How should he proceed? He عليه السلام said: He should sprinkle with one handful in front of him, one handful behind him, one handful to his right, and one handful to his left, then perform ghusl. So this does not contradict the earlier report, because it is possible that what is meant by ghusl here is other than ghusl al-janābah, among the recommended ghusls. For what is not permitted is the use of water with which ghusl has been performed when the ghusl is for janābah; but if it is recommended, then that takes the same ruling as wudu (ablution). It is also possible that this is specific to a state of necessity, and it must also be specific to one upon whose body there is nothing of najāsah, because if there were najāsah there, the water would become najis and its use would not be permitted in any case. And that which indicates that it is specifically for the state of necessity...

What Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from Mūsā ibn al-Qāsim al-Bajalī and Abī Qatādah, from ʿAlī ibn Jaʿfar, from Abī al-Ḥasan al-Awwal عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who comes upon water in a channel or a pond: may he perform ghusl from janabah with it, or perform wudu from it for salat, if he cannot find any other water, while the water does not amount to a saʿ for janabah nor a mudd for wudu, and it is scattered? So what should he do, while he fears that wild beasts may have drunk from it? He said: If his hand is clean, then let him take a handful of water with one hand and sprinkle it behind him, and a handful in front of him, and a handful to his right, and a handful to his left. If he fears that it will not suffice him, he should wash his head three times, then wipe his skin with his hand, for that will suffice him. And if it is wudu, he should wash his face and wipe his hand over his forearms, his head, and his feet. And if the water is scattered and he is able to gather it, then he should do so; otherwise, he should perform ghusl from this and from that. So if it is in one place and it is a small amount that does not suffice him for his ghusl, there is no blame upon him if he performs ghusl and returns the water into it, for that will suffice him.

Abu al-Husayn ibn Abi Jid al-Qummi informed me, from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn al-Walid, from al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan ibn Aban, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Fadalah, from Mu'awiyah ibn 'Ammar, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: Do not perform the obligatory prayer in the Ka'bah, for the Prophet صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم did not enter the Ka'bah during any hajj or 'umrah; rather, he entered it on the Day of the Conquest, the Conquest of Makkah, and he prayed two rak'ahs between the two pillars, and Usamah ibn Zayd was with him.
From him, from Ṣafwān and Faḍālah, from al-ʿAlāʾ, from Muḥammad, from one of the two عليهما السلام, who said: The obligatory salat (prayer) is not valid inside the interior of the Kaʿbah.

As for what al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from al-Hasan ibn 'Ali ibn Faddal, from Yunus ibn Ya'qub, who said: I said to Abi 'Abdillah عليه السلام: The obligatory salat (prayer) has become due while I am inside the Ka'bah; should I perform salat (prayer) in it? He said: Perform salat (prayer). So this report does not conflict with the first two reports, because the proper way regarding this report is that we carry it upon the state of necessity in which a person is unable to leave it. At that point, salat (prayer) in it is permissible for him, though that is disliked and not prohibited. This was made explicit in his saying, “The obligatory salat (prayer) is not proper inside the interior of the Ka'bah,” and that is explicit in indicating dislike. The first report, even if its wording is the wording of prohibition, its meaning is dislike, as indicated by what he explained in the second report and what has come concerning its permissibility in the third report.

Al-Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan ibn Aban, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Hammad, from Mu'awiyah ibn Wahb or Ibn 'Ammar, from al-Sabbah ibn Sayabah, who said: Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام said to me: Do not omit the adhan in any of the prayers. But if you do omit it, then do not omit it in Maghrib and Fajr, for there is no shortening in them.

From him, from Abū al-Qāsim Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb, from Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad, from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ḥamzah, from Abū Baṣīr, from one of the two of them عليه السلام, who said: I asked him: “Is a single adhan sufficient?” He said: “If you pray in congregation, nothing suffices except an adhan and an iqamah. But if you are alone and hastening to something that you fear may escape you, an iqamah suffices for you, except in the fajr and maghrib prayers, for it is appropriate that you give the adhan in them both and perform the iqamah, because shortening is not done in them as it is done in the rest of the prayers.”

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from al-Hasan, from Zur'ah, from Sama'ah, who said: Abu 'Abdillah عليه السلام said: The dawn prayer and the maghrib prayer are not performed except with adhan and iqamah. Concession was given in the rest of the prayers for iqamah alone, though the adhan is more excellent.
From him, from al-Naḍr ibn Suwayd, from Ibn Sinān, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: In the salat, one iqamah suffices for you, except in the dawn prayer and the maghrib prayer.

As for what Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Jaʿfar ibn Bashir, from ʿUmar ibn Yazid, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbd Allah عليه السلام about the iqamah without adhan in the Maghrib prayer, and he said: There is no harm in it, but I do not like that you make a habit of that. So this does not contradict what we have presented earlier, because it is only permissible for him to suffice with the iqamah in these prayers when there is some incidental circumstance or impediment. His statement, 'I do not like that you make a habit of that,' indicates that what is preferable is to perform it.

As for what Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb narrated from Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī, from ʿAmr ibn Saʿīd, from Muṣaddiq ibn Ṣadaqah, from ʿAmmār al-Sābāṭī, who said: I heard Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام saying: The sick person must give the adhān and iqāmah when he intends salat, even within himself if he is unable to speak them. He was asked: And if he is in severe pain? He said: There is no alternative but that he give the adhān and iqāmah, because there is no salat except with adhān and iqāmah. So the correct understanding of this report is the emphasis of recommendation and encouragement toward the greatness of the reward in it, not that what is intended by it is obligation.

Al-Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan ibn Aban, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Fadalah, from al-Husayn ibn 'Uthman, from 'Amr ibn Abi Nasr, who said: I said to Abi 'Abdillah عليه السلام: May a man speak during the adhan? He said: There is no harm. I said: During the iqamah? He said: No.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from Salih ibn 'Uqbah, from Abi Harun al-Makfuf, who said: Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام said: O Aba Harun, the iqamah is part of the salat (prayer), so when you pronounce the iqamah, do not speak and do not gesture with your hand.

Al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from Ḥammād ibn ʿĪsā, from Ḥarīz, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, who said: Abu ʿAbdillah عليه السلام said: Do not speak when you have commenced the iqamah for the salat, for if you speak, you must repeat the iqamah.

As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Muḥammad ibn Sinān, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muskān, from Muḥammad al-Ḥalabī, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام about a man speaking during his adhan or during his iqamah, and he said: There is no harm in it.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Ja'far ibn Bashir, from Hammad ibn 'Uthman, who said: I asked Aba 'Abdillah عليه السلام about a man who speaks after he has pronounced the iqamah for the salat (prayer). He said: Yes.

Ja'far ibn Bashir narrated from al-Husayn ibn Shihab, who said: I heard Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام saying: There is no harm in a man speaking while he is giving the iqamah for salat (prayer), and after he gives it as well, if he wishes. So the proper way regarding these reports is that we understand them to mean that it is permissible to speak about something connected to the rulings of salat (prayer), such as appointing an Imam or straightening a row, and that this is before he says, "Qad qāmati al-salāh." Once he says that, speaking becomes forbidden except for what has been exempted, and this is indicated by that.

What al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Fadalah, from Husayn ibn 'Uthman, from Ibn Miskan, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, who said: I asked Aba 'Abdillah عليه السلام about a man speaking during the iqamah. He said: Yes. But when the mu'adhdhin says, “The salat has been established,” then speech becomes forbidden for the people of the mosque, unless they have gathered from different places and do not have an Imam; then there is no harm in some of them saying to another, “Go forward, O so-and-so.”

From him, from al-Ḥasan, from Zur‘ah, from Samā‘ah, who said: Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام said: When the mu’adhdhin stands for the salat, speech has become haram, unless it is that the people do not have an Imam known for them.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Hammad, from Rib'i, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I said to Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام: May a man recite the adhan while he is sitting? He said: Yes; but he should not recite the iqamah except while he is standing.

From him, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from ʿAbd Ṣāliḥ عليه السلام, who said: A man may give the adhan while he is sitting, but he should not give the iqamah except while standing. And he said: You may give the adhan while riding, but do not give the iqamah except while you are on the ground.

As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā narrated from Muḥammad ibn Sinān, from Abī Khālid, from Ḥumrān, who said: I asked Abā Jaʿfar عليه السلام about giving the adhān while seated. He said: No one gives the adhān while seated except a rider or a sick person. Thus, the proper approach regarding this report is that we carry it upon a kind of recommendation rather than obligation.

Al-Husayn ibn Ubayd Allah informed me, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub, from Salamah ibn al-Khattab, from Abi Jamilah, from Ibn Bukayr, from Zurarah, from Abi Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: I said to him: A man forgets the adhan and the iqamah until he says the takbir. He said: He continues with his salat and does not repeat.

From him, from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn, from Jaʿfar ibn Bashīr, from Nuʿmān al-Rāzī, who said: I heard Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, and Abū ʿUbaydah al-Ḥadhdhāʾ asked him about the case of a man who forgot to give the adhān and iqāmah until he pronounced the takbīr and entered into the salat (prayer). He said: If he had entered the mosque with the intention that he would give the adhān and the iqāmah, then he should continue in his salat (prayer) and not turn away.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Fudayl, from Abi al-Sabbah, from Abi 'Abdillah عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who forgot the adhan until he had prayed. He said: He does not repeat.

Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub narrated from Ali ibn al-Sindi, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Shu'ayb ibn Ya'qub, from Abu Basir, from Abu Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who forgot to pronounce the iqamah for the salat (prayer) until he had finished; should he repeat his salat (prayer)? He said: He does not repeat it, and he should not return to doing the like of it.

As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Yaqṭīn, from his brother al-Ḥusayn, from ʿAlī ibn Yaqṭīn, who said: I asked Abā al-Ḥasan عليه السلام about a man who forgets to make the iqāmah for the salat (prayer) after he has already begun the salat (prayer). He said: If he has finished his salat (prayer), then his salat (prayer) is complete; and if he has not finished his salat (prayer), then let him repeat. So this report is to be understood as referring to a type of recommendation.

As for what Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb narrated from Muḥammad ibn Ismāʿīl, from al-Faḍl ibn Shādhān, from Ṣafwān, from al-ʿAlāʾ ibn Razīn, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, that he said: Regarding a man who forgets the adhān and the iqāmah until he has entered into the salat (prayer), he said: If he remembers before he recites, then let him send blessings upon the Prophet صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم; and if he has already recited, then let him complete his salat (prayer).

Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from ʿAlī ibn al-Nuʿmān, from Saʿīd al-Aʿraj and Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Ḥammād, from al-Ḥalabī, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: If you begin the salat (prayer) and forget to give the adhan and iqamah, then remember before you perform ruku', turn away, give the adhan and iqamah, and begin the salat (prayer). But if you have already performed ruku', then complete your salat (prayer).

Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Mahbub narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Ishaq ibn Adam, from Abu al-'Abbas al-Fadl ibn Hassan al-Dalani, from Zakariyya ibn Adam, who said: I said to Abu al-Hasan al-Rida عليه السلام, “May I be made your ransom, I was in my salat (prayer), and in the second rak'ah, while I was reciting, I remembered that I had not said the iqamah, so what should I do?” He عليه السلام said: “Pause at the point of your recitation and say: ‘Qad qamati al-salat, qad qamati al-salat.’” Then continue with your recitation and your salat (prayer), and your salat has been completed.”

From him, from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn, from Ṣafwān, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Abī al-ʿAlāʾ, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who begins his obligatory salat (prayer), then remembers that he did not recite the iqamah. He said: If he remembers that he did not recite the iqamah before he has begun reciting, then let him send salutations upon the Prophet صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم, then recite the iqamah and perform the salat (prayer). But if he remembers after he has recited part of the surah, then let him continue with his salat (prayer). The proper way regarding these reports as well is that we interpret them as indicating a kind of recommendation, just as we interpreted the first report in that manner, so that the reports do not conflict; and that is indicated by what follows.

What Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Ja'far ibn Bashir, from Hammad ibn 'Uthman, from 'Ubayd ibn Zurarah, from his father, who said: I asked Aba Ja'far عليه السلام about a man who forgot the adhan and the iqamah until he had entered into the salat. He said: Let him continue in his salat, for the adhan is only a sunnah (prophetic tradition).

From him, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn Abī Naṣr, from Dāwūd ibn Sirḥān, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, concerning: A man forgot the adhān and the iqāmah until he had entered into the salat (prayer). He said: There is nothing upon him.

Al-Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Abū al-Qāsim Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb, from ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā ibn ʿUbayd, from Abān ibn ʿUthmān, from Ismāʿīl al-Juʿfī, who said: I heard Abā Jaʿfar عليه السلام say: The adhān and the iqāmah are thirty-five phrases. He counted that with his hand one by one: the adhān is eighteen phrases, and the iqāmah is seventeen phrases.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from 'Abd Allah ibn Sinan, who said: I asked Aba 'Abd Allah عليه السلام about the adhan, and he said: You say: Allah is greater, Allah is greater. I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, I bear witness that there is no god but Allah. I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم, I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم. Come to salat (prayer), come to salat (prayer). Come to success, come to success. Come to the best of deeds, come to the best of deeds. Allah is greater, Allah is greater. There is no god but Allah, there is no god but Allah.

Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub narrated from Ali ibn al-Sindi, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Umar ibn Udhaynah, from Zurarah and al-Fudayl ibn Yasar, from Abu Ja'far عليه السلام, who said: When the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم was taken on the Night Journey and reached al-Bayt al-Ma'mur, the time of salat came. Jibra'il عليه السلام gave the adhan and the iqamah, then the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم stepped forward, and the angels and the prophets formed rows behind the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم. He said: We asked him, 'How did he give the adhan?' He said: 'Allahu Akbar, Allahu Akbar. I testify that there is no god but Allah, I testify that there is no god but Allah. I testify that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم, I testify that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم. Hayya 'ala al-salat, hayya 'ala al-salat. Hayya 'ala al-falah, hayya 'ala al-falah. Hayya 'ala khayr al-'amal, hayya 'ala khayr al-'amal. Allahu Akbar, Allahu Akbar. There is no god but Allah, there is no god but Allah.' And the iqamah is like it, except that in it there is 'Qad qamat al-salat, qad qamat al-salat' between 'Hayya 'ala khayr al-'amal, hayya 'ala khayr al-'amal' and 'Allahu Akbar, Allahu Akbar.' So the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم instructed Bilal to use it, and he continued to call the adhan with it until the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم passed away. And from him, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn, from Fadalah, from Sayf ibn Umayrah, from Abu Bakr al-Hadrami, from Abu Abdillah عليه السلام, and Kulayb al-Asadi, from Abu Abdillah عليه السلام: He recounted to them the adhan and the iqamah, and said: 'Allahu Akbar, Allahu Akbar, Allahu Akbar, Allahu Akbar. I testify that there is no god but Allah, I testify that there is no god but Allah. I testify that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم, I testify that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم. Hayya 'ala al-salat, hayya 'ala al-salat. Hayya 'ala al-falah, hayya 'ala al-falah. Hayya 'ala khayr al-'amal, hayya 'ala khayr al-'amal. Allahu Akbar, Allahu Akbar. There is no god but Allah, there is no god but Allah.' And the iqamah is likewise.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Fadalah, from Hammad ibn 'Uthman, from Ishaq ibn 'Ammar, from al-Mu'alla ibn Khunays, who said: I heard Aba 'Abdillah عليه السلام giving the adhan, and he said: Allah is greatest, Allah is greatest, Allah is greatest, Allah is greatest. I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, I bear witness that there is no god but Allah. I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم, I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم. Come to salat (prayer), come to salat (prayer). Come to success, come to success. Come to the best of deeds, come to the best of deeds—until he completed the adhan. And he said at its end: Allah is greatest, Allah is greatest; there is no god but Allah, there is no god but Allah. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: As for the first two hadiths, although they include the mention of 'Allahu Akbar' two times at the beginning of the adhan, it is possible that he only limited himself to that because he intended only to make the questioner understand how to pronounce it, while it was already known to him that it is not permissible to suffice with that short of four times. And that which clarifies what we have mentioned is...

What Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb narrated from Muḥammad ibn Ismāʿīl, from al-Faḍl ibn Shādhān, from Ḥammād ibn ʿĪsā, from Ḥarīz, from Zurārah, from Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said: He said: O Zurārah, you begin the adhān with four takbīrs, and you conclude it with two takbīrs and two tahlīls.
As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Faḍālah, from Muʿāwiyah ibn Wahb, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, he said: The adhān is in pairs, and the iqāmah is one by one.

And among what Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from Faḍālah ibn Ayyūb, from Sayf ibn ʿAmīrah and Ṣafwān ibn Yaḥyā, from ʿAbd Allah ibn Sinān, from Abī ʿAbd Allah عليه السلام, who said: The iqamah is once, once, except for the phrase “Allah is the Greatest,” for it is twice. So the explanation regarding these two reports is that they are a form of taqiyyah, because they agree with the doctrines of some of the general populace. And it is possible that the basis in them may be in a state of necessity and haste; and that which reveals what we have mentioned...

What Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from Faḍālah, from al-ʿAlāʾ, from Abū ʿUbaydah al-Ḥadhdhāʾ, who said: I saw Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام pronouncing the takbīr one by one, so I said to him: “Why do you pronounce the takbīr one by one?” He said: “There is no harm in it when you are in haste in the adhan.”
Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Ibn Abi Najran, from Safwan ibn Mihran al-Jammal, who said: I heard Aba Abdillah عليه السلام saying: The adhan is in pairs, in pairs, and the iqamah is in pairs, in pairs.

And from him, from Faḍālah, from Ḥusayn ibn ʿUthmān, from Ibn Miskān, from Yazīd, the client of al-Ḥakam, from the one who narrated to him, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: I heard him saying: That I pronounce the iqāmah two by two is more beloved to me than that I give the adhān and the iqāmah one by one. 12—Al-Ḥusayn, from al-Qāsim ibn ʿUrwah, from Burayd ibn Muʿāwiyah, from Abī Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said: The adhān is shortened during travel just as the salat (prayer) is shortened; and the adhān is one by one, and the iqāmah is one by one.

Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Ja'far ibn Bashir, from Nu'man al-Razi, who said: I heard Aba 'Abd Allah عليه السلام saying: It suffices you in the iqamah to say the phrases once each during travel.

The call and the tathwib in the adhan are from the sunnah (prophetic tradition). As for what Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Mahbub narrated from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan, from al-Husayn, from Hammad ibn 'Isa, from Shu'ayb ibn Ya'qub, from Abi Basir, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said:

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Fadalah, from al-'Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far عليه السلام, who said: My father used to call out in his house, 'al-salat is better than sleep,' and if you were to repeat that, there would be no harm in it. And whatever resembles these two reports among that which includes mention of these expressions, they are to be understood as taqiyyah, due to the consensus of the sect upon leaving action by them; and that is also indicated by...

What al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Fadalah, from Hammad ibn 'Isa, from Mu'awiyah ibn Wahb, who said: I asked Abā 'Abdillāh عليه السلام about the tathwīb that takes place between the adhan and the iqamah, so he said: We do not recognize it.

Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Mahbub narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Najran, from Hammad ibn 'Isa, from Hariz, from Zurarah, who said: Abu Ja'far عليه السلام said to me: O Zurarah, you begin the adhan with four takbirs, and you end it with two takbirs and two tahlils. And if you wish, you may add in the tathwib: “Hayya 'ala al-falah” in place of “al-salatu khayrun min al-nawm.” For if this phrase were a prescribed sunnah, it would not have been permitted for him to repeat some expressions and to depart from them. Moreover, repeating the wording is only permissible when he intends by it to alert someone else to the salat, or to wait for another, and what resembles that clarifies what we have mentioned.

What Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb narrated from Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from Ibn Maḥbūb, from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ḥamzah, from Abū Baṣīr, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: If a muʾadhdhin were to repeat in the two shahadahs, and in ḥayya ʿalā al-salat or ḥayya ʿalā al-falāḥ, two times, three times, or more than that, if by it he only intends the group of people so as to gather them, there would be no harm in it.

Al-Husayn ibn ʿUbayd Allah informed me, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Muhammad ibn ʿAli ibn Mahbub, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from al-Hasan ibn ʿAli ibn Yusuf, from Sayf ibn ʿAmirah, from some of our companions, from Abi ʿAbd Allah عليه السلام, who said: Between every two calls there is a sitting, except for al-Maghrib, for indeed between them there is only a breath.

As for what Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Muhammad ibn ʿIsa ibn ʿUbayd, from Saʿdan ibn Muslim, from Ishaq al-Jariri, from Abu ʿAbd Allah عليه السلام, who said: Whoever sits in the period between the adhan of Maghrib and the iqamah is like one struggling in his own blood in the way of Allah. So the correct way to reconcile these reports is that if it is the beginning of the time, it is permissible for him to separate the two with a sitting; but if the time becomes constrained, one breath suffices for that.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id informed me, from Fadalah, from al-'Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abi Ja'far عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about one who does not recite Fatihat al-Kitab in his salat; he said: There is no salat for him except with its recitation, whether aloud or quietly. I said: Which of the two is more beloved to you, if he is fearful or in haste: that he recite a surah or Fatihat al-Kitab? He said: Fatihat al-Kitab.

As for what al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from al-Nadr, from 'Abd Allah ibn Sinan, who said: Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام said: Allah, Most High, has made obligatory in the salat (prayer) the ruku' (bowing) and the sujud (prostration). Do you not see that if a man were to enter Islam and not be able to recite the Qur'an well, it would suffice him to say the takbir, perform tasbih, and pray? Thus, the proper way regarding this report is that we interpret it as applying to one who does not recite Fatihat al-Kitab well, in accordance with what it contains. And his statement, "Allah has made obligatory in the salat (prayer) the ruku' (bowing) and the sujud (prostration)," means an obligation such that if he leaves them deliberately or forgetfully, he must repeat the salat (prayer), because they are two pillars. The recitation is not like that, because one who forgets the recitation until he has entered into ruku' (bowing) is not required to repeat the salat (prayer). So the difference between them is from this perspective.

Al-Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan ibn Aban, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Najran, from Safwan, who said: I prayed behind Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام for several days, and he would recite in Fatihat al-Kitab: Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim. Then when it was a prayer in which the recitation is not done aloud, he would recite Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim aloud, and keep the rest lower.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from 'Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from Yunus, from Mu'awiyah ibn 'Ammar, who said: I said to Abī 'Abdillāh عليه السلام: When I stand for salat (prayer), do I recite “In the Name of Allah, the All-beneficent, the All-merciful” in Fātiḥat al-Kitāb? He said: Yes. I said: Then when I have recited Fātiḥat al-Kitāb, do I recite “In the Name of Allah, the All-beneficent, the All-merciful” along with the surah? He said: Yes.

And from him, from Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from ʿAlī ibn Mahzīyār, from Yaḥyā ibn Abī ʿImrān al-Hamadhānī, who said: I wrote to Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام: May I be made your ransom, what do you say regarding a man who begins with Bismillāh al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm in his salat only in Umm al-Kitāb, then when he proceeds to other than Umm al-Kitāb from the surah, he leaves it? Al-ʿAyyāshī said: There is no harm in that. So he wrote in his own hand: He must repeat it twice, despite his objection — meaning al-ʿAyyāshī.

Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Mahbub narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Muhammad ibn Hammad ibn Zayd, from 'Abd Allah ibn Yahya al-Kahili, who said: Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام led us in prayer in the mosque of Banu Kahil. He recited Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim aloud twice, performed qunut in the fajr prayer, and gave one taslim toward the direction of the qiblah.

As for what was narrated by Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Mahbub, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Safwan, from 'Abd Allah ibn Bukayr, from Mismā' al-Basri, who said: I prayed with Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, and he recited: In the Name of Allah, the All-beneficent, the All-merciful, al-Hamdu lillahi Rabb al-'Alamin. Then he recited the surah after al-Hamd and did not recite Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim. Then he stood in the second rak'ah and recited al-Hamd and did not recite Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim. Then he recited another surah. So this report does not contradict the reports that we have presented earlier, because it contains the account of an action. It is possible that Mismā' did not hear Aba 'Abd Allah عليه السلام reciting Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim due to a distance between him and the Imam, and it is also possible that he only omitted it due to a kind of taqiyyah and necessity.

As for what Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb narrated from ʿAlī ibn al-Sindī, from Ḥammād, from Ḥarīz, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about a man who is acting as an Imam and begins with al-Ḥamd, and does not say Bismillāh al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm. He said: It does not harm him, and there is no problem in that. The correct way regarding it is that we understand it as applying to the state of taqiyyah, not the state of choice; that is indicated by this.

What Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah narrated from Ahmad and Muhammad, from al-'Abbas ibn Ma'ruf, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Abi Hariz Zakariyya ibn Idris al-Qummi, who said: I asked Abā al-Ḥasan al-Awwal عليه السلام about a man who leads people in prayer while they dislike that he recite aloud, 'In the Name of Allah, the All-beneficent, the All-merciful.' He said: 'He should not recite it aloud.'

As for what Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Abi ʿUmayr, from Hammad ibn ʿUthman, from ʿUbayd Allah ibn ʿAli al-Halabi; and al-Husayn ibn Saʿid, from ʿAli ibn al-Nuʿman and Muhammad ibn Sinan and ʿAbd Allah ibn Miskan, from Muhammad ibn ʿAli al-Halabi, from Abi ʿAbd Allah عليه السلام, that the two of them asked him about one who recites بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمٰنِ الرَّحِيمِ when he wants to recite Fatihat al-Kitab, and he said: He may recite it for them, if he wishes, quietly, and if he wishes, aloud. He said: Then does he recite it with the other surah? He said: No. Thus, the proper way to understand this report is what we stated regarding the first report, namely interpreting it in light of taqiyyah. It is also possible that what is meant is one who is in a supererogatory salat and wishes to recite part of a surah; in that case it is permissible for him not to recite بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمٰنِ الرَّحِيمِ. This clarifies what we have mentioned.

What Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from Faḍālah ibn Ayyūb, from Abān ibn ʿUthmān, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, from Abī Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who begins the recitation in the salat (prayer): should he recite Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim? He said: Yes. When he begins the salat (prayer), then let him say it at the beginning of what he starts, then that suffices him for what comes after that.

Hariz narrated from Zurarah, from Abu Ja'far عليه السلام, concerning: A man who recited aloud where it is not appropriate to recite aloud, or recited quietly where it is not appropriate to recite quietly — he said: whichever of the two he did deliberately, then he has invalidated his salat (prayer), and repetition is upon him. But if he did that forgetfully, absentmindedly, or without knowing, then there is nothing upon him, and his salat (prayer) is complete.

As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from Mūsā ibn al-Qāsim, from ʿAlī ibn Jaʿfar, from his brother Mūsā عليه السلام, he said: I asked him about a man who performs the obligatory prayer in which the recitation is done aloud: is it required of him not to recite aloud? He said: If he wishes, he may recite aloud, and if he wishes, he may refrain from doing so. So this report is in agreement with the generality, and we do not act upon it; rather, practice is based on the first report.

Al-Husayn ibn 'Ubayd Allah informed me, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Yahya, from his father, from Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Mahbub, from Musa ibn 'Umar, from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan al-Maythami, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, from his grandfather, who said: I asked Aba 'Abd Allah عليه السلام about a well into which a mouse or some other animal falls and dies, then dough is kneaded from its water: may that bread be eaten? He said: If the fire has touched it, then there is no problem in eating it.

From him, from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn, from Muḥammad ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from one who narrated it, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, concerning: Regarding dough that was kneaded and baked, then it became known that there was carrion in the water in it, he said: There is no harm; the fire has consumed what was in it.

As for what was narrated by Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb, from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from one of our companions—and I do not think him to be anyone but Ḥafṣ ibn al-Bakhtarī—who said: It was said to Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام regarding dough kneaded with impure water: what should be done with it? He said: It should be sold to one who deems eating carrion permissible.

From him, from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from some of our companions, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: It should be buried and not sold. The proper way regarding these two reports is that we carry them upon a kind of recommendation. It is also possible that what is intended by the two reports is water whose one of whose qualities has changed, while the first two reports concern well-water, whose ruling is not that, and which can be purified by drawing out water, because that is a lighter impurity than water changed by najasah.

Al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿUbayd Allah informed me, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā, from his father, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb, from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn, from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Faḍḍāl, from some of our companions, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: The sunnah (prophetic tradition) regarding the salat (prayer) of the day is reciting quietly, and the sunnah (prophetic tradition) regarding the salat (prayer) of the night is reciting aloud.

As for what Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb narrated from ʿAlī ibn al-Sindī, from ʿUthmān ibn ʿĪsā, from Samāʿah, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, he said: I asked him about a man: should he recite aloud in voluntary prayer during the day? He said: Yes. The proper way to reconcile between the two is that we carry the first narration upon merit and recommendation, not obligation and requirement, and the other narration upon permissibility and the lifting of prohibition.

Al-Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Abū al-Qāsim Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb, from Aḥmad ibn Idrīs, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd, from Sayf ibn ʿUmayrah, from Manṣūr ibn Ḥāzim, who said: Abū ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام said: “Do not recite in the obligatory prayer less than one surah, nor more than that.”

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Safwan, from al-'Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from one of the two of them عليهما السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who recites two surahs in one rak'ah, so he said: For every rak'ah there is one surah.

As for what Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from ʿAli ibn Riʾab, from Abi ʿAbd Allah عليه السلام, who said: I heard him saying: Indeed, Fatihat al-Kitab alone is sufficient in the obligatory prayer. So the proper way regarding this report is that we interpret it as applying to a state of necessity, not to a state of choice; that is indicated by what follows.

What al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Muḥammad ibn Sinān, from Ibn Muskān, from al-Ḥasan al-Ṣayqal, who said: I said to Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام: Is it sufficient for me to recite in the obligatory prayer Fātiḥat al-Kitāb alone, if I am in haste or something causes me to hurry? He said: There is no harm in it.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from 'Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from Yunus, from 'Abd Allah ibn Sinan, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: It is permissible for the sick person to recite in the obligatory prayer only Fatihat al-Kitab, and it is permissible for the healthy person in making up the supererogatory prayer by night and day.

Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Hammad ibn 'Uthman, from 'Ubayd Allah ibn 'Ali al-Halabi, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: There is no harm in a man reciting in the obligatory prayer only Fatihat al-Kitab in the first two rak'ahs when a need has pressed him or something occurs.

As for what Saʿd narrated from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from al-ʿAbbās ibn Maʿrūf, from Ṣafwān ibn Yaḥyā, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muskān, from al-Ḥasan ibn al-Sirrī, from ʿUmar ibn Yazīd, who said: I said to Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام: May a man recite the same surah in the two rakʿahs of the obligatory prayer? He said: There is no harm, if it is more than three verses. The proper way concerning this report is that we understand it to mean that it is permissible for him to repeat it in the second rakʿah without dividing it, and that is when he does not recite well any other than it. But if he recites other than it well, then that is disliked. That which indicates this is as follows.

What Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb narrated from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from Mūsā ibn al-Qāsim, from ʿAlī ibn Jaʿfar, from his brother Mūsā ibn Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who recites one single surah in the two rakʿahs of the obligatory prayer while he is able to recite other than it. If he does that, what is upon him? He said: If he is able to recite other than it, then he should not do so; but if he is not able to recite other than it, then there is no harm.

As for what Saʿd narrated from Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā, from Yāsīn al-Ḍarīr, from Ḥarīz ibn ʿAbd Allāh, from Abī Baṣīr, from Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, that he was asked about a surah with which a man prays in the two rakʿahs of the obligatory prayer. He said: Yes; if it is six verses, he may recite half of it in the first rakʿah and the other half in the second rakʿah. So this report is to be understood as applying to the state of taqiyyah, not to the state of choice; that is indicated by what follows.

What al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Muḥammad ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Abān ibn ʿUthmān, from Ismāʿīl ibn al-Faḍl, who said: Abū ʿAbdillāh or Abū Jaʿfar, peace be upon him, led us in prayer, and he recited Sūrat al-Fātiḥah and the end of Sūrat al-Māʾidah. Then when he gave salām, he turned toward us and said: Indeed, I only intended to teach you.

As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from al-Barqī, from Saʿd ibn Saʿd al-Ashʿarī, from Abī al-Ḥasan al-Riḍā عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who recited al-Ḥamd and half of a surah in one rakʿah: would it suffice him in the second that he not recite al-Ḥamd and instead recite what remained of the surah? He said: He should recite al-Ḥamd, then recite what remained of the surah. So the proper way regarding this report is that we understand it as applying to supererogatory prayers rather than the obligatory prayers; that is indicated by what follows.

What Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Yaqṭīn, from his brother al-Ḥusayn, from ʿAlī ibn Yaqṭīn, who said: I asked Abā al-Ḥasan عليه السلام about dividing the surah, and he said: I dislike it, but there is no problem with it in the supererogatory prayer.

The Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from his father, from al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Ḥasan ibn Abān, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from al-Qarawī, from Abān, from ʿUmar ibn Yazīd, who said: I said to Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام: May I recite two surahs in one rakʿah? He said: Yes. I said: Is it not said, “Give every surah its due of bowing and prostration”? He said: That is in the obligatory prayer; but as for the supererogatory prayer, there is no harm in it.

Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Mahbub narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Safwan, from 'Abd Allah ibn Bukayr, from Zurarah, who said: Abu Ja'far عليه السلام said: It is only disliked to combine two surahs in the obligatory prayer; as for the supererogatory prayer, there is no harm in it.

As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Yaqṭīn, from his brother al-Ḥusayn, from ʿAlī ibn Yaqṭīn, who said: I asked Abū al-Ḥasan عليه السلام about combining two surahs in the obligatory prayer and the supererogatory prayer. He said: There is no harm in it. So the proper approach concerning this report is that we carry it upon a kind of concession, even though what we presented earlier is preferable, because combining two surahs is not among the things that invalidate the prayer. And the narrations have come explicitly indicating dislike.

As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Faḍālah, from al-ʿAlāʾ, from Zayd al-Shaḥḥām, who said: Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام led us in the fajr prayer and recited al-Ḍuḥā and Alam Nashraḥ in one rakʿah. So this does not contradict what we have stated regarding the dislike of joining two surahs together, because these two surahs are one surah according to Āl Muḥammad عليهم السلام, and one should recite them together in one place and not separate between them with Bismillāh al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm in the obligatory prayers, and this report does not contradict that.

What Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from al-Ḥusayn, from Faḍālah, from al-Ḥusayn, from Ibn Muskān, from Zayd al-Shaḥḥām, who said: Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام led us in salat (prayer). Then he recited for us: al-Ḍuḥā and Alam Nashraḥ. Because in this report it is not stated whether he recited them in one rakʿah or in two rakʿahs. So when this very narrator himself has narrated this very ruling itself and clarified that he recited them in a single rakʿah, then interpreting this unrestricted narration in a way that accords with that is more appropriate, and that does not contradict it.

What Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from some of our companions, from Zayd al-Shaḥḥām, who said: Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام led us in prayer, and in the first rakʿah he recited وَالضُّحَى, and in the second, أَلَمْ نَشْرَحْ. So this narration, even though it indicates that he recited them in the two rakʿahs, does not state that he recited them in an obligatory prayer or a supererogatory prayer. It is possible that he recited them in two rakʿahs of supererogatory prayers, and that is permissible, as we have explained.

The Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Abū al-Qāsim Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb, from ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Mughīrah, from Jamīl ibn Darrāj, from Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said: When you are behind an Imam and he recites al-Ḥamd and finishes its recitation, then say: “You are the praise, for Allah, Lord of the worlds,” and do not say: “Āmīn.”

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Ibn Muskan, from Muhammad al-Halabi, who said: I asked Aba 'Abdillah عليه السلام, “Should I say ‘Amin’ when I finish Fatihat al-Kitab?” He said, “No.”

As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Jamīl, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about the people’s saying in congregational salat (prayer), when Fātiḥat al-Kitāb is recited, “Āmīn.” He said: “How good it is, and lower the voice with it.” So the first thing concerning this report is that its narrator is Jamīl, and he has narrated the opposite of that, namely what we have presented earlier from his statement: “Do not say Āmīn; rather say: al-ḥamdu lillāhi rabbi al-ʿālamīn.” When he has narrated what contradicts this narration and agrees with the narration of others, then acting upon that is necessary instead of the other. And even if it were accepted, it would be possible to interpret it as a form of taqiyyah, due to the consensus of the rightful sect upon abandoning acting by it; and also, indeed...

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Hammad ibn 'Isa, from Mu'awiyah ibn Wahb, who said: I said to Abī 'Abdillah عليه السلام: Should I say “Āmīn” when the Imam says “not of those who have incurred wrath, nor of those who are astray” He said: They are the Jews and the Christians. And he did not answer on this point; so his turning away عليه السلام from answering what the questioner asked is evidence for the reprehensibility of this expression, even if he was not able to state its reprehensibility explicitly due to taqiyyah and necessity, so he turned away from answering him altogether.

Al-Husayn ibn 'Ubayd Allah informed me, from a number of our companions, from Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from 'Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, that he was asked about a man who recites a surah containing the sajdah at the end of the surah. He said: He performs sajdah, then stands, recites Fatihat al-Kitab, then performs ruku', and performs sajdah.

As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from Muḥammad ibn Khālid, from Abū al-Bakhtarī Wahb ibn Wahb, from Abū ʿAbdillāh, from his father, from ʿAlī عليه السلام, that he said: If the sajdah is at the end of the surah, it suffices you to go into rukuʿ with it. So this does not contradict the first report, because this report is to be understood as applying to one who prays with a group and is not able to perform sajdah and then stand and recite al-Ḥamd; in that case, there is no harm in his going into rukuʿ. And the first report is to be understood as applying to one praying alone. And that which indicates this is...

What al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from 'Uthman ibn 'Isa, from Sama'ah, who said: Whoever recites Iqra' bismi rabbika, then when he completes it, let him perform sajdah; then when he rises, let him recite Fatihat al-Kitab and perform ruku'. He said: If you are tried with an Imam who does not perform sajdah, then indication by gesture and ruku' will suffice you. And do not recite it in the obligatory prayer; recite it in the supererogatory prayer.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id informed me, from Fadalah ibn Ayyub, from al-Husayn ibn 'Uthman, from سماعة, from Abi Basir, from Abi 'Abdillah عليه السلام, who said: If you pray with a group and the Imam recites, "Recite in the name of your Lord who created," or something from the verses of obligatory prostration, and he finishes his recitation and does not prostrate, then indicate by gesture; and the menstruating woman prostrates when she hears the verse of prostration.

As for what al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated, from Fadalah, from Aban ibn 'Uthman, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi 'Abd Allah, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, he said: I asked him about a menstruating woman: does she recite the Qur'an and perform a sajdah when she hears the verse of sajdah? He said: She should not recite and she should not perform sajdah. So this does not contradict the first report, because the first report is understood as indicating recommendation rather than obligation, and this report is understood as indicating the permissibility of leaving it; thus there is no contradiction between them.

The Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Abu al-Qasim Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from 'Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from 'Umar ibn Udhaynah and Ibn Bukayr, from Zurarah, from Abi Ja'far عليه السلام, who said: Nothing of the recitation and the du'a is recorded except what he makes himself hear.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from al-'Abbas ibn Ma'ruf, from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from 'Ali ibn Ri'ab, from al-Halabi, who said: I asked Aba 'Abdillah عليه السلام: May a man recite in his salat (prayer) while his garment is over his mouth? He said: There is no harm in that, if he makes his two ears hear the murmuring.

As for what Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā narrated from al-ʿAmrakī, from ʿAlī ibn Jaʿfar, from his brother Mūsā ibn Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man: is it proper for him to recite in his salat (prayer) and move his tongue with the recitation in his throat without making himself hear it? He said: There is no problem if he does not move his tongue, and merely imagines it inwardly. So the proper way regarding this report is that we understand it as applying to one who prays behind someone who is not to be followed; it is permissible for him to recite within himself, like inner self-talk. This indicates that.

What Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā narrated from Yaʿqūb ibn Yazīd, from Muḥammad ibn Abī Ḥamzah, from one whom he mentioned, from Abū ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said: What suffices you of the recitation with them is the like of the speech of the النفس.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, from Hammad ibn 'Isa, from Hariz, from Zurarah, who said: I said to Abi Ja'far عليه السلام: What suffices of speech in the last two rak'ahs? He said: That you say, “Subhan Allah, wal-hamdu lillah, wa la ilaha illa Allah, wa Allahu akbar,” then you pronounce takbir and bow.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from Yahya al-Halabi, from 'Ubayd ibn Zurarah, who said: I asked Aba 'Abdillah عليه السلام about the last two rak'ahs of Zuhr. He said: You glorify Allah, praise Allah, and seek forgiveness for your sin; and if you wish, then [recite] Fatihat al-Kitab, for it is praise and supplication.

Saʿd narrated from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Faḍḍāl, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Bukayr, from ʿAlī ibn Ḥanẓalah, from Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about the last two rakʿahs: what should I do in them? He said: If you wish, recite Fātiḥat al-Kitāb; and if you wish, then remember Allah, for it is the same. He said: I said, Then which of the two is more virtuous? He said: By Allah, they are equal: if you wish, you may recite tasbīḥ, and if you wish, you may recite.

As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā narrated from Muḥammad ibn Abī al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAllān, from Muḥammad ibn Ḥakīm, who said: I asked Abā al-Ḥasan عليه السلام: Which is more excellent in the last two rakʿahs, recitation or tasbīḥ? He said: Recitation is more excellent. So the correct way to understand this narration is that when he is an Imam, recitation is more excellent; that is indicated by this.

What al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Safwan, from Mansur ibn Hazim, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: If you are an Imam, then recite in the last two rak'ahs Fatihat al-Kitab. And if you are by yourself, then it is sufficient for you whether you do it or do not do it.

As for what Saʿd narrated from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from Muḥammad ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Ḥammād ibn ʿUthmān, from ʿUbayd Allah al-Ḥalabī, from Abū ʿAbd Allah عليه السلام, he said: When you stand in the last two rakʿahs, do not recite in them; rather say: al-ḥamdu lillāh, subḥāna Allāh, and Allāhu akbar. He only forbade him from reciting while believing that anything other than recitation is not permissible, not from reciting it by way of choice and seeking merit. And it is possible that his statement, 'Do not recite in them,' is informative, not prohibitive; as though he said: If you are not among those who recite, then say: al-ḥamdu lillāh, subḥāna Allāh, and Allāhu akbar.

Al-Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Abū al-Qāsim Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from his father, from Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, and Muḥammad ibn Khālid al-Barqī, and al-ʿAbbās ibn Maʿrūf, from al-Qāsim ibn ʿUrwah, from Hishām ibn Sālim, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbd Allah عليه السلام about the tasbih in rukuʿ and sujud. He said: In rukuʿ you say, “Glory be to my Lord, the Magnificent,” and in sujud, “Glory be to my Lord, the Most High.” The obligatory minimum of that is one tasbih, the sunnah is three, and the merit is in seven.

From him, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from ʿAlī ibn Ḥadīd and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Najrān and al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from Ḥammād ibn ʿĪsā, from Ḥarīz ibn ʿAbd Allāh, from Zurārah, from Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said: I said to him, “What suffices of utterance in the rukuʿ and the sujud?” He said, “Three tasbihat in one measured manner, and one complete utterance suffices.”

From him, from Ayyūb ibn Nūḥ al-Nakhaʿī, from Muḥammad ibn Abī Ḥamzah, from ʿAlī ibn Yaqṭīn, from Abū al-Ḥasan al-Awwal عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about rukūʿ and sujūd: how much tasbīḥ is sufficient in them? He said: Three, and one suffices for you if you have firmly placed your forehead upon the ground.

And from him, from Abū Jaʿfar, from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Yaqṭīn, from his brother al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī ibn Yaqṭīn, from his father, from Abī al-Ḥasan al-Awwal عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who performs سجود: how much tasbih suffices him in his rukūʿ and his sujūd? He said: Three, and one suffices him.

As for what al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Safwan, from Misma', from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, he said: Less than three tasbihat, or their equivalent amount, does not suffice for a man in his salat (prayer).
From him, from al-Naḍr, from Yaḥyā al-Ḥalabī, from Dāwūd al-Abzārī, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: The minimum tasbih is three times while you are in sajdah; do not be hasty in them.

From him, from Muḥammad ibn Sinān, from Ibn Miskān, from Abī Baṣīr, who said: I asked him about the minimum amount of tasbīḥ that suffices in rukuʿ and sujud, so he said: three tasbīḥāt. Thus, the proper way to reconcile these reports is in two ways. One of them is that limiting oneself to a single tasbīḥ is only permissible when it is a specific tasbīḥ, namely saying: “Subḥāna Rabbīya al-ʿAẓīm” in rukuʿ, and “Subḥāna Rabbīya al-Aʿlā” in sujud, according to what is indicated by the narration we transmitted at the beginning of the chapter from Hishām ibn Sālim. But if he says: “Subḥāna Allāh,” then fewer than three repetitions do not suffice for him, as is indicated by that.

What was narrated by Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Mahbub, from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan, from al-Husayn, from al-Hasan, from Zur'ah, from Sama'ah, who said: I asked him about ruku' and sujud: have they been revealed in the Qur'an? He said: Yes. The saying of Allah, the Exalted: “O you who have faith, bow and prostrate.” So I said: What is the limit of ruku' and sujud? He said: As for what suffices you in ruku', it is three tasbihat: you say, “Subhan Allah, Subhan Allah, Subhan Allah,” three times.

From him, from al-‘Abbās ibn Ma‘rūf, from Ḥammād ibn ‘Īsā, from Mu‘āwiyah ibn ‘Ammār, who said: I said to Abū ‘Abdillāh عليه السلام: What is the least that suffices of tasbih in the salat (prayer)? He said: Three tasbihat, uttered deliberately and unhurriedly; you say: “Subḥān Allāh, Subḥān Allāh, Subḥān Allāh.” And the second possibility is that we interpret the latter reports as referring to merit and recommendation, not obligation and requirement. And that which clarifies what we have mentioned...

What Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā narrated, from ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥakam, from Yaḥyā ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, from Abū Bakr al-Ḥaḍramī, who said: I said to Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام: What is the minimum limit of rukūʿ and sujūd? So he said: You say, “Subḥāna Rabbīya al-ʿAẓīmi wa bi-ḥamdih” three times in rukūʿ, and “Subḥāna Rabbīya al-Aʿlā wa bi-ḥamdih” three times in sujūd. So whoever omits one, he has diminished one third of his salat (prayer), and whoever omits two, he has diminished two thirds of his salat (prayer), and whoever does not recite tasbīḥ, then there is no salat (prayer) for him. So this report indicates that they only negated completeness and merit. Do you not see that they said: whoever omits one, he has diminished one third of his salat (prayer), and whoever omits two, he has diminished two thirds of his salat (prayer)? For were the matter not as we have mentioned, there would be no difference between failing to recite one of them such that it would invalidate the salat (prayer), and failing to recite all of them; and we have known that they differentiated between the two.

As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from Ibn Faḍḍāl, from Ibn Bukayr, from Ḥamzah ibn Ḥumrān and al-Ḥasan ibn Ziyād, they both said: We entered upon Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام while there were people with him and he was leading them in the ʿAṣr salat, and we had already performed salat. So we counted for him in his rukūʿ: “Subḥāna Rabbiyal-ʿAẓīm” thirty-four or thirty-three times. And one of the two said in his narration: “wa bi-ḥamdih” in the rukūʿ and the sujūd. So this narration is specific to his action عليه السلام and his salat with one whom he knew could bear that, because the principle in congregational salat is lightening it, as we shall explain.

Abu al-Hasan ibn Abi Jayd al-Qummi informed me, from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn al-Walid, from al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan ibn Aban, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Fadalah, from al-'Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I saw Aba Abdillah عليه السلام place his hands before his knees when he performed sajdah.

From him, from al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad al-Jawharī, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Abī al-ʿAlāʾ, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about a man placing his hands before his knees in the salat (prayer). He said: Yes.
From him, from Safwan, from al-'Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: He was asked about a man placing his hands on the ground before his knees. He said: Yes—meaning in the salat (prayer).

As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Faḍālah, from al-Ḥusayn, from Samāʿah, from Abī Baṣīr, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: There is no harm, when a man performs salat (prayer), in placing his knees on the ground before his hands. So the proper way regarding this report is that we interpret it as applying to a state of necessity in which a person is unable to meet the ground with his hands first, due to an ailment, illness, or something similar.

As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Faḍālah, from Abān ibn ʿUthmān, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī ʿAbd Allāh, from Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man: when he bows and then raises his head, should he begin and place his hands on the ground first or his knees? He said: It does not harm him whichever of the two he begins with; it is accepted from him. His statement عليه السلام, 'It does not harm him,' means that the salat (prayer) is not invalidated for him, or that he does not deserve punishment for leaving it, because that is from the etiquettes of salat (prayer), not from its obligations for whose omission punishment is deserved.

Al-Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Abu al-Qasim Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah, from Hamzah ibn Ya'la, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, who said: Some of our companions narrated to me from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام. He عليه السلام said: There is no objection to performing wudu (ablution) with water that is placed in the sun.

As for what was narrated by Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Mahbub, from Muhammad ibn 'Isa al-'Ubaydi, from Durust, from Ibrahim ibn 'Abd al-Hamid, from Abi al-Hasan عليه السلام, he said: The Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم entered upon 'A'ishah while she had placed her ewer in the sun. He said: “O Humayra', what is this?” She said: “I am washing my head and my body.” He said: “Do not do it again, for it causes leprosy.” So it is to be understood as indicating a kind of karahah (dislike) rather than prohibition.

Al-Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from his father, from al-Ṣaffār, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā, from Abī ʿAbdillāh al-Barqī, from Muḥammad ibn Muṣādif, who said: I heard Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام saying: Sajdah is only upon the forehead, and there is no sajdah upon the nose.

Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Mahbub narrated from Musa ibn 'Umayr, from al-Hasan ibn 'Ali ibn Faddal, from Ibn Bukayr and Tha'labah ibn Maymun, from Burayd, from Abi Ja'far عليه السلام, who said: From the forehead to the nose—whichever part of that you place upon the ground in sajdah, it suffices for you; but performing sajdah upon all of it is more virtuous.

Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Faḍḍāl, from Marwān ibn Muslim and ʿAmmār al-Sābāṭī, who said: What is between the hairline and the tip of the nose is the place of prostration; whichever part of that you make touch the ground will suffice you.

As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā, from ʿAmmār, from Jaʿfar, from his father عليه السلام, who said: ʿAlī عليه السلام said: No salat (prayer) is valid if the nose does not touch what the forehead touches. So this narration is to be understood as indicating a type of dislike rather than obligation, because the obligation is sajdah upon the forehead, while pressing the nose to the ground is sunnah (prophetic tradition), as we have explained. And what we have said is further confirmed.

What Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb narrated from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from Ibn Abī Najrān, from Ḥammād ibn ʿĪsā, from Ḥarīz, from Zurārah, who said: Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام said: The Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم said: Sajdah is upon seven bones: the forehead, the two hands, the two knees, and the two big toes of the feet. And press your nose down in humility. As for the obligation, it is these seven; and as for pressing the nose down, it is a sunnah from the Prophet صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم.

The Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from his father, from al-Ṣaffār, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from Faḍālah, from al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿUthmān, from Samāʿah, from Abī Baṣīr, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: Do not sit in the iqʿāʾ posture between the two sajdahs.

As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Ḥammād ibn ʿUthmān, from ʿUbayd Allāh al-Ḥalabī, from Abū ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said: There is no harm in iqʿāʾ during salat (prayer) between the two sajdahs. The proper understanding of this narration is concession or a state of necessity, except that what we have previously presented in the first narration is more virtuous; and that also accords with the narrations that we cited in our major book, and this also confirms that.
What was narrated by Mu'awiyah ibn 'Ammar, Ibn Muslim, and al-Halabi, all together, who said: He said: Do not sit between the two sajdahs like the sitting of a dog.

The Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from al-Saffar, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Abu Ayyub al-Khazzaz, from Abd al-Hamid ibn Awwad, from Abu Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: I saw him: when he raised his head from the second sajdah of the first rak'ah, he sat until he became settled, then he stood.

Sama'ah, from Abu Basir, said: Abu 'Abdillah عليه السلام said: When you raise your head from the second sajdah of the first rak'ah, at the time when you intend to stand, then sit upright evenly, then stand.

As for what was narrated by ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥakam, from Raḥīm, who said: I said to Abī al-Ḥasan al-Riḍā عليه السلام: I see that when you pray, and you raise your head from sajdah in the first and third rakʿah, you sit upright and then stand. So should we do as you do? He said: Do not look at what I do; do what you are commanded. He عليه السلام only said, 'Do not look at what I do,' so that they would not believe that this was obligatory upon them by way of obligation, not that he had forbidden them from following his act as a matter of merit and perfection. This sitting is among the etiquettes of salat (prayer), not among its obligatory acts, and that which indicates this is as follows.

What Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā narrated from al-Ḥajjāl, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Bukayr, from Zurārah, who said: I saw Abū Jaʿfar and Abū ʿAbd Allāh, peace be upon them, that when they raised their heads from the second sajdah, they rose and did not sit.

Al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿUbayd Allāh informed me, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā, from his father, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from Ibn Abī Najrān, from Ḥammād ibn ʿĪsā, from Ḥarīz, from Zurārah, who said: Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام said: The Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم said: Sajdah is upon seven bones: the forehead, the two hands, the two knees, and the two big toes; and you press your nose down as an act of irghām. As for what is obligatory, it is these seven; and as for the irghām, it is a sunnah (prophetic tradition) from the Prophet صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم.

As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from Muḥammad ibn Ismāʿīl ibn Bazīʿ, from Abū Ismāʿīl al-Sarrāj, from Hārūn ibn Khārijah, who said: I saw Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام while he was in sajdah, and he had raised his feet from the ground, with one of his feet upon the other. So the proper interpretation of this report is that it is possible that he عليه السلام only did that due to a necessity that compelled him to it, not in a state of choice.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Safwan, from Ishaq ibn 'Ammar, from a man of Banu 'Ijl, who said: I asked Aba 'Abdillah عليه السلام about a place upon which there is dust, so I blow it away when I intend sajdah. He said: There is no harm in it.

As for what Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb narrated from al-Faḍl, from Ḥammād ibn ʿĪsā, from Ḥarīz, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, he said: I said to him: A man blows in salat (prayer) at the place of his forehead. He said: No. So the sound understanding of this narration is that it indicates a kind of reprehensibility, not prohibition. And it is possible that this was only disliked when it is something by which people are annoyed; that is what this indicates.

What Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from Abū Muḥammad al-Ḥajjāl, from Abū Isḥāq, from Abū Bakr al-Ḥaḍramī, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: There is no harm in blowing during salat (prayer) at the place of sajdah (prostration), so long as it does not harm anyone.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Mu'awiyah ibn Hukaym, from Abi Malik al-Hadrami, from al-Hasan ibn Hammad, who said: I said to Abi 'Abdillah عليه السلام: I perform sajdah, and my forehead falls upon an elevated spot. He said: Raise your head, then place it down again.

As for what Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb narrated from Muḥammad ibn Ismāʿīl, from al-Faḍl ibn Shādhān, from Ṣafwān ibn Yaḥyā, from Muʿāwiyah ibn ʿAmmār, who said: Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام said: When you place your forehead on a raised spot, do not lift it; rather, drag it onto the ground.

Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Mahbub narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Mughirah, from Ibn Muskan, from Husayn ibn Hammad, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: I said to him: I place my face down for sajdah, and my face lands on a stone or on an elevated spot; should I move my face to a level place?
