He said: Yes, drag your face along the ground without lifting it.

Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā, from Mūsā ibn Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who performs sajdah upon pebbles, but his forehead cannot settle upon the ground. He said: He should move his forehead until it becomes properly placed, then move the pebbles away from his forehead, and he should not raise his head. Thus, the correct approach regarding these reports is to understand them as applying to the case in which a person is able to place his forehead evenly without raising his head, because if he raises his head, he would have added an extra sajdah in the salat, and that is not permissible. The first report is to be understood as referring to a state of necessity in which this cannot be achieved except by raising the head.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Muhammad ibn Khalid, from al-Qasim ibn 'Urwah, from Abu al-'Abbas al-Fadl ibn 'Abd al-Malik, who said: Abu 'Abdillah عليه السلام said: Do not perform sajdah except upon the earth or that which the earth grows, except cotton and linen.

ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from Ḥammād ibn ʿĪsā, from Ḥarīz, from Zurārah, from Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said: I said to him, ‘May I perform sajdah upon tar, meaning upon bitumen?’ He said, ‘No, nor upon cloth made from cotton, nor upon wool, nor upon anything from an animal, nor upon food, nor upon anything from the fruits of the earth, nor upon anything from furnishings.’

As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from Aḥmad ibn Isḥāq, from Yāsir al-Khādim, who said: Abū al-Ḥasan عليه السلام passed by me while I was praying on al-Ṭabarī, and I had placed something upon it on which I would perform sajdah. So he said to me: Why do you not perform sajdah on it? Is it not from the vegetation of the earth? So the proper way regarding this report is that we carry it upon the state of taqiyyah; that is indicated by this.

What Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Yaqṭīn, from his brother al-Ḥusayn, from his father ʿAlī ibn Yaqṭīn, who said: I asked Abā al-Ḥasan al-Māḍī عليه السلام about a man who performs sajdah on a coarse cloth and a carpet. He said: There is no harm if he is in a state of taqiyyah.

Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn Abi al-Khattab, from Wahb ibn Hafs, from Abi Basir, who said: I asked Aba 'Abd Allah عليه السلام about a man who performs sajdah upon a coarse cloth, and he said: If he is in taqiyyah, then there is no harm.

As for what Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Dawud al-Sarmi, he said: I asked Abu al-Hasan al-Thalith عليه السلام: Is sajdah on linen and cotton permissible without taqiyyah? He said: It is permissible. So the meaning in this report is that sajdah on these two materials is permissible when there is no taqiyyah, on condition that another necessity arises, such as heat or cold and what is similar to them. And he did not say that this is permissible without taqiyyah or anything that takes its place; that indicates this.

What was narrated by Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Hamid, from Sayf ibn 'Umayrah, from Mansur ibn Hazim, from more than one of our companions, who said: I said to Abī Ja'far عليه السلام: We are in a cold land where there is snow; should we perform sajdah upon the snow? He said: No. Rather, place something between yourself and it, cotton or linen.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from al-Muthanna al-Hannat, from 'Uyaynah, the seller of reeds, who said: I said to Abu 'Abdillah عليه السلام: I enter the mosque on an intensely hot day, and I dislike praying upon the pebbles, so I spread my garment and perform sajdah upon it. He said: Yes, there is no harm in it.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from 'Ali ibn Abi Hamzah, from Abi Basir, from Abi Ja'far عليه السلام, who said: I said to him: I may be traveling, and the time for salat (prayer) arrives, and I fear the burning heat of the ground on my face; what should I do? He said: Perform sajdah on part of your garment. I said: Not every garment allows me to perform sajdah on its edge or hem. He said: Perform sajdah on the back of your hand, for it is one of the places of sajdah.

Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from Abū Ṭālib ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ṣalt, from al-Qāsim ibn al-Fuḍayl, who said: I said to al-Riḍā عليه السلام: May I be made your ransom, a man prostrates on his sleeve because of the harm of heat and cold. He said: There is no harm in it.

From him, from ʿAbbād ibn Sulaymān, from Saʿd ibn Saʿd, from Muḥammad ibn al-Qāsim ibn al-Fuḍayl, from Aḥmad ibn ʿUmar, who said: I asked Abā al-Ḥasan عليه السلام about a man who performs sajdah on his sleeve to protect himself from the harm of heat and cold, or on his cloak when beneath it there is a coarse cloth or something else upon which sajdah is not performed. He said: There is no harm in it.

From him, from ʿAbbād ibn Sulaymān, from Saʿd ibn Saʿd, from Muḥammad ibn al-Qāsim ibn al-Fuḍayl ibn Yasār, who said: A man wrote to Abī al-Ḥasan عليه السلام: May a man perform sajdah upon a garment by which he protects his face from the heat and the cold, and from a thing upon which he dislikes to perform sajdah? He said: Yes, there is no harm in it.

As for what Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn Ja'far, from al-Husayn ibn 'Ali ibn Kaysan al-San'ani, who said: I wrote to Abī al-Hasan al-Thalith عليه السلام asking him about sajdah upon cotton and linen without taqiyyah and without necessity. So he wrote back to me: That is permissible. So this does not contradict the earlier reports upon which we have compiled, because it is possible that he only permitted it while negating a necessity that reaches the destruction of the soul, even though there may be a lesser necessity than that, such as heat or cold and whatever resembles that, as we have explained.
Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from ʿAlī ibn Ismāʿīl, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr ibn Saʿīd, from Abū al-Ḥasan al-Riḍā عليه السلام, who said: Do not perform sajdah upon pitch, nor upon al-qufr, nor upon saruj.

As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from al-Naḍr, from Muḥammad ibn Abī Ḥamzah, from Muʿāwiyah ibn ʿAmmār, who said: Al-Muʿallā ibn Khunays asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, while I was with him, about performing sajdah on al-qufr and on al-qīr. He said: There is no harm. So the correct approach regarding this narration is that we interpret it as applying to a state of necessity or taqiyyah, not to a state of choice.
Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Fadalah, from Jamil ibn Darrāj, from Abī 'Abdillāh عليه السلام. That he disliked that one should perform sajdah upon paper on which there is writing.

As for what ʿAlī ibn Mahziyār narrated, he said: Dāwūd ibn Farqad asked Abā al-Ḥasan عليه السلام about sheets and papers upon which there is writing: is sajdah upon them permissible or not? So he wrote: It is permissible.

Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Najrān, from Ṣafwān al-Jammāl, who said: I saw Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام in the litter; he performed sajdah upon paper, and most of that time he would indicate by gesturing. So there is no contradiction between these two reports and the first report, because the purport of the first report is a type of karāhah, and he explicitly stated that in his saying that he disliked making sajdah upon paper that has writing on it. Thus the two reports are to be understood as indicating permissibility. Also, the report of Ṣafwān al-Jammāl, in which he narrated the action of Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, does not state that the paper upon which he was making sajdah had writing on it; rather, the karāhah is directed only to that which has this description. It is possible that it had no writing, and thus it accords with the first report.

Al-Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan ibn Aban, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Fadalah, from Jamil ibn Darrāj, from Aban, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi 'Uqbah, from Humran, from one of the two عليهما السلام, who said: My father used to perform salat (prayer) on the khumrah; he would place it on the carpet and perform sajdah upon it. When there was no khumrah, he would place pebbles on the carpet where he would perform sajdah.

Ali, from his father, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from 'Umar ibn Udhaynah, from al-Fudayl ibn Yasar and Burayd ibn Mu'awiyah, from one of the two of them عليه السلام, who said: There is no objection to the praying person standing upon hair and wool, so long as he performs sajdah upon the earth. But if it is from the vegetation of the earth, then there is no objection to standing and performing sajdah upon it.

As for what ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm narrated from his father, from Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā, from Ghiyāth ibn Ibrāhīm, from Jaʿfar, from his father, from ʿAlī عليه السلام, that he said: A man does not perform sajdah upon something that the rest of his body is not upon. So this does not contradict the first two reports, because this report conforms to the generality, and its basis is taqiyyah rather than the state of choice.

Al-Shaykh Abu 'Abd Allah informed me, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Hammad, from Mu'awiyah ibn 'Ammar, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: I heard him saying: The garment is not washed, and the salat (prayer) is not repeated, because of what falls into the well, unless it becomes foul-smelling. If it does become foul-smelling, the garment is washed, the salat (prayer) is repeated, and the well is drained.

And al-Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Abu al-Qasim Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Qulawayh, from his father, from Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Abu Talib 'Abd Allah ibn al-Salt, from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Mughirah, from Mu'awiyah ibn 'Ammar, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, concerning: A mouse falls into the well, and a man performs wudu (ablution) from it and prays while he does not know. Should he repeat the salat (prayer) and wash his garment? He said: He does not repeat the salat (prayer), and he does not wash his garment.

The Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan, from his father, from al-Ṣaffār, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥakam, from Abān ibn ʿUthmān, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: He was asked about a mouse that falls into the well, and it is not known about until after wudu (ablution) has been performed from it. Should the salat (prayer) be repeated? He said: No.

Al-Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Abi al-Qasim Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Ja'far ibn Bashir, from Abi 'Uyaynah, who said: Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام was asked about a mouse that falls into a well, and he said: If it comes out, then there is no harm; but if it decomposes, then seven buckets [should be drawn]. He said: And he was asked about a mouse that falls into the well, and no one knows about it until after one has performed wudu (ablution) from it. Should he repeat his wudu (ablution) and his salat (prayer), and wash whatever it touched? He said: No. The people of the house have already used it and sprinkled with it.

With this chain of transmission, from Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from ʿAli ibn al-Hakam, from Aban, from Abi Usamah and Abi Yusuf Yaʿqub ibn ʿUthaym, from Abi ʿAbd Allah عليه السلام, who said: If a bird, a chicken, or a mouse falls into the well, then draw seven buckets from it. We said: What do you say regarding our salat (prayer), our wudu (ablution), and what has touched our clothes? He said: There is no harm in it.

Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn Abī Naṣr, from ʿAbd al-Karīm, from Abū Baṣīr, who said: I said to Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام: A well is drawn from, wudu is performed with it, clothes were washed from it, and dough was kneaded with it, then it became known that there had been a dead creature in it. He said: There is no harm, the garment is not to be washed, and the salat (prayer) performed with it is not to be repeated. Shaykh Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan, may Allah have mercy on him, said: What these reports contain regarding the dropping of repetition in wudu and salat (prayer) for one who used these waters does not indicate that drawing out water is not obligatory when there is no change, because it is not impossible that the required amount of drawing out in everything that falls into it is obligatory, even though when he used it, repeating wudu and salat did not become binding upon him, because repetition is a second obligation. So it is not for anyone to make that a proof that what is meant by the specified amounts of drawing out is a kind of recommendation. Rather, what ought to be acted upon is that if he used these waters before knowing of the occurrence of impurity in them, then repeating wudu and salat is not binding on him; but whenever he used them while knowing that, repeating wudu and salat becomes binding on him. And that which indicates this is:

What Ishaq ibn 'Ammar narrated from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام concerning: Regarding a man who finds a mouse in his vessel, after having performed wudu (ablution) from that vessel many times, washed his clothes from it, and performed ghusl from it, while the mouse had become decomposed: he said, if he had seen it in the vessel before performing ghusl, or performing wudu (ablution), or washing his clothes, and then did that after seeing it in the vessel, then he must wash his clothes, wash everything that that water touched, and repeat the wudu (ablution) and the salat (prayer). But if he only saw it after he had finished all of that and done it, then he should not touch any of the water, and there is nothing upon him, because he does not know when it fell into it. Then he said: perhaps it only fell into it at that very time when he saw it.

As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from Muḥammad ibn Ismāʿīl, from al-Riḍā عليه السلام, he said: The water of the well is ample; nothing renders it najis except if its smell or its taste changes. Then water is drawn from it until the smell goes away and its taste becomes good, because it has a source. So the meaning in this report is that nothing spoils it in such a way that use of any part of it is impermissible unless all of it must be drawn out, except what changes it. As for that which does not change it, then a measured amount is drawn from it and use is made of the remainder, according to what we explained in the Book of Tahdhīb al-Aḥkām.

As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from Ibn Maḥbūb, from al-Ḥasan ibn Ṣāliḥ al-Thawrī, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, he said: If the water in the well-reservoir is a kurr, nothing renders it impure. I said: And how much is the kurr? He said: Three spans and a half in its length, by three spans and a half in its depth, by three spans and a half in its width. This report may bear two possibilities: one of them is that what is meant by al-rakī is the constructed reservoir that does not have a supply from a spring, as opposed to wells that do have a supply from it; for that is what consideration of kurr applies to, as we have explained. The second is that this may have been issued in the context of taqiyyah, because among the jurists are those who equate wells and ponds in their smallness and abundance, so it is possible that the report was issued in agreement with them. What clarifies that is that al-Ḥasan ibn Ṣāliḥ, the narrator of this hadith, is a Zaydī, Batrī, whose hadith is abandoned in what he is alone in narrating.
Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Mu'ammar ibn Khallad, said: I asked Aba al-Hasan عليه السلام about performing sajdah on snow. He said: Do not perform sajdah on saline ground, nor on snow.

As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from Dāwūd al-Ṣirmī, who said: I asked Abā al-Ḥasan عليه السلام and said to him: I go out on this route, and sometimes there is no place in which I can perform salat except snow, so what should I do? He said: If it is possible for you not to perform sajdah upon the snow, then do not perform sajdah upon it; and if it is not possible for you, then level it and perform sajdah upon it. So the bearing of this report concerns the state of necessity, according to what we have already presented in the first report, and what he also clarified in the report of Manṣūr ibn Ḥāzim, which we have already presented earlier.

Al-Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Abu al-Qasim Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from 'Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Mu'awiyah ibn 'Ammar, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: The takbirs in the obligatory prayer, in the five prayers, are ninety-five takbirs; among them are five takbirs for the qunut.

From him, from ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Mughīrah; and he explained them in... For al-Ẓuhr, twenty-one takbirs; and in al-ʿAṣr, twenty-one takbirs; and in al-Maghrib, sixteen takbirs; and in al-ʿIshāʾ al-Ākhirah, twenty-one takbirs; and in al-Fajr, eleven; and five takbirs in the qunut in five prayers.

Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā, from Mūsā ibn ʿUmar, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Mughīrah, from Abī al-Ṣabbāḥ al-Muzanī, who said: Amīr al-Muʾminīn عليه السلام: There are ninety-five takbīrs in the day and night for the prayers; among them is the takbīr of the qunūt. Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan said: These narrations that we have mentioned are those upon which practice should be based, and according to them our Shaykh al-Mufīd, may Allah have mercy on him, used to give fatwa formerly. Then, near the end of his life, he came to abandon acting upon them and adopted acting upon raising the hands without takbīr. The first view is more appropriate due to the existence of the narrations concerning it, and besides this I do not know of any hadith at all. And it is not for anyone to interpret these reports by saying: What exceeds ninety takbīrs, I take to mean that when he rises from the first tashahhud to the third rakʿah, he rises with a takbīr—for several reasons: One of them is that reports are only interpreted away from their apparent meanings, and their outward sense left, when they conflict and some of them oppose others. Here, there is nothing that opposes these narrations, so it is not permissible to turn away from their apparent meanings by any kind of interpretation. The second is that not all prayers contain a rising from the second rakʿah to the third; rather, that is found only in four prayers. If that were what was meant, then it would have said: ninety-four takbīrs. The third is that the detailed hadith includes mention of eleven takbīrs in the dawn prayer, and a takbīr after that for the qunūt added to them. If the matter were as interpreted in that way, then the takbīr in it would have been only eleven takbīrs. The fourth is that separate narrations have been transmitted stating that a person should rise from the first tashahhud to the third rakʿah and say: “By the power of Allah and His strength I rise and sit,” and they did not mention the takbīr. If rising with takbīr had been obligatory, then it would have said: “Then he says takbīr and rises to the third,” just as, when they mentioned bowing and prostration, they said: “Then he says takbīr and bows,” and “he says takbīr and prostrates,” and “he raises his head from prostration and says takbīr.” So if there had been a takbīr here, it would have said the like of that.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated that from Hammad ibn 'Isa, from Hariz, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: When you sit in the first two rak'ahs and recite the tashahhud, then stand up, say: “By the power of Allah and His strength I stand and I sit.”

And from him, from Fadalah, from Rifa'ah ibn Musa, who said: I heard Aba 'Abd Allah عليه السلام saying: 'Ali عليه السلام, when he rose from the first two rak'ahs, would say: “By Your power and Your strength I rise and sit.”

And from him, from Faḍālah, from Sayf, from Abī Bakr, who said: Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام said: When you rise from the first two rakʿahs, then rely upon your two palms and say: By the power of Allah and His strength, I rise and I sit.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Ibn Abi Najran, from Safwan al-Jammal, who said: I prayed behind Abi 'Abdillah عليه السلام for some days, and he used to perform qunut in every salat (prayer), whether he recited aloud in it or did not recite aloud in it.
From him, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from ʿUmar ibn Udhaynah, from Zurārah, from Abī Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said: Qunut is in every salat (prayer), in the second rakʿah, before the rukuʿ.

From him, from Safwan and Ibn Abi Umayr, from Abdullah ibn Bukayr, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I asked Abu Ja'far عليه السلام about qunut in all five salat (prayers), and he said: Perform qunut in all of them. He said: Then after that I asked Abu Abdullah عليه السلام, and he said: As for those in which you recite aloud, then do not doubt about it.

From him, from Faḍālah, from Ibn Muskān, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: Qunūt in the Maghrib prayer is in the second rakʿah, and in the ʿIshāʾ and Ghadāh prayers it is likewise, and in the Witr prayer it is in the third rakʿah.

From him, from al-Ḥasan, from Zurʿah, from Samāʿah, who said: I asked him about qunut—during which salat it is. He said: In every prayer in which you recite aloud, there is qunut; and the qunut is before the ruku' and after the recitation.

Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā narrated from ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥakam, from Abū Ayyūb al-Khazzāz, from Abū Baṣīr, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: One of our companions asked him, while I was with him, about the qunut in Jumuʿah. He said to him: “In the second rakʿah.” Abū Baṣīr said to him: “Some of your companions have narrated to us that you said: ‘In the first rakʿah.’” He said: “In the last.” Then when he saw the people’s inattentiveness regarding it, he said: “O Abā Muḥammad, in the first and the last.” After that, Abū Baṣīr said: “Before the rukuʿ or after it?” Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام said to him: “Every qunut is before the rukuʿ except Jumuʿah; for indeed the first rakʿah in it is before the rukuʿ, and the last is after the rukuʿ.”

From him, from Ibn Udhaynah, from Wahb, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: Qunut is in the Friday prayer, the maghrib prayer, the 'atamah prayer, the witr, and the morning prayer. So whoever abandons the qunut out of aversion to it, then there is no salat (prayer) for him.

From him, from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Faḍḍāl, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Bukayr, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, from Abī Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said: Qunūt is in every two rakʿahs of supererogatory prayer or obligatory prayer. Al-Ḥasan said: And ʿAbd Allāh ibn Bukayr informed me, from Zurārah, from Abī Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said: Qunūt is in all prayers. Muḥammad ibn Muslim said: So I mentioned that to Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, and he said: As for that in which there is no doubt, it is that in which the recitation is made aloud.

As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā narrated from ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥakam, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Jamīl ibn Ṣāliḥ, from ʿAbd al-Malik ibn ʿAmr, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about the qunut, whether it is before the rukuʿ or after it. He said: Neither before it nor after it.

And from him, from al-Barqi, from Sa'd ibn Sa'd al-Ash'ari, from Abi al-Hasan al-Rida عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about qunut: is qunut performed in all salat (prayer), or only in those in which the recitation is audible? He said: There is no qunut except in the morning prayer, the witr, Jumu'ah, and the maghrib prayer.

And Saʿd narrated from Abū Jaʿfar, from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Faḍḍāl, from Yūnus ibn Yaʿqūb, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about qunūt: in which prayers should I perform qunūt? He said: Do not perform qunūt except in the Fajr prayer. So the proper way regarding these reports is that we understand them to mean that in these prayers qunūt is not on the level of special merit and emphasized recommendation to the extent established in other prayers in which recitation is audible, and after that in the obligatory prayers, because the merit of qunūt in the prayers is graded. Thus, qunūt in the obligatory prayers is more excellent than in the supererogatory prayers, and in those obligatory prayers in which recitation is audible it is more excellent than in those in which it is not audible, and the Maghrib and Fajr prayers, among the audible prayers, are more strongly emphasized in this regard. And when we interpret the reports according to these aspects, a sound basis is established for each of them that does not conflict with the others. It is also possible that they only negated qunūt in some prayers and specified it in others as a form of taqiyyah and practical consideration, because among the generality there are those who hold that view, and that which indicates this is as follows.

What ʿAlī ibn Mahziyār narrated from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from Abū al-Ḥasan al-Riḍā عليه السلام, who said: Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام said regarding the qunut: If you wish, then perform qunut, and if you wish, then do not perform qunut. Abū al-Ḥasan said: And when there is taqiyyah, then do not perform qunut, and I adopt this. And Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb narrated from ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from Ibn Faḍḍāl, from Ibn Bukayr, from Abū Baṣīr, who said: I asked Abū ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام about the qunut, and he said: In that in which the recitation is made aloud. He said: So I said to him: I had asked your father about that, and he said: In all five. So he said: May Allah have mercy on my father. Indeed, the companions of my father came to him and asked him, so he informed them of the truth. Then they came to me in doubt, so I informed them in accordance with taqiyyah.

As for what al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad al-Jawhari, from Aban ibn 'Uthman, from Isma'il al-Ju'fi and Ma'mar ibn Yahya, from Abi Ja'far عليه السلام, who said: Qunut is before the ruku', and if you wish, then after it. The correct way to understand his saying عليه السلام, "and if you wish, then after it," is that we carry it upon the case of making it up for one who missed it in its proper place, or the case of taqiyyah, because it is the position of some of the 'ammah.

Al-Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Abū al-Qāsim Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from his father, from Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allāh, from al-ʿAbbās ibn Maʿrūf, from ʿAlī ibn Mahziyār, from Ḥammād ibn ʿĪsā, from Ḥarīz ibn ʿAbd Allāh, from Zurārah, who said: I said to Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام: What statement suffices in the tashahhud in the first two rakʿahs? He said: That you say: I bear witness that there is no god but Allah alone, having no partner. I said: Then what suffices of the tashahhud in the last two rakʿahs? He said: The two testimonies.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from al-Hajjal, from Tha'labah ibn Maymun, from Yahya ibn Talhah, from Saurah ibn Kulayb, who said: I asked Aba Ja'far عليه السلام about the minimum that suffices of the tashahhud. He said: the two testimonies.

Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Saʿd ibn Bakr, from Ḥabīb al-Khathʿamī, from Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said: I heard him saying: when a man sits for the tashahhud, and he praises Allah and extols Him, that suffices for him.

From him, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn Abī Naṣr, who said: I said to Abū al-Ḥasan عليه السلام: May I be made your ransom, is the tashahhud that is in the second [rakʿah] sufficient for me to say in the fourth? He said: Yes.

As for what Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb narrated from Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from ʿUthmān ibn ʿĪsā, from Manṣūr ibn Ḥāzim, from Bakr ibn Ḥabīb, who said: I asked Abā Jaʿfar عليه السلام about the tashahhud, and he said: If it were obligatory upon the people as they say, they would have perished. The people only used to say the easiest of what they knew. When you praise Allah, it suffices you. So the correct way to understand this report is that the negation of obligation is directed only to what exceeds the two testimonies, because that is recommended and not obligatory like the two testimonies. And what indicates that is:

What Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥakam, from Abū Ayyūb al-Khazzāz, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, who said: I said to Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام: The tashahhud in salat (prayer)? He said: Twice. He said: I said: And how is it twice? He said: When you have settled sitting, then say: I bear witness that there is no god but Allah alone, having no partner, and I bear witness that Muḥammad is His servant and His Messenger; then you depart. He said: I said to him: The servant’s saying, “All greetings are for Allah, and the salats and the good things are for Allah”? He said: This wording is from du'a (supplication) by which the servant speaks gently to his Lord.

As for what Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb narrated from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan, from Ṣafwān, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Bukayr, from ʿUbayd ibn Zurārah, who said: I said to Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام: A man experiences hadath after he has raised his head from the final sajdah. He said: His salat is complete; the tashahhud in the salat is only sunnah. So he performs wudu (ablution), sits in his place or in a clean place, and then recites the tashahhud. The proper way regarding this narration is that we understand it to apply to one who experiences hadath after the two testimonies, even if he has not completed the remainder of the testimony; then he completes his salat. But if the hadath had occurred before that, it would have been obligatory for him to repeat it from its beginning, as we have explained. As for his statement, 'the tashahhud in the salat is only sunnah,' its meaning is what goes beyond the two testimonies, as we have explained, and his instruction to repeat it after wudu is understood as recommendation.

As for what Saʿd narrated from Abū Jaʿfar, from his father, from Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā and al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd and Muḥammad ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Ibn Udhaynah, from Zurārah, from Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام, concerning: Regarding a man who incurs hadath after raising his head from the final sajdah and before performing tashahhud, he said: He turns away and performs wudu (ablution). Then, if he wishes, he may return to the mosque; if he wishes, then in his house; and if he wishes, wherever he wishes, he sits and performs tashahhud, then gives salām. And if the hadath occurred after the two shahadahs, then his salat has passed validly. So the sound way regarding this report is that we understand it as applying to one who entered into the salat with tayammum, then incurred hadath forgetfully before the two shahadahs. In that case, he performs wudu (ablution) if he has found water and completes the salat with the two shahadahs, and repeating it is not required of him, just as he may complete it if he had incurred hadath before that, as we explained previously. It is also possible that his saying, 'before he performs tashahhud,' only meant completing the recommended tashahhud in full, not that what was meant by it was the two shahadahs, as we said concerning the first report equally.

Ibn Abi ʿUmayr, from Abi Basir, from Zurarah, from Abi ʿAbdillah عليه السلام, that he said: Part of the completion of fasting is giving zakat, just as salat upon the Prophet صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم is part of the completion of prayer. Whoever fasts and does not render it, then there is no fasting for him if he leaves it deliberately; and whoever performs prayer and does not send salat upon the Prophet صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم, and leaves that deliberately, then there is no prayer for him. Indeed, Allah, Exalted is He, began with it before prayer, so He said: “Certainly successful is he who purifies himself, and mentions the name of his Lord, then prays.”

As for what Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb narrated from ʿAlī ibn Khālid, from Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan, from ʿAmr ibn Saʿīd, from Muṣaddaq ibn Ṣadaqah, from ʿAmmār al-Sābāṭī, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: If a man forgets the tashahhud in the salat and remembers that he said only “Bismillah,” then his salat has been valid. But if he does not remember anything from the tashahhud, he repeats the salat. The correct understanding of this report is that if he remembers that he said “Bismillah,” then his salat is complete, and he completes the two testimonies by way of qaḍāʾ, and he does not repeat the salat. And if he remembers nothing at all, he repeats the salat if he had left it deliberately. There is nothing in the report stating whether this applies when he did not remember it after leaving it forgetfully or deliberately. And if he had left it inadvertently and then remembered, then the qaḍāʾ of the tashahhud would be upon him, as we have explained.

As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Saʿd ibn Bakr, from Ḥabīb al-Khathʿamī, from Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said: I heard him saying: When a man sits for the tashahhud and praises Allah, that suffices him. So the proper way to understand this report is taqiyyah, because it is the view of many among the common people, and we have already explained the obligation of the two testimonies and salat upon the Prophet صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Fadalah, from Jamil ibn Darrāj, from Muhammad ibn Muslim and Zurārah ibn A'yan, who said: We asked Abā Ja'far عليه السلام about a man who forgets the qunūt until he bows. He said: He should perform the qunūt after the ruku'. But if he does not remember, then there is nothing upon him.

And from him, from Hammad ibn 'Isa, from Hariz, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I asked Aba 'Abdillah عليه السلام about the qunut that a man forgets, and he said: He should perform qunut after he bows in ruku'. If he does not remember until he finishes and departs, then there is nothing upon him.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from al-Hasan ibn 'Ali ibn Faddal, from 'Ubayd ibn Zurarah, who said: I said to Abī 'Abdillāh عليه السلام: A man remembered that he had not recited the qunut until he had bowed. He said: Then he said, he should recite the qunut when he raises his head.

From him, from ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥakam, from Abū Ayyūb, from Abū Baṣīr, who said: I heard it being mentioned in the presence of Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام; he said concerning a man who forgets the qunūt: he should perform the qunūt after he finishes and while he is sitting.

As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā narrated from Muḥammad ibn Sahl, from his father, who said: I asked Abā al-Ḥasan عليه السلام about a man who forgot the qunūt in the obligatory prayer. He said: There is no repetition required upon him.

As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Faḍālah, from Muʿāwiyah ibn ʿAmmār, he said: I asked him about a man who forgets the qunūt until he bows: should he perform qunūt? He said: No. So it is possible that the meaning in these two reports is that making it up is not obligatory upon him; rather, it is only recommended, because initiating it is recommended, so how then would making it up be otherwise? And it is possible that what is meant by it is that he does not make it up when the circumstance is a circumstance of taqiyyah; that is indicated by this.

From what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from him, who said: Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام said to me regarding the qunut in the fajr prayer: If you wish, then perform qunut, and if you wish, then do not perform qunut. And he said: when there is taqiyyah, then do not perform qunut, and I adhere to this.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Fadalah, from Aban, from Zurarah, from Abu Ja'far عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who performs salat (prayer), then sits and breaks wudu (ablution) before giving taslim. He said: His salat (prayer) is complete.

As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from ʿUthmān ibn ʿĪsā, from Samāʿah, from Abī Baṣīr, who said: I heard Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام saying about a man who had performed the dawn prayer, then when he sat in the two rakʿahs before reciting the tashahhud, he had a nosebleed: He said: Let him go out, wash his nose, then return and complete his salat (prayer). He said: Indeed, the end of the salat (prayer) is the taslīm. His statement عليه السلام, “Indeed, the end of the salat (prayer) is the taslīm,” is to be understood as referring to merit and perfection. As for completing the salat (prayer), that is indispensable, because part of its completion is bringing the two testimonies and the salat upon the Prophet صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم, as we have explained.

Abu al-Husayn ibn Abi al-Jayd al-Qummi informed me, from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn al-Walid, from al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan ibn Aban, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Ibrahim al-Khazzaz, from 'Abd al-Hamid ibn 'Awwad, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: If you are leading a people, one taslim to your right suffices for you. If you are with an Imam, then two taslims. And if you are alone, then one, while facing the qiblah.

From him, from Safwan, from Mansur ibn Hazim, who said: Abu 'Abdillah عليه السلام said: The Imam gives one taslim, and those behind him give two taslims; but if there is no one on his left, he gives one taslim.

From him, from Faḍālah, from Ḥusayn, from Ibn Muskān, from ʿAnbasah ibn Muṣʿab, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about a man who stands in the row behind the Imam, while there is no one on his left—how should he give salām? He said: One taslīmah to his right.

As for what al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from 'Umar ibn Udhaynah, from Zurarah and Muhammad ibn Muslim and Ma'mar ibn Yahya and Isma'il, from Abi Ja'far عليه السلام, who said: He gives one taslim, whether he is an Imam or otherwise. The proper way regarding this report is that we understand it to mean when the follower has no one on his left, as he explained in the narration of Mansur ibn Hazim and 'Anbasah ibn Mus'ab; and what follows further clarifies that.

What al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Ibn Muskan, from Abi Basir, from Abi 'Abdillah عليه السلام, who said: When you are an Imam, the taslim is only that you send salutation upon the Prophet صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم and say: “Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of Allah.” Then when you have said that, the salat has ended. Then you signal to the people and say, while facing the qiblah: “Peace be upon you, and the mercy of Allah, and His blessings.” Likewise, when you are alone, you say: “Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of Allah,” just as you gave salutation while being an Imam. So when you are in a congregation, then say the same as you said, and give salutation to those on your right and your left. If there is no one on your left, then give salutation to those on your right, and do not omit the taslim to your right if there is no one on your left.

Al-Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn al-Walid, from his father, from al-Saffar, from Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from Hafs al-Jawhari, who said: Abu al-Hasan 'Ali ibn Muhammad عليه السلام led us in the maghrib prayer. Then he performed the sajdah of shukr after the seventh, so I said to him, "Your forefathers used to prostrate after the third." He said, "None of my forefathers ever prostrated except after the seventh."

As for what was narrated by Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn al-Walid, from al-Saffar, from al-'Abbas ibn Ma'ruf, from Sa'dan ibn Muslim, from Jahm ibn Abi Jahm, who said: I saw Abū al-Ḥasan Mūsā ibn Ja'far عليه السلام, and he had performed a sajdah after the three rak'ahs of Maghrib. So I said to him: May I be your ransom, I saw you perform sajdah after the three. He said: You saw me? I said: Yes. He said: Then do not leave it, for du'a in it is answered. The proper way regarding this narration is that we carry it upon a kind of recommendation, and the first one upon permissibility. And his statement in the first report, 'None of my forefathers would perform sajdah except after the seventh,' is to inform that they did not choose to do it, or that they did not perform it as an obligation, even if they did perform it by way of merit.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from 'Uthman ibn 'Isa, from Ibn Muskan, from Sulayman ibn Khalid, from Abi 'Abdillah عليه السلام, who said: Al-witr is three rak'ahs; separation is made between them, and in all of them Sūrat Qul Huwa Allahu Ahad is recited.
From him, from Hammad, from Shu'ayb, from Abi Basir, from Abi 'Abdillah عليه السلام, who said: The witr is three rak'ahs: two separated, and one.

From him, from al-Naḍr, from Muḥammad ibn Abī Ḥamzah, from Muʿāwiyah ibn ʿAmmār, who said: I said to Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام: “The taslīm in the two rakʿahs of al-watr?” He said: “It awakens the sleeper, and you may speak concerning a need.”

From him, from al-Naḍr, from Muḥammad ibn Abī Ḥamzah, from Abū Wallād Ḥafṣ ibn Sālim, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about the taslim in the two rakʿahs of al-watr. He said: Yes. So if you have a need, then go out and fulfill it, then return and perform one rakʿah.
Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from al-Barqī, from Saʿd ibn Saʿd al-Ashʿarī, from Abī al-Ḥasan al-Riḍā عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about al-witr: is it separation or joining? He said: separation.

As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from al-Naḍr, from Muḥammad ibn Abī Ḥamzah, from Yaʿqūb ibn Shuʿayb, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about the taslīm in the two rakʿahs of al-watr. He said: If you wish, you may say the taslīm; and if you wish, you may refrain from saying the taslīm.

From him, from al-Naḍr, from Muḥammad ibn Abī Ḥamzah, from Muʿāwiyah ibn ʿAmmār, who said: I said to Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام: “The taslīm in the two rakʿahs of al-watr?” He said: “If you wish, you may say the taslīm, and if you wish, you may refrain from saying the taslīm.”

From him, from Muḥammad ibn Ziyād, from Kurdawayh al-Hamadanī, who said: I asked al-ʿAbd al-Ṣāliḥ عليه السلام about the witr, and he said: Join it. So the proper way regarding all of these narrations is that we carry them upon a form of taqiyyah, because they agree with the doctrines of many of the ʿammah, while the purport of two hadiths among them is choice, and that is not the doctrine of anyone. For whoever deems joining obligatory does not permit separation, and whoever deems separation obligatory does not permit joining. And it is possible that his statement, 'if he wishes he gives salām, and if he wishes he does not give salām,' is an indication toward the speech which becomes permissible by the taslīm, because that is not a condition in it, clarifying what we have mentioned.

What al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Ṣafwān, from Manṣūr, from a mawlā of Abī Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said: As for the two rakʿahs of al-watr, if you wish, you may speak between them and the third; and if you wish, you may refrain from doing so.

Al-Husayn ibn ʿUbayd Allah informed me, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn ʿAbd al-Hamid, from Sayf ibn ʿAmirah, from Mansur ibn Hazim, who said: A number of our companions narrated to me from Abi ʿAbd Allah عليه السلام. He said: Seven buckets are to be drawn from it when a boy urinates into it, or a mouse falls into it, or something similar to it.

As for what Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā narrated from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥakam, from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ḥamzah, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, he said: I asked him about the urine of a weaned boy that falls into the well, so he said: one bucket. I said: the urine of a man? He said: forty buckets are to be drawn from it. So this does not contradict the first report, because it is possible that it be understood as referring to the urine of a boy who had not eaten food.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Ali ibn Muhammad al-Qasani, from Sulayman ibn Hafs al-Marwazi, said: Abu al-Hasan al-Akhir عليه السلام said: Beware of sleeping between Salat al-Layl and al-Fajr; rather, a brief lying down without sleep. For indeed, its practitioner is not praised for what he has sent ahead of his prayer.

As for what Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated from Ahmad and ʿAbd Allah, the two sons of Muhammad ibn ʿIsa, from ʿAli ibn al-Hakam, from ʿAbd Allah ibn Bukayr, from Zurarah, from Abi Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said: It is only upon one of you, when half the night has passed, to rise and perform his salat all together in one sequence: thirteen rakʿahs. Then, if he wishes, he may sit and make du'a; if he wishes, he may sleep; and if he wishes, he may go wherever he wishes. So this narration came as a concession, lifting the prohibition. What is more excellent, however, is to leave sleeping aside, in accordance with what the other narration contains.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Abu Ja'far, from Abu al-Jawza', from al-Husayn ibn 'Ulwan, from 'Amr ibn Khalid, from 'Asim ibn Abi al-Najud al-Asadi, from Ibn 'Umar, from al-Hasan ibn 'Ali عليه السلام, who said: I heard my father, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib عليه السلام, saying: The Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم said: Any Muslim man who sits in his place of prayer in which he performed the fajr prayer, remembering Allah until the sun rises, there shall be for him a reward like that of one who performed hajj to the House of Allah, and he shall be forgiven. And if he remains sitting there until there comes an hour in which prayer becomes permissible, then he performs two rak'ahs or four, what has previously passed of his sins shall be forgiven for him, and there shall be for him a reward like that of one who performed hajj to the House of Allah.

Al-‘Alā’ narrated from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, from one of the two of them, peace be upon him, who said: I asked him about sleeping after the morning prayer, and he said: Indeed, rizq is spread out during that hour, so I dislike that a man should sleep during that hour. And al-Ṣādiq عليه السلام said: The sleep of early morning is ill-omened; it drives away rizq, yellows the complexion, makes it ugly, and alters it. It is the sleep of every ill-fated one. Indeed, Allah, Exalted is He, apportions sustenance between the rising of dawn and the rising of the sun.

As for what Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb narrated from Mūsā ibn ʿUmar, from Muʿammar ibn Khallād, who said: Abū al-Ḥasan al-Riḍā عليه السلام sent for me regarding a need, so I entered upon him. He said: 'Return, and when it is tomorrow, then come; and do not come except after sunrise, for I sleep when I have performed the fajr prayer.'

From him, from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Hāshim, from Sālim ibn Abī Khadījah, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: A man asked him while I was listening, and he said: “I perform the fajr prayer, then I remember Allah, the Exalted, with whatever I wish to remember of what is obligatory upon me. I want to lie on my side and sleep before sunrise, but I dislike that.” He عليه السلام said: “And why?” He said: “I dislike that the sun should rise from other than its place of rising.” He عليه السلام said: “There is no obscurity in that. Look to where the dawn rises, and from there the sun rises. There is no hardship upon you in sleeping if you have remembered Allah.” So the interpretation of these two narrations is that they indicate a kind of concession, even though what we have presented in the earlier narrations is more virtuous.

The Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn al-Walid, from his father, from al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan ibn Aban, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Safwan, from Ibn Bukayr, from 'Ubayd ibn Zurarah, who said: I asked Aba 'Abd Allah عليه السلام about a man who began the salat (prayer) and forgot to say the takbir until he had commenced the salat (prayer). He said: He repeats the salat (prayer).
From him, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Jamīl, from Zurārah, who said: I asked Abā Jaʿfar عليه السلام about a man who forgets the takbīrat al-iḥrām. He said: He repeats.

From him, from Faḍālah, from Ṣafwān, from al-ʿAlāʾ, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, from one of the two عليهما السلام, concerning about one who remembers that he did not say the takbir at the beginning of his salat (prayer). He said: If he becomes certain that he did not say the takbir, then let him repeat; but how can he be certain?

Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā, from ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥakam, from Dhurayḥ ibn Muḥammad al-Muḥāribī, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who forgets to pronounce the takbīr until he has recited. He said: He should pronounce the takbīr.

From him, from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Yaqṭīn, from his brother al-Ḥusayn, from his father ʿAlī ibn Yaqṭīn, who said: I asked Abā al-Ḥasan عليه السلام about a man who forgets to begin the salat (prayer) until he bows in rukuʿ. He said: He must repeat the salat (prayer).

As for what Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from Muḥammad ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Ḥammād ibn ʿUthmān, from ʿUbayd Allah al-Ḥalabī, from Abī ʿAbd Allah عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who forgot to say the takbir until he had entered into the salat (prayer). He said: “Was it not his intention to say the takbir?” I said: “Yes.” He said: “Then let him continue in his salat (prayer).”

Saʿd narrated from Abū Jaʿfar, from ʿAlī ibn Ḥadīd and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Najrān, from Ḥammād ibn ʿĪsā, from Ḥarīz ibn ʿAbd Allāh, from Zurārah, from Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said: I said to him: A man forgets the first takbir of the opening. He said: If he remembers it before the rukuʿ, he should say the takbir, then recite, then perform rukuʿ. And if he remembers it during the salat, he should say it while standing, in the place of the takbir, before the recitation and after the recitation. I said: Then if he remembers it after the salat? He said: Then let him make it up, and there is nothing upon him.

ʿAlī ibn Mahziyār, from Faḍālah ibn Ayyūb, from al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿUthmān, from Samāʿah ibn Mihrān, from Abī Baṣīr, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about a man who stood in salat (prayer) and forgot to say the takbīr, so he began with the recitation. He said: If he remembers it while standing, before he performs rukuʿ, then let him say the takbīr; and if he has already performed rukuʿ, then let him proceed in his salat (prayer). The proper way regarding these reports is that we interpret them as applying to one who doubts the opening takbīrah and does not remember it with certainty. So if this is his state, then he says the takbīr so long as he has not yet performed rukuʿ, as a precaution; but once he has performed rukuʿ, he proceeds in his salat (prayer), because he has moved to another state. But if he knew with certain knowledge, then repeating the salat (prayer) would be required of him, according to what we have already presented in the earlier reports.

Al-Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Abū al-Qāsim Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Muḥammad al-Ashʿarī, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀmir, from ʿAlī ibn Mahziyār, from Faḍālah, from Abān, from al-Faḍl ibn ʿAbd al-Malik or Ibn Abī Yaʿfūr, from Abū ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, that he said: Regarding a man who performs salat (prayer) but did not begin with the takbir, does the takbir of rukūʿ suffice for him? He said: No. Rather, he must repeat his salat (prayer) if he is certain that he did not say the takbir.

As for what Saʿd narrated from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn ibn Abī al-Khaṭṭāb, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn Abī Naṣr, from Abū al-Ḥasan al-Riḍā عليه السلام, he said: I said to him: A man forgot to pronounce the opening takbīrah until he said the takbīrah for rukūʿ. He said: It suffices him. The proper understanding of this report as well is what we stated regarding the previous reports: that it is not established that he did not pronounce the opening takbīrah. So if he pronounces the takbīrah for rukūʿ, that suffices for the takbīrah about which we said he should take precaution with it. But if omitting it were established with certainty, then it would be necessary to restart the salat (prayer), as we have explained.

Al-Husayn ibn Ubayd Allah al-Ghada'iri informed me, from a number of our companions, from Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Rib'i ibn Abd Allah, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from one of the two of them عليهما السلام, who said: Indeed Allah, Mighty and Majestic, made ruku' and sujud obligatory, while recitation is sunnah (prophetic tradition). So whoever deliberately leaves the recitation must repeat the salat (prayer), and whoever forgets the recitation, then his salat (prayer) is complete, and there is nothing upon him.

From him, from Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from Ibn Faḍḍāl, from Yūnus ibn Yaʿqūb, from Manṣūr ibn Ḥāzim, who said: I said to Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام: I performed the obligatory prayer, but I forgot to recite throughout my entire prayer. He said: Have you not completed the bowing and the prostration? I said: Yes. He said: Then your prayer has been completed, if it was out of forgetfulness.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Hammad ibn 'Isa, from Fadalah, from Mu'awiyah ibn 'Ammar, from Abi 'Abdillah عليه السلام, who said: I said: A man forgets the recitation in the first two rak'ahs, then remembers in the last two rak'ahs that he did not recite. He said: Has he completed the ruku' and the sujud? I said: Yes. He said: Indeed, I dislike that I should make the end of my salat its beginning.

From him, from Faḍālah, from Ḥusayn ibn ʿUthmān, from Samāʿah, from Abī Baṣīr, who said: If he forgets to recite in the first and second rakʿahs, the tasbih of the rukuʿ and sujud suffices for him. And if it is the morning prayer and he forgets to recite in it, then he should continue in his salat.

As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Faḍālah, from al-ʿAlāʾ, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, from Abī Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about one who does not recite Fātiḥat al-Kitāb in his salat (prayer). He said: There is no salat (prayer) for him unless he recites it, whether aloud or quietly. So the proper way regarding this narration is that we interpret it as applying to one who deliberately did not recite it, not one who forgot. For indeed, he has no salat (prayer), according to what we have explained in the earlier reports, and what follows further clarifies that.

What al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from 'Uthman ibn 'Isa, from Sama'ah, who said: I asked him about a man who stands in salat (prayer) and forgets Fatihat al-Kitab. He said: Then let him say: “I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan.” Indeed, Allah is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing. Then let him recite it so long as he has not yet bowed, for there is no salat (prayer) for him until he recites it, whether aloud or quietly. But if he has bowed, that will suffice for him, if Allah wills.

As for what Sa'd narrated from Abū al-Jawzā’, from al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿUlwān, from ʿAmr ibn Khālid, from Zayd ibn ʿAlī عليه السلام, he said: I prayed behind my father in the Maghrib prayer, and he forgot Fātiḥat al-Kitāb in the first rakʿah, so he recited it in the second.

Saʿd narrated from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from Ibn Abī Naṣr, from ʿAbd al-Karīm ibn ʿAmr, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Ḥammād, from Abū ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said: I said to him: I become heedless regarding the recitation in the first rakʿah. He said: Recite in the second. I said: I become heedless in the second. He said: Recite in the third. I said: I become heedless in my entire salat (prayer). He said: If you have preserved the rukuʿ and the sujud, then your salat (prayer) is complete. His statement عليه السلام, 'If it escaped you in the first, then recite in the second,' did not mean that he should repeat the recitation that he missed in the first; rather, he meant that he should recite in the second and the third what pertains to each of them from the recitation. As for the first, its ruling has already passed. The correct understanding of that is that whoever forgets the recitation in the first two rakʿahs must recite in the third and fourth and leave the tasbih that would have been permissible for him had he recited in the first two, so that his salat (prayer) does not remain entirely without recitation.

Al-Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan ibn Aban, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Safwan, from Abi Basir, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: If a man becomes certain that he omitted a rak'ah of the salat (prayer), and he has already performed two sajdahs while having omitted the ruku', he must restart the salat (prayer).

From him, from Faḍālah, from Rifāʿah, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who forgot to perform ruku' until he had performed sajdah and stood up. He said: He starts over.
From him, from Ibn Abi ʿUmayr, from Rifāʿah, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about a man who forgot to bow until he prostrated and stood up. He said: He restarts.
From him, from Muḥammad ibn Sinān, from Ibn Muskān, from Abī Baṣīr, who said: I asked Abā Jaʿfar عليه السلام about a man who forgot to perform the bowing. He said: repeating the prayer is upon him.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Safwan, from Ishaq ibn 'Ammar, who said: I asked Aba Ibrahim عليه السلام about a man who forgets to perform the ruku'. He said: He is to begin again, until he places everything of that in its proper place.

As for what Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from al-Hakam ibn Miskin, from al-'Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abi Ja'far عليه السلام, concerning: A man who doubts, after having performed sajdah, that he did not do ruku'. He said: if he becomes certain, then let him discard the two sajdahs for which there is no rak'ah, then let him continue his salat to completion. And if he did not become certain until after he had finished and departed, then let him stand and perform one rak'ah and two sajdahs, and there is nothing upon him. The correct way regarding this narration is that we interpret it as referring to one who forgot the ruku' in the last two rak'ahs; then he discards the two sajdahs and completes his salat. But if his forgetfulness was in the first two rak'ahs, then repeating the salat is obligatory upon him, in accordance with what the earlier reports have contained.

As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Ṣafwān, from Manṣūr, from Abī Baṣīr, who said: If a man becomes certain that he has omitted a rakʿah from the salat (prayer), and he has already performed two sajdahs and omitted the rukuʿ, then he restarts the salat (prayer). This does not contradict what we have said, because we interpret this report as referring to one who forgot the rukuʿ in a salat (prayer) in which inadvertence is not allowed, such as the dawn prayer or the maghrib prayer, or concerning the first two rakʿahs, according to what we stated in the earlier reports. And that which clarifies what we have mentioned...

What Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Ja'far ibn Bashir, from Hammad ibn 'Uthman, from Hakam ibn Hukaym, who said: I asked Aba 'Abd Allah عليه السلام about a man who forgets a rak'ah from his salat (prayer), or a sajdah, or more than that, then remembers. He said: He makes up exactly that itself. I said: Does he repeat the salat (prayer)? He said: No.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Fadalah, from Hammad, from 'Imran al-Halabi, who said: I said: A man doubts while he is standing, and does not know whether he has performed ruku' or not. He said: Then let him perform ruku'.

From him, from Muḥammad ibn Sinān, from Ibn Muskān, from Abī Baṣīr, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about a man who doubts while he is standing and does not know whether he has performed rukuʿ or has not performed rukuʿ. He said: He performs rukuʿ and prostrates.

From him, from Faḍālah, from Ḥusayn, from Ibn Muskan, from Abū Baṣīr and al-Ḥalabī, concerning: A man who does not know whether he has performed ruku' or has not performed ruku'—he said: he should perform ruku'.

As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Faḍālah, from Abān, from al-Fuḍayl ibn Yasār, who said: I said to Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام: I become fully upright standing, then I do not know whether I performed rukuʿ or not? He said: Yes, you have performed rukuʿ, so continue in your salat, for that is only from al-Shayṭān. So this does not contradict what we mentioned, because the correct way regarding this report is that we interpret it as referring to one who has become fully upright standing from sajdah to the second rakʿah, or to the third after the first tashahhud, and then doubts the rukuʿ in the rakʿah whose ruling has already passed. He does not pay attention to that doubt, because he has already moved on to another state, and that doubt does not entail any ruling. And that which indicates this is...

What al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Faḍālah, from Ḥammād ibn ʿUthmān, who said: I said to Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام: I doubt while I am in sajdah, and I do not know whether I performed rukuʿ or not. He said: Proceed.

From him, from Safwan, from Hammad ibn 'Uthman, who said: I said to Abī 'Abdillāh عليه السلام: I doubt while I am in sajdah, and I do not know whether I performed ruku' or not. So he said: You have performed ruku'; continue.

Saʿd narrated from Abū Jaʿfar, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from Faḍālah, from al-ʿAlāʾ ibn Razīn, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, from one of the two عليهما السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who doubts, after he has performed sajdah, that he did not perform rukuʿ. He said: He should continue in his salat (prayer).

From him, from Abū Jaʿfar, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn Abī Naṣr, from Abān ibn ʿUthmān, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī ʿAbdillāh, who said: I said to Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام: A man moved down toward sajdah and does not know whether he performed rukuʿ or did not perform rukuʿ. He said: He has performed rukuʿ.

Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Mughirah, from Isma'il ibn Jabir, who said: Abu Ja'far عليه السلام said: If he doubts about the ruku' after he has already performed sajdah, then let him proceed. And if he doubts about the sujud after he has stood up, then let him proceed. Everything about which he doubts, from that which he has already passed beyond and entered into something else, then let him proceed upon it.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Ibn Miskan, from Abi Basir, who said: I asked him about one who forgot to perform one sajdah and then remembered it while he was standing. He said: He should perform it when he remembers it, so long as he has not yet bowed in ruku'. But if he has already performed ruku', then he should continue with his salat, and when he finishes, he should make it up; and there is no sahw upon him.

Sa'd narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Mughirah, from Isma'il ibn Jabir, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, concerning: A man forgot to perform one sajdah from the second [unit] until he stood up, then remembered while he was standing that he had not performed the sajdah. He عليه السلام said: Let him perform the sajdah so long as he has not gone into ruku'. But if he has gone into ruku' and then remembers after his ruku' that he did not perform the sajdah, then let him continue with his salat until he gives salām, then he should perform it, for it is a qada'.

From him, from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan ibn 'Ali ibn Faddal, from 'Amr ibn Sa'id, from Musaddiq ibn Sadaqah, from 'Ammar al-Sabati, from Abi 'Abdillah عليه السلام, concerning Regarding a man who forgets one sajdah, then remembers it after he has stood up and performed ruku', he said: He continues in his salat and does not perform the sajdah until he gives salam. Then when he gives salam, he performs a sajdah like the one he missed. I said: And if he does not remember except after that? He said: He makes up what he missed when he remembers it.

As for what Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā narrated from ʿAlī ibn Ismāʿīl, from a man, from Muʿallā ibn Khunays, who said: I asked Abā al-Ḥasan al-Māḍī عليه السلام about a man who forgets a sajdah in his salat. He said: If he remembers it before his rukuʿ, he performs it and continues his salat; then he performs the two sajdahs of sahw after finishing. But if he remembers it after his rukuʿ, he repeats the salat, and forgetting a sajdah in the first two rakʿahs and the last two is the same. What this report contains in his statement, 'If he remembers it after his rukuʿ, he repeats the salat,' admits two possibilities. One of them is that it refers to one who left both sajdahs together, for whoever is in this condition must repeat the salat; and for this reason he said, 'Forgetting the sajdah in the first two rakʿahs and the last two is the same,' meaning with respect to the two sajdahs together. The second is that this is to be understood regarding a single sajdah, and that this ruling is specific to the first two rakʿahs; and that his statement, 'Forgetting the sajdah in the first two rakʿahs and the last two is the same,' is a new ruling concerning the two sajdahs together. And that which indicates the distinction that we have mentioned...

What Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā narrated from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn Abī Naṣr, who said: I asked Abā al-Ḥasan عليه السلام about a man who prayed two rakʿahs, then remembered in the second while he was in rukuʿ that he had left out one sajdah in the first. He said: Abū al-Ḥasan عليه السلام used to say: If you leave out a sajdah in the first rakʿah and do not know whether it was one or two, then you begin again so that two valid rakʿahs are established for you. And if it is in the third and fourth, and you have left out a sajdah after having preserved the rukuʿ, then you repeat the sajdah.

As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā narrated from ʿAlī ibn Aḥmad, from Mūsā ibn ʿUmar, from Muḥammad ibn Manṣūr, who said: I asked him about one who forgets the second sajdah of the second rakʿah, or doubts concerning it. So he said: If you fear that you only placed your face down once, then when you give salām, perform one sajdah and place your face down once, and there is no sahw upon you. So this does not contradict the detail that we presented earlier, because his statement, 'the one who forgets the second sajdah of the second rakʿah,' may mean that he intended the second rakʿah of the last two rakʿahs. In the apparent wording of the report, it is not specified whether it is the second rakʿah of the first two or of the last two; rather, it can bear both meanings together. So when that is possible, we interpret it as the second rakʿah of the last two, so that it accords with what was detailed in the first report.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Safwan, from Ibn Abi Ya'fur, from Abi 'Abdillah عليه السلام, that he said: If a man forgets one sajdah and is certain that he omitted it, then he should perform it after he sits, before he gives salām. But if he is doubtful, then he should give salām, then perform it, and let him recite a light tashahhud. And he should not call it a peck, for the peck is the peck of the crow.

Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā narrated from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from some of our companions, from Sufyān ibn al-Simṭ, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: You perform the two sajdahs of forgetfulness for every addition that occurs in your prayer or any omission. And this report does not contradict the report we presented in the first chapter from Abū Baṣīr in his statement, 'There is no sahw upon him,' because the meaning of his statement 'There is no sahw upon him' is only that his ruling is not the ruling of one who is forgetful; rather, his ruling is the ruling of one who has cut off and resumed. For when he remembers what he missed and makes it up, no doubt concerning it remains upon him, so he departs from the state of forgetfulness.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from 'Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, who said: Abu 'Abdillah عليه السلام was asked about a man who became forgetful and did not know whether he had performed one sajdah or two. He said: He should perform one more sajdah, and after the completion of the salat, the two sajdahs of forgetfulness are not required upon him.

From him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Ibn Miskan, from Abi Basir, who said: I asked Aba Abdillah عليه السلام about a man who doubted and did not know whether he had performed one sajdah or two sajdahs. He said: He should perform sajdah until he becomes certain that they are two sajdahs.

From him, from ʿAlī, from his father, from ʿAmr ibn ʿUthmān, from al-Mufaḍḍal ibn Ṣāliḥ, from Zayd al-Shaḥḥām, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, concerning: A man became confused and did not know whether he had performed one sajdah or two. He said: Then let him perform another one.

Saʿd narrated from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from Ibn Abī Naṣr, from Abān ibn ʿUthmān, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī ʿAbd Allāh, who said: I said to Abū ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام: A man raised his head from sajdah, then doubted before becoming fully settled in a sitting position, and he did not know whether he had performed sajdah or had not performed sajdah. He said: He should perform sajdah. I said: Then a man rose from his sajdah before becoming fully upright standing, and he did not know whether he had performed sajdah or had not performed sajdah. He said: He should perform sajdah.

As for what Saʿd narrated from Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan, from ʿAmr ibn Saʿīd, from Muṣaddaq ibn Ṣadaqah, from ʿAmmār al-Sābāṭī, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, concerning: A man upon whom confusion frequently occurs in salat (prayer), so he doubts regarding the rukuʿ, not knowing whether he bowed or not, and he doubts regarding the sujud, not knowing whether he prostrated or not—so he said: He should not prostrate nor bow; rather, he should continue in his salat (prayer) until he becomes certain with certainty. So this report bears two possibilities: one of them is that he doubts after having entered into another state, and he does not remember with certainty having omitted the bowing or the prostration; then he ought to continue in his salat (prayer) according to what we explained previously. The second is that it is specific to one upon whom forgetfulness frequently occurs, so he was given concession to continue in his salat (prayer) as a facilitation, because the forgetful person, whenever he prostrates and then doubts, would need to prostrate again and thus would never be free of it; for that reason, he was given concession to continue in it.

Al-Husayn ibn ʿUbayd Allah informed me, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Muhammad ibn ʿAli ibn Mahbub, from Ahmad, from his father, from ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Mughirah, from ʿUmar ibn Yazid, who said: ʿAmr ibn Saʿid ibn Hilal narrated to me, saying: I asked Aba Jaʿfar عليه السلام about what falls into the well, from a mouse and a cat up to a sheep. So he said: For all of that, seven buckets are prescribed. He said: Then when I reached the donkey and the camel, he said: A kurr of water.

As for what Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb narrated from Aḥmad ibn Idrīs, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Jabbār, from Ṣafwān, from Ibn Muskān, from al-Ḥalabī, from Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said: If a small thing falls into the well and dies in it, then draw out buckets from it. If a person in janabah falls into it, then draw out seven buckets from it. And if a camel dies in it, or wine is poured into it, then all of the water must be drawn out.

And among what al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated, from al-Nadr, from 'Abd Allah ibn Sinan, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: If a small animal falls into the well, or a person in janabah enters it, seven buckets are drawn from it. But if a bull dies in it, or wine is poured into it, then all of the water is drawn out. So what these two reports contain regarding the obligation of drawing out all the water when a camel falls into it is what I act upon and according to which I give fatwa. That does not conflict with the first report in his saying, “a kurr of water,” when the questioner asked about the donkey and the camel, because it is not impossible that he عليه السلام answered with what specifically concerns the ruling of the donkey, and relied regarding the ruling of the camel upon what had already been heard from him concerning the obligation of drawing out all the water. As for wine, then all the water of the well is to be drawn out if any of it falls into it, in accordance with what the two reports contain, and that is also supported by...

What Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb narrated from Yaʿqūb ibn Yazīd, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Muʿāwiyah ibn ʿAmmār, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, concerning A well into which a child urinates, or urine is poured into it, or wine is poured into it—he said: all of the water is to be drawn out. So what this report includes of mentioning urine together with wine is to be understood as when one of the qualities of the water has changed, because if it has not changed, then it has a specific fixed amount to be drawn out, as we shall explain later.

As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Muḥammad ibn Ziyād, from Kurdawayh, who said: I asked Abā al-Ḥasan عليه السلام about a well into which a drop of blood, or intoxicating nabīdh, or urine, or wine falls. He said: Thirty buckets are to be drawn from it.

And what Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā narrated from Abū Isḥāq, from Nūḥ ibn Shuʿayb al-Khurāsānī, from Bashīr, from Ḥarīz, from Zurārah, who said: I said to Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام: A well into which a drop of blood or wine has dripped. He said: Blood, wine, carrion, and pig meat are all one in that regard: twenty buckets are to be drawn from it; and if the odor prevails, it should be drained until it becomes wholesome. So these two reports are not acted upon, because they are solitary reports, and the reports that we have presented earlier are not opposed by them. Also because impurity is known by the occurrence of wine in it, and we do not know with certainty its purification except by drawing out all the water of the well, so practice should accordingly be based on that. It is also possible that the report is specific to the ruling of urine, because the urine of a man necessitates drawing forty buckets, as we explained in Tahdhīb al-Aḥkām; and likewise is the ruling of blood, carrion, and pig meat. Thus, the addition of wine to that may be an error from the narrator.

Al-Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from al-Saffar, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from al-Husayn ibn Abi al-Ala', who said: I asked Abu Abdillah عليه السلام about a man who prays the first two rak'ahs of an obligatory prayer and does not sit in them until he bows in the third. He said: Let him complete his salat, then let him give salam, and perform the two sajdahs of forgetfulness while seated before he speaks.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Hisham ibn Salim, from Sulayman ibn Khalid, who said: I asked Abu 'Abdillah عليه السلام about a man who forgot to sit in the first two rak'ahs. He said: If he remembers before he bows in ruku', then he should sit; but if he does not remember until he has bowed, then he should complete the salat (prayer), and when he has finished and given salām, he should perform the two sajdahs of forgetfulness.

From him, from Faḍālah, from al-ʿAlāʾ, from Ibn Abī Yaʿfūr, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about a man who prays the first two rakʿahs of the obligatory prayer and does not sit in them until he bows. He said: He completes his salat, then gives salām, and performs the two sajdahs of forgetfulness while seated before speaking.

As for what Saʿd narrated from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from Muḥammad ibn Sinān, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muskān, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī al-Ḥalabī, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام about a man who becomes forgetful in salat (prayer) and forgets the tashahhud. He said: He returns and performs the tashahhud. I said: Should he perform the two sajdahs of forgetfulness? He said: No, in this there are no two sajdahs of forgetfulness. The correct way to understand this report is that if he remembers before the rukūʿ, then returns and performs the tashahhud, there are no two sajdahs of forgetfulness upon him. Rather, they are only obligatory upon one who does not remember until he has bowed; then he continues in his salat (prayer), gives salām, makes up the tashahhud, and then performs the two sajdahs of forgetfulness, as we have explained.
Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from al-Nadr, from 'Asim, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I asked Abu Ja'far عليه السلام about a man who doubted in the first rak'ah. He said: He must begin again.
From him, from Muḥammad ibn Sinān, from Ibn Miskān, from ʿAnbasah ibn Muṣʿab, who said: Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام said to me: If you doubt concerning the first two rakʿahs, then repeat.

From him, from al-Qarawī, from Abān, from Ismāʿīl al-Juʿfī and Ibn Abī Yaʿfūr, from Abī Jaʿfar and Abī ʿAbdillāh عليهما السلام, that they both said: If you do not know whether you have prayed one rakʿah or two, then begin again.
From him, from al-Naḍr, from Mūsā ibn Bakr, who said: Al-Fuḍayl asked him about forgetfulness, so he said: If you doubt concerning the first two rakʿahs, then repeat.

From him, from al-Ḥasan, from Zur‘ah, from Samā‘ah, who said: He said: If a man becomes forgetful concerning the first two rak‘ahs of al-Ẓuhr, al-‘Aṣr, and al-‘Atamah, and he does not know whether he has prayed one or two, then he must repeat the salat (prayer).
From him, from Faḍālah, from Rifāʿah, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about a man who does not know whether he has prayed one rakʿah or two. He said: He repeats.

From him, from Faḍālah, from Ḥusayn ibn ʿUthmān, from Hārūn ibn Khārijah, from Abī Baṣīr, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: If you become forgetful concerning the first two rakʿahs, then repeat them until you establish them with certainty.
From him, from Faḍālah, from Ḥammād, from al-Faḍl ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, who said: He said to me: If you do not retain certainty about the first two rakʿahs, then repeat your salat (prayer).

ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from Ḥammād, from Ḥarīz, from Zurārah, from one of the two (Imams) عليهما السلام, who said: I said to him: A man does not know whether he has prayed one rakʿah or two. He said: He repeats.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Hasan ibn Ali al-Washsha', who said: Abu al-Hasan al-Rida عليه السلام said to me: Repetition is required regarding the first two rak'ahs, and inadvertence concerns the last two rak'ahs.

As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā narrated from ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥakam, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Abī al-ʿAlāʾ, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about a man who does not know whether he has prayed two rakʿahs or one. He said: He completes it.
