And among what Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā narrated, from al-Sindī ibn al-Rabīʿ, from al-Ḥasan ibn Maḥbūb, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Ḥajjāj, from Abī Ibrāhīm عليه السلام, who said: Concerning a man who does not know whether he has prayed one rakʿah or two, he said: He builds upon one rakʿah.

And among what Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from ʿAbd al-Karim ibn ʿAmr, from ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Yaʿfur, who said: I asked Aba ʿAbd Allah عليه السلام about a man who does not know whether he has prayed two rakʿahs or one. He said: He completes it with one rakʿah. So the first point concerning these reports is that they do not contradict what we have previously presented, because those are many times more than these, and it is not permissible to turn away from the greater number to the lesser, as we have explained in more than one place. And even if they were opposing them and equal to them, there would still be no contradiction in them, because there is nothing in any of these reports stating that the doubt occurred in the first and second rakʿahs of the obligatory prayers or the supererogatory prayers. And when this is not present in the report, we interpret them as referring to the supererogatory prayers, because in our view there is no sahw in the supererogatory prayers, and the one praying may build on the lesser if he wishes and on the greater if he wishes, though building on the lesser is better. So we have understood these reports according to what we mentioned regarding the supererogatory prayers, so that the reports do not contradict one another.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from 'Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Hafs ibn al-Bakhtari and others, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: If you doubt in the Maghrib prayer, then repeat; and if you doubt in the Fajr prayer, then repeat.

From him, from ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from Ḥammād, from Ḥarīz, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about a man who is performing salat and does not know whether he has prayed one rakʿah or two. He said: He starts again until he becomes certain that he has completed it; and this applies in the Friday prayer, the maghrib prayer, and the prayer during travel.
From him, from ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā, from Yūnus, from a man, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: There is no sahw in the Maghrib and Fajr prayers.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Ibn Muskan, from 'Anbasah ibn Mus'ab, who said: Abu 'Abdillah عليه السلام said: If you doubt concerning the maghrib prayer, then repeat; and if you doubt concerning the fajr prayer, then repeat.

From him, from al-Hasan, from Zur‘ah, from Sama‘ah, who said: I asked him about forgetfulness in the morning prayer. He said: If you do not know whether you prayed one or two, then repeat the salat (prayer) from its beginning. And likewise the Friday prayer: if the Imam becomes forgetful in it, then he must repeat the salat (prayer), because it is two rak‘ahs. And the Maghrib prayer, if forgetfulness occurs in it and he does not know how many rak‘ahs he prayed, then he must repeat the salat (prayer).

From him, from Faḍālah, from al-ʿAlāʾ, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who doubts in the Fajr prayer. He said: He repeats it. I said: The Maghrib? He said: Yes, and the Witr and the Jumuʿah, without my asking him.

From him, from Ibn Abi ʿUmayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abi ʿAbdillah عليه السلام; and Ibn Abi ʿUmayr, from Hafs ibn al-Bakhtari and more than one person, from Abi ʿAbdillah عليه السلام, who said: If you doubt in the maghrib prayer, then repeat; and if you doubt in the fajr prayer, then repeat.

As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā narrated from Muʿāwiyah ibn Ḥukaym, from Muḥammad ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Ḥammād al-Nāb, from ʿAmmār al-Sābāṭī, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about a man who does not know whether he has prayed the fajr prayer as two rakʿahs or one rakʿah. He said: He should recite the tashahhud and depart, then stand and pray one rakʿah. If he had already prayed two rakʿahs, then this would be supererogatory; and if he had prayed one rakʿah, then this would complete the prayer. And this, by Allah, is from that which is never made up. So this is an anomalous report, contrary to all the other reports, and the sect has agreed upon leaving action according to it. However, it is possible that the doubt concerned the two supererogatory rakʿahs of fajr, so it was permissible for him to build upon one and pray another rakʿah as a precaution. There is no mention of the obligatory prayer in the report; rather, it mentions the fajr prayer, and that expression may be used for both the obligatory and the sunnah prayer. According to this interpretation, it does not contradict the reports previously mentioned.

As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Ṣafwān, from al-ʿAlāʾ, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, from Abī Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said: He was asked about a man who joined the Imam in his salat (prayer) after the Imam had preceded him by one rakʿah. Then when the Imam finished, he left with the people, and afterward remembered that one rakʿah had escaped him. He said: He repeats it as one rakʿah.

From him, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Bukayr, from Ibn Zurārah, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام about a man who performs the dawn prayer as one rakʿah, recites the tashahhud, then leaves and goes away and comes back, and then later remembers that he had only performed one rakʿah. He said: He should add to it one rakʿah. So there is no contradiction between these two reports and the earlier reports, because the doubt that necessitates repetition is only when he does not remember how much he prayed. But as for one who assumed that he had prayed two rakʿahs and acted upon that, then later remembered and came to know afterward that he had in fact prayed one rakʿah, he is not considered doubtful, and his duty is to complete what he missed so long as he has not turned away from the qiblah. This indicates that.

What was narrated by Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā, from Yaʿqūb ibn Yazīd, from ʿAlī ibn al-Nuʿmān, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Abī al-ʿAlāʾ, from Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said: I said: I come to the Imam while he had preceded me by one rakʿah in the fajr prayer. Then when he gave salām, it occurred in my heart that I had completed [the prayer], so I continued remembering Allah until the sun rose. Then when it rose, I stood up and remembered that the Imam had preceded me by one rakʿah. He said: If you are still in your place, then complete it with one rakʿah; but if you have already departed, then you must repeat [the prayer]. His statement عليه السلام, 'but if you have already departed, then you must repeat [the prayer],' is to be understood as referring to when he has turned his back to the qiblah. And what is contained in the report of ʿUbayd ibn Zurārah in his statement, 'then he goes and comes,' is to be understood as referring to when he has not turned his back to it. Thus there is no contradiction between them; this detail indicates that.

ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥasan and ʿAlī ibn Muḥammad narrated to me, from al-ʿUbaydī, from Yūnus, from al-ʿAlāʾ, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, from one of the two عليهما السلام. He said: He was asked about a man who joined the Imam in his salat (prayer) after the Imam had preceded him by one rakʿah. When the Imam finished, he left with the people, then remembered that he had missed one rakʿah. He said: He repeats one rakʿah only; that is permissible for him so long as he has not turned his face away from the qiblah. But if he has turned his face, then he must begin the salat (prayer) anew.

As for what Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Jaʿfar ibn Bashir, from Hammad ibn ʿUthman, from ʿUbayd ibn Zurarah, who said: I asked Aba ʿAbd Allah عليه السلام about a man who prayed one rakʿah of the dawn prayer, then turned away and went out for his needs, then remembered that he had prayed only one rakʿah. He said: Let him complete what remains.

From him, from Ibn Abī Najrān, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from Ḥammād, from Ḥarīz, from Zurārah, from Abī Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who prayed two rakʿahs in al-Kūfah, then remembered while he was in Makkah, or al-Madīnah, or al-Baṣrah, or in a town among the towns, that he had prayed two rakʿahs. He said: he should pray two rakʿahs. The way to understand these two reports is that we carry them upon the case where the doubt occurred in the nawāfil, not the faraʾiḍ. It is also possible that this is specific to one who thinks that he had left something out of the salat, but has not ascertained it; then repetition is not obligatory upon him, for he has moved on to another state and doubt has no effect in it. Thus, what is included of the command to complete the salat is to be understood as bearing a mode of istiḥbāb. This indicates that.

What al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Abū Ayyūb al-Khazzāz, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, concerning: A man who doubts after he has departed from his salat (prayer) — he said: So he said, he does not repeat, and there is nothing upon him. However, the second report only included mention of one who prayed two rakʿahs and forgot two rakʿahs, and that occurs in the four-rakʿah prayers rather than salat al-ghadāh. Yet even if that is so, the ruling in that case also is like the ruling in salat al-ghadāh: that whenever he turns away to face away from the qiblah, repeating the salat (prayer) is incumbent upon him. And that which indicates this is:

What al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from al-Ḥasan, from Zurʿah, from Samāʿah, from Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said: Whoever has preserved awareness of his forgetfulness and then completes it, there are no two sajdahs of forgetfulness upon him. For indeed, the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم led the people in the ẓuhr prayer, then forgot and gave salām. Dhū al-Shimālayn said to him, “O Messenger of Allah, has something been revealed concerning the prayer?” He said, “And what is that?” He said, “You only prayed two rakʿahs.” So the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم said, “Do you say the like of what he says?” They said, “Yes.” Then he stood and completed the prayer with them, and performed the two sajdahs of forgetfulness. He said: I said, “What do you see regarding one who prayed two rakʿahs, then thought they were four, so he gave salām and departed, then remembered after he had gone that he had only prayed two rakʿahs?” He said: “He begins the prayer again from its beginning.” He said: I said, “Then why was it that the Messenger صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم did not begin the prayer again, and only completed with them what remained of his prayer?” He said: “Indeed, the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم had not left his place. So if he has not left his place, then let him complete what is lacking from his prayer.”

Al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from Ṣafwān and Faḍālah, from al-ʿAlāʾ, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, from one of the two عليهم السلام, who said: I asked him about forgetfulness in Salat al-Maghrib, so he said: He repeats it until he retains it correctly, for it is not like the even-numbered prayer.

From him, from al-Naḍr, from Mūsā ibn Bakr, from al-Fuḍayl, who said: I asked him about forgetfulness, and he said: In Salat al-Maghrib, if you do not retain certainty between the three and the four, then repeat your prayer.

From him, from Faḍālah, from Ḥusayn ibn ʿUthmān, from Hārūn ibn Khārijah, from Abī Baṣīr, who said: Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام said: If you commit forgetfulness in the Maghrib prayer, then repeat the salat (prayer). Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan said: Most of the narrations that we have cited in the first chapter also include mention of the Maghrib prayer along with mention of the morning prayer, and they reinforce these reports.

As for what Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn, from Faḍālah, from Sayf ibn ʿUmayrah, from Abū Bakr al-Ḥaḍramī, who said: I prayed al-Maghrib with my companions, and when I had prayed two rakʿahs, I said the salām. Some of them said, “You only prayed two rakʿahs,” so I repeated it. Then I informed Abū ʿAbd Allah عليه السلام, and he said, “Perhaps you repeated it?” I said, “Yes.” So he laughed, then said, “It is only sufficient for you to stand and perform one rakʿah.” Indeed, the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم forgot and gave salām after two rakʿahs, then he mentioned the hadith of Dhū al-Shimālayn. He said: then he stood and added two rakʿahs to it.”

Saʿd ibn ʿAbdillah narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Jaʿfar ibn Bashir, from al-Harith ibn al-Mughirah al-Nadri, who said: I said to Abu ʿAbdillah عليه السلام: We prayed Maghrib, and the Imam erred, so he gave salām after two rakʿahs, and we repeated the prayer. He said: Why did you repeat it? Did not the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم conclude after two rakʿahs and then complete it with two rakʿahs? Why did you not complete it? So there is nothing in these two reports that conflicts with what we stated earlier, because the inadvertence here occurred only in that he gave salām in the second rakʿah, and the inadvertence did not occur in the number of the prayer. Whoever forgetfully gives salām in the first two rakʿahs is not required to repeat the prayer; rather, he is required to make it up with one rakʿah, according to what the two reports contain. And that which clarifies what we have mentioned is...

What Saʿd narrated from Ayyūb ibn Nūḥ, from ʿAlī ibn al-Nuʿmān al-Rāzī, who said: I was with some companions of mine on a journey, and I was their Imam. I performed the maghrib salat, then gave salām after the first two rakʿahs. My companions said, “You only performed two rakʿahs for us.” I spoke to them and they spoke to me, and they said, “As for us, we will repeat.” I said, “But I will not repeat; rather, I will complete it with one rakʿah.” So I completed it with one rakʿah. Then we departed, and I came to Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام and mentioned to him what had occurred in our matter. He said to me, “You were more correct than they in action. Only the one who does not know how much he has prayed repeats.” Thus, he عليه السلام clarified in this report that whoever does not know what he has prayed must repeat, as opposed to one who is certain. Alongside that, in the two hadiths there is that which prevents reliance upon them, namely the hadith of Dhū al-Shimālayn and the forgetfulness of the Prophet صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم, and that is among the things prevented by decisive proofs establishing that forgetfulness and error are not permissible for him صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم.

As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Ḥammād and al-Ḥakam ibn Miskīn, from ʿAmmār al-Sābāṭī, who said: I said to Abū ʿAbdillāh, peace be upon him: A man doubts during the Maghrib prayer and does not know whether he has prayed two rakʿahs or three. He said: He should give salām, then stand and add one rakʿah to it. Then he said: By Allah, this is among that which can never be made up for me.

And among what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated, from Muʿāwiyah ibn Ḥukaym, from Muḥammad ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Ḥammād Dhī al-Nāb, from ʿAmmār al-Sābāṭī, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about a man who prayed Maghrib, then did not know whether he had prayed two or three. He said: He recites the tashahhud and concludes, then he stands and prays one rakʿah. If he had prayed three, then this would be a supererogatory prayer; and if he had prayed two, then this would complete the salat. And this, by Allah, is among that which can never be established for me. So the proper approach regarding these two reports is that the earlier reports are not to be opposed by them, because their source is one and the same, namely ʿAmmār al-Sābāṭī, and he is weak and corrupt in doctrine; what is exclusively reported by him is not acted upon. The sect has agreed to abandon acting upon this report. It is also possible that the intended meaning in these two reports concerns one who became forgetful in the supererogatory Maghrib prayer, in which case it is permissible for him to build upon what the report contains and complete what remains. It is also possible that it is to be understood regarding one whose assumption inclines strongly to that, and even if he is not certain, it is permissible for him to build upon the greater number, while the addition of the rakʿah mentioned therein is taken as a recommendation.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Hammad, from Hariz, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I asked Aba 'Abdillah عليه السلام about a man who has prayed two rak'ahs and does not know whether they are two or four. He said: He gives salām, then stands and prays two rak'ahs with Fatihat al-Kitab, then departs, and there is nothing upon him.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from 'Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from Yunus, from Ibn Muskan, from Ibn Abi Ya'fur, who said: I asked Aba 'Abdillah عليه السلام about a man who does not know whether he has prayed two rak'ahs or four. He said: He should recite the tashahhud and give salām, then stand and pray two rak'ahs and four sajdahs, reciting in them Fātiḥat al-Kitāb; then he should recite the tashahhud and give salām. So if he had in fact prayed four, then these two would be supererogatory; and if he had prayed two rak'ahs, then these two would complete the four. And if he spoke, then he should perform the two sajdahs of forgetfulness.

From him, from ʿAlī, from his father, from Ḥammād, from Ḥarīz, from Zurārah, from one of the two عليهما السلام, who said: I said to him: One who does not know whether he is in four or in two, while he has secured the two? He said: He performs two rakʿahs and four sajdahs while standing, with Fātiḥat al-Kitāb, and he recites the tashahhud, and there is nothing upon him. And if he does not know whether he is in three or in four, while he has secured the three, he stands and adds to it one other rakʿah, and there is nothing upon him. And he does not overturn certainty by doubt, nor does he admit doubt into certainty, nor does he mix one of them with the other; rather, he overturns doubt by certainty, and completes upon certainty, so he builds upon it, and he gives no consideration to doubt in any state among the states.

As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Faḍālah, from al-ʿAlāʾ, from Muḥammad, he said: I asked him about a man who does not know whether he has prayed two rakʿahs or four. He said: He repeats the salat (prayer). So it does not conflict with the earlier reports, because the proper way regarding it is that we carry it upon a salat (prayer) in which doubt is not permissible, such as the morning prayer and the maghrib prayer, as we have stated before.

Al-Husayn ibn 'Ubayd Allah informed me, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Yahya, from his father, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from 'Ali ibn Isma'il, from Hammad, from Hariz, from Ibn Abi Ya'fur, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: If you doubt and do not know whether you are in three, or two, or one, or in four, then repeat the salat and do not proceed on the basis of doubt.

From him, from ʿAbbād ibn Sulaymān, from Saʿd ibn Saʿd, from Ṣafwān, from Abū al-Ḥasan عليه السلام, who said: If you do not know how much you have prayed, and your conjecture does not settle upon anything, then repeat the salat (prayer).

As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Yaqṭīn, from his brother, from his father, who said: I asked Abā al-Ḥasan عليه السلام about a man who does not know how many he has prayed—one, two, or three. He said: He builds upon certainty, performs the two sajdahs of forgetfulness, and recites a light tashahhud. So it does not contradict the first two reports, because he said: he builds upon certainty, and what certainty requires is recommencing the salat (prayer), as we have explained. The command to perform the two sajdahs of forgetfulness is therefore understood as recommendation, not as compensation for the salat (prayer).

As for what Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā narrated from Muʿāwiyah ibn Ḥukaym, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Mughīrah, from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ḥamzah, from a righteous man, peace be upon him, who said: I asked him about a man who doubts and does not know whether he has prayed one, or two, or three, or four; his prayer becomes confused for him. He said: “All of that?” He said: I said: “Yes.” He said: “Then let him proceed in his prayer and seek refuge in Allah from al-Shayṭān al-Rajīm, for it is likely soon to go away from him.” The proper understanding of this report is one of two possibilities. One of them is that we interpret it as applying to a supererogatory prayer, for there is nothing in the report indicating that he doubted in an obligatory prayer. The second possibility is that what is meant is one whose forgetfulness is frequent and who is unable to guard against it; it is permissible for him to proceed in his prayer, because if repetition were made obligatory upon him while forgetfulness is his condition, he would never be free of prayer in any state. As for one whose doubt occurs only sometimes, then repetition is obligatory upon him according to what we have stated before; that is indicated by this.

What Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb narrated from ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, and Muḥammad ibn Ismāʿīl, from al-Faḍl ibn Shādhān, all together from Ḥammād ibn ʿĪsā, from Ḥarīz, from Zurārah and Abū Baṣīr, who said: We said to him: A man doubts frequently in his salat (prayer), to the point that he does not know how much he has prayed or what remains upon him. He said: He repeats it. We said: That happens to him often; whenever he repeats, he doubts again. He said: He should proceed despite his doubt. Then he said: Do not accustom the wicked one from among yourselves to breaking the salat (prayer), lest you make him hopeful; indeed al-Shayṭān is wicked and becomes accustomed to what he is accustomed to. So let one of you proceed in the uncertainty and not frequently break the salat (prayer), for if he does that three times, the doubt will not return to him. Zurārah said: And he said: He only wants to be obeyed, so when he is disobeyed, he does not return to any one of you.

Al-Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Abū al-Qāsim Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb, from ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from Ḥammād ibn ʿĪsā, from Ḥarīz, from Zurārah, from one of the two of them عليهما السلام, who said: I said to him: A man does not know whether he has prayed one rakʿah or two. He said: He repeats. He said: I said: A man does not know whether he has prayed two or three. He said: If doubt comes to him after his entering into the third, he proceeds with the third, then he prays the other one, and there is nothing upon him; then he gives salām, and there is nothing upon him.

As for what Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā narrated from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn, from Jaʿfar, from Ḥammād, from ʿUbayd ibn Zurārah, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, he said: I asked him about a man who did not know whether he had prayed two rakʿahs or three. He said: He repeats. I said: Is it not said, “A faqih does not repeat the prayer”? So he said: That only applies to three and four. Thus it is understood as referring to the maghrib prayer or the morning prayer, because in these two prayers there is no sahw, and repeating is obligatory in them in every case.

As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from Muḥammad ibn Sahl, he said: I asked Abā al-Ḥasan عليه السلام about a man who does not know whether he has prayed three or two rakʿahs. He said: He builds upon the lesser amount and takes what is certain, and after finishing he recites a light tashahhud, likewise from the beginning of the salat (prayer) and its end. The correct way to understand this report is that he only builds upon the lesser amount when his conjecture inclines toward it, and he prays its completion as a recommended act. But when the conjecture is balanced, then building upon the greater amount is more precautionary, when he completes after finishing the salat (prayer) as we have explained. And that which confirms this is...

What Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from Muḥammad ibn Khālid, from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī, from Muʿādh ibn Muslim, from ʿAmmār ibn Mūsā al-Sābāṭī, who said: Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام said: Whenever any doubt enters upon you in your salat (prayer), then act upon the greater number; then when you have finished, complete what you thought you had omitted. And it is possible that the report is specific to the nawāfil, for the more excellent practice in the nawāfil is to build upon the lesser number, as we have explained.

As for what Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā narrated from Ayyūb ibn Nūḥ, from Ṣafwān, from ʿAnbasah, who said: I asked him about a man who does not know whether he has performed one rakʿah or three. He said: He builds his salat (prayer) upon one rakʿah, then recites in it Sūrat al-Fātiḥah, and performs the two sajdahs of forgetfulness. So the proper way regarding this report as well is that we interpret it as applying to the nawāfil, because the prescribed sunnah in them is to build upon the lesser number, and that is not the case in the obligatory prayers.

Al-Husayn ibn 'Ubayd Allah informed me, from a number of our companions, from Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from 'Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Ibn Udhaynah, from Zurarah and Bukayr, the two sons of A'yan, from Abu Ja'far عليه السلام, who said: If he becomes certain that he added to the prescribed salat (prayer), he does not count it, and he begins his salat (prayer) anew, when he has become certain with certainty.
ʿAlī ibn Mahziyār, from Faḍālah ibn Ayyūb, from Abān ibn ʿUthmān, from Abī Baṣīr, who said: Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام said: Whoever adds to his salat (prayer), then repetition is obligatory upon him.

As for what Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā narrated from Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Hilāl, from al-ʿAlāʾ, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, who said: I asked Abā Jaʿfar عليه السلام about a man who became certain, after he had performed the ẓuhr prayer, that he had prayed five [rakʿahs]. He said: How did he become certain? I said: He knew. He said: If he knew that he had sat in the fourth [rakʿah], then the ẓuhr prayer is complete; so let him stand and add to the fifth rakʿah another rakʿah, and perform the two sajdahs of forgetfulness, and they will be counted as two rakʿahs of supererogatory prayer, and there is nothing upon him.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Abi Nasr, from Jamil ibn Darrāj, from Zurārah, from Abī Ja‘far عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who prayed five [rak‘ahs]. He said: If he had sat in the fourth [rak‘ah] for the measure of the tashahhud, then his salat (prayer) is complete. So there is no contradiction between these two reports and the first two reports, because whoever sat in the fourth [rak‘ah] and recited the tashahhud, then stood and prayed an additional rak‘ah, has not omitted a pillar from the pillars of the salat (prayer). He only omitted the taslim, and omission of the taslim does not necessitate repeating the salat (prayer), according to what we have stated earlier.

As for what Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated from Abū al-Jawzāʾ, from al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlwān, from ʿAmr ibn Khālid, from Zayd ibn ʿAlī, from his forefathers, from ʿAlī عليه السلام, who said: The Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم led us in the ẓuhr prayer as five rakʿahs, then he turned away. Some of the people said to him, "O Messenger of Allah, has something been added to the prayer?" He said, "And what is that?" They said, "You led us in five rakʿahs." He said: then he faced the qiblah, said the takbir while seated, then performed two sajdahs in which there was no recitation and no rukuʿ, then he gave salām, and he used to say, "They are the two that humiliate [Shaytan]." So the proper way regarding this report is that we understand it to mean that the Prophet صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم only performed the two sajdahs because the statement of one person does not produce certainty for him such that he would need to restart the prayer. Rather, it only entails doubt; and whoever doubts an addition, his obligation is to perform the two sajdahs of sahw, as we have explained in our major book. And they are the two that humiliate [Shaytan].

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn and Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, all together from Safwan ibn Yahya, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, who said: I asked Aba 'Abdillah عليه السلام about a man who speaks forgetfully during the salat (prayer), saying, "Straighten your rows." He said: "He completes his salat (prayer), then performs two sajdahs." I said: "Are the two sajdahs of forgetfulness before the taslim or after it?" He said: "After it."

As for what Saʿd narrated from Abū Jaʿfar, from his father, and al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from Muḥammad ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from ʿUmar ibn Udhaynah, from Zurārah, from Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام, concerning: Regarding a man who becomes heedless in the two rakʿahs and speaks, he said: He completes what remains of his salat (prayer), whether he spoke or did not speak, and there is nothing upon him. So this does not contradict the first report concerning the obligation of the two sajdahs of forgetfulness, because there is nothing in the report stating that the two sajdahs of forgetfulness are not upon him. Rather, it only says that there is nothing upon him, and it is possible that this is an indication to something other than that, such as sin and burden.

As for what Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb narrated from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Hilāl, from ʿUqbah ibn Khālid, from Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, concerning... About a man whom another man called while he was performing salat, so he became inattentive and answered him regarding his need—what should he do? He said: he continues with his salat and says takbīr many times. So this does not contradict the first two reports regarding the obligation of the two sajdahs of forgetfulness upon him, because there is nothing in the report stating that the two sajdahs of forgetfulness are not upon him. Rather, he only commanded him to say takbīr, and it is not impossible that he should say takbīr as a recommended act and perform the two sajdahs of forgetfulness as compensation. As for speaking deliberately, it necessitates repeating the salat without disagreement, and that is not contradicted by this.

What al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Faḍālah, from al-Qāsim ibn Burayd, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, from Abī Jaʿfar عليه السلام, concerning: A man prayed two rakʿahs of the obligatory prayer, then gave salām while thinking that he had completed the prayer, and he spoke. Then he remembered that he had not prayed two rakʿahs, so he عليه السلام said: He should complete what remains of his prayer, and there is nothing upon him.

And Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā narrated from Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Faḍḍāl, from ʿAmr ibn Saʿīd, from Muṣaddaq ibn Ṣadaqah, from ʿAmmār ibn Mūsā, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, concerning: A man who forgot the tashahhud in the salat (prayer)—he said: if he remembers that he said only “Subḥāna Allāh,” then his salat (prayer) is valid; but if he does not remember having said anything of the tashahhud, he repeats the salat (prayer). And he said: regarding a man who remembers, after he has stood up, spoken, and gone about his needs, that he had only prayed two rakʿahs of ẓuhr, ʿaṣr, ʿatamah, or maghrib—he said: he builds upon his salat (prayer) and completes it, even if he had reached China, and he does not repeat the salat (prayer). So there is no contradiction between these two reports and what we have mentioned, because one who errs, gives salām, and then speaks afterward has not intentionally spoken during the salat (prayer); rather, he only speaks when he thinks that he has finished the salat (prayer). Thus, he takes the ruling of one who is in the salat (prayer) and spoke because he thought he was not in it. But if, when he remembered that something from this salat (prayer) had been missed, he then spoke deliberately afterward, it would be obligatory for him to repeat the salat (prayer), in accordance with what we have already stated regarding deliberate speech. However, we have already discussed the last report earlier and that it is not acted upon, because it conflicts with the principles. For the reports that are acted upon establish that if he has turned his back to the qiblah, restarting the salat (prayer) becomes obligatory upon him; rather, building upon it is only permissible if he remembers while still facing the qiblah. This report implies that even if he had reached China, he would not repeat the salat (prayer), and that is contrary to what we have stated.

The two sajdahs of forgetfulness are after the taslim and before speaking. The Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Abu al-Qasim Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah, from Musa ibn al-Hasan, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn Abi al-Khattab, from al-Hasan ibn 'Ali ibn Faddal, from 'Abd Allah ibn Maymun al-Qaddah, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, from 'Ali عليه السلام, who said:

As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā narrated from al-Barqī, from Saʿd ibn Saʿd al-Ashʿarī, he said: Al-Riḍā عليه السلام said regarding the two sajdahs of forgetfulness: if there has been a deficiency, then before the taslim, and if there has been an addition, then after it.

And among what Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā narrated from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from Ibn Sinān, from Abū al-Jārūd, who said: I said to Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام: When should I perform the two sajdahs of forgetfulness? He said: Before the taslīm, for when you give the taslīm, the sanctity of your salat has departed. So the proper way regarding these two reports is that we interpret them as a kind of taqiyyah, because they agree with the doctrines of many of the ʿāmmah. And Abū Jaʿfar Ibn Bābawayh al-Qummī, may Allah have mercy on him, said: I give fatwa according to them in a state of taqiyyah.

Al-Husayn ibn ʿUbayd Allah informed me, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Yahya, from his father, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Ayyub ibn Nuh, from Safwan, from Ismaʿil ibn Jabir, who said: I said to Abi ʿAbd Allah عليه السلام: “What is the water that nothing renders impure?” He said: “Its depth is two cubits, and its breadth is one cubit and a span.”

And with this chain of transmission, from Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from al-Barqī, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Sinān, from Ismāʿīl ibn Jābir, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام about water that nothing renders impure. He said: “Kurr.” He said: I said: “And what is kurr?” He said: “Three spans by three spans.”

Al-Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Abu al-Qasim Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from 'Uthman ibn 'Isa, from Ibn Muskan, from Abu Basir, who said: I asked Abu 'Abdillah عليه السلام about the kurr of water: how much is its measure? He عليه السلام said: When the water is three and a half spans by the like of it, and three and a half spans in its depth in the ground, then that is the kurr of water.

As for what Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā narrated from Yaʿqūb ibn Yazīd, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from some of our companions, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, he said: The kurr of water, which nothing renders impure, is one thousand and two hundred ritls. So this report does not conflict with the reports that preceded it, because we had mentioned in our book Tahdhīb al-Aḥkām that acting upon this report is according to what the Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, supported. And we interpreted what was reported concerning specification by spans as being in conformity with that, such that their measure would be the measure that corresponds to it. Thus it is as though two methods were established for us: one of them is that we consider ritls when we have a way to determine them, and if there is no way to that, we consider spans, because that is not impossible in any circumstance. The Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, chose regarding the ritls that they be according to the Baghdadi measure, while others among our companions held that they be according to the Madani measure. There is no report here that includes mention of ritls other than this report, and despite that it is also mursal, even if it is repeated in the books, for its basis is Ibn Abī ʿUmayr from some of our companions. The view that the Baghdadi ritls are to be considered is closer to correctness, because they approximate the measure that we adopted in spans; but if we consider the Madani measure, the approximation between them becomes remote. So acting upon that is more appropriate for what we have already stated, and what further strengthens this consideration is also what...

It was narrated to me from ʿAbd Allah — meaning Ibn al-Mughirah — raising it to Abu ʿAbd Allah عليه السلام that the kurr is six hundred ratls. 6- And this report was narrated by Muhammad ibn ʿAli ibn Mahbub, from al-ʿAbbas, from ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Mughirah, from Abu Ayyub, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu ʿAbd Allah عليه السلام. He said: I said to him: A pond has collected water in it; beasts urinate in it, dogs lap from it, and the person in janabah performs ghusl in it. He said: If it is the measure of a kurr, nothing makes it najis, and the kurr is six hundred ratls. The manner of preferring this report in considering the Iraqi ratls is that what is intended by it is the ratl of Makkah, because it equals two ratls. And it is not impossible that they عليهم السلام gave the questioner a fatwa according to the customary measure of his land, because it is not permissible that what is intended by it be the ratls of the people of Iraq nor the ratls of the people of al-Madinah, since none of our companions considered that, so it is abandoned by consensus. As for the preference of the one who considered the ratls of the people of al-Madinah by saying that precaution requires it, because if we carry it upon the greater measure the lesser enters into it, this is unsound, because one may say that this is contrary to precaution, since it is required of a person that he not perform the salat except by making wudu with water when it exists, and that he not judge a present water to be najis except with a legal proof. There is no disagreement among our companions that if water is less than the amount that we considered, then it becomes najis by what falls into it; and there is no proof here that if it exceeds what we considered, then it becomes najis by what falls into it. As for what was preferred on the basis of their custom, inasmuch as they were from the people of al-Madinah عليهم السلام, there is no preference in that, because they used to give fatwa according to what was customary in the questioner’s practice and usage. For that reason, in considering the ratls of the saʿ we regarded it as nine ratls in the Iraqi measure, and that is contrary to their own custom. Likewise, the report about which we have spoken, regarding their consideration of six hundred ratls, is only a consideration according to the custom of the people of Makkah. Thus they عليهم السلام used to

Al-Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan ibn Aban, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from al-Qasim, from 'Ali, who said: I asked Aba 'Abd Allah عليه السلام about a mouse that falls into a well. He said: seven buckets. He said: And I asked him عليه السلام about a bird and a chicken falling into the well. He said: seven buckets; and for a cat, twenty or thirty or forty buckets; and for a dog and the like of it.

With this chain of transmission, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from ʿUthmān ibn ʿĪsā, from Samāʿah, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about a mouse that falls into the well, or a bird. He said: If you reach it before it becomes putrid, you should draw seven buckets from it. If it is a cat or something larger than it, you should draw thirty buckets or forty buckets from it. And if it has become putrid such that the smell of rottenness is found in the water, you should drain the well until the foul smell goes away from the water.

As for what al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Ibn Udhaynah, from Zurarah, Muhammad ibn Muslim, and Burayd ibn Mu'awiyah al-'Ijli, from Abi 'Abdillah and Abi Ja'far, peace be upon them, concerning: About a well into which a beast, a mouse, a dog, or a bird falls and dies, he said: It is removed, then buckets are drawn from the well, then drink from it and perform wudu (ablution) with it.

And from him, from al-Qasim, from Aban, from Abi al-'Abbas al-Fadl al-Baqbaq, who said: Abu 'Abdillah عليه السلام said concerning a well into which a mouse, or a beast, or a dog, or a bird falls and dies: It is taken out, then buckets are drawn from the well, then one may drink from it and perform wudu (ablution) with it.

Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated from Ayyub ibn Nuh al-Nakhaʿi, from Muhammad ibn Abi Hamzah, from ʿAli ibn Yaqtin, from Abu al-Hasan Musa ibn Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a well into which a pigeon, a chicken, a mouse, a dog, or a cat falls. He said: It suffices you to draw from it buckets, for that purifies it, if Allah, Exalted is He, wills. The sound approach concerning these reports is one of two possibilities: either that he عليه السلام answered regarding the ruling of some of what the question included, namely the mouse and the bird, and relied regarding the ruling of the rest upon what is well known from his doctrine or from other reports that became widespread from them عليهم السلام; or secondly, that there is no contradiction in that, because his statement, 'draw from it buckets,' is a plural indicating abundance, which means what exceeds ten, and it is not impossible that what is intended by it is forty buckets, in accordance with what the earlier reports contain. If what was intended were less than ten, its plural would come on the pattern afʿilah rather than fiʿāl. Moreover, knowledge has been established that impurity has occurred, and by drawing forty buckets the ruling of impurity is also removed, and that is known; whereas anything less than that belongs to the category of solitary reports, so practice should be according to what we have stated.

As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Jamīl ibn Darrāj, from Abū Usāmah Zayd al-Shaḥḥām, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, concerning: the mouse, the cat, the chicken, the dog, and the bird, he said: If it has not decomposed, or the taste of the water has not changed, then five buckets will suffice you. But if the water has changed, then draw from it until the odor goes away. So this report also admits two possibilities: one of them is what we mentioned in the earlier reports, namely that he was answering about the ruling of the chicken and the bird. The second is that we understand it to mean that if the dog fell into it and came out alive, then this amount up to seven buckets is drawn from it; and there is nothing in the report indicating that it died in it. That which indicates this is what...

Al-Husayn ibn 'Ubayd Allah informed us of it, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Yahya, from his father, from Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Mahbub, from al-'Abbas ibn Ma'ruf, from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Mughirah, from Abi Maryam, who said: Ja'far عليه السلام narrated to us. He said: Abu Ja'far عليه السلام used to say: When a dog dies in the well, it is to be drained. And Ja'far عليه السلام said: If it falls into it and then is taken out of it alive, seven buckets are to be drawn from it. His statement عليه السلام, 'When a dog dies in the well, it is to be drained,' is to be understood as referring to when one of the qualities of the water changes because of it, for that necessitates draining all of it. But if it does not change, then the ruling concerning it is what we have mentioned previously.

As for what Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā narrated from Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Faḍḍāl, from ʿAmr ibn Saʿīd, from Muṣaddaq ibn Ṣadaqah, from ʿAmmār al-Sābāṭī, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, he said: He was asked about a well into which a dog, a mouse, or a pig falls. He said: All of it is to be drawn out. The proper way to understand this report, and the hadith of Abī Maryam in his statement, ‘If the dog dies in the well, it is to be drained,’ is that we carry them upon the case where one of the qualities of the water has changed—its color, taste, or smell. But when that is absent, then the ruling is what we have mentioned.

As for what Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā narrated from al-Ḥasan ibn Mūsā al-Khashshāb, from Ghiyāth ibn Kullūb, from Isḥāq ibn ʿAmmār, from Jaʿfar, from his father, that ʿAlī عليه السلام used to say: If a chicken, or something like it, dies in the well, two or three buckets are drawn from it; and if it is a sheep or something similar, then nine or ten. So it does not contradict what we have presented earlier, because this report is anomalous, while what we have presented earlier accords with all the reports. Also, if we act upon those reports, then we have also acted upon these reports because they are included within them; but if we act upon this report, we would need to discard those reports altogether. And because certainty of the removal of impurity is attained by acting upon those reports, whereas it is not attained by acting upon this report.

The Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Abu al-Qasim Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah, from Abu Ja'far, from Muhammad ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Hammad ibn 'Uthman, from 'Ubayd Allah ibn 'Ali al-Halabi, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, that he said: If you do not know whether you have prayed four or five, or whether you have decreased or increased, then recite the tashahhud and give salām, and perform the two sajdahs of forgetfulness without ruku' and without recitation, and recite in them a light tashahhud.

As for what Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated from Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Faḍḍāl, from ʿAmr ibn Saʿīd al-Madāʾinī, from Muṣaddaq ibn Ṣadaqah, from ʿAmmār ibn Mūsā al-Sābāṭī, from Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about the two sajdahs of forgetfulness: is there takbīr or tasbīḥ in them? He said: No, they are only two sajdahs. If the one who forgot is the Imam, he says takbīr when he prostrates and when he raises his head, so that those behind him may know that he has forgotten. There is no obligation upon him to recite tasbīḥ in them, and there is no tashahhud in them after the two sajdahs. The meaning of this report is that there is no tasbīḥ or tashahhud in them by way of prolongation, because what is prescribed in them is a light tashahhud, as was contained in the first report.

Al-Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan ibn Aban, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Hammad, from Hariz, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I asked Aba 'Abdillah عليه السلام about fox skins: may one perform salat in them? He said: I do not like to perform salat in them.
From him, from Muḥammad ibn Ibrāhīm, who said: I wrote to him asking him about salat (prayer) in the skins of rabbits, and he wrote: It is disliked.

Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from Ibn Abī Zayd, who said: Al-Riḍā عليه السلام was asked about the properly slaughtered skins of foxes, and he said: Do not perform salat (prayer) in them.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, from Ali ibn Mahziyar, from a man who asked al-Rida عليه السلام about prayer in fox skins, so he forbade prayer in them and in the garment that is next to them. He did not know which of the two garments was the one that sticks to the fur or the one that sticks to the skin, so he wrote in his own hand: the garment that sticks to the skin. And Abu al-Hasan mentioned that he asked him about this issue, and he said: Do not pray in the one above it, nor in the one beneath it.

As for what al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Jamil, from Abu 'Abdillah عليه السلام, he said: I asked him about salat (prayer) in the skins of foxes, and he said: If they have been properly slaughtered, then there is no harm.

Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Mahbub narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Safwan, from Jamil, from al-Hasan ibn Shihab, who said: I asked Aba 'Abdillah عليه السلام about the skins of foxes, when they have been properly slaughtered: may one perform salat (prayer) in them? He said: Yes.

From him, from ʿAlī ibn al-Sindī, from Ṣafwān ibn Yaḥyā, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥajjāj, who said: I asked him about a covering made from foxes or Khwārazmī fur: may one perform salat (prayer) in it or not? He said: If it has been properly slaughtered, then there is no objection to it. So the proper way regarding these reports is that we interpret them as a form of taqiyyah, not as applying in a state of free choice, because that is the doctrine of all the generality, and this confirms what we have already presented.

What Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from al-Walīd ibn Abān, who said: I said to al-Riḍā عليه السلام: May I perform salat (prayer) in al-fanak and al-sinjāb? He said: Yes. Then I said: May one perform salat (prayer) in foxes' skins when they have been duly slaughtered? He said: Do not perform salat (prayer) in them.

ʿAlī ibn Mahziyār said: Ibrāhīm ibn ʿUqbah wrote to him: “We have socks and waistbands made from rabbit fur. Is salat (prayer) permissible in them without necessity and without taqiyyah?” So he, peace be upon him (AS), wrote: “Salat (prayer) in them is not permissible.”

Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Mahbub narrated from Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from 'Ali ibn Mahziyar, from Ahmad ibn Ishaq al-Abhari, who said: I wrote to him: May I be made your ransom, among us there are socks and waist-ties made from rabbit fur. Is salat (prayer) permissible in rabbit fur without necessity and without taqiyyah? So he, peace be upon him, wrote: Salat (prayer) in them is not permissible.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, said: I wrote to Abu Muhammad عليه السلام asking him: May one perform salat (prayer) in a cap upon which there is the fur of that whose flesh is not eaten, or in a belt of pure silk, or in a belt made from the fur of rabbits? So he wrote: Salat (prayer) is not lawful in pure silk. But if the fur is from a duly slaughtered animal, salat (prayer) in it is lawful, if Allah wills.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from 'Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Ibn Bukayr, who said: Zurarah asked Aba 'Abdillah عليه السلام about salat (prayer) in fox, fennec, squirrel, and other furs. So he brought out a book which he stated was dictated by the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم: Indeed, salat (prayer) in the fur of every thing whose eating is forbidden is invalid; so salat (prayer) in its fur, hair, skin, urine, dung, and everything from it is invalid. That salat (prayer) is not accepted until he prays in something other than it, from what Allah has made lawful to eat. Then he said: O Zurarah, this is from the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم, so preserve that, O Zurarah. If it is from that whose flesh is eaten, then salat (prayer) in its fur, urine, hair, dung, milk, and everything from it is permissible, when you know that it is properly slaughtered and that slaughter has purified it. But if it is other than that, from what you have been prohibited from eating or what has been made forbidden for you to eat, then salat (prayer) in everything from it is invalid, whether slaughter has purified it or it has not been purified.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Umar ibn Ali ibn Yazid, from Ibrahim ibn Muhammad al-Hamadhani, said: I wrote to him: Fur and hair from that whose flesh is not eaten falls onto my garment, without taqiyyah and without necessity. So he wrote, peace be upon him: Salat is not permissible in it.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from 'Ali ibn Muhammad, from 'Abd Allah ibn Ishaq, from one whom he mentioned, from Muqatil ibn Muqatil, who said: I asked Abū al-Ḥasan عليه السلام about salat (prayer) in al-sammūr, al-sinjāb, and fox furs. He said: There is no good in all of that except for al-sinjāb, for it is a creature that does not eat meat.

ʿAlī ibn Mahziyār narrated from Abū ʿAlī ibn Rāshid, who said: I said to Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام: What do you say about furs—which of them may one perform salat in? He said: Which furs? I said: al-fanak, al-sinjāb, and al-sammūr. He said: So perform salat in al-fanak and al-sinjāb; but as for al-sammūr, do not perform salat in it. I said: And foxes—may one perform salat in them? He said: No, but they may be worn after the salat. I said: May I perform salat in the garment that is directly against it? He said: No.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Dawud al-Sarmi, who said: Bashir ibn Yasar narrated to me, saying: I asked him about salat (prayer) in fanak fur, fira', squirrel fur, sable, and hawasil that are hunted in the lands of shirk or in the lands of Islam: may I perform salat (prayer) in it without taqiyyah? He said: So he said: Perform salat (prayer) in squirrel fur and the Khwarazmian hawasil, and do not perform salat (prayer) in foxes nor in sable.

As for what Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā narrated from al-ʿAbbās, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Ḥammād, from al-Ḥalabī, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, he said: I asked him about al-firāʾ, al-sinjāb, al-sammūr, foxes, and the like. He said: There is no harm in praying in it.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Hasan ibn 'Ali ibn Yaqtin, from his brother al-Husayn, from his father 'Ali ibn Yaqtin, who said: I asked Abā al-Ḥasan عليه السلام about wearing al-firā', al-sammūr, al-fanak, foxes, and all skins. He said: There is no harm. So the proper way regarding these two reports is that we interpret them as a kind of taqiyyah, as we have explained in other reports, because no one agrees with us on that. And it is possible that his statement, “there is no harm in it,” is specific to some of what the question included, namely al-sinjāb, because permission has been given for salat in it, as we have explained in some reports. And it may be that in the answer regarding what is other than al-sinjāb, he relied upon what had already preceded from him and from his forefathers عليهم السلام of clarification. As for al-sammūr in particular, it also indicates its reprehensibility.

What Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from al-Barqī, from Saʿd ibn Saʿd al-Ashʿarī, from al-Riḍā عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about the skins of al-sammūr. He said, “What kind of thing is that? Is it the dark-colored one?” I said, “It is the black one.” He said, “Does it hunt?” I said, “Yes, it takes chickens and pigeons.” He said, “No.”

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Ahmad ibn Idris, from Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Jabbar, who said: I wrote to Abu Muhammad عليه السلام asking him whether one may perform salat (prayer) in a cap made of pure silk or a cap of dibaj. So he عليه السلام wrote: Salat (prayer) is not lawful in pure silk.
Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā, from Ismāʿīl ibn Saʿd al-Ashʿarī, said: I asked him about a garment of silk: may a man perform salat (prayer) in it? He said: No.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Ya'qub ibn Yazid, from a number of our companions, from 'Ali ibn Asbat, from Abi al-Harith, who said: I asked al-Rida عليه السلام: May a man perform salat (prayer) in a garment of silk? He said: No.

As for what Saʿd narrated from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from Muḥammad ibn Ismāʿīl ibn Bazīʿ, who said: I asked Abū al-Ḥasan عليه السلام about salat (prayer) in a garment of brocade, and he said: So long as there are no images in it, there is no objection. So the first point regarding this report is that we have already narrated from Abū al-Ḥasan عليه السلام that which conflicts with this narration, and it is not permissible for his statements to differ except for a valid aspect or a sound interpretation. Moreover, the apparent wording of the report does not indicate that there is no objection in every circumstance; so when that is not the case in it, we interpret it as applying to the state of الحرب rather than the state of choice, and that is indicated by what follows.

What Saʿd narrated from Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā, from Samāʿah ibn Mihrān, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about wearing silk and dībāj, So he said: As for in warfare, there is no harm, even if it contains images. And it is possible that what is meant by dībāj is that which is mixed with cotton and linen, because salat (prayer) in that is permissible, and its being called dībāj would be by way of figurative usage; that indicates this.

What al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Yusuf ibn Ibrahim, from Abi 'Abdillah عليه السلام, who said: There is no harm in a garment whose warp, buttons, and trimming are of silk; rather, only solid silk has been considered disliked for men.

Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Mahbub, from al-'Abbas, from 'Ali ibn Mahziyar, from Fadalah ibn Ayyub, from Musa ibn Bakr, from Zurarah, who said: I heard Abu Ja'far عليه السلام forbidding silk clothing for men and women, except that which is of silk mixed with khazz, such that its weft or its warp is khazz, or linen, or cotton. Rather, it is only pure silk that is disliked for men and women.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from a number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, who traces it up to Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, concerning: Pure khazz—there is no harm in it. But as for that in which rabbit fur or other such similar things are mixed, one should not perform salat (prayer) in it.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from Ayyub ibn Nuh, who raised it, said: Abu 'Abdillah عليه السلام said: There is no problem with salat (prayer) in pure khazz. But as for that in which rabbit fur or other similar things are mixed, then do not perform salat (prayer) in it.

As for what Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā narrated from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from Dāwūd al-Ṣirmī, who said: Bashīr ibn Yasār narrated to me, saying: I asked him about salat (prayer) in khazz that is adulterated with the fur of rabbits, so he wrote: That is permissible. So this is an anomalous report; none narrated it except Dāwūd al-Ṣirmī, even if it is repeated in the books with different chains. And it is possible that its basis is a form of taqiyyah, as we have stated regarding other reports.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Ya'qub ibn Yazid, from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from some of our companions, from one of them, peace be upon him, who said: Wearing a garment over the shoulders above wrapping it crosswise in salat (prayer) is disliked, and wrapping it crosswise over the shirt is disliked.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from 'Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Hisham ibn Salim, from Abi Basir, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: It is not appropriate that you wrap yourself with an izar over a qamis while you are performing salat, and do not gird yourself with an izar over the qamis when you pray, for indeed that is from the attire of the Jahiliyyah.

From him, from ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from Ḥammād, from Ḥarīz, from Zurārah, from Abī Jaʿfar عليه السلام, that he said: Beware of wrapping oneself in al-ṣammāʾ. I said: And what is wrapping oneself in al-ṣammāʾ? He said: It is that you insert the garment from beneath your side and place it over one shoulder.

As for what Saʿd narrated from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn, from Mūsā ibn ʿUmar ibn Bazīʿ, he said: I said to al-Riḍā عليه السلام: "May I tie the waist-wrapper and the kerchief over my shirt during salat (prayer)?" He said: "There is no harm in it."
From him, from Abū Jaʿfar, from Mūsā ibn al-Qāsim al-Bajalī, who said: I saw Abā Jaʿfar al-Thānī عليه السلام praying in a qamīṣ, having girded himself above it with a cloth, while he was praying.

From him, from ʿAlī ibn Ismāʿīl, from Ḥammād ibn ʿĪsā, who said: Al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Yaqṭīn wrote to al-ʿAbd al-Ṣāliḥ عليه السلام: “May a man perform the salat (prayer) while wearing an izār wrapped around himself over the qamīṣ?” So he wrote: “Yes.” Thus, the import of these reports is the lifting of prohibition and permissibility, while the earlier reports pertain to virtue and recommendation; and there is no contradiction between them.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from 'Umar ibn Udhaynah, from Zurarah, who said: I asked Aba Ja'far عليه السلام about the minimum in which a woman may perform salat (prayer). He said: a shift and a wrap, which she spreads over her head and with which she covers herself.

From him, from Safwan, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, from Abu al-Hasan عليه السلام, who said: It is not upon the bondwomen to cover themselves with a head-cover in the salat, and it is not proper for a woman to perform salat except in two garments.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from 'Uthman ibn 'Isa, from Ibn Miskan, from Ibn Abi Ya'fur, who said: Abu 'Abdillah عليه السلام said: A woman performs salat (prayer) in three garments: a waist-wrapper, a shift, and a khimar; and it does not harm her that she cover herself with the khimar. If she does not find that, then with two garments: she wraps herself with one of them and covers herself with the other. I said: Then if it is a shift and a wrap, and she does not have a head-covering? He said: There is no problem if she covers herself with a wrap; and if it does not suffice her, then she should wear it lengthwise.

As for what Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Ansari, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from ʿAbd Allah ibn Bukayr, from Abu ʿAbd Allah عليه السلام, who said: There is no harm in a free Muslim woman performing salat (prayer) while her head is uncovered.

From him, from Abū ʿAlī Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Ayyūb al-Makkī, from ʿAlī ibn Asbāṭ, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Bukayr, from Abū ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said: There is no harm in a Muslim woman praying while there is no head-covering upon her head. So the proper way regarding these two reports is that we interpret them as referring to young girls among women, excluding those who are mature, because it is not permissible for them to pray without a head-covering. It is also possible that this was only permitted for them in a situation where they are unable to obtain anything with which to cover themselves; then it is permissible, in the circumstance as we have described, for them to pray without a head-covering. And it is possible that what is meant by that is when she has upon herself a garment that covers her from her head to her feet, such as a wrap and the like. As for the final report, it does not mention the free woman, and it is possible that this is specific to bondwomen, because it is permissible for a bondwoman to pray while there is no head-covering upon her. What we have previously presented of the reports indicates this, and clarifies it further.

What Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah narrated from Ahmad and 'Abd Allah, the two sons of Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from al-'Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: I said to him: Should the female slave cover her head? He said: No, and it is not upon Umm al-Walad to cover her head if she does not have a child.

As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Jamīl ibn Darrāj, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about a woman praying in a shift and a khimār. He said: There should be over her a wrap which she draws closely around herself. So the proper way to understand this report is that it indicates a kind of recommendation. It is also possible that what is meant is when the shift and the khimār are of the sort that do not conceal anything; for when that is so, a covering is unavoidable. And that which indicates what we have said is...

What Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb narrated from ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Ḥammād, from al-Ḥalabī, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: It is not proper for a Muslim woman to wear, from among khimārs and garments, that which does not cover anything.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Fadalah, from al-Husayn ibn 'Uthman, from Ibn Muskan, from Abi Bakr al-Hadrami, who said: I asked Aba 'Abdillah عليه السلام about a man who performs salat while his dye-cloth is upon him. He said: He should not perform salat while it is upon him; rather, he should remove it when he wants to perform salat. I said: His henna and his cloth are clean. He said: He should not perform salat while it is upon him, and the woman also should not perform salat while her dye-cloth is upon her.

As for what Saʿd narrated from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from al-Ḥasan ibn Maḥbūb, from Rifāʿah, who said: I asked Abā al-Ḥasan عليه السلام about a person dyed with henna: if he is able to perform sajdah and recitation, may he perform salat in his henna? He said: Yes, if his cloth is tahir and he is in a state of wudu (ablution).

From him, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from Muḥammad ibn Sahl ibn al-Yasaʿ al-Ashʿarī, from his father, from Abī al-Ḥasan عليه السلام, who said: I asked him: May a man perform salat (prayer) while in his dye, if he is in a state of taharah (ritual purity)? He said: Yes.

From him, from Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan, from ʿAmr ibn Saʿīd, from Muṣaddaq ibn Ṣadaqah, from ʿAmmār al-Sābāṭī, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about a woman who performs salat (prayer) while her hands are bound with henna. He said: If she had performed wudu (ablution) for the salat (prayer) before that, then there is no harm in the salat (prayer) while she is dyed with henna and her hands are bound.

From him, from Abi Ja'far, from Musa ibn al-Qasim, from 'Ali ibn Ja'far, from his brother Musa عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man and a woman who apply dye and perform salat (prayer) while they are covered with henna and wasmah. He said: If the mouth and the nostril are left exposed, then there is no harm. The first report is to be understood as indicating karahah, while these reports are to be understood as indicating permissibility.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Fadalah, from al-'Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who performs salat (prayer) and does not bring his hands out from his garment. He said: If he brings out his hands, that is good; and if he does not bring them out, then there is no harm.

Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from ʿAli ibn Riʾab, from Ziyad ibn Suqah, from Abi Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said: There is no harm in one of you praying in a single garment while its buttons are undone. Indeed, the religion of Muhammad صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم is upright and inclining to truth.

Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Faḍḍāl, from a man, who said: I said to Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام: The people say that if a man performs salat (prayer) while his buttons are undone and his hands are inside the shirt, then he is only praying as one naked. He said: There is no harm.

As for what Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb narrated, from Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī, from ʿAmr ibn Saʿīd, from Muṣaddaq ibn Ṣadaqah, from ʿAmmār al-Sābāṭī, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, he said: I asked him about a man who performs salat (prayer) and puts his hand inside his garment. He said: If he is wearing another garment, a waist-wrapper or trousers, then there is no problem. But if he is not, then that is not permissible for him. And if he puts in one hand and does not put in the other, then there is no problem.

From him, from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn, from Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā, from Ghiyāth, from Jaʿfar, from his father عليه السلام, who said: A man should not perform salat (prayer) with his buttons undone when he is not wearing an izar. The meaning in these two reports is a degree of reprehensibility, not prohibition; that is indicated by this.

What al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Safwan, from 'Abd Allah ibn Bukayr, from Ibrahim al-Ahmar, who said: I asked Aba 'Abd Allah عليه السلام about a man who performs salat (prayer) while his buttons are undone. He said: That is not proper.

Al-Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Abu al-Qasim Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from 'Abd Allah ibn Sinan, who said: My father asked Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام while I was present: I lend my garment to a dhimmi, and I know that he drinks wine and eats the flesh of swine. Then he returns it to me, so should I wash it before I perform salat in it? So Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام said: Perform salat in it, and do not wash it on account of that, for you lent it to him while it was tahir, and you have not become certain that he made it najis. So there is no problem in performing salat in it until you become certain that he made it najis.

As for what was narrated by ʿAlī ibn Mahziyār, from Faḍālah, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Sinān, who said: My father asked Abā ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام about a person who lends his garment to someone whom he knows eats al-jirrī and drinks wine, then he returns it: may he perform salat (prayer) in it before washing it? He said: He should not perform salat (prayer) in it before washing it. Thus, both of these reports are narrated by ʿAbd Allāh ibn Sinān, and in both of them the account concerns his father's question to Abā ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام. It is not permissible, as you can see, for them to be contradictory such that he says at one time, 'Perform salat (prayer) in it,' and at another time says, 'Do not perform salat (prayer) in it,' unless his statement, 'Do not perform salat (prayer) in it,' is to be understood as indicating dislike rather than prohibition.

The Shaykh Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام informed me, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from his father, from al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Ḥasan ibn Abān, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from Ḥammād and Faḍālah, from Muʿāwiyah ibn ʿAmmār, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about a mouse and a gecko that fall into the well. He said: Three buckets are to be drawn from it.
And from him, from Faḍālah, from Ibn Sinān, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام. Its like.
As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from al-Qāsim, from ʿAlī, he said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about a mouse that falls into the well. He said: seven buckets.

And from him, from 'Uthman ibn 'Isa, from Sama'ah, who said: I asked him about a mouse that falls into the well, or a bird. He said: If you reach it before it becomes putrid, you draw seven buckets from it. So the proper way regarding these two reports is that we interpret them to mean that if the mouse had decomposed, then seven buckets are to be drawn from it; and we interpret the first two reports to mean that it was removed before it decomposed. And that which indicates this detailed distinction is what follows.

The Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me of it from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from 'Ali ibn al-Hakam, from 'Uthman ibn 'Abd al-Malik, from Abi Sa'id al-Mukari, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: If a mouse falls into the well and its skin comes off, then draw out seven buckets from it. Thus this report came as an explanation for all the reports.

As for what Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā narrated from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Hāshim, from Abū Khadījah, from Abū ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said: He was asked about a mouse falling into a well. He said: If it dies and does not rot and stink, then forty buckets; and if it swells in it and stinks, all of the water is to be drawn out. So the sound approach regarding what this report contains of the command to draw forty buckets if it has not stunk is that it is to be understood as a form of recommendation, not obligation and requirement, because none of our companions held obligation in this amount.

As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā narrated from ʿAlī ibn Ḥadīd, from some of our companions, who said: I was with Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام on the road to Makkah. We came to a well, and the servant of Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام drew up a bucket, and two mice came out in it. So Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام said: “Pour it out.” Then he drew another, and a mouse came out in it, so Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام said: “Pour it out.” Then he drew a third, and nothing came out in it, so he said: “Pour it into the vessel.” So he poured it into the vessel. So the first thing about this report is that it is mursal, and its narrator is weak, namely ʿAlī ibn Ḥadīd; and this weakens using his report as proof. And even if it is accepted, it is possible that what is meant by the well is a reservoir in which there is an amount of water exceeding the measure of a kurr, so no water needs to be drawn out from it; and that is what is customary on the road to Makkah. Moreover, there is nothing in the report stating that he performed wudu (ablution) with that water; rather, he said to his servant: “Pour it into the vessel,” and in that there is no proof for the permissibility of using water of this ruling-status in wudu (ablution). It is also possible that he only ordered him to pour it into the vessel because they needed it for watering beasts and camels, or for drinking in a state of necessity requiring it, and that is permissible. It is also possible that the two mice came out alive, and if that was so, then using what remained of the water is permissible, because that does not render the water najis, as has preceded earlier. And what further clarifies it is what...

The Shaykh Abū ʿAbd Allāh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me of it, from Abū Jaʿfar Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn ibn Bābawayh, from his father, from Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā, from Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā, from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn ibn Abī al-Khaṭṭāb and al-Ḥasan ibn Mūsā al-Khashshāb together, from Yazīd ibn Isḥāq, from Hārūn ibn Ḥamzah al-Ghanawī, from Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a mouse, a scorpion, and the like falling into water and then coming out alive: may that water be drunk from and wudu (ablution) performed from it? He said: It should be poured out three times, and its small amount and large amount are of one rank; then one may drink from it and perform wudu (ablution) from it, except for the gecko, for no benefit is taken from what it falls into. And we have already spoken about this report previously.

Al-Husayn ibn 'Ubayd Allah informed me, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Mahbub, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from 'Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Aban, from Ya'qub ibn 'Uthaym, who said: I said to Abī 'Abd Allāh عليه السلام: A gecko was found, and we found that it had decomposed in the well. He said: You are only required to draw seven buckets from it.

As for what Jābir ibn Yazīd al-Juʿfī narrated, he said: I asked Abā Jaʿfar عليه السلام about a gecko falling into the well, and he said: It is nothing; stir the water with the bucket in the well. So this does not contradict the first report, because the first report is to be understood as recommendation, and this report accords with what we have already presented from the reports: that whatever has no flowing blood does not spoil the water by its death, and the gecko is of that kind.

Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥakam, from Abān ibn ʿUthmān, from Zurārah, from Abī Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about the shādhakūnah upon which janabah is present: may one pray upon it in the litter? He said: There is no harm.

From him, from al-‘Abbās ibn Ma‘rūf, from Ṣafwān, from Ṣāliḥ al-Naylī, from Muḥammad ibn Abī ‘Umayr, who said: I said to Abū ‘Abdillāh عليه السلام: May I perform salat (prayer) on a shādhakūnah when janabah has affected it? He said: There is no harm.

As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Ṣafwān, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Bukayr, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام about the shādhakūnah that is affected by semen from a wet dream: may one pray on it? He said: No. So the proper understanding of this report is that it indicates a kind of recommendation, not prohibition.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from al-'Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I said to Abī Ja‘far عليه السلام: May I perform salat (prayer) while images are in front of me and I am looking at them? He said: There is no problem; cast a cloth over them. And there is no problem with them if they are on your right, or your left, or behind you, or beneath your feet, or above your head. But if they are in the qiblah direction, then throw a cloth over them and perform salat (prayer).

As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from Saʿd ibn Ismāʿīl, from his father, who said: I asked Abū al-Ḥasan al-Riḍā عليه السلام about a person praying while there is a carpet with images on it: may he stand on it and perform salat (prayer), or not? He said: “By Allah, I indeed dislike it.” And concerning a man who entered upon another man who had a carpet with an image on it, he said: “Do not sit on it, and do not perform salat (prayer) on it.” Thus, the correct understanding of this report is that it indicates a degree of reprehensibility, not prohibition.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from 'Ali ibn Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah, from Ibn al-Barqi, from his father, from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Fadl, from one who narrated to him, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: There are ten places in which one does not perform salat (prayer): mud, water, the bathhouse, graves, the beaten parts of the road, ant colonies, the resting places of camels, the course of water, saline ground, and snow.

As for what was narrated by Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb, from ʿAlī ibn Khālid, from Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan, from ʿAmr ibn Saʿīd, from Muṣaddaq ibn Ṣadaqah, from ʿAmmār al-Sābāṭī, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about salat (prayer) in the bathhouse. He said: If it is a clean place, then there is no harm in it. So the correct way regarding this report is that we understand it as referring to the dressing area of the bathhouse, or as a kind of concession, because doing that is disliked, though not prohibited.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Al-Hasan, from Zur'ah, from Sama'ah, who said: I asked him about salat (prayer) in the resting-places of camels and in the tethering-places of cattle and sheep. He said: If you sprinkle it with water and it is dry, then there is no harm in praying in them. But as for the tethering-places of horses and mules, then no.

As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Ḥammād, from Ḥarīz, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about salat (prayer) in the resting places of camels. He said: If you fear loss regarding your belongings, then sweep it, sprinkle it with water, and perform salat (prayer); and there is no objection to salat (prayer) in the sheepfolds.
