So the proper understanding of this report is the state of necessity, in accordance with what the report contains of fear for one’s belongings or something similar.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from al-Hasan, from Zur'ah, from Sama'ah, who said: I asked him about salat (prayer) in saline land, and he said: There is no harm in it. As for the previous report and what it contained of prohibition regarding salat (prayer) in marshy saline ground, it is only to be understood as indicating a kind of recommendation. It is also possible that it is to be understood as referring to a saline ground in which the forehead cannot be firmly placed for sajdah (prostration). This is indicated by what follows.

What al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Hammad ibn 'Isa, from Shu'ayb ibn Ya'qub, from Abi Basir, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about salat (prayer) in saline marshland, and he disliked it because the forehead does not settle evenly. So I said: If there is level ground in it? He said: There is no harm in it.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan, from Amr ibn Sa'id, from Musaddaq ibn Sadaqah, from Ammar al-Sabati, from Abu Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: A man should not perform salat (prayer) while there is fire or iron in front of him in the direction of his qiblah.

Muhammad ibn Yahya, from al-'Umarki, from 'Ali ibn Ja'far, from Abu al-Hasan عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who performs salat (prayer) while a lamp is placed before him in the direction of the qiblah. He said: It is not proper for him to face fire.

As for what Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā narrated from al-Ḥasan, from al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAmr, from his father ʿAmr ibn Ibrāhīm al-Hamadānī, he raised the hadith and said: Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام said: There is no harm in a man performing salat (prayer) while a fire, a lamp, and an image are before him. Surely, the One for whom he performs salat (prayer) is nearer to him than that which is before him. So this is an anomalous narration with a disconnected sanad/isnad, and it is to be understood as a kind of concession, even though what we mentioned previously is preferable.

Al-Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Abū al-Qāsim Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb, from Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī, from ʿAmr ibn Saʿīd, from Muṣaddaq ibn Ṣadaqah, from ʿAmmār al-Sābāṭī, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who performs salat (prayer) between the graves. He said: That is not permissible unless, when he performs salat (prayer), he places between himself and the graves ten cubits in front of him, ten cubits behind him, ten cubits on his right, and ten cubits on his left; then he may perform salat (prayer) if he wishes.

As for what Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā narrated from Muʿāwiyah ibn Ḥakīm, from Muʿammar ibn Khallād, from al-Riḍā عليه السلام, who said: There is no harm in praying toward the قبر so long as the قبر is not taken as a qiblah.

And what Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb narrated from Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā al-ʿAbdī, from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Yaqṭīn, from his brother, from his father ʿAlī ibn Yaqṭīn, who said: I asked Abā al-Ḥasan al-Māḍī عليه السلام about salat (prayer) between the graves: is it valid? He said: There is no objection. So the proper way regarding these two reports is that we understand them to mean that this is when there is a barrier between him and the grave, or when there are ten cubits between him and the grave, according to what he explained in the first report.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, from Hammad ibn 'Isa, from Rib'i, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far عليه السلام, who said: I said to him: May a man perform salat (prayer) while he is veiled over the mouth? He said: As for on the ground, no; but as for on a riding animal, there is no harm.

As for what al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from 'Uthman ibn 'Isa, from Sama'ah, who said: I asked Aba 'Abdillah عليه السلام about a man who performs salat (prayer) and recites the Qur'an while his face is covered with a litham, and he said: There is no harm in it.

Sa'd narrated from Abū Ja'far, from al-'Abbās ibn Ma'rūf, from 'Alī ibn Mahziyār, from al-Ḥusayn ibn 'Alī, from someone he mentioned, from one of the two (Imams) عليهما السلام, that he said: There is no harm in a man reciting in salat (prayer) while his garment is over his mouth. So the proper way regarding these two reports is that we understand them to mean that if the face-covering does not prevent the Qur'an from being heard, then there is no harm in it. It is only considered disliked when it prevents the recitation from being heard. This is indicated by that.

What Saʿd ibn ʿAbdillah narrated from Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan, from al-Ḥasan ibn Maḥbūb, from ʿAlī ibn Riʾāb, from al-Ḥalabī, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillah عليه السلام: May a man recite in his salat (prayer) while his garment is over his mouth? He said: There is no harm in that, if he can hear the murmuring.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Safwan, from al-'Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from one of the two عليهما السلام, who said: I asked him about a man praying in one corner of the room while his wife or his daughter is praying beside him in the other corner. He said: That is not appropriate; but if there is a span between them, it suffices—that is, when the man is ahead of the woman by a span.

From him, from Faḍālah, from Ḥusayn ibn ʿUthmān, from al-Ḥasan al-Ṣayqal, from Ibn Miskān, from Abū Baṣīr, who said: I asked him about a man and a woman praying in one house, while the woman is on the right side of the man, parallel with him. He said: No, unless there is between them a handspan or a cubit. Then he said: The length of the saddle-pack of the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم was a cubit, and he would place it in front of himself when he performed salat, so that it would screen him from one who might pass in front of him.

From him, from Ṣafwān and Faḍālah, from al-ʿAlāʾ, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, from one of the two عليهما السلام, who said: I asked him about a woman being alongside a man in the howdah while they both perform salat together. He said: No; rather, the man should perform salat, and when he has finished, the woman should perform salat.

From him, from Muḥammad ibn Sinān, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muskān, from Abī Baṣīr, from Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man and a woman performing salat (prayer) together in a house, with the woman on the man's right, aligned beside him. He said: No, not until there is between them a handspan, or a cubit, or something similar.

A man is praying while a woman is parallel to him or at his side, so he said: If her prostration is aligned with his bowing, then there is no harm. 6—From him, from Ya'qub ibn Yazid, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from 'Umar ibn Udhaynah, from Zurarah, from Abi Ja'far عليه السلام. He said: I asked him about a woman praying near a man, so he said: A woman should not pray directly in line with a man unless he is in front of her, even if only by the measure of his chest.

As for what Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā narrated from Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan, from ʿAmr ibn Saʿīd al-Madāʾinī, from Muṣaddaq ibn Ṣadaqah, from ʿAmmār al-Sābāṭī, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, that he was asked about a man: is it proper for him to perform salat while his wife is performing salat in front of him? He said: He should not perform salat until he places between himself and her more than ten cubits. If she is on his right or his left, he should place between himself and her the like of that. If she is performing salat behind him, then there is no harm, even if she touches his garment. And if the woman is sitting, lying down, or standing without being in salat, then there is no harm wherever she may be. Thus, the proper way regarding this report is that we understand it as indicating a form of recommendation. It is also possible that the consideration of ten cubits between them applies only when they are on a single line; but if the man is ahead of her, even by a handspan, then this consideration falls away, according to what he detailed in the earlier reports.

As for what Saʿd narrated from Yaʿqūb ibn Yazīd, from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Faḍḍāl, from one who informed him, from Jamīl ibn Darrāj, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, concerning: A man prays while a woman prays beside him. He said: There is no harm. The proper way to understand this report is that it is to be understood as referring to when the man is slightly ahead of the woman, such that his saying, ‘she prays beside him,’ is in a figurative sense due to her closeness to him.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Hasan ibn 'Ali al-Washsha', from Ahmad ibn 'A'idh, from 'Umar ibn Hanzalah, who said: I said to Abu 'Abdillah عليه السلام: There may be a heap of food plastered with clay like a rooftop? He said: Pray upon it.

As for what Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb narrated from Aḥmad, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from Faḍālah, from Ḥusayn ibn ʿUthmān, from Ibn Muskān, from Muḥammad ibn Muḍārib, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a heap of wheat that had been plastered with clay: may I perform salat (prayer) on top of it? He said: Do not perform salat (prayer) on top of it. I said: But it is level like a roof. He said: Do not perform salat (prayer) upon it. So the proper understanding of this report is that it indicates a kind of disapproval short of prohibition.

Al-Shaykh Abu 'Abd Allah, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah and al-Saffar together, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from 'Abd Allah ibn Yahya, from Ibn Muskan, who said: Abu Basir narrated to me, saying: I asked Aba 'Abd Allah عليه السلام about excrement falling into a well. He said: Ten buckets are to be drawn from it; if it has dissolved, then forty or fifty buckets.

As for what Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated from Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan, from ʿAmr ibn Saʿīd, from Muṣaddaq ibn Ṣadaqah, from ʿAmmār, who said: Abu ʿAbd Allah عليه السلام was asked about a well into which a basket of dry or moist excrement falls, and he said: There is no harm, if there is abundant water in it.

And what Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb narrated from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn, from Mūsā ibn al-Qāsim, from ʿAlī ibn Jaʿfar, from his brother Mūsā ibn Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a well of water into which a basket of dry or wet feces had fallen, or a basket of manure. Is wudu (ablution) from it valid? He said: There is no harm in it. The proper way to understand these two reports is one of two possibilities: one of them is that the intended meaning is that there is no harm in it after drawing out fifty buckets, in accordance with what the first report contained. The second is that what is meant by the well is a constructed reservoir in which there is more than a kurr of water; and for this reason he said there is no harm in it when there is abundant water in it, because that is where smallness and abundance are taken into consideration, unlike specified wells.

As for what Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated, from Musa ibn al-Hasan, from Abu al-Qasim ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Hammad al-Kufi, from Bashir, from Abu Maryam al-Ansari, who said: I was with Abu ʿAbd Allah عليه السلام in a garden belonging to him when the time for salat (prayer) came. He drew up a bucket for wudu (ablution) from a well of his, and on it there came out a piece of dry feces, so he tilted off its top and performed wudu (ablution) with what remained. This report may also bear two possibilities: one of them is what we mentioned in the two previous reports, that what is meant by al-rakiyy is the reservoir in which there is abundant water; and the second is that the feces is understood to have been the feces of an animal whose meat is eaten, and that does not render the water impure in any case.

As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Muḥammad ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Kurdawayh, who said: I asked Abā al-Ḥasan عليه السلام about a well into which rainwater enters, containing urine, feces, the urine of beasts, their dung, and the droppings of dogs. He said: Thirty buckets should be drawn from it. And even if it is malodorous, this report does not conflict with what we specified regarding drawing fifty buckets, because this report is specific to rainwater with which one of these impure things becomes mixed and then enters the well. In that case, its use is permissible after drawing forty buckets. And the report we cited earlier applies to when the feces itself falls into the well, so there is no contradiction between them in any way.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from Mansur ibn Yunus, from Abi Bakr al-Hadrami, from Abi Ja'far and Abi 'Abd Allah, peace be upon them, that they said: Nothing cuts off the salat except four things: defecation, urination, wind, and sound.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from 'Abbad ibn Sulayman, from Sa'd ibn Sa'd, from Muhammad ibn al-Qasim ibn al-Fudayl ibn Yasar, from al-Hasan ibn al-Jahm, who said: I asked him about a man who performed Zuhr or 'Asr, then breaks his wudu (ablution) when he sits in the fourth [rak'ah]. He said: If he had said, "I bear witness that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah," then he does not repeat [the prayer]. But if he had not recited the tashahhud before breaking his wudu (ablution), then he must repeat.

From him, from Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Faḍḍāl, from ʿAmr ibn Saʿīd, from Muṣaddaq ibn Ṣadaqah, from ʿAmmār al-Sābāṭī, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, concerning: A man is in his salat (prayer), and a pumpkin seed comes out from him; then there is nothing upon him, and it has not invalidated his wudu (ablution). But if it comes out smeared with feces, then he must repeat the wudu (ablution); and if he is in his salat (prayer), he must break the salat (prayer) and repeat the wudu (ablution) and the salat (prayer).

As for what was narrated by ʿAlī ibn Mahziyār, from Ḥammād ibn ʿĪsā, from Ḥarīz, from al-Fuḍayl ibn Yasār, who said: I said to Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام: I may be in salat (prayer) and feel a cramp in my stomach, or discomfort, or throbbing. So he said: Turn away, then perform wudu (ablution), and build upon what has passed of your salat (prayer), so long as you have not invalidated the salat (prayer) by speaking deliberately. And if you spoke forgetfully, then there is no harm upon you; it is like one who speaks in salat (prayer) forgetfully. I said: What if he turns his face away from the qiblah? He said: Yes, even if he turns his face away from the qiblah. So this report does not contradict what we have previously presented of the reports, because there is nothing in the report beyond that he found discomfort in his stomach, and not everyone who finds discomfort has entered a state of hadath. There is nothing in the report stating that he actually passed hadath. As for his statement, “so long as he has not invalidated the salat (prayer) deliberately,” it does not indicate that if he was forgetful then repetition is not required, except by way of an implication of wording; and such implication may be left aside, according to those who accept it, on account of other evidence. We have already shown that through the preceding reports. As for his ordering him to perform wudu (ablution), that may be understood as carrying a sense of recommendation. It is also possible that this was specific to speech, because one who speaks forgetfully is not required to repeat. For that reason he said immediately after this statement, “And if you spoke forgetfully, then there is no harm upon you,” which indicates that by his statement, “so long as he has not invalidated the salat (prayer) deliberately,” he intended deliberate invalidation by speech and not anything else.

As for what was narrated by Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb, from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn, from Ṣafwān, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Bukayr, from ʿUbayd ibn Zurārah, who said: I said to Abū ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام: A man experiences hadath after he has raised his head from the final sajdah. He said: His salat is complete. The tashahhud is only a sunnah in the salat, so he should perform wudu (ablution), sit in his place or in a clean place, and then recite the tashahhud. The proper way to understand this report is to interpret it as referring to one who experienced hadath after the two testimonies and before completing the recommended part of the tashahhud. In that case, he performs wudu (ablution) and repeats the tashahhud by way of recommendation. But if it had occurred before the two testimonies, then repeating the salat would have been required of him, as we explained in the earlier reports.

As for what Saʿd narrated from Abū Jaʿfar, from his father, from Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā and al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd and Muḥammad ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from ʿUmar ibn Udhaynah, from Zurārah, from Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام, concerning: Regarding a man who experiences hadath after raising his head from the final sajdah and before performing tashahhud, he said: He should leave and perform wudu (ablution). Then, if he wishes, he may return to the mosque, and if he wishes, then in his house, and if he wishes, wherever he wishes, he may sit and recite the tashahhud, then give salām. And if the hadath occurred after the two testimonies, then his salat (prayer) has passed as valid. So this report may be understood as being specific to one who entered into the salat (prayer) with tayammum and then experienced hadath forgetfully; in that case it is permissible for him to perform wudu (ablution) and continue his salat (prayer), according to what we explained in the Book of Taharah in the larger book. It is also possible that he only experienced hadath after the two testimonies, which are a condition for the validity of the salat (prayer), and that his statement, 'And if the hadath occurred after the two testimonies, then his salat (prayer) has passed,' indicates completion of the two testimonies, with the recommended prolongation therein; and the instruction to repeat the tashahhud is to be understood as carrying a sense of recommendation.

Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah, from Musa ibn al-Husayn, from al-Sindi ibn Muhammad, from al-'Ala' ibn Razin, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who is overcome by nosebleed or vomiting during the salat (prayer): what should he do? He said: He should turn away, wash his nose, and return to the salat (prayer). But if he speaks, then he must repeat the salat (prayer).

Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥakam, from Ismāʿīl ibn ʿAbd al-Khāliq, who said: I asked him about a man who is among a group of people praying the obligatory salat, then a nosebleed occurs to him—what should he do? He said: He should leave, and if he finds water before speaking, then let him wash his nose of the nosebleed, then return and continue building upon his salat.

As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Yaqṭīn, from his brother al-Ḥusayn, from his father ʿAlī ibn Yaqṭīn, who said: I asked Abā al-Ḥasan عليه السلام about nosebleeding, cupping, and vomiting. He said: These do not invalidate anything of the wudu (ablution), but they do invalidate the salat (prayer).

Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from Muḥammad ibn Sinān, from Abī Khālid, from Abī Ḥamzah, from Abī Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said: Nothing cuts off the salat (prayer) except a nosebleed and rumbling in the belly, so deal with them promptly as much as you are able. The proper way regarding these two reports is that we carry them upon a nosebleed whose sufferer needs to turn away from the qiblah or to speak. But when that is absent, then it does not cut off the salat (prayer), as has been detailed in the first two reports; and this is also indicated by further evidence.

What was narrated by ʿAlī ibn Mahziyār, from Faḍālah, from Abān, from Muslim, from Abī Ḥafṣ, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, that ʿAlī عليه السلام used to say: A nosebleed, blood, and vomiting do not invalidate the salat (prayer). So whoever experiences discomfort should take the hand of a man from the people in the row and bring him forward—that is, if he is an Imam.

Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb, from ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Ḥammād, from al-Ḥalabī, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who is afflicted with a nosebleed while he is in salat (prayer). He said: If he is able to reach water near him, to his right, or to his left, or in front of him, while he is still facing the qiblah, then he should wash it off and then complete what remains of his salat (prayer). But if he is not able to reach water before turning his face away or speaking, then his salat (prayer) has been invalidated.

As for what Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā narrated from al-ʿAmrakī, from ʿAlī ibn Jaʿfar, from his brother Mūsā ibn Jaʿfar عليه السلام, he said: I asked him about a man who has a wart or a wound: is it permissible for him to cut off the wart while he is in his salat (prayer), or to pluck some flesh from that wound and lance it? He said: If he does not fear that blood will flow, then there is no problem; but if he fears that blood will flow, then he should not do it. And about a man who is in his salat (prayer), then another man throws something at him and wounds his head, so blood flows. He turns away, washes it, and does not speak until he returns to the mosque. Should he count what he has already prayed, or should he begin the salat (prayer) anew? He said: He should begin the salat (prayer) anew and not count anything of what he had prayed. So the proper way regarding this report is that we interpret it as referring to one who turned around until he faced away from the qiblah, for that invalidates his salat (prayer). It is also possible that it was issued in the context of taqiyyah, because according to many of the ʿAmmah, the خروج of blood nullifies wudu (ablution), and when wudu (ablution) is nullified, it necessitates repeating the salat (prayer) from its beginning, as we have mentioned before.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from 'Umar ibn Udhaynah, from Zurarah, that he heard Aba Ja'far عليه السلام saying: Turning away breaks the salat (prayer) when it is done with the whole body.

From him, from Safwan, from al-'Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far عليه السلام, who said: I asked him: May a man turn around in his salat (prayer)? He said: No, and he should not crack his fingers.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from 'Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Hammad, from Hariz, from Zurarah, from Abu Ja'far عليه السلام, who said: When you face the qiblah with your face, then do not turn your face away from the qiblah, lest you invalidate your salat. For Allah, Exalted is He, said to His Prophet صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم regarding the obligatory prayer: “So turn your face toward al-Masjid al-Haram; and wherever you are, turn your faces toward it.” And be humble with your gaze, and do not raise it toward the sky; rather, keep it level with your face at the place of your sajdah.

As for what Saʿd narrated from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn, from Jaʿfar ibn Bashīr, from Ḥammād ibn ʿUthmān, from ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd, from ʿAbd al-Malik, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about turning in salat (prayer): does it invalidate the salat (prayer)? He said: No, but I do not like that you do it. So the correct way regarding this report is that we interpret it as referring to one who does not turn toward what is behind him, but rather turns to the right and left; then this does not invalidate his salat (prayer), although he has left what is more excellent, according to what he explained in this report and other reports. And what further clarifies that will come.

What was narrated by ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Ḥammād, from al-Ḥalabī, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: If you turn around during an obligatory salat (prayer) before completing it, then repeat the salat (prayer) if the turning was excessive; but if you had already recited the tashahhud, then do not repeat.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from Mu'awiyah ibn Wahb, from Abi 'Abdillah عليه السلام, who said: The Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم used to place the spear before him when he performed salat (prayer).

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Ibn Sinan, from Ibn Miskan, from Abi Basir, from Abi 'Abdillah عليه السلام, who said: The length of the saddle of the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم was one cubit, and when he performed salat, he would place it before himself and screen himself with it from anyone who might pass in front of him.
Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from ʿAbd Allah ibn Ghiyath, from Abu ʿAbd Allah عليه السلام. The Prophet صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم placed a cap and performed salat (prayer) toward it.

As for what Ibn Muskan narrated from Abi Basir, from Abi ʿAbdillah عليه السلام, he said: Nothing cuts off the salat (prayer): neither a dog, nor a donkey, nor a woman. But screen yourselves with something; if there is before you, to the measure of a forearm, something raised from the ground, then you have screened yourself.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from 'Uthman ibn 'Isa, from Ibn Miskan, from Ibn Abi Ya'fur, who said: I asked Aba 'Abdillah عليه السلام about a man: does anything that passes before him cut off his salat (prayer)? He said: Nothing cuts off the salat (prayer) of a Muslim, but ward off what you can.

Ali narrated from his father, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abi 'Abdillah عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man: does anything that passes in front of him cut off his salat (prayer)? He said: Nothing cuts off the salat (prayer) of a Muslim, but ward off whatever you can.

Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Mahbub, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from 'Amr ibn Khalid, from Sufyan ibn Khalid, from Abi 'Abdillah عليه السلام, that he was praying one day when a man passed in front of him while his son Musa was sitting there. When he finished, he said: to him: “O my father, did you not see the man who passed in front of you?” So he said: “O my son, the One for whom I pray is nearer to me than the one who passed in front of me.” So the correct understanding of this report is permissibility, while the merit is in what we have previously presented among the reports, and this further clarifies that.

What Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā narrated from Mūsā ibn ʿUmar, from Muḥammad ibn Ismāʿīl, from al-Riḍā عليه السلام, concerning: Regarding a man who is performing salat (prayer), he said: there should be before him a small heap of dust, or he should draw a line before himself.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Ibrahim ibn Hashim, from al-Nawfali, from al-Sukuni, from Ja'far, from his father, from his forefathers, peace be upon them, who said: The Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him and his family, said: When one of you prays in an open land, let him place before himself something like the rear part of a saddle. If he does not find that, then a stone; if he does not find that, then an arrow; and if he does not find that, then let him draw a line on the ground before himself.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad, from al-Washsha', from Hammad ibn 'Uthman, from Sa'd Bayya' al-Sabiri, who said: I said to Abī 'Abdillāh عليه السلام: “Should a man force himself to weep in salat (prayer)?” He said: “Excellent, excellent, even if it be like the head of a fly.” Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: This report is to be understood as meaning that he intended when one weeps out of خشية of Allah, not that he should weep for something from the afflictions of the world; that is indicated by what supports this.

What Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb narrated from ʿAlī ibn Muḥammad, from al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad, from Sulaymān ibn Dāwūd, from al-Nuʿmān, from ʿAbd al-Salām, from Abū Ḥanīfah, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about crying during salat (prayer): does it invalidate the salat (prayer)? He said: If he cries due to the remembrance of jannah (paradise) or nar (hellfire), then that is among the best of deeds in salat (prayer). But if it is because he remembered a deceased person of his, then his salat (prayer) is invalid.

Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Mahbub, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad al-'Alawi, from al-'Amraki, from 'Ali ibn Ja'far, from his brother Musa عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about the boy: when do fasting and prayer become obligatory upon him? He said: when he approaches puberty and comes to know prayer and fasting.

From him, from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn, from Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī, from ʿAmr ibn Saʿīd, from Muṣaddaq ibn Ṣadaqah, from ʿAmmār al-Sābāṭī, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about the boy: when does salat (prayer) become obligatory upon him? He said: When he reaches thirteen years of age. But if he experiences iḥtilām before that, then salat (prayer) has become obligatory upon him and the pen has begun to run upon him. And the girl is like that: if she reaches thirteen years of age, or menstruates before that, then salat (prayer) has become obligatory upon her and the pen has begun to run upon her.

As for what al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Muhammad ibn al-Fudayl, from Ishaq ibn 'Ammar, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, he said: When the boy reaches six years, salat (prayer) becomes obligatory upon him; then when he is able to fast, sawm (fasting) becomes obligatory upon him.

Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb, from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn, from Ṣafwān, from al-ʿAlāʾ, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, from one of the two عليهما السلام, concerning: the child: when does he perform salat (prayer)? He said: when he understands the salat (prayer). I said: when does he understand the salat (prayer), such that it becomes obligatory upon him? He said: at six years.

From him, from al-‘Abbās ibn Ma‘rūf, from Ḥammād ibn ‘Īsā, from Mu‘āwiyah ibn Wahb, who said: I asked Abā ‘Abdillāh عليه السلام: At what age is the child to be held to salat (prayer)? He said: Between seven years and six years. I said: At what age is he to be held to sawm (fasting)? He said: Between fifteen or fourteen. And if he fasts before that, then leave him, for indeed a certain son of mine fasted before that and I left him.

Ali ibn Ibrahim narrated from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abi Abd Allah, from his father, peace be upon them both, who said: We command our children to perform salat (prayer) when they are five years old, so command your children to perform salat (prayer) when they are seven years old. And we command our children to observe sawm (fasting) when they are seven years old, according to whatever they are able to bear of the day's fast, even if it is until midday, or more than that, or less; then when thirst and hunger overcome them, they break the fast, so that they become accustomed to fasting and are able to bear it. So command your children, when they are nine years old, to observe sawm (fasting) as much of the day's fast as they are able; then when thirst overcomes them, they break the fast. Thus, the proper approach regarding these reports is that we carry them upon a mode of recommendation, encouragement, and disciplining, while the former is carried upon obligation, so that the reports do not conflict.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya and others, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, who said: Abu al-Hasan عليه السلام said: The supererogatory prayer on Friday is six rak'ahs at the beginning of the day, and six rak'ahs when it rises higher, and two rak'ahs when the sun declines. Then you perform the obligatory prayer, then pray six rak'ahs after it.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Hammad ibn 'Isa, from al-Husayn ibn al-Mukhtar, from 'Ali ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, from Murad ibn Kharijah, who said: Abu 'Abdillah عليه السلام said: As for me, when it is Friday, and the sun is in the east at the same measure as it would be from the west at the time of salat al-'asr, I pray six rak'ahs. Then when the day has broadened, I pray six rak'ahs. Then when the sun declines or passes the meridian, I pray two rak'ahs, then I pray al-zuhr, then I pray six after it.

From him, from Ya'qub ibn Yaqtin, from al-'Abd al-Salih عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about supererogatory prayer on Friday. He said: If you wish to perform supererogatory prayer on Friday while not traveling, then pray six rak'ahs at the rising of the day, six rak'ahs before midday, two rak'ahs when the sun declines before the Friday prayer, and six rak'ahs after the Friday prayer. And it has also been narrated that it is permissible for him to pray the same as he prays on the rest of the days.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated that from al-Nadr, from Hisham ibn Salim, from Sulayman ibn Khalid, who said: I said to Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام: What about the supererogatory prayer on Friday? He said: Six rak'ahs before the sun's decline, and two rak'ahs at its decline. The recitation in the first is Surat al-Jumu'ah and in the second Surat al-Munafiqun, and after the obligatory prayer there are eight rak'ahs. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Acting upon the first narrations is preferable, and that is also indicated by this.

What Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn Abī Naṣr, who said: I asked Abū al-Ḥasan عليه السلام about the supererogatory prayers on Friday. He said: Six rakʿahs at the beginning of the day, six rakʿahs before zawāl, two rakʿahs when the sun passes the meridian, and six rakʿahs after الجمعة; that makes twenty rakʿahs besides the obligatory prayer. And what I practice upon and give fatwa by is that bringing forward all the nawāfil on Friday to before zawāl is more excellent; this indicates that.

What was narrated by Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Yaqtin, from his brother al-Husayn, from his father Ali ibn Yaqtin, who said: I asked Aba al-Hasan عليه السلام about the nafilah that is performed on Friday: is it better before the Jumu'ah or after it? He said: Before the salat.

Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from al-Barqī, from Saʿd ibn Saʿd al-Ashʿarī, from Abī al-Ḥasan al-Riḍā عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about the prayer on Friday: how many rakʿahs is it before zawal? He said: six rakʿahs early in the morning, and six after that, making twelve rakʿahs, and six after that, making eighteen rakʿahs, and two rakʿahs after zawal, so these are twenty rakʿahs, and two rakʿahs after ʿasr, so these are twenty-two rakʿahs. Also, if the earlier narrations have been reported permitting the advancement of the nawafil to the beginning of the day, then acting upon them is more appropriate and more virtuous, because a person is not secure from sudden death, so he may have hastened that in which there is reward and merit for him.

As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from Muḥammad ibn Ismāʿīl, from ʿAlī ibn al-Nuʿmān, from Isḥāq ibn ʿAmmār, from ʿUqbah ibn Muṣʿab, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام and said: Which is better: that I perform the rakʿahs earlier on Friday, or that I pray them after the obligatory prayer? He said: No; rather, pray them after the obligatory prayer.

And among what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated, from Muḥammad ibn Sinān, from Ibn Miskān, from Sulaymān ibn Khālid, who said: I said to Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام: Should I advance some rakʿahs on Friday? He said: Yes, six rakʿahs. I said: Which of the two is more excellent: that I advance the rakʿahs on Friday, or that I perform them after the obligatory prayer? He said: Performing them after the obligatory prayer is more excellent. So these two reports do not contradict what we presented and said was more excellent, because the proper way regarding them is that we understand them to mean that when the sun has passed the meridian, delaying the nawāfil is more excellent than advancing them. Advancing is only more excellent so long as the sun has not passed the meridian and the time of the obligatory prayer has not entered; for when it has passed the meridian, one should begin with the obligatory prayer on this day rather than the nawāfil. And that which indicates this is:

What al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Muḥammad ibn Sinān, from Ibn Miskān, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAjlān, who said: Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام said: If you are doubtful about zawāl, then perform the two rakʿahs; and when you are certain of zawāl, then perform the obligatory prayer.

From him, from Muḥammad ibn Sinān, from Ibn Muskān, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr and Faḍālah, from Ḥusayn, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, who said: He narrated to me that he asked him about the two rakʿahs at the time of zawāl on Friday. He said: So he said: As for me, when the sun declines, I begin with the obligatory prayer.
From him, from Faḍālah, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Sinān, from Abū ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said: There is no salat at midday except on the day of al-Jumuʿah.

From him, from Safwan, from Ibn Muskan, from Isma'il ibn 'Abd al-Khaliq, who said: I asked Aba 'Abdillah عليه السلام about the time of Zuhr, so he said: After the sun’s decline by a footspan or about that, except on Friday or during travel, for indeed its time then is when the sun declines. And this report does not contradict.

What al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Safwan, from 'Abd Allah ibn Bukayr, from Abi Basir, who said: I entered upon Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام on a Friday, and I had already performed the Friday prayer and the 'asr prayer. I found that he had engaged in intercourse — meaning from al-bah, that is, he had had relations. He came out to me wrapped in his cloak, then called his maidservant and instructed her to place water for him to pour over himself. So I said to him, "May Allah set you right, have you not performed ghusl?" He said, "I have not yet performed ghusl, nor have I prayed." I said to him, "I have performed al-zuhr and al-'asr together." He said, "There is no harm, because it is not impossible that he عليه السلام only delayed al-zuhr from the time of zawal due to an excuse he had. It only becomes obligatory at zawal when no preventing obstacle from among the obstacles is present. And this also indicates the permissibility of advancing the nawafil."

What al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from al-Nadr, from Musa ibn Bakr, from Zurarah, from 'Umar ibn Hanzalah, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: The salat of supererogatory prayer on Friday, if you wish, may be performed from the beginning of the day; and whatever you intend to perform after Jumu'ah, then if you wish, you may advance it and perform it from the beginning of the day, at whatever part of the day you wish, before the sun declines.

Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from al-Ḥusayn, from al-Naḍr, from Muḥammad ibn Abī Ḥamzah, from Saʿīd al-Aʿraj, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about the nafilah prayer on Friday, So he said: Sixteen rakʿahs before al-ʿaṣr. Then he said: And ʿAlī عليه السلام used to say: Whatever is added is better. And he said: If a man wishes, he may perform six rakʿahs of it in the early part of the day, and six rakʿahs in the middle of the day, and pray al-ẓuhr, then pray four of it, then pray al-ʿaṣr.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Safwan, from Abi Ayyub, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I said to Abu 'Abdillah عليه السلام: “As for recitation in the salat (prayer), is there anything fixed in it?” He said: “No, except in الجمعة, in which al-Jumu'ah and al-Munafiqun are recited.”

From him, from 'Uthman ibn 'Isa, from سماعة, from Abu Basir, who said: Recite on the night of Friday Surat al-Jumu'ah and Sabbih isma rabbika al-A'la; and in the dawn prayer, Surat al-Jumu'ah and Qul huwa Allahu Ahad; and in the Friday prayer, Surat al-Jumu'ah and al-Munafiqun.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from 'Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Mughirah, from Jamil, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abi Ja'far عليه السلام, who said: Indeed, Allah honored the believers by means of Jumu'ah, so the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم established it as glad tidings for them and as a rebuke to the hypocrites. It is not proper to abandon it, and whoever abandons it deliberately, then there is no salat (prayer) for him.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Al-Husayn ibn 'Abd al-Malik al-Ahwal, from his father, from Abi 'Abdillah عليه السلام, who said: Whoever does not recite in the Friday prayer Surat al-Jumu'ah and al-Munafiqun, then there is no Jumu'ah for him. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: All of these reports are to be understood as indicating strong recommendation and emphatic censure regarding its omission, not that reciting these two surahs is a condition for the validity of the salat (prayer). And that which indicates this is:

What al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Ḥammād ibn ʿĪsā, from Ḥarīz and Ribʿī, who raised it to Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said: When it is the night of Friday, it is recommended that in the ʿatamah prayer, Sūrat al-Jumuʿah and Sūrat Idhā Jāʾaka al-Munāfiqūn be recited; and in the morning prayer likewise; and in the Friday prayer likewise; and in the ʿaṣr prayer likewise.

And Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā narrated from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Yaqṭīn, from his brother al-Ḥusayn, from his father ʿAlī ibn Yaqṭīn, who said: I asked Abā al-Ḥasan al-Awwal عليه السلام about a man who recites in Salat al-Jumuʿah something other than Surat al-Jumuʿah deliberately. He said: There is no harm in that.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from Muhammad ibn Sahl al-Ash'ari, from his father, who said: I asked Abā al-Hasan عليه السلام about a man who recites in Salat al-Jumu'ah something other than al-Jumu'ah intentionally. He said: There is no problem.

As for what Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb narrated from ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Muʿāwiyah ibn ʿAmmār, from ʿUmar ibn Yazīd, who said: Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام said: Whoever performs the Friday prayer without reciting Sūrat al-Jumuʿah and al-Munāfiqīn must repeat the salat (prayer), whether in travel or residence. The proper understanding of this report is encouragement that one should treat what he prayed without al-Jumuʿah and al-Munāfiqīn as being among the supererogatory prayers, and begin the salat (prayer) anew so that he may attain the merit of these two surahs; this clarifies what we have mentioned.

What was narrated by Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from Yūnus, from Ṣabbāḥ ibn Ṣabīḥ, who said: I said to Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام: A man intended to perform the Friday prayer, then he recited “Say: He is Allah, One.” He عليه السلام said: He completes it as two rakʿahs, then begins again. And that which indicates what we have said...

What Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā narrated, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from Abī al-Faḍl, from Ṣafwān ibn Yaḥyā, from Jamīl, from ʿAlī ibn Yaqṭīn, who said: I asked Abā al-Ḥasan عليه السلام about al-Jumuʿah during travel: what should I recite in them both? He said: Recite in them both: Qul huwa Allāhu Aḥad. So in this report he permitted the recitation of Qul huwa Allāhu Aḥad, while in the report it states that he repeats, whether he was in travel or in residence. Thus, if what was intended were other than what we have mentioned of encouragement, he would not have allowed that for him.

Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Safwan, from 'Abd Allah ibn Sinan, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: I heard him say concerning Salat al-Jumu'ah: there is no harm in reciting in it other than Surat al-Jumu'ah and al-Munafiqun, if you are in haste.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Mu'awiyah ibn Hakim, from Aban, from Yahya al-Azraq, the seller of Sabiri cloth, who said: I asked Aba al-Hasan عليه السلام, and I said: A man performed the Jumu'ah prayer and recited "Glorify the Name of your Lord, the Most High" and "Say: He is Allah, One." He عليه السلام said: “It sufficed him.”

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from 'Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, who said: I asked Abā 'Abdillāh عليه السلام about the recitation on Friday: if I pray alone four rak'ahs, should I recite aloud? He said, "Yes."

Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Ja'far ibn Bashir, from Hammad ibn 'Uthman, from 'Imran al-Halabi, who said: I heard Aba 'Abd Allah عليه السلام saying, and he was asked about a man who prays the Jumu'ah prayer as four rak'ahs: should he recite aloud in it? He said: Yes, and the qunut is in the second rak'ah.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from 'Ali ibn al-Nu'man, from 'Abd Allah ibn Muskan, from Hariz ibn 'Abd Allah, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: He said to us: Perform salat al-Jumu'ah during travel in congregation without a khutbah, and recite aloud. So I said: Indeed, our reciting aloud in it during travel is disapproved of by others against us. He said: Recite aloud in it.

From him, from Faḍālah, from al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿUbayd Allāh al-Arrajjānī, from Muḥammad ibn Marwān, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about the Zuhr prayer on Friday: how should we perform it while traveling? He said: You perform it while traveling as two rakʿahs, and the recitation in it is aloud.

As for what al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Jamil, who said: I asked Aba 'Abdillah عليه السلام about congregational prayer on Friday while traveling. He said: You do as you do on days other than Friday for Zuhr prayer, and the Imam does not recite aloud in it; rather, he only recites aloud when there is a sermon.

From him, from al-‘Alā’, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, who said: I asked him about Salat al-Jumu‘ah during travel, and he said: You do as you do in Zuhr, and the Imam does not recite aloud in it. He only recites aloud when there is a sermon. So the proper way regarding these two reports is that we interpret them as applying to a state of taqiyyah and fear; that indicates this.

What al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Ṣafwān, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Bukayr, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about a people in a village who do not have anyone to lead the Jumuʿah for them: should they pray Zuhr on Friday in congregation? He said: Yes, if they do not fear.
Sulaymān ibn Khālid narrated to me from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام. He said: The qunūt on the day of الجمعة is in the first rakʿah.

From him, from Faḍālah, from Abān, from Ismāʿīl al-Juʿfī, from ʿUmar ibn Ḥanẓalah, who said: I said to Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام: “The qunūt on Friday?” He said: “You are my messenger to them regarding this: when you pray in congregation, then it is in the first rakʿah; and when you pray individually, then it is in the second rakʿah.”
The qunut is in the first rak'ah before the ruku'. From him, from al-Hasan, from Zur'ah, from Abi Basir, who said:

ʿAlī ibn Mahziyār narrated from Faḍālah ibn Ayyūb, from Muʿāwiyah ibn ʿAmmār, who said: I heard Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام say regarding the qunut of Jumuʿah: if he is an Imam, he performs qunut in the first rakʿah; and if he is praying four rakʿahs, then in the second rakʿah before the rukuʿ.

As for what al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Muhammad ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Jamil ibn Salih, from 'Abd al-Malik ibn 'Amr, who said: I said to Abu 'Abdillah عليه السلام: Is the qunut of الجمعة in the first rak'ah before the ruku' and in the second after it? He said to me: Neither before nor after.

Saʿd ibn ʿAbdillah, from Jaʿfar ibn Bashir, from Dawud ibn al-Husayn, said: I heard Muʿammar ibn Abi Riʾab asking Aba ʿAbdillah عليه السلام, while I was present, about the qunut in Jumuʿah, so he said: “There is no qunut in it.” So the proper approach regarding these two reports is that we carry them upon the circumstance of taqiyyah, and that which indicates this is as follows.

What al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Abī Ayyūb, from Abī Baṣīr, who said: ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd asked Abā ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, while I was with him, about the qunūt on the Day of Jumuʿah, so he said: In the second rakʿah. He said to him: Some of our companions have narrated to us that you said: In the first rakʿah. So he said: In the last one. There were many people with him, so when he saw their heedlessness, he said: O Abā Muḥammad, in the first and the last. He said: I said, May I be your ransom, before the rukūʿ or after it? He said: Every qunūt is before the rukūʿ except Jumuʿah; for in the first rakʿah the qunūt in it is before the rukūʿ, and in the last it is after the rukūʿ.

Al-Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan ibn Aban, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from al-Qasim, from 'Ali, who said: I asked Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام about a mouse that falls into the well. He said: seven buckets. He said: And I asked him about a bird and a chicken that fall into the well. He said: seven buckets.

As for what Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā narrated from al-Ḥasan ibn Mūsā al-Khashshāb, from Ghiyāth ibn Kallūb, from Isḥāq ibn ʿAmmār, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, from his father عليه السلام, that ʿAlī عليه السلام used to say: Regarding a chicken and the like that dies in the well, two or three buckets are drawn from it. But if it is a sheep and what resembles it, then nine or ten. The proper way regarding this report is that we interpret it as indicating permissibility, and the first report as indicating merit and recommendation. Acting upon the first is preferable, because whenever we act upon the first report, this report is included within it, and our practice is then based on precaution and we attain certainty of taharah (ritual purity). But if we act upon this one, we would not be certain of taharah (ritual purity). It is also possible that the first refers to when it has decomposed, and the second to when it died and was removed immediately.

Al-Husayn ibn Ubayd Allah informed me, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Yahya, from his father, from Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub, from al-Abbas, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Rib'i, from Umar ibn Yazid, from Abi Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: If they are seven on Friday, then let them pray in congregation.

From him, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from his father, from Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā, from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn, from al-Ḥakam ibn Miskīn, from al-ʿAlāʾ, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, from Abī Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said: Jumuʿah becomes obligatory upon seven persons from among the Muslims, and it is not obligatory upon fewer than them: the Imam, his judge, the one claiming a right, the one against whom the claim is made, the two witnesses, and the one who carries out the prescribed penalties before the Imam.

ʿAlī ibn Mahziyār, from Faḍālah, from Abān ibn ʿUthmān, from Abī al-ʿAbbās, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: The minimum that suffices for Jumuʿah is seven, or five at the lowest. Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan said: There is no contradiction between these two reports, because obligation is connected to the number when they are seven; and when the number is five, that is recommended and encouraged, and it is not an obligatory duty. If it is less than five, then the Jumuʿah does not take place at all. That which indicates this is:

What al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Ṣafwān, from Manṣūr ibn Ḥāzim, from Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said: The people hold Jumuʿah on Friday when they are five or more. If they are fewer than five, then there is no Jumuʿah for them. Jumuʿah is obligatory upon every person; the people are not excused from it except five: the woman, the owned slave, the traveler, the child, and the sick person.
From him, from ʿUthmān ibn ʿĪsā, from Ibn Miskān, from Ibn Abī Yaʿfūr, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: There is no Jumuʿah unless the people are five.

ʿAlī, from his father, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Ibn Udhaynah, from Zurārah, who said: Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام used to say: the khutbah, the Jumuʿah, and the two-rakʿah salat are not to be held with fewer than five persons: the Imam and four others.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Safwan, from al-'Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from one of the two of them عليهما السلام, who said: I asked him about some people in a village: do they perform the Jumu'ah prayer in congregation? He said: They should pray four rak'ahs if there is no one to deliver the sermon.

From him, from Faḍālah, from Abān ibn ʿUthmān, from al-Faḍl ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, who said: I heard Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام saying: If there are people in a village, they pray the Jumuʿah as four rakʿahs. Then, if they have someone who can deliver the sermon for them, they hold the Jumuʿah when they are five persons. Jumuʿah was only made two rakʿahs because of the two sermons.

From him, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Hishām ibn Sālim, from Zurārah, who said: Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام strongly urged us regarding salat al-jumuʿah until I thought that he wanted us to come to him. So I said, “Shall we go early to you?” He said, “No, I only meant among yourselves.”

Zurārah narrated to me, from ʿAbd al-Malik, from Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said: He said: He said: One like you is ruined while he has not performed an obligatory prayer that Allah has made obligatory. He said: I said: What should I do? He said: He said: Pray in congregation, meaning the Friday prayer.

As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā, from Ṭalḥah ibn Zayd, from Jaʿfar, from his father, from ʿAlī عليه السلام, who said: There is no Jumuʿah except in a city in which the prescribed punishments are carried out. So the interpretation of this report is taqiyyah, because it conforms to the doctrines of most of the ʿāmmah, and likewise.

What Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā narrated from Abū Jaʿfar, from his father, from Ḥafṣ ibn Ghiyāth, from Jaʿfar, from his father عليه السلام, who said: There is no Jumuʿah upon the people of the villages, nor going out for the two ʿEids. The aspect of it here also is taqiyyah, and it is possible that what is meant is one whose village is farther from the town by more than two farsakhs, and in whom there is not the number by which Jumuʿah becomes obligatory upon them, nor have their conditions been fulfilled among them.

ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm narrated from his father, from Ḥammād, from Ḥarīz, from Ibn Muslim, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about the Friday prayer, and he said: It is obligatory upon one who is at a distance of two farsakhs from it; but if he is farther than that, then nothing is incumbent upon him.

Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Mahbub narrated from 'Ali ibn al-Sindi, from Muhammad ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Jamil ibn Darraj, from Zurarah and Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far عليه السلام, who said: Jumu'ah becomes obligatory upon one who is within two farsakhs of it.

As for what was narrated by Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb, from Yaʿqūb ibn Yazīd, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from ʿUmar ibn Udhaynah, from Zurārah, who said: Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام said: Jumuʿah is obligatory upon one who, if he performs the morning prayer among his family, can still reach the Friday prayer. And the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم would only perform the ʿaṣr prayer at the time of ẓuhr on the rest of the days, so that when they had completed the prayer with the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم, they would return to their dwellings before nightfall. And that is a sunnah until the Day of qiyamah. So the proper way regarding this report is that we carry it upon a form of recommendation rather than obligation and requirement, because the obligation pertains to one who is at the distance of two farsakhs.

ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Ḥammād ibn ʿUthmān, from al-Ḥalabī, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about one who did not catch the khutbah on Friday. He said: He prays two rakʿahs. But if the prayer has passed him and he did not catch it, then let him pray four. And he said: If you catch the Imam before he bows in the last rakʿah, then you have caught the prayer. But if you catch him after he has bowed, then it is ẓuhr, four rakʿahs.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from al-Qasim, from Aban ibn 'Uthman, from Abi Basir and Abi al-'Abbas al-Fadl ibn 'Abd al-Malik, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: If a man catches one rak'ah, then he has caught the Jumu'ah prayer; but if it has escaped him, then let him pray four.

As for what al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Fadalah, from Ibn Sinan, from Abi 'Abdillah عليه السلام, he said: The Friday prayer is not valid except for one who has attended the two sermons. So the correct understanding of this report is that it is not fully meritorious and complete except for one who has attended the two sermons, and by that he did not intend to negate sufficiency, according to what he explained in the first two reports; and this further clarifies that.

What Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥakam, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-ʿArzamī, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: If you catch the Imam on Friday and he has preceded you by one rakʿah, then add another rakʿah to it and recite aloud in it. And if you catch him while he is reciting the tashahhud, then pray four [rakʿahs].

Al-Husayn ibn 'Ubayd Allah informed me, from a number of our companions, from Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from a number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Fadalah, from al-Husayn ibn 'Uthman, from Ibn Miskan, from Abi Basir, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: Five do not lead the people in prayer under any circumstance: the one afflicted with leprosy, the one afflicted with vitiligo, the insane person, the child born of zina, and the Bedouin Arab.

As for what Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Ismaʿil ibn Baziʿ, from Zarif ibn Nasih, from Thaʿlabah ibn Maymun, from ʿAbd Allah ibn Yazid, who said: I asked Aba ʿAbd Allah عليه السلام about the leper and the one afflicted with vitiligo leading the Muslims in prayer. He said: “Yes.” I said: “Does Allah test the believer by means of them?” He said: “Yes; and was tribulation written for anyone except the believer?” So the proper way regarding this report is that we interpret it as applying to a state of necessity in which no one suitable for the Imamate of prayer is found except one with this description. And it is possible that the meaning in it is permissibility, even though the merit is in the first division.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Safwan and Fadalah, from al-'Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from one of them, peace be upon them, that he was asked about a slave: may he lead the people in prayer if they are pleased with him and he is the most versed among them in the Qur'an? He said: There is no harm in it.

From him, from Hammad, from Hariz, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I asked Aba Abdillah عليه السلام about a slave: may he lead the people in prayer if they are pleased with him and he is the most proficient of them in the Qur'an? He said: There is no harm in it.

From him, from al-Hasan, from Zur'ah, from Sama'ah, who said: I asked him about the owned slave: may he lead the people in prayer? He said: No, unless he is the most learned of them in fiqh and the most knowledgeable of them.

As for what Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā narrated from Abū Isḥāq, from al-Nawfalī, from al-Sukūnī, from Jaʿfar, from his father, from ʿAlī عليه السلام, that he said: “The servant does not lead anyone except his own household” is to be understood as pertaining to merit and recommendation, although it is permissible for him to lead his household and others besides his household.

Al-Husayn ibn Ubayd Allah informed me, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from al-Hasan ibn Musa al-Khashshab, from Ghiyath ibn Kallub, from Ishaq ibn Ammar, from Ja'far, from his father, that Ali عليه السلام used to say: There is no harm in a boy giving the adhan before he reaches puberty, but he should not lead in prayer until he reaches puberty. If he does lead, his prayer is valid, but the prayer of those behind him is invalid.

As for what Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā narrated from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā, from Ṭalḥah ibn Zayd, from Jaʿfar, from his father, from ʿAlī عليه السلام, who said: There is no harm in a boy who has not yet had a wet dream giving the adhān and leading the prayer. So the proper way regarding this report is that we carry it upon one who is complete in intellect, even if he has not reached puberty; and the first report upon one in whom the conditions of legal responsibility have not been realized before reaching puberty, so that the two reports may be reconciled.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from 'Abbad ibn Suhayb, who said: I heard Aba 'Abdillah عليه السلام saying: One who has performed tayammum does not lead in prayer a people who have performed wudu (ablution).

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Bunan ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Ibn al-Mughirah, from al-Sakuni, from Ja'far, from his father عليه السلام, who said: The one performing tayammum must not lead in prayer those who have wudu (ablution), and the one afflicted with paralysis must not lead the healthy.

As for what Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā narrated from Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd, from Abū Jamīlah, from Abū Usāmah, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, concerning: A man becomes junub while he does not have any water with him, and he is the Imam of the people. He said: Yes, he performs tayammum and leads them.

Sa'd narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Fadalah ibn Ayyub, from 'Abd Allah ibn Bukayr, who said: I asked Aba 'Abd Allah عليه السلام about a man who became junub, then performed tayammum, and led us in prayer while we were in a state of taharah. He said: There is no problem with that.

From him, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from Muḥammad ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Ḥamzah ibn Ḥumrān and Jamīl ibn Darrāj, who said: I said to Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام: An Imam of a people is afflicted with janabah during travel, and he does not have with him enough water for ghusl. Should some of them perform wudu and he lead them in salat? He said: No. Rather, the junub performs tayammum and leads them in salat, for indeed Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has made earth a purifier.

From him, from Abū Jaʿfar, from his father, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Mughīrah, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Bukayr, from Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said: I said to him: A man led a people in salat while he was junub, and he had performed tayammum, while they were in a state of taharah. He said: There is no harm in that. So the proper way regarding these reports, and reconciling them with the first report, is that we carry the first report upon preference, and these upon permissibility, so that the reports do not contradict one another.

Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Ḥasan al-Luʾluʾī, from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Faḍḍāl, from Abī al-Miʿzā Ḥumayd ibn al-Muthannā, from ʿImrān, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī, that he asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about a travelling man when he enters into... ...the salat (prayer) with the residents. He said: Then let him perform his salat (prayer), then give salām, and make the last two as supererogatory prayer.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Muhammad ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Hammad ibn 'Uthman, who said: I asked Aba 'Abdillah عليه السلام about the traveler who performs salat (prayer) behind the resident. He said: He performs two rak'ahs and then goes wherever he wishes.

As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Faḍālah ibn Ayyūb, from Ḥusayn ibn ʿUthmān, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muskān, from Abī Baṣīr, who said: Abū ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام said: The traveler should not pray with the resident; and if he does pray, then he should conclude at the two rakʿahs.

Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah, from Abu Ja'far, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from Dawud ibn al-Husayn, from Abu al-'Abbas al-Fadl ibn 'Abd al-Malik, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: A resident should not lead a traveler, nor should a traveler lead a resident. If one is tried with something of that, and he leads resident people, then when he completes the two rak'ahs he gives salām, then takes one of them by the hand and puts him forward, and he leads them. And when the traveler prays behind resident people, then let him complete his prayer as two rak'ahs and give salām. And if he prays al-zuhr with them, then let him make the first two al-zuhr and the last two al-'asr. So the correct understanding regarding these two reports is a degree of dislike short of prohibition, according to what he عليه السلام detailed of its rulings.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from 'Uthman ibn 'Isa, from Sama'ah ibn Mihran, who said: I asked Aba 'Abdillah عليه السلام about a woman leading women in prayer, and he said: There is no problem with it.

Sa'd narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Hasan ibn 'Ali ibn Faddal, from 'Abd Allah ibn Bukayr, from some of our companions, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, concerning: About a man leading a woman in prayer, he said: Yes, she stands behind him. And about a woman leading women in prayer, he said: Yes, she stands in the middle among them and does not stand ahead of them.

As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Faḍālah, from Ibn Sinān, from Ibn Muskān, from Sulaymān ibn Khālid, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about a woman leading women in prayer. He said: If they are all together, she may lead them in the supererogatory prayer; but as for the obligatory prayer, then no. And she should not stand in front of them; rather, she stands in the middle among them.

And among what was narrated by Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Mahbub, from Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Hamid, from al-Hasan ibn al-Jahm, from Ibn Muskan, from al-Halabi, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: A woman may lead women in salat (prayer), and she stands in the middle among them, while they stand to her right and her left. She leads them in supererogatory prayer, and she does not lead them in the obligatory prayer. Thus, the proper way regarding these two reports is one of two possibilities: the first is that we carry the earlier unrestricted reports upon these detailed ones, so that what has been reported regarding the permissibility of a woman leading women applies only to the supererogatory prayers, according to what they explained in the later reports. The second is that we carry them upon a degree of reprehensibility rather than prohibition; and likewise so.

Al-Faḍl ibn Shādhān narrated to us from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Ḥammād, from Ḥarīz, from Zurārah, from Abī Jaʿfar عليه السلام. He said: I said, “Can a woman lead women?” He said: “No, except over the deceased, when there is no one more entitled than her. She stands in the middle with them in the row, then she pronounces the takbir and they pronounce the takbir.” So the proper understanding of this report as well is that it indicates a form of recommendation, not obligation.

Al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿUbayd Allāh informed me, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā, from his father, from Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā al-Ashʿarī, from al-ʿAmrakī, from ʿAlī ibn Jaʿfar, from his brother Mūsā ibn Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who slaughtered a sheep, and it convulsed and fell into a water well while its veins were gushing blood. May wudu (ablution) be performed from that well? He said: Thirty to forty buckets are drawn from it, then wudu (ablution) is performed, and there is no harm in it. He said: And I asked him about a man who slaughtered a chicken or a pigeon and it fell into a well. Is it suitable that wudu (ablution) be performed from it? He said: A few buckets are drawn from it, then wudu (ablution) is performed from it. And I asked him about a man drawing water from a well and having a nosebleed into it. May he perform wudu (ablution) from it? He said: A few buckets are drawn from it.

As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from Muḥammad ibn Ismāʿīl ibn Bazīʿ, he said: I wrote to a man asking him to ask Abū al-Ḥasan al-Riḍā عليه السلام about a well that is in the house for wudu (ablution), into which drops of urine or blood fall, or something else falls into it, such as droppings or the like: what is it that purifies it so that wudu (ablution) from it for salat (prayer) becomes permissible? So he عليه السلام wrote in my letter, in his own handwriting: “Buckets are to be drawn from it.” The proper way regarding this report is that we understand it as referring to when the blood is little, because that is how he asked him. Do you not see that he said, “Drops of blood fall into it,” and from that smallness is understood? And what the report includes of thirty to forty buckets is to be understood as when the blood is abundant; for that reason he paired it with the slaughter of a sheep that fell into the well while gushing blood, and what is customary in that is abundance. But when that is little, as in the slaughter of a chicken or a pigeon or a nosebleed, he permitted that a small number of buckets be drawn from it, and that is detailed and explained in the first report.

As for what al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Muhammad ibn Ziyad, from Kurdawayh, who said: I asked Aba al-Hasan عليه السلام about a well into which a drop of blood, or intoxicating nabidh, or urine, or wine falls. He said: Thirty buckets are to be drawn from it. So this report is anomalous and rare, and we have already discussed it earlier, because it includes mention of wine and intoxicating nabidh, which necessitate drawing out all of the water, in addition to the mention of blood. We have already clarified the basis regarding it, and it is possible that, concerning a drop of blood, it may be understood as indicating a type of recommendation, while the reports we cited earlier are understood as indicating obligation, so that the reports do not contradict one another.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn and Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, all together from Safwan ibn Yahya, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, who said: I asked Aba 'Abdillah عليه السلام about salat (prayer) behind the Imam: Should I recite behind him? He عليه السلام said: As for the prayer in which the recitation is not done aloud, that has been assigned to him, so do not recite behind him. And as for the prayer in which recitation is done aloud, he has only been commanded to recite aloud so that those behind him may listen attentively; so if you hear, then listen attentively, and if you do not hear, then recite.

From him, from ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Ḥammād ibn ʿUthmān, from al-Ḥalabī, from Abū ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said: When you pray behind an Imam whom you follow, then do not recite behind him, whether you hear his recitation or do not hear, unless it is a prayer in which recitation is done aloud and you do not hear, then recite.

And from him, from ʿAlī, from his father, from Ḥammād ibn ʿĪsā, from Ḥarīz, from Zurārah, from one of the two of them عليهما السلام, who said: When you are behind an Imam whom you follow, then remain silent and recite tasbih within yourself.

From him, from ʿAlī, from his father, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Mughīrah, from Qutaybah, from Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said: If you have prayed behind an Imam whom you approve of in a salat in which the recitation is said aloud, and you do not hear his recitation, then recite for yourself. But if you can hear the murmuring, then do not recite. Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā, from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Faḍḍāl, from Yūnus ibn Yaʿqūb, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام about praying behind one whom I approve of: should I recite behind him? He said: Behind one whom you approve of, do not recite behind him.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from Hisham ibn Salim, from Sulayman ibn Khalid; and 'Ali ibn al-Nu'man, from 'Abd Allah ibn Muskan, from Sulayman ibn Khalid, who said: I said to Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام: Should a man recite in the first two rak'ahs and in al-'Asr behind the Imam while he does not know whether he is reciting? He said: It is not appropriate for him to recite; he should leave it to the Imam.

As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā narrated from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Ḥammād ibn ʿUthmān, from al-Ḥalabī, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, he said: When you pray behind an Imam whom you follow, then do not recite behind him, whether you hear his recitation or do not hear it. So this does not contradict what we have presented before: that whenever he does not hear the recitation in a prayer in which the recitation is said aloud, then he should recite. That is because it is possible that the narrator transmitted only part of the hadith, for we have already presented in the narration of ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Ḥammād ibn ʿUthmān, from al-Ḥalabī, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, this very hadith, and he added: “unless it is a prayer in which recitation is aloud and you do not hear, then recite.” And if this is part of the complete report, then it agrees with the rest of the reports. It is also possible that what is meant by that is when he hears the recitation, but hears it faintly such that it is not distinguishable to him, like a murmur; then that also suffices for him. And that which indicates this is:

What al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from al-Ḥasan, from Zurʿah, from Samāʿah, who said: I asked him about a man who leads the people, and they hear his voice but do not understand what he is saying. He said: If he hears his voice, then that suffices him; and if he does not hear his voice, he should recite for himself. And it has also been narrated that regarding what he does not hear, he has the choice between reciting and not reciting; but the more precautionary view is what we have already stated.

Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated that from Abū Jaʿfar, from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Yaqṭīn, from his brother al-Ḥusayn, from his father ʿAlī ibn Yaqṭīn, who said: I asked Abū al-Ḥasan al-Awwal عليه السلام about a man who prays behind an Imam who is followed, in a prayer in which the recitation is audible, but he does not hear the recitation. He said: There is no problem whether he remains silent or recites.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from 'Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Hammad ibn 'Uthman, from al-Halabi, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: When you pray behind an Imam who is not to be followed, then recite behind him, whether you hear his recitation or you do not hear.

Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn Abi al-Khattab, from al-Hasan ibn Musa al-Khashshab, from 'Ali ibn Asbat, from some of his companions, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام and Abu Ja'far عليه السلام, concerning: A man is behind the Imam, not following him in اقتداء, and the Imam gets ahead of him in the recitation. He said: If he has already recited Umm al-Kitab, that suffices for him, and he stops and bows.

As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Ṣafwān, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Bukayr, from his father Bukayr ibn Aʿyan, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام about the nāṣib who leads us in prayer: what do you say regarding prayer with him? He said: As for when he recites aloud, then remain silent for the Qur'an and listen; then bow and prostrate yourself for yourself.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Hammad ibn 'Isa, from Mu'awiyah ibn Wahb, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who leads the people in prayer while you are not pleased with him, in a prayer in which the recitation is audible. So he said: When you hear the Book of Allah being recited, then listen silently to it. I said: But he testifies against me with shirk. He said: If he disobeys Allah, then obey Allah. I repeated the matter to him, but he refused to grant me a concession. He said: So I said to him: Shall I then pray in my house and then go out to him? He said: That is up to you. So the correct understanding regarding these two reports is the state of taqiyyah and fear, because when the situation is like that, it is permissible for a person to recite to himself inwardly and not raise his voice; this indicates that.

What Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq and Muḥammad ibn Abī Ḥamzah, from one whom he mentioned, from Abū ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said: It suffices you, when you are with them, to recite like the speech of the النفس within oneself.

Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā narrated from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Yaqṭīn, from his brother al-Ḥusayn, from his father ʿAlī ibn Yaqṭīn, who said: I asked Abā al-Ḥasan عليه السلام about a man who prays behind one whose prayer is not followed, while the Imam recites aloud. He said: Recite for yourself, and if you do not make yourself hear yourself, then there is no harm.

As for what Sa'd narrated from Musa ibn al-Husayn and al-Hasan ibn 'Ali, from Ahmad ibn Hilal, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from Ahmad ibn 'A'idh, who said: I said to Abu al-Hasan عليه السلام: I enter with these people in the maghrib salat, and they hurry me before I can give the adhan and iqamah, so I do not recite anything, until when they perform ruku', I perform ruku' with them. Will that suffice for me? He said: Yes. So the correct understanding of his statement, "I do not recite," is that it is carried upon what is additional to al-Hamd, because the recitation of al-Hamd is indispensable. What indicates that is that Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, the narrator of this hadith, narrated this same incident itself and said: I am not able to recite what is additional to al-Hamd, so he said to him: Yes.

Sa'd narrated that from Musa ibn al-Husayn and al-Hasan ibn 'Ali, from Ahmad ibn Hilal, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from Abu al-Hasan عليه السلام, who said: I said to him: I join these people in the maghrib salat (prayer), and they hasten me such that I do not have the chance to give the adhan and iqamah, and I recite nothing but al-Hamd until he bows. Will that suffice me? He said: Yes, al-Hamd alone suffices you. And it is possible that the report is specific to the state of taqiyyah, for that is permissible when one performs the ruku' and sujud.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated that from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Muhammad ibn al-Fudayl, from Ishaq ibn 'Ammar, who said: I said to Abī 'Abdillāh عليه السلام: I enter the masjid and find that the Imam has already gone into ruku' and the people have gone into ruku', so I am unable to give the adhan, perform the iqamah, and say the takbir. He said to me: When that is so, then enter with them and count it, for it is among the best of your rak'ahs. Ishaq said: When I heard the adhan for maghrib while I was sitting at my door, I said to the servant: Go see, has the salat been commenced? He came back to me and said: Yes. So I got up quickly and entered the masjid, and I found that the people had already gone into ruku', so I performed ruku' with the first row that I reached and counted it. Then after the conclusion, I prayed four rak'ahs and then departed. Thereupon, five or six of my neighbors from the Makhzumis and the Umayyads came up to me and said: O Aba Hashim, may Allah reward you well for yourself; for by Allah, we saw contrary to what we had thought about you and what had been said to us. I said: And what was that?
