They said: We followed you when you rose for the salat while we thought that you did not count the salat with us, but we found that you had counted the salat with us and had prayed with our salat. May Allah be pleased with you and reward you well. He said: So I said to them: Glory be to Allah, is such a thing said to one like me? He said: Then I came to know that Abā 'Abdillāh عليه السلام only instructed me so because he feared for me this and things like it.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Hasan ibn 'Ali ibn Faddal, from 'Abd Allah ibn Bukayr; and al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Fadalah, from 'Abd Allah ibn Bukayr, who said: Hamzah ibn Humran asked Aba 'Abd Allah عليه السلام about a man who led us in salat during travel while he was junub, and he knew it while we did not know. He said: There is no harm.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Safwan, from al-'Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abi Ja'far عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who leads the people in prayer while he is not in a state of taharah, and he does not know until his prayer is finished. He said: He must repeat, but those who prayed behind him do not repeat, even if he informs them that he was not in a state of taharah.

From him, from 'Uthman ibn 'Isa, from 'Abd Allah ibn Muskan, from 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Ya'fur, who said: Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام was asked about a man who led a people in prayer while he was without wudu (ablution). He said: There is no repetition upon them, but he himself must repeat.

From him, from Hammad, from Hariz, from Zurarah, from Abi Ja'far عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a people whose Imam led them in salat while he was without taharah. Is their salat valid, or must they repeat it? He said: There is no repetition upon them; their salat is complete. The repetition is upon him, and it is not incumbent upon him to inform them. This is waived from him.

As for what ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥakam narrated from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-ʿArzamī, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, he said: ʿAlī عليه السلام led the people in salat while not in a state of ritual purity, and it was the noon prayer. Then his caller went out and proclaimed: Surely Amīr al-Muʾminīn عليه السلام performed salat without ritual purity, so repeat, and let the one present convey it to the absent. So this is an anomalous report, contrary to the hadiths, and that whose ruling is such is not to be acted upon. It also contains a further defect that undermines its soundness, namely that Amīr al-Muʾminīn عليه السلام led the people in salat without wudu (ablution), whereas the indication of his ʿismah (infallibility) عليه السلام gives us certainty against that. And Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn ibn Bābawayh mentioned, saying: I heard a group of our shaykhs saying: There is no repetition upon them for anything in which he recited aloud, but they must repeat what he led them in of that in which he did not recite aloud.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Mu'awiyah ibn 'Ammar, who said: I asked Aba 'Abdillah عليه السلام about a man who comes to the mosque while they are in the salat, and the Imam has preceded him by one rak'ah or more; then the Imam becomes ill, takes him by the hand, and since he is the nearest of the people to him, brings him forward. He عليه السلام said: He completes the salat with the people, then he sits. When they have finished the tashahhud, he signals to them with his hand to the right and the left, and it is as though his signaling to them with his hand stands in place of the tashahhud and the completion of their salat. Then he completes what he had missed, or what remained upon him.

As for what Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā narrated from al-ʿAbbās ibn Maʿrūf, from Ibn Sinān, from Ṭalḥah ibn Zayd, from Jaʿfar, from his father عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who led a people in salat, then a nosebleed afflicted him after he had performed one rakʿah or two rakʿahs, so he put forward one who had prayed though one rakʿah or two rakʿahs had been missed by him. He said: he completes the salat with them, then he puts forward a man to give the salām for them, and he himself stands and completes the remainder of his salat. The proper way regarding this report is that we carry it upon a kind of recommendation, even though indication by gesture is sufficient according to what was contained in the first report.

As for what Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā narrated from Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī, from al-Ḥakam ibn Miskīn, from Muʿāwiyah ibn Shurayḥ, who said: I heard Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام saying: When the Imam breaks wudu (ablution) while he is in the salat (prayer), it is not fitting that anyone step forward except one who witnessed the iqāmah. Thus, the proper understanding of this report is that it indicates a kind of recommendation. For that reason, he said, “it is not fitting,” and did not say, “it is not permissible,” and that is explicit in indicating reprehensibility.

As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from al-Naḍr, from Hishām ibn Sālim, from Sulaymān ibn Khālid, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about a man who is leading the people in prayer, then breaks his state of purity, and puts forward a man who has missed one rakʿah. What should he do? He said: He should not put forward one who has missed one rakʿah; rather, he should take the hand of someone else and put him forward. So this report, even though its apparent wording is the apparent wording of prohibition, we interpret it as indicating a type of dislikeability, based on the indication of the reports that came earlier.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Jamil, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abi Ja'far عليه السلام, who said: He said to me: If you do not catch up with the people before the Imam says the takbir for the rak'ah, then do not enter with them in that rak'ah.
From him, from Safwan, from al-'Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far عليه السلام, who said: Do not count the rak'ah in which you did not witness its takbir along with the Imam.
From him, from al-Naḍr, from ʿĀṣim, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, from Abī Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said: If you catch the takbir before the Imam bows in rukuʿ, then you have caught the salat (prayer).

As for what al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from al-Nadr, from Hisham, from Sulayman ibn Khalid, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, that he said: Concerning a man who catches the Imam while he is in ruku', so the man says the takbir while standing upright, then goes into ruku' before the Imam raises his head: he has indeed caught that rak'ah.

And among what Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb narrated, from ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Ḥammād, from al-Ḥalabī, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: If you catch the Imam while he has already gone into rukuʿ, and you pronounce takbir and perform rukuʿ before he raises his head, then you have caught the rakʿah. But if the Imam raises his head before you go into rukuʿ, then it has passed you by. So the proper way regarding these two reports is that we understand his saying, 'if you catch him while he is in rukuʿ,' and in the last report, 'while he has already bowed,' as referring to joining him in the row, from which one should not remain behind when able, even if he had already caught the takbir of rukuʿ before that place. Because whoever hears the Imam pronouncing takbir for rukuʿ while there is a distance between them, it is permissible for him to pronounce takbir and bow with him wherever the place comes to an end for him; then he may walk while in his rukuʿ, if he wishes, until he catches up with him, or he may perform sajdah in his place. Then when he finishes his two sajdahs, he joins him. Whichever of these he wishes, he may do. And whenever we understand these two reports in this manner, the reports do not contradict one another. And that which indicates the permissibility of what we have mentioned is:

What al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Ḥammād ibn ʿĪsā, from Ḥarīz, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, from one of the two عليهما السلام, that he was asked about a man who enters the mosque and fears that he will miss the rakʿah, so he said: He bows before reaching the people, and walks while he is bowing until he reaches them.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from 'Abd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from 'Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Aban, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi 'Abd Allah al-Basri, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: When you enter the masjid and the Imam is in ruku', and you think that if you walk toward him he will raise his head before you catch him, then say the takbir and perform ruku'. When he raises his head, then perform sajdah in your place. If he stands, then join the row; and if he sits, then sit in your place; then when he stands, join the row.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from 'Umar ibn Udhaynah, from Zurarah, from Abi Ja'far عليه السلام, who said: If a man catches part of the salat (prayer) and misses part of it behind an Imam whose prayer behind him he counts as valid, he makes the first part he catches the first part of his own salat (prayer). If he catches the first two rak'ahs of Zuhr, 'Asr, or 'Isha' and misses two rak'ahs, he recites quietly to himself in every rak'ah that he catches behind the Imam: Umm al-Kitab and a surah. If he is unable to complete the surah, Umm al-Kitab suffices him. Then when the Imam gives salām, he stands and prays two rak'ahs in which he does not recite, because recitation in the salat (prayer) is only in the first two rak'ahs, in every rak'ah with Umm al-Kitab and a surah; and in the last two there is no recitation. Rather, they consist of tasbih, takbir, tahlil, and du'a, and there is no recitation in them. And if he catches one rak'ah, he recites in it behind the Imam. Then when the Imam gives salām, he stands and recites Umm al-Kitab and a surah, then sits and recites the tashahhud, then stands and prays two rak'ahs in which there is no recitation.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Safwan, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, who said: I asked Aba 'Abdillah عليه السلام about a man who catches the second rak'ah of the salat (prayer) with the Imam, while it is his first. What should he do when the Imam sits for the tashahhud? He said: He should sit lightly without settling himself fully in sitting. Then when it is the Imam’s third rak'ah and it is his second, he should remain briefly when the Imam rises, to the measure of what he would recite for the tashahhud, then he should catch up with the Imam. He said: And I asked him about one who catches the last two rak'ahs of the salat (prayer): what should he do regarding recitation? He said: Recite in them, for they are your first two rak'ahs; and do not make the beginning of your salat (prayer) its end.

Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā narrated from Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā, from Ṭalḥah ibn Zayd, from Jaʿfar, from his father, from ʿAlī عليه السلام, who said: A man makes what he catches with the Imam the beginning of his salat (prayer). Jaʿfar said: And we do not say as the foolish ones say.

As for what Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated from Yaʿqub ibn Yazid, from Marwak ibn ʿUbayd, from Ahmad ibn al-Nadr, from a man, from Abu Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said: He said to me: “What do these people say regarding a man who has missed two rakʿahs with the Imam?” He said: “They say that in the two rakʿahs he recites al-Hamd and a surah.” So he said: “This turns his salat around, making its beginning its end.” I said: “How should he act?” He said: “He recites Fatihat al-Kitab in every rakʿah.” So this report does not contradict the reports we presented earlier, because his statement that he recites al-Hamd alone in the two rakʿahs means in the two missed rakʿahs, not in the two that he caught. For the two that he caught, he recites in them al-Hamd and a surah. For that reason, he refuted the one who said that he recites al-Hamd and a surah, for this turns his salat around, because among the common people are those who say that he recites al-Hamd and a surah in what he missed, since the two he missed were the first two, so he would need to make them up. Therefore he said in the narration of Talhah ibn Zayd: ‘And we do not say as the foolish say.’

As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Ḥammād ibn ʿĪsā, from Muʿāwiyah ibn Wahb, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about a man who catches the end of the Imam’s salat, while it is the beginning of the man’s salat, and he does not give him time to recite; should he then make up the recitation at the end of his salat? He said: Yes. His statement, 'he makes up the recitation at the end of his salat,' is figurative usage. What is meant by it is that which pertains to the end of the salat of the recitation of al-Ḥamd, not that he intended by it making up the recitation of what pertains specifically to the first and second rakʿah.

Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Sahl al-Ashʿari, from his father, from Abu al-Hasan عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about one who performed ruku' with an Imam whom he was following, then raised his head before the Imam. He said: He repeats his ruku' with him.

As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā narrated from his father, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Mughīrah, from Ghiyāth ibn Ibrāhīm, who said: Abū ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام was asked about a man who raises his head from ruku' before the Imam: should he return and bow again if the Imam is slow, and then raise his head with him? He said: No. So the proper understanding of this report is one of two things: one is that he is praying behind one whose leadership is not to be followed; in that case, it is not permissible for him to return to ruku', because that would become an addition in the salat. The second is that he did that deliberately; then likewise it is not permissible for him to return to ruku'. Rather, he should return only if he raised his head forgetfully, so that his raising of the head may coincide with the Imam's raising of the head.

Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā narrated from ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥakam, from Sulaym al-Farrāʾ, who said: I asked him about a man who is the muʾadhdhin of a people and their Imam, and he is on the road to Makkah or elsewhere, so he leads them in the ʿasr prayer in its time. Then a man enters who does not know and thinks that it is the first prayer; would it suffice for him if it is actually the ʿasr prayer? He said: No.

As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Ḥammād ibn ʿUthmān, he said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about a man who leads a people in prayer and prays the ʿaṣr prayer, while for them it is the ẓuhr prayer. He said: It sufficed for them, and it sufficed for him. So this does not conflict with the first report, because the proper way regarding it is that we interpret it as applying to one who does not follow the Imam in the prayer itself and intends ẓuhr for himself; then his prayer is valid even if the Imam is praying ʿaṣr. The first report applies to one who follows his prayer and binds his prayer to it. So if the Imam’s prayer is ʿaṣr, and the one who prayed behind him did not intend ẓuhr for himself, then his ʿaṣr prayer is invalid, because he has not yet prayed ẓuhr, and the ʿaṣr prayer is not valid for one who has not prayed ẓuhr, unless its time has become constrained, as we have explained.

Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥakam, from Ismāʿīl ibn ʿAbd al-Khāliq, who said: I heard him say: It is not proper for the Imam to stand up after he has prayed until everyone behind him has completed what he missed of the salat (prayer).

As for what Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah narrated from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan, from 'Amr ibn Sa'id, from Musaddiq ibn Sadaqah, from 'Ammar, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who became forgetful behind an Imam after he had begun the salat (prayer), so he said nothing, did not say the takbir, did not utter tasbih, and did not recite the tashahhud until he gave salam. He said: His salat (prayer) is valid, and there are no two sajdahs of forgetfulness upon him when he forgets behind the Imam, because the Imam is guarantor for the salat (prayer) of those behind him. So the proper way of understanding this report is one of two possibilities; one of them is that he guarantees only the recitation and nothing else, which indicates that.

What al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Zurʿah, from Samāʿah, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام: that a man asked him about recitation behind the Imam, so he said: No. Indeed, the Imam is responsible for the recitation, and the Imam does not guarantee the salat (prayer) of those behind him; rather, he only guarantees the recitation. The second possibility is that what is meant by negating guarantee is the completion of the prayer, because he is not secure from ritual invalidation; that is indicated by this.

What Jamil narrated from Zurarah, from one of the two of them عليهما السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who led a people in two rak'ahs, then informed them that he was not in a state of wudu (ablution). He said: The people complete their salat (prayer), for there is no liability upon the Imam.

Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from his father, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Mughīrah, said: ʿUtbah narrated to me from Ibrāhīm ibn Maymūn. He asked Abā ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام about salat in congregation on a ship, and he said: There is no harm in it.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Muhammad ibn Ahmad al-'Alawi, from al-'Umarki al-Nawfali, from 'Ali ibn Ja'far, from Musa ibn Ja'far عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a people who performed salat in congregation on a ship: where should the Imam stand? And if there are women with them, what should they do? Should they pray standing or sitting? He said: They should pray standing, and if they are not able to stand, they should pray sitting. The Imam stands in front of them, and the women are behind them. If the ship tosses, the women sit and the men pray, and there is no harm in the women being alongside them.

As for what Sahl ibn Ziyad narrated from Abū Hāshim al-Jaʿfarī, he said: I was with Abū al-Ḥasan عليه السلام on a boat on the Tigris when the time for salat came. So I said: “May I be made your ransom, shall we perform salat in congregation?” He said: “Do not perform salat in congregation in the middle of a valley.” So the intended meaning in this narration is a form of reprehensibility, or a state of necessity in which one is not able to perform salat in congregation.

Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Mahbub, from al-'Abbas, from Safwan, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from Sulayman Mawla Tirbal, from 'Ubayd ibn Zurarah, who said: I heard Aba 'Abdillah عليه السلام saying: The whole earth is a masjid, except a well of excrement, or a graveyard, or a bathhouse.

As for what was narrated by Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb, from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn, from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Faḍḍāl, from Thaʿlabah ibn Maymūn, from Muḥammad ibn Muḍārib, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: There is no objection to a masjid being made over excrement. Thus, this does not contradict the first report, because the proper way to reconcile the two is that it is only permissible for it to be made a masjid when it has been covered with earth and the odor has ceased. This is indicated by that.

What Sahl ibn Ziyad narrated from Ibn Abi Nasr, from Aban ibn Uthman, from Abi al-Jarud, who said: I asked Aba Ja'far عليه السلام about a place that had been a latrine, then is cleaned and made into a masjid. He said: Soil should be spread over it until it covers it, then it is purer.

Sa‘d narrated from Harun ibn Muslim, from Mas‘adah ibn Sadaqah al-Raba‘i, from Ja‘far ibn Muhammad عليه السلام, who said: He was asked: Is it suitable for the place of a latrine to be made into a masjid? He said: If enough soil is cast over it to cover that, or to cut off its odor, then there is no harm. That is because the soil purifies it; with this the sunnah (prophetic tradition) has passed.

Sa'd, from Abū Ja'far, from his father, from 'Abd Allāh ibn Sinān, who said: I asked Abū 'Abd Allāh عليه السلام about a place that had been a privy for a period of time, then it is cleaned and taken as a masjid. He said: Cast some soil over it until it is covered over, for that purifies it, if Allah, Exalted is He, wills.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ghiyath ibn Ibrahim, from Ja'far, from his father, that 'Ali عليه السلام said: Spitting in the mosque is a sin, and its expiation is to bury it.

Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Mahbub, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Musa ibn Yasar, from 'Ali ibn Ja'far al-Sakkuni, from Isma'il ibn Muslim al-Sha'iri, from Ja'far, from his father, from his forefathers, peace be upon them, who said: Whoever defiles the mosque with his phlegm shall meet Allah on the Day of Resurrection smiling, having been given his book in his right hand.

From him, from Abū Isḥāq al-Nahāwandī, from al-Barqī, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Sinān, who said: I heard Abā ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام saying: Whoever coughs up phlegm in the mosque and then returns it into his body, it will not pass by any illness within his body except that it cures him from it.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Muhammad ibn Mihran, from 'Abd Allah ibn Sinan, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: I said to him: A man is in the masjid, in salat, and wants to spit. So he said: To his left. And if he is not in salat, then he should not spit facing the qiblah, and he may spit to his right and his left.
As for what ʿAlī ibn Mahziyār narrated, he said: I saw Abā Jaʿfar al-Thānī عليه السلام spit in al-Masjid al-Ḥarām between al-Rukn al-Yamānī and al-Ḥajar al-Aswad, and he did not bury it.

Sa'd, from Abi Ja'far, from al-'Abbas ibn Ma'ruf, from Safwan, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from Sulayman Mawla Tirbal, from 'Ubayd ibn Zurarah, who said: I heard Aba 'Abdillah عليه السلام saying: Abu Ja'far عليه السلام would perform salat in the masjid, then spit in front of him, to his right, to his left, and behind him upon the pebbles, and he would not cover it. So the correct view regarding these reports is permissibility and the lifting of prohibition, even though the more virtuous course, according to the previous reports, is to refrain from both.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Hamid, from Abi Jamilah, from Abi Usamah, from Abi Abdillah عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about the takbir in the two Eids. He said: seven and five. And he said: the salat of the two Eids is an obligation.
Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Jamil, from Abi 'Abdillah عليه السلام, who said: The salat of the two 'Ids is obligatory, and the salat of the eclipse is obligatory.

As for what Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated from Abū Jaʿfar, from ʿAlī ibn Ḥadīd and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Najrān, from Ḥammād ibn ʿĪsā, from Ḥarīz, from Zurārah, who said: Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام said: The salat of the two Eids with the Imam is a sunnah, and there is no salat before it nor after it on that day until noon. So the proper way concerning this narration is that we understand his statement that it is a sunnah with the Imam to mean that its obligation was known through the sunnah, not that it is therefore non-obligatory. We have treated that fully in our major book, and we will devote a chapter to the fact that it is not obligatory except with the presence of the Imam.

Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Muḥammad, from al-Muʿallā ibn Muḥammad, from al-Washshāʾ, from Ḥammād ibn ʿUthmān, from Maʿmar ibn Yaḥyā, from Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said: There is no salat (prayer) on the day of al-Fiṭr and al-Aḍḥā except with the Imam.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Ibn Udhaynah, from Zurarah, from Abi Ja'far عليه السلام, who said: Whoever does not perform the prayer with the Imam in congregation on the day of Eid, then there is no Eid prayer for him, and no make-up is due upon him.

From him, from Safwan, from al-'Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from one of the two (Imams) عليهما السلام, who said: I asked him about the salat (prayer) on the day of al-Fitr and al-Adha, so he said: There is no salat (prayer) except with an Imam.

As for what was narrated by ʿAlī ibn Ḥātim, from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī, from his father, from Faḍālah, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Sinān, from Abū ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said: Whoever does not attend the congregation of the people in the two ʿIds, then let him perform ghusl, apply whatever perfume he finds, and pray by himself just as he prays in congregation.

From him, from al-Hasan, from his father, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, who said: Abu 'Abdillah عليه السلام was asked about a man who does not go out on the Day of al-Fitr and al-Adha: is there a salat (prayer) upon him by himself? He said: Yes.

From him, from Muḥammad ibn Jaʿfar, who said: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muḥammad and Muḥammad ibn al-Walīd narrated to us, from Yūnus ibn Yaʿqūb, from Manṣūr ibn Ḥāzim, from Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said: My father fell ill on the Day of al-Aḍḥā, so he performed two rakʿahs in his house, then he offered the sacrifice. Thus, the proper approach regarding these reports is that we interpret them as indicating a kind of recommendation, because this prayer with the Imam is obligatory, while when performed individually it is an emphasized sunnah (prophetic tradition); and that which indicates this is:

What al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from ʿUthmān ibn ʿĪsā, from Samāʿah, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: There is no salat in the two Eids except with an Imam; and if you pray by yourself, then there is no harm.

Abu Qays narrated to me from Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad عليه السلام, who said: The salat on the day of ʿEid is only upon the one who goes out to the open prayer ground, and whoever does not go out, then there is no salat upon him. So this does not contradict what we have mentioned earlier, because the meaning of his saying عليه السلام, 'there is no salat upon him,' is: not as an obligation, as it is when one goes out to the open prayer ground; and likewise.

What Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb narrated from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn, from Yazīd ibn Isḥāq Shaʿīr, from Hārūn ibn Ḥamzah al-Ghanawī, from Abū ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said: Going out on the Day of al-Fiṭr and the Day of al-Aḍḥā to the open prayer-ground is good for one who is able to go out to it. So I said: Tell me, if he is ill and unable to go out, should he pray in his house? He said: No. So the correct view concerning it also is what we have said: that this is not an obligatory duty upon him; rather, it is only on the basis of recommendation and desirability.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Fadalah, from 'Abd Allah ibn Sinan, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: The salat of the two Eids is two rak'ahs, without adhan and without iqamah, and there is nothing before them nor after them.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from 'Ali ibn Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from Yunus, from Mu'awiyah ibn 'Ammar, who said: I asked him about the salat of the two 'Eids, and he said: They are two rak'ahs; there is nothing before them and nothing after them.

Sa'd, from Musa ibn al-Hasan, from Mu'awiyah ibn Hakim, from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Mughirah, who said: Some of our companions narrated to me, saying: I asked Aba 'Abd Allah عليه السلام... about the salat of al-Fitr and al-Adha. So he said: Pray them as two rak'ahs, in congregation and outside congregation, and say the takbir five and seven times.

As for what Aḥmad ibn Abī ʿAbd Allāh narrated from his father, from Abī al-Bakhtarī, from Jaʿfar, from his father, from ʿAlī عليه السلام, who said: Whoever misses the salat of the ʿEid should pray four rakʿahs. The proper understanding of this narration is option, because one who prays alone has the choice between praying two rakʿahs according to the arrangement of the salat of the two ʿEids, and between praying four however he wishes, although the superior form is the two rakʿahs according to the arrangement of the salat of the ʿEid.

Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from Muḥammad ibn Sinān, from Ḥammād ibn ʿUthmān and Khalaf ibn Ḥammād, from Ribʿī ibn ʿAbd Allāh and al-Fuḍayl ibn Yasār, from Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said: There is no Jumuʿah in travel, nor Fiṭr, nor Aḍḥā.

As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from Saʿd ibn Saʿd al-Ashʿarī, from Abī al-Ḥasan al-Riḍā عليه السلام, he said: I asked him about the traveler to Makkah and elsewhere: is the salat of the two ʿIds, al-Fiṭr and al-Aḍḥā, obligatory upon him? He said: Yes, except at Minā on the Day of Sacrifice. So the proper understanding of this report is that it indicates a kind of recommendation, not obligation and mandatory duty.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Muhammad ibn al-Fudayl, from Abi al-Sabbah, who said: I asked Aba 'Abdillah عليه السلام about the takbir in the two Eids. He said: Twelve takbirs: seven in the first [rak'ah] and five in the latter.
From him, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Jamīl, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about the takbīr in the two ʿĪds. He said: seven and five.

As for what Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb narrated from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan, from Yazīd ibn Isḥāq Shaʿīr, from Hārūn ibn Ḥamzah al-Ghanawī, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, he said: I asked him about the takbīr in the two ʿĪds. He said: seven and five.

From him, from Harun ibn Hamzah al-Ghanawi, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about the takbir in al-Fitr and al-Adha. He said: Five and four; so it does not harm you if you conclude upon an odd number.

And among what al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Ibn Udhaynah, from Zurarah, that 'Abd al-Malik ibn A'yan asked Aba Ja'far عليه السلام about the salat in the two Eids. So he said: The salat in both of them is the same. The Imam says the opening takbir of the salat completely, as he does in the obligatory prayer, then he adds in the first rak'ah three takbirs and in the second three, apart from the takbir of the salat, and the ruku' and the sujud. And if he wishes, three and five; and if he wishes, five and seven, after attaching that to the odd number. Thus, the way to understand these two narrations is taqiyyah, because they accord with the doctrines of many among the 'ammah, and we do not act upon it; and the consensus of the rightly guided sect is upon what we have stated earlier.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from 'Ali, from Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from Yunus, from Mu'awiyah, who said: I asked about the salat of the two 'Eids, so he said: They are two rak'ahs; there is nothing before them nor after them, and there is no adhan in them nor iqamah. He says twelve takbirs in them. He begins, says takbir, and opens the salat, then recites Fatihat al-Kitab. Then he recites: “By the sun and its brightness.” Then he says five takbirs, then says takbir and bows, so he has bowed with the seventh. He performs two sajdahs, then stands and recites Fatihat al-Kitab. And: “Has there come to you the حديث of al-Ghashiyah?” Then he says four takbirs, performs two sajdahs, recites the tashahhud, and gives salam. He said: And thus did the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم do.

From him, from ʿAlī, from Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā, from Yūnus, from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ḥamzah, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, concerning: Regarding the salat of the two Eids, he said: He says takbīr, then recites, then says takbīr five times, making qunūt between every two takbīrs. Then he says the seventh takbīr and performs rukūʿ with it. Then he performs sajdah. Then he rises in the second rakʿah and recites, then says takbīr four times, making qunūt between every two takbīrs. Then he says takbīr and performs rukūʿ with it.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Muhammad ibn Muskan, from Sulayman ibn Khalid, from Abi 'Abdillah عليه السلام, concerning the salat of the two Eids, who said: Say six takbirs and perform ruku' with the seventh. Then stand in the second rak'ah and recite, then say four takbirs and perform ruku' with the fifth.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Hammad ibn 'Isa, from Shu'ayb, from Abi Basir, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: The takbirs in al-Fitr and al-Adha are twelve takbirs: you say one takbir in the first rak'ah, then recite, then after the recitation you say five takbirs, and with the seventh you perform ruku'. Then you rise in the second rak'ah and recite, then say four takbirs, and with the fifth you perform ruku'.

From him, from Ya'qub ibn Yaqtin, who said: I asked al-'Abd al-Salih عليه السلام about the takbir in the two 'Eids: is it before the recitation or after it? How many takbirs are there in the first and in the second rak'ah, and the supplication with them, and is there qunut in them or not? He عليه السلام said: The takbir of the two 'Eids for the prayer is before the khutbah. He says one takbir by which he opens the prayer, then he recites and says five takbirs, making supplication between them. Then he says another takbir and performs ruku' with it; that makes seven takbirs including the one with which he opened. Then in the second rak'ah he says five takbirs: he stands and recites, then says four takbirs and makes supplication between them, then performs ruku' with the fifth takbir.

From him, from Aḥmad ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Qarawī, from Abān ibn ʿUthmān, from Ismāʿīl al-Jabalī, from Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام, concerning: the salat (prayer) of the two Eids, he said: He pronounces one takbīr with which he opens the salat (prayer), then recites Umm al-Kitāb and a surah, then pronounces five takbīrs, performing qunūt between them, then pronounces one takbīr and bows with it. Then he stands and recites Umm al-Qurʾān and a surah. He recites in the first: “Glorify the Name of your Lord, the Most High,” and in the second: “By the sun and its morning brightness.” Then he pronounces four takbīrs, performing qunūt between them, then he bows with the fifth.

And from him, from ʿAbd Allah ibn Baḥr, from Ḥarīz ibn ʿAbd Allah, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, who said: I asked Abu ʿAbd Allah عليه السلام about the takbir in al-Fiṭr and al-Aḍḥā. He said: Begin and pronounce one takbir, then recite; then after the recitation pronounce five takbirs, then perform rukuʿ with the seventh. Then stand and recite, then pronounce four takbirs, then perform rukuʿ with the fifth.

As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from al-Naḍr ibn Suwayd, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Sinān, from Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said: The takbīr in the two ʿĪd prayers is seven in the first [rakʿah] before the recitation, and in the second, five after the recitation.

And among what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from Ismāʿīl ibn Saʿdān al-Ashʿarī, from al-Riḍā عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about the takbīr in the two ʿĪds. He said: the takbīr in the first is seven takbīrs before the recitation, and in the second is five takbīrs after the recitation.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from al-Hasan, from Zur'ah, from Sama'ah, who said: I asked him about the salat (prayer) on the day of al-Fitr, and he said: It is two rak'ahs without adhan and no iqamah, and it is proper for the Imam to perform the salat before the sermon. And the takbir in the first rak'ah is that he says takbir six times, then recites, then says the seventh takbir, then bows with it; so those are seven takbirs. Then he rises to the second rak'ah and recites; when he finishes the recitation, he says takbir four times, then says the fifth takbir and bows with it.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Fudayl, from Abi al-Sabbah, who said: I asked Aba Abdillah عليه السلام about the takbir in the two Eids, So he said: They are twelve: seven in the first [rak'ah] and five in the last. And when you stand in the salat, then say one takbir, and say: I bear witness that there is no god but Allah alone, having no partner, and I bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and His Messenger—up to the end of the report.

Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb, from Yaʿqūb ibn Yazīd, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Hishām ibn al-Ḥakam, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, concerning the salat of the two Eids. He said: He joins the recitation to the recitation. Then he said: He begins with the takbir in the first rakʿah, then he recites and bows with the seventh.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Hisham ibn al-Hakam, from Abi 'Abdillah عليه السلام; and Hammad ibn 'Uthman, from 'Ubaydillah al-Halabi, from Abi 'Abdillah عليه السلام, similarly. So the proper way regarding these reports is that we interpret them as being upon a kind of taqiyyah, because they agree with the doctrines of some of the 'ammah.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from 'Uthman ibn 'Isa, from Sama'ah, from Abi 'Abdillah عليه السلام, who said: The ghusl (ritual bath) of the day of al-Fitr and the day of al-Adha is a sunnah (prophetic tradition); I do not like abandoning it.

As for what was narrated by Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Mahbub, from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan ibn 'Ali, from 'Amr ibn Sa'id, from Musaddaq ibn Sadaqah, from 'Ammar al-Sabati, who said: I asked Aba 'Abdillah عليه السلام about a man who forgets to perform ghusl on the day of Eid until he has prayed. He said: If it is still within the time, then he must perform ghusl and repeat the salat (prayer); but if the time has passed, then his salat (prayer) is valid. The proper way to understand this report is that it indicates a form of recommendation, because we have already clarified that the ghusl of the two Eids is sunnah (prophetic tradition). We also discussed this fully in the chapter on ghusl in our major book, and we have also clarified that whoever misses the salat (prayer) of the two Eids has no qada' upon him; rather, it is only recommended for him to pray individually.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Safwan, from Musa ibn Bakr or 'Abd Allah ibn al-Mughirah, from Talhah ibn Zayd, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, from his father. That the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم performed the salat of istisqa' as two rak'ahs, and he began with the salat before the sermon, and he said seven and five takbirs, and he recited aloud.

As for what al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Fadalah, from Aban, from Ishaq ibn 'Ammar, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, he said: The sermon in the prayer for rain is before the salat, and he says seven takbirs in the first and five in the second. So this narration is anomalous, opposing the consensus of the rightful Shi'a, because their practice is upon the first narration due to its conformity with the reports that were narrated stating that salat al-istisqa' is like the salat of the two 'Ids.

Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb narrated that from ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Hishām ibn al-Ḥakam, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about salat al-istisqa' (the prayer for rain). He said: It is like the prayer of the two Eids.

Al-Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan ibn Aban, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from 'Uthman ibn 'Isa, from Sama'ah, who said: I asked Aba 'Abdillah عليه السلام about a man who falls asleep while he is in sajdah. He said: He should leave and perform wudu (ablution).

With this chain of transmission, from Hammad, from 'Umar ibn Udhaynah and Hariz, from Zurarah, from one of the two (Imams) عليه السلام, who said: Nothing invalidates wudu (ablution) except what comes out from your two passages, or sleep.

Al-Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Abū al-Qāsim Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from his father, from Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allāh, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā, from Muḥammad ibn ʿUbayd Allāh and ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Mughīrah, who said: We asked al-Riḍā عليه السلام about a man who sleeps on his mount, and he said: If sleep takes away the intellect, then he must repeat the wudu (ablution).

With this chain of transmission, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā, from Muḥammad ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Isḥāq ibn ʿAbdillāh al-Ashʿarī, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: Nothing invalidates wudu (ablution) except a state of hadath, and sleep is a state of hadath.

Al-Husayn ibn 'Ubayd Allah informed me, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Yahya, from his father, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from 'Imran ibn Musa, from al-Hasan ibn 'Ali ibn al-Nu'man, from his father, from 'Abd al-Hamid ibn 'Awwad, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: I heard him say: Whoever sleeps while he is in ruku', or in sajdah, or walking, in whichever of these states, then wudu (ablution) is obligatory upon him.

As for what Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā narrated from al-ʿAbbās, from Abī Shuʿayb, from ʿImrān ibn Ḥumrān, that he heard a righteous servant say: Whoever falls asleep while he is sitting, not intending sleep, then no wudu (ablution) is required upon him.

And what Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā, from ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥakam, from Sayf ibn ʿAmīrah, from Bakr ibn Abī Bakr al-Ḥaḍramī, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام: Does a man sleep while he is sitting? He said: My father used to say: When a man sleeps while sitting, gathered together, then there is no wudu (ablution) upon him; but when he sleeps lying down, then wudu (ablution) is upon him. And whatever proceeds along the lines of these two reports among what has been transmitted, containing the negation of repeating wudu (ablution) due to sleep, is abundant; we did not mention it because the discussion concerning it is one and the same: that we carry it upon sleep which does not overcome the intellect, and with which the person remains composed and aware of what proceeds from him. And that which indicates this interpretation is what al-Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me of, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from his father, from al-Ṣaffār, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā and al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Ḥasan ibn Abān together, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from Muḥammad ibn al-Fuḍayl, from Abī al-Ṣabbāḥ al-Kinānī, from Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who dozes while he is in salat (prayer). He said: If he does not retain awareness of any hadath issuing from him, then wudu (ablution) and repeating the salat (prayer) are upon him. But if he is certain that no hadath occurred, then there is no wudu (ablution) upon him, nor any repetition.

With this chain of transmission, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from ʿUmar ibn Udhaynah, from Ibn Bukayr, who said: I said to Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام: His, Exalted is He, saying: “When you rise for salat (prayer)” What is meant by that, “when you rise for salat (prayer)”? He said: “When you rise from sleep.” I said: “Does sleep invalidate wudu (ablution)?” He said: “Yes, when it overcomes hearing and he does not hear the sound.”

With this chain of transmission, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from Faḍālah, from al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿUthmān, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Ḥajjāj, from Zayd al-Shaḥḥām, who said: I asked Abū ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام about a doze and two dozes, He said: I do not know what a doze and two dozes are. Indeed, Allah, Exalted is He, says: “Rather, the human being is fully aware of himself.” Indeed, ʿAlī عليه السلام used to say: Whoever experiences the taste of sleep, then wudu (ablution) has become obligatory upon him.

As for what Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb narrated from al-ʿAbbās, from Muḥammad ibn Ismāʿīl, from Muḥammad ibn ʿUdhāfir, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Sinān, from Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, concerning: Regarding a man: is his wudu (ablution) invalidated when he sleeps while sitting? He said: If it is on the day of الجمعة, then there is no wudu upon him, and that is because he is in a state of necessity. So this report is to be understood to mean that there is no wudu upon him, but tayammum is upon him, because that which invalidates wudu (ablution) is not specific to the day of الجمعة to the exclusion of other days. Thus, the correct understanding in it is that he performs tayammum and offers salat (prayer), then when the gathering disperses he performs wudu (ablution) and repeats the salat (prayer), because he may not have been able to get out due to the crowding. And that which indicates this is what...

Al-Husayn ibn Ubayd Allah informed me of it, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Yahya, from his father, from Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub, from al-Abbas ibn Maruf, from Abd Allah ibn al-Mughirah, from al-Sakuni, from Jafar, from his father, from Ali عليه السلام, that he was asked about a man who is in... in the midst of the crowd on Friday or on the Day of Arafah, unable to leave the mosque because of the large number of people, and he breaks his wudu (ablution). He said: He performs tayammum and prays with them, then repeats when he departs.
Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from 'Ali ibn al-Hakam, from 'Ali ibn Abi Hamzah, from Abi Basir, who said: I asked him about salat of the eclipse, and he said: ten rak'ahs and four sajdahs.

Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Mahbub narrated from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan ibn 'Ali, from 'Ali ibn Ya'qub al-Hashimi, from Marwan ibn Muslim, from Ibn Abi Ya'fur, from Abi 'Abdillah عليه السلام, who said: Salat al-kusuf consists of ten rak'ahs and four sajdahs. The eclipse of the sun is more severe upon people and animals.

As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from Muḥammad ibn Khālid al-Barqī, from Abū al-Bakhtarī, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, that ʿAlī عليه السلام prayed during... the salat of the eclipse as two rakʿahs with four sajdahs and four rukūʿs: he stood and recited, then bowed; then he raised his head and recited, then bowed; then he stood and did likewise for two rakʿahs; then he performed two sajdahs; then he stood and did the like of what he had done in the first, equal in its recitation, standing, bowing, and prostration.

Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Mahbub narrated from Bunan ibn Muhammad, from al-Muhassin ibn Ahmad, from Yunus ibn Ya'qub, who said: Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام said: The moon was eclipsed, so my father went out, and I went out with him to al-Masjid al-Haram. Then he prayed eight rak'ahs, praying as one normally prays a rak'ah and two sajdahs. So these two reports agree with the doctrines of the 'ammah, while practice is based on the first two reports, because they agree with the narrations that contain the detailed description of Salat al-Kusuf. We have cited them in our major book, and the entire group acts upon them.

Al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿUbayd Allāh narrated to me from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from his father, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb, from Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan, from ʿUbayd ibn Zurārah, from his father, from Abī Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said: The sun was eclipsed while I was in the bathhouse, and I came to know only after I had come out, so I did not make it up.

From him, from Ahmad, from Musa ibn al-Qasim and Abi Qatadah, from Ali ibn Ja'far, from his brother Musa ibn Ja'far عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about salat al-kusuf: is qada' due upon one who leaves it? He said: If it passes you by, then there is no qada' upon you.

Muhammad ibn Sinan narrated from Ibn Muskan, from Ubayd Allah al-Halabi, who said: I asked Abu Abd Allah عليه السلام about salat al-kusuf: should we make it up if it passes us by? He said: “There is no qada' for it.” Yet it had been held by us that it is to be made up. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: the proper way regarding these reports is that we understand the falling away of qada' to apply when the disk has not been completely eclipsed; but if it has been completely eclipsed, then qada' is unavoidable. This is indicated by that.

What al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Ḥammād, from Ḥarīz, from one who informed him, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: If the moon is eclipsed and a man wakes up but is too lethargic to perform the prayer, then he must perform ghusl on the following day and make up the prayer. But if he did not wake up and did not know of the eclipse of the moon, then nothing is upon him except making up the prayer without ghusl.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Hammad, from Zurarah and Muhammad, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: If the sun was completely eclipsed and burned over, and you did not know, then later came to know of that, then the qada' is upon you. But if it did not burn over completely, then there is no qada' upon you. And this detail does not contradict.

What ʿAmmār al-Sābāṭī narrated from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, that he said: If you did not know until the eclipse had passed, then came to know after that, then there is no salat of the eclipse upon you. But if one person informed you while you were asleep, and you came to know, then your eye overpowered you and you did not pray, then its qaḍāʾ is upon you. For the correct approach regarding this narration is that we interpret it to mean that when part of the disc was obscured and one was informed of that but did not pray, then qaḍāʾ was upon him; but if he did not know at all, then qaḍāʾ was not binding upon him. As for when the entire disc was obscured, then qaḍāʾ was upon him in every case, whether he knew or did not know; and if he had known, then ghusl was also upon him together with the qaḍāʾ, according to what we have explained previously.

Al-Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, informed me from Abū al-Qāsim Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb, from ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from Ḥammād ibn ʿĪsā, who said: I heard Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام when he was asked about salat (prayer) in a ship, and he said: If you are able to go out to the firm ground, then go out. But if you are not able, then perform salat standing; and if you are not able, then perform salat sitting, and seek out the qiblah.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad al-Jawhari, from Ibn Abi Hamzah, from 'Ali ibn Ibrahim, who said: I asked him about salat in a ship, and he said: He should perform salat while sitting if he is not able to stand in the ship. And he should not perform salat in the ship while he is able to reach the shore. And he said: He performs salat in the ship and turns his face toward the qiblah, then performs salat however it turns.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Yazid ibn Ishaq, from Harun ibn Hamzah al-Ghanawi, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about salat (prayer) in a ship. He said: If it is heavily loaded, such that when you stand in it, it does not move, then perform salat standing; but if it is light and tilts, then perform salat sitting.

As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Yaqṭīn, from his brother al-Ḥusayn, from his father ʿAlī ibn Yaqṭīn, from Abī al-Ḥasan عليه السلام, he said: I asked him about a ship whose occupant is not able to stand: should he perform salat in it while sitting, gesturing, or should he perform sajdah? He said: He should stand, even if he bends his back. So this narration is to be understood as applying to one who is able to perform salat with a bent back, even if he is not able to stand fully upright. That is permissible according to the order that was detailed previously in the reports, and this is also confirmed by what follows.
What Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from more than one of our companions, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: Salat (prayer) in the ship is by gesture.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from 'Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, who said: I asked Aba 'Abd Allah عليه السلام about salat al-khawf (the prayer of fear). He said: The Imam stands, and a group from his companions comes and stands behind him, while another group faces the enemy. The Imam leads them in one rak'ah, then he stands and they stand with him; then he remains standing while they perform the second rak'ah. Then some of them give salam to one another, then they depart and take the place of their companions, and the others come and stand behind the Imam. He then leads them in the second rak'ah, then the Imam sits, and they stand and perform another rak'ah; then he gives salam to them, and they depart with one taslim. He said: And in the Maghrib prayer it is similar to that. The Imam stands and a group comes and stands behind him; then he leads them in one rak'ah. Then he stands and they stand; the Imam remains standing while they perform the two rak'ahs, recite the tashahhud, and some of them give salam to one another. Then they depart and stand in the position of their companions, and the others come and stand behind the Imam. He leads them in one rak'ah in which he recites, then he sits and recites the tashahhud, then he stands and they stand with him, and he leads them in another rak'ah. Then he sits, and they stand and complete one more rak'ah, then he gives salam to them.

As for what Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb narrated from Yaʿqūb ibn Yazīd, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from ʿUmar ibn Udhaynah, from Zurārah, from Abī Jaʿfar عليه السلام, that he said: When the maghrib salat (prayer) is performed in a state of fear, he divides them into two groups. He leads one group in two rakʿahs, then he sits with them. Then he signals to them with his hand, and each person among them stands and performs one rakʿah, then they give salām and go to the place of their companions. Then the other group comes; they say the takbīr and enter into the salat (prayer). The Imam stands and leads them in one rakʿah, then gives salām. Then each man among them stands and performs one rakʿah, joining it to the one he performed with the Imam, then he stands and performs one rakʿah in which there is no recitation. Thus the Imam completes three rakʿahs, the first group has two rakʿahs in congregation, and the latter ones individually. So the first ones have the takbīr and opening of the salat (prayer), and the latter ones have the salām.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated this hadith from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from 'Umar ibn Udhaynah, from Zurarah, Fudayl, and Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abi Ja'far عليه السلام. The proper way regarding this narration and its conformity with the other narration is that we interpret it as indicating choice, and that a person has the option to act according to either one of them. However, acting upon the first narration is more apparent, and Zurarah, the narrator of this hadith, has indeed narrated something like the first report.

Sa'd narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from 'Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Aban ibn 'Uthman, from Zurarah, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: In salat al-khawf, for the Maghrib prayer, he leads the first group in one rak'ah, and they complete two rak'ahs; then he leads the latter group in two rak'ahs, and they complete one rak'ah.

ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Ḥafṣ ibn al-Bakhtarī, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: I heard him saying concerning the one who has fainted: He said: Whatever Allah has overcome him with, then Allah is more entitled to excuse for it.

From him, from Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā, from Yūnus, from Ibrāhīm al-Khazzāz Abī Ayyūb, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who had been unconscious for several days and did not perform salat (prayer), then regained consciousness: should he perform the missed prayers? He said: There is nothing upon him.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from 'Ali ibn Hadid, from Murazim, who said: I asked Aba 'Abdillah عليه السلام about the sick person who is unable to perform salat (prayer). He said: Whatever Allah has overpowered him with, then Allah is more entitled to excuse.

From him, from al-Hajjal, from Tha'labah, from Ma'mar ibn 'Umar, who said: I asked Aba Ja'far عليه السلام about the sick person: does he make up the salat (prayer) if he had been rendered unconscious? He said: No.

Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Mahbub narrated from 'Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Sulayman, who said: I wrote to the jurist, Abi al-Hasan al-'Askari عليه السلام, asking him about one who has fallen unconscious for a day or more: should he make up what he missed of the salat (prayer), or not? So he wrote عليه السلام: He does not make up the sawm (fasting), nor does he make up the salat (prayer).

Sa'd narrated from Ayyub ibn Nuh, who said: I wrote to Abu al-Hasan al-Thalith عليه السلام asking him about one who has fallen unconscious for a day or more: should he make up what he missed of the salat (prayer), or not? So he wrote: He does not make up the sawm (fasting), nor does he make up the salat (prayer).

As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from al-Ḥasan, from Zurʿah, from Samāʿah, he said: I asked him about the sick person who becomes unconscious. He said: If it exceeds three days, then there is no make-up duty upon him. But if he was rendered unconscious for three days, then he must make up the salat (prayer) during those days.

Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb narrated from Yaʿqūb ibn Yazīd, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Ḥafṣ, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about the one who had fainted. He said: then he said, he makes up the salat (prayer) of one day.

From him, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Jabbār, from Muḥammad ibn Sinān, from al-ʿAlāʾ ibn al-Fuḍayl, who said: I asked Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about a man who is rendered unconscious for a day until night, then regains consciousness. He said: If he regains consciousness before sunset, then he must make up this day of his. And if he was unconscious for several numbered days, then he is not required to make up except the last of his days, if he regains consciousness before sunset; otherwise, there is no make-up upon him. So the proper way regarding these reports is that we carry them upon a mode of recommendation, because the proofs indicate that making up what he missed during the state of unconsciousness is not obligatory upon him. These reports are thus understood as encouraging the making up of what he missed. As for the salat (prayer) whose time remains when he regains consciousness, then making it up is binding upon him in every case; that is indicated by the evidence.

What Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from al-Ḥasan ibn Maḥbūb, from ʿAlī ibn Riʾāb, from Abū Baṣīr, from one of the two of them, peace be upon them, who said: I asked him about the sick person who loses consciousness and then regains awareness: how does he make up his salat (prayer)? He said: He makes up the salat (prayer) whose time he had reached.

Sa'd, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Hammad, from 'Ubayd Allah al-Halabi, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about the sick person: does he make up the salat (prayer) when he had lost consciousness? He said: No, except for the salat (prayer) during which he regained consciousness.
Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Hafs, from Abi 'Abdillah عليه السلام, who said: He makes up the salat (prayer) during whose time he regained consciousness.

As for what al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Fadalah, from Ibn Sinan, from Abi 'Abdillah عليه السلام, he said: Every salat (prayer) that you left due to an illness in which you lost consciousness, then make it up when you recover consciousness.

From him, from Safwan, from al-'Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who loses consciousness and then regains consciousness. He said: He makes up what he missed; he gives the adhan for the first one and performs the iqamah for the remainder.
From him, from Safwan, from Mansur ibn Hazim, from Abi Abdillah عليه السلام, concerning: Regarding the one who was unconscious, he said: He makes up whatever he missed.

From him, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Rifāʿah, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about one who remained unconscious for a month: what of the salat (prayer) must he make up? He said: He makes up all of it, for the matter of salat (prayer) is severe.

From him, from ʿAbd Allah ibn Muhammad, who said: I wrote to him: May I be made your ransom. It has been narrated from Abi ʿAbd Allah عليه السلام regarding a sick person who remains unconscious for several days. Some of them said: he makes up the salat (prayer) of the day in which he regained consciousness; and some said: he makes up the salat (prayer) of three days and leaves what is beyond that; and some said: there is no make-up upon him. So he wrote: he makes up the salat (prayer) of the day in which he regains consciousness. Thus, the proper way to understand these reports is what we mentioned first: that it is on the basis of recommendation and desirability, not obligation and requirement.

As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Shuʿayb, from Abū Baṣīr, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who faints during the day and then regains consciousness before sunset. He said: He should perform ẓuhr or ʿaṣr. And during the night, if he regains consciousness before dawn, he should make up the night prayer. So this report accords with what we have stated earlier: that it is obligatory upon him to make up the prayer whose time he regains consciousness within. And this time is the end of the time allotted to the constrained person; thus making it up becomes obligatory at that point.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from al-Hasan, from Zur'ah, from Sama'ah, who said: Abu 'Abdillah عليه السلام said to me: Pray on the night of the twenty-first and the night of the twenty-third of Ramadan, in each one of them, if you have the strength for that, one hundred rak'ahs, apart from the thirteen rak'ahs.

ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥasan ibn Faḍḍāl, from Muḥammad ibn Khālid, from Sayf ibn ʿUmayrah, from Isḥāq ibn ʿAmmār, from Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh, who said: Indeed, Abū ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام said to him: These companions of ours have refused to increase in their salat (prayer) during the month of Ramaḍān, while the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم did increase in his salat (prayer) during the month of Ramaḍān.

From him, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī, from ʿAlī ibn al-Nuʿmān, from Manṣūr ibn Ḥāzim, from Abū Baṣīr, that he asked Abā ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام: Should a man increase in salat (prayer) in the month of Ramadan? He said: Yes. Indeed, the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم used to increase in salat (prayer) in Ramadan.

From him, from Isma'il ibn Mihran, from al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan al-Marwazi, from Yunus ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from al-Ja'fari, that he heard al-'Abd al-Salih عليه السلام saying: On the night of the twenty-first and the twenty-third, one hundred rak'ahs are performed; in every rak'ah, Qul Huwa Allahu Ahad is recited ten times.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from 'Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn 'Isa ibn 'Ubayd, from Yunus ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from Abu al-'Abbas al-Baqbaq and 'Ubayd ibn Zurarah, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: The Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم would increase in his salat (prayer) during the month of Ramadan. When he had performed the night prayer, he would pray after it; the people would stand behind him, so he would go inside and leave them. Then he would come out again, and they would come and stand behind him; so he would go inside and leave them. Then he would come out again, and they would come and stand behind him; so he would go inside and leave them, repeatedly. He said: And he said: He would not pray after the night prayer in other than the month of Ramadan.

ʿAlī ibn Ḥātim, from Ḥumayd ibn Ziyād, said: ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Aḥmad al-Nahīkī narrated to us, from ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥasan, from Muḥammad ibn Ziyād, from Abū Khadījah, from Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said: When the month of Ramadan entered, the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم would increase in salat (prayer); so I increase, therefore increase.

From him, from Muḥammad ibn Jaʿfar al-Muʾaddib, who said: Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan al-Ṣaffār narrated to us, from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn, from al-Naḍr ibn Shuʿayb, from Jamīl ibn Ṣāliḥ, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: If you are able to perform one thousand rakʿahs in the day and night during the month of Ramaḍān and other than it, then do so, for indeed ʿAlī عليه السلام used to perform one thousand rakʿahs in the day and night.

ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥasan ibn Faḍḍāl, from Ismāʿīl ibn Mihrān, from al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Ḥasan al-Marwazī, from Yūnus ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā, who said: I was with Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, and he was asked: “Is there an addition in the supererogatory prayers during the month of Ramaḍān?” He said: “Yes.” The Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم used to pray after al-ʿatamah in his place of prayer and pronounce the takbīr, and the people would gather behind him to pray with his prayer. So when they pronounced takbīr behind him, he left them and entered his house. Then when the people dispersed, he returned to his place of prayer and prayed as he had been praying. Then when the people pronounced takbīr behind him, he left them and went inside, and he did that repeatedly.

From him, from Hārūn ibn Muslim, from Mas‘adah ibn Ṣadaqah, from Abī ‘Abdillāh عليه السلام, who said: Among what he used to do in the month of Ramadan was that he would perform supererogatory prayers every night, and he would add to the prayers he had been performing before that. From the first night until the completion of twenty nights, in every night he would pray twenty rak‘ahs: eight rak‘ahs of them after al-Maghrib, and twelve after al-‘Ishā’ al-Ākhirah. In the last ten nights, in every night he would pray thirty rak‘ahs: twelve of them after al-Maghrib, and eighteen after al-‘Ishā’ al-Ākhirah. And he would make du‘a and strive with intense exertion. He would pray one hundred rak‘ahs on the night of the twenty-first, and he would pray one hundred rak‘ahs on the night of the twenty-third, and he would strive in them both.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from al-Hasan, from Zur'ah, from Sama'ah ibn Mihran, who said: I asked him about Ramadan: how much should one pray in it? He said: As he prays in other than it, except that Ramadan has over the rest of the months such virtue that it is appropriate for the servant to increase in his voluntary prayers. So if he wishes and is able to do that, then from the first night of the month until twenty nights, every night he should add twenty rak'ahs besides what he used to pray before that; of these twenty, twelve rak'ahs are between al-Maghrib and al-'Atamah, and eight rak'ahs are after al-'Atamah. Then he prays the night prayer that he used to pray before that: eight rak'ahs, and al-Witr, three rak'ahs—two rak'ahs in which he gives salām, then he rises and prays one rak'ah in which he recites qunūt; this is al-Witr. Then he prays the two rak'ahs of al-Fajr when dawn breaks, and these are thirteen rak'ahs. Then when ten nights remain of Ramadan, he should pray thirty rak'ahs every night besides these thirteen rak'ahs: he prays twenty-two rak'ahs between al-Maghrib and al-'Isha', and eight rak'ahs after al-'Atamah. Then after the night prayer he prays thirteen rak'ahs as I described. And on the night of the twenty-first and the twenty-third, in each one of them, if he is able to do so, he prays one hundred rak'ahs besides these thirteen rak'ahs. And he should stay awake in those two until morning, for it is recommended that this be in prayer, du'a, and humble supplication, for it is hoped that Laylat al-Qadr may be in one of them.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from al-Qasim, from 'Ali ibn Abi Hamzah, who said: We entered upon Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, and Abu Basir said to him: What do you say regarding the salat (prayer) in Ramadan? He said: Indeed, Ramadan has a sanctity and a right unlike anything from the other months. Pray as much voluntary salat (prayer) as you are able in Ramadan, by night and day. And if you are able to pray one thousand rak'ahs each day, then pray. Indeed, 'Ali عليه السلام, in the latter part of his life, would pray one thousand rak'ahs in every day and night. And pray extra in Ramadan, O Aba Muhammad. He said: How much, may I be your ransom? He said: During the twenty nights that pass, in every night twenty rak'ahs: eight rak'ahs before al-'atamah and twelve after it, besides what you used to pray before that. Then when the last ten nights begin, pray thirty rak'ahs every night: eight rak'ahs before al-'atamah and twenty-two after al-'atamah, besides what you used to do before that.

Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb, from ʿAlī ibn Muḥammad, from Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Muṭahhar, that he wrote to Abū Muḥammad عليه السلام informing him of what had come in the narration: that the Prophet صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم would not pray in... the month of Ramaḍān and other nights except thirteen rakʿahs, including al-witr and the two rakʿahs of dawn. So he wrote: May Allah open your mouth to good. Pray in the month of Ramaḍān, for twenty nights, twenty rakʿahs each night: eight after al-maghrib and twelve after al-ʿishāʾ al-ākhirah. And perform ghusl on the night of the seventeenth, the night of the nineteenth, the night of the twenty-first, and the night of the twenty-third; and pray on these nights thirty rakʿahs: twelve after al-maghrib and eighteen rakʿahs after al-ʿishāʾ al-ākhirah. And pray in those two nights one hundred rakʿahs, reciting in every rakʿah al-Fātiḥah once and Qul huwa Allāhu Aḥad ten times. And pray until the end of the month, every night, thirty rakʿahs, as I have explained.

ʿAlī ibn Ḥātim, from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī, from his father, who said: A man wrote to Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام asking him about the salat of the nawafil of the month of Ramadan and about increasing them. So he عليه السلام wrote back to him a letter, which I read in his own handwriting: Pray in the first part of the month of Ramadan, over twenty nights, twenty rakʿahs. Pray eight rakʿahs of them between al-Maghrib and al-ʿAtamah, and after al-ʿIshaʾ twelve rakʿahs. And in the last ten nights, pray eight rakʿahs between al-Maghrib and al-ʿAtamah, and twenty-two rakʿahs after al-ʿAtamah, except on the night of the twenty-first and the twenty-third; then one hundred will suffice you, if Allah wills. And that is besides the fifty. And increase your recitation of: “Indeed, We sent it down.”

From him, from Aḥmad ibn ʿAlī, who said: Muḥammad ibn Abī al-Ṣahbān narrated to me from Muḥammad ibn Sulaymān, who said: A number of our companions agreed upon this hadith. Among them were Yūnus ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Sinān, from Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام; Ṣabbāḥ al-Ḥadhdhāʾ, from Isḥāq ibn ʿAmmār, from Abī al-Ḥasan عليه السلام; and Samāʿah ibn Mihrān, from Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام. Muḥammad ibn Sulaymān said: I asked al-Riḍā عليه السلام about this hadith, and he informed me of it, and said: All of these together asked us about the salat (prayer) in the month of Ramadan—how it is, and how the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم acted. They all said: When the first night of the month of Ramadan entered, the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم performed the Maghrib salat (prayer), then he performed four rakʿahs which he used to perform after Maghrib every night, then he performed eight rakʿahs. Then when he had performed the ʿIshāʾ al-Ākhirah and the two rakʿahs which he used to perform after the ʿIshāʾ al-Ākhirah while seated every night, he stood and performed twelve rakʿahs, then entered his house. When the people saw that and observed that the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم had increased in prayer when the month of Ramadan entered, they asked him about that. He informed them: I performed this salat because of the excellence of the month of Ramadan over the months. Then, when it was night, he stood to perform salat, and the people formed rows behind him. So he turned toward them and said: O people, this salat is supererogatory, and there shall be no congregational gathering for supererogatory prayer. Let each man among you perform salat by himself, and let him recite what Allah has taught him from His Book. And know that there is no congregation in a supererogatory prayer. So the people dispersed, and each one of them performed salat on his own, for himself. Then when it was the night of the nineteenth of the month of Ramadan, he performed ghusl (ritual bath) when the sun had set and performed the Maghrib salat (prayer) with ghusl. After he had performed Maghrib and the four rakʿahs which he used to perform every night after Maghrib before that, he entered his house. When Bilāl gave the iqāmah for the ʿIshāʾ al-Ākhirah, the Prophet صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم came out and led the people in salat. Then when he finish

ʿAlī ibn Ḥātim narrated from Muḥammad ibn Jaʿfar, from Aḥmad ibn Buṭṭah al-Qummī, from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn, from Muḥammad ibn Sinān, from al-Mufaḍḍal ibn ʿUmar, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, that he said: He performs an additional one thousand rakʿahs in the month of Ramadan. He said: I said, “And who is able to do that?” He said: “It is not as you think. Do you not perform in the month of Ramadan an additional one thousand rakʿahs? In nineteen nights of it, in every night twenty rakʿahs; and on the night of the nineteenth, one hundred rakʿahs; and on the night of the twenty-first, one hundred rakʿahs; and on the night of the twenty-third, one hundred rakʿahs; and you perform in eight nights of it during the last ten, thirty rakʿahs. So these are nine hundred and twenty rakʿahs.” He said: I said, “May Allah make me your ransom, you have relieved me. The matter had indeed become constricted for me, but when you brought the explanation, you relieved me. So how is the completion of the one thousand rakʿahs?” He said: “You perform on every Friday in the month of Ramadan four rakʿahs for Amīr al-Muʾminīn عليه السلام, and you perform two rakʿahs for the daughter of Muḥammad صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم, and after the two rakʿahs you perform four rakʿahs for Jaʿfar al-Ṭayyār عليه السلام. And you perform on the night of Friday during the last ten, for Amīr al-Muʾminīn عليه السلام, twenty rakʿahs, and you perform on Friday evening, the night of Saturday, twenty rakʿahs for the daughter of Muḥammad صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم.” Then he said: “Listen, retain it, and teach it to the trustworthy ones among your believing brothers.” And he continued the hadith.

Ibrahim ibn Abi Ishaq al-Ahmari al-Nahawandi, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, and 'Amr ibn 'Uthman, and Muhammad ibn Khalid, and 'Abd Allah ibn al-Salt, and Muhammad ibn 'Isa, and a group also, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, who said: Al-Rida عليه السلام said: My father used to add, during the last ten nights of the month of Ramadan, twenty rak'ahs every night.

As for what al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Safwan, from Ibn Muskan, from al-Halabi, who said: I asked him about salat (prayer) in the month of Ramadan, so he said: Thirteen rak'ahs, including the witr and the two rak'ahs of dawn after fajr. That is how the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم used to pray, and I likewise pray in that manner; and if it had been good, the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم would not have left it.

From him, from Hammad, from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Mughirah, from Ibn Sinan, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about the salat (prayer) in the month of Ramadan. He said: Thirteen rak'ahs, including al-Witr, and two rak'ahs before Salat al-Fajr. Thus was the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم praying; and if there had been any additional merit, the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم would have acted upon it and would have had more right to it.

Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Faddal, from Muhammad ibn Ubayd Allah al-Halabi and al-Abbas ibn Amir al-Thaqafi, both from Abd Allah ibn Bukayr, from Abd al-Hamid al-Ta'i, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I heard Abu Abd Allah عليه السلام say: When the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم had performed the later evening prayer, he would retire to his bed and would not perform any prayer until after the middle of the night, neither in Ramadan nor in other than it. Thus, the proper understanding of these reports and others of the same kind is that the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم did not perform supererogatory prayer in congregation during the month of Ramadan; and if there had been good in it, he would not have abandoned it. What is not intended is that it is impermissible for one to perform it individually, contrary to what some people have held; and that which indicates this is as follows.

Among what al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated, from Hammad ibn 'Isa, from Hariz, from Zurarah, Ibn Muslim, and al-Fudayl, they said: We asked them both about performing the supererogatory prayer in Ramadan at night in congregation. So they both said: The Prophet صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم, when he had performed the later evening prayer, would depart to his home. Then he would come out at the end of the night to the mosque, stand, and pray. On the first night of the month of Ramadan he came out to pray as he used to pray, and the people formed rows behind him. So he fled from them to his house and left them. They did this for three nights. Then on the fourth day he stood upon his pulpit, praised Allah and extolled Him, then said: O people, indeed praying at night in the month of Ramadan, in the supererogatory prayer, in congregation, is a bid'ah, and Salat al-Duha is a bid'ah. Lo, do not gather at night in the month of Ramadan for Salat al-Layl, and do not perform Salat al-Duha, for that is disobedience. Lo, every bid'ah is misguidance, and every misguidance, its path is to the Fire. Then he descended while saying: A little in a sunnah (prophetic tradition) is better than much in a bid'ah. Do you not see that when he صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم objected, he objected to gathering in it and forbade it, but he did not object to the prayer itself? Had the prayer itself been an objectionable bid'ah, he would have objected to it just as he objected to gathering in it. We have already fully covered what pertains to this chapter in our larger book, so whoever wishes to examine it may do so there.

Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā narrated from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from al-Naḍr ibn Suwayd, from Hishām ibn al-Ḥakam, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: I said to him: Is the funeral salat performed over the wine-drinker, the fornicator, and the thief when they die? He said: Yes.

Sa'd narrated from Ayyub ibn Nuh, from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from Ibrahim ibn Mihzam, from Talhah ibn Zayd, from Abu 'Abd Allah, from his father, peace be upon them both, who said: Perform salat over whoever dies from among the people of the qiblah, and his reckoning is upon Allah.

From him, from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan ibn 'Ali, from Abu Hammam Isma'il ibn Hammam, from Muhammad ibn Sa'id ibn Ghazwan, from al-Sakuni, from Ja'far, from his father, from his forefathers, peace be upon them, who said: The Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him and his family, said: Perform salat over the one who is stoned from my Ummah, and over the one who kills himself from my Ummah. Do not leave anyone from my Ummah without salat.

As for what Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā narrated from Hārūn ibn Muslim, from Masʿadah ibn Ṣadaqah, from Jaʿfar, from his father, from his forefathers: that ʿAlī عليه السلام did not perform ghusl on ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir, may Allah have mercy on him, nor on Hāshim ibn ʿUtbah, who was al-Mirqāl. He buried them in their blood and did not perform salat over them. So what this report contains, that he did not perform salat over them, is an error from the narrator, because we have already explained the obligation of salat over every deceased person, and this is a matter of consensus among the rightful sect. We have mentioned in the rulings concerning martyrs that wherein there is sufficiency in our larger book.
