It was also narrated by Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb al-Kulaynī, from a number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyād, from Muḥammad ibn Ismāʿīl, from some of his companions, from Abū ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said: Indeed Allah, Mighty and Majestic, created the world in six days, then reduced them from the days of the year, and the year is three hundred and fifty-four days. Shaʿbān is never complete, and the month of Ramaḍān never decreases, by Allah, ever; and an obligation is never deficient. Indeed Allah, Exalted is He, says: “And that you complete the number.” And Shawwāl is twenty-nine days, and Dhū al-Qaʿdah is thirty days. Because of the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: “And We appointed for Mūsā thirty nights, and We completed them with ten, so the appointed term of his Lord was completed as forty nights.” And Dhū al-Ḥijjah is twenty-nine days, and al-Muḥarram is thirty days; then after that, the months are one complete month and one deficient month. This report also resembles what has preceded, in that it is not sound to argue by it, for the same reasons we have already mentioned: namely, that it is a solitary report that yields neither knowledge nor practice, and that the apparent meaning of the Qur’an and the mutawātir reports are not opposed by the like of it. Also, its wording and meanings differ while the report is one. Moreover, it contains reasoning that reveals that it was not established from an Imam of guidance عليه السلام. Among that is that His saying, Exalted is He, “And We appointed for Mūsā thirty nights,” does not necessitate the perpetual completeness of a similar month in Dhū al-Qaʿdah. The coincidence of Dhū al-Qaʿdah being complete in the days of Mūsā عليه السلام does not require its completeness in future times, nor does it indicate that it had always been like that in the past. If that is so, then attributing an everlasting rationale for the completeness of Dhū al-Qaʿdah to what the Qur’an included of its being complete at one time is invalid as a truthful report from Allah, Mighty and Majestic—especially since it is also offered as a rationale for the completeness of the month of Ramaḍān, though there is no relation between them in mention of completeness. The deduction of six days from the year does not prevent deficiency from occurring in two or three consecutive months, nor the completeness of three or four consecutive month

What was narrated by ʿAlī ibn Mahziyār, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Yasār, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jundab, from Muʿāwiyah ibn Wahb, who said: Abū ʿAbd Allāh said: The month about which it is said that it does not diminish is Dhū al-Qaʿdah, while there is no month among the months of the year that is more subject to diminution than it. As for the statement that the year is three hundred and fifty-four days because the heavens and the earth were created in six days, which were reduced from three hundred and sixty days, this does not establish that any particular month among them must always be thirty days. Rather, it implies that the six days are distributed throughout all the months without specification or designation of which among them is deficient, such that one that may happen to be complete would be so instead of being deficient. As for the statement that the months of the year differ in completeness and deficiency, such that among them there is a complete month and a deficient month, this also does not necessitate the opponent’s claim regarding the month of Ramaḍān as he alleged, nor regarding Shaʿbān what he ruled of its deficiency in every case. For they may indeed be as described in terms of completeness and deficiency, but they are not so according to a fixed sequence and order. Rather, it is not to be denied that within them two consecutive months may both be complete, and two successive months may both be deficient, and even three months as we have described. And along with what we have mentioned, this still accords with the statement that among them there is a deficient month and a complete month, since explicit wording of that does not require either continuity or separation.

As for what Ibn Rabah narrated from Sama'ah, from al-Hasan ibn Hudhayfah, from Mu'awiyah ibn 'Ammar, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, concerning... His, Exalted is He, saying: “and that you complete the number.” He said: fasting thirty days. So this report is like what has preceded, in that it is a solitary report that does not establish knowledge nor practice. The discussion regarding it is like the discussion regarding that one: it is not permissible to object by means of it to the outward meaning of the Qur'an and the mutawatir reports. And even if it were sound, there would be nothing in it contrary to what we have said regarding the obligation of acting upon the crescents. That is because ruling that the count be completed for fasting as thirty days does not prevent the completion of what is in the month, if it is deficient, from being the fasting of twenty-nine days, since what is meant by completing the count is the days that are the days of the month in whatever state it may be. And there is no disagreement that a month which is twenty-nine days is truly a month, not metaphorically. And we do not deny that what is obligatory upon us, when there is obscurity regarding the crescent of Shawwal, is that we complete the month as thirty days, and that this is also obligatory when there is knowledge of the month’s completeness. And when the matter is as we have described it, reliance upon it in opposition to what is known from the Shari'ah falls away.

1. ʿAlī ibn Ḥātim, from Muḥammad ibn Jaʿfar, from Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā, from Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā, said: I wrote to him, peace be upon him: May I be your ransom, sometimes the الهلال becomes obscured from us in the month of Ramadan, then on the following day we see the الهلال before midday, and sometimes we see it after midday. Do you hold that we should break the fast before midday when we see it, or not? And how do you instruct me regarding that? So he, peace be upon him, wrote: Complete it until night, for if it were complete, it would have been seen before midday. 2. From him, from al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī, from his father, from al-Ḥusayn, from Yūsuf ibn ʿAqīl, from Muḥammad ibn Qays, from Abī Jaʿfar, peace be upon him, who said: Amīr al-Muʾminīn, peace be upon him, said: When you see the الهلال, then break the fast, or a just one from among the Muslims bears witness to it. But if you do not see the الهلال except from the middle of the day or its end, then complete the fasting until night. And if it is obscured from you, then count thirty and then break the fast. 3. Al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from al-Naḍr ibn Suwayd, from al-Qāsim ibn Sulaymān, from Jarrāḥ al-Madāʾinī, who said: Abū ʿAbdillāh, peace be upon him, said: Whoever sees the الهلال of Shawwāl by day during Ramadan should complete his fasting. 4. And from him, from Faḍālah, from Abān ibn ʿUthmān, from Isḥāq ibn ʿAmmār, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh, peace be upon him, about the الهلال of Ramadan becoming obscured from us on the twenty-ninth of Shaʿbān, and he said: Do not fast it unless you see it. If the people of another town testify that they saw it, then make it up. And if you see it in the middle of the day, then complete your fast until night—meaning, complete your fast until night on the basis that it is from Shaʿbān, without intending that it is from Ramadan. 5. As for what Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb narrated, from ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Ḥammād ibn ʿUthmān, from Abī ʿAbdillāh, peace be upon him, who said: If they see the الهلال before midday, then it belongs to the previous night; and if they see it after midday, then it belongs to the coming night. 6. And what Saʿd ibn ʿAbdillāh narrated, from Abī Jaʿfar, from Abī Ṭālib ʿAbdillāh ibn al-Ṣalt, from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Faḍḍāl, from ʿUbayd ibn Zurārah and ʿAbdillāh ibn Bukayr, who both said: Abū ʿAbdillāh, peace

If the الهلال disappears before the twilight, then it is for one night; and if it disappears after the twilight, then it is for two nights. 2. Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah, from Ya'qub ibn Yazid, from Muhammad ibn Murazim, from his father, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: If the الهلال becomes encircled, then it is for two nights; and if you see the shadow of your head in it, then it is for three nights. Because the proper understanding of these two reports, and others that run along the same meaning, is that they only serve as an indicator for considering the beginning of the month when there is some impediment in the sky, such as clouds and the like. In that case, it is permissible to consider it for the coming night by the encircling of the الهلال and its setting before or after the twilight. But when the impediment has cleared and the sky is clear, then these things are not to be considered. This is similar to what we mentioned regarding the testimony of two men from outside the town, for it is only considered when there is an impediment; and whenever there is no impediment, it is not permissible to consider that in any way. Rather, one then needs the testimony of fifty persons, according to what we mentioned earlier. This interpretation upon which we have understood these two reports was only stated so that the reports would not be dismissed, even though the more precautious position is what has preceded, and upon it action must be based, if Allah wills.

1- Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb, from ʿAlī ibn Muḥammad, from some of our companions, from Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā ibn ʿUbayd, from Ibrāhīm ibn Muḥammad al-Madanī, from ʿImrān al-Zaʿfarānī, who said: I said to Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام: Indeed, the sky remains overcast for us in Iraq for two or three days, so on which day should we fast? He said: Look at the day on which you fasted in the previous year, and fast on the fifth day. 2- From him, from a number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyād, from Manṣūr ibn al-ʿAbbās, from Ibrāhīm al-Aḥwal, from ʿImrān al-Zaʿfarānī, who said: I said to Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام: Indeed, in winter we remain for a day or two without seeing the sun or a star, so on which day should we fast? He said: Look at the day on which you fasted in the previous year, count five days, and fast on the fifth day. These two reports do not contradict what we have presented regarding acting on sighting, for the same reason that we mentioned in the first chapter: that they are solitary reports which do not establish knowledge or practice. Also, their transmitter is ʿImrān al-Zaʿfarānī, and he is unknown, and in the chains of the two hadiths are weak men whose exclusive narrations we do not act upon. Even if all of that were sound, it would still not oppose the position of sighting; rather, it would support it, because if what were to be observed were the number, then it would be necessary to refer back to it and not to the previous year and to counting five days from it. For the discussion concerning the previous year and by what thing the month is known in it is like the discussion concerning the present year, so that must necessarily be based on sighting for the report to have any benefit. The benefit in the two reports is that a person should fast—if his situation is as described in the two reports—on the fifth day from the previous year as a precaution, and he should intend by it fasting from Shaʿbān if he has no decisive proof that it is from Ramaḍān. Then afterward he should observe; if it becomes clear to him that it was from Ramaḍān, it has sufficed him, and if not, then his fast was supererogatory and he deserves reward for it. 3- As for what Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb narrated from a number of our companions, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā, from Ḥamzah Abī Yaʿlā, from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan ibn Abī Khālid, raising it to Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who s

1. Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb narrated from Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā, from ʿĪsā ibn Hishām, from al-Khaḍir ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, from Muḥammad ibn Ḥakīm, who said: I asked Abū al-Ḥasan عليه السلام about the day concerning which there is doubt. The people claim that whoever fasts it is like one who broke the fast for a day of the month of Ramadan. He said: They have lied. If it is from the month of Ramadan, then it is a day to which he was granted success; and if it is from other than it, then it is like the past days. 2. From him, from ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā, from Yūnus, from Samāʿah, who said: I asked him about the day concerning which there is doubt in relation to the month of Ramadan, and it is not known whether it is from Shaʿbān or from Ramadan, and he fasted it from the month of Ramadan. He said: It is a day to which he was granted success, and there is no qaḍāʾ upon him. 3. From him, from Aḥmad, from Muḥammad ibn Abī al-Ṣahbān, from Muḥammad ibn Bakr ibn Janāḥ, from ʿAlī ibn Shajarah, from Bashīr al-Nabbāl, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about fasting the Day of Doubt, and he said: Fast it; if it is from Shaʿbān, it will be supererogatory, and if it is from the month of Ramadan, then it is a day to which you were granted success. 4. Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb narrated from a number of our companions, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from Ḥamzah ibn Yaʿlā, from Zakariyyā ibn Ādam, from al-Kāhilī, who said: I asked Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about the day of Shaʿbān concerning which there is doubt. He said: That I fast a day from Shaʿbān is more beloved to me than that I break the fast for a day from the month of Ramadan. 5. From him, from a number of our companions, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from Muḥammad ibn Abī al-Ṣahbān, from ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥasan ibn Ribāṭ, from Saʿīd al-Aʿraj, who said: I said to Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام: I fasted the day concerning which there is doubt, and it turned out to be from the month of Ramadan. Shall I make it up? He said: No. It is a day to which you were granted success. 6. As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Muḥammad ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Hishām ibn Sālim and Abī Ayyūb, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, from Abī Jaʿfar عليه السلام: Regarding a man who fasts the day concerning which there is doubt as part of Ramadan, he said: Its qaḍāʾ is upon him. If that is so, then the proper way concerning this report is one

Musa ibn al-Qasim said: al-Nakha'i, Abu al-Husayn, narrated to me. He said: 'Ubayd ibn al-Harith narrated to me, from Hammad al-Minqari, who said: Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام said to me: 'If you want to increase your wealth, then lengthen your standing at al-Safa.'

As for what Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb narrated from ʿAlī ibn Muḥammad, from Ṣāliḥ ibn Abī Ḥamzah, from Aḥmad ibn al-Jahm al-Kharrāz, from Muḥammad ibn ʿUmar ibn Yazīd, from some of his companions, who said: I was behind Abī al-Ḥasan Mūsā عليه السلام on al-Ṣafā or on al-Marwah, and he was not adding to more than two phrases: “O Allah, I ask You for good opinion of You in every state, and sincerity of intention in reliance upon You.” So this does not contradict the first report, because the first is to be understood as recommendation and encouragement, while this one is to be understood as indicating permissibility and lifting restriction.

Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from al-Nakha'i, Abu al-Husayn, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Mu'awiyah ibn 'Ammar, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: I said to him: A man forgot the sa'y between al-Safa and al-Marwah. He said: He must repeat the sa'y. I said: What if he has departed? He said: He must return and repeat the sa'y. This is not like the throwing of the jamarat; indeed, the throwing is a sunnah, while the sa'y between al-Safa and al-Marwah is an obligation. And he said regarding a man who deliberately abandoned the sa'y: He has no hajj.

As for what Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated from Musa ibn al-Hasan, from Muhammad ibn ʿAbd al-Hamid, from Abu Jamilah al-Mufaḍḍal ibn Ṣaliḥ, from Zayd al-Shaḥḥam, from Abu ʿAbd Allah عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who forgot the saʿy between al-Ṣafā and al-Marwah until he returned to his family, and he said: It is performed on his behalf. The proper way regarding this report is that we interpret it as applying to one who is unable to return to Makkah; for it is permissible for him to appoint another in his place for that. But whoever is able, nothing is permissible for him except returning, in accordance with what was contained in the first report.

Mūsā ibn al-Qāsim narrated from Ṣafwān ibn Yaḥyā, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muḥammad, from Abū al-Ḥasan عليه السلام, who said: The obligatory tawaf, if you add to it, is like salat; so when you add to it, repetition is required of you. And likewise is the sa'y.

As for what Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb narrated from Abū ʿAlī al-Ashʿarī, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Jabbār, from Ṣafwān ibn Yaḥyā, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Ḥajjāj, from Abū Ibrāhīm عليه السلام, concerning a man who performed saʿy between al-Ṣafā and al-Marwah for eight circuits—what is upon him? So he said: If it was done by mistake, he should disregard one and count seven.

And from him, from ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn Abī Naṣr, from Jamīl ibn Darrāj, who said: We performed hajj while we were doing it for the first time, and we performed saʿy between al-Ṣafā and al-Marwah fourteen circuits. So we asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about that, and he said: There is no problem; seven are for you, and seven are discarded.

Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from Muḥammad ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Hishām ibn Sālim, who said: I performed saʿy between al-Ṣafā and al-Marwah, I and ʿUbayd Allah ibn Rāshid. So I said to him, “Keep count for me.” He began counting one trip going and returning as a single circuit. When it reached that amount, I said to him, “How are you counting?” He said, “Going and returning as one circuit.” So we completed fourteen circuits. Then we mentioned that to Abū ʿAbd Allah عليه السلام, and he said: “They have added beyond what is required of them; there is nothing upon them.” Thus, the proper way regarding these reports is that we understand them as referring to one who did that forgetfully or ignorantly: repetition is not required of him. The first report is to be understood as referring to one who did that deliberately. This has been clarified in the narration of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Ḥajjāj in his statement, “If he made a mistake, he drops one,” which indicates that when he acted deliberately, the ruling is what we have already stated.

As for what Mūsā ibn al-Qāsim narrated from Ṣafwān, from ʿAlāʾ, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, from one of the two of them, peace be upon them, who said: Indeed, in the Book of ʿAlī عليه السلام, if a man performs the obligatory tawaf of the House in eight circuits and is certain of eight, he adds six to it. Likewise, if he is certain that he has performed eight circuits of saʿy, he adds six to it. So the proper way regarding this report is that we interpret it as applying to one who did that forgetfully, according to what we have previously stated; and along with that, when he has performed eight circuits of saʿy, he is at al-Ṣafā. But if he knows that he has performed eight circuits while he is at al-Marwah, then repetition becomes obligatory upon him in every case, because that would mean he began with al-Marwah; and it is not permissible for one who did that to build upon it. And that which indicates this is:

What al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Fadalah and Safwan ibn Yahya, from Mu'awiyah ibn 'Ammar, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: If a man performs nine circuits between al-Safa and al-Marwah, then let him continue on one and discard eight. And if he performs eight circuits between al-Safa and al-Marwah, then let him discard them and restart the sa'y. And if he begins with al-Marwah, then let him discard what he has performed and begin with al-Safa.

Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah, from Musa ibn al-Hasan, from Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Hamid, from Abu Jamilah al-Mufaddal ibn Salih, from Zayd al-Shahham, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who performs sa'y between al-Safa and al-Marwah without wudu (ablution), so he said: There is no harm.

Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from Safwan, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Rifa'ah ibn Musa, who said: I said to Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام: May I perform some part of the rites while I am without wudu (ablution)? He said: Yes, except for the tawaf of the House, for indeed there is salat (prayer) in it.

As for what Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb narrated from Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from Ibn Faḍḍāl, who said: Abū al-Ḥasan عليه السلام said: Do not perform tawaf, nor sa'y, except in a state of wudu (ablution). The interpretation of this report is one of two possibilities: one of them is that he only forbade combining the two, because we have already clarified that tawaf is not valid without wudu (ablution), and he did not mean the sa'y being performed separately from tawaf without wudu. The other possibility is that it is to be understood as recommendation and desirability, because performing sa'y in a state of wudu is preferable in every circumstance; that is indicated by this.

What Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb narrated from a number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyād, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from Ḥammād ibn ʿUthmān, from Yaḥyā al-Azraq, from Abī al-Ḥasan عليه السلام, who said: I said to him: A man performs saʿy between al-Ṣafā and al-Marwah for three circuits or four, then he urinates; may he complete his saʿy without wudu (ablution)? He said: There is no harm. But if he were to complete his rite with wudu (ablution), that would be more beloved to me.

Musa ibn al-Qasim, from Safwan, from Mu'awiyah ibn 'Ammar, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: There is no harm in performing all of the rites without wudu (ablution), except for the tawaf, for in it there is salat (prayer). And wudu (ablution) is preferable in every circumstance.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from 'Abd Allah ibn Muskan, from Ishaq ibn 'Ammar, from Abi Basir, who said: I asked Aba 'Abd Allah عليه السلام about a mutamatti' who intended to shorten his hair, but shaved his head. He said: A blood-offering is upon him, which he must spill; then when the Day of Sacrifice comes, he should pass the razor over his head when he intends to shave. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: Blood is only required of him if he did that deliberately. But if he did it forgetfully, then nothing is upon him; that which indicates this is as follows.

What Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb narrated from Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from ʿAlī ibn Ḥadīd, from Jamīl ibn Darrāj, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about a mutamattiʿ who shaved his head in Makkah. He said: If he was ignorant, then there is nothing upon him. If he did that deliberately in the first of the months for hajj, thirty days before, then there is nothing upon him. But if he did it deliberately after the thirty days in which hair is left to grow for hajj, then a blood-sacrifice is upon him, which he must shed.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Ishaq ibn 'Ammar, who said: I said to Abī Ibrāhīm عليه السلام: A man performs tamattu', then forgets to shorten his hair until he enters into iḥrām for hajj. So he said: A blood-offering is upon him, which he must spill.

As for what Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb narrated from ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Muʿāwiyah ibn ʿAmmār, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: I asked Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about a man who entered into iḥrām for the ʿumrah and forgot to shorten his hair until he entered the hajj. He said: He should seek Allah’s forgiveness, and there is nothing upon him, and his ʿumrah has been completed. So this does not contradict the first report, because his statement, “there is nothing upon him,” is to be understood as meaning that there is nothing upon him in terms of punishment, and his ʿumrah has indeed been completed.

As for what Mūsā ibn al-Qāsim narrated from Ṣafwān, from Isḥāq ibn ʿAmmār, from Abī Baṣīr, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, he said: The one performing tamattuʿ, when he has performed tawaf and saʿy, then recites the talbiyah before trimming the hair, then he may not trim the hair, and he no longer has mutʿah. So this report is to be understood as applying to one who did that deliberately; but if he did it forgetfully, then his ʿumrah is not invalidated, according to what the first report indicated, and this gives further clarification of that.

What Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb narrated from Abū ʿAlī al-Ashʿarī, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Jabbār, from Ṣafwān ibn Yaḥyā, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Ḥajjāj, who said: I asked Abā Ibrāhīm عليه السلام about a man who performed tamattuʿ with the ʿumrah leading to hajj, then entered Makkah, performed tawaf and saʿy, put on his clothes, exited ihram, and forgot to shorten his hair until he went out to ʿArafāt. He عليه السلام said: There is no problem with it. He builds upon the ʿumrah and its tawaf, and the tawaf of hajj follows after it.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Hammad ibn 'Isa, and Safwan, and Fadalah, from Mu'awiyah ibn 'Ammar, who said: I asked Aba 'Abdillah عليه السلام about a man who entered into ihram for the 'umrah and forgot to shorten his hair until he entered into the hajj. He said: He should seek Allah’s forgiveness, and there is nothing upon him, and his 'umrah is complete.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from a number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Hammad ibn 'Isa, from Muhammad ibn Maymun, who said: Abu al-Hasan عليه السلام arrived performing tamattu' on the night of 'Arafah. He performed tawaf, exited the state of ihram, and went to some of his bondwomen; then he entered into ihram for hajj and departed.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Fadalah, from Abi al-Mi'za, from Abi Basir, who said: I said to Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام: A man exited his ihram, while his wife had not yet exited hers, and he had intercourse with her. He said: Upon her is a badanah, which her husband must pay for.

From him, from Muḥammad ibn Sinān, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Miskān, from Muḥammad al-Ḥalabī, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام about a woman performing tamattuʿ whose husband approached her before she had shortened [her hair]. So when she feared that he would overpower her, she reached toward the braids of her hair and clipped some of it with her teeth and cut it with her nails. Is there anything upon her? He عليه السلام said: No. Not everyone finds scissors.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from 'Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Hammad ibn 'Uthman, from al-Halabi, who said: I said to Abu 'Abdillah عليه السلام: May I be made your ransom, when I completed the rites of my 'umrah, I went to my wife before cutting my hair short. He said: A camel is due from you. He said: I said: When I wanted that from her and she had not yet cut her hair short, she refused; then when I overpowered her, she bit off some of her hair with her teeth. He said: May Allah have mercy on her; she was more knowledgeable than you. A camel is due from you, and there is nothing upon her.

As for what Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan al-Ṣaffār narrated from Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā, from Sulaymān ibn Ḥafṣ al-Marwazī, from al-Faqīh عليه السلام, who said: When a man performs hajj, then enters Makkah in tamattuʿ, circles the House, performs two rakʿahs behind the Station of Ibrāhīm عليه السلام, and goes between al-Ṣafā and al-Marwah, then everything becomes lawful for him except women, because for the lawfulness of women there is still upon him a tawaf and a prayer. So this does not contradict what we have mentioned, because there is nothing in the report stating that the tawaf and saʿy after which intercourse is not lawful until after ṭawāf al-nisāʾ are for the ʿumrah or for the hajj. When that is not specified in the report, we interpret it as referring to one who performed tawaf and saʿy for the hajj; thus it is not permissible for him to have intercourse with women. This interpretation is more appropriate, because his saying عليه السلام in the report by way of explanation, 'because for the lawfulness of women there is upon him a tawaf and a prayer,' indicates that. The ʿumrah by which one performs tamattuʿ up to the hajj does not require ṭawāf al-nisāʾ; rather, ṭawāf al-nisāʾ is only obligatory in the separate ʿumrah and the hajj, and that indicates it.

What Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā narrated from Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā, who said: Abū al-Qāsim Mukhalad ibn Mūsā al-Rāzī wrote to ask him about the detached ʿumrah: is ṭawāf al-nisāʾ obligatory upon the one performing it? And about the ʿumrah by which one performs tamattuʿ up to hajj. So he wrote: As for the detached ʿumrah, ṭawāf al-nisāʾ is obligatory upon the one performing it. But as for the one by which tamattuʿ is performed up to hajj, ṭawāf al-nisāʾ is not obligatory upon the one performing it.

Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from ʿAsim ibn Humayd, who said: I said to Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام: “May anyone enter the Haram except in a state of ihram?” He said: “No, except one who is ill or suffering from an abdominal ailment.”

From him, from Aḥmad ibn ʿĪsā, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Najrān, from ʿĀṣim ibn Ḥumayd, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, who said: I asked Abā Jaʿfar عليه السلام: “May a man enter the Ḥaram without iḥrām?” He said: “No, unless he is ill or has an abdominal ailment.”

As for what Mūsā ibn al-Qāsim narrated from Ṣafwān ibn Yaḥyā and Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Rifāʿah, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about a man afflicted with a stomach ailment and severe pain: may he enter Makkah without ihram? He said: He must not enter it except in a state of ihram. He said: And he said: Indeed, the woodcutters and those who brought goods came to the Prophet صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم and asked him, so he permitted them to enter without ihram. So the proper understanding of this report is that it indicates a kind of recommendation, not obligation and requirement.

As for what Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Jamīl ibn Darrāj, from Abū ʿAbd Allah عليه السلام, concerning regarding a man who goes out to Najd for some need. He said: He may enter Makkah without ihram. The correct way to understand this report is that we interpret it as applying to one who went out and returned within that same month, for ihram is not required of him. But as for one who enters it initially, or returns to it after the end of the month, then ihram is obligatory upon him. This detail is indicated by the evidence.

What al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Ḥafṣ ibn al-Bakhtarī and Abān ibn ʿUthmān, from a man, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, concerning: A man who goes out from the Haram for some need—he said: if he returns in the same month in which he left, he may enter without ihram; but if he enters in another month, he enters with ihram.

Musa ibn al-Qasim, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: The one performing tamattu' circles the House and performs sa'y between al-Safa and al-Marwah so long as he catches up with the people at Mina.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from a number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Faddal, from Ibn Bukayr, from some of our companions: he asked Aba 'Abdillah عليه السلام about mut'ah—when does it take place? He said: He may perform mut'ah as long as he thinks that he will catch up with the people at Mina.

Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn Abi al-Khattab, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from Murazim ibn Hakim, who said: I said to Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام: The one performing tamattu' enters Makkah on the night of 'Arafah, and the menstruating woman—until when does tamattu' remain for the two of them? He said: As long as they catch up with the people at Mina.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from 'Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Isma'il ibn Marrar, from Yunus, from Ya'qub ibn Shu'ayb al-Maythami, who said: I heard Aba 'Abdillah عليه السلام say: There is no harm for the one performing tamattu' if he does not enter ihram on the night of al-Tarwiyah; whenever it becomes possible for him, so long as he does not fear missing the two standing places.

Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah, from Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Jamil ibn Darrāj, from Abī 'Abd Allāh عليه السلام, who said: The one performing tamattu' has mut'ah available to him until the sun passes the meridian on the Day of 'Arafah, and he has hajj available to him until the sun passes the meridian on the Day of al-Nahr.

From him, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar, from Muḥammad ibn Surūr, who said: I wrote to Abū al-Ḥasan al-Thālith عليه السلام: What do you say about a man performing tamattuʿ with the ʿumrah up to the hajj, who arrives on the morning of ʿArafah while the people have departed from Minā to ʿArafāt? Is his ʿumrah still valid, or has it lapsed from him? Until what time does his ʿumrah remain valid if he is performing tamattuʿ with the ʿumrah up to the hajj, but he did not arrive on the Day of Tarwiyah nor on the night of Tarwiyah? So what should he do? So he wrote back عليه السلام: At the hour he enters Makkah, if Allah wills, he performs tawaf, prays two rakʿahs, performs saʿy, cuts short his hair, enters ihram for his hajj, proceeds to the standing place, and departs with the Imam.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from 'Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Hisham ibn Salim, and Murazim, and Shu'ayb, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, concerning: Regarding a man performing tamattu' who enters on the night of 'Arafah: he performs tawaf and sa'y, then exits ihram, then enters ihram again, and comes to Mina. He said: There is no harm in that.

From him, from a number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Hasan ibn Sa'id, from Hammad ibn 'Isa, from Muhammad ibn Maymun, who said: Abu al-Hasan عليه السلام arrived performing tamattu' on the night of 'Arafah. He performed tawaf, exited ihram, went to some of his bondwomen, then entered into ihram for hajj and departed.

Musa ibn al-Qasim, from al-Hasan, from al-'Ala' ibn Razin, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I said to Abi 'Abdillah عليه السلام: Until when is there an 'umrah for the pilgrim? He said: Until dawn-time in the night of 'Arafah.

From him, from Safwan, from al-'Ala', from 'Is ibn al-Qasim, who said: I asked Aba 'Abdillah عليه السلام about the mutamatti' who arrives in Makkah on the Day of Tarwiyah at the time of salat al-'Asr: does the mut'ah pass him by? He said: No. He has the time between then and sunset. And he said: The Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم had indeed done that.

And from him, from Muḥammad ibn Sahl, from his father, from Isḥāq ibn ʿAbd Allāh, who said: I asked Abā al-Ḥasan Mūsā عليه السلام about the mutamattiʿ who enters Makkah on the Day of Tarwiyah. He said: For the mutamattiʿ, there is time until sunset.

From him, from Muḥammad ibn ʿUdhāfir, from ʿUmar ibn Yazīd, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: When you arrive in Makkah on the Day of Tarwiyah while you are performing tamattuʿ, then you have the time between your arrival and the night to perform tawaf of the House, perform saʿy, and make it a mutʿah.

From him, from al-Hasan, from al-'Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I said to Abu 'Abdillah عليه السلام: Until when does the pilgrim have 'umrah? He said: Until dawn-time in the night of 'Arafah.

Musa ibn al-Qasim said: A trustworthy person from the Ahl al-Bayt narrated to us from Abu al-Hasan Musa عليه السلام that he said: Enter into ihram for tamattu' in hajj—meaning on the Day of Tarwiyah—until the decline of the sun, and after al-'Asr, and after al-Maghrib, and after the later al-'Isha', and all that in between is expansive.

As for what Mūsā ibn al-Qāsim narrated from Muḥammad ibn Sahl, from Zakariyyā ibn ʿImrān, he said: I asked Abā al-Ḥasan عليه السلام about the mutamattiʿ when the Day of ʿArafah has begun. He said: There is no tamattuʿ for him; he makes it into a separate ʿumrah.

From him, from Muḥammad ibn Sahl, from his father, from Isḥāq ibn ʿAbd Allāh, from Abū al-Ḥasan عليه السلام, who said: If the mutamattiʿ arrives on the night of ʿArafah, then he no longer has mutʿah; rather, he makes it into an individual hajj. Mutʿah is only up to the Day of Tarwiyah.

From him, from Muḥammad ibn Sahl, from his father, from Mūsā ibn ʿAbd Allāh, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام about one performing tamattuʿ who arrives in Makkah on the night of ʿArafah. He said: There is no tamattuʿ for him; he makes it into an individual hajj, performs tawaf of the House, goes between al-Safa and al-Marwah, and goes out to Mina. There is no sacrificial offering upon him; rather, the sacrificial offering is only upon the one performing tamattuʿ.

And from him, from Ṣafwān ibn Yaḥyā, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Aʿyan, from ʿAlī ibn Yaqṭīn, who said: I asked Abū al-Ḥasan Mūsā عليه السلام about a man and a woman who are performing tamattuʿ with the ʿumrah leading to hajj, then they enter Makkah on the Day of ʿArafah—what should they do? He said: They should make it into an individual hajj, and the limit of tamattuʿ is until the Day of al-Tarwiyah.

If you arrive in Makkah on the Day of Tarwiyah after the sun has set, then there is no mut'ah for you; proceed with your hajj as you are. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: The proper way to reconcile these reports is to say that the mutamatti' has a complete 'umrah so long as he reaches the two standings, whether that is on the Day of Tarwiyah, the night of 'Arafah, or the Day of 'Arafah until after zawal. But once the sun has passed the meridian on the Day of 'Arafah, mut'ah has been missed, because he can no longer catch the people at 'Arafat in the manner we described. However, people's ranks differ in merit and reward: whoever reaches on the Day of Tarwiyah at the sun's decline has greater reward and a more complete mut'ah than one who arrives at night, and whoever reaches at night has less reward than that but more than one who arrives on the Day of 'Arafah until after zawal. The reports stating that whoever does not reach the Day of Tarwiyah has missed mut'ah mean the loss of the perfection that he had hoped for by arriving on the Day of Tarwiyah. And what they, peace be upon them, said: 'Let him make it an ifrad hajj,' is directed only to one who strongly expects that if he occupies himself with tawaf, sa'y, exiting ihram, and then entering ihram for hajj, he will miss the two standings. If we carry these reports according to what we have mentioned, we do not discard any of them; this interpretation is indicated by that. 6. What Ibn Abi 'Umayr narrated from Hammad, from al-Halabi, who said: I asked Aba 'Abd Allah عليه السلام about a man who entered into ihram for both hajj and 'umrah together, then arrived in Makkah while the people were at 'Arafat, and he feared that if he performed tawaf and sa'y between al-Safa and al-Marwah he would miss the standing. So he said: He leaves the 'umrah, and when he completes his hajj he does as 'A'ishah did, and there is no sacrificial offering upon him. From him, from Muhammad ibn 'Udhafir, from 'Umar ibn Yazid, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said:

From him, from al-Ḥasan ibn Maḥbūb, from ʿAlī ibn Riʾāb, from Zurārah, who said: I asked Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام about a man who is on the Day of ʿArafah, and between him and Makkah are three miles, while he is performing tamattuʿ with ʿumrah leading to hajj. He said: He cuts off the talbiyah of the tamattuʿ, and begins the hajj with the talbiyah when he has performed Fajr salat (prayer), then proceeds to ʿArafāt and stands with the people, completes all the rites, and remains in Makkah until he performs the ʿumrah of al-Muḥarram, and there is nothing upon him. Do you not see that in the first report he directed the address to one who feared missing the standing, and in the second report to one between whom and Makkah are three miles? And it is known that one whose condition is like this cannot enter Makkah, become occupied with exiting ihram and then entering ihram afterward, and still catch up with the people at ʿArafāt. Whenever that is not possible for him, then his duty is to continue in his ihram and make it an individual hajj, as we have mentioned.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from 'Ali ibn al-Salt, from Zur'ah, from Abi Basir, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: When you intend to enter into ihram on the Day of Tarwiyah, then do as you did when you intended to enter ihram: trim your moustache, clip your nails, and remove from your pubic hair if you have hair; pluck your armpits, perform ghusl, and put on your two garments. Then go to the mosque and perform six rak'ahs there before entering ihram, and supplicate to Allah and ask Him for help, and say—then he mentioned the supplication.

As for what Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn Abi al-Khattab, from ʿAli ibn al-Nuʿman, from Suwayd al-Qallaʾ, from Ayyub ibn al-Hurr, from Abi ʿAbd Allah عليه السلام, who said: I said to him: We have already used depilatory, plucked, and trimmed our nails in al-Madinah, so what should we do at the time of hajj? He said: Do not use depilatory, do not pluck, and do not move anything. Thus, the proper understanding of this report is that it indicates the permissibility of that, because the first narration is to be understood as referring to merit and recommendation, not obligation and requirement.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Muhammad ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Hammad ibn 'Uthman, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I heard Abu Ja'far عليه السلام say: Nothing that the fasting person does harms him, so long as he avoids three qualities: food, drink, women, and immersion.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from 'Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, and Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, all from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Jamil ibn Darrāj, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, that he was asked about a man who deliberately broke the fast one day in the month of Ramadan, and he said: A man came to the Prophet صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم and said, “I am ruined, O Messenger of Allah.” He said, “What is the matter with you?” He said, “The Fire, O Messenger of Allah.” He said, “And what is the matter with you?” He said, “I had intercourse with my wife.” So he said, “Give charity and seek forgiveness from your Lord.” The man said, “By the One who has magnified your right, I have left nothing in the house, neither little nor much.” He said: Then a man from the people entered with a basket of dates containing twenty sa's. The Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم said to him, “Take these dates and give them in charity.” He said, “O Messenger of Allah, to whom should I give them in charity, when I have informed you that there is nothing in my house, neither little nor much?” He said, “Then take it and feed it to your dependents, and seek forgiveness of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.” He said: When we went out, our companions said, “He began with emancipation.” He said, “Free a slave, or fast, or give charity.”

From him, from ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Sinān, from Abū ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, concerning A man who had intercourse with his wife in the month of Ramadan and could not find what he could give in charity to sixty poor persons—he said: He should give charity according to the amount he is able.

From him, from Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā, from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn, from Ṣafwān, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Ḥajjāj, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about a man who fondles his wife in the month of Ramadan until he ejaculates. He said: Upon him is an expiation like that which is upon one who has sexual intercourse.

As for what Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Faḍḍāl narrated from ʿAmr ibn Saʿīd, from Muṣaddaq ibn Ṣadaqah, from ʿAmmār ibn Mūsā al-Sābāṭī, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about a man who is fasting and has intercourse with his wife. He said: He performs ghusl, and nothing is due upon him. So this report admits of two possibilities: one of them is that he did that absentmindedly or forgetfully, for then nothing is binding upon him and his fast has been completed. We have already clarified that in our larger book. The second is that he did that while not knowing that it is not permissible to do it in the state of fasting, and that which indicates this is:

What was narrated by ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥasan ibn Faḍḍāl, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī, from ʿAlī ibn al-Nuʿmān, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muskān, from Zurārah and Abū Baṣīr, from Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said: Together we asked Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام about a man who had intercourse with his wife in the month of Ramaḍān, and had intercourse with his wife while he was in iḥrām, and he saw that as nothing but lawful for him. He said: There is nothing upon him.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from 'Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Mu'awiyah ibn 'Ammar, from Abi 'Abdillah عليه السلام, who said: When you reach al-Rawha' before al-Radm, and overlook al-Abtah, then raise your voice in the talbiyah until you come to Mina.

Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Sulayman ibn Jarir, from Hariz, from Zurarah, who said: I said to Abī 'Abd Allah عليه السلام: When should I recite the talbiyah for hajj? He said: When you depart toward Mina. Then he said: When you place Shi'b al-Dubb on your right and al-'Aqabah on your left, then recite the talbiyah for hajj.

As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from ʿAlī ibn al-Ṣalt, from Zurʿah, from Abū Baṣīr, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, he said: Then you recite the talbiyah from al-Masjid al-Ḥarām just as you recited the talbiyah when you entered iḥrām, and you say: “Labbayka for a hajj whose completion and conveyance are upon You.” If you are able, let your departure to Minā be at the decline of the sun; otherwise, then whenever it is made easy for you on the Day of Tarwiyah. This does not conflict with the first two reports, because the one walking recites the talbiyah from the place where he performs salat for iḥrām, while the rider recites the talbiyah at al-Raqṭāʾ or at Shiʿb al-Dubb, and neither of them raises the voice in the talbiyah except when overlooking al-Abṭaḥ. This is indicated by that.

What Mūsā ibn al-Qāsim narrated from Muḥammad ibn ʿUmar ibn Yazīd, from Muḥammad ibn ʿUdhāfir, from ʿUmar ibn Yazīd, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: When it is the Day of Tarwiyah, do as you did at al-Shajarah, then pray two rakʿahs behind the Maqām, then enter into the state of ihram for hajj. If you are walking, then recite the talbiyah at the Maqām, and if you are riding, then when your camel sets out with you. Pray Zuhr, if you are able, at Minā, and know that it is broad for you to enter ihram after an obligatory prayer, or after a supererogatory prayer, or by night, or by day.

Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā, from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Yaqṭīn, from his brother al-Ḥusayn, from ʿAlī ibn Yaqṭīn, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about one who wants to go ahead in it, for which there is no time earlier than it. He said: “When the sun passes the meridian.” And about one who wishes to remain behind in Makkah on the eve of al-Tarwiyah—until what hour is it permissible for him to remain behind? He said: “That is broader for him, until he reaches Minā by morning.”

As for what Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb narrated from a number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyād, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from Rifāʿah, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: I asked him: Do the people depart to Minā in the morning? He said: Yes, until sunset. So it does not contradict the first report, because this report is to be understood as referring to what we mentioned regarding one who has excuses, the sick person, and others; that indicates this.

What Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb narrated from Abū ʿAlī al-Ashʿarī, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Jabbār, from Ṣafwān, from Isḥāq ibn ʿAmmār, from Abū al-Ḥasan عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who is an elderly shaykh or ill, and fears the pressure of the people and their crowding: may he enter into ihram for hajj and go out to Minā before the Day of Tarwiyah? He said: Yes. I said: Then may a healthy man go out seeking a place or seeking comfort thereby? He said: No. I said: May he go early by one day? He said: Yes. I said: By two days? He said: Yes. I said: By three? He said: Yes. I said: More than that? He said: No.

Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from one of his companions, who said: I said to Abī al-Ḥasan عليه السلام: A man hastens ahead of al-Tarwiyah by one day or two because of the crowding and the pressure of the people. So he said: There is no harm.

As for what al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Safwan ibn Yahya and Fadalah, from al-'Ala' ibn Razin, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from one of the two of them عليهما السلام, who said: It is not appropriate for the Imam to perform the Zuhr salat on the Day of Tarwiyah except at Mina, and he should remain there through the night until sunrise.

From him, from Safwan and Fadalah ibn Ayyub and Ibn Abi Umayr, from Jamil ibn Darrāj, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: It is not proper for the Imam to perform the Zuhr prayer except at Mina on the Day of Tarwiyah; and he should spend the night there, remain until the sun rises, and then depart.

From him, from Faḍālah, from Muʿāwiyah ibn ʿAmmār, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: It is upon the Imam to perform the Zuhr prayer on the Day of Tarwiyah at Masjid al-Khayf, and to perform the Zuhr prayer on the Day of Nafr in al-Masjid al-Haram. The correct way to understand these reports is that they apply specifically to the Imam, to the exclusion of others; that is what they indicate, and there is no contradiction between them and what we have previously presented.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Al-Hasan, from Zur'ah, from Sama'ah, who said: I asked him about combining the maghrib and the later 'isha' at Jam', so he said: Do not perform them until you reach Jam', even if as much of the night as has passed should pass. For indeed the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him and his family, combined them with one adhan and two iqamahs, just as he combined the zuhr and the 'asr at 'Arafat.

From him, from Safwan, from al-'Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from one of the two عليهما السلام, who said: Do not perform the Maghrib salat until you come to Jam', even if one-third of the night has passed.

As for what Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn Abī Naṣr, from Muḥammad ibn Samāʿah ibn Mihrān, he said: I said to Abū ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام: May a man perform the Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ at al-Mawqif? He said: The Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم had indeed done that; he performed them both in the mountain pass. Thus, the correct way regarding this report is that it is to be understood as applying to one whom some impediment prevents from coming to Jamʿ until it becomes quite late in the evening. But when there is choice, that is not permissible in any circumstance. And that which indicates that what is intended is what we have mentioned...

What Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Saʿid, from Hammad, from Ribʿi ibn ʿAbd Allah, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abi ʿAbd Allah عليه السلام, who said: My father’s litter stumbled between ʿArafah and al-Muzdalifah, so he dismounted and prayed al-maghrib, and he prayed the later ʿisha prayer at al-Muzdalifah.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Hisham ibn al-Hakam, from Abi 'Abdillah عليه السلام, who said: There is no harm in a man performing the Maghrib prayer when evening comes upon him at 'Arafah.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Mansur ibn Hazim, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: The salat of al-Maghrib and al-'Isha' at Jam' are with one adhan and two iqamahs, and do not perform anything between them. He said: And this is how the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم performed salat. From him, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from 'Abd Allah ibn Muskan, from 'Anbasah ibn Mus'ab, who said: I said to Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام: If I perform salat al-Maghrib at Jam', should I perform the rak'ahs after al-Maghrib? He said: No. Perform al-Maghrib and al-'Isha', then perform the rak'ahs afterward.

As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Ḥajjāj, from Abān ibn Taghlib, who said: I prayed Maghrib behind Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام at al-Muzdalifah. Then he stood and prayed Maghrib, then prayed the later ʿIshāʾ, and he did not perform any rakʿah between them. Then I prayed behind him a year after that, and when he had prayed Maghrib, he stood and performed four rakʿahs of supererogatory prayer. So there is no contradiction between the two actions, nor between it and the earlier reports, because the earlier reports are interpreted as recommendation and desirability rather than obligation and requirement, while this action is interpreted as indicating permissibility.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from a number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ibn Mahbub, from Ibn Ri'ab, from Misma', from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, concerning: A man stood with the people at Jam', then departed before the people departed. He said: If he was ignorant, then there is nothing upon him; but if he departed before the rise of dawn, then upon him is the blood-offering of a sheep.

As for what Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from Muḥammad ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Hishām ibn Sālim and others, from Abū ʿAbd Allah عليه السلام, that he said: There is no harm in going ahead from Minā to ʿArafāt before sunrise, and in going ahead from al-Muzdalifah to Minā so that they stone the jamarāt and perform salat al-fajr in their lodgings at Minā, there is no harm. The proper way regarding this report is that we understand it as applying to one who has excuses, such as the sick person, women, the menstruating woman, and other such excuses. But when the excuse has ceased, then it is not permissible, according to what we have stated before; that is indicated by this.

What Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb narrated from a number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyād, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ḥamzah, from one of the two of them عليهما السلام, who said: Any woman and any fearful man who departs from al-Mashʿar al-Ḥarām at night, there is no harm in that; so let him cast the pebble at the Jamrah. And he mentioned the hadith to its end.

From him, from ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Jamīl ibn Darrāj, from some of our companions, from one of the two of them عليهما السلام, who said: There is no harm in a man departing by night if he is fearful.

From him, from a number of our companions, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from Abī al-Mighrāʾ, from Abī Baṣīr, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: The Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم gave permission to the women and children to depart by night, to stone the jamarāt by night, and to perform the morning prayer in their lodgings. And if the women feared menstruation, they could proceed to Makkah and appoint someone to perform the sacrifice on their behalf.

Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Musa ibn al-Qasim, from Mu'awiyah ibn Hakim, who said: I asked Abū Ibrāhīm عليه السلام: “At what time is it more beloved to you that we depart from Jam'?” He said: “A little before the sun rises; that is the most beloved of times to me.” I said: “If we remain until the sun rises?” He said: “There is no harm in it.”

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Abi 'Ali al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Jabbar, from Safwan, from Ishaq ibn 'Ammar, who said: I asked Aba Ibrahim عليه السلام, “At what time is it more beloved to you that we depart from Jam'?” He said, “A little before the sun rises; that is the most beloved of times to me.” I said, “If we remain until the sun rises?” He said, “There is no harm in it.”

As for what Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-'Abbas ibn Ma'ruf, from 'Ali ibn Mahziyar, from the one who narrated to him, from Hammad ibn 'Uthman, from Jamil ibn Darrāj, from Abī 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: It is appropriate for the Imam to remain at Jam' until the sun rises, while the rest of the people, if they wish, may hasten, and if they wish, may delay. So the proper understanding of this report is the removal of hardship from whoever does that, and the first two reports are to be understood as indicating a kind of recommendation.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from 'Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about ghusl when one has performed the ramy of the jimar. He said: I have perhaps done it at times, but as for the sunnah, then no; rather, it is because of the heat and sweat.

From him, from Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥakam, from al-ʿAlāʾ, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, who said: I asked Abā Jaʿfar عليه السلام about the pebbles-throwing ritual, and he said: Do not throw the jamarāt except while you are in a state of taharah (ritual purity).

As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā narrated from al-Barqī, from Jaʿfar, from Abī Ghassān Ḥumayd ibn Masʿūd, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about pelting the jamarāt while not in a state of taharah. He said: The jamarāt, with us, are like al-Ṣafā and al-Marwah—walls; if you were to go between them while not in a state of taharah, it would not harm you. But taharah is more beloved to me, so do not leave it while you are able to do it. Thus, the correct understanding of this report is permissibility, and the first report is to be understood as referring to merit and recommendation.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Ibn Miskan, from Sa'id al-A'raj, who said: Abu 'Abdillah عليه السلام said: Whoever performs tamattu' in the months of hajj, then remains in Makkah until the hajj of the following year arrives, then upon him is the blood-sacrifice of a sheep. And whoever performs tamattu' outside the months of hajj, then resides nearby until the hajj arrives, then there is no blood-sacrifice upon him. It is only a separate hajj, and the udhiyah is only upon the people of the towns.

As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Ṣafwān ibn Yaḥyā, from al-ʿĪṣ ibn al-Qāsim, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, that he said: Regarding a man who performed ʿumrah in Rajab, he said: if he remains in Makkah until he departs from it as a pilgrim, then the hady has become obligatory upon him. But if he leaves Makkah so that he enters ihram from somewhere other than it, then there is no hady upon him. So the proper way to understand this report is one of two things: either it is to be understood as referring to merit and recommendation rather than obligation and requirement; or it is to be understood as referring to one who performed ʿumrah in Rajab and remained in Makkah until the months of hajj, then performed tamattuʿ from it by ʿumrah toward hajj. For whoever is like that, the hady is binding upon him according to what this report contains, and that indicates it.

What Mūsā ibn al-Qāsim narrated from Muḥammad ibn Sahl, from his father, from Isḥāq ibn ʿAbd Allāh, who said: I asked Abā al-Ḥasan عليه السلام about a person performing ʿumrah who resides in Makkah: should he perform hajj ifrād, or should he perform tamattuʿ once again? He said: Performing tamattuʿ is more beloved to me, and let his ihram be from the distance of a journey of one night or two nights.

Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb, from ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from Ḥammād ibn ʿĪsā, from Ḥarīz, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, concerning: Regarding a mutamattiʿ who finds the price but does not find sheep, he said: He should leave the price with some of the people of Mecca and instruct one who will buy for him and slaughter on his behalf, and that suffices for him. فإذا مضى ذو الحجة، he delays that until the coming year in Dhū al-Ḥijjah.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from al-Nadr ibn Qirwash, who said: I asked Abu 'Abdillah عليه السلام about a man who performed tamattu' with the 'umrah up to the hajj, so the sacrificial rite became obligatory upon him. He sought it but could not find it, while he was well-off and in good condition, yet he was too weak to fast. So what should he do? He عليه السلام said: He should pay the price of the nusuk to someone who will slaughter it in Makkah, if he intends to depart to his family, and it should be slaughtered in Dhu al-Hijjah. So I said: If he gave it to someone to slaughter on his behalf, but he did not find a nusuk in Dhu al-Hijjah and found one after that? He عليه السلام said: He must not slaughter it on his behalf except in Dhu al-Hijjah, even if he delays it until the following year.

As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn Abī Naṣr narrated from ʿAbd al-Karīm, from Abū Baṣīr, from one of the two of them, peace be upon them, he said: I asked him about a man performing tamattuʿ who did not find what he could offer as hady, until when it was the Day of Nafr he found the price of a sheep. Should he slaughter, or should he fast? He said: Rather, he should fast, for the days of slaughter have already passed. So this does not contradict what we have stated, because what is meant in this report is one who did not find the hady nor its price and fasted three days, then later found the price of the hady. It is upon him to fast whatever remains due upon him to complete the ten days, and the hady is not obligatory upon him. This is indicated by that.

What Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb narrated from a number of our companions, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yaḥyā, from Ḥammād ibn ʿUthmān, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام about a mutamattiʿ who fasted three days during the hajj, then obtained a sacrificial animal on the day he departed from Minā. He said: His fasting suffices him.

As for what was narrated by Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā, from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Hilāl, from ʿUqbah ibn Khālid, who said: I asked Abū ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام about a man who performed tamattuʿ hajj while not having with him what he could buy a sacrificial offering with; then, after he had fasted three days during the hajj, he became financially able. Should he buy a sacrificial offering and slaughter it, or leave that and fast seven days when he returns to his family? He عليه السلام said: He should buy a sacrificial offering and slaughter it, and the fasting that he already performed will count as supererogatory for him. The proper way regarding this report is that we carry it upon a degree of recommendation and desirability, because whoever obtains the price of the sacrificial offering after having fasted three days has the choice: if he wishes, he may fast the remainder of what is due upon him, and if he wishes, he may slaughter the sacrificial offering; and the sacrificial offering is more virtuous.

Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb, from a number of our companions, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from Faḍālah, from Muʿāwiyah ibn ʿAmmār, who said: Whoever dies and does not have a sacrificial offering for his tamattuʿ, then his guardian should fast on his behalf.

As for what Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb narrated from ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Ḥammād, from al-Ḥalabī, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام. He was asked about a man who performed tamattuʿ with ʿumrah up to hajj, and he did not have a sacrificial offering, so he fasted three days in Dhū al-Ḥijjah. Then he died after he had returned to his family, before fasting the seven days. Is it upon his guardian to make them up on his behalf? He said: I do not see any make-up duty upon him. So this does not contradict the first report, because the command to make up the fasting in the first report was directed only to the three days. As for the seven days, it is not obligatory upon his guardian to make them up on his behalf, though it is recommended for him to make up all of them on his behalf.
Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr and Fadalah, from Jamil, from Zurarah and Abi Basir, from Abi Ja'far عليه السلام, who said: A kiss does not invalidate the fast.

Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Fadalah, from Aban, from Muhammad ibn Muslim and Zurarah, from Abi Ja'far عليه السلام. He was asked whether the fasting person may engage in مباشَرَة or kiss during the month of Ramadan. So he said: Indeed, I fear for him, so let him refrain from that, unless he is confident that his semen will not precede him.

From him, from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿUlwān, from Saʿd ibn Ṭarīf, from al-Aṣbagh ibn Nubātah, who said: A man came to Amīr al-Muʾminīn عليه السلام and said: “O Amīr al-Muʾminīn, may I kiss while I am fasting?” He عليه السلام said to him: “Keep your fast chaste, for the beginning of fighting is the slap.” So these two reports are to be understood as indicating a kind of karahah, because what is better is that a person should not expose himself to these things, in order to keep his fast above reproach and to avoid that with which he would not be safe from committing what is prohibited.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Al-Hasan ibn 'Ali ibn Faddal, from Ibn Bukayr, from Al-Hasan al-'Attar, who said: I asked Abu 'Abdillah عليه السلام about a man who instructed his owned slave to perform tamattu' with the 'umrah up to the hajj: is he required to slaughter on his behalf? He said: No. Because Allah, Exalted is He, says: “A slave, owned, who has no power over anything.”

From him, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Saʿd ibn Abī Khalaf, who said: I asked Abā al-Ḥasan عليه السلام and said: I instructed my slave to perform tamattuʿ. He said: If you wish, then slaughter on his behalf; and if you wish, then instruct him to fast.

Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Jamil ibn Darraj, who said: A man asked Aba 'Abd Allah عليه السلام about a man who instructed his slave to perform tamattu'. He said: Then instruct him to fast, and if you wish, then slaughter on his behalf.

As for what al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Safwan ibn Yahya, from al-'Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from one of the two of them عليهما السلام, who said: He was asked about the mutamatti', how much suffices him. He said: one sheep. And I asked him about the enslaved mutamatti', so he said: upon him is the like of what is upon the free man, either a sacrifice or fasting. The proper way of understanding this report is one of several possibilities. One of them is that this is informing of his equality to the free man in the amount of what is due upon him, even if what is binding regarding the enslaved person, by way of choice, rests with his master; for if he wishes, he offers a sacrificial animal on his behalf, and if he wishes, he instructs him to fast. If he instructs him to fast, then what is binding upon him of fasting is the same as what is binding upon the free man, namely fasting ten days. This is not treated like zihar, in which half of what is binding upon the free man is binding upon him. Likewise, if he wishes to slaughter on his behalf, it is binding upon him to offer on his behalf the like of what is offered on behalf of the free man. From this aspect he is like the free man, not from the standpoint of the sacrificial offering being initially obligatory upon him. The second possibility is that it is to be understood regarding one who was enslaved and then emancipated before missing either of the two standing-places; then the sacrificial offering becomes binding upon him, because he reached the hajj while he was free, so what is binding upon the free man becomes binding upon him, according to what has previously been stated concerning it. And the third is that if the master does not instruct his slave to fast until the final departure, then it becomes binding upon him to slaughter on his behalf, and fasting does not suffice him. That is indicated by what follows.

What al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad, from Abī Ibrāhīm عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a غلام whom I brought with me, and I instructed him, so he performed tamattuʿ, then he entered into hajj on the Day of al-Tarwiyah, and I did not slaughter on his behalf. Does he have the option to fast after the departure, when the days which Allah, Exalted is He, mentioned have already passed? So he said: Why did you not instruct him to perform hajj separately (ifrād)? I said: I sought the good. He said: Since you sought the good, then go and slaughter on his behalf a fat sheep. And that was on the final day of departure.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from a number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad and Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Mahbub, from Ibrahim al-Karkhi, from Abi 'Abdillah عليه السلام, regarding: A man who arrived in Makkah with his hady during the ten days—he said: if it is an obligatory hady, then he should not slaughter it except at Mina; and if it is not obligatory, then let him slaughter it in Makkah if he wishes. And if he had marked it and garlanded it, then he should not slaughter it except on the Day of al-Adha.

As for what Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb narrated from ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Muʿāwiyah ibn ʿAmmār, who said: I said to Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام: The people of Makkah objected to you that you slaughtered your sacrificial offering in your house in Makkah. So he said: Indeed, all of Makkah is a place of slaughter. So the proper way regarding this report is that we understand it as referring to a sacrificial offering that is not obligatory, for that may be slaughtered in Makkah, as was explained in detail in the first report.

Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā, from Mūsā ibn al-Qāsim al-Bajalī and Abū Qatādah ʿAlī ibn Muḥammad ibn Ḥafṣ al-Qummī, from ʿAlī ibn Jaʿfar, from his brother Mūsā ibn Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about al-Aḍḥā: how long is it in Minā? He said: Four days. And I asked him about al-Aḍḥā outside Minā, and he said: Three days. I said: What do you say about a traveling man who arrives two days after al-Aḍḥā—may he offer the sacrifice on the third day? He said: Yes.

From him, from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Faddal, from Amr ibn Sa'id, from Musaddaq ibn Sadaqah, from Ammar al-Sabati, from Abu Abdillah عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about the udhiyah in Mina, and he said: four days. And about the udhiyah in the rest of the towns, he said: the udhiyah is three days. 3—Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Muhammad ibn Ghiyath, from Ja'far, from his father عليهما السلام, from Ali عليه السلام, who said: The udhiyah is three days, and the best of them is the first of them.

As for that which Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb narrated from a number of our companions, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from Faḍālah ibn Ayyūb, from Kulayb al-Asadī, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about al-naḥr, and he said: As for Minā, it is three days; and as for the towns, it is one day.

From him, from ʿAlī, from his father, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Jamīl ibn Darrāj, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, from Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said: Al-Aḍḥā is two days after the Day of Sacrifice in Minā, and one day only in the towns. The correct way regarding these two reports is that we interpret them to mean that the days of sacrifice during which fasting is not permitted are three days in Minā, and one day in the rest of the lands; because after the sacrifice day, fasting is permitted in the other towns, whereas that is not permitted in Minā except after three days. And that which indicates this is:

What Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā narrated from Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd, from Sayf ibn ʿUmayrah, from Manṣūr ibn Ḥāzim, from Abū ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said: I heard him saying: Slaughtering at Minā is for three days, so whoever wishes to fast must not fast until the three days have passed. And slaughtering in the towns is for one day, so whoever wishes to fast may fast from the following day.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Hammad ibn 'Isa, from Shu'ayb, from Abi Basir, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: He should not offer the sacrifice except with that by which he has performed the standing at 'Arafat.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, said: He was asked about a castrated animal: may one offer it as a sacrifice? He said: If you want meat, then it is available to you. And he said: One should not offer as a sacrifice except that by which it has been prescribed.

As for what Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from 'Abd Allah ibn Miskan, from Sa'id ibn Yasar, who said: I asked Aba 'Abd Allah عليه السلام about one who bought a sheep and it had not been identified as such. He said: There is no problem with it, whether it was identified as such or it was not identified as such. The correct way regarding this report is that we understand it to mean that the buyer had not identified it as such, while the seller mentioned that he had identified it as such. So he is believed in that, and it suffices for him. This is indicated by that.

What al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Safwan, from Sa'id ibn Yasar, who said: I said to Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام: We buy sheep in Mina, and we do not know whether they have been taken to 'Arafah or not. So he said: They do not lie; there is no problem upon you; offer it as the sacrifice.

Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from Abu al-Husayn al-Nakha'i, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: A cow and a camel suffice for seven in the cities, but at Mina they do not suffice except for one.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Fadalah and Safwan, from al-'Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from one of the two (Imams) عليهما السلام, who said: A camel for sacrifice and a cow are not valid except on behalf of one person at Mina.

As for what Mūsā ibn al-Qāsim narrated from Abū al-Ḥusayn al-Nakhaʿī, from Muʿāwiyah ibn ʿAmmār, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: A cow suffices for five at Minā when they are people of one table.
Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Ibn Faddal, from Yunus ibn Ya'qub, who said: I asked Aba 'Abdillah عليه السلام about a cow offered as sacrifice. He said: It suffices for seven.

And Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn Abi al-Khattab, from Wuhayb ibn Hafs, from Abu Basir, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: A camel and a cow suffice for seven people, when they gather together from one household or from others besides them.

From him, from Abu Ja'far, from al-'Abbas ibn Ma'ruf, from al-Husayn ibn Yazid, from Isma'il ibn Abi Ziyad, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, from his father عليه السلام, from 'Ali عليه السلام, who said: A cow and a jadha'ah suffice for three members of one household, a musinnah suffices for seven separate individuals, and a jazur suffices for ten separate individuals.

From him, from ʿAbd Allah ibn Jaʿfar al-Ḥimyarī, from ʿAlī ibn al-Rayyān ibn al-Ṣalt, from Abū al-Ḥasan al-Thālith عليه السلام, who said: I wrote to him asking about the water buffalo: for how many does it suffice in the udhiyah? The reply came: if it is a male, then for one; and if it is a female, then for seven.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from a number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Hasan ibn 'Ali, from a man whom he named Sawadah, who said: We were a group at Mina, and the sacrificial animals had become scarce. So we looked, and there was Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام standing by the flock, bargaining for sheep and haggling with them intensely, while we were waiting. When he had finished, he turned toward us and said: I think you were surprised by my haggling. We said: Yes. He said: Indeed, the one who is cheated is neither praised nor rewarded. Do you have some need? We said: Yes, may Allah set you aright; the sacrificial animals have become too costly for us. He said: Gather together and buy a camel, then sacrifice it among yourselves. We said: Our means do not reach that. He said: Then gather together and buy a cow among yourselves. We said: Our means still do not reach that either. He said: Then gather together and buy a sheep and slaughter it among yourselves. We said: Will it suffice for seven? He said: Yes, and for seventy.

From him, from ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Ibn Udhaynah, from Ḥumrān, who said: The sacrificial camels became scarce one year at Minā until a single camel reached one hundred dinars. So Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام was asked about that, and he said: “Share in it together.” He said: I said, “How many?” He said: “The fewer it is, the better.” He said: I said, “On behalf of how many does it suffice?” He said: “On behalf of seventy.”

Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from al-Hasan ibn 'Ali ibn Faddal, from Sawadah al-Qattan and 'Ali ibn Asbat, from Abu al-Hasan al-Rida عليه السلام, who said: We said to him: May we be your ransom, sacrificial animals have become scarce for us in Makkah; is it sufficient for two people to share in one sheep? He said: Yes, and on behalf of seventy. The discussion concerning these reports, despite the variation in their wording and the incompatibility of their meanings, is from two angles. One of them is that there is nothing in any of them explicitly stating that sufficiency on behalf of seven, or five, or seventy—according to the variation of their wordings—applies to the obligatory offering or the supererogatory one; so when there is no explicit statement about that, we interpret them to mean that what is intended is that which is not obligatory, not that which is an obligatory duty. This is because in the obligatory case, only one on behalf of one is sufficient, according to what we mentioned first; and that which indicates this interpretation is...

What al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Muḥammad ibn Sinān, from Ibn Muskān, from Muḥammad al-Ḥalabī, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about a group for whom one cow would suffice, He said: As for the hady, no; but as for the uḍḥiyah, yes. Another possible interpretation is that this was only allowed in a state of necessity and not in a state of choice; and there has already appeared, throughout these reports, that which indicates this and clarifies it further.

What Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb narrated from Abū ʿAlī al-Ashʿarī, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Jabbār, from Ṣafwān ibn Yaḥyā, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Ḥajjāj, who said: I asked Abā Ibrāhīm عليه السلام about a group for whom the sacrificial animals had become expensive, while they were performing tamattuʿ and traveling together. They were not the people of a single household, but rather a company who had gathered together on their journey and whose campsite was one. Could they slaughter a cow? He said: I do not approve of that except in necessity.

ʿAlī ibn Jaʿfar narrated from his brother Mūsā ibn Jaʿfar عليه السلام that he asked him about a man who buys a one-eyed sacrificial animal and does not come to know of its defect until after purchasing it: would it suffice for him?
