He said: Yes, unless it is an obligatory hady, for a deficient one does not suffice.

As for what al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Hammad ibn 'Isa, from 'Imran al-Halabi, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: Whoever buys a sacrificial animal and does not know that it has a defect until he has paid its price, then comes to know after paying the price, it suffices him. So this report admits two possibilities: one of them is that his hady is not obligatory, for that is permissible for him according to what was detailed in the first report. The second is that this may be a concession for one who has already paid the price and is unable to recover it; in that case, it is permissible for him to suffice with it.

As for what Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb narrated from ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Muʿāwiyah ibn ʿAmmār, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام: A man bought a sacrificial offering, and it had a defect, one-eyed or otherwise, so he said: If he has already paid its price, then it has sufficed for him. But if he has not paid its price, he should return it and buy another in its place. The proper way to understand this report is what we mentioned regarding the first report: that it is to be understood as applying to the obligatory sacrificial offering, not the voluntary one. It is also possible that it is to be understood as indicating a kind of recommendation rather than obligation.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Safwan ibn Yahya and Fadalah, from al-'Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from one of the two (Imams) عليهما السلام, who said: I asked him about the sacrificial animal that is garlanded or marked, then perishes. He said: If it was voluntary, then nothing else is due upon him; but if it was an expiation or a vow, then a replacement is due upon him.

From him, from Faḍālah, from Muʿāwiyah ibn ʿAmmār, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who had offered a sacrificial animal and it became injured. He said: If it was guaranteed, then a replacement is upon him; and what is guaranteed is that which was for a vow, or an expiation, or an oath. And he may eat from it. But if it was not guaranteed, then nothing is upon him. His statement عليه السلام, “And he may eat from it,” is understood to mean when it is voluntary and not when it is obligatory, because that which is obligatory is not permissible for him to eat from. That is indicated by what follows.

What al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from Muhammad ibn Abi Hamzah, from Mu'awiyah ibn 'Ammar, from Abi 'Abdillah عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about the sacrificial offering when it becomes disabled before it reaches the place of slaughter: does it suffice on behalf of its owner? He said: If it is voluntary, then let him slaughter it and eat from it, and it has sufficed for him whether it reached the place of slaughter or did not reach it, and there is no compensation upon him. But if it is guaranteed, then he may not eat from it, whether it reached the place of slaughter or did not reach it, and a replacement is due from him.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from 'Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Hammad, from Hariz, from one who informed him, from Abu 'Abdillah عليه السلام, who said: Whoever drives a sacrificial animal voluntarily and it becomes incapacitated, then nothing is due upon him. He should slaughter it, take the sandal of taqlid, dip it in the blood, and strike with it the side of its hump, and no replacement is due upon him. But whatever is from the compensation for hunting or a vow, and it becomes incapacitated, he should do the like of that, and a replacement is due upon him. And everything that, once it has entered the Haram, becomes incapacitated, then no replacement is due upon its owner, whether it was voluntary or otherwise. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: This report does not contradict what we have previously presented, namely that a replacement is due whether it reached its destination or did not reach it, because this is to be understood as referring to when it becomes incapacitated in a way short of death, such as a fracture, illness, or the like. In that case, as we have described, it suffices on behalf of its owner. This is indicated by that.

What Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn, from Hammad ibn 'Isa and Fadalah ibn Ayyub, from Mu'awiyah ibn 'Ammar, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who had designated a sacrificial offering while it was fat, then illness afflicted it and its eye burst or it became broken, yet it reached the place of sacrifice while still alive. He said: He should slaughter it, and it has sufficed for him. And it is possible that what is meant by this is one who is not able to provide a substitute, because one whose condition is such is excused; but as for when one has the ability, then a substitute is unavoidable. This is indicated by that.

What Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb narrated from Abū ʿAlī al-Ashʿarī, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Jabbār, from Ṣafwān, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Ḥajjāj, who said: I asked Abā Ibrāhīm عليه السلام about a man who bought a sacrificial animal for his mutʿah, then brought it to his منزل and tied it, but it got loose and perished. Does it suffice for him, or must he repeat it? He عليه السلام said: It does not suffice him, unless he had no power over it.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Ibn Muskan, from Abi Basir, who said: I asked Aba 'Abdillah عليه السلام about a man who bought a ram, then it was lost from him. He said: He should buy another in its place. I said: If he bought another in its place and then found the first? He said: If both of them are still present, then he should slaughter the first and sell the latter; and if he wishes, he may slaughter it. And if he had already slaughtered the latter, he should slaughter the first along with it. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: The slaughter of the first only becomes obligatory upon him, when he has slaughtered the latter, if he had already marked the first sacrificial animal. But if he had not marked it, then that is not binding upon him. What indicates this is as follows.

What Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, who said: I asked Aba Abdillah عليه السلام about a man who buys a camel for sacrifice, then it goes missing before he marks it or garlands it, and he cannot find it until he comes and slaughters [a replacement], and then finds his sacrificial animal. He عليه السلام said: If he had not marked it, then it remains part of his property: if he wishes, he may slaughter it, and if he wishes, he may sell it. But if he had marked it, he must slaughter it.

Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah, from Abu Ja'far, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id and Ya'qub ibn Yazid, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Hafs ibn al-Bakhtari, from Mansur ibn Hazim, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, concerning: A man whose sacrificial animal goes astray, then another man finds it and slaughters it—he عليه السلام said: If he slaughtered it in Mina, then it has sufficed on behalf of its owner from whom it had gone astray. But if he slaughtered it in a place other than Mina, it has not sufficed on behalf of its owner.

As for what Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb narrated from a number of our companions, from Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad, from ʿAlī ibn Ḥadīd, from Jamīl, from some of our companions, from one of the two of them, peace be upon them, concerning: A man bought a sacrificial animal and slaughtered it. Then another man passed by it and recognized it. He said: This is my badanah; it was lost from me yesterday. And two men testified to that for him. So he said: Its meat belongs to him, but it does not suffice on behalf of either of them. Then he said: For that reason, the sunnah has proceeded with marking it and garlanding it when it is identified. So this does not contradict the first report, because it only counted for its owner, in accordance with what the first report contained, when the one who found it slaughtered it on behalf of its owner. But the latter report includes one who slaughtered it on behalf of himself and claimed it for himself, so it did not suffice for the first one. He is only permitted the meat because of the two witnesses according to the outward legal ruling.

Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb, from ʿAlī, from his father, from Ismāʿīl ibn Marrār, from Yūnus, from Ibn Muskān, from Abī Baṣīr, who said: I asked him about a man who had offered a sacrificial animal and it became broken. He said: If it was guaranteed, and the guaranteed one is that which was due because of an oath—meaning a vow or an expiation—then its compensation is upon him. I said: May he eat from it? He said: No; it is only for the needy. But if it was not guaranteed, then nothing is upon him. I said: May he eat from it? He said: He may eat from it.

From him, from ʿAlī, from his father, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Ḥammād, from al-Ḥalabī, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about the compensation for hunted game: may he eat some of its meat? He said: He may eat from his sacrifice, and he gives the compensation in charity.

Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā, from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī, from al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿĀmir, from Abān ibn ʿUthmān, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī ʿAbd Allāh, from Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about the sacrificial offering: what may be eaten from it? He said: Every offering that is due to a deficiency in the hajj, then do not eat from it; and every offering that is part of the completion of the hajj, then eat.

As for what Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah narrated from Abu Ja'far, from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from 'Abd Allah ibn Yahya al-Kahili, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: One may eat from all of the hady, whether it is guaranteed or not guaranteed.

From him, from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn, from Jaʿfar ibn Bashīr, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about the camels that are due as compensation for oaths, women, and other than that: may one eat from them? He said: Yes, one may eat from all the sacrificial camels. So in these two reports there is no unrestricted permission for that in every circumstance. Since that is not present in them, we interpret them as applying to the state of necessity, and the owner is liable for the value of what he ate, which he gives in charity; that is indicated by what follows.

What Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā narrated from Bunān ibn Muḥammad, from his father, from Ibn al-Mughīrah, from al-Sakūnī, from Jaʿfar, from his father عليه السلام, who said: If a man eats from the sacrificial offering voluntarily given, then there is nothing upon him; but if it was obligatory, then the value of what he ate is upon him.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from al-Qasim, from 'Ali, from Abi Basir, who said: I asked Aba 'Abdillah عليه السلام about a man who places his hand on the body of his wife while he is fasting. So he said: There is no harm, and if madhy is emitted, it does not break the fast. He said: And His saying, “Do not have direct contact with them,” means intercourse during the daytime in the month of Ramadan.

From him, from al-Qāsim, from ʿAlī, from Abī Baṣīr, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about a man who spoke intimately with his wife in the month of Ramadan while he was fasting. He said: There is nothing upon him; and if madhy is emitted, then there is nothing upon him. And mubāsharah is not objectionable, and there is no making up of his day, but it is not appropriate for him to expose Ramadan to risk.

As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā narrated from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Ibn Abī Ḥamzah, from Rifāʿah ibn Mūsā, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about a man who touched a slave-girl in the month of Ramadan and emitted madhy. He said: If it was unlawful, then let him seek forgiveness from his Lord with the seeking forgiveness of one who never returns to it, and let him fast one day in place of one day. And if it was from what is lawful, then let him seek forgiveness from his Lord and not return, and let him fast one day in place of one day. So this is an anomalous report, contrary to the fatwa of our companions, and it is likely that it is an error from the narrator, or that it was issued in the mode of recommendation rather than obligation and requirement.

Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā, from Ibrāhīm al-Ḥadhdhāʾ, from Fuḍayl ibn ʿUthmān, from Abī al-Zubayr, from Jābir ibn ʿAbdillāh al-Anṣārī, who said: The Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم commanded us not to eat the meat of the sacrificial animals after three days; then he permitted us to eat, preserve it as dried meat, and send it as a gift to our families.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from Hanan ibn Sadir, from his father, from Abu Ja'far عليه السلام; and from Muhammad ibn al-Fudayl, from Abu al-Sabbah, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: The Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم forbade the meat of the sacrificial offerings after three days, then he permitted it. He said: Eat from the meat of the sacrificial offerings after three days and store it.

As for what Mūsā ibn al-Qāsim narrated from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from Muḥammad ibn Ḥumrān, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, from Abī Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said: Indeed, the Prophet صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم forbade that the meat of the sacrifices be kept for more than three days. This does not contradict the first report, because it is possible that Muḥammad ibn Muslim shared with Abū al-Ṣabbāḥ in hearing the report, and that the Prophet صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم forbade that, then later said: then he permitted after that its consumption. Muḥammad ibn Muslim forgot it, while Abū al-Ṣabbāḥ narrated it. And even if it were accepted as it stands, it would be permissible to interpret it as a type of recommendation, because what remains after three days is better to be given in charity.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Fadalah, from al-'Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from one of the two of them, peace be upon them, who said: I asked him about meat: may it be taken out of the Haram? He said: Nothing is taken out from it except the hump, after three days.
From him, from Faḍālah, from Muʿāwiyah ibn ʿAmmār, who said: Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام said: Do not take out anything from the meat of the hady.

And from him, from Hammad, from Ali ibn Abi Hamzah, from one of the two عليهما السلام, who said: The pilgrim should not take provisions from his sacrificial animal, but he may eat in Mina. He said: and this is the issue of Shihab; he wrote to him about it.

As for what Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb narrated from ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Jamīl ibn Darrāj, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, he said: I asked him about taking out the meat of the sacrificial animals from Minā, and he said: We used to say that nothing should be taken out, because of the people’s need for it. But as for today, the people have become numerous, so there is no harm in taking it out. Thus, it does not contradict the first two reports, because it does not state in it that it is permissible to take out the meat of the uḍḥiyyah from what a person himself sacrifices or from what he purchases. So when that is not present in its apparent meaning, we interpret it to mean that whoever purchases from the meat of the sacrificial animals, there is no harm in his taking it out. And that which indicates this is...

What al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from 'Ali, from Abi Ibrahim عليه السلام, who said: I heard him saying: The pilgrim should not take provisions from his sacrificial animal, though he may eat from it during its days, except for the hump, for indeed it is a remedy. Ahmad said: And he said: There is no harm in the pilgrim purchasing some of the meat of Mina and taking it as provisions.

Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Mu'awiyah ibn 'Ammar, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: The Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم slaughtered on behalf of the Mothers of the Believers one cow each, and he himself sacrificed sixty-six camels, and 'Ali عليه السلام sacrificed thirty-four camels. He did not give the butchers anything from their coverings, nor from their garlands, nor from their hides; rather, he gave it in charity.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Hammad and Fadalah, from Mu'awiyah ibn 'Ammar, who said: I asked Aba 'Abdillah عليه السلام about the hide. He said: Give it in charity, or make it into a musalla to be used in the house, and do not give it to the butchers. And he said: The Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم forbade that its coverings, its hides, and its collars be given to the butchers, and he commanded that they be given in charity.

As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Ṣafwān, and Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad from Ḥammād, both together from Isḥāq ibn ʿAmmār, from Abū Ibrāhīm عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about the sacrificial offering: may anything from it be taken out of the Haram? He said: The hide, the hump, and a thing from which benefit is taken. I said: It has reached us from your father that he said: Nothing is to be taken out from the guaranteed sacrificial offering. He said: Yes, a thing from which benefit is taken may be taken out. And Aḥmad added in it: And none of its meat is to be taken out from the Haram. So this does not conflict with the reports we mentioned earlier, because the report does not contain unrestricted permission for that in every circumstance. And it is possible that he only permitted it for one who gives its price in charity; that is indicated by this.

What Mūsā ibn al-Qāsim narrated from ʿAlī ibn Jaʿfar, from his brother Mūsā ibn Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about the skins of the sacrificial animals: is it permissible for the one who offered them as sacrifice to make them into a sack? He said: It is not permissible for him to make them into a sack unless he gives its price in charity.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd and Safwan, from Ibn Sinan; and Hammad, from Ibn al-Mughirah, from Ibn Sinan, from Abi 'Abdillah عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who performed tamattu' and did not find a sacrificial offering. He said: then let him fast three days, excluding the Days of Tashriq from them; rather, he should remain in Makkah until he fasts them, and seven when he returns to his family. And he mentioned the hadith of Budayl ibn Warqa'.

From him, from al-Naḍr ibn Suwayd, from Hisham ibn Salim, from Sulayman ibn Khalid and ʿAli ibn al-Nuʿman, from Ibn Muskan, who said: I asked Abu ʿAbd Allah عليه السلام about a man who performed tamattuʿ and did not find a sacrificial offering. He said: He should fast three days. I said to him: Are the Days of Tashriq included among them? He said: No, but he should remain in Mecca until he fasts them, and seven when he returns to his family. If his companions do not remain for him and he is unable to stay in Mecca, then let him fast ten days when he returns to his family. And he mentioned the hadith of Budayl ibn Warqaʾ.

From him, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Abu al-Hasan عليه السلام, who said: I said to him: Ibn al-Sarraj mentioned that he wrote to you asking you about a mutamatti' who did not have a sacrificial offering, and you replied to him in your letter: He should fast on the days of Mina; and if that escapes him, he should fast on the morning of al-Hasbah and two days after that. He said: As for the days of Mina, they are days of eating and drinking; there is no fasting in them, and seven days when he returns to his family.

As for what Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn, from al-Ḥasan ibn Mūsā al-Khashshāb, from Ghiyāth ibn Kallūb, from Isḥāq ibn ʿAmmār, from Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, that ʿAlī عليه السلام used to say: Whoever misses the fasting of the three days that are during hajj, then let him fast them during the Days of Tashrīq, for that is permissible for him.

And among what was narrated by Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā, from Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Maymūn al-Qaddāḥ, from Jaʿfar, from his father, that ʿAlī عليه السلام used to say: Whoever misses fasting the three days during hajj—and they are the day before al-Tarwiyah, the Day of al-Tarwiyah, and the Day of ʿArafah—then let him fast during the Days of al-Tashrīq, for permission has been granted to him. These two reports have come as anomalous, opposing the rest of the reports, and it is not permissible to adopt them and abandon the many hadiths except by a proof that removes excuse. It is possible that the two men were mistaken in attributing that to Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, and that they heard it from someone else who ascribed himself to the Ahl al-Bayt عليهم السلام, because it has been narrated that this was something ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥasan used to say, so they attributed it to him by mistake. Moreover, even if these two reports opposed the many earlier reports and those reports did not possess the advantage of greater number over them, it would still be necessary to set all of them aside and turn to what Abū al-Ḥasan Mūsā عليه السلام narrated, because his narration has a manifest advantage over the narration of others due to his 'ismah, purity, integrity, and freedom from error.

Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from Abu al-Husayn al-Nakha'i, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, who said: I was standing performing salat (prayer), while Abu al-Hasan Musa عليه السلام was sitting before me and I did not know. Then 'Abbad al-Basri came to him, greeted him, and sat down. He said to him: O Abu al-Hasan, what do you say about a man who performed tamattu' and had no sacrificial offering? He said: He fasts the days that Allah, Exalted is He, has stated. He said: So I turned my hearing toward them. 'Abbad said to him: Which days are they? He said: They are one day before al-Tarwiyah, the Day of al-Tarwiyah, and the Day of 'Arafah. He said: If he misses that, then what? He said: He fasts the morning of al-Hasbah and two days after that. He said: Will you not say as 'Abd Allah ibn al-Hasan said? He said: And what did he say? He said: He fasts the days of al-Tashriq. He said: Ja'far used to say: The Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم ordered Bilal to proclaim: These are days of eating and drinking, so no one should fast. He said: O Abu al-Hasan, indeed Allah, Exalted is He, said: “then a fast of three days during the hajj (pilgrimage) and seven when you return.” He said: Ja'far used to say: The whole of Dhu al-Hijjah is among the months of hajj (pilgrimage).

As for what Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb narrated from ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Ḥafṣ ibn al-Bakhtarī, from Manṣūr ibn Ḥāzim, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: Whoever did not fast in Dhū al-Ḥijjah until the crescent of al-Muḥarram is sighted, then a sheep-sacrifice is due upon him, and there is no fasting for him, and he should slaughter at Minā.

And among what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Ḥammād ibn ʿĪsā, from ʿImrān al-Ḥalabī, who said: Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام was asked about a man who forgot to fast the three days that were incumbent upon the mutamattiʿ when he did not find the sacrificial offering, until he returned to his family. He said: He should send a blood-offering. So there is no contradiction between these two reports and the report that we presented earlier from Ibn Miskān, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, that he said: If his companions did not remain with him and he was not able to fast on the road, he should fast ten days when he returns to his family. That is because this is to be understood as referring to one who returned to his family before the end of Dhū al-Ḥijjah, in which case fasting the ten days was permissible for him. But when Dhū al-Ḥijjah has ended, then nothing is permissible for him except the blood-offering, in accordance with what the two reports indicate.

Musa ibn al-Qasim, from Muhammad, from Ahmad, from Mufaḍḍal ibn Ṣaliḥ, from ʿAbd al-Raḥman ibn al-Ḥajjaj, from Abu ʿAbdillah عليه السلام, concerning: Whoever fasts on the Day of al-Tarwiyah and the Day of ʿArafah—he عليه السلام said: it suffices him to fast one other day.

From him, from al-Nakhaʿī, from Ṣafwān, from Yaḥyā al-Azraq, from Abī al-Ḥasan عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who arrived on the Day of al-Tarwiyah performing tamattuʿ, and he did not have a sacrificial offering, so he fasted on the Day of al-Tarwiyah and the Day of ʿArafah. He said: He should fast one more day after the Days of al-Tashrīq.

As for what was narrated by Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā, from ʿImrān ibn Mūsā, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd, from ʿAlī ibn al-Faḍl al-Wāsiṭī, who said: I heard him saying: If the mutamattiʿ fasts two days and does not follow them with the fasting of the third day, then the fasting of three days during the hajj has escaped him. So let him fast in Makkah three consecutive days; and if he is not able, and the camel-driver does not remain for him, then let him fast them on the roads; or when he arrives to his family, he should fast ten consecutive days. So this is not contrary to what we have mentioned, because it is not stated in the report which two days he fasted. Since that is not explicit in its outward wording, we interpret it as referring to one who did not fast on the Day of Tarwiyah and the Day of ʿArafah, but fasted two days after the Days of Tashrīq and did not add to them the third day; that is not permissible for him, because after the completion of the Days of Tashrīq, nothing is permissible except the fasting of three consecutive days. This is indicated by that.

What Mūsā ibn al-Qāsim narrated from Muḥammad ibn ʿUmar ibn Yazīd, from Muḥammad ibn ʿUdhāfir, from Isḥāq ibn ʿAmmār, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: He must not fast the three days separately.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Safwan and Fadalah, from Rifa'ah ibn Musa, who said: I asked Aba 'Abd Allah عليه السلام about one performing tamattu' who cannot find a sacrificial offering. He said: He fasts one day before al-Tarwiyah, the day of al-Tarwiyah, and the day of 'Arafah. I said: What if he arrived on the day of al-Tarwiyah and then went out to 'Arafat? He said: He fasts three days after the day of al-nafr, one day after al-Tarwiyah and the day of al-nafr. I said: What if his camel-driver does not stay for him? He said: He fasts on the day of al-Hasbah and two days after it. I said: Does he fast while he is traveling? He said: Yes. Is he not traveling on the day of 'Arafah? For Allah, Exalted is He, says: “three days during the hajj.” He said: I said: May Allah عزّ وجلّ honor you, Allah, Exalted is He, says: in Dhu al-Hijjah? Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام said: And we, the Ahl al-Bayt, say: in Dhu al-Hijjah.

From him, from Hammad ibn 'Isa, who said: I heard Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام say: 'Ali عليه السلام said: The fasting of three days during hajj is one day before al-Tarwiyah, the Day of al-Tarwiyah, and the Day of 'Arafah. So whoever misses that should take the pre-dawn meal on the night of al-Hasbah — meaning the night of al-Nafr — and begin the morning fasting, and [fast] two days after it, and seven when he returns.

As for what Mūsā ibn al-Qāsim narrated from al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Mukhtār, from Ṣafwān ibn Yaḥyā, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Ḥajjāj, from Abī al-Ḥasan عليه السلام, he said: ʿAbbād al-Baṣrī asked him about one performing tamattuʿ hajj who did not have a sacrificial offering with him. He said: He fasts three days before the Day of al-Tarwiyah. He said: If the fasting of these days escapes him? He said: He must not fast on the Day of al-Tarwiyah nor on the Day of ʿArafah, but rather he fasts three consecutive days after the Days of al-Tashrīq. So this does not conflict with what we presented earlier: that whoever fasts the Day of al-Tarwiyah and the Day of ʿArafah may add to them another day, because he only forbade fasting the Day of al-Tarwiyah and the Day of ʿArafah separately, and he did not forbid fasting them by way of combination, such that the addition of the third day to them is valid, as we have already presented.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Muhammad ibn Aslam, from Ishaq ibn Ammar, who said: I said to Abu al-Hasan Musa عليه السلام: I came to Kufah and had not fasted the seven days, until I departed on a need to Baghdad. He said: Fast them in Baghdad. I said: May I separate them? He said: Yes.

As for what was narrated by Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad al-'Alawi, from al-'Umarki al-Khurasani, from 'Ali ibn Ja'far, from his brother Musa ibn Ja'far عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about fasting three days during hajj and the seven: should he fast them consecutively, or separate them? He said: He fasts the three days without separating between them, and the seven without separating between them, and he does not combine the seven and the three all together. So this does not contradict the first narration, because his statement عليه السلام, 'he does not separate between the three,' is what is acted upon, since we have already stated that they are to be fasted consecutively. And his statement, 'and the seven, he does not separate between them,' is upon the basis of recommendation and desirability. And his statement, 'and he does not combine the three and the seven all together,' the explanation of it is that fasting the three days is required in hajj, and seven when he returns to his family, so how could he combine them both? But as for the one who missed the three days in hajj until he returned to his family, it is permissible for him to combine them with the seven, as we have already mentioned.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Hammad ibn 'Isa, from Mu'awiyah ibn 'Ammar, who said: A righteous servant, peace be upon him, narrated to me. And I asked him about one performing tamattu' who does not have a sacrificial offering, and the fasting has passed him by until he departs, and he has no stay. He said: He may fast three days on the road if he wishes, and if he wishes he may fast ten among his family.

Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah, from al-Husayn, from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from Hisham ibn Salim, from Sulayman ibn Khalid; and ʿAli ibn al-Nuʿman, from ʿAbd Allah ibn Muskan, from Sulayman ibn Khalid, who said: I asked Aba ʿAbd Allah عليه السلام about a man who performed tamattuʿ and did not find a sacrificial offering. He said: He should fast three days in Makkah and seven when he returns to his family. If his companions do not wait for him and he is unable to remain in Makkah, then let him fast ten days when he returns to his family. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: These two reports do not contradict the report of Rifaʿah that we cited in the first chapter, in his statement, ‘He fasts while he is traveling,’ because he did not make fasting during travel obligatory and nothing beyond that. Rather, he intended to clarify the permissibility of fasting these days during travel, in response to those who disallowed it and did not permit fasting them during travel. That which further clarifies what we have mentioned is that he intended choice in that matter.

What Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn, from Fadalah ibn Ayyub, from Mu'awiyah ibn 'Ammar, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: The Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم said: Whoever is performing tamattu' and cannot find a sacrificial offering, then he must fast three days during the hajj and seven when he returns to his family. If he misses that, and he remains after the departure, he should fast three days in Makkah; and if he does not remain, he should fast on the road or among his family. And if he remains in Makkah and wishes to fast the seven, he should leave off fasting for the length of his travel to his family, or for a month, then fast after that.

As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Faḍālah ibn Ayyūb, from al-ʿAlāʾ, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, from one of the two of them, peace be upon them, who said: The fasting is the three days; if he fasts them, then the last of them is the Day of ʿArafah. And if he is not able to do that, then let him defer them until he fasts them among his family, and he should not fast them during travel. The correct manner of understanding this report is that it is not permissible for him to fast them during travel while believing that no option other than that is allowed for him; rather, he should believe that he is given the choice between fasting them during travel and fasting them when he returns to his family.

As for what al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Hammad ibn 'Isa, from 'Imran al-Halabi, who said: Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام was asked about a man who forgot to fast the three days that are due upon the mutamatti' when he does not find the sacrificial offering, until he returned to his family. He said: He should send a sacrificial blood-offering. The proper way to understand this report is what we have already mentioned in the previous chapter: that he sends a blood-offering if Dhu al-Hijjah has passed and he did not fast. It is only permissible for him to fast the three days so long as he remains within Dhu al-Hijjah.

Sa'd ibn Abdillah, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Nu'man and Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Abdillah ibn Muskhan, who said: Aban al-Azraq narrated to me, from Zurarah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), that he said: Whoever does not have the offering (hady) and wishes to fast the three days at the beginning of the ten [days of Dhul-Hijjah], there is no harm in that. This does not contradict the reports we have previously mentioned stating that the last of these three days is the Day of Arafah, because those reports are understood as referring to the preferred/virtuous act (fadl), while this report is understood as referring to the concession (rukhsah) for one who fears being unable to perform the offering. There is no contradiction between them on this basis.

Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from Ali (peace be upon him) who said: He should not shave his head nor visit (the shrine) until he offers the sacrifice, then he shall shave his head and visit whenever he wishes.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Wahb ibn Hafsh, from Abu Basir, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: When you buy your sacrificial animal (Udhiyah) and wrap it, and it is placed beside your saddle, the Hady (sacrificial animal for Hajj) has reached its designated place; so if you wish to shave [your head], then shave.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from a number of our companions from Sahl ibn Ziyad from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr who said: I said to Abu Ja'far (the second Imam), peace be upon him: 'I am your ransom, indeed a man from our companions threw the Jamarah on the day of Nahr (sacrifice) and shaved [his head] before he slaughtered [the animal].' He said: 'Indeed, the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) was visited on the day of Nahr by groups of Muslims who said: O Messenger of Allah, we slaughtered before we threw [the Jamarah] and we shaved before we slaughtered, so nothing that ought to be done first was left except that it was delayed, and nothing that ought to be done last was left except that it was done first.' The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'No harm, no harm.' Therefore, the interpretation of this report is that we should understand it as applying to one who did that out of forgetfulness or unintentionally, and indeed doing that is not permissible on the path of deliberate intent.

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Jamil ibn Darraj, said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the man who visits the House (Kaaba) before shaving [his head], he said: It is not appropriate unless he is forgetful. Then he said: Indeed, the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) came to him some people on the Day of Sacrifice, and some of them said: O Messenger of Allah, I shaved before I sacrificed, and some of them said: I shaved before I threw [the pebbles]. They did not leave anything that it was appropriate for them to delay except that they hastened it, so he said: There is no blame.

Musa ibn al-Qasim from Abd al-Rahman from Abd Allah ibn Sinan said: I asked him about a man who shaved his head before sacrificing (his animal). He said: There is no harm, and there is nothing upon him, and he should not do it again.

Musa ibn al-Qasim from Ibn Abi 'Umayr from Hammad from al-Halabi said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who forgot to shorten his hair or shave it until he departed from Mina. He said: He returns to Mina until he discards his hair there, whether it was by shaving or shortening.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Ali ibn Abi Hamzah, from Abu Basir, who said: I asked him about a man who did not know whether to trim or shave his head, so he departed from Mina. He said: Let him return to Mina so that he may shave his hair there or trim it, and upon the forehead is the shaving of the head.

Musa ibn al-Qasim from Ali ibn Ri'ab from Mis'mam said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who forgot to shave his head or shorten [his hair] until he departed [from Mina]. He said: He should shave [or shorten] on the road or wherever he is, and this does not contradict the first two reports, because this narration is applied to one who is unable to return to Mina. As for one who is able to return, it is necessary to do so according to what we have previously mentioned. And with that, if he is unable to return, he should bring his hair back to Mina and bury it there, which indicates that.

Muhammad ibn al-Qasim, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon him) used to bury his hair in his tent in Mina, and he said: 'They used to prefer that.' He (Abu Abdillah) said: 'So Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) disliked that the hair be taken out of Mina, and he said: Whoever takes it out must return it.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hafs ibn al-Bakhtari, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding a man who shaves his head in Mecca, he said: He should return the hair to Mina.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Ibn Faddal from Al-Mufaddal ibn Salih from Abu Basir from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding a man who visited the House (Kaaba) and did not shave his head, he said: He should shave it in Mecca and carry his hair to Mina, and there is no penalty upon him.

Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from Hasan ibn al-Husayn al-Lu'lu'i from Ali ibn Ri'ab from Abu Basir who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who forgets to shave his head until he departs from Mina. He said: 'I do not like that he casts off his hair except in Mina, and he has not placed anything upon it.' The meaning in this report is that whoever does not do so is not obliged to pay expiation, except that he has left the preferable act.

Musa ibn al-Qasim from Muhammad ibn Saif from Mansur ibn Hazim said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who threw [the pebbles] and shaved [his head]: does he eat anything that has a yellowish tint? He said: No, until he performs Tawaf around the House and Sa'i between Safa and Marwah. Then all things become permissible for him except women, until he performs another Tawaf around the House. Then women become permissible for him.

From him, from Abd al-Rahman, from 'Ullah, who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): I performed Tamattu', slaughtered [the sacrificial animal], and shaved [my head]. Should I apply henna to my head? He said: Yes, provided you do not touch anything of the perfume. I said: Should I wear the shirt? He said: Yes, if you wish. I said: Should I cover my head? He said: Yes.

From him, from Muhammad ibn 'Umar, from Muhammad ibn 'Uthayfir, from 'Umar ibn Yazid, from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Know that when you shave your head, everything becomes permissible for you except women and perfume.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Abu Ali al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn al-Jabbar, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Sa'id ibn Yasar, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the Mutamatti' (one who performs Hajj al-Tamattu'), and he said: When he shaves his head, he anoints it with henna, and garments, perfume, and everything become permissible for him except women. I repeated this to him two or three times. He said: And I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about it, and he said: Yes. Henna, garments, perfume, and everything become permissible for him except women. This does not contradict what we mentioned, because in the apparent meaning of the report, it is not stated that when he shaves his head these things become permissible for him even if he has not performed Tawaf. Rather, it is possible that he meant the one who shaved and performed the Tawaf of Hajj and Sa'i, in which case these things have become permissible for him even if not mentioned in the wording, due to his knowledge that the addressee is aware of that, or relying on other reports. And we have previously presented reports that indicate this, so acting upon them is more appropriate, because they are detailed, whereas this report is general.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Abu Ali al-Ash'ari from Muhammad ibn al-Jabbar from Safwan from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj who said: A child was born to Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) in Mina, so he sent to us on the Day of Sacrifice (Nahr) khabis (a type of bread) with saffron, and we had already shaved [our heads]. Abd al-Rahman said: 'I ate, and Abu al-Kahili and Murazm said they would eat from it, and they said: We have not yet visited the House (performed Tawaf). Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) heard our speech and said to Musaffa, who was the messenger who brought it to us: 'In what matter were they speaking?' He said: 'Abd al-Rahman ate, and the other two said they had not yet visited [the House].' He said: 'Abd al-Rahman was correct.' Then he said: 'Do you not remember when it was brought to us on a day like this, and I ate from it, and my brother Abu Abdillah said he would eat from it? When my father came, he urged him upon me, and I said: O father, indeed Musa ate khabis with saffron and had not yet visited [the House].' My father said: 'He is more learned than you. Have you not shaved your heads?'

And Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Fadalah from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Ibn 'Abbas was asked: 'Did the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) use perfume before visiting the House?' He said: 'I saw the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) bandaging his head with musk before visiting.' Therefore, in these two reports, it is not established that he permitted the use of perfume upon completion of shaving the head and before the visitation for the Mutamatti' or for the Hajj pilgrim who is not Mutamatti'. And if that is not explicit in their apparent meaning, we interpret them regarding the non-Mutamatti', because it is permissible for him to use everything upon shaving his head except women (i.e., excluding the prohibition of women), and the use of perfume is not permissible at that time for the Mutamatti' alone, and that which indicates this distinction...

Musa ibn al-Qasim from Abd al-Rahman from Muhammad ibn Humran said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the pilgrim who is not performing Tamattu' on the Day of Sacrifice: what is permissible for him? He said: Everything except women. And about the one performing Tamattu': what is permissible for him on the Day of Sacrifice? He said: Everything except women and perfume.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) that he asked him about a man who uses enema, where the illness is in the month of Ramadan. He said: The fasting person is not permitted for him to use enema.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ali ibn al-Hasan from his father who said: I wrote to Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him): What do you say regarding lubrication that a person inserts while he is fasting? He wrote: There is no harm with the solid (form), so it does not contradict the first report, because the first report only permitted the use of the solid from it, and the first report addressed the liquid that reaches the cavity (stomach), and there is no contradiction between them in any state.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Safwan and Fadala from al-Ala' said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'I shaved my head and sacrificed [the animal] while I was in the state of Tamattu', and I anointed my head with henna.' He said: 'Yes, provided you do not touch anything of perfume.' I said: 'And I wear the qamis [seamless garment] and cover my head [with the edge of the ihram]?' He said: 'Yes.' I said: 'Before I perform Tawaf around the House?' He said: 'Yes.'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Hammad ibn Isa from Hariz from Muhammad ibn Muslim said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who performed Umrat al-Tamattu', then stood at Arafat and stood at Al-Mash'ar, and threw the Jamarat, and sacrificed, and shaved [his head]. Should he cover his head? He said: No, until he performs Tawaf with the House and with As-Safa and Al-Marwah. It was said to him: If he did [shave before Tawaf], he said: I do not see any blame upon him.

And from him, from Safwan, from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, from Idris al-Qummi, who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'My slave performed Tamattu' (pilgrims who perform Umrah then Hajj). When he shaved his head, he put on his clothes before visiting the Kaaba. He said: 'What a bad thing he did.' I said: 'Is there anything wrong with him?' He said: 'No.' I said: 'For I saw Ibn Abi Sammak running between Safa and Marwah, wearing two socks, a qaba' (tunic), and a belt.' He said: 'What a bad thing he did.' I said: 'Is there anything wrong with him?' He said: 'No.' The way to reconcile these two narrations is to carry them upon being recommended (mustahabb) rather than obligatory (fard/wajib). That which indicates this is what he narrated.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Safwan from Mansur ibn Hazim from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) that he said: Regarding a man who was performing Tamattu' Hajj, so he stood at Arafat and Al-Mash'ar, sacrificed his animal, and shaved his head. He said: 'He should not cover his head until he performs Tawaf with the House and Sa'i between As-Safa and Al-Marwah.' For indeed my father (Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq) disliked that and forbade it. We said to him: 'If he did [cover his head before completing these acts]?' He said: 'I do not see any blame upon him.' And if he did not [cover his head], that was more beloved to me.

Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from Abd al-Rahman from Ulā' from Muhammad ibn Muslim from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about the Mutamatti' (pilgrim who performs Umrah then Hajj), when does he perform the visitation? He said: On the Day of Sacrifice.

From him, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Mansur ibn Hazim, who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: The Mutamatti' (pilgrim who performs Hajj al-Tamattu') does not spend the night in Mina on the Day of Sacrifice until he has visited the House.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Hammad ibn Isa from 'Imran al-Halabi from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: It is appropriate for the Mutamatti' (pilgrim performing Hajj al-Tamattu') to visit the House (Kaaba) on the Day of Sacrifice and from its night, and not to delay that day.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Safwan ibn Yahya from Isḥaq ibn 'Ammar said: I asked Abu Ibrahim (peace be upon him) about the visitation of the House (Kaaba) being delayed until the third day. He said: 'Hastening it is more beloved to me, and there is no harm in it if one delays it.'

From him, from Safwan, from Abdillah ibn Sinan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: There is no harm in delaying the visitation of the House until the Day of Nafr; only the hastening of that is recommended, out of fear of incidents and obstructions.

From him, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a man who forgot to visit the House (Kaaba) until morning [of Eid]. He said: Perhaps he delayed it until the days of Tashreeq pass, but he should not approach women or use perfume. The correct interpretation of these narrations is to apply them to one who is not a Mutamatti' (pilgrim performing Tamattu' Hajj), for he is given leeway to delay that [visiting the Kaaba] after the Day of Nahr (10th Dhu al-Hijjah) and the next day.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Hammad ibn 'Isa and Fadala from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: I asked him about the Mutamatti' (one who performs Hajj al-Tamattu'), when does he visit the House? He said: On the Day of Sacrifice or the next day, and he should not delay it. The Mufrid and the Qarin are not the same; they are given more leeway, in that it is only disliked for the Mutamatti' to delay that (visiting the House) for more than two days, although that delay does not invalidate the Hajj, which indicates that.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr and Safwan, from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), in the chapter of Visiting the House on the Day of Sacrifice, said: Visit it (the Kaaba), and if you are occupied, it will not harm you to visit the House the next day. Do not delay visiting from your day, for it is disliked for the Mutamatti' (one performing Hajj with combination of Umrah and Hajj) to delay it, and it is permissible for the Mufrid (one performing single Hajj) to delay it.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Safwan, he said: Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) said: Some people asked me about a man who spent a night from the nights of Mina in Mecca, so I said: I do not know. Then I said to him: May I be your ransom, what do you say about it? He said: There is a blood-guilt (dam) on him if he spent the night. I said: If his staying was due to the matter he was engaged in from his tawaf and sa'i, and it was not for sleep or pleasure, is there upon him the same as upon this one? He said: This is not in the same position as that one, and I do not like for the dawn to break for him except while he is in Mina.

From him, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Ibn Muskān, from Ja'far ibn Nājīyah, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about one who spent the nights of Mina in Mecca, and he said: 'Three from the livestock, he slaughters them.'

And Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from Ali ibn Ja'far, from his brother Musa ibn Ja'far (peace be upon him), from a man who spent the night in Mecca during the nights of Mina until morning. He said: If he came to it during the day and spent the night in it until morning, then upon him is a dam (blood of sacrifice) that he must shed.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Safwan from al-'Is ibn al-Qasim said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who missed a night from the nights of Mina. He said: There is no penalty upon him, but he has done poorly.

And Sa'd ibn Abdillah narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from Muhammad ibn 'Isa from Safwan from Sa'id ibn Yasar, who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'The night of staying in Mina was missed by me due to busyness.' He said: 'There is no harm.' The explanation in these two narrations is one of two things: one is that he stayed in Mecca in supplication and performing rituals until the dawn rose, so nothing is required of him, and the state is as we described, and we have clarified that previously, and this adds to its clarification.

Sa'd ibn Abd Allah narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn, from Hammad ibn Isa and Fadala and Safwan, from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who visited the House (Kaaba) and did not cease from his tawaf, supplication, and sa'i and supplication until the dawn broke. He said: 'There is no penalty upon him, for he was in obedience to Allah, Exalted and Glorious.' The other view is that he may have left Mina after midnight, for whenever he leaves after midnight for the visitation, no penalty is obligatory upon him, although it is preferable that he does not leave until morning, which indicates that.

Sa'd ibn Abd Allah, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from al-Nadr ibn Shu'ayb, from Abd al-Ghaffar al-Harithi, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who left Mina intending to go to the House (Kaaba) before the middle of the night, and thus spent the dawn in Mecca. He said: 'It is not valid for him until he gives it as charity (sadaqah) or sheds blood (dams). But if he left Mina after the middle of the night, nothing will harm him.'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Safwan and Fadala from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Do not spend the nights of Tashriq anywhere except in Mina. If you spend the night elsewhere, then a dam (blood sacrifice) is upon you. If you leave at the beginning of the night, you must not be absent from Mina when the night is half gone, unless a ritual duty (nusk) occupies you or you have already left Mecca. And if you leave after the middle of the night, it does not harm you if you spend the morning elsewhere.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Hammad ibn 'Isa, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from 'Ali, from Abu Ibrahim (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a man who performed Ziyarah to the House, circled the House, and [circled] between al-Safa and al-Marwah, then returned. His eyelids overpowered him during the circling, so he slept until morning. He said: 'A sheep is due from him.' This does not contradict what the first report contained from his statement, except if he had left Mecca, because that report is applicable to one who left Mecca and passed the pass of the Madaniyyun. Indeed, it is permissible for him to sleep, and the state as we described it indicates that.

Sa'd ibn Abdillah, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) who said: Regarding a man who performs ziyarah and sleeps before Mina, he said: When he has passed the pass of al-Madaineen, there is no harm in him sleeping.

From him, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Jamil ibn Darraj, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Whoever performs Ziyarah and sleeps on the road, if he spends the night in Mecca, he owes a blood-offering (dam); and if he has already left it, there is no penalty upon him; and if he arrives before Mina, [penalty applies]. And that which indicates that the preferable course is not to leave [Mecca] except after dawn, is according to what we have mentioned.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Fudayl from Abu al-Subah al-Kinani who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the night journey to Mecca during the days of Mina, while I intended to visit the House. He said: No, until the dawn breaks, out of dislike that the man should spend the night without being in Mina.

Al-Husayn ibn Said narrated from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr from Jamil ibn Darraj from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: There is no harm if a man comes to Mecca and performs Tawaf during the days of Mina and does not stay overnight there.
And from him, from Fadala, from Rifa'ah, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about visiting the House (Kaaba) during the days of Tashriq, and he said: 'It is good (hasan).'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Abu Ali al-Ash'ari from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar from Safwan from Isa ibn al-Qasim said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the visitation (of the Prophet's shrine) after the pilgrimage in the days of Tashriq, and he said: 'No.' He added: 'It does not contradict the first report, because the meaning in this report is that we should understand it as indicating preference and recommendation, rather than prohibition.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Faddal, from al-Mufaddal ibn Salih, from Layth al-Muradi, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who comes to Mecca during the days of Mina after finishing his visit to the House, and performs tawaf around the House as a voluntary act. He said: Staying in Mina is better and more beloved to me.
Musa ibn al-Qasim from Abd al-Rahman from Safwan ibn Mihran said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: 'Throwing [the Jamarat] is from the rising of the sun until its setting.'

From him, from Muhammad, from Saif, from Mansur ibn Hazim, who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: Casting the stones (at the Jamarat) is [permitted] from the rising of the sun until its setting.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Throw [the pebbles] each day at the decline of the sun, and say [the supplication], and he mentioned the supplication. Therefore, the meaning in this report is that we should interpret it as recommended virtue and preference, rather than obligatory duty and compulsion.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Fudaylah ibn Ayyub, from Mu'awiyah ibn 'Ammar, who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) say: Regarding a woman who was unaware that she had not thrown the Jamarat until she returned to Mecca, he said: She should return and throw the Jamarat as she had been throwing them, and the man is the same.

Musa ibn al-Qasim from al-Nakha'i from Ibn Abi 'Umayr from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'A man forgot throwing the Jamarat.' He said, 'He returns and throws them.' I said, 'If he forgot them until he arrived in Mecca?' He said, 'He returns and throws them separately, and separates between each two throws by an hour.' I said, 'If he forgot or was unaware until it passed and he left?' He said, 'There is no obligation upon him to repeat it.' Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: His saying 'There is no obligation upon him to repeat it' means he is not obligated to repeat it in this year, although repeating it may be obligatory upon him in the coming year, either by himself if able, or by ordering someone to act on his behalf. And this is because the days of throwing are the days of Tashriq; so if they pass him, nothing is obligatory upon him except in the coming year during similar days.

Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from Muhammad ibn 'Umar ibn Yazid from Muhammad ibn 'Udhafir from 'Umar ibn Yazid from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Whoever neglects throwing the Jamarat or part of it until the days of Tashreeq have passed, he must throw them the following year. If he does not perform Hajj, his guardian should throw on his behalf. If he has no guardian, he should seek assistance from a Muslim man to throw on his behalf, for the throwing of the Jamarat occurs only during the days of Tashreeq. And it has been narrated that whoever deliberately leaves throwing the Jamarat, women are not permissible to him, and he must perform Hajj the following year. He narrated that.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Ya'qub ibn Yazid, from Yahya ibn al-Mubarik, from Abd Allah ibn Jabala, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Indeed, whoever deliberately leaves throwing the Jamarat, women are not permissible to him, and he must perform Hajj again next year. Therefore, this report is interpreted as indicating preference (istihbab), because we have clarified in our Great Book that throwing is a sunnah and not obligatory (fard). And if it is not obligatory, nor is it one of the pillars of Hajj, then re-performing Hajj is not required due to leaving it.

Sa'd ibn Abdillah, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, that he saw Abu Ja'far (the second) (peace be upon him) throwing the stones while riding. Sa'd ibn Abdillah, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, that he saw Abu Ja'far (the second) (peace be upon him) throwing the stones while riding.

From him, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from some of our companions, from one of them, regarding the casting of the pebbles (at the Jamarat). That the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) cast the pebbles while riding his mount.

From him, from Abu Ja'far, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Najran, that he saw Abu al-Hasan al-Thani (peace be upon him) throwing the Jamarat while he was riding, until he threw all of them. He saw Abu al-Hasan al-Thani (peace be upon him) throwing the Jamarat while he was riding, until he threw all of them.

From him, from Abu Ja'far, from al-Abbas, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Najran, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who threw the pebbles (at the Jamarat) while he was riding, and he said: There is no objection (it is permissible).

Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from Ali ibn Ja'far, from his brother, from his father, from his forefathers (peace be upon them), who said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) used to throw the pebbles at the Jamarat while walking.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd from 'Asim from 'Anbasah ibn Mus'abb said: I saw Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) in Mina walking and riding. I told myself that I would ask him when I enter upon him, but he initiated the narration and said: Indeed, Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon him) used to leave his house on foot when he threw the Jamarat (stones at the pillars in Hajj). And my house today is further from his than his house was from his [previous location], so I ride until I reach him. When I arrive at him, I walk until I throw the Jamarat. The way to reconcile these two narrations is to interpret them as indicating a type of recommended status (mustahabb) rather than obligatory (fard) or compulsory (ijbar).

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Hammad from Hariz from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the saying of Allah, Exalted and Mighty: 'Remember Allah during known days.' He said: The Takbir (saying Allahu Akbar) during the Days of Tashriq from the Dhuhr prayer, and whoever stays in Mina and prays Dhuhr and Asr there, let him recite the Takbir.

Hammad narrated from Hariz from Zurara who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'Is the Takbir during the Days of Tashriq after the obligatory prayers?' He said: 'The Takbir is in Mina after fifteen prayers, and in the other cities after ten prayers. So the first Takbir is after the Dhuhr prayer on the Day of Nahr (Sacrifice),' and he continued the hadith.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Fadhal, from Amr ibn Sa'id, from Musaddiq ibn Sadaqah, from 'Ammar ibn Musa al-Sabati, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Takbir (saying Allahu Akbar) is obligatory after every obligatory or voluntary prayer during the days of Tashriq.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan, from Amr ibn Sa'id, from Musaddiq ibn Sadaqah, from 'Ammar ibn Musa, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a man who forgets to say the Takbir during the days of Tashriq. He said: If he forgets until he rises from his place, there is nothing upon him. This does not indicate the negation of obligation regarding what we said, because it only entails the dispensation of re-performance (i'adah) for the one who forgets. And not everything in which re-performance is not obligatory serves as proof that it is not obligatory, because the Friday prayer is obligatory, yet not everyone who forgets it fulfills it with a single Friday prayer; rather, another obligation falls upon him. And there are many similar cases. Likewise, the menstruating woman is not required to make up the prayer, and this does not indicate that the prayer is not obligatory. As for what the report of 'Ammar al-Sabbati included, that it is obligatory after every obligatory and voluntary prayer, the way to handle what relates to the voluntary prayer is to interpret it as a type of preferability (istihbab) rather than obligation and compulsion, which indicates that.

Sa'd ibn Abd Allah, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Dawud ibn Farqad, who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: The Takbir (saying 'Allahu Akbar') is [required] in every obligatory [prayer], and there is no Takbir in the voluntary [prayers] during the days of Tashriq.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, and Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, from Safwan, from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: If you intend to depart on one of the two days, you are not permitted to depart until the sun passes its zenith; and if you delay until the last of the days of Tashriq, which is the final day of departure, there is no blame upon you regardless of what time you depart and throw [the pebbles], before or after the zenith.

From him, from several of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Dawud ibn al-Nu'man, from Abu Ayyub, who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): We wish to hasten the departure, and it was the night of the first departure when I asked him, so at what time do we depart? He said to me: As for the second day, do not depart until the sun sets, and it was the night of the first departure. And as for the third day, when the sun has turned white (risen clearly), then depart, according to the word of Allah, Exalted and Mighty.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The fasting person immerses himself in the water and does not rub his head.
From him, from Hammad, from Hariz, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The fasting person and the person in Ihram do not submerge their head in water.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from al-Ala' ibn Razin, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: The fasting person immerses himself in the water, pours water over his head, cools himself with his garment, sprinkles the hand fan, and sprinkles the awning beneath him, and he does not submerge his head in the water.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad ibn 'Uthman from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I heard Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) saying: 'What the fasting person does will not harm him, provided he avoids three things: food, drink, and women, and submerging himself in water.'

Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Faddal, from Muhammad ibn Abdillah, from Abdillah ibn Sinan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: It is disliked for the fasting person to immerse himself completely in water.

Sa'd ibn 'Abdillah narrated from 'Imran ibn Musa from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from 'Abdullah ibn Jabalah from Isḥaq ibn 'Ammar who said: I said to Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him): A man who is fasting deliberately immersed himself in water; is he required to make up that day? He said: There is no making up required for him, and he need not repeat it. The explanation for these two narrations and what follows their pattern is that we should attribute it to a form of precautionary dissimulation (taqiyyah), because that is consistent with the general public (Sunnis). It is permissible that this applies specifically to the removal of the make-up day and the expiation, even if the action is prohibited, because it is not impossible that the action is prohibited and its commission is not permissible, even if it does not necessitate the make-up day and the expiation. And I do not know a hadith regarding the obligation of the make-up day and the expiation, or the obligation of one of them, upon the one who immerses himself in water.

Musa ibn al-Qasim from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad from al-Halabi said: I asked Abu Abdillah about a man who arrives after the people have departed from Arafat. He said: If he has time to go to Arafat from its night, stand there, then depart and catch the people at al-Mash'ar before they depart, his Hajj is not complete until he goes to Arafat. And if a man arrives and Arafat has been missed for him, let him stand at al-Mash'ar al-Haram, for indeed Allah the Exalted has excused His servant, and his Hajj is complete if he catches al-Mash'ar al-Haram before the sunrise and before the people depart. If he does not catch al-Mash'ar al-Haram, then Hajj has been missed for him, and let him make it a separate Umrah, and upon him is the Hajj next year.

From him, from Muhammad ibn Sahl, from al-Idris ibn Abdillah, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who reached the people at Jamarat al-Aqaba (Jam'ah), and feared that if he proceeded to 'Arafat, the people would depart from Jam'ah before he reached it. He (AS) said: If he expects that the people will be at Jam'ah before sunrise, let him go to 'Arafat. And if he fears that he will not reach Jam'ah, let him stand at Jam'ah, then depart with the people, and his Hajj is complete. These two reports indicate that when one is able, standing at 'Arafat is obligatory. And in case of necessity, it is permissible to restrict oneself to al-Mash'ar al-Haram. And it also indicates the obligation of that.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Ali ibn Abi Hamzah, from Abu Basir, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: When you stand at Arafat, draw near to the hills, and the hills are the mountains, for the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'Those who stand at the Arak trees have no Hajj,' meaning those who stand at the Arak trees.

From him, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) said during the standing: 'Raise yourselves from the bottom of Bait Uraynah.' And he said: 'The people of al-Arak have no Hajj.' Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: The basis of inference from these two is that the Prophet (peace be upon him) invalidated the Hajj of anyone who left the boundary of Arafat, even if he was standing. Had standing in it not been obligatory, he would not have invalidated the Hajj of someone who stood outside its boundary; rather, he would have permitted him to not stand at all.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Ya'qub ibn Yazid, from Ibn Faddal, from some of our companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Standing at Al-Mash'ar is an obligation (fard), and standing at Arafah is a sunnah. This does not contradict what we mentioned, because the meaning in this report is that its obligation was known from the side of the Sunnah, rather than from the explicit text of the Quran. And whatever its obligation is known from the side of the Sunnah, it is permissible to call it by the name of 'Sunnah'. We have explained this in other places. But it is not so for standing at Al-Mash'ar, because its obligation is known from the explicit text of the Quran. So when you depart from Arafat, remember Allah at Al-Mash'ar Al-Haram. Thus He obligated upon us remembrance at Al-Mash'ar. And there was no command in the explicit text of the Quran regarding standing at Arafat, so for that reason it was attributed to the Sunnah. And this also indicates the obligation of standing at Arafat.

Musa ibn al-Qasim, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) was on a journey, and behold, there was an elderly man. He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what do you say about a man who catches the Imam at Jam'?' He said to him: 'If he expects that he will reach 'Arafat and stand there for a short while, then catch Jam' before the sunrise, let him go to Jam'. And if he expects that he will not reach it until the people depart from Jam', then let him not go to it, for his Hajj is complete.'

Musa ibn al-Qasim from Muhammad ibn Sinan said: I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about the one whom the [time of] Hajj catches [late], [asking if] he has caught Hajj? He said: If he arrives at Jam' while the people are at al-Mash'ar al-Haram before the sunrise, he has caught Hajj and his Umrah is not valid. And if he catches Jam' after the sunrise, it is a separate Umrah and he has no Hajj. If he wishes to stay in Mecca, he stays; and if he wishes to return to his family, he returns, and Hajj is incumbent upon him next year.

From him, from Muhammad ibn Sahl, from his father, from Ishaq ibn Abdillah, who said: I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about a man who entered Mecca performing Hajj al-Mufrad and feared that the two standings (at Arafat and Muzdalifah) would be missed. He said to him: 'Your day lasts until the sunrise of the Day of Nahr (Eid al-Adha). When the sun rises, his Hajj is complete.' I asked him: 'What should he do with his Ihram?' He said: 'He should go to Mecca and perform Tawaf around the House and Sa'i between al-Safa and al-Marwah.' I asked him: 'When he does that, what does he do afterwards?' He said: 'If he wishes, he stays in Mecca; and if he wishes, he returns to the people in Mina and is not among them in any way; and if he wishes, he returns to his family, and Hajj is incumbent upon him next year.'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Hammad ibn 'Isa from Hariz said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man performing Hajj al-Tamattu' (or Mufrad, contextually implying the Hajj ritual) who missed both standings (at Arafat and Muzdalifah). He said to him: [Wait] until the sunrise of the Day of Nahr (Eid al-Adha). If the sun rises on the Day of Nahr, then he has not performed Hajj, and he makes it a single Umrah, and upon him is the Hajj next year.

From him, from Muhammad ibn Fudayl, who said: I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about the limit: if a man reaches it, he has reached Hajj. He said: If he arrives at Jam' while the people are in al-Mash'ar before the sunrise, he has reached Hajj and his Umrah is not valid. If he does not arrive at Jam' until the sun rises, then it is a separate Umrah and he has no Hajj. If he wishes, he stays in Mecca, and if he wishes, he returns, and Hajj is incumbent upon him next year.

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar narrated from Abdullah ibn Amir, from Ibn Abi Najran, from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr, from Abdullah ibn al-Mughira, who said: A man came to us in Mina and said, 'I did not catch up with the people at both standing places (al-Mawqifayn) together.' Abdullah ibn al-Mughira said to him, 'Then your Hajj is not valid.' He asked Isma'il ibn 'Ammar, but he did not answer him. So Isma'il entered upon Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) and asked him about that. He said, 'If he catches up with Muzdalifah and stands at it before the sun moves (sets) on the Day of Nahr (Eid al-Adha), then he has caught up with the Hajj.'

And Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Jamil, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Whoever reaches the Mash'ar al-Haram on the Day of Nahr (sacrifice) before the decline of the sun has attained the Hajj. These two reports carry two meanings: one is that whoever reaches al-Muzdalifah before the decline of the sun has attained the virtue and reward of Hajj, without it being intended that by reaching it the obligation of the Hajj of Islam is dropped upon him. It also carries the meaning that this ruling is specific to one who reached 'Arafat then came to the Mash'ar before the decline of the sun, for he has attained the Hajj, because one in this state has attained one of the two stations in its proper time, and his Hajj is complete, which indicates that.

Musa ibn al-Qasim from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Ali ibn Ri'ab from al-Hasan al-Attar from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: When the pilgrim reaches 'Arafat before the rising of the dawn, then turns back from 'Arafat, and does not catch the people at Jam', and finds that they have already proceeded (to Muna), then he should stand for a short while at al-Mash'ar al-Haram and join the people at Muna, and there is no penalty upon him.

Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from Muhammad ibn Sinan, who said: I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about the one whom this [time] overtakes, and he has thereby attained Hajj. He said: If he arrives at Jam' while the people are at al-Mash'ar al-Haram before the sunrise, he has attained Hajj and his Umrah is not valid. If he attains Jam' after the sunrise, it is a separate Umrah and he has no Hajj. If he wishes to stay in Mecca, he stays; and if he wishes to return to his family, he returns, and Hajj is incumbent upon him next year.

From him, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Muawiya ibn 'Ammar, from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Whoever catches the 'Jam' (concurrent Hajj and 'Umrah), has caught the Hajj. And Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: Whichever pilgrim, bringing his offering (Hady) or performing individual Hajj or performing 'Umrah with conjunction to Hajj, arrives and his Hajj has been missed, let him make it an 'Umrah, and upon him is the Hajj next year.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Safwan from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): A man came as a pilgrim but missed the Hajj, and he had not performed Tawaf. He said: He stays with the people as a Harami (one in the state of Ihram for Hajj) during the Days of Tashriq, and there is no Umrah in them. When they end, he performs Tawaf with the House and Sa'i between As-Safa and Al-Marwah, and he becomes Muhsin (free from Ihram restrictions), and Hajj is incumbent upon him next year. He enters Ihram from where he entered Ihram.

Musa ibn al-Qasim from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Ali ibn Ri'ab from Durays ibn A'yan, who said: I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about a man who set out performing Tamattu' (combining Umrah and Hajj) for the Hajj, but did not reach Mecca except on the Day of Sacrifice. He said: He remains in his state of Ihram, and cuts off the Talbiyah when he enters Mecca, and performs Tawaf and Sa'i between al-Safa and al-Marwah, and shaves his head, and returns to his family if he wishes. And he said: This is for the one who made a condition upon his Lord at the time of his Ihram. If he did not make the condition, then upon him is the Hajj of the following year.

Sa'd ibn Abdillah narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from Muhammad ibn Abi Hamzah, and Safwan ibn Yahya, and Ali ibn al-Nu'man, from Ya'qub ibn Shu'ayb, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'Does a woman wear a qamis (shirt) with its pile/nap on it, and wear khazz (silk fabric), silk, and dibbaj (silk brocade)?' He said: 'Yes, there is no objection.' I asked: 'And does she wear the two khalkhal (anklets) and the mask (silk veil)?' He said: 'It does not contradict the first report, because the way to interpret it is to carry it upon silk that is not pure, in that it is mixed with cotton or linen or pure khazz.
