Sa'd ibn Abd Allah narrated that from Ibrahim ibn Hashim, from Isma'il ibn Marar, from Abd al-Jabbar ibn al-Mubarak, from Yunus ibn Abd al-Rahman, from Abd Allah ibn Muskhan, from Abu Basir and Sama'ah ibn Mihran, who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) asked us about a man who is obligated to fast two consecutive months, but he is unable to fast and is unable to pay the fidya (compensation). He said: 'Let him fast eighteen days: for every ten days, three days.'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from 'Uthman ibn 'Isa from Sama'ah who said: I asked him about a man who had intercourse with his wife in Ramadan intentionally, and he said: freeing a slave, feeding sixty poor people, fasting two consecutive months, and making up that day, and I am like that day for him. This report contains two possibilities: one is that the intended meaning of the 'waw' (and) in it is 'or', which indicates choice rather than the 'waw' that implies conjunction, and it may be used in this manner. Allah, the Exalted, said: 'Marry of those who are lawful to you, two or three or four.' He only meant two or three or four. The second possibility is that this is specific to one who had intercourse with his wife at a time when it is not permissible for him, except in a state of necessity, or he breaks his fast on something forbidden, such as an intoxicant or other than it. If the matter is thus, then three expiations are obligatory upon him by conjunction, and this is indicated by... Marry of those who are lawful to you, two or three or four. The second possibility is that this is specific to one who had intercourse with his wife at a time when it is not permissible for him, except in a state of necessity, or he breaks his fast on something forbidden, such as an intoxicant or other than it. If the matter is thus, then three expiations are obligatory upon him by conjunction.

Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn Babawayh al-Qummi (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated from Abd al-Wahid ibn Muhammad ibn Abdus al-Naysaburi, from Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Qutaybah, from Hamdan ibn Sulayman, from Abd al-Salam ibn Salih al-Harawi, who said: I said to al-Rida (peace be upon him): 'O son of the Messenger of Allah, it has been narrated from your fathers (peace be upon them) that for one who has intercourse or breaks his fast in the month of Ramadan, there are three expiations. And it has also been narrated from them that there is only one expiation. Which of the two reports should we follow?' He said: 'We take both. So whenever a man has unlawful intercourse or breaks his fast unlawfully in the month of Ramadan, he is obligated to three expiations: freeing a slave, fasting for two consecutive months, and feeding sixty poor people, plus making up that day. And if he had lawful intercourse or broke his fast lawfully, he is obligated to only one expiation.'

Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Ali ibn Ahmad ibn Ashyam from Sulayman ibn Ja'far al-Ja'fari who said: I asked Abu al-Hasan al-Rida (peace be upon him) about a man who intends to travel during the month of Ramadan and leaves his home after morning prayer. He said: If he is in his home at morning, fasting for that day becomes obligatory upon him, unless he departs after a late morning (delaying departure).

From him, from Al-Hasan ibn Ali, from Rifah, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man for whom travel arises during the month of Ramadan such that he remains traveling until morning. He said: 'He completes his fast for that day.' I said to him: 'But he arrived in the month of Ramadan, and between him and his family there was only the mid-morning part of the day.' He said: 'When the dawn breaks while he is traveling, he has the choice: if he wishes, he fasts, and if he wishes, he breaks his fast.'

Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Fadhal narrated from Ayub ibn Nuh, from Muhammad ibn Abi Hamzah, from Ali ibn Yaqtin, from Abu al-Hasan Musa (peace be upon him), concerning: A man who travels during the month of Ramadan, does he break his fast at his home? He (peace be upon him) said: If he decides in the night while traveling that he will break his fast, he breaks his fast when he leaves his home. And if he did not decide in the night, but then decided while traveling during the day, he completes his fast.

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar narrated from Abdullah ibn Amir, from Ibn Abi Najran, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from one who narrated from Abu Basir, who said: When you depart after the rising of the dawn, and you did not intend travel during the night, then complete the fast and count it as being from the month of Ramadan.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him), that he was asked: About a man who leaves his house intending to travel while he is fasting. He said: If he leaves before midday, he should break his fast and make up that day. And if he leaves after midday, he should complete his day.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from al-'Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: If a man travels during the month of Ramadan and departs after midday, he is obligated to fast that day and count it as part of Ramadan. If he enters a land before dawn rises, intending to reside there, he must fast that day. But if he enters after dawn rises, there is no fasting obligation upon him; if he wishes, he may fast. The correct approach in these two reports and what follows their pattern is to interpret them as meaning: if he had intended travel from the night, fasting is obligatory upon him if he departs before noon (zawal); if he departs after noon, it is recommended for him to complete the fast. If he does not fast, there is no penalty upon him, which indicates what we have mentioned.

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar narrated from Abdullah ibn Amir, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Najran, from Safwan, from Sama'ah or Ibn Muskhan, from a man, from Abu Basir, who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: When you intend to travel in the month of Ramadan and you intend to depart from the night, if you depart before dawn or after it, you are one who breaks the fast, and upon you is the making up of that day.

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar from 'Imran ibn Musa from Musa ibn Ja'far from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from al-Hasan ibn 'Ali ibn Fadhl from Ibn Bukayr from 'Abd al-A'la, the freedman of the House of Sam, regarding the man who intends to travel in the month of Ramadan, he said: He breaks the fast, even if he departs a little before the sun sets. The ruling in this is what we have previously stated: that whoever departs after the sun has passed its zenith (dhuhr) and had spent the night with the intention of travel, it is permissible for him to break the fast, although it is preferable for him to fast until nightfall, according to what has preceded from the earlier narrations, and there is no contradiction between them.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from al-Karram, who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): I have made it upon myself to fast until the Rising of the Qa'im (peace be upon him). He said: Fast, but do not fast during travel, and do not fast on the two Eids, and do not fast on the Days of Tashriq, and do not fast on the day of doubt in the month of Ramadan.

Al-Husayn ibn Said from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad al-Jawhari from Ali ibn Abi Hamzah from Abu Ibrahim (peace be upon him) said: I asked him about a man who made it upon himself to fast a month in Kufa, a month in Medina, and a month in Mecca due to a trial he was tested with. It was ruled for him that he fasted a month in Kufa, then entered Medina and fasted eighteen days there, and did not stay with al-Jammal. He said: He fasts what remains of it when he reaches his home, and he does not fast it while traveling.

Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Fadhal narrated from Amr ibn Uthman, from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from Abdillah ibn Sinan, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who fasts a fast that he has appointed upon himself, or who fasts the sacred months, and a month or two pass without him making it up. He said: He does not fast during travel, and he does not make up anything from voluntary fasting except the three days that he used to fast every month, and he does not make them equivalent to the obligatory fast, unless I love for you to persist in good deeds. He said: And the one who fasts the sacred months, it suffices him to fast three days in place of each month of the sacred months.

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar from al-Qasim ibn Abi al-Qasim al-Siqlal said: I wrote to him: 'O our master, a man vowed to fast one of the Fridays permanently for as long as he lives. That day coincided with Eid al-Fitr or Eid al-Adha, or a Friday, or the days of Tashriq, or travel, or illness. Is he required to fast that specific day, or make it up, or what should he do, O our master?' He wrote back to him: 'Fasting has been waived for you during all these days, and you shall fast one day in place of one day, if God wills.'

Sa'd ibn Abd Allah narrated from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Fadhl, from Abd Allah ibn Bukayr, from Zurarah, who said: I said to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him): My mother had made a vow upon herself that if God restored to her some of her children from an ailment she feared for them, she would fast on that day on which the remainder of them arrived. So she traveled with us to Mecca, and it became unclear to us; we did not know whether she should fast or break her fast. He said: 'She should not fast, for God Almighty has lifted the obligation of her vow from her, and she fasts what she made upon herself.' I said: 'What do you think if she returns home, should she make up for it?' He said: 'No.' I said: 'So she leaves it?' He said: 'No, for I fear she will see in what she vowed that which she dislikes.'

Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Fadhal narrated from Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Abi al-Subbah, from Ibrahim ibn Abd al-Hamid, from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a man who makes it incumbent upon himself for the sake of God to fast a specific day. He said: He always fasts, both in residence and during travel. The meaning in this report is that if he stipulated upon himself during the vow that he would fast during travel and residence, then that is binding upon him. And if he spoke generally without stipulating, then it is lifted from him during travel, according to what we have previously mentioned, and that which indicates this distinction.

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad and Abd Allah ibn Muhammad from Ali ibn Mahziyar, who said: Bundar, the freedman of Idris, wrote: 'O our master, I vowed to fast every Saturday. If I do not fast it, what expiation (kaffarah) will be incumbent upon me?' He (peace be upon him) wrote back and I read it: 'Do not leave it, except due to an excuse. And you are not required to fast it during travel or illness, unless you intended that. And if you broke it without an excuse, then give charity for the count of each day to seven poor people. We ask Allah for success in what He loves and is pleased with.'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad who said: I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about fasting in Mecca and Medina while we were traveling. He said: 'It is obligatory (fard).' I said: 'No, but it is voluntary (ta-taww'u), just as prayer is performed voluntarily.' He said: 'You say: today and tomorrow.' I said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Do not fast.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from a number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Mansur ibn al-Abbas, from Muhammad ibn Abdillah ibn Wasir, from Ismail ibn Sahl, from a man, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) left Medina in the remaining days of Sha'ban, and he would fast. Then the month of Ramadan entered upon him while he was traveling, so he broke his fast. He was asked: 'You fast in Sha'ban but break your fast in the month of Ramadan?' He said: 'Yes, Sha'ban is up to me; if I wish I fast, and if I wish I do not. And the month of Ramadan is a divine obligation upon me to break the fast [i.e., to perform the obligatory fast].'

And from him, from a number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ali ibn Bilal, from Al-Hasan ibn Bassam al-Jammal, from a man who said: I was with Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) between Mecca and Medina in the month of Sha'ban, and he was fasting. Then we saw the crescent of Ramadan, so he broke his fast. I said to him, 'May I be your ransom, yesterday was from Sha'ban and you were fasting, and today is from Ramadan and you are breaking your fast.' He said, 'That was voluntary (fasting), and we may do what we wish, and this is obligatory (fasting), and we may do only what we are commanded.' The explanation of these two reports is that they should be understood as a form of concession (rukhsah), and that whoever fasts a voluntary fast while traveling is not blameworthy, although breaking the fast is preferable. We said this because both reports are mursal (disconnected chain) and not musnad (connected chain). The earlier reports are musnad and agree with the general reports we mentioned in our book Al-Kabir regarding the prohibition of fasting while traveling, such as their saying: 'Fasting while traveling is not from piety.' So it is as if he broke his fast in the city. And those [general reports] apply to both obligatory and voluntary fasting, and the two preceding reports agree with them, and acting upon them is more worthy and more appropriate.

Al-Husayn ibn Said, from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad ibn Uthman, from Ubaydullah al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about an elderly man who is too weak to fast in the month of Ramadan, so he said: He should give charity in the form of feeding one poor person for each day.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa narrated from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Abd al-Malik ibn Utbah al-Hashimi, who said: I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about the elderly man and the elderly woman who are too weak to fast in the month of Ramadan. He said: They give charity for each day with a mud of wheat.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from al-'Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, said: I heard Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) saying: The elderly man and the one suffering from thirst, there is no blame upon them if they break their fast in the month of Ramadan, and each of them must give charity one mudd of food every day, and there is no make-up (qada) upon them; if they are unable [to give food], then there is nothing upon them.

As for this narration of Saad, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn Abi al-Khattab, who said: 'Ja'far ibn Bashir and Muhammad ibn Abdullah ibn Hilal narrated to us from Ula' ibn Razin from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I heard Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) and he mentioned the hadith.' Except that he said: 'And each of the two shall give charity every day with two mudds of food.' So it does not contradict the earlier narrations, because this narration can be understood as a type of recommendation (mustahabb), while the earlier ones are understood as obligatory (fard/wajib).

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Safwan from al-'Iyyas ibn al-Qasim said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the Fitrah (alms of fasting), when is it? He said: Before the prayer on the day of Eid al-Fitr. I said: If some of it remains after the prayer? He said: There is no harm. We give our dependents from it, then it remains and we divide it.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad from al-Hasan from Abu Bakr al-Hadrami from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) regarding the saying of Allah, Exalted and Mighty: He has certainly succeeded who purifies himself and mentions the name of his Lord and prays. He said: He goes to the prayer place (al-jabbanah) and prays.

From him, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, from Ibrahim ibn Maymun, who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: The Fitrah (alms of breaking the fast) is considered Fitrah if you give it before you go out to the Eid prayer, and if you give it after you go out to the Eid prayer, it is considered Sadaqah (general charity). Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: There is no contradiction between this narration and the first narration, because the way to reconcile them is that it is obligatory to discharge the Fitrah before the prayer, and it is set apart; if one gives it afterwards to the worthy recipient, there is no harm in it.

And similarly, the report narrated by Sa'd ibn Abdillah from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn Abi al-Khattab from Dinār ibn Hakīm from al-Hārith from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: There is no harm in delaying the breaking of the fast (Iftar) until the crescent of Dhu al-Qa'dah. The aspect in this report is also what we said in the first report, equally, and that which indicates what we said.

Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Fadhal narrated from Ya'qub ibn Yazid, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from some of our companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding the fitrah (small cloth used for wiping after urination), if you set it aside while you are seeking a place for it or waiting for a man (to use it), there is no harm in it.

Sa'd from Muhammad ibn 'Isa from Yunus from Ishaq ibn 'Ammar and others said: I asked him about the fitrah (semen emission), he said: When you isolate it (perform ghusl), it does not harm you when you give it (perform ghusl), before the prayer or after the prayer.

As for what Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Najran and al-'Abbas ibn Ma'ruf, from Hammad ibn 'Isa, from 'Umar ibn Udhaynah, from Zurarah and Bukayr, sons of A'yan, and al-Fudayl ibn Yasar, and Muhammad ibn Muslim, and Burayd ibn Mu'awiya, from Abu Ja'far and Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon them), that they said: It is upon the man to give for every person he supports, whether free or slave, young or old. He should give on the day of al-Fitr before the prayer, as that is superior. If he is in ease, he may give it from the first day he enters until the last day of Ramadan. If he gives dates, a sa' for each head; and if he does not give dates, half a sa' of wheat or barley for each head. Wheat and barley are equal: whatever the wheat discharges, the barley discharges. The aspect in this narration is a form of concession (rukhsah) in advancing the payment of Zakat al-Fitr before its appointed time, as we said regarding the advancement of Zakat al-Mal, although the preference is to discharge it at its proper time, as explicitly stated in the narration.

Al-Husayn ibn Ubayd Allah informed us from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Yahya, from his father, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Muhammad, from al-Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: When a man travels during Ramadan, he should not approach women during the day in Ramadan, for that is forbidden for him.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Mahbub, from Ibn Sinan, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who travels in the month of Ramadan and has a female servant with him, is it permissible for him to have intercourse with her during the day? He said: Glory be to Allah, does he not know the sanctity of the month of Ramadan? For him there is a long night. I said: Is it not permissible for him to eat, drink, and shorten (prayer)? He said: Indeed, Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, granted permission to the traveler to break the fast and shorten (prayer) as a mercy and to alleviate the burden of fatigue, exertion, and difficulty of travel, but He did not grant him permission for intercourse with women while traveling during the day in the month of Ramadan. So He made it obligatory upon him to make up the fasting, but did not make it obligatory upon him to complete the prayer when he returns from his journey. Then he said: And the Sunnah is not to be measured (by the ruling of the traveler), and indeed when I travel in the month of Ramadan, I do not eat all the food nor drink all the drink.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa narrated from Muhammad ibn Sahl from his father who said: I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about a man who had intercourse with his wife during the month of Ramadan while he was a traveler, and he said: There is no objection.

Sa'd ibn 'Abdillah narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from 'Ali ibn al-Hakam who said: I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about a man who has intercourse with his wife while traveling during the month of Ramadan. He said: There is no harm in it. So do not see a contradiction between this report and the earlier reports, because the first report included the question about one who had intercourse with his wife during Ramadan, and he answered that there is no harm. It is not impossible that he did so out of ignorance, not knowing that it was not permissible for him. And he did not say in the report that it is permissible in every case. As for the last two hadiths and what is added to them from what has come in the books, it is not mentioned therein that he did so at night or during the day. It is not impossible that the permission came regarding the state of the night, not the day. And it can be understood, with acceptance, that they include mentioning the day for one upon whom desire overcomes and he cannot control himself and does not fear falling into the prohibited, so He granted him concession to attain from the permissible. And if it is the other case, it is as we have mentioned. And a report has been narrated that included mention of the day, and the explanation for it is what we have mentioned.

Sa'd ibn 'Abdillah narrated from Muhammad ibn 'Isa ibn 'Ubayd from 'Uthman ibn 'Isa from Hariz from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I asked Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who returns from his journey after the 'Asr prayer in the month of Ramadan, and he has intercourse with his wife when she has become pure from her menses. Is it permissible for him to have sexual relations with her? He said: There is no harm in it.

The Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) informed us from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan ibn Aban, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammam, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), that he was asked about a man who converted to Islam in the middle of the month of Ramadan, what is incumbent upon him regarding fasting? He said: There is not incumbent upon him except what he converted to Islam in.

And from him, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from al-‘Is ibn al-Qasim, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a group of people who embraced Islam during the month of Ramadan, and some days had passed from it. Is it upon them to make up for the days that passed, or is their day the one in which they embraced Islam? He said: There is no making up (qada) upon them, nor is their day the one in which they embraced Islam, unless they embraced Islam before the rising of dawn (Fajr).

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Harun ibn Muslim, from Mas'adah ibn Sadah, from Abu Abdillah, from his fathers, that Ali (peace be upon him) used to say: Regarding a man who converted to Islam in the middle of the month of Ramadan, he is only obligated for what he faces (i.e., the remainder of the days).

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad from Aban ibn Uthman from al-Halabi who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who entered the month of Ramadan for some days and then converted to Islam. He said to me: 'He must make up what was missed.' The approach in this narration is to interpret it as referring to one who converted in the month of Ramadan but did not know that fasting was obligatory upon him, so he fasted (or ate), and then learned afterwards. Indeed, it becomes obligatory upon him to make up (the missed days). This is indicated by his saying 'make up what was missed.' And 'missing' does not occur except after the obligation of the duty has directed towards the accountable person, without the condition of Islam. And one who converts in the month of Ramadan, what passed of it was not directed towards him except by the condition of Islam. And one with this description is not obliged to make up (the fasts) without disagreement.

The Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) informed me from Abu al-Qasim Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Sa'd ibn Abdillah, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn Abi al-Khattab, from Uthman ibn Isa, from Sama'ah ibn Mihran, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who entered Ramadan while he was ill and unable to fast, and he died in the month of Ramadan or in the month of Shawwal. He said: 'There is no fasting upon him, nor is it compensated on his behalf.' I said: 'And a postpartum woman who entered Ramadan and was unable to fast, and she died in the month of Ramadan or in the month of Shawwal?' He said: 'It is not compensated on her behalf.'

And from him, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Hamid, from Saif ibn Umayrah, from Mansur ibn Hazim, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the sick person in the month of Ramadan who does not recover until he dies; he said: His fasts are not made up for him. And about the menstruating woman who dies in the month of Ramadan; he said: Her fasts are not made up for her.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad, from al-Wassaq, from Hammad ibn 'Uthman, from the one he mentioned, from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a man who dies while he has a debt from the month of Ramadan. Who will pay it off on his behalf? He said: The people most entitled to do so. I said: And if the person most entitled to do so is a woman? He said: No, only men.

And from him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad, who said: I wrote to the latter (Imam al-Rida, peace be upon him) regarding a man who died with a debt of making up ten days from the month of Ramadan, and he had two heirs. Is it permissible for both of them to make up for him together, one of the heirs making up five days and the other heir making up five days? He replied: 'Make up for him ten days as heirs, if God wills.' There is no contradiction between these two reports and the earlier reports, because they only included the heir making up for the deceased who has a debt of making up the month of Ramadan. And whoever died in his illness, nothing is upon him, so it does not need to be made up for him, because the obligation is what became due upon him. The way to understand both is that they are applied to one who missed the month of Ramadan due to illness or otherwise, then recovered and was able to make it up, but did not make it up, then became ill and died. It becomes obligatory upon his heir to make it up for him, because the making up became obligatory upon him in the state of his ability, so he was negligent. And reports have come with this detail, some of which:

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Zarif ibn Nasih, from Abu Maryam, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: If a man fasts something from the month of Ramadan and remains ill until he dies, there is nothing upon him [to make up]. And if he recovered, then became ill again, then died, and he had wealth, charity is given on his behalf; and if he did not have wealth, his heir gives charity on his behalf.

And in the narration of Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad, from al-Wasshash, from Aban ibn 'Uthman, from Abu Maryam, similar to it, except that he said: 'His guardian fasts on his behalf.'

Al-Saffar narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Abu Basir, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a woman who fell ill in Ramadan and died in Shawwal, and she instructed me to make up the fasts on her behalf. He said: 'Did she recover from her illness?' I said: 'No, she died while still ill.' He said: 'Then do not make up the fasts on her behalf, for Allah did not impose it upon her.' I said: 'But I wish to make up the fasts on her behalf, and she had instructed me to do so.' He said: 'How can you make up for something that Allah did not impose upon her? If you wish to fast for your own sake, then fast.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from al-Ala' ibn Razin, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from one of the two Imams (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about a man whom the month of Ramadan caught while he was ill, and he died before he recovered. He said: There is no obligation upon him, but the one who recovers then dies before fulfilling the obligation must have it fulfilled on his behalf.

The Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) informed us from Abu al-Qasim Ja'far ibn Muhammad from Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Hammad ibn Isa from Hariz from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: We asked them (peace be upon them) about a man who fell ill and did not fast until another Ramadan arrived. They said: If he recovered and then delayed (paying the makeup) until another Ramadan arrived, he should fast the days he missed and give charity for each day with a mud of food to a poor person, and he must also pay the makeup. If he remained ill until another Ramadan arrived, he should fast the days he missed and give charity for the first (missed days), one mud for each day to a poor person, and he does not have to pay the makeup.

And from him, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr and Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Jamil, from Zurarah, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) Regarding a man who falls ill and Ramadan overtakes him while he is ill and does not recover until another Ramadan overtakes him, he said: He gives charity for the first [year] and fasts the second [year]. And if he recovered in between but did not fast until another Ramadan overtook him, he fasts both [years] and gives charity for the first [year].

And from him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from Muhammad ibn al-Fudayl, from Abu al-Subah al-Kinanī, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who owes a portion of [fasts] from the month of Ramadan, and then the next month of Ramadan catches him [before he makes them up]. He said: If he was sick in between, until the next month of Ramadan caught him, then there is not upon him except fasting, if he is healthy. But if the illness continues upon him, then upon him is to feed a poor person for each day.

Al-Husayn ibn Said from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad from Ali from Abu Basir from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: If a man falls ill between one Ramadan and the next, then recovers, then for every day he broke his fast, he owes the ransom of food, which is a mudd for each poor person. He said: And likewise in the expiation of the oath and the dhihar [verbal divorce], a mudd for a mudd. If he recovers in between the two Ramadans, then he only owes making up the fast. And if he was negligent with it and has recovered, then upon him is the charity and the fasting together for each day, a mudd, when he finishes that Ramadan.

Sa'd ibn Abdillah narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from 'Abbad ibn Sulayman, from Sa'd ibn Sa'd, from a man, from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about a man who is ill during the month of Ramadan, then recovers afterwards, and delays making up the missed days for a year or less than that, or more than that. He said: 'I like for him to hasten the fasting. If he delays it, there is nothing upon him (no penalty).' Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: 'There is no contradiction between these narrations, because whoever is ill in Ramadan until another Ramadan, if he recovers in between with a strong health enabling him to make up the fasts, and does not make them up out of negligence, then upon him is both making up the fasts and expiation (kaffarah) when he fasts the current Ramadan. And if he recovers and intends to make them up, but it does not coincide with him and the days keep passing, then upon him is only making up the fasts without expiation. And if he does not recover in between and the illness persists until another Ramadan, he fasts the current Ramadan, expiates for the first one, and there is no making up (fasts) upon him.'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from 'Uthman ibn 'Isa from Sama'ah who said: I asked him about a man whom Ramadan arrived while he had Ramadan from before upon him, which he did not fast. He said: He should give charity in place of each day of the Ramadan that was upon him with a mud of food, and he should fast this Ramadan that arrived. When he breaks his fast (in this current Ramadan), then let him fast the Ramadan that was upon him. For indeed, I was ill, and three Ramadans passed over me and I was not healthy in them, then I caught another Ramadan. So I gave charity in place of each day that passed with a mud of food. Then Allah healed me and I fasted them. So there is nothing in it that contradicts what we mentioned, that when the illness persists, only charity is obligatory upon him, not the making up (of fasts), because in the report it is not stated that he was not healthy in between them. Rather, he said: 'Three Ramadans passed over me and I was not healthy in them, then I caught another Ramadan.' And this implies that he was not healthy in the Ramadans themselves, not in between them. And if it did not bear except that he was not healthy in between them, then his action would be for him on the path of recommendation and voluntary act, and that which reveals what we mentioned.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Fadalah ibn Ayyub from Abdullah ibn Sinan from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Whoever breaks his fast for a portion of Ramadan due to an excuse, then is overtaken by another Ramadan while he is ill, he must give charity with a mud for each day. As for me, I fasted and gave charity. Do you not see that he made charity obligatory upon the one who missed Ramadan, rather than making the makeup fast obligatory, and he attached the makeup fast to himself along with the charity? If it were not that it was on the path of voluntary giving and supererogation, he would not have singled himself out for that, but rather he would have made it general for whoever shared in that, according to what he attached to himself.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Uthman ibn Isa, from Sama'ah, who said: I asked him about a traveler who entered his home before the sun's declination (midday) and had already eaten. He said: It is not appropriate for him to eat anything that day, nor to have sexual intercourse during the month of Ramadan, if he has a family.

And from him, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yunus, who said: He said regarding the traveler who enters to his family in the month of Ramadan and has eaten before entering: He should refrain from eating for the remainder of the day, and upon him is the making up (of the fast). And he said regarding the traveler who enters to his family while he is in a state of major ritual impurity before midday, and he had not eaten: It is upon him to complete his fast, and there is no making up upon him, meaning if his impurity was from a nocturnal emission.

Sa'd ibn Abdillah narrated from Muhammad ibn 'Isa ibn 'Ubayd, from 'Uthman ibn 'Isa, from Hariz ibn Abdillah, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who arrives from a journey after the afternoon prayer in the month of Ramadan, and he has intercourse with his wife when she has become pure from menstruation. He said: There is no harm in it, so it does not contradict what we mentioned, because we did not command him to abstain as an obligation or necessity, but rather we mentioned it as encouragement and recommendation. And we have clarified in what preceded that it is not permissible for one who breaks his fast in Ramadan for an excuse to have intercourse with his family, unless he fears on himself committing the indecent act and entering into the forbidden, for then it is permissible, and the state is as we described.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Ibn Abi Umayr from Ibn Udhaynah, who said: I wrote to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) asking him: What is the limit of the illness that causes its owner to break his fast, and the illness that causes its owner to leave the prayer while standing? He said: Rather, the person has sight (discernment) over himself, and he said: That is for him, as he is more knowledgeable about himself.

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Sulayman ibn Hafsh al-Marwazi, who said: The Jurist (peace be upon him) said: The sick person only prays sitting if he reaches a state in which he cannot walk for the duration of his prayer until he finishes standing. Thus, there is no contradiction with the first two narrations, because the foundation is what the first two narrations contain, which is what a person knows about his own condition, and this is referred to. This narration is to be understood as referring to a type of preference (istihbab), and it is not impossible that this is a ruling specific to prayer, distinct from fasting, and there is no contradiction between them in any case.

Abu al-Husayn ibn Abi Jeed informed me from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn al-Walid, from al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan ibn Aban, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: If a man has remaining days of fasting from the month of Ramadan, let him make them up in whichever month he wishes, as consecutive days. If he is unable [to fast consecutively], let him make them up however he wishes, and let him specify the days. If he separates them, it is good; and if he continues them, it is good. I said: What do you think if there remains upon him something from the fasting of the month of Ramadan, should he make it up in Dhu al-Hijjah? He said: Yes.

From him, from Hammad, from Abdillah ibn al-Mughira, from Ibn Sinan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Whoever breaks the fast for a part of the month of Ramadan due to an excuse, if he makes it up consecutively, that is better; and if he makes it up separately, it is good.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from a number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn Ahmad ibn Ashyam, from Sulayman ibn Ja'far al-Ja'fari, who said: I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about a man who has missed days from the month of Ramadan, should he make them up separately? He said: There is no harm in separating the making up of the month of Ramadan. The fasting that must not be separated is the expiation for Dhihar, the expiation for blood (diyah), and the expiation for an oath.

Sa'd ibn Abdillah, from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Fadhal, from Amr ibn Sa'id al-Mada'ini, from Musaddiq ibn Sadaqa, from Ammar ibn Musa al-Sabati, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about a man who has missed days from the month of Ramadan, how should he make them up? He said: If he has two days, he should break fast (skip one day) between them; and if he has five days, he should break fast between them (skip days); and he is not permitted to fast more than eight consecutive days. And if he has eight or ten days, he should break fast between them (skip one day). The meaning in this narration is that whoever is obligated to make up the month of Ramadan is not required to make them up consecutively, according to what was obligatory for him to fast initially. Thus, what this report contains regarding the command to break fast and separate between these days is merely a command of choice and permission, not obligation or recommendation, because we have clarified that making them up consecutively is superior in the first narration.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Khalid, from Sa'd ibn Sa'd al-Ash'ari, from Abu al-Hasan al-Rida (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about the Fitrah (alms of breaking the fast), how much should be paid for every head from wheat, barley, dates, and raisins? He said: A sa' with the sa' of the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family).

And from him, from several of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Abi Najran, and Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Safwan al-Jammal, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the Fitrah (alms of fasting), so he said: Upon the young and the old, the free and the slave, for every person, one Sa' of wheat, or one Sa' of dates, or one Sa' of raisins.

Sa'd ibn Abd Allah, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Abd Allah ibn al-Mughira, from Abu al-Hasan al-Rida (peace be upon him) in the Fitrah (alms of breaking the fast), he said: A sa' is given from wheat, and from barley, and from aqit, a sa'.

From him, from Muhammad ibn al-Jabbar, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn Abi Hamzah, from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The owners of camels, cattle, and sheep give in alms-tax (fitrah) from aqit (dried curds) one sa'.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Hammad ibn Isa from Abd Allah ibn Maymun from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) from his father (peace be upon him) said: The Zakat al-Fitr is a sa' of dates, or a sa' of raisins, or a sa' of barley, or a sa' of aqit, for every person, free or slave, young or old. And there is no blame on one who cannot find what to give in charity.

Abu al-Qasim Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Qulawayh narrated from Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Mas'ud from Ja'far ibn Ma'ruf, who said: I wrote to Abu Bakr al-Razi regarding the Zakat al-Fitr, and asked him to write about that to our Master, meaning Ali ibn Muhammad (peace be upon him). He wrote that the ruling had been sent to Ali ibn Mahziyar, stating that from every item, a sa' is to be given out, such as dates, wheat, and others. After his response, there is no difference of opinion among us regarding that.

Al-Husayn ibn Said from Safwan from Ibn Muskhan from Al-Halabi said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the Zakat al-Fitr, and he said: Upon every person whom the man supports, from the free and the slave, the small and the large, is one Sa' of dates or half a Sa' of wheat, and the Sa' is four Madad.

From him, from Hammad, from Abdullah ibn al-Mughira, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), regarding the Zakat al-Fitr. He said: Give charity on behalf of all those you provide for, whether young or old, free or slave. For every person, half a sa' of wheat or one sa' of barley, and the sa' is four mudds.

From him, from Hammad, from Hariz, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: For the one who does not find wheat and barley, the release of the alms-tax (Fitr) is fulfilled by emmer wheat, sifted emmer, lentils, and mustard; half a sa' of each of these suffices, or one sa' of dates or raisins. The rationale in these narrations and those that follow their pattern is that we should understand them as being based on a form of precautionary dissimulation (taqiyyah). The basis of this taqiyyah is that the Sunnah was previously practiced by giving one sa' of every type of food for the Fitr alms. However, during the time of Uthman and subsequently in the days of Mu'awiya, half a sa' of wheat was established in exchange for one sa' of dates, and the people followed them in this. Thus, these narrations came in accordance with them, based on taqiyyah, which indicates the reason.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Fadala, from Aban ibn Uthman, from Salama ibn Hafsh, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), from his father (peace be upon him), who said: The Zakat al-Fitr is due on every small and large person, free or slave, for every person one supports (meaning: upon whom one spends), a sa' of dates, or a sa' of barley, or a sa' of raisins. Then, when the time of Uthman came, he changed it to two mudds of wheat.

From him, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Mu'awiya ibn Wahb, who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying regarding Fitrah: The Sunnah was established with a Sa' of dates, or a Sa' of raisins, or a Sa' of barley. Then when the time of Uthman came and wheat became abundant, the people standardized it, saying: Half a Sa' of wheat is equivalent to a Sa' of barley.

Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Fadhal narrated from Abbad ibn Ya'qub, from Ibrahim ibn Abi Yahya, from Abu Abdillah, from his father, from the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family), that the first person to establish two mudds of wheat as equivalent to one sa' of dates was Uthman.

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar, from Ya'qub ibn Yazid, from al-Yasir al-Qummi, from Abu al-Hasan al-Rida (peace be upon him) who said: The Fitrah (alms of breaking the fast) is one Sa' of wheat, or one Sa' of barley, or one Sa' of dates, or one Sa' of raisins; and it was Mu'awiyyah who lightened [the obligation] to wheat.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad al-Jawhari from Aban ibn Uthman from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Abdillah said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about making up the days of Ramadan in the month of Dhu al-Hijjah, and whether to break the fast (of the make-up days) or not. He said: Make it up in the month of Dhu al-Hijjah, and break it if you wish.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn 'Isa narrated from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ghiyath ibn Ibrahim from Ja'far from his father (peace be upon him) who said: Imam Ali (peace be upon him) said regarding the making up of the month of Ramadan: If one is unable to perform it continuously, one should divide it. And he said: One does not make up the month of Ramadan during the ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah. The meaning of this report regarding his statement 'one does not make up the month of Ramadan during the ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah' is that we interpret it as applying to one who is a pilgrim, because he will be traveling. And it is not permissible for the traveler to make up the month of Ramadan unless he stays in a town and intends to remain there for ten days or more. And that which indicates this is what we have previously mentioned from the reports regarding the permissibility of making up the month of Ramadan during Dhu al-Hijjah. As for that which indicates that it is not permissible to make up the month of Ramadan while traveling...

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Muhammad ibn Abdillah ibn Hilal, from Uqbah ibn Khalid, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) in a man who fell ill during the month of Ramadan, and when he recovered he wished to perform Hajj; what should he do regarding the making up of the fast? He said: When he returns, let him make it up.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Fadala ibn Ayyub, from Al-Husayn ibn Uthman, from Sama'a, from Abu Basir, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a woman who is making up the month of Ramadan, and her husband forces her to break the fast; he said: It is not proper for him to force her after midday.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from the multitude of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Mahbub, from al-Harith ibn Muhammad, from Burayd al-Ajli, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) Regarding a man who had relations with his wife on a day he is making up from the month of Ramadan, he said: If he had relations with his wife before midday (zuwal), there is nothing upon him except one day in place of one day; and if he had relations with his wife after midday, then upon him is to give charity to ten poor people.

Sa'd ibn 'Abdillah narrated from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) from Ayyub ibn Nuh from Muhammad ibn Abi 'Umayr from Hisham ibn Salim who said: I said to Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'A man had intercourse with his wife while he was making up the days of Ramadan.' He said, 'If he had intercourse with her before the 'Asr prayer, there is no penalty upon him; he fasts one day in its place. And if he did it after 'Asr, he fasts that day and feeds ten poor people. If he is unable to do so, he fasts three days as expiation for that.' Muammad ibn al-Hasan said, 'There is no contradiction between the two reports because when the time for the two prayers is at the decline of the sun, except that Dhuhr is before 'Asr as we have established previously, it is permissible to describe what is before the decline as being before 'Asr due to the closeness between the two times, and to describe what is after 'Asr as being after the decline in the same way. And it is permissible to carry this narration if one determines the time and meaning within it to be obligatory, and the first case to be recommended.'

Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Fadhal narrated from Muhammad ibn Isma'il from Hammad ibn Isa from Hariz from Zurara, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who made up a day from the month of Ramadan and then had intercourse with his wife. He said: Upon him is the expiation that is upon the one who had intercourse during Ramadan, because that day, in the sight of God, is from the days of Ramadan. This report came as rare and unusual (shadh), and it can be meant for the one who broke his fast on that day after midday (zuwal) in a manner of轻视 and negligence regarding the obligation of God Almighty, in which case that expiation is obligatory upon him as a strict punishment. As for the one who was not like that, but rather believed that completing the fast was preferable, but desire overcame him and compelled him to break the fast, then only what we have previously mentioned is obligatory upon him.

Ahmad ibn 'Abdun narrated to me from Ali ibn Muhammad ibn al-Zubayr, from Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Faddal, from Ibrahim ibn Abi Bakr ibn Abi Sammak, from Zakariyya al-Mu'min, from Isma'il ibn 'Ammar, from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: He who fasts Ramadan has the choice to break his fast at any time between dawn (fajr) and sunset (maghrib), and for voluntary fasting, he has the choice to break it at any time between dawn and sunset.

Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Faddal narrated from Harun ibn Muslim from Mas'ada ibn Sadqa from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) from his father that Ali (peace be upon him) said: One who fasts a voluntary fast has the choice [to break it] between himself and the middle of the day. When the day has passed its midpoint, the fast becomes obligatory. The view in this narration is that the first [period], if it is after midday (zawal), is for him to fast it, and it may be said that what he does in the first [period] is obligatory, and we have explained this in other places as has preceded.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Fadala ibn Ayyub from Isma'il ibn Abi Ziyad from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) from his father (peace be upon him) from Ali (peace be upon him) who said: When the child is capable of fasting for three consecutive days, then fasting the month of Ramadan becomes obligatory upon him. The approach in this narration is to understand that it is obligatory upon him for the sake of discipline (ta'dib), and although it is expressed with the wording of obligation (wujub), it is according to a type of concession, because it is appropriate that the child be made to fast when he is capable, to the extent of his capacity, so that he may become accustomed.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), that he said: We command our young boys to fast when they are seven years old, to the extent they can endure fasting for the day, whether it is until midday or more or less. When thirst and hunger overcome them, they break their fast, until they become accustomed to fasting and are able to endure it. So command your young boys, when they are nine years old, to fast to the extent they can endure, and when thirst overcomes them, they break their fast.

The Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) informed us from Abu al-Qasim Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Muhammad ibn Qulawayh from his father from Sa'd ibn Abd Allah from Ibrahim ibn Hashim from Isma'il ibn Marar and Abd al-Jabbar ibn al-Mubarik from Yunus ibn Abd al-Rahman from Hisham ibn Salim from Sulayman ibn Khalid, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who was obligated to fast two consecutive months, so he fasted twenty-five days, then he became ill. When he recovered, should he build upon what he had fasted, or should he repeat the entire fast? He said: Rather, he builds upon what he had fasted. Then he said: This is what Allah, Exalted and Majestic, has made easy for him, and there is no penalty upon him for what Allah, Exalted and Majestic, has made easy for him.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr and Fadala from Rifah said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man upon whom is the fasting of two consecutive months, so he fasted one month and became ill. He said: 'O my son, the holding (of the fast) is upon him.' I said: 'A woman upon whom was the fasting of two consecutive months, so she fasted and broke her fast during her days of menstruation.' He said: 'She makes them up.' I said: 'And if she made them up, then she despaired of menstruation.' He said: 'She does not repeat them; that suffices for her.'
And from him (al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl) from al-Nu'man ibn Suwayd from 'Asim ibn Humayd from Muhammad ibn Muslim from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) like that. Like that.

And Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from Ali, from Abu Basir, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about interrupting the fast of expiation for an oath, expiation for zihar, and expiation for blood (diyah). He said: If upon a man is the fasting of two consecutive months, and he breaks his fast or falls ill in the first month, it is upon him to restart the fasting. And if he fasts the first month and fasts some part of the second month, then an excuse befalls him for which he has a valid reason, then it is only upon him to make up (the missed days). The approach in these narrations is to interpret them as: if his illness is one that does not prevent him from fasting, although it causes him some difficulty, then whenever the matter is as we mentioned, it becomes obligatory upon him to restart (the two months) according to what these narrations imply. And it is also possible to interpret them as a type of recommendation (istihbab) rather than obligation (fard) and necessity (ijab).

The Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) informed me from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from his father from al-Saffar from Muhammad ibn Isa from al-Qasim al-Siqqal that he wrote to him: O our Master, a man vowed to fast one day for Allah, and during that day, intercourse with his wife occurred upon him, incurring the expiation (kaffarah). He asked for a ruling, and he was answered: He must fast one day in place of the vowed day, and free a believing slave.

As for what al-Saffar narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad and Abdullah ibn Muhammad from Ali ibn Mahziyar, who said: Bundar, the master of Idris, wrote: 'O my master, I vowed to fast every Saturday.' He wrote back and I read it: 'Do not leave it except due to an excuse, and you are not required to fast it during travel or illness unless you intended that. If you broke your fast in it without an excuse, then give charity for the count of each day to seven poor people. We ask Allah for success in what He loves and is pleased with.' So it does not contradict the first two reports, because the way to reconcile between them is that the expiation is only obligatory according to the capacity of the person. Whoever is able to free a slave, that is required of him; if he is unable, he feeds seven poor people; if he is unable to do that as well, there is nothing upon him. And thus we said regarding one who intentionally breaks a fast in the month of Ramadan, and upon this we have collected the reports.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from a number of our companions from Sahl ibn Ziyad from Ibn Mahbub from Umar ibn Yazid who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'What do you say regarding i'tikaf (seclusion for worship) in Baghdad, in some of its mosques?' He said, 'There is no i'tikaf except in a mosque of congregation where an upright Imam has prayed the congregational prayer.' And there is no objection to performing i'tikaf in the mosque of Kufa, the mosque of Medina, and the mosque of Mecca.
And in the narration of Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Faddal, from Muhammad ibn Ali, from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from Umar ibn Yazid, like that [previous narration]. And he added to it the mosque of Basra.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from a number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Dawud ibn Sirhan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: There is no I'tikaf (spiritual retreat) except in the last ten days of the month of Ramadan. And he said: Indeed, Ali (peace be upon him) used to say: I do not consider I'tikaf to be valid except in the Sacred Mosque (Mecca), or the Prophet's Mosque (Medina), or in a congregational mosque. And it is not fitting for the one in I'tikaf to leave the mosque except for a necessity that is unavoidable, then he should not sit [outside] until he returns. And the woman is the same [in this ruling].

Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Faddal from Muhammad ibn Ali from Ali ibn al-Nu'man from Abu al-Subah al-Kinani from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about al-I'tikaf (seclusion in mosque) in Ramadan during the ten days. He said: Indeed Ali (peace be upon him) used to say: I do not see al-I'tikaf except in the Sacred Mosque or the Messenger's Mosque or in a congregational mosque.
Ali ibn al-Hasan, from Ahmad ibn Sabih, from Ali ibn Ghurab, from Abu Abdillah, from his father, said: The one who performs i'tikaf performs it in the congregational mosque.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Fadala ibn Ayyub from Abdullah ibn Sinan who said: The one performing i'tikaf in Mecca may pray in whichever of its houses he wishes; it is the same for him whether he prays in the Mosque or in its houses, and this does not contradict the earlier reports which state that i'tikaf is not valid except in the specific places, because what this report entails is the permissibility of prayer in Mecca outside the Mosque, unlike i'tikaf, and this is not prevented, because in case of necessity, if a person leaves the Mosque in Mecca and the time for prayer enters him, it is permissible for him to pray in whichever place he wishes. But the ruling for other mosques is not like this, because it is not permissible for him to pray until he returns to the Mosque in which he performed i'tikaf, and this indicates that.

Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Fadhal narrated from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Najran from Abd Allah ibn Sinan from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I heard him say: The one who performs i'tikaf in Mecca may pray in whichever of its houses he wishes; it is the same for him whether in the Mosque or in its houses. And he said: I'tikaf is not valid elsewhere except in the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah or in a mosque of the congregation. And the one who performs i'tikaf may not pray in a house other than the mosque in which he has performed i'tikaf, except in Mecca, for he performs i'tikaf in Mecca wherever he wishes because all of it is a sanctuary. And the one who performs i'tikaf does not leave the mosque except for a need.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Abu Ali al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn al-Jabbar, from Safwan, from Mansur ibn Hazim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: The one performing i'tikaf in Mecca prays in whichever of its houses he wishes, and the one performing i'tikaf elsewhere does not pray except in the mosque that he has specified.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from the multitude of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Mahbub, from Abu Ayyub, from Abu Basir, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I'tikaf (seclusion in the mosque) is not valid for less than three days. Whoever performs I'tikaf must fast. It is appropriate for the one performing I'tikaf, when he enters it, to make a condition (of intention), just as the one who enters Ihram makes a condition.

Ali ibn al-Hasan, from Muhammad ibn Ali, from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from Umar ibn Yazeed, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: When the servant performs i'tikaf, he should fast. And he said: I'tikaf is not valid for less than three days. And stipulate with your Lord during your i'tikaf, just as you stipulate when entering ihram, that He releases you from your i'tikaf in the event of an occurrence, if a cause befalls you from the command of God.

Ali ibn al-Hasan, from Amr ibn Uthman, from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from Abu Ayyub, from Abu Ubaydah, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: The one in i'tikaf (seclusion in mosque) should not smell perfume, nor delight in basil (or pleasant scent), nor bargain, nor buy, nor sell. He said: Whoever performs i'tikaf for three days, on the fourth day he has the option: if he wishes, he adds more days, and if he wishes, he exits the mosque. But if he stays two days after the three, he does not exit the mosque until he completes three days. This report is predicated on the condition that he did not stipulate (a specific duration), because whoever is in such a state and stays two days, completing three days is obligatory upon him. And whoever stipulated (a specific duration), cancellation is permissible for him at any time he wishes, except that it is preferred for him, if two days have passed, to complete the three days. This indicates that.

Ali ibn al-Hasan, from Abu Ayyub, from al-Hasan, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said: If he performs i'tikaf for one day and has not stipulated (a condition for duration), then he may exit and break his i'tikaf. And if he stays for two days and has not stipulated, then he may not exit and break his i'tikaf until three days have passed.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from a number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Mahbub, from Abu Wallad al-Hannat, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a woman whose husband was absent; he returned while she was performing i'tikaf (spiritual retreat) in the mosque with his permission. She left the mosque upon hearing of his arrival and went to her house, preparing for her husband until they consummated the marriage. He said: If she left the mosque before three days had passed and she had not stipulated in her i'tikaf [that leaving for her husband does not break it], then she bears the same ruling as the one who performs kaffarat al-zhihar (expiation for zhihar).

From him, from several of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Najran, from Abd Allah ibn al-Mughira, from Sama'ah ibn Mihran, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the person in i'tikaf (seclusion in the mosque) who had intercourse with his wife, and he said: 'He is in the same position as one who broke his fast for a day in the month of Ramadan.'

Ali ibn al-Hasan, from Muhammad ibn Ali, from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from Ali ibn Ri'ab, from Zurarah, who said: I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about the one who performs i'tikaf (secludes himself in the mosque) and has sexual intercourse, so he said: If he does so, then upon him is what is upon the one who performs dhikr al-zhahir (expiation for divorcing by comparison to one's mother's back).

From him, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Najran, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Sama'ah ibn Mihran, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about a person performing i'tikaf (spiritual retreat) who had intercourse with his wife. He said: Upon him is what is upon the one who deliberately broke his fast for a day in the month of Ramadan: freeing a slave, or fasting two consecutive months, or feeding sixty poor people.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family), when it was the last ten days, would perform i'tikaf in the mosque, and a tent of hair was pitched for him, and he would roll up his apron and fold his bedding. Some said: 'And he abstained from the women.' Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'As for abstaining from the women, no; it does not contradict the earlier reports, because what is meant by his saying:

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from some of our companions from Muhammad ibn 'Isa from Ali ibn Bilal who said: I wrote to the man asking him about the Fitrah (alms of fasting) and how much should be paid. He wrote back: Six Artals of dates in the Madani measure, and that is nine Artals in the Baghdadi measure.

From him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Ja'far ibn Ibrahim ibn Muhammad al-Hamadani, and he was with us as a pilgrim, he said: I wrote to Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) via my father, 'May I be your ransom, our companions have differed regarding the Sa' (measure). Some say the Fitrah (alms of fasting) is paid with the Meccan Sa', and some say with the Iraqi Sa'. He wrote to me: 'The Sa is six Artals in the Meccan measure and nine Artals in the Iraqi measure.' He informed me that by weight it is one thousand and seventy mithqals.

Muhammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā narrated from Muhammad ibn ʿĪsā from Muhammad ibn al-Rayyān who said: I wrote to the man (Imam al-Ridha, peace be upon him) asking him about the Fitrah (alms of the body) and its zakat, how much should be paid? He wrote back: Four Artals measured with the Madani measure. The explanation of this report is one of two things: Either he meant four Amadds (a smaller unit of volume) and it was misread by the narrator as Artals, and we have presented this earlier; or he meant four Artals from milk and Aqit (dried curds), because whoever's staple food is that, this amount is obligatory from it. The mention of this has preceded, and this adds clarification.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Ibrahim ibn Hashim, who said: Abu al-Hasan Ali ibn Sulayman narrated to us, from al-Hasan ibn Ali, from al-Qasim ibn al-Hasan, who raised it to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: He was asked about a man from the desert who is unable to give the fidyah (ransom for missing fasting), so he said: Let him give charity of four artals of milk.

Ahmad ibn 'Abdun narrated to me from Abu al-Hasan Ali ibn Muhammad ibn al-Zubayr, from Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Faddal, from Ya'qub ibn Yazid, from Abu Hammam, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi 'Abdillah, from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) who said: Fasting the Day of 'Arafah is equivalent to a year [of fasting], and he said: Al-Hasan (peace be upon him) did not fast it, but Al-Husayn (peace be upon him) fasted it.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Sulayman al-Ja'fari said: I heard Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) saying: 'My father used to fast on the Day of 'Arafah while standing at the station (of 'Arafah) on a hot day, and he would order a high shade to be set up for him, so he would perform ritual bath from the heat that reached him.'

Ali ibn al-Hasan from Muhammad and Ahmad, the two sons of al-Hasan, from their father, from Thalabah ibn Maymun, from Muhammad ibn Qays, who said: I heard Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) saying: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) did not fast the Day of Arafah since the fasting of the month of Ramadan was revealed. So this does not contradict the first two narrations, because the narration only implies that the Prophet (peace be upon him) did not fast it, and it is permissible that the Prophet (peace be upon him) did so due to an excuse, even though it has merit, because the merit of fasting this day is specific to one who is strong upon it and it does not weaken him from supplication and asking [of God]. For it is a day of supplication and asking. As for one who is not strong upon it, it is better for him to break the fast. This indicates that.

Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Fadhal narrated from Amr ibn Uthman from Hanan ibn Sadir from his father from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about fasting the Day of Arafah, and I said, 'May I be your ransom, they claim that it equals the fasting of a year.' He said, 'My father did not fast it.' I said, 'And why is that?' He said, 'Indeed, the Day of Arafah is a day of supplication and asking, and I fear that it will weaken me from supplication, and I dislike that I fast it, and I fear that the Day of Arafah might be the Day of Eid (Al-Adha), so it is not a day of fasting.'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Fadala, from Aban ibn Uthman, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about fasting the Day of 'Arafah. He said: 'If you are strong enough for it, it is good, provided it does not prevent you from supplication, for it is a day of supplication and asking [of God]. So fast it, but if you fear that you will become weak to do so, then do not fast it.'
From him, from Ya'qub ibn Yazid, from Abu Hammam, from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) who said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) fasted on the day of 'Ashura.

Sa'd ibn Abdillah, from Abu Ja'far, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Abdillah, from Abdillah ibn Maymun al-Qaddah, from Ja'far, from his father (peace be upon them), said: Fasting the day of Ashura is an expiation for a year.

From him, from Al-Hasan ibn Ali Al-Hashimi, from Muhammad ibn Musa, from Ya'qub ibn Yazid, from Al-Wassah, who said: Najiyyah ibn Al-Harith Al-Attar narrated to me. He said: I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about the fasting of the day of Ashura, and he said: It is a discontinued fast with the descent of the month of Ramadan, and that which is discontinued is an innovation. Najiyyah said: Then I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about that after his father, and he answered me with the same answer as his father. Then he said: Indeed, it is the fasting of a day for which no Book was revealed and no Sunnah was established, except the Sunnah of the family of Ziyad regarding the killing of Al-Husayn (peace be upon him).

From him, from Al-Hasan ibn Ali Al-Hashimi, from Muhammad ibn Isa ibn Ubayd, who said: My brother Ja'far ibn Isa narrated to me, saying: I asked Al-Imam Al-Rida (peace be upon him) about the fasting of Ashura and what people say about it. He said: The fasting of Ibn Marjanah is what you are asking me about. It is a day that the claimants from the family of Ziyad fasted for the killing of Al-Husayn (peace be upon him). It is a day that the family of Muhammad (peace be upon him) consider unlucky, and the people of Islam consider unlucky. The day that Islam and its people consider unlucky is not fasted and is not blessed. Monday is a day in which Allah took His Prophet (peace be upon him), and the family of Muhammad (peace be upon him) were afflicted only on Monday, so we considered it unlucky, but our enemies considered it blessed. On the day of Ashura, Al-Husayn (peace be upon him) was killed, and Ibn Marjanah considered it blessed, and the family of Muhammad (peace be upon him) consider it unlucky. So whoever fasts them or considers them blessed will meet Allah, Almighty and Majestic, with a changed heart, and his gathering place will be with those who instituted their fasting and considered them blessed.

From him, from Al-Hasan ibn Ali Al-Hashimi, from Muhammad ibn Isa, who said: Muhammad ibn Abi Umair narrated to us from Zayd al-Rassi, who narrated to us from Ubayd ibn Zurarah, who said: I heard Zurarah asking Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the fasting of the day of Ashura. He (peace be upon him) said: Whoever fasts it, his portion from fasting that day is the portion of Ibn Marjanah and the family of Ziyad. I said: And what is their portion from that day? He said: The Fire (Hell). The way to reconcile these narrations is what our Sheikh (may God have mercy on him) used to say: Whoever fasts the day of Ashura on the path of grief due to the calamity of the family of Muhammad (peace be upon him) and the distress over what befell his progeny, he has succeeded. And whoever fasts it based on what our opponents believe regarding the virtue of its fasting, seeking blessings in it, and believing in its barakah and happiness, he has sinned and erred.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad, from al-Washsha', from Hammad ibn 'Uthman, from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I heard him (peace be upon him) say: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) fasted until it was said, 'He does not break his fast,' then he broke his fast until it was said, 'He does not fast,' then he fasted the fast of David (peace be upon him): one day and one night (or one day and one night of rest), then he was commanded to fast three days in the month. He said: 'The fast of the whole year is equal to it, and it removes the heat of the chest.' Hammad said: I said, 'What is the heat of the chest?' He said, 'The heat of the chest is the whispering (of Satan).' Hammad said: I said, 'Which are the days?' He said: 'The first Thursday of the month, the first Wednesday after the tenth, and the last Thursday of it.' I said to him, 'Why did these days become the ones that are fasted?' He said: 'Indeed, those before us from the nations, when punishment was sent down upon one of them, it would descend on these fearful days.'

Sa'd ibn Abdillah, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad al-Jawhari, from Ali ibn Abi Hamzah, from Abu Basir, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the fasting of the Sunnah, so he said: Fasting the three days of every month: Thursday, Wednesday, and Thursday, removes the clots of the heart and the heat of the chest. (He repeated) Thursday, Wednesday, and Thursday. And if he wishes, (he may fast) Monday, Wednesday, and Thursday. And if he wishes, he may fast one day in every ten days, for that is thirty good deeds. And if he wishes to increase, let him increase.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from al-Husayn ibn Muhammad from Muhammad ibn 'Imran from Ziyad al-Qandi from 'Abd Allah ibn Sinan who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to me: If there are two Thursdays at the beginning of the month, then fast the first of them, for it is superior. And if there are two Thursdays at its end, then fast the last of them, for it is superior.

And regarding what Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from al-Husayn ibn Muhammad ibn 'Imran al-Ash'ari from Zur'a from Sama'ah from Abu Basir, who said: I asked him about fasting three days in the month, so he said: In every ten days, Thursday, Wednesday, and Thursday; and in the following month, Wednesday, Thursday, and Wednesday. This does not contradict the earlier reports because the person is free to choose between fasting Wednesday between two Thursdays, or fasting Thursday between two Wednesdays. Whichever he acts upon is permissible, as indicated by that.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Musa ibn Ja'far al-Mada'ini, from Ibrahim ibn Isma'il ibn Dawud, who said: I asked al-Rida (peace be upon him) about fasting, and he said: 'Three days in the month: Wednesday, Thursday, and Friday.' I said: 'Indeed, our companions fast on Wednesday between two Thursdays.' He said: 'There is no objection to that, and there is no objection to Thursday between two Wednesdays.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from a number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad and Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father, all from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Salama, the companion of al-Sabiri, from Abu al-Subah al-Kinani, who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: Fasting the month of Sha'ban and the month of Ramadan consecutively is an expiation (or act of repentance) from Allah, the Exalted.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Al-Husayn ibn Alwan from 'Amr ibn Khalid from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) used to fast in Sha'ban and the month of Ramadan, connecting them, and he would forbid the people from connecting them. And he would say: 'They are the two months of Allah, and they are expiation for what is before them and what is after them.'

Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Faddal, from Muhassin ibn Ahmad, and Muhammad ibn al-Walid, and Umar ibn Uthman, and Sindiyy ibn Muhammad, all of them from Yunus ibn Ya'qub, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: And I asked him about the fasting of Sha'ban, so I said to him, 'May I be your ransom, did one of your fathers fast in Sha'ban?' He said, 'The best of my fathers is the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family); his most frequent fasting was in Sha'ban.' And we have cited a good portion of the narrations regarding the virtue of Sha'ban in our book Al-Kabir. As for what has been narrated regarding the dislike of fasting in Sha'ban and the prohibition from it, and that none of the Imams (peace be upon them) fasted it, the explanation is that none of the Imams (peace be upon them) fasted it in this specific manner. Because its fasting is treated like the fasting of the month of Ramadan in terms of obligation and necessity, for some people said that its fasting is obligatory, and Abu al-Khattab, Muhammad ibn Abi Zaynab (may Allah curse him) and his companions went along with this, saying that whoever breaks his fast for one day in it incurs the same expiation as one who breaks his fast for a day in Ramadan. So criticism came from them (peace be upon them) regarding this, and that none of the Imams (peace be upon them) fasted it in this manner. And the narrations that included encouragement for separation between the months of Ramadan and Sha'ban, the meaning in them is the prohibition of Sawm al-Wisal (continuous fasting), which we explained in our book Al-Kabir as being forbidden, and it is that one fasts two consecutive days without breaking the fast at night. And this is indicated by that.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Muhammad from some of his companions from Muhammad ibn Sulayman from his father who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'What do you say about a man who fasts in Sha'ban and the month of Ramadan?' He said, 'They are the two months that Allah, the Exalted, said: two consecutive months, as a repentance from Allah.' I said, 'So he does not separate between them?' He said, 'If he breaks the fast during the night, that is a separation.' And the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) said, 'No continuous fasting (Wisal) in fasting,' meaning a man does not fast two consecutive days without breaking the fast. And it is recommended for the servant not to leave the pre-dawn meal (Suhoor). The book of Fasting from al-Istibsar is completed.
