Musa ibn al-Qasim from al-Mu'afa ibn Wahb from al-Saffan from al-'Ala' ibn Muhammad from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I said to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), regarding His Exalted's saying: 'For those who can afford it, there is a duty to carry out to the House of God,' he said: 'He must have what enables him to perform Hajj.' I said: 'If Hajj is presented to him and he feels shy (of the cost/effort),' he said: 'He is among those who can afford it, and why should he feel shy? Even if it is on a single-humped camel.' He said: 'If he is able to walk part of the way and ride part of the way, let him do so.'

Al-Husayn ibn Said from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad from Ali from Abu Basir said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'And for God upon people is the pilgrimage to the House, whoever is able to find a way to it.' He said: 'He goes out and walks, if he does not have what he rides.' I said: 'He cannot manage walking.' He said: 'He walks and rides.' I said: 'He cannot manage that, meaning walking.' He said: 'He serves the people and goes out with them.'

From him, from Fadala ibn Ayyub, from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who has a debt; is it upon him to perform Hajj? He said: Yes. Indeed, the Hajj of Islam is obligatory upon every Muslim who is able to walk. And indeed, most of those who performed Hajj with the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) did so on foot. And indeed, he (peace be upon him and his family) passed by Kura' al-Ghaim, and they complained to him of exhaustion and hardship, so he said: 'Tighten your girdles and walk slowly,' so they did that and it went away from them. So do not see a contradiction between these two reports and the earlier reports, because the explanation for them is one of two things: One is that they are to be understood as referring to recommendation (istihbab), because whoever is able to walk is recommended to perform Hajj, and if it is not obligatory, he incurs punishment for leaving it, and the utterance of the name of obligation upon it is a form of concession. And we have already explained that what is strongly recommended is permissible to be called obligatory even if it is not a duty. And the second explanation is that they are to be understood as a form of precautionary piety (taqiyyah), because that is the view of some of the Sunnis, and that which indicates that the Hajj of the debtor (mu'sir) does not suffice for him if he becomes wealthy is the Hajj of Islam.

Sahl ibn Ziyad narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Abdullah ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Asam, from Mis'a ibn Abd al-Malik, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: If a slave performed Hajj ten times, the obligation of Hajj of Islam would still remain upon him if he had the means to do so. And if a boy (who was not yet of age) performed Hajj for ten years, then reached puberty, the obligation of Hajj of Islam would be upon him. And if a slave performed Hajj ten times, then was freed, the obligation of Hajj of Islam would be upon him if he had the means to do so.

First: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Safwan and Fadala from Abd Allah ibn Sinan from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'God is not worshipped by anything more enduring than walking, nor is there anything superior.' Second: Musa ibn al-Qasim from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad from al-Halabi said: 'I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the virtue of walking, so he said: Indeed, Al-Hasan ibn Ali (peace be upon him) made a pact with his Lord three times, until [he received] a pair of sandals, a pair of sandals, a garment, a garment, a dinar, a dinar, and [the reward of] Hajj for twenty pilgrimages, walking on his feet.' Third: From him [Musa ibn al-Qasim] from Fadl ibn Amr from Muhammad ibn Ismail ibn Rajaa' al-Zabiri from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'God is not worshipped by anything superior to walking.' Fourth: As for what Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa narrated from Al-Hasan ibn Ali from Rifa'a, who said: 'A man asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): Is riding superior or walking?' He said: 'Riding is superior to walking because the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) rode.' Fifth: And what Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from Ibn Abi Umayr from Saif al-Tammarr said: 'I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): It reached us that we were walking from you that year, and that you say regarding riding...' He said: 'Indeed, people perform Hajj walking and riding.' I said: 'I am not asking you about this.' He said: 'What are you asking me about?' I said: 'Which is more beloved to you, that we walk or ride?' He said: 'Riding is more beloved to me, for that is stronger for supplication and worship.' Thus, the resolution between these two narrations is that whoever is strong in walking and is not weakened by it from supplication and rituals, or who has brought with him something to ride if exhausted, then walking is superior for him over riding. And whoever is weakened by walking and does not have what to resort to for riding when exhausted, then it is not permissible for him to depart except as a rider, according to what was explained in the narration. And this meaning is also indicated by what Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from Safwan from Abd Allah ibn Bukayr, who said: 'I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): We intend to depart to Mecca.' He said: 'Do not walk, but ride.' I said: 'May God perfect you, it reached us that Al-Hasan ibn Ali (peace be upon

And Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa narrated this meaning from al-Hasan ibn Ali from Hisham ibn Salim, who said: We entered upon Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), myself and 'Anbasah ibn Mus'ab and more than ten of our companions, and we said: 'May we be your ransom, which is better: walking or riding?' He said: 'Nothing is worshipped by God that is better than walking.' We said: 'Which is better: that we ride to Mecca and hasten, so we stay there until the walker arrives, or we walk?' He said: 'Riding is better.'

First: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Humayd ibn Ziyad, from Ibn Sama'ah, from a number of our companions, from Aban ibn Uthman, from al-Fadl ibn Abd al-Malik, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who had no wealth, and a group of his companions financed his pilgrimage; does he fulfill the obligation of Hajj al-Islam? He said: Yes. And if he becomes wealthy afterwards, he must perform Hajj again. I asked: Is his Hajj complete or deficient, if it was not from his own wealth? He said: Yes, the obligation of Hajj al-Islam is fulfilled for him, and it is complete, not deficient. If he becomes wealthy, let him perform Hajj. Second: As for what al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Fadalah ibn Ayyub, from Mu'awiyah ibn 'Ammar, who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): A man who had no wealth, and a brother financed his pilgrimage, does that suffice for him as Hajj al-Islam, or is it deficient? He said: No, it is a complete Hajj. This does not contradict the first report which stated that he must repeat Hajj if he becomes wealthy, because he only informed us that his Hajj is complete, and there is no disagreement that it is complete, and he deserves reward for its performance. As for his statement in the first report: 'and he has fulfilled the obligation of Hajj al-Islam,' the meaning is the Hajj that was recommended for him during his period of poverty. That is expressed as Hajj al-Islam, insofar as it was the first Hajj. And the report does not say that if he becomes wealthy he is not required to perform Hajj, but it explicitly states that if he becomes wealthy, let him perform Hajj. And that is consistent with the sound principles indicated by the evidence and reports.

1- Musa ibn al-Qasim from Muhammad ibn Sahl from Adam ibn Ali from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) who said: Whoever performs Hajj on behalf of a person who does not have the wealth to perform it, it suffices for him until God grants him the means to perform it and Hajj becomes obligatory upon him. 2- Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from a number of our companions from Ahmad ibn Muhammad and Sahl ibn Ziyad, all of them, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr from Ali ibn Abi Hamzah from Abu Basir from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: If a poor man were performed Hajj on his behalf by another man, it would count as one Hajj for him; and when he becomes wealthy afterwards, Hajj becomes obligatory upon him. 3- As for what Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Ibn Abi Umayr from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who performed Hajj on behalf of another; does that suffice for him for the Hajj of Islam? He said: Yes. I said: Is the Hajj of the wealthy person complete or incomplete? He said: Complete. I said: Is the Hajj of the poor person complete or incomplete? He said: Complete. So it does not contradict the first two narrations, because his saying 'it suffices for him for the Hajj of Islam' refers to the Hajj that is recommended in the state of poverty, not the one that is obligatory upon him in the state of wealth, because that latter one can be expressed as the Hajj of Islam as we have clarified.

1- Musa ibn al-Qasim from Safwan and Ibn Abi Umayr from Umar ibn Udhaynah from Burayd ibn Muawiya al-Ajli said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who performed Hajj while he did not know this matter (Imamate), then God granted him knowledge and devotion to it. Is the Hajj of Islam obligatory upon him, or has he fulfilled his duty? He said: He has fulfilled his duty, and if he performed again, it would be more beloved to me. I asked him about a man who performed while he was from one of the categories of the People of the Qibla, a Nasib (devout but not of the Ahl al-Bayt), then God granted him and he knew this matter. Does he fulfill the Hajj of Islam? He said: He fulfills it, it is more beloved to me. And he said: Every deed he performed while in the state of his Nasib and misguidance, then God granted him and he was made to know the Wilayah, he is rewarded for it except for Zakat, for he returns it, because he placed it in its non-places, because it is for the People of the Wilayah. As for the Prayer, Hajj, and Fasting, there is no need for him to make them up. 2- As for what Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from a number of our companions from Sahl ibn Ziyad from Ali ibn Mahziyar who said: Ibrahim ibn Muhammad ibn Imran al-Hamadani wrote to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) saying: I performed Hajj while I was opposing (the Wilayah), and I was single, so I entered performing Tamattu' with Umrah to Hajj. He wrote to him: Repeat your Hajj. 3- And what he also narrated from Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from a number of our companions from Ahmad ibn Muhammad and Sahl ibn Ziyad together from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr from Ali ibn Abi Hamzah from Abu Basir from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Nasibi, when he knows (the Wilayah), upon him is the Hajj. And if he had already performed, the ruling in these two narrations is a type of preference (Istihbab) rather than obligation (Fard/Ijbab). And Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) explicitly stated this in the narration of Burayd al-Ajli in his saying: 'He has fulfilled his duty, and if he performed, it would be more beloved to me.' And this also indicates it. 4- What Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Ibn Abi Umayr from Umar ibn Udhaynah who said: I wrote to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) asking him about a man who performed while he did not know and was un
Musa ibn al-Qasim from Ali ibn Ja'far from his brother Musa ibn Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: The slave, if he performs Hajj and then is freed, then upon him is the re-performance of Hajj.
Muawiya ibn 'Ammar said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'A slave who is freed on the Day of 'Arafah.' He said: 'If one attains one of the two stations, then he has attained the Hajj.'

This issue has no disagreement among the Muslims, and there is consensus that the obligation of Hajj is a single payment. We have included some of the narrations regarding this in our Great Book, and therefore we have not included them here. 1. As for what Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Muhammad ibn Sinan from Hudhayfah ibn Mansur from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: God, the Mighty and Majestic, made Hajj obligatory upon the wealthy every year. 2. From him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya from Ya'qub ibn Yazid from Ibn Abi Umayr from Abu Jarir al-Qummi from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Hajj is obligatory upon the wealthy every year. 3. And Ali ibn Ja'far narrated from his brother Musa ibn Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: Indeed, God the Exalted made Hajj obligatory upon the wealthy every year. And this is His saying, the Mighty and Majestic: 'And to God belongs the pilgrimage to the House for whoever is able to find a way to it.' And whoever disbelieves, then indeed God is free of need of the worlds. He said: I said, 'And whoever among us does not perform Hajj has disbelieved?' He said: 'No, but whoever says that this is not so has disbelieved.' Therefore, the interpretation of these narrations is one of two things: either they are to be understood as recommending (mustahabb) rather than obligatory (fard/wajib), or the meaning is that for every year, in the manner of substitution (badal), because whoever upon whom Hajj became obligatory in the first year and did not perform it, it becomes obligatory upon him in the second year, and likewise if he did not perform it in the second year, it becomes obligatory upon him in the third year. And thus is the ruling for every year until he performs it, and it was not meant that he is obligated in every year in the manner of repetition.

1- Musa ibn al-Qasim from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad from al-Halabi who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): A man vowed to walk to the House of Allah (Exalted and Mighty), and he became unable to walk. He said: Let him ride and offer a camel, for that will suffice for him if Allah knows effort from him. 2- From him from Safwan and Ibn Abi Umayr from Dharih al-Muharibi who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who swore to perform Hajj on foot, and he became unable to do so and could not manage it. He said: Let him ride and offer the sacrifice. 3- As for what Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Ali ibn Ri'ab from Abu Ubaydah al-Hadda' who said: I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about a man who vowed to walk to Mecca barefoot. He said: Indeed, the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) went out for Hajj and looked at a woman walking among the camels. He said: Who is this? They said: The sister of Uqbah ibn Amir, who vowed to walk to Mecca barefoot. The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: O Uqbah, go to your sister and tell her to ride, for Allah is富 from her walking and her bare feet. She rode. 4- From him from Ibn Abi Umayr from Rifa'ah ibn Musa al-Nakhas who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): A man vowed to walk to the House of Allah. He said: Let him walk. I said: But he becomes weary. He said: When he becomes weary, let him ride. Do not see a contradiction between these two narrations and the first two regarding the obligation of expiation for the one who rides, because the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) did not say: Tell her to ride and there is no sin upon her. Rather, he ordered her to ride so that it would not be said that this is not permissible in any state. And if expiation is required alongside that due to the context of the camel, as explained in the first two narrations.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from Yunus ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'We do not know of any Hajj for Allah other than Al-Mut'ah. When we meet our Lord, we will say: We acted according to Your Book and the Sunnah of Your Prophet. And the people will say: We acted according to our own opinion. So Allah will place us and them wherever He wills.'

From him, from several of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from Safwan al-Jammal, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Whoever does not have his offering (hady) with him and performs Hajj al-Ifrad with a preference over Hajj al-Tamattu', he has preferred (disliked) the religion of Allah. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: All these narrations indicate that the obligatory duty upon the accountable person in Hajj is Tamattu' rather than Ifrad and Qiran. Therefore, whoever performs Ifrad or Qiran while having the ability to perform Tamattu', that does not suffice him as the Hajj of Islam. We said this because these narrations contain the command to perform Tamattu'; so whoever does not perform Tamattu' has not done what he was commanded to do. And because they (the Imams) attributed the practice of Tamattu' to the Book of Allah and the Sunnah, and the practice of other forms to opinions and desires. And every action that contradicts the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger (peace be upon him and his family) does not suffice for what Allah Almighty imposed upon the people. Furthermore, they have clarified in some of the narrations we presented earlier that Ifrad in Hajj is from the opinion of Umar, and the saying of Umar is not a proof in Islamic jurisprudence. They also mentioned that they do not know for Allah any Hajj other than Tamattu'. This phrase indicates that whoever does not perform Tamattu' while having the ability, it does not suffice him as the Hajj of Islam. As for when the state is one of necessity and he is not able to perform Tamattu' therein, then there is no harm in restricting himself to Qiran and Ifrad. This indicates that.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Ibn Muskān, from Abd al-Malik ibn 'Amr, that he asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about Tamattu', so he said: I said: He performed Hajj al-Qada (compensatory Hajj), that he had performed Hajj al-Tamattu' in that year or after it. I said: May Allah make you prosperous, I asked you and you ordered me to perform Tamattu', yet I see that you have performed Hajj al-Qada this year. He said: By Allah, the merit is in what I ordered you to do, but I am weak, so the two circumambulations (Tawaf) between As-Safa and Al-Marwah were difficult for me, therefore I performed Hajj al-Qada.

Ali ibn al-Sindi, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Jamil, said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'I never entered [the state of Ihram for Hajj] except as a Mutamatti', except in this year. For by Allah, I do not finish the Sa'i until my molars are chattering [from hunger/exertion], and the 'Adh' you performed is superior. If it is said: 'How do they say that the obligatory act is Tamattu', while they have divided Hajj into three types: Tamattu', Ifrad, and Qiran?' Then, if the matter were as you claim, this division would have no benefit.'

That was narrated by Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: Hajj is of three types: Ifrad, Qiran, and Tamattu' (with Umrah to Hajj). And the Prophet of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) commanded with it, and the virtue is in it, so we do not command the people except with it.

From him, from Abu Ali al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn al-Jabbar, from Safwan, from Isḥaq ibn 'Ammar, from Mansur al-Siqalli, who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: Hajj with us is upon three forms: a Mutamatti' pilgrim, and a Mufrid pilgrim who brings his Hadi (sacrificial animal), and a Mufrid pilgrim for Hajj alone. It was said: There is nothing in these two narrations that contradicts what we have previously mentioned, because they divided Hajj into three types for all the obligated people, then distinguished each group from them with a specific obligation. Thus, the obligation for one who is distant from the Haram is Tamattu', and the obligation for one who resides in the Haram is either Ifrad or Qiran. For this reason, he said in the first narration: 'And by it commanded the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family), and we command the people only by it,' meaning those who are distant from the Haram from among the people of the lands. So if it were said: 'If the command were as you mentioned, there would be no benefit in their preferring Tamattu' over other types of Hajj,' because its superiority over others only exists if it equals them in sufficiency and in being an act of obedience for which reward is earned, and adds to it. But if the obligation is Tamattu' alone, there is no basis for preferring it over other types of Hajj.

That was narrated by Sa'd ibn Abd Allah from Ya'qub ibn Yazid from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hafs ibn al-Bakhtari and al-Hasan ibn Abd al-Malik from Zurara, all from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: Al-Mut'ah, by God, is the best; with it the Quran was revealed, and with it the Sunnah proceeded. And from him (Abu Abdillah) from Ya'qub ibn Yazid from Ibn Abi Umayr from Abu Ayyub Ibrahim ibn Isa, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'Which type of Hajj is best?' He said, 'Al-Mut'ah.' And how could anything be better than it, while the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) says: 'If I could reverse my matter from what I have concluded, I would do as the people did.'

Muhammad ibn al-Qasim narrated from Safwan and Ibn Abi Umayr and others from Abdullah ibn Sinan, who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'I combined [the Umrah and Hajj] this year and brought the sacrificial animal.' He said: 'Why did you do that? The Tamattu' is better, by Allah. Do not return [to doing Qiran].'
Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Ibn Abi Umayr from Abu Ayyub al-Kazzaz who said:

Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from Safwan ibn Yahya, and Hammad ibn Isa, and Ibn Abi Umayr, and Ibn al-Mughira, from Muawiya ibn Ammar, who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), while we were in Medina: 'I have performed the Umrah of Rajab, and I intend to perform Hajj, so should I send the sacrificial animal (Hady) and perform Hajj al-Ifrad, or perform Hajj al-Tamattu?' He said: 'In each there is merit, and each is good.' I said: 'Which of them is superior?' He said: 'Indeed, Ali (peace be upon him) used to say that for every month, Umrat Tamattu' is superior, and by God, it is superior.' Then he said: 'Indeed, the people of Mecca say that his Umrah was Iraqi and his Hajj was Meccan, and they are lying. Is he not bound to his Hajj? He does not depart until he completes it.'

From him, from Safwan and Ibn Abi Umayr, from Yazid and Yunus ibn Dhabyan, who said: We asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who enters into ihram in the month of Rajab or in the month of Ramadan, so when the time for Hajj arrives, he performs Hajj al-Tamattu'. He said: 'There is no harm in that.' And we have fully covered what relates to this chapter in our Great Book, and what we have mentioned is sufficient, if God wills.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from a number of our companions from Sahl ibn Ziyad from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr from Muthanna from Zurara from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: Hajj is in known months: Shawwal, Dhu al-Qi'dah, and Dhu al-Hijjah. No one may enter the state of Ihram for Hajj in any other time, and no one may enter Ihram before the time designated by the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family). The example of this is like one who prays four rak'ahs during travel and leaves the two (rak'ahs).

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from a number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a man who performs the ritual bath for Ihram, then sleeps before entering the state of Ihram. He said: He must repeat the ritual bath.

From him, from several of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from Ali ibn Abi Hamzah, who said: I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about a man who performed the ritual bath for Ihram, then slept before entering the state of Ihram. He said: He must repeat the ritual bath.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Safwan from al-'Iyyas ibn al-Qasim said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who performs the ritual bath for Ihram in Medina, wears two garments, and then sleeps before entering the state of Ihram. He said: 'There is no obligatory bath upon him.' Therefore, it does not contradict the two previous narrations, because he (peace be upon him) only said there is no obligatory bath, and he did not negate the bath from him as a recommended and preferred act.

Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from Ali ibn Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: I asked my brother Musa ibn Ja'far (peace be upon him) about whether the Muhrim (person in Ihram) may wear a garment saturated with saffron. He said: If there is no perfume in it, there is no harm. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: This report is a concession (rukhsah), but leaving it is better.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa narrated from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Abu al-Faraj, from Aban ibn Taghlib, who said: He asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), his brother while I was present, about the garment that is dyed with safflower and then washed; should one wear it while in ihram? He said: Yes, safflower is not perfume, but I dislike that you wear what makes you conspicuous to people.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Nasr, from Najih, from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him), who said: There is no harm in the Muhrim (person in Ihram) wearing a ring.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Ibrahim ibn Mahziyar from al-Salih ibn al-Sandiy from Ibn Mahbub from al-'Ali from al-Mismaa, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) regarding a man who forgot to shave or trim [his hair/nails] until he departed [for Hajj]. He [the Imam] said: He shaves if he remembers while on the road or wherever he is. I asked him: Does the Muhrim wear the ring? He said: He does not wear it for adornment.

Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from Ali ibn Abi Hamzah, from Abu Basir, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: One prays six rak'at for the Ihram, entering into Ihram after the last of them, and this does not contradict what has been narrated.

Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from Safwan, from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: When you intend to enter the state of Ihram outside the time of a mandatory prayer, pray two rak'ahs and then enter Ihram after them, because the meaning in the first narration is one of excellence and preference, and this narration is understood as referring to the minimum amount of prayer sufficient for entering Ihram.

Abu al-Qasim Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Qulawayh narrated from his father, from Sa'd ibn Abdillah, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yunus, from Ishaq ibn Ammar al-Sayrafi, who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'May I be your ransom, what do you say regarding the Fitrah (alms of fasting)? Is it permissible for me to pay it in silver at the value of these specific items that you have mentioned?' He said, 'Yes, indeed that is more beneficial for him.'

Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Faddal, from Thalabah ibn Maymun, from Ishaq ibn Ammar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: There is no harm in the Qimah (payment in kind) for Fitrah (Zakat al-Fitr).

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Sulayman ibn Ja'far al-Marwazi, who said: I heard him say: If you do not find someone to place the Fitrah (Zakat al-Fitr) upon, then set it aside at that moment before the prayer. The charity is a sa' of dates, or its value in that land in dirhams.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn al-Fudayl, from Abu al-Subah al-Kinani, who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): What do you think if a man entered into the state of Ihram after a non-obligatory prayer, would that suffice for him? He said: Yes.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) that he said: The Ihram (entering the state of ritual consecration for Hajj) is not valid except after a prescribed (fard) prayer. If you enter Ihram after it, following the Taslim (conclusion), then the meaning in this narration is excellence and recommendation, because it is most excellent for a person to enter Ihram immediately after a obligatory prayer, as the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) did. And the most excellent of the obligatory prayers is that it be after the Dhuhr prayer. And that which indicates this is that Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, the narrator of this hadith, narrated after quoting this report what the Imam (peace be upon him) said: 'And if it is a voluntary prayer, you pray two rak'ahs and enter Ihram after them.' So we know that he meant by the first (narration) what we mentioned of excellence, otherwise it would be contradictory. And that which indicates this also...

Musa ibn al-Qasim from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad from al-Halabi said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): Did the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) enter the state of Ihram at night or during the day or at night? He said: Rather, during the day. I said: At which hour? He said: After the Dhuhr prayer.

From him, from Safwan, from Mu'awiya, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: When you intend to enter the state of Ihram at a time other than that of an obligatory prayer, pray two rak'ahs, then enter Ihram after them.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Ibn Abi 'Umayr from Hammad ibn 'Uthman from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: I said to him, 'I intend to perform Umrah with the right of enjoyment until Hajj; so what should I say?' He said, 'You should say: O Allah, I intend to perform Umrah with the right of enjoyment until Hajj, according to Your Book and the Sunnah of Your Prophet (SAWW). And if you wish, you can keep in mind what you intend.'

From him, from Hammad, from Ibrahim ibn Umar, from Abu Ayyub, who said: Abu al-Subbah, the freedman of Bassam al-Sayrafi, narrated to me, saying: I intended to enter into Ihram for Tamattu' (the Hajj of Tamattu'), so I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'How should I say?' He said, 'You should say: O Allah, I intend to perform the Tamattu' of Umrah until Hajj, according to Your Book and the Sunnah of Your Prophet. And if you wish, you may keep silent (intend) what you desire.'

And from him, from al-Nuḍr ibn Suwayd, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Sinān, and from Ḥammād, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Mughīrah, from Ibn Sinān, from Abū ʿAbd Allāh (peace be upon him), who said: When you intend to enter into iḥrām and perform tamattuʿ, say: 'O God, I intend what You have commanded regarding the performance of ʿumrah followed by ḥajj; facilitate that for me and accept it from me.'

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from Ibn Abi Nasr, from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about a man performing Tamattu', what should he do? He said: He intends the 'Umrah and enters into Ihram for the Hajj.

Musa ibn al-Qasim from Ibn Abi Umayr from Abd Allah ibn Muskān from Abū Basīr who said: I asked Abū 'Abdillāh (peace be upon him) about a man who stipulates in his Hajj that if he is prevented, he is exempt; is the Hajj obligatory upon him for the following year? He said: Yes.

From him, from Muhammad ibn al-Fudayl, from Abu al-Subah al-Kinani, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who stipulates a condition during Hajj. How does he stipulate? He said: He says when he intends to enter the state of Ihram: 'Release me from my obligation where you detain me, and if you detain me, then it is Umrah.' I said to him: 'Then is Haj obligatory upon him next year?' He said: 'Yes.' And Safwan said: 'Several of our companions have narrated this narration, all of them say: Indeed, Haj is obligatory upon him next year.'

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Jamil ibn Salih from Dharih al-Muharibi who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who performed Umrah until Hajj (Tamattu') and was prevented after entering the state of Ihram, what should he do? He said: Did he not stipulate to his Lord before entering Ihram that his release from Ihram would be upon any incident that befalls him from Allah's command? I said: Yes, he did stipulate that. He said: Let him return to his family, free (from the obligation of Hajj), there is no sin upon him, for Allah is more deserving to fulfill what was stipulated upon Him. I said: Then is Hajj obligatory upon him next year? He said: No. The meaning in this report is that we interpret it as: if his Hajj is voluntary (Nafl), Hajj is not obligatory upon him next year. But if it is the Hajj of Islam (Fard), then Hajj is necessary next year, according to what the earlier narrations contained.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from a number of our companions from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd from Abd Allah ibn Sinan from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) regarding a man performing Tamattu' who forgot to shorten his hair until he entered the state of Ihram for Hajj, he said: He seeks forgiveness of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

From him, from Abu Ali al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn al-Jabbar, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, who said: I asked Abu Ibrahim (peace be upon him) about a man who performed Tamattu' (combining Umrah and Hajj) by entering into Ihram for Hajj after Umrah, entered Mecca, performed Tawaf and Sa'i, put on his clothes, and exited Ihram, but forgot to shorten his prayer (of four rak'ahs) until he went out to Arafat. He said: There is no harm with him. He builds upon the Umrah and its Tawaf, and the Tawaf of Hajj follows after it.

From him, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Muawiya ibn Ammar, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who entered into Umrah and forgot to shorten [his garments] until he entered into Hajj. He said: He seeks forgiveness of Allah, and there is no penalty upon him, and his Umrah is complete.

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from al-Ala' ibn al-Fudayl, who said: I asked him about a man performing Tamattu' who circled the Kaaba, then entered the state of Ihram for Hajj before shortening his hair. He said: His Tamattu' is invalidated; it is a Hajj that is 'mutabathala' (flawed/compensated). The meaning in this report is that we interpret it as applying to one who did that intentionally. As for one who did it unintentionally, his Tamattu' is not invalidated, according to what the earlier reports contained.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Mutamatti' (pilgrim performing Hajj al-Tamattu') cuts off the Talbiyah when he looks at the houses of Mecca.

From him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from Hanan ibn Sadir, from his father, who said: Abu Ja'far and Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: When you see the houses of Mecca, cut off the Talbiyah.

Musa ibn al-Qasim, from Ibrahim ibn Abi Sammak, from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: When you enter Mecca while you are a Mutamatti' (one performing Hajj al-Tamattu'), look at the houses of Mecca, then cease the Talbiyah. And when you reach the boundary of the houses of Mecca that existed before that day, if you reach the 'Aqabah of the Madaniyyin, cease the Talbiyah. And upon you is the Tahleel, Takbir, and praising Allah your Lord as much as you can. And if you are Mufrid (performing Hajj al-Ifrad), do not cease the Talbiyah until the Day of Arafah at the decline of the sun. And if you are Mu'tamir (performing Umrah), cease the Talbiyah when you enter the Haram.

Sa'd ibn Abdillah narrated from Musa ibn al-Hasan, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Hamid, from Abu Jamilya al-Mufaddal ibn Salih, from Zayd al-Shahham, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about the Talbiyah of al-Mut'ah (Hajj al-Tamattu'), when is it cut off? He said: When one enters the Haram (sanctuary of Mecca). The correct approach in this narration is to consider it permissible (mubah), while the earlier one is for excellence and recommendation, so that the reports do not contradict each other.

And from him, from Muhassan ibn Ahmad, from Yunus ibn Ya'qub, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the man who performs an Umrah al-Mufradah (independent Umrah); from where does he terminate the Talbiyah? He said: When you see the houses of Dhi Tuwa, then terminate the Talbiyah.

And Umar ibn Yazid narrated from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: Whoever wishes to leave Mecca to perform Umrah should enter the state of Ihram from Al-Ji'ranah and Al-Hudaybiyah and similar places. And whoever leaves Mecca intending Umrah, then enters in the state of Ihram, he does not break the Talbiyah until he looks at the Ka'bah.

And al-Fudayl ibn Yasar narrated, he said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), saying: 'I entered [Mecca] with an Umrah, so where do I terminate the Talbiyah?' He said: 'Opposite the pass of the people of Medina (Aqabat al-Madiniyyin).' I asked: 'Where is the pass of the people of Medina?' He said: 'Opposite the dyers (Qassarin).' Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: The way to reconcile these narrations is to apply the last narration to those who came specifically via the Medina route, for they terminate the Talbiyah at the pass of the people of Medina. And the narration in which he said he terminates the Talbiyah at Dhi Taww is applied to those who came via the Iraq route. And the narration that included terminating it while looking at the Ka'bah is applied to one who had left Mecca for the Umrah. And in this way, there is no contradiction or conflict between them. And the narration we mentioned in the first chapter, that the Umrah pilgrim terminates the Talbiyah when entering the Haram, we apply it as permissible (optional). And these narrations, despite their differing states, are upon excellence and recommendation. And when Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn Babawayh (may Allah have mercy on him) narrated these narrations, he applied them to choice (option), thinking they were contradictory. And according to what we explained, they are not contradictory. And if they were contradictory, the way he mentioned would still be correct.

Musa ibn al-Qasim, from Ibrahim, from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Beware of killing all beasts, and do not touch anything of the perfume, nor of the oil, during your Ihram. Beware of the perfume in your provisions (zad). Keep the pleasant scent upon your nose, and do not keep the foul scent, for it is not fitting that one should delight in a pleasant scent. So whoever is afflicted with something of that, upon him is its ghusl (ritual bath), and he should give charity in proportion to what he did.

From him, from Abd al-Rahman, from Hammad, from Hariz, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him said The Muhrim (person in Ihram) should not touch anything of the perfume, nor of the basil (or fragrant plant), nor should he delight in it. So whoever is tested by something of that, let him give charity in proportion to what he did, in proportion to his satiety from the food.

From him, from Ali al-Jarimi, from Durusta al-Wasiti, from Ibn Muskān, from al-Hasan ibn Harun, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I said to him, 'I ate khabeeṣ (a type of bread/dough) containing saffron until I was full.' He said, 'When you have completed your rituals and intend to leave Mecca, buy dates with one dirham and then give them in charity; it will be an expiation for what you ate and for what entered upon you during your state of iḥrām that you are unaware of.'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Hammad, from Rabi', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from one of the Imams (peace be upon him), regarding the saying of Allah, Exalted and Mighty: 'Then let them end their impurity'. The hair surrounding the man's body (from shaving/perfuming).

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Ja'far ibn Bashir, from Isma'il, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about sa'ut (snuff) for the muhrim (one in ihram) in which there is perfume, and he said: There is no objection. Therefore, the approach in this report is to carry it upon the state of necessity, rather than the state of choice.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Safwan ibn Yahya from Isma'il ibn Jabir A wind (puffiness/swelling) had befallen his face due to an ailment that struck him while he was in the state of Ihram. He said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'The doctor who treats me prescribed for me a sa'ut (nasal drops) containing musk.' He said, 'Use it.'

Muhammad ibn al-Qasim, from al-Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Only four things from perfume are forbidden to you: musk, ambergris, waras (a type of plant), and saffron; except that it is disliked for the person in ihsar (ritual consecration for Hajj/Umrah) to use scented oils.

Yaqub ibn Yazid from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hisham ibn al-Hakam from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: I heard him (peace be upon him) say: There is no harm with the pleasant scent between As-Safa and Al-Marwah from the scent of the perfumers, and one does not need to hold one's nose, so it does not contradict the report of Muawiya ibn Ammar, who said in it: One holds one's nose from the pleasant scent for two reasons: one is that the command to hold the nose is directed only at the one who is directly engaging in the act with his own self, so it is appropriate for him to hold his nose; but if he is passing by on a path and the scent reaches him, then it is not obligatory upon him to do so. The other aspect is that we consider the command to hold the nose to be a type of recommendation (istihbab), and this is upon permissibility.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd from Ibn Sinan said: I asked him about henna, so he said: Indeed, the person in ihram may touch it and use it to treat his camel, and it is not considered perfume, and there is no harm in it.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Muhammad ibn al-Fudayl, from Abu al-Subah al-Kinanī, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about a woman who feared discord (shiqāq) and wished to enter the state of ihram (for pilgrimage or umrah); should she dye her hand with henna before that? He said: 'I do not like her to do it,' and the appropriate interpretation is that this is a degree of dislike (karāhiyah) rather than prohibition (ḥaẓr).

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar narrated from Muhammad ibn Isa who said: Ibrahim ibn Uqbah wrote to him asking about Fitrah (alms of fasting), how much is it, in the weight of Baghdad, for every head? And is it permissible to give it to a non-believer? So he wrote to him: You must give from yourself one Sa' (measure) in the Sa' of the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family), and from your dependents also, and it is not appropriate that you give your Zakat except to a believer.

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar from Muhammad ibn Isa said: He narrated to me Ali ibn Bilal, and it seemed to me that I had heard it from Ali ibn Bilal, who said: I wrote to him: Is it permissible for a man to be in one town and another man, one of his brothers, in another town, who needs him, to pay the Fitrah to him or not? So he wrote: He distributes the Fitrah among those who are present in that town and does not send it to another town, even if he does not find a suitable recipient there.

And Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yunus, from Ishaq ibn 'Ammar, from Abu Ibrahim (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about the Zakat al-Fitr (charity of breaking the fast): should it be given to those who are not from the Ahl al-Wilayah (the Imams' family/followers) among the poor of my neighbors? He said: Yes. The neighbors are more entitled to it due to the prevalence of their status. Therefore, the meaning in these two narrations and what follows their pattern is that it should be understood as being given to one who is not known to be from the Umayyads (rivals of the Ahl al-Bayt), who is poor, and this is in the absence of those who are known (to be from the Ahl al-Wilayah). As for when they exist, it is not permissible to give it to others, and that which indicates this.

Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Fadhal narrated from Ibrahim ibn Hashim from Hammad from Hariz from al-Fudayl from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: My grandfather, the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family), would give his fitrah to the weak, and to the one who has no one, and to the one who has no guardian. And his father (Imam al-Hassan) (peace be upon him) said: It belongs to its owners, unless they are not found; if they are not found, then to the one who is not set up (i.e., not appointed as a recipient). And it is not transferred from one land to another. And the Imam places it wherever he wishes and does in it what he sees fit.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Do not anoint yourself with oil containing musk or ambergris when you intend to enter the state of Ihram, because its scent will remain in your head after you have entered Ihram. And anoint yourself with whatever oil you wish when you intend to enter Ihram. Once you have entered Ihram, the oil becomes forbidden for you until you exit the state of Ihram.

Muhammad al-Halabi asked him about the oil of henna and the oil of violet, asking: 'Do we anoint ourselves with it when we intend to enter the state of Ihram?' He said: He said: 'Yes, and it does not contradict the earlier narrations, because the prohibition in the earlier narrations was directed only towards oils that contain perfume, such as musk and ambergris. There is no prohibition on the oil of violet and what resembles it, even if it is perfumed, and there is no contradiction between them in any case. It is permissible that the permissibility of using the oil of violet applies only when its scent disappears at the time of contracting the Ihram, or that this is specific to the state of necessity and need for its use, where one finds no alternative. It is also permissible that the oil of violet is among those whose scent has already faded, because if it is so, it follows the ruling of the Shiraj (a type of oil), which indicates this.'

Ibn Abi Umayr narrated from Hisham ibn Salim, who said: Ibn Abi Ya'fur asked him, 'What do you say regarding using perfume after the ritual bath for Ihram?' He replied, 'Before, after, and during; there is no harm in it.' Then he called for a bottle of pure musk containing nothing else, and ordered us to anoint ourselves with it. When we intended to leave, he said, 'It is not upon you to perform the ritual bath if you find water, when you reach Dhat al-Hulayf.'

Sa'd ibn Abd Allah, from Ya'qub ibn Yazid, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from some of our companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about apples, oranges (citrus), and quinces, and whatever has a pleasant scent; he said: 'One should hold one's nose (to block the scent) and eat.'

Ammar al-Sabati said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the person in Ihram, can he use a comb? He said: Yes, there is no harm in it. I said to him: Can he eat the orange (citrus)? He said: Yes. I said to him: For it has a pleasant scent. He said: Indeed, the orange is food and it is not among the perfumes, so it does not contradict the first report, because he only mentioned the permissibility of eating it and did not say that smelling it is permissible, and the first report is detailed, so acting upon it is more appropriate.

Muhammad ibn al-Qasim narrated from Abd al-Rahman from Muthanna from al-Hasan al-Siqall from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him from the Muhrim (one in ihram) who performed cupping, he said: He may perform cupping unless he fears harm to his life or is unable to pray. And he said: If the blood causes him pain, there is no objection, and he performs cupping and does not shave his hair.
From him, from Muhassan ibn Ahmad, from Yunus ibn Ya'qub, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the person in ihram who gets cupped (hijamah). He said: 'I do not like it.'

Musa ibn al-Qasim, from Abd al-Rahman, from Hammad, from Hariz, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: It is not objectionable for the Muhrim (one in Ihram) to undergo cupping, provided he does not shave or cut the hair. The correct view is to apply it to the state of necessity, based on the report we narrated from al-Hasan al-Siqill, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him). That report is detailed, and this one is general, so acting upon this one is more appropriate.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa narrated from al-Abbas ibn Ma'ruf, from Fadala ibn Ayyub, from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him); and al-Hasan ibn 'Ali ibn Fadhal, from some of our companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: There is no harm in the Muhrim (one in Ihram state) entering the bathhouse, but he should not rub his body (scrub vigorously).

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Muhammad ibn Abdillah ibn Hilal, from Uqbah ibn Khalid, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about the person in ihram entering the bathhouse. He said: 'He does not enter.' The meaning in this report is that we should interpret it as a form of dislike (karahah) rather than prohibition (haram), and the first report as permissible, removing the prohibition.

Muhammad ibn al-Qasim from Hammad ibn Isa from Hariz said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the person in ihram who covered his head unintentionally. He said: He should remove the head-cover from his head, say the Talbiyah, and there is no penalty upon him.

Sa'd ibn Abd Allah, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from Ali ibn Ri'ab, from Zurarah, who said: I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him): 'A man in ihram wishes to sleep and cover his face from flies.' He said: 'Yes, but he should not cover his head.' And for the woman in ihram, there is no harm if she covers her entire face.

As for what Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah narrated from Musa ibn al-Hasan and al-Hasan ibn 'Ali from Ahmad ibn Hilal and Muhammad ibn Abi 'Umayr and Umayyah ibn 'Ali al-Qaysi from 'Ali ibn 'Atiyyah from Zurarah from one of the Imams (peace be upon him) regarding the Muhrim (one in Ihram), he said to him that he should cover his head and face if he wants to sleep. Therefore, the face in this report is to be understood as referring to the state of necessity, in which a person fears harm from uncovering the head, rather than the state of choice.

Al-Husayn ibn Saeed from Bakr ibn Salih said: I wrote to Abu Ja'far (the second Imam, peace be upon him) that my aunt was with me and she was my companion (traveling partner), and the heat was severe upon her when she entered the state of Ihram, so she desired that I provide shade for her and for myself. He wrote back: 'Provide shade for her alone.'

Sa'd ibn Abdillah from al-Hasan ibn Ali from al-Abbas ibn Ma'ruf from some of our companions from al-Rida (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about the person in Ihram who has a sick companion, and he shaded his head; is it permissible for him to shade himself? He said: Yes. And it does not contradict the first report, because his saying 'Is it permissible for him to shade himself?' does not specify that it is for the sick person to shade himself. It is possible that the reference returns to the sick person, and the question was about that, whether it is permissible for him or not. He said: Yes.

Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from Ibn Jabala, from Isḥāq ibn ʿAmmār, from Abū al-Ḥasan (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about the person in iḥrām who is shaded while he is in iḥrām. He said: 'No, except for a sick person, or one who has an ailment, or the one who cannot endure the sun.'

From him (al-Hasan ibn Muhammad al-Warraq), from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi and Ibn Sinan, from Ibn Muskhan, from al-Halabi, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the person in Ihram riding in the Qubbah (a covered saddle/canopy). He said: 'I do not like that, except if he is ill.'

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa narrated from Ali ibn Ahmad from Musa ibn Umar from Muhammad ibn Mansur from him, who said: I asked him about the shading for the Muhrim (one in Ihram), he said: He is not shaded except due to a defect or illness.

From him, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Isma'il ibn 'Abd al-Khaliq, who said: I asked Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him): Does the Muhrim (person in Ihram) seek shade from the sun? He said: No, unless he is an old man. And he said: This is the reason.

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar narrated from Ali ibn Muhammad who said: I wrote to him (peace be upon him): 'Does the person in Ihram shade himself if the sun or rain bothers him, or if he is sick, or not? And if he shades himself, is there a fidya (ransom/expiation) upon him, or not?' He wrote back: 'He may shade himself, and he sheds blood, if God wills.'

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa narrated from al-Barqi, from Sa'd ibn Sa'd al-Ash'ari, from Abu al-Hasan al-Rida (peace be upon them) who said: I asked him about the person in Ihram who shades himself. He said: Is it due to an illness/cause? I said: The heat of the sun harms him while he is in Ihram. He said: It is a cause; he may shade himself and offer the ransom.

From him, from Muhammad ibn Isma'il ibn Bazee', who said: A man asked him about the shade for the Muhrim (person in Ihram) from the harm of rain or sun, and I was listening, so he ordered him to pay the ransom (fidyah) by slaughtering a sheep in Mina.

From him, from Ibrahim ibn Abi Mahmud, who said: I said to Al-Reza (peace be upon him): The Muhrim (one in Ihram) may be shaded on his mount and offer a ransom (Fida) if the sun or rain harms him. He said: Yes. I asked him: What is the ransom? He said: A sheep. So no one should say that these narrations contradict the earlier narrations in that they stipulate the obligation of expiation (Kaffarah) on the one who is shaded due to necessity, because the earlier narrations only stipulated permission for the necessitated and the sick on condition of committing to the expiation; as for without it, it is not permissible in any case. And if there is no harm there, shading is not permissible even if he commits to the expiation. This indicates that.

Sa'd ibn 'Abdullah from al-'Abbas ibn Ma'ruf from 'Abdullah ibn al-Mughirahra said: I said to Abu al-Hasan al-Awwal (peace be upon him): 'Do I shade myself while I am in ihram?' He said: 'No.' I said: 'Then do I shade myself and offer expiation?' He said: 'No.' I said: 'If I get sick?' He said: 'Shade yourself and offer expiation.'

Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah, from Abu Ja'far, from Muhammad ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Jamil ibn Darraj, from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: There is no harm in shading women, and permission has been granted for it for men. Thus, the meaning of His saying 'and permission has been granted for it for men' is that we should understand it as applying to a state of necessity and obligation of expiation, as we have clarified in the preceding narrations.

Musa ibn al-Qasim from Ibn Abi Umayr and Safwan from al-Mu'afi ibn 'Ammar from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: It is no objection if a man prays in the Masjid al-Shajara and says what he wishes to say, and does not say the Talbiyah, then he goes out and catches game or other things, there is no blame on him for that.

From him, from Safwan and Ibn Abi Umayr, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), in the matter of a man who has sexual intercourse with his wife after he has contracted the Ihram but has not yet recited the Talbiyah, he said: There is no penalty upon him.

From him, from Safwan ibn Yahya and Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hafs ibn Bukhtari and Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) That he prayed two rak'at in the Mosque of the Tree, and concluded the Ihram, then went out, and was brought a dish of khabis containing saffron, and he ate from it.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Jamil ibn Darraj, from some of our companions, from one of the two Imams (peace be upon him) regarding: Regarding a man who prayed Dhuhr in the Mosque of the Tree, and contracted the Ihram, then touched perfume or hunted game or had intercourse with his wife, he said: There is no penalty upon him as long as he has not said the Talbiyah.

From him, from Ali, from his father and Isma'il ibn Marar, from Yunus, from Ziyad ibn Marwan, who said: I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him): What do you say about a man who prepared for Ihram and completed everything except the prayer and all the conditions, except that he had not yet recited the Talbiyah? Is it permissible for him to break that state and have intercourse with women? He said: Yes.

From him, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Hammad, from Hariz, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding a man who prepares for Ihram, it is permissible for him to have intercourse with women as long as he has not yet pronounced the Talbiyah or committed to it.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Muhammad ibn Isa from Ahmad ibn Muhammad who said: I heard my father saying regarding a man who wears his Ihram garments and prepares for Ihram, then has intercourse with his wife before he pronounces the Talbiyah for Ihram: He bears the blood (damm, i.e., the sacrificial animal penalty). The interpretation of this report is one of two things: First, we interpret it as referring to one who did not proclaim the Talbiah aloud, even if he recited it silently between himself and his soul. For if the matter is so, the Ihram is established and the expiation (kaffarah) becomes obligatory upon him for whatever he commits. The second interpretation is that we interpret it as referring to a type of recommended act (istihbab), rather than an obligatory duty (farad) or binding requirement (ijbar).

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from a number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from Sabbah al-Hadda', from Isحاق ibn 'Ammar, who said: I asked Abu al-Hasan Musa (peace be upon him): 'Inform me about a man who was in the state of Ihram (unconsecrated) and had intercourse with his female slave who was in the state of Ihram (consecrated for Hajj).' He said: 'For the wealthy or the poor?' I said: 'Answer me regarding both.' He said: 'If he ordered her to enter Ihram or did not order her and she entered Ihram on her own behalf?' I said: 'Answer me regarding both cases.' He said: 'If he was wealthy and knew that it was not appropriate for him, and he was the one who ordered her to enter Ihram, then upon him is a camel, or if he wishes, a cow, or if he wishes, a sheep. And if he did not order her to enter Ihram, then there is nothing upon him, whether he was wealthy or poor. And if he ordered her and he was poor, then upon him is the blood of a sheep or fasting.'

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from Ali ibn Ri'ab, from Durays, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who ordered his slave-girl to enter the state of ihram from a specific time, so she entered ihram while he had not yet entered ihram, and he had intercourse with her after she had entered ihram. He said: He orders her to perform ghusl, then she enters ihram, and there is no penalty upon him. This does not contradict the first report because the way to understand it is to assume that she had not yet recited the talbiyah, for if the matter is so, no penalty is incumbent upon him, as we indicated in the first chapter.
Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from some of our companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Do not give anyone less than a head.

Al-Husayn ibn Said from Safwan from Ishaq ibn al-Mubarak said: I asked Abu Ibrahim (peace be upon him) about the Zakat al-Fitr, is it from what Allah said: 'Establish prayer and give zakat'? He said: Yes. And he said: The charity of dates is more beloved to me because my father (peace be upon him) used to give charity in dates. I said: Should its value be made silver and given to one man or two? He said: Distributing it is more beloved to me, and there is no harm in making it silver, and dates are more beloved to me. I said: Should it be given to those other than the Ahl al-Wilayah from these neighbors? He said: Yes, the neighbors are more entitled to it. I said: Should I give the one man three sa' and four sa'? He said: Yes. So this report implies several things: First, that he chose distribution in the state of Taqiyyah (dissimulation) because the belief of all the Sunnis agrees with that, and it does not agree with us regarding the obligation of giving one sa' to one person. Second, that the report does not indicate that it is permissible to distribute one sa', and it is possible that he referred to one who is obligated to provide Fitr for many heads, so distributing it among a group of needy people is better than giving it to one person. Third, that he meant that when the needy are gathered, and there is not enough to distribute the one sa' among them, then distribution is permissible, and perhaps that is the better option.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from a number of our companions from Sahl ibn Ziyad and Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, all from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Ali ibn Ri'ab from Mis'mam, Abu Sayyar, who said: He (peace be upon him) said to me: 'O Abu Sayyar, the state of the Muhrim (one in Ihram) is restrictive. If he kisses his wife while not desiring (sexual release) and he is Muhrim, then upon him is the blood of a sheep. And if he kisses his wife while desiring and he ejaculates, then upon him is the blood of a camel, and he seeks forgiveness from Allah. And whoever touches his wife while Muhrim with desire, then upon him is the blood of a sheep. And whoever looks at his wife with desire and ejaculates, then upon him is the blood of a camel. And if he touches his wife and stays close to her without desire, then there is nothing upon him.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, and Muhammad ibn Isma'il from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, from Ibn Abi Umayr and Safwan ibn Yahya from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about a person in ihram who looked at his wife and emitted semen or pre-seminal fluid while he was in ihram. He said: 'There is no penalty upon him.' The meaning in this report is that we interpret it as him looking at her without lust, so no penalty was incumbent upon him. And the penalty is only incumbent if he looked with lust, causing emission, according to what was detailed in the first report.

And as for what Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah narrated from Abu Ja'far, from al-Husayn, from Safwan, from Ishaq ibn 'Ammar, from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) regarding a person in ihram who looked at his wife with desire and emitted semen, he said: There is no penalty upon him. The correct interpretation of this report is that we understand it as referring to the state of heedlessness and forgetfulness, because whoever looks while heedless or forgetful looks with desire and emits semen, there is no penalty upon him, just as if he had intercourse while forgetful, no expiation would be incumbent upon him, as we have clarified in our book Al-Kabir.

Musa ibn al-Qasim from Safwan from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man in ihram who had intercourse with his wife in what is below the private part. He said: Upon him is a camel (as ransom), and he is not required to perform Hajj next year.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Ibn Abi Umayr and Muhammad ibn Isma'il from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan from Ibn Abi Umayr and Safwan ibn Yahya from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding the Muhrim (person in Ihram) who has intercourse with his wife, he said: If he has fully penetrated her, then upon him is a camel and Hajj next year; and if he has not fully penetrated her, then upon him is a camel and he is not required to perform Hajj next year.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Amr ibn Uthman al-Kazzaz from Sabbah al-Hadda' from Isma'il ibn 'Ammar from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) who said: I asked: What do you say about a person in ihram who played with his penis and thereby ejaculated? He said: I see upon him the same as what is upon the one who had intercourse with his wife while in ihram: a camel and the hajj next year. This does not contradict the first two reports because it is not impossible that the ruling for the one who played with his penis is stricter than the ruling for the one who had intercourse in what is below the genital organ, because he committed a prohibition that is not permissible in any way, whereas the one who had intercourse did not commit a prohibition except in that he did it at a time when permission for that was not legislated for him. And it is possible that this report is to be understood as indicating a degree of emphasis and strictness of preference, rather than it being obligatory.

Al-Husayn ibn Said, from Safwan and al-Nadr, from Ibn Sinan, and Hammad, from Ibn al-Mughira, from Ibn Sinan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The person in ihram is not permitted to marry nor to give someone in marriage; if he marries or gives someone in marriage while he is a muhrim, his marriage is invalid.

From him, from Hammad, from Hariz, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Abdillah, who said: He said to him: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: Indeed, a man from the Ansar married while he was in the state of Ihram, so the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) annulled his marriage.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from al-Hasan ibn Ali, from Umar ibn Aban al-Kalbi, who said: I went to the door of Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), and al-Mufaddal came out. I faced him and he said, 'What is the matter with you?' I said, 'I intend to do something, but I have not done it until Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) orders me. I intend for Allah to preserve my chastity and lower my gaze while in ihram.' He said, 'As you are,' and entered. He asked him about that, and he said, 'This al-Kalbi is at the door, and he intends to enter ihram and intends to marry, so that Allah will lower his gaze by that. If you order him to do it, he will do it, otherwise he will turn away from that.' He said to me, 'Order him to do it and let him be modest.' The meaning in this report is one of two things: one is that he ordered him to do that before entering into ihram; as for after the contract of ihram, it is not permissible in any case. The other meaning is that it is to be taken as a form of taqiyya (dissimulation), because that is the view of some of the Sunnis.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Ali ibn Ri'ab from Abu Basir said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who trimmed one of his fingernails while he was in the state of Ihram. He said: Upon him is, for every nail, the value of a Mudd of food, until it reaches ten. If he trimmed the nails of both his hands entirely, then upon him is the blood of a sheep. I said: If he trimmed the nails of both his feet and hands entirely? He said: If he did that in one sitting, then upon him is one blood (of a sheep). And if he did it separately in two sittings, then upon him are two bloods (of sheep).

From him, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Ibn Muskhan, from al-Halabi, that he asked him about a person in ihram who trimmed his fingernails, he said: Upon him is a mud for each finger. If he trimmed all ten of them, then upon him is the blood of a sheep.

Musa ibn al-Qasim from Abd al-Rahman from Hammad from Hariz from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) When the one in Ihram forgets and trims one of his fingernails, he gives one handful of food as charity. I said: 'And for two?' He said: 'Two handfuls.' I said: 'And for three?' He said: 'And for three?' He said: 'Three handfuls. Each nail is one handful until it becomes five. If he trims five, then upon him is one blood-expiation (dam). Whether it was five or ten or whatever it was.' The correct interpretation of this report is to take it as indicating a type of recommendation (istihbab), because obligation (wujub) applies only to the one who trims all ten fingers. What confirms that it is a recommendation is that he said: 'When the one in Ihram forgets and trims a nail,' and the one who does this while forgetting is not bound by anything originally. Thus it is known that he meant recommendation. And that which indicates that the one who does this while forgetting is not bound by anything...

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Hammad from Abu Hamrah who said: I asked him about a man who trimmed his fingernails except for one finger. He said: 'He forgot.' I said: 'Yes.' He said: 'There is no harm.'

Musa ibn al-Qasim from Abd al-Rahman from Hammad from Hariz from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) passed by Ka'b ibn Ujrah al-Ansari, and lice were falling from his head. He said: 'Do the insects of your head annoy you?' He said: 'Yes.' Then this verse was revealed: 'So whoever among you is ill or has an ailment of the head [from fasting] must offer a ransom of fasting [three days] or charity or a sacrifice.' The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) ordered him, so he shaved his head. He made upon him fasting for three days, and charity for six poor people, two mudds for each poor person, and the sacrifice is one sheep. Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'And everything in the Quran that says

Musa ibn al-Qasim from Muhammad ibn 'Umar ibn Yazid from Muhammad ibn 'Udhafir from 'Umar ibn Yazid from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Allah the Exalted said in His Book: 'So whoever among you is ill or has an ailment of the head [from fasting] - then ransom is from fasting by day or charity or sacrifice.' So whoever is afflicted with an ailment or pain and uses what is not permissible for the Muhrim when he is healthy, then [the ransom is] fasting for three days, and charity to ten poor people, feeding them from food, and the sacrifice is a sheep which he slaughters, eats from, and feeds [others] from. And indeed, he is only obligated with one of those, so it does not contradict the first report which said in it 'And charity to six poor people, for each poor person two measures,' because the matter in both is optional, because the person is chosen between feeding six poor people, two measures for each poor person, and feeding ten poor people to the extent of their satiety, so there is no contradiction between them in any case, and that which confirms the first narration.

Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from Muhammad ibn Ahmad, from Muthanna, from Zurara, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: If a man is detained (from completing the Hajj rites) and sends his sacrificial animal, but his head is affected (by hair regrowth or other impediment) before the animal is slaughtered, then he must slaughter a sheep in place of what he was detained from, or fast, or give charity to six poor people; and the fasting is three days, and the charity is half a Sa' for each poor person.

Musa ibn al-Qasim from Abd al-Rahman from Hammad ibn Isa said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the person in ihram who removes a louse from his body and throws it away; he said: He feeds in its place one meal.

From him, from Abu Ja'far, from Abd al-Rahman, from al-Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about the Muhrim (person in Ihram) who removes a louse from his body and throws it away; he said: He gives food in its place. From him, from Husayn ibn Abi al-Ala', from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Muhrim should not deliberately remove a louse from his body or from his garment; and if he kills any of them by mistake, he should give food in its place, a handful with his hand.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Safwan ibn Yahya from Murra, the freedman of Khalid, said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the person in ihram who throws off the louse, so he said: 'Throw it off, may God Almighty distance it, [it is] not blameworthy and not lost.'

From him, from Fadala, from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'If the Muhrim scratches his head and a louse and two lice fall from him,' he said, 'There is no penalty upon him, and they do not return.' I said, 'How does he scratch his head?' He said, 'With his fingernails, as long as he does not draw blood and does not cut the hair.'

From him, from Fadala, from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): What do you say about a person in ihram who kills a louse? He said: There is no specific penalty upon him for the louse, and it is not appropriate for him to intentionally kill it. Thus, the meaning in these narrations is that what is meant by his saying 'there is no penalty upon him' is that there is no specific [fixed] penalty, as is specified in the case of other [insects/creatures] among the expiations.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Safwan from Abu Sa'id from Mansur from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): When the person in Ihram touches his beard and hair falls from it, he said: He gives a handful of food or two handfuls.

From him, from Fadala, from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'If the one in Ihram plays with his beard and a hair (or eight hairs) fall from it,' he said, 'He feeds (a poor person) something.'

Sa'd ibn Abdillah narrated from Abu Ja'far, from al-Husayn, from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from Hisham ibn Salim, who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: When one of you places his hand on his head or beard while in the state of Ihram, and some hair falls out, he should give charity of a handful of food or a handful of Sowiq.

Sa'd ibn 'Abdillah narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from Ja'far ibn Bashir from al-Haytham ibn 'Urwah al-Tamimi who said: A man asked Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the person in ihsar (state of consecration for Hajj/Umrah) who wishes to perfect his wudu (ablution), and a hair or two hairs fall from his beard, so he said: 'It is of no consequence. What God has placed upon you in the religion is not a hardship.'

From him, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Ja'far ibn Bashir, from al-Mufaddal ibn 'Umar, who said: Al-Nabbahi entered upon Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) and said: 'What do you say about a person in ihram who touched his beard and two hairs fell from it?' Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'If I touched my beard and ten hairs fell from it, there would be nothing upon me.' The explanation for these two narrations is that we should interpret them as applying to one who did that unintentionally, not deliberately, because the unintentional person and the forgetful person are not obligated to pay any expiation.

Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Ali ibn Ri'ab from Zurarah who said: I heard Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) saying: 'Whoever shaves his head or plucks the hair of his armpit, forgetting or heedless or ignorant, there is no penalty upon him. And whoever does it deliberately, then upon him is the blood (damm).'

Sa'd ibn 'Abdullah, from Abu Ja'far, from al-Hasan ibn 'Ali ibn Fadhl, from al-Mufaddal ibn Salih, from Layth al-Maradi, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who touches his beard while he is in the state of Ihram, playing with it, and plucks out tufts of hair from it by hand, whether by mistake or intentionally. He said: It does not harm him. The meaning of his saying 'It does not harm him' is that he does not incur punishment, because whoever gives charity with a handful of food does not suffer harm from that; rather, the harm is in the punishment or what resembles it. And it also indicates that he is obliged to pay the expiation (Kaffarah).

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Hammad from Hariz from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: When a man plucks the hairs of his two armpits after entering the state of Ihram, he is liable for a blood sacrifice (dam).

Sa'd ibn Abdillah, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn Abi al-Khattab, from Muhammad ibn Abdillah ibn Hilal, from Abdillah ibn Jabalah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding the one in Ihram who plucks the hair from his armpit, he said: He must feed three poor people. The correct interpretation of this report is that we apply it to the one who plucked from one armpit, because the first [part of the report] is directed toward the one who plucked from both armpits entirely, so a sheep's blood [expiation] became obligatory for him.
Ibn Abi Umayr from Hafs from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: For the pigeon, one dirham; and for the chick, half a dirham; and for the egg, a quarter of a dirham.

Ali ibn Ibrahim narrated from his father, from Hammad, from Hariz, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: If the one in Ihram kills a pigeon, the penalty is a sheep; and if he kills its chicks, the penalty is a camel; and if he crushes the eggs, he owes a dirham. The correct interpretation of this report is that we understand it to apply to the one who kills the pigeon while he is in Ihram. As for the first [penalties mentioned], they apply to the one who kills it while he is Muhrim (in Ihram), and the latter [referring to the lighter penalty or specific context] applies to the one who kills it while he is Muhtal (not in Ihram), for he is not obligated to pay more than its value.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Ibn Fudayl from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) said: I asked him about a man who killed a pigeon from the pigeons of the Sanctuary (Haram) while he was not in a state of Ihram. He said: Upon him is its value, which is one dirham, which he gives as charity or uses to buy food for the pigeons of the Sanctuary. And if he killed it while he was in Ihram in the Sanctuary, then upon him is a sheep and the value of the pigeon. And that which also indicates that whenever he slaughtered it in the Sanctuary while he was Muhrim (not in Ihram), it did not obligate him more than the value.
