Musa ibn al-Qasim from Muhammad ibn Saif from Mansur who said: A trustworthy companion of ours narrated to me who said: I was walking in some of the streets of Mecca when a man met me and said to me, 'Slaughter these two birds for me.' So I slaughtered them, forgetting, while I was in the state of Ihram (Halal). Then I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), and he said, 'Upon you is the price (compensation).'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd from Ibn Sinan from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) that he said: Regarding a person in ihram who slaughters a bird, indeed upon him is the blood of a sheep which he must pay. If it is a chick, then a young goat or a small lamb from the sheep. And that which indicates that it is incumbent upon him is the value of the egg, one dirham, when he is in ihram.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Hammad, from Hariz, from Zurarah, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): What is the limit of the Jizya (poll tax) upon the People of the Book, and is there a fixed amount upon them in this matter that they must not exceed? He said: That is up to the Imam; he takes from each of them whatever he wishes, according to their wealth and their capacity. They are a people who ransomed their lives from being enslaved or killed, so the Jizya is taken from them according to what they can bear to give until they convert to Islam. Indeed, Allah, Exalted and Mighty, said: 'Until they give the Jizya with a willing hand.' And how can one be 'humbled' if he does not care about what is taken from him, until he finds humiliation in what was taken from him, and thus feels pain because of it, and then converts? He said: And Muhammad ibn Muslim said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): What do you think about what these [rulers/collectors] take from the Khums of the land of the Jizya, and what they take from the peasants as the Jizya of their heads? Is there a fixed amount upon them in this? He said: It is upon them whatever they authorized upon themselves, and the Imam does not take more than the Jizya. If the Imam wishes, he places that upon their heads, and there is nothing upon their wealth; and if he wishes, he places it upon their wealth, and there is nothing upon their heads. I said: And what about this Khums? He said: This is merely something that the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) made a treaty with them upon.

Hariz narrated from Muhammad ibn Muslim who said: I asked him about the People of the Dhimma (covenant), what is upon them by which their blood and wealth are secured? He said: The land tax (Kharaj). If the Jizya is taken from their heads, then there is no claim on their lands; and if it is taken from their lands, then there is no claim on their heads.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from a number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn Abi Hamzah, from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about a man who killed an ostrich egg while he was in ihram (pilgrimal state). He said: He should send a male camel among the camels for the number of eggs. I said: If the eggs are all spoiled and all viable? He said: Whatever is produced from the sacrificial animal is considered a valid sacrifice reaching the Ka'bah, and if it is not produced, there is nothing upon him. If he does not find camels, then for each egg there is a sheep upon him, and if he does not find [sheep], then charity for ten poor people, for each poor person a mudd. If he does not find [that], then fasting for three days.

Musa ibn al-Qasim from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad from al-Halabi from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: Whoever collects an ostrich egg while he is in the state of ihram, upon him is to send a male camel in the number equal to the count of the eggs from the camels, for perhaps all of them spoil, and perhaps all of them hatch, and perhaps some of them are viable and some spoil; whatever the camels give birth to, they are a offering (hady) reaching the Ka'bah.

Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Fudayl, Safwan, and others, from Abu al-Subah al-Kinani, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a person in ihram who trod on an ostrich egg and broke it. He said: The Commander of the Faithful ruled regarding it that a male camel should be sent for each female camel corresponding to the number of eggs; whatever was fertilized and survived, the offspring would be a sacrifice reaching the Kaaba. And Abu Abdillah said: Whatever you trod upon, or your camel or beast of burden trod upon, while you are in ihram, then the redemption (fidyah) is upon you.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Abu Ali al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn al-Jabbar, from Safwan, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, from Sulayman ibn Khalid, who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said in the Book of Ali (peace be upon him): Regarding the egg of the sandgrouse, the compensation is one sheep; if the person in ihram kills it, the compensation is like that of the ostrich egg, which is one camel. The correct interpretation of this report is to apply it to the egg in which the chick has moved, because it follows the same ruling as the ostrich egg, which indicates this.

Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from Ali ibn Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him (peace be upon him) about a man in ihram who broke an ostrich egg, and in the egg were chicks that had moved. He said: Upon him is, for every chick that moved, a camel which he slaughters in the place of slaughter.

Muhammad ibn al-Qasim narrated from Safwan, from Mansur ibn Hazim and Ibn Muskhan, from Sulayman ibn Khalid, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a person in ihram who trod upon the eggs of sandgrouse and crushed them. He said: He sends a male camel as compensation for a number of eggs equal to the number of eggs, from the sheep, just as he sends a male camel for the number of eggs of the ostrich from the camels.

From him, from Mu'awiya ibn Hakim, from Ibn Ribat, from some of his companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about the eggs of the sandgrouse (qatā). He said: They are treated like the eggs of the ostrich in the case of camels.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Abu Ali al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn al-Jabbar, from Safwan, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, from Sulayman ibn Khalid, who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said in the Book of Ali (peace be upon him): Regarding the eggs of the sandgrouse (qat), the compensation is one sheep; if the person in ihram consumes it, [the compensation] is like what is in the eggs of the ostrich: one camel.

And what Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from Muhammad ibn Ahmad from Abd al-Malik from Sulayman ibn Khalid, who said: I asked him about a man who trod on the eggs of the sandgrouse (qatā) and crushed them. He said: He should send a male goat in number equal to the number of the eggs from the sheep, just as he sends a male goat in number equal to the count of the eggs from the camels. And whoever hits an ostrich egg, upon him is a young sheep (makhāḍ). There is no contradiction between these two reports and the earlier reports, because a young sheep from the sheep is only obligatory by specification if there is a chick inside the egg, as we said regarding the eggs of the ostrah that a yearling camel (badanah) is obligatory if there are chicks inside it. And that which indicates that the ruling of the eggs of the sandgrouse is the ruling of the eggs of the ostrich.

Musa ibn al-Qasim from Safwan from Sulayman ibn Khalid from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: In the Book of Ali (peace be upon him), regarding the eggs of the sandgrouse (quail-like bird), the expiation is like that of the ostrich eggs.

Musa ibn al-Qasim from Abu al-Hasan al-Tamimi from Safwan from Yazid ibn Khalifa said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) was asked while I was with him, and a man said to him: 'My slave threw a basket in my house, and in it are two eggs from the pigeons of the Sanctuary (Haram).' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Upon him is the value of the two eggs; he should feed them to the pigeons of the Sanctuary.'

Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from Muhammad ibn Ahmad, from al-Karim, from Yazid ibn Khalifa, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I said to him: There was a basket in my house containing eggs from the pigeons of the Sanctuary (Mecca). My servant went and overturned the basket, not knowing there were eggs in it, and broke them. I went out and met Abdullah ibn al-Hasan, and I mentioned that to him. He said: Give charity with two handfuls of fine flour. I said: Then I met Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) and informed him. He said: The price of two birds, which you feed to the pigeons of the Sanctuary. I met Abdullah ibn al-Hasan after that and informed him. He said: He is truthful, so follow his ruling, for he took it from his forefathers (peace be upon them).

Musa ibn al-Qasim from Abbas from Aban from al-Halabi Ubayd Allah said: A boy moved a basket and broke two eggs in the Haram (sanctuary). I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), and he said: 'Two Jaddayn or two Hamalayn.' This is not contradictory to what we said earlier, because this report is understood to mean that if the egg is one in which the chick has already moved, then at that time a ransom of one Hamal or one Jaddayn is obligatory upon him. And if there was no movement of the chick in it, then its value (Qimah) is due upon him, according to what we presented earlier, which indicates that.

Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from Ali ibn Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: I asked my brother Musa ibn Ja'far (peace be upon him) about a man who broke the eggs of pigeons, and in the eggs were chicks that had moved. He (peace be upon him) said: He must give charity for every chick that had moved inside it by sacrificing a sheep, and give charity with its meat if he is in ihram. And if the chicks had not moved, he must give charity for their value in silver, and buy with it fodder and throw it for the pigeons of the Sanctuary.

Ali ibn Ja'far narrated from his brother Musa ibn Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a man who shot an animal for game, broke its leg or arm, and left it, so the animal died. He said: One-fourth of the blood money (fidyah) is due.

Musa ibn al-Qasim from Safwan from Abd Allah ibn Sinan from Abu Basir who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): A man hunted a gazelle while he was in the state of Ihram, and he broke its arm or leg, so the gazelle went on its face (limping), and he did not know what to do with it. He said: Upon him is its fidyah (ransom). I said: But he saw it afterwards walking. He said: Upon him is one-quarter of its value.

Musa ibn al-Qasim from Ali al-Jarmi from Muhammad ibn Abi Hamzah, and you studied from Abd Allah ibn Muskān from Abū Basīr from Abū Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a person in ihram who threw [a stone at] game and hit its leg, causing it to limp. He said: If the gazelle walked on it and grazed while he was looking at it, there is no penalty upon him. And if the gazelle went on its face (died) while he was raising its leg, he does not know what it did, so upon him is its ransom (fidyah) because he does not know, perhaps it has perished. This does not contradict the two previous narrations because the quarter of the value is only obligatory upon him if he broke its leg or foot and then saw it healed afterwards. And in this narration, it hit it, it limped, then it walked and grazed, and there is no contradiction between them. Because the one whose ruling is this does not incur a specific expiation, but rather gives charity in whatever amount he can.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from al-'Abbas ibn Ma'ruf, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from some of our companions, from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: He (peace be upon him) disliked that game be shot while it is heading towards the Sanctuary (Mecca).

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from al-Haytham ibn Abi Masruq, from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from Ali ibn Ri'ab, from Mis'ma, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding a man from the open land (Hill) who shot game in the open land, and the game carried itself until it entered the Sanctuary (Haram), he said: Its meat is forbidden, like the dead animal.

And from him, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Ibn Faddal, from Ali ibn Uqba, from his father Uqba ibn Khalid, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a man who completed his Hajj, then turned back, and when he exited the Sanctuary, game approached him near the Sanctuary, and the game was heading towards the Sanctuary. He threw at it and killed it. What is upon him in that regard? He said: He must ransom it.

Musa ibn al-Qasim from Abu al-Husayn al-Nakha'i, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding a man who hunts while aiming for the Sanctuary (Haram), and the arrow strikes him, and he carries it until he enters the Sanctuary and dies in it: He said, 'There is no penalty upon him.' It is like the case of a man who sets a net in the open country (Hill), and game falls into it, and struggles until it enters the Sanctuary and dies in it. I said, 'This is considered by them to be analogical reasoning (Qiyas).' He said, 'No, I merely compared one thing to another for you, so it does not contradict the earlier narrations, because his statement 'there is no penalty upon him' is to be understood as meaning 'no penalty from the punishment,' because doing so is disliked (Makruh), and it is not something that deserves punishment by virtue of the act, as it would if he did it inside the Sanctuary. He explicitly stated this in the first narration, although a ransom (Kaffarah) would be obligatory upon him along with that, according to what the later narration implies, and that which indicates that the ransom is obligatory in addition to what has preceded.

Musa ibn al-Qasim from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad from al-Halabi from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: When you are in the state of Ihram in the open land (al-Hill) and you kill game between yourself and the distance of al-Bareed to the Sanctuary (al-Haram), then upon you is its compensation. If you blind its eye or break its horn, you give charity.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Hammad from Hariz from Zurara from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding a person in ihram who killed a locust, he said: He gives a date, and a date is better than a locust.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Salih ibn Uqbah, from 'Urwah al-Hannat, from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding a man who caught a locust and ate it, he said: 'It has blood.' The meaning in this report is that we should interpret it as referring to one who killed many locusts, even if the term 'al-tawhid' (the singular/unique one) was used for it, because he meant the species, and that which indicates this is...

Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from Abd al-Rahman from 'Ula' from Muhammad ibn Muslim from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a person in ihram who killed a locust. He said: A handful of food, and if it was more, then upon him is the blood money of a sheep.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Fadala from Mu'awiya said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'Locusts are on the side of the road, and people are praying (in a state of Ihram); what should they do?' He said: 'They should avoid them as much as they can.' I said: 'If they kill some of them, is there anything upon them?' He said: 'There is nothing upon them.' The meaning in this narration is what has been clarified, that they kill them in a manner in which they cannot avoid them, so no expiation is required of them, and this adds to the clarification.'

Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from Hammad from Hariz from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: It is upon the Muhrim (one in Ihram) to be watchful of the locusts if they are on his path; if he finds no alternative, he may kill them, and there is no objection.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Hammad, from Hariz, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: Whatever of beasts, snakes, and others the Muhrim fears, he should kill it; and if it does not attack you, do not attack it.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Baraqi, from Dawud ibn Abi Yazid al-Attar, from Abu Sa'id al-Makari, who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): A man killed a lion in the Haram (sanctuary). He (AS) said: Upon him is a sheep that he must slaughter. The ruling is that we hold him liable because he killed it, even if he did not intend it, for if the matter is thus, the expiation becomes obligatory upon him.

Muhammad ibn al-Hassan al-Saffar narrated from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ali ibn Ibrahim from Ibrahim ibn Hashim from Musa ibn al-Qasim from Muhammad ibn Saif ibn 'Amirah from Mansur ibn Hazim, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a person in ihram who was compelled to eat game or meat of an animal that died naturally. He said: 'Which is more preferable to you, to eat from the game or the meat of an animal that died naturally?' I said: 'The meat of an animal that died naturally, because the game is forbidden to the person in ihram.' He said: 'Which is more preferable to you, to eat from your own wealth or the meat of an animal that died naturally?' I said: 'I eat from my own wealth.' He said: 'Then eat from the game and redeem it.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali from his father from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad from al-Halabi from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a person in ihram who is compelled (by hunger) and finds a carcass (dead animal not slaughtered ritually) and game (caught meat), which of the two should he eat? He said: He should eat the game. I said: Does he not like to eat from his own wealth (to compensate)? He said: The compensation is upon him, so let him eat and let him pay the compensation.

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar from Isḥāq from Jaʿfar from his father (peace be upon him) that ʿAlī (peace be upon him) used to say: When the Muḥrim (person in iḥrām) is compelled to [eat] game and carrion, let him eat the carrion that Allah has permitted him, so as not to contradict the earlier reports, because in the report it is not specified that he was compelled to [eat] game and carrion while he was capable of and able to consume them. And if that is not explicit in its apparent meaning, we interpret it as referring to one who cannot find game nor is able to reach it, but is able to consume carrion; at that time it is permissible for him to consume carrion. As for when game is available and he is able to consume it, then it is not permissible under any condition.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ibn Faddal from Yunus ibn Ya'qub said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the one who is compelled to eat the dead animal (beast of burden) while he finds game (to eat). He said: He should eat the game. I said: Indeed, Allah, Exalted and Mighty, has permitted him the dead animal if he is compelled to it, and has not permitted him the game. He said: Which is more beloved to you, to eat from your wealth or the dead animal? I said: I will eat from my wealth. He said: It is your wealth because the ransom is upon you. I said: If there is no wealth with me? He said: You will pay it off when you return to your wealth.

And as for what Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd from Abd al-Ghaffar al-Jazi who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the person in ihram (ritual consecration for Hajj/Umrah) who is compelled to eat carrion (meat of an animal that died naturally), and he finds it, and also finds game (freshly killed or alive). He said: He eats the carrion and leaves the game. The meaning in this report is one of two things: One is that it is to be attributed to a form of taqiyya (dissimulation/prudence), because that is the view of some of the Sunnis. And the second is that it is directed to one who finds the game not yet slaughtered (or alive), for he eats the carrion and frees the game (lets it go). And we said this because when the person in ihram slaughters the game, its ruling is the ruling of the carrion. And if it is so, and he finds the carrion, he should restrict himself to it and not slaughter the living animal, but rather let it go.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding the Muhrim (one in Ihram) who hunts game, he said (peace be upon him): The expiation is upon him for every thing he catches.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Ibn Abi Umayr from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'If a person in ihram kills game, he said: 'Upon him is the expiation.' I said, 'And if he repeats?' He said: 'Upon him, every time he repeats, an expiation.'

Al-Husayn ibn Said from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad from Al-Halabi from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: The Muhrim (one in Ihram), if he kills game, is upon him its compensation (Jaza'), and he gives the game as charity to a poor person. If he returns and kills another game, there is no Jaza' upon him, and Allah takes retribution from him, and the retribution is in the Hereafter. This does not contradict what we have presented from the narrations, because the aspect of it is that we carry it upon the one from whom killing game repeats via the path of intentionality (Al-'Amad). For if the matter is so, the expiation (Kaffarah) is obligatory upon him in the first time, and nothing is obligatory upon him in the second time, and he is among those from whom Allah takes retribution. And if that is upon the mode of inadvertence (Al-Sahw) and forgetfulness (An-Nisyan), the expiation is obligatory upon him every time it repeats from him. This indicates this distinction.

Yaqub ibn Yazid from Ibn Abi Umayr, from some of his companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: When the Muhrim (person in Hajj/Umrah state) catches game by mistake, upon him is the Kaffarah (expiation). If he catches it a second time by mistake, upon him is the Kaffarah always, if it is by mistake. If he catches it intentionally, upon him is the Kaffarah. If he catches it a second time intentionally, he is among those from whom Allah takes vengeance, and there is no Kaffarah upon him.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Abu Ali al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn al-Jabbar, from Safwan, from Abd Allah ibn Sinan, who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: Whoever is obliged to pay the ransom (fidyah) for game he caught while in the state of ihram, if he is a pilgrim (hajj), he slaughters his sacrificial animal (hady) which is obligatory upon him at Mina; and if he is a pilgrim of Umrah, he slaughters it in Mecca opposite the Ka'bah.

From him, from Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from Al-Mu'alla ibn Muhammad, from Al-Hasan ibn Ali, from Aban, from Zurarah, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) that he said: Regarding the Muhrim (one in Ihram) who catches game, making a Hady (sacrificial animal) obligatory upon him: he must slaughter it if he is performing Hajj in Mina where people slaughter, and if he is performing Umrah, he slaughters it in Mecca. And if he wishes, he may leave it until he returns and buys it, for his saying suffices. And if he wishes, he may leave it until he returns and buys it; this is a concession (rukhsah) in delaying the Fidyah (expiation) to Mecca or Mina. And the preferable course is to redeem it from where he caught it.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, who said: The person in ihsar (ritual consecration) offers the ransom for the game from wherever it is found.

Musa ibn al-Qasim from Safwan from Ibn Abi Umayr from Mansur ibn Hazim said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the expiation of the individual Umrah, where should it be? He said: In Mecca, unless its owner wishes to delay it to Mina, but making it in Mecca is more beloved to me and superior. Thus, the meaning in this report is one of two things: either it is informing about sufficiency (validity), and the earlier reports include the aspect of superiority, as explicitly stated in the report by his words 'and making it in Mecca is more beloved to me'; or this is specific to what is other than the expiation of game, because that which cannot be slaughtered except in Mecca is the expiation of game. Therefore, what is other than that among the expiations, their slaughter is permissible in Mina, even if slaughtering them in Mecca is superior.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from a number of our companions from Sahl ibn Ziyad from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from some of his men from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: Whoever is obliged to offer a sacrificial animal (hady) while in the state of consecration (ihram), he may slaughter it wherever he wishes, except for the redemption of game, for indeed Allah, the Exalted, says: 'A sacrificial animal reaching the Ka'ba.'

Ahmad ibn 'Abdun narrated to me from Abu al-Hasan Ali ibn Muhammad ibn al-Zubayr al-Qurashi, from Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Faddal, from Muhammad ibn 'Abdullah ibn Zur'ar, from al-Hasan ibn Ali, from al-'Ala' ibn Razin, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from one of the Imams (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about a man who permits the sexual intimacy of his slave-girl to his brother, and he said: 'She is permissible for him as long as he permits her to him.'
From him, from his two brothers, from their father, from Abdullah ibn Bukayr, from Durays ibn Abd al-Malik, who said: There is no harm in a man making his concubine permissible for his brother.

From him, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Hakim, from Karram ibn Amr, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said: I said to him, 'If a man makes the private part of his slave-girl permissible for his brother,' he said, 'Yes, there is no objection; he has whatever he made permissible for him from her.'

From him, from Muhammad ibn Abdillah, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hisham ibn Salim, from Muhammad ibn Mudabbir, who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to me: 'O Muhammad, take this slave girl; she will serve you and you may have sexual relations with her. So when you go out, return her to us.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from a number of our companions from Sahl ibn Ziyad and Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad and Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father, all from Ibn Mahbub from Ibn Ri'ab from Abu Basir, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a woman who made her slave girl's private part permissible for her son. He said: 'It is permissible for him.' I said: 'Then is the price (dowry/value) permissible for him?' He said: 'No, only what she made permissible for him is permissible for him.'

From him, from several of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from Abd al-Karim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I said to him, 'A man permits the private part of his slave-girl to his brother.' He said, 'Yes, for him whatever he permitted from her.'

From him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Isma'il ibn Bazee', who said: I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about a woman who made her slave girl permissible for me. He said: 'That is for you.' I said: 'For she was joking.' He said: 'What is there for you regarding what is in her heart? If you know that she was joking, then do not [take it as binding].'

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa narrated from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Yaqtin, from his brother al-Husayn, from Ali ibn Yaqtin, who said: I asked him about a man who makes the vagina of his female slave permissible (for another man), and he said: 'I do not like that.' There is nothing in it that necessitates the prohibition of what we mentioned, because it came in the place of dislike (karaahah). He explicitly stated this in his saying 'I do not like that.' The reason for the dislike of this is that this is something upon which none of the general public (Sunni scholars) agree with us, and it is something they use to criticize us. Therefore, abstaining from it is superior, even if it is not forbidden. It is also possible that he disliked it only if the freedom of the child was not stipulated; so if that is stipulated, this dislike is removed, which indicates that.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Safwan ibn Yahya from Ishaq ibn 'Ammar who said: I asked Abu Ibrahim (peace be upon him) about a woman who makes her female slave girl permissible (for intercourse) for her husband. He said: 'I dislike this.' I said: 'If she becomes pregnant?' He said: 'You say: If she becomes pregnant by you, then it is for you.' He said: 'There is no problem with this.' I said: 'So a man does this with his brother?' He said: 'There is no problem.'

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan, from Amr ibn Sa'id, from Musaddiq ibn Sadaqah, from 'Ammar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) in When a woman says to her husband, 'My slave girl is for you,' he said: 'Her private part is not permissible to him unless she sells it to him or gifts it to him.' The meaning in this report is that we interpret it as: if she says, 'It is for you, excluding the private part,' regarding her service, because it is known from the custom of women that they do not consider their husbands' intercourse with their slave girls to be permissible [by default], and if the matter is as we have said, then his private part is not permissible to her in any case.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from Abu al-Hasan al-Rida (peace be upon them) who said: Temporary marriage (Mut'ah) is a marriage with inheritance and a marriage without inheritance. If inheritance is stipulated, it exists; if it is not stipulated, it does not exist.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from al-Nadr from 'Asim ibn Humayd from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'What is the dowry, meaning in al-Mut'ah (temporary marriage)?' He said: 'Whatever they agree upon for whatever duration they choose.' I said: 'What do you think if she becomes pregnant?' He said: 'The child is his.' If he wishes to enter into a new matter, he may do so, and there is no waiting period for her from him. And from another man, she has five and forty nights. And if they stipulate inheritance, then they are upon their stipulation.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Barqi, from al-Hasan ibn Jahm, from al-Hasan ibn Musa, from Sa'id ibn Yasar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a man who marries a woman for a fixed term (mut'ah) and does not stipulate inheritance. He said: There is no inheritance between them, whether he stipulated it or not. This does not contradict the first two narrations, because the matter is that there is no inheritance between them, whether the negation of inheritance was stipulated or not, because the negation of mutual inheritance is among the necessary rulings in mut'ah, and the establishment of inheritance requires a stipulation, and that which indicates what we mentioned.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Ja'far ibn Bashir, from Hammad ibn 'Uthman, from Jamil ibn Salih, from 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about al-Mut'ah, and he said: 'It is permissible by Allah and His Messenger.' I said: 'What is its limit/condition?' He said: 'Among its conditions is that she does not inherit you, nor do you inherit her.' I said: 'What is her waiting period (Iddah)?' He said: 'Forty-five days, or three pure menstrual cycles.'

And as for what Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ibn Faddal from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I heard Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) saying regarding a man who marries a woman for a specified term (mut'ah): 'The two inherit from each other if they do not stipulate [a condition], and the condition is after the marriage. Therefore, the approach in this report is to interpret it as: if the term is not stipulated, then they inherit from each other, and that which indicates this...'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from 'Amr ibn 'Uthman from Ibrahim ibn al-Fadl from Aban ibn Taghlib who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'How should I say to her when I am alone with her?' He said, 'You should say: I marry you for a mut'ah (temporary marriage) according to the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Prophet (peace be upon him and his family), not as an inheritor nor as an inherited one, for such and such a day, and if you wish, such and such a year, for such and such a dirham, and you specify the term, whether it be little or much, whatever you two agree upon. When she says 'Yes', she is pleased, and she is your wife, and you are the most entitled of people to her.' I said, 'But I am shy to mention the condition of the days.' He said, 'It is more detrimental to you.' I said, 'How so?' He said, 'Indeed, if you do not stipulate it, it becomes a permanent marriage, necessitating maintenance upon you during the waiting period, and she becomes an inheritor, and you cannot divorce her except with a Sunnah divorce.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Ibn Abi Umayr from Al-'Ala' ibn Rawbab from Ibn Muskān from Ibn Abi Ya'fur from Al-Hasan ibn Mahran from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: I said to him, 'May God perfect you: A man divorced his wife while she was in a state of purity, without sexual intercourse, with the testimony of two just witnesses.' He said, 'When she enters the third menstruation, her waiting period is completed and she becomes permissible for marriage.' I said to him, 'May God perfect you, indeed the people of Iraq narrate from Ali (peace be upon him) that he said: He has more right to take her back as long as she has not bathed from the third menstruation.' He said, 'They lie.'

From him, from Abu Ali al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, from Safwan, from Isḥāq ibn ʿAmmār, from Ismāʿīl al-Jaʿfī, from Abū Jaʿfar (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him, 'A man divorced his wife.' He said, 'He has more right to take her back (revocation of divorce) as long as the blood has not fallen from the third menstruation.'

And with this chain, from Safwan, from Ibn Muskhan, from Zurarah, from one of the Imams (peace be upon him), he said: The divorced woman inherits and is inherited from until she sees the third blood [of menstruation]; when she sees it, then it is severed.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Humayd, from al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Sama'ah, from Safwan, from Musa ibn Bakr, from Zurarah, who said: I said to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him): 'I heard al-Rabi'ah al-Ra'y say: When the woman sees blood from the third menstruation, she is thereby divorced (baanat minhu), and the Quru' (period of purity) is only what is between the two menstruations. And he claimed that he took this by his own opinion (ra'y).' Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: 'He did not lie by my life; he did not say that by his own opinion, but he took it from Ali (peace be upon him).' I said to him: 'And what did Ali (peace be upon him) say regarding this?' He said: 'He used to say: When she sees blood from the third menstruation, her waiting period (iddah) is completed, and there is no way for the husband to take her back. And the Quru' is only what is between the two menstruations. And she is not permitted to marry until she performs the ritual bath (ghusl) from the third menstruation.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad, from al-Hasan ibn Ali, from Aban ibn 'Uthman, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi 'Abdillah, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the woman whose husband divorces her, when does she become free to dispose of herself (i.e., complete her waiting period)? He said: When she sees the blood of the third menstruation, she is free to dispose of herself. I said: And if the blood comes early for her before the days of her menses? He said: If the blood is before ten days, it is considered hers (as a second menstruation), and it is from the menstruation from which she purified herself. And if the blood is after the ten days, it is from the third menstruation, so she is free to dispose of herself.

From him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from some of his companions (I think it is Muhammad ibn Abdillah ibn Hilal or Ali ibn al-Hakam), from al-Ala' ibn Razin, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a man who divorces his wife: when does she become fully divorced (mutallaqah) from him? He said: When the blood of the third menstrual period appears, she gains control of herself. I said: Then is she permitted to marry in that state? He said: Yes, but she should not allow herself to be married until she is purified from the blood. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: What these narrations encompass is what we act upon, which is that when she sees the blood of the third menstrual period, she gains control of herself and becomes permissible for husbands, and it is valid for her to contract marriage upon herself. However, it is preferable that she delay marriage until she performs the ritual bath (ghusl). If she contracts marriage, she should not allow herself to be married until after the bath. This is the view of al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Sama'ah and Ali ibn Ibrahim ibn Hashim. Ja'far ibn Sama'ah said: She becomes fully divorced upon seeing the blood, except that it is not permissible for her to contract marriage until after the bath. And what we have chosen is more appropriate, and by this our Sheikh (may God have mercy on him) used to issue fatwas. Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) explicitly stated this in the narration of Zurarah, which Umar ibn Udhaynah narrated from him, from his saying: 'And she becomes permissible for husbands.' And the narration which Musa ibn Bakr narrated from Zurarah from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), from his saying: 'And she is not permitted to marry until she bathes from the third menstrual period,' is to be understood as referring to the dislike (karahah) we previously mentioned, that contracting marriage upon her is valid. Muhammad ibn Muslim also narrated it, and we have previously presented the narration from him, and it is mentioned therein that she is not permitted to allow herself to be married until after the bath, according to what we have presented.

Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Fadhal narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn al-Jahm from Abdullah ibn Maymun from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) from his father (peace be upon him) who said: Ali (peace be upon him) said: When a man divorces his wife, he has more right to her as long as she has not performed the ritual bath (ghusl) from the third (divorce).

From him, from Ayyub ibn Nuḥ, from Ṣafwān ibn Yaḥyā, from Isḥāq ibn ʿAmmār, from whoever narrated to him, from Abū ʿAbdillāh (peace be upon him) who said: A woman came to ʿUmar asking him about her divorce. He said, 'Go to this man and ask him,' meaning ʿAlī (peace be upon him). She said to ʿAlī (peace be upon him), 'My husband has divorced me.' He said, 'Did you wash your private part?' She returned to ʿUmar and said, 'He sent me to a man who plays (is joking).' He said, 'I sent you to him twice,' every time she returned saying, 'He plays.' He said, 'Go to him, for he is the most knowledgeable of us.' He said, and ʿAlī (peace be upon him) said to her, 'Did you wash your private part?' She said, 'No.' He said, 'Then your husband has more right to your private part as long as you have not washed your private part.' The explanation in these two narrations and what came in their meaning is that they are not repelled by the preceding narrations, because the explanation in them is that we carry them on a type of taqiyyah (dissimulation) or on the manner of attributing the opinion to them, so the saying of Abū ʿAbdillāh (peace be upon him) 'ʿAlī (peace be upon him) said' means 'These people say that,' not that he was informing in reality about the opinion of the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him). And Abū Jaʿfar (peace be upon him) explicitly stated in the narration of Zurārah and others what is a refutation of it, and his saying 'They lied about ʿAlī (peace be upon him).' And if the matter is as we have said, then there is no contradiction between the narrations.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn 'Isa from Ibn Abi 'Umayr from Hammad from al-Halabi from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: The number of periods for which menstruation is established and becomes regular is three menstrual cycles, and these are three menstruations.

Sa'd ibn 'Abdillah narrated from Ayub ibn Nuh from Safwan from 'Abdullah ibn Muskhan from Abu Basir who said: The number of periods during which menstruation becomes established and regular is three menstrual cycles, and these are three menstruations. The explanation for these two narrations is one of two things: either they are both based on taqiyya (dissimulation), because they both interpret the 'cycles' (aqra') as 'menstruations' (hiyad), whereas for us the 'cycles' are the periods of purity between two menstruations, and that which indicates this is...

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, and a number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ibn Abi Nasr, from Jamil ibn Darraj, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said: The Quru' (period of purity) is the time between the two menstruations.

From him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Hajjāl, from Thaʿlabah, from Zurārah, from Abū Jaʿfar (peace be upon him) who said: The qarāʾ (monthly periods) are the aṭhār (clean periods). The other interpretation in the two reports is that the expression was used to refer to three qarāʾ, in that they do not become clear (i.e., the woman is considered pure) except upon seeing the blood of the third period. Thus, he expressed the first sighting of blood as another period by way of metaphor, even if it is not a condition of that to complete the third period, as we have previously stated. And in the report it is not established that she is required to complete the third period, nor does this interpretation contradict it.

Sa'd ibn Abdillah narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from Ja'far ibn Bashir from Rifa'ah from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a divorced woman when she menstruates, is the right of return upon her for her husband? He said: Yes, until she becomes pure, because in this report there is no indication that he has the right of return upon her until she becomes pure from the third menstruation. And if that is not in it, we interpret it to mean that he has the right of return upon her in the first or second menstruation.

Sa'd ibn Abdillah, from Ayub ibn Nuh, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Abdillah ibn Muskān, from al-Hasan ibn Ziyād, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: She inherits and is inherited from as long as she has the right of return (raj'ah) from the first two divorces, until she performs the ritual bath. The solution regarding these two reports is what we have previously presented, by interpreting them as being based on precaution (taqiyyah). Our Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) reconciled these reports by saying: If he divorces her at the end of her purity period, she observes the waiting period by counting her menstrual cycles; and if he divorces her at the beginning of it, she observes the waiting period by counting the purity periods (which are the clean days). This is a close (plausible) solution, except that the first one is what we have previously presented.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Bunan ibn Muhammad, from Musa ibn al-Qasim, from Ali ibn Ja'far, from his brother Musa ibn Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: I asked him about a man who divorces his wife with one or two divorces, then leaves her until her waiting period expires. What is her status? He said: If he leaves her intending not to remarry her, she becomes fully divorced from him and is not permissible to him until she marries another husband. And if he leaves her intending to remarry her, and a year passes, then he has more right to her revocation (of the divorce).

From him, from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ali, from Amr ibn Sa'id, from Musaddaq ibn Sadaqah, from 'Ammar al-Sabati, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), that he was asked: About a man who divorced his wife with two divorces during the waiting period, then left her until her menstrual periods (quru') passed. He said: If he left her with the intention of not revoking the divorce, she is completely divorced from him and not permissible to him until she marries another husband. And if his intention was to revoke the divorce, then he left her for six months, there is no harm in him revoking the divorce. These two reports are accepted by consensus, because there is no disagreement among the Ummah that when she exits the waiting period, the husband has no claim over her, and she becomes master of her own self.

Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Fadhal narrated from Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Hakim from Jamil from some of our companions from one of the two Imams (peace be upon him) who said: The woman with continuous menstruation (mustahadha) counts her waiting period based on the blood if it is during her menstrual days, or based on the months if it preceded them. If it becomes mixed and her menstrual days are not known, then that does not remain hidden, for the blood of menstruation is thick and warm, and the blood of continuous menstruation is yellow and cool.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from a number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Abd al-Karim, from Abi Basir, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The waiting period of the woman with irregular menstruation (mustahadha) who does not purify is three months, and the waiting period of the woman who menstruates and whose menstruation becomes regular is three quru', and the qur' is the gathering of blood between two menstruations.

From him, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The waiting period ('iddah) of the woman who does not menstruate and the woman who has irregular bleeding (mustahadha) and does not become pure is three months. And the waiting period of the woman who menstruates and whose menses are regular is three menstrual cycles. The method for reconciling these narrations is that if it is possible for the mustahadha to know the days of her menstruation, she must observe the cycles that are her pure days. And if it is not possible for her due to the confusion of blood upon her, it suffices for her to observe three months, according to what the last two narrations contained.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: It is not appropriate for the divorced woman to leave except with the permission of her husband, until her waiting period (iddah) expires, which is three menstrual periods, or three months if she does not menstruate.

From him, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Uthman ibn Isa, from Sama'ah, who said: I asked him about the divorced woman (revocable divorce), where does she observe her waiting period? He said: In her house, she does not go out. And if she wishes to visit, she goes out after half the night, and she does not go out during the day. And she is not permitted to perform Hajj until her waiting period is completed. And I asked him about the woman whose husband dies, is she the same? He said: Yes, and she performs Hajj if she wishes.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan and Abu Ali al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn al-Jabbar, from Safwan, from al-Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: The divorced woman performs Hajj and pays her dues. This report carries two meanings: one is that it is permissible for her to perform the Hajj of Islam (Fard), because there is no obedience to the husband for her in that matter, as we have indicated in the Book of Hajj; and the second is that it is permissible for her to perform the voluntary Hajj if her husband grants her permission.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Humayd ibn Ziyad, from Ibn Sama'ah, from Muhammad ibn Zaid, from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I heard him (peace be upon him) say: The divorced woman (triple or revocable) performs Hajj during her waiting period if her husband is pleased with it. As for what the report included regarding that it is permissible for her to attend to legal rights, it should be understood according to the detail contained in the report of Sama'ah, that it is permissible for her to do so if she leaves after mid-night and returns to her home during the night, and that is the first [instance/ruling].

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Musa ibn Bakr, from al-Zurari, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: The woman who is thrice divorced has no maintenance (nafaqah) from her husband; that is only for the one whose husband has the right of return (raj'ah).

From him, from Humayd ibn Ziyad, from Ibn Sama'ah, from Muhammad ibn Ziyad, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about the woman who has been thrice divorced according to the Sunnah, does she have residence (housing) or maintenance (nafaqah)? He said: No.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Ibn Sinan said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the thrice-divorced woman during her waiting period: does she have residence or maintenance? He said: Yes. The meaning in this report is one of two things: either it is to be understood as recommended (not obligatory), or the intended meaning is when she is pregnant, which indicates that.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad from al-Halabi from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) that he was asked about the thrice-divorced woman Does she have maintenance and residence? He said: Is she pregnant? I said: No. He said: Then no.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Ibn Abi Umayr from Jamil from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) in A slave woman who was under a man, he divorced her, then she was freed. He said: She observes the waiting period of a free woman.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Fadala from al-Qasim ibn Yazid from Muhammad ibn Muslim from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: If a free man divorces his slave-girl, and she observes part of her waiting period from him, and then she is manumitted, then she observes the waiting period of a slave-girl, and this does not contradict the first report, because the way to reconcile between them is that if the slave-girl is divorced with the first divorce, with which he retains the right of return, and then she is manumitted after that, then her waiting period is the waiting period of a free woman; and if she is divorced with the second divorce, with which the bond of marriage is severed, then her waiting period is the waiting period of a slave-girl. This indicates this distinction.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Abu Ayyub al-Kazzaz from Mihzam from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding a slave woman under the ownership of a free man who divorced her during a period of purity without sexual intercourse, with one revocable divorce, and then she was freed after he had divorced her for thirty days, and her waiting period had not yet expired. He said: If she is freed before her waiting period expires, she observes the waiting period of a free woman from the day he divorced her, and he has the right of return (raj'ah) over her before the expiration of the waiting period. If he divorced her with two divorces, one after the other, and then she was freed before the expiration of her waiting period, then he has no right of return over her, and her waiting period is the waiting period of a slave woman.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from al-Husayn ibn Muhammad from al-Mu'alla ibn Muhammad from al-Hasan ibn Ali from Aban from Zurarah, who said: I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about the waiting period of the woman who undergoes khul' (divorce by redemption), how many is it? He said: The waiting period of the divorced woman, and she should observe it in her house. And the woman who undergoes mubarat (mutual divorce) is in the same status as the woman who undergoes khul'.

From him, from Humayd ibn Ziyad, from al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Sama'ah, from Dawud ibn Sirhan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding the mu'talah (mutual divorce for compensation), it was said: her waiting period is the same as that of the divorced woman, and she observes it in her house; and the mu'talah is in the position of the mubar'ah (divorce by mutual agreement).

Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Ibn Bukayr from Zurarah from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) that he said: The waiting period of a woman who gives khula' (divorce by mutual consent) is forty-five days. This report carries two interpretations: one is that if the woman is a slave who does not menstruate, but a similar slave does menstruate, her waiting period is forty-five days when her husband grants her khula'. The other interpretation is that the report is specific to a woman whose habit is to menstruate three times within this period, which amounts to forty-five days. On both interpretations, it does not contradict the earlier reports.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from a number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ibn Abi Najran, from Safwan, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'Three [types of women] may marry at any time [without waiting for a waiting period]: the one who has not yet menstruated, and her like who does not menstruate.' I asked: 'What is her limit/definition?' He said: 'When she is less than nine years old.' And the one who has not been entered into (consummated), and the one who has despaired of menstruation, and her like who does not menstruate.' I asked: 'What is her limit/definition?' He said: 'When she is fifty years old.'

From him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Mahbub, from Hammad ibn Uthman, from Zurara, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding the young girl who does not menstruate like her, and the one who has despaired of menstruation, he said: There is no waiting period (iddah) upon her, even if intercourse occurs with her.

From him, from Abu Ali al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn al-Jabbar and al-Razzaz together, and Humayd ibn Ziyad, from Ibn Sama'ah, from Safwan, from Muhammad ibn Hakim, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said: the one who does not conceive (like her), there is no waiting period ('iddah) upon her.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Humayd ibn Ziyad, from Ibn Sama'ah, from Muhammad ibn Ziyad, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) ruled regarding a woman whose husband died before consummating the marriage with her, saying: 'She shall not marry until she completes a waiting period of four months and ten days, which is the waiting period for a woman whose husband has died.'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Safwan, from al-'Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from one of the Imams (peace be upon him), regarding: If a man dies while his wife is under his guardianship, but he has not yet consummated the marriage with her, he said: She receives half of the dowry, and she inherits fully, and upon her is the complete waiting period.

From him, from Safwan, from Abdullah ibn Bukayr, from Ubayd ibn Zur'arah, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who married a woman but did not consummate the marriage with her. He said: If she dies or he dies or he divorces her, then she is entitled to half of the dowry, and she must observe the full waiting period, and she is entitled to inheritance.

From him, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: If he has not yet entered into her, and he has already designated a dowry for her, then she is entitled to half of what he designated for her, and she inherits, and she must observe the waiting period.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr from Muhammad ibn Umar al-Sabati who said: I asked Imam al-Rida (peace be upon him) about a man who married a woman and divorced her before consummating the marriage. He said: 'There is no waiting period (iddah) upon her.' And I asked him about a woman whose husband died before consummating the marriage. He said: 'There is no waiting period upon her. The two cases are equal.'

From him, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from Dawud ibn al-Husayn, from Ubayd ibn Zurara, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who divorced his wife before consummating the marriage, is there a waiting period (iddah) upon her? He said: No. I said to him: What about the one whose husband dies before consummation? Is there a waiting period upon her? He said: Hold back from this [question], for these two reports do not contradict the reports we have previously presented, because the first reports are consistent with the apparent meaning of the Quran. Allah, the Exalted, said: 'Those of you who die and leave wives should be tested by their wives for four months and ten [days].' And He did not specify anything other than the consummated [marriage] from that, so it is appropriate that it be general, and the reports we presented confirm this, and that should not be abandoned for the sake of these two anomalous reports. With the understanding that the latter report does not explicitly state that he said: 'There is no iddah upon her,' but rather he said: 'Hold back from this,' and it is not impossible that he ordered him to hold back from that for a certain type of expediency in the moment. And since Ubayd ibn Zurara, the narrator of the latter hadith, narrated that there is a complete iddah upon her, and we have previously presented that narration from him, then taking what is explicitly stated in it is more worthy of being acted upon than acting upon what did not explicitly state the intended meaning.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from a number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ibn Mahbub, from Ali ibn Ri'ab, from Umar ibn Hanzalah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: He stipulates for her whatever days he wishes.

From him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from Abu al-Hasan al-Rida (peace be upon him), who said: I said to him: 'A man marries in mut'ah for a year, or less, or more.' He said: 'If it is with a known amount (dowry) until a known term.' I said: 'And it ends (terminates) without divorce?' He said: 'Yes.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Faddal, from Ibn Bukayr, from Zurara, who said: I asked him: Is it permissible for a man to enjoy [temporary marriage] with a woman for an hour or two hours? He said: For the hour and the two hours, there is no fixed limit, but rather the period and the two periods, and the day and the two days, and similar to that.

From him, from a number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ibn Faddal, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from a man he named, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who marries a woman for a single 'arad' (temporary period), so he said: 'There is no objection, but when he finishes, let him turn his face and not look.' The 'face' in these two narrations is a form of concession. The more precautionary approach, as contained in the earlier narrations, is that the mention of the term should be known days or specified months. As for the hour and the two hours, and the 'daffah' (session/instance) and the two 'daffahs', these are from what cannot be established with certainty. And the first view is that the intended meaning of 'daffah' and 'two daffahs' in the two narrations is only permissible when added to a specific day or specific days. As for if he mentions 'daffah' vaguely without adding it to a specific day, that is a permanent contract that does not dissolve except by divorce, which indicates that.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from Musa ibn Sa'dan from Abd Allah ibn al-Qasim from Hisham al-Jawaliqi who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'Should I marry a woman for a mut'ah (temporary marriage) for a specific, indefinite period?' He said: 'That is more difficult for you; she inherits you and you inherit her, so it is not permissible for you to divorce her except after a period of purity and with two witnesses.' I said: 'May God improve you, then how should I marry her?' He said: 'For a numbered number of days, with a specified amount, according to what you have agreed upon. When her days are completed, her divorce is by virtue of the condition, and there is no maintenance for her upon you.' I said: 'What do we say to her?' He said: 'You say to her: I marry you upon the Book of God and the Sunnah of His Prophet (peace be upon him and his family), and God is my guardian and your guardian, for such and such a month for such and such a dirham, on the condition that God guarantees for me that you will fulfill [the terms] for me, and I will not swear to you, nor will I claim your offspring, nor is there a waiting period for you upon me.' When your condition expires, do not marry until forty-five days have passed for you, and if childbirth occurs to you, inform me.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Abdillah ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hisham ibn Salim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) In the case of a man who had a wife under him, then he divorced her, and then he died regarding her before her waiting period ended, he said: She observes the waiting period of the longer of the two periods, the waiting period of the one whose husband died regarding her.

From him, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Najran, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from Asim ibn Humayd, from Muhammad ibn Qays, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: I heard him saying: Any woman who is divorced and then her husband dies before her waiting period (iddah) expires and she is not yet forbidden to him, then she inherits him. Then she observes the waiting period of the one who died for her (the deceased husband). If she dies while in her waiting period and she is not yet forbidden to him, then he inherits her.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Jamil ibn Darraj, from some of our companions, from one of the two Imams (peace be upon him), in [a hadith]: Regarding a man who divorced his wife with a revocable divorce (Talaq Raj'i), then her husband died, she said: She observes the waiting period (Iddah) of the nearer of the two periods, which is four months and ten days.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ahmad ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn al-Fudayl, from Abu al-Subah al-Kinani, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), that he said: Regarding the pregnant woman whose husband dies, is she entitled to maintenance (nafaqah)? He said: No.

From him, from Ali, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), that he said: Regarding the pregnant woman whose husband dies, that there is no maintenance (nafaqah) for her.

From him, from a number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ibn Abi Nasr, from Muthanna al-Hannat, from Zurarah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) regarding the pregnant woman whose husband dies, is she entitled to maintenance (nafaqah)? He said: No.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Faddal from al-Mufaddal ibn Salih from Zayd, Abu Usamah, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the pregnant woman whose husband died, is she entitled to maintenance (nafaqah)? He said: No.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from al-'Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from one of the two Imams (peace be upon him), who said: If her husband dies, he provides for her from his wealth; this does not contradict what we have previously stated, because the saying of the Imam (peace be upon him): 'He provides for her from his wealth,' we interpret as meaning he provides for her from the wealth of the child if she is pregnant, and the child, even if not yet mentioned by name, is something we are permitted to estimate/assume, as the evidence for it is established, just as we have done in many places in the Quran and elsewhere, and that which indicates this.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isma'il from Muhammad ibn al-Fudayl from Abu al-Subah al-Kinani from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The pregnant woman whose husband dies, is maintained from the wealth of the child in her womb. It is noted that Muhammad ibn Muslim, the narrator of this hadith, has narrated it in agreement with what we have previously presented; he narrated that.

Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from al-Saffan, from al-'Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from one of the Imams (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about a woman whose husband dies while she is in her waiting period (iddah); does she receive maintenance (nafaqah)? He said: No, she is not maintained from her own wealth.

Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Barqi, from Abdullah ibn al-Mughira, from al-Sakuni, from Ja'far, from his father, from Ali (peace be upon him) who said: The maintenance (nafaqah) of the pregnant woman whose husband has died is paid from all the estate until she gives birth. The interpretation of this report is one of two matters: either it is understood as recommended (mustahabb) if the heirs agree to it, or the correct view is that she is maintained from all the estate because the share of the fetus has not yet been distinguished; it is only distinguished when she gives birth and it is known whether it is male or female. At that point, his estate is partitioned. When it is distinguished, what was spent on her is taken from her share and returned to the heirs. The benefit of this report is that maintenance is not obligatory upon one heir to the exclusion of the other, but they are equal in this matter.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from al-Qasim from 'Ali from Abi Basir said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the divorce of a female slave, so he said: Two divorces. And he said, Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: The waiting period of the female slave whose husband dies is two months and five days. And the waiting period of the divorced female slave is one month and a half.

From him, from Uthman ibn Isa, from Sama'ah, who said: I asked him about a female slave whose husband dies, and he said: Her waiting period is two months and five days. And he said: The waiting period of the female slave who does not menstruate is forty-five days.

Ali ibn Isma'il from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad from al-Halabi from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: The waiting period ('iddah) of a female slave whose husband dies is two months and five days, and the waiting period of the divorced woman who does not menstruate is one month and a half.

Al-Husayn ibn Said from Ibn Abi Umayr and Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Jamil ibn Darraj from Muhammad ibn Muslim from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: When the wife of a slave woman dies, her waiting period (iddah) is two months and five days.

From him, from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from 'Asim ibn Humayd, from Muhammad ibn Qays, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: I heard him saying: The divorce of a male slave for his female slave involves two divorces, and her waiting period is two menstruations if she menstruates, and if she does not menstruate, her waiting period is one and a half months. And if her husband dies for her, her waiting period is half the waiting period of a free woman, which is two months and five days.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from a number of our companions from Sahl ibn Ziyad and Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad and Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father, all from Ibn Mahbub from Ibn Ri'ab and Abdullah ibn Bukayr from Zurara from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: Indeed, the slave woman and the free woman, both of them, when her husband dies, are equal in the waiting period (Idda), except that the free woman observes mourning (Ihadd) and the slave woman does not observe mourning.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Nu'man, from Ibn Muskhan, from Sulayman ibn Khalid, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a female slave who is divorced, what is her waiting period? He said: Two menstrual cycles or two months. I said: And if her husband dies for her? He said: Indeed Ali (peace be upon him) said regarding the mothers of children: They do not marry until they complete a waiting period of four months and ten days, even if they are slaves.

Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from Wahb ibn Abd Rabbih, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about a man who had an Umm al-Walad (concubine who bore him a child), and he married her to a man, and she bore him a boy. Then the man died, and she returned to her master. Is it permissible for him to have sexual relations with her? He said: She observes the waiting period (Iddah) from the deceased husband for four months and ten days. Then he can have relations with her by virtue of ownership (Milk), without a new marriage contract.

And as for what al-Saffar narrated from Muhammad ibn 'Isa from Ali ibn al-Hakam from Zur'ah from Samaan from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about the waiting period ('iddah) of a female slave whose husband dies, and he said: one and a half months. This is a report in which the narrator may have erred in its transmission, because it is not impossible that he heard this ruling regarding a divorced female slave, since we have clarified that the waiting period of a divorced female slave, if she is among those who do not menstruate but is of an age where she could menstruate, is one and a half months. Thus, it became confused for him, and he narrated it regarding the one whose husband dies. On this basis, it does not contradict the previously mentioned reports.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Ali ibn Isma'il from Safwan from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a woman whom a man marries in mut'ah (temporary marriage), then her husband dies. Is there a waiting period ('iddah) upon her? He said: She observes a waiting period of four months and ten days. And if she stays with him for days, she observes the waiting period and also observes mourning (hudd). I said: Does she observe mourning? He said: Yes, if she stayed with him for days, she observes the waiting period and also observes mourning. And if she was with him for one day or two days or an hour of the day, then the full waiting period is obligatory upon her and she does not observe mourning.

From him, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Umar ibn Udhaynah, from Zurarah, who said: I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him): What is the waiting period (iddah) of the Mut'ah woman if the husband from whom she enjoyed dies? He said: Four months and ten days. He then said: O Zurarah, in all marriages, if the husband dies, the waiting period for the woman is four months and ten days, whether she was free or a slave, and regardless of whether the marriage was Mut'ah, permanent marriage (Tazwij), or ownership by right (of a concubine). The waiting period of the divorced woman is three months, and for the slave woman who is divorced, it is half of what is upon the free woman, and likewise for the Mut'ah woman, it is what is upon the slave woman.

Ali ibn al-Hasan al-Tathari said: My father Ali ibn Abdullah ibn Ali ibn Abi Shu'ba al-Halabi narrated from his father, from a man, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a man who married a woman for temporary marriage (mut'ah), then he died, what is her waiting period ('iddah)? He said: Fifty-six days. It is understood that this refers to if the wife was a slave-girl owned by a group of people, and the man enjoyed her with their permission, so her waiting period is the waiting period of slave-girls, fifty-six days, as we have previously established, if she was not a mother of children.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Khalid, from al-Qasim ibn 'Urwah, from Zurarah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The divorced woman may apply kohl, dye (her hair), perfume herself, and wear whatever clothes she wishes. Because Allah, the Exalted, says: 'Perhaps Allah will bring about after that some new matter (of reconciliation).'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from a number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Shummun, from Abdullah ibn Abd al-Rahman, from Mis'ma ibn Abd al-Malik, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), from Ali (peace be upon him), who said: The divorced woman observes waiting (iddah) just as the wife whose husband has died observes waiting; she does not apply kohl, nor perfume herself, nor dye (her hair/nails), nor comb her hair. Therefore, the meaning in this report is that we interpret it as applying when the divorce is final (ba'in); it is recommended for her to observe waiting (hidad) because the use of adornment is only recommended for her in a revocable divorce (raj'i) so that the man may see her, and perhaps he will reconcile with her.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Humayd ibn Ziyad, from Ibn Sama'ah, from Muhammad ibn Ziyad, from Abdillah ibn Sinan and Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about a woman whose husband has died, whether she observes her waiting period (iddah) in her own house or wherever she wishes. He said: 'Rather, wherever she wishes.' Indeed, when 'Umar died, Ali (peace be upon him) came to Umm Kulthum and took her to his house.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd from Hisham ibn Salim from Sulayman ibn Khalid said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a woman whose husband died, asking: Where does she observe her waiting period (iddah)? In her husband's house or wherever she wishes? He said: 'Wherever she wishes.' Then he said: 'Indeed, when 'Umar died, 'Ali (peace be upon him) came to Umm Kulthum, took her by the hand, and led her to his house.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn and Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from Yunus, from a man, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about a woman whose husband has died: if she observes her waiting period ('iddah) in a house where she stays for a month or less than a month, or more, then moves to another, and stays in the new house for a duration equal to what she stayed in the previous one, and continues this practice until her waiting period is completed. He said: That is permissible for her, and there is no objection.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Uthman ibn Isa from Sama'ah ibn Mihran who said: I asked him about the divorced woman, where does she observe her waiting period? He said: In her house, she does not go out. And if she wishes to visit, she goes out after half the night, and she does not go out during the day. And she is not permitted to perform Hajj until her waiting period expires. And I asked him about the woman whose husband dies, is she like that? He said: Yes, and she performs Hajj if she wishes.

From him, from Humayd ibn Ziyad, from Ibn Sama'ah, from Ibn Ribat, from Ibn Muskhan, from Abu al-Abbas, who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'What is the ruling for a woman whose husband has died?' He said: 'She should not apply kohl for adornment, nor perfume herself, nor wear a dyed garment, nor go out during the day, nor stay away from her house overnight.' I said: 'What if she wishes to go out for a need, what should she do?' He said: 'She should go out after midnight and return at nightfall.'

From him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from al-Ala' ibn Razin, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from one of the Imams (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about a woman whose husband dies while she is away from her home: where does she observe her waiting period (iddah)? He said: Wherever she wishes, provided she does not spend the night away from her home. Therefore, the meaning in these narrations is that we interpret them as being of the type of recommendation (istihbab), rather than obligation (farḍ) and compulsion (ijbar).

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Umar ibn Udhaynah, from Zurarah and Muhammad ibn Muslim and Burayd ibn Mu'awiya, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), that he said: Regarding the absent man, if he divorces his wife, she counts her waiting period (iddah) from the day he divorced her.

From him, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from al-Ala' ibn Razin, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: When a man divorces his wife while he is absent, he should bear witness to that. When three menstrual periods have passed from that day, her waiting period (iddah) is completed. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: This ruling is valid for her only if clear evidence establishes that he divorced her on a specific day. If such evidence does not establish that, she should observe the waiting period from the day the news reaches her, indicating that.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad from al-Halabi from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a man who divorces his wife while he is absent from her: from which day does she observe the waiting period? He said: If a just testimony is presented that she was divorced on a known day, she shall observe the waiting period from the day she was divorced. And if she does not remember which day and which month, she shall observe the waiting period from the day the news reaches her.

From him, from a number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ibn Abi Nasr, from al-Muthanna al-Hannat, from Zurara, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who divorced his wife while he was absent. When does she begin her waiting period? He said: If a clear evidence is established for her that she was divorced on a known day and month, let her begin her waiting period from the day she was divorced.
