He said: She inherits him as long as she is in her waiting period. And if he divorced her in a state of harm (delaying the final pronouncement), she does not inherit him until a year. If one day is added to the year, she does not inherit him, and she observes a waiting period of four months and ten days, which is the waiting period of the one whose husband has died.

Al-Husayn ibn Said from Safwan ibn Yahya, from al-Azraq, from Abd al-Rahman, from Musa ibn Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: I asked him about a man who divorces his wife with the final divorce (talaq al-khulas or talaq al-mughallazah), he said: Yes, they inherit from each other during the waiting period (iddah).

Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Fadhal narrated from Ali ibn Asbat from Ala' ibn Razin from Muhammad ibn Muslim from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a man who divorces his wife with two divorces, then divorces her with the third while he is ill. He said: She inherits him.

From him, from the two brothers, from their father, from Abdullah ibn Bukayr, from Ubayd ibn Zurara, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), in [the matter of] A man divorces his wife with two divorces, then he divorces her a third time while he is ill, then she inherits him.

Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Fadhal narrated from his two brothers, from Asim ibn Humayd, from Muhammad ibn Qays, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: Regarding the woman who is divorced, then her husband dies while she is in her waiting period from him, provided she has not become permanently prohibited to him: she inherits him and he inherits her as long as she remains in the blood of her second menstruation during the two initial divorces. If he divorces her three times, then she does not inherit from her husband, nor does he inherit from her. And if she is killed, he inherits from her blood money, and if he is killed, she inherits from his blood money, provided one did not kill the other. This does not contradict the earlier reports, because this report is understood to mean that he divorces her while in good health, then dies afterwards. For whoever divorces his wife while he is healthy, inheritance is established between them as long as he has a right of return. And if he does not have a right of return, there is no inheritance between them. The sick person is specifically exempted from this, with the establishment of inheritance between them even if the bond is severed and the right of return ceases. Just as he is specifically exempted in that she inherits him between her and one year, and this is not the case for others. And we have previously presented what indicates this.

Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Faddal from Muhammad and Ahmad, the two sons of al-Hasan, from their father from Abdullah ibn Bukayr from Zurara, who said: I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about a man who divorced his wife. He said: 'He inherits her and she inherits him as long as the revocable divorce (raj'ah) remains for him over her.' The discussion regarding this report is the same as the discussion regarding the first report. As for the two reports that we presented earlier, one from Ubayd ibn Zurara and the other from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from his saying: 'When he divorces her for the third time, she inherits him,' these do not indicate that he does not inherit her except through the implication of the context (dalil al-khitab), which may be set aside for a stronger evidence. And we have already presented what indicates that from it, namely the hadith of Abd al-Rahman from Musa ibn Ja'far (peace be upon him), when he asked him about a man who divorced his wife with her final divorce, he said: 'They inherit each other during the waiting period (iddah).' And this is explicit regarding what we said.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Ahmad ibn Abi Abdillah, from al-Hasan, from Muhammad ibn al-Qasim al-Hashimi, who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: The Khul' (mutual divorce) wife, the Mubar'ah (divorce by mutual consent with compensation) wife, and the Musta'marah (divorce by request) wife do not inherit anything from the husband in their divorce if that divorce was initiated by them during the husband's illness, and even if he dies, because the bond of marriage has been severed from them and from him. Therefore, the correct interpretation of this report is to restrict it to those specifically named in the report as Khul', Mubar'ah, and Musta'marah wives, because the cause for this ruling is on their part due to their request for divorce, unlike the Mutlaqah (simply divorced) wife who does not request it, but may even be reluctant to it. And upon this basis, there is no contradiction between the reports.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad (peace be upon him) from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Safwan from al-'Ala' from Muhammad from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: If a male slave has a female slave under his ownership, and he divorces her, and then his master frees her, she remains with him in the state of one (i.e., she is not freed independently but remains a slave alongside him).

From him, from Abu al-Maghra', from al-Halabi, who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: Regarding a male slave who has a female slave under his ownership, if he divorces her with one divorce and then frees them both, she remains with him based on that single divorce.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Abu Abdillah al-Razi, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from Ahmad ibn Ziyad, from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about a man who marries his male slave to his female slave, then the man has a preference for the female slave and separates her from his male slave, then he purifies her (from menstruation) and has intercourse with her, then he returns her to his male slave. Then later he has a preference for her again and separates her from his male slave. Is the master's separation of the female slave from her husband twice considered a double divorce, such that she is not permissible to him until she marries another man? He wrote: She is not permissible to him except by marriage. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: His statement 'She is not permissible to him except by marriage' means from another husband who marries her, then divorces her, or dies, and then she becomes permissible to him at that time.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from Ibn Abi Najran, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from al-'Is, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a slave who divorced his wife, and then both were freed. Is it permissible for him to remarry her before she marries another? He said: Yes. This does not contradict the reports we have previously mentioned, because in their apparent meaning it was not specified that he divorced her with a single divorce or two divorces. And if that is not specified in their apparent meaning, we interpret it to mean that if he divorced her with a single divorce, then it is permissible for him to remarry her before she marries another husband. And that which adds to what we mentioned is for clarification.

Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn, from Ibn Abi Umayr and Fadala, from al-Qasim, from Rifah, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the male slave and the female slave whom he divorces with two divorces, then both are freed. Does he remarry her? He said: No, until she marries another husband and is divorced from him.

From him, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from al-Ala' ibn Fudayl, from one of the Imams (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about a man who married off his male slave to his female slave, then he divorced her with two divorces. If the master wished, would he remarry her? He said: No. I said: What if the master had sexual intercourse with her? Would it be permissible for the slave to remarry her? He said: No, until she marries another husband, and he consummates the marriage with her, so that the marriage is like the first marriage. And if he had divorced her with one divorce, and the master wished, he would remarry her.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Humayd ibn Ziyad, from Ibn Sama'ah, from Ibn Ribat, from Isa ibn al-Qasim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a man who gave his wife the choice (of divorce), and she chose herself (to be divorced), so she was separated from him. He said: No, this was a matter specific to the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family), who was commanded to do so. And if they had chosen themselves, they would have been divorced. O Prophet, say to your wives, 'If you should desire the worldly life and its adornment, then come, that I may provide for you and give you a gracious release.' Al-Hasan ibn Sama'ah said: With this report, we take the ruling regarding the choice (of divorce).

From him, from Humayd ibn Ziyad, from Ibn Sama'ah, from Muhammad ibn Ziyad and Ibn Ribat, from Abu Ayyub al-Kazzaz, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'I heard your father saying: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) gave his wives the choice, and they chose Allah and His Messenger, so he did not keep them bound by divorce. And if they had chosen themselves, he would have divorced them.' He (Abu Abdillah) said: 'This is a hadith that my father used to narrate from Aishah. And what is there for the people regarding the choice? This is something Allah specifically granted to His Messenger (peace be upon him).'

From him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Faddal, from Marwan ibn Muslim, from some of our companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him, 'What do you say about a man who puts the matter of his wife in her hand (giving her the choice of divorce)?' He said, 'The matter was assumed by one who is not its rightful authority, and he contradicted the Sunnah, and he did not validate the marriage.'

Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Faddal narrated from Muhammad and Ahmad, the two sons of al-Hasan, from Ali ibn Ya'qub from Marwan ibn Muslim from Ibrahim ibn Muhraz, who said: A man asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) while I was with him. He said: A man said to his wife, 'Your affair is in your hand.' He (the Imam) said: 'How can that be, when Allah the Exalted says, Men are the protectors/maintainers of women. This is not valid.

Ali ibn al-Hasan narrated from Muhammad and Ahmad, the two sons of al-Hasan, from their father, from al-Qasim ibn 'Urayrah, from 'Abdullah ibn Bukayr, from Zurarah, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: I said to him, 'A man gave his wife the option [of divorce].' He said, 'The option belongs to both of them as long as they remain in their session [of marriage/negotiation]; but when they separate, there is no option for either of them.'

From him, from Ya'qub ibn Yazid, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Jamil, from Zurarah and Muhammad ibn Muslim, from one of the two, who said: There is no option (for the wife to choose divorce) except during a period of purity from which intercourse has been avoided, in the presence of witnesses.

From him, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Hakim, from Jamil ibn Darraj, from Zurarah, from one of the Imams (peace be upon him), who said: If she chooses herself (to be divorced), then she is a final divorce, and he is suitor among suitors (free to marry others); and if she chooses her husband, then there is no penalty.

Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Ali ibn Ri'ab from Humran said: I heard Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) saying: The woman granted the choice (of divorce) is considered divorced from that moment without a formal pronouncement of divorce, and there is no inheritance between them, because the bond of marriage has been severed.

Ali ibn al-Hasan from Ali ibn Asbat from Ibn Riab from Umar ibn Udhaynah from Zurarah from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: I said to him, 'A man gave his wife the option of divorce.' He said, 'The option belongs to her as long as they remain in their session; when they separate, there is no option for either of them.' I said, 'May God perfect you, but if she divorces herself three times before they separate from their session,' he said, 'It will not be more than one [divorce], and he has more right to take her back before her waiting period is completed.' And indeed, the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) gave his wives the option, and they chose him, so that became a divorce. I said to him, 'If they had chosen themselves, it would have been for us.' He said to me, 'What do you think of the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) if they had chosen themselves? Would he have kept them?' The approach in these narrations, despite the difference in their wording and the contradiction in their meanings, is to carry them upon a type of taqiyyah (dissimulation), because they are consistent with the belief of the general public. And if we did not carry these narrations upon what we said, we would have to discard the narrations that contained that this was not a real event, and that this was something specific to the Prophet (peace be upon him), and that this was something that my father narrated from Aisha, and whatever words followed that pattern, and we were unable to act upon them in any manner, and that is not permissible in any case.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Her khul' (redemption/divorce initiated by wife) is not valid until she says to her husband: 'By Allah, I will not fulfill your oath, nor obey your command, nor perform ghusl for you from janabah, and I will surely bed your bed, and I will surely give adhan (call to prayer) upon you without your permission.' The people used to grant permission (for khul') for less than this. So when the woman says that to her husband, what he took from her becomes lawful for him, and she remains with him having two remaining divorces. And the khul' was considered one divorce. And he said: The speech must come from her (not the husband). And he said: If the matter were up to us, we would not validate a divorce except for the waiting period (i.e., khul' counts as one irrevocable divorce, not three).

From him, from several of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from Uthman ibn Isa, from Sama'ah, who said: I asked him about the woman who performs khal' (redeems herself from divorce). He said: It is not permissible for her husband to grant her khal' until she says: 'I will not be dutiful to you with an oath, and I will not establish God's boundaries within you, and I will not perform the ritual bath for you from major impurity, and I will surely bed your bed, and I will surely bring into your house whom you dislike, without you knowing this.' And he does not speak, and she is the one who says this. When she performs khal', she becomes irrevocably divorced (bain), and he has the right to take from her wealth whatever he can manage, but he does not have the right to take from the mubari'ah (the compensation amount) more than what he had given her.

From him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from Muhammad ibn al-Fudayl, from Abu al-Subah al-Kinani, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: When a man performs khul' (divorce by redemption) with his wife, she is one irrevocable divorce, and he is suitor-like among the suitors. It is not permissible for him to take back what he gave until she is the one who requests that from him without him harming her, and until she says: 'I will not be dutiful to you with an oath, nor will I bathe for you from major impurity, and I will surely bring into your house someone you dislike, and I will lie on your bed and not establish God's boundaries.' If this is from her, then what he took from her is pleasing to him.

From him, from a number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from Abd al-Karim, from Abi Basir, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: It is not permissible for her to perform khul' (divorce by redemption) until she says to her husband: Then he mentioned what our companions mentioned, Then Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'It was permitted for women in what is less than this.' So when she says to her husband, 'My khul' is lawful, and it is lawful for my husband what he took from me,' and there remain two talaqs upon him, then the khul' counts as one talaq. And the statement (of khul') must come only from her. Then he said: 'If the matter were up to us, the divorce would not be except for the waiting period (i.e., one talaq would suffice, and khul' would not count as a separate divorce).

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa narrated from Ali ibn al-Hakam from Zur'ah from Sama'ah ibn Mihran who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'It is not permissible for a man to take from the woman who pays khul' (compensation for divorce) until she speaks all of this statement.' He said: 'When she says to him,

Al-Husayn ibn Said narrated from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr, from Jamil ibn Darraj, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: When the woman says to her husband in a general statement: 'I will not obey you in any matter, specified or unspecified,' it becomes permissible for him to take from her (her dowry/mahr) without having to return it to her.

As Al-Hasan ibn Ayyub narrated from Ibn Bukayr, from Ubayd ibn Zurara, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: Whatever you hear from me that resembles the speech of the people, there is taqiyya (dissimulation) in it. And whatever you hear from me that does not resemble the speech of the people, then there is no taqiyya in it. And the saying that khul' (divorce by wife's initiative) causes separation resembles the speech of the people, so it should be considered as being due to taqiyya. And that which indicates this as well.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa narrated from Muhammad ibn Isma'il ibn Bazee' from Safwan from Musa ibn Bakr from Zurara from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: The khul' (divorce initiated by the wife) does not take effect until she says: 'I will not obey you in any matter, nor will I fulfill your oath, nor will I uphold your ruling for you; so take from me and divorce me.' When she says this, it becomes permissible for him to release her (in khul') for whatever amount they mutually agree upon, whether small or large. This does not occur except in the presence of a ruler (judge). When she does this, she is more entitled to herself than others, without it being named as a talaq (husband-initiated divorce).

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa narrated from Muhammad ibn Isma'il ibn Bazee' who said: I asked Abu al-Hasan al-Rida (peace be upon him) about a woman who gives herself to her husband in exchange for release, or who pays him to divorce her (khal'), with the testimony of two witnesses regarding her purity (from menstruation) without sexual intercourse. Does she become fully divorced (tabin) from him by that, or is she still his wife as long as the divorce has not followed? He said: She becomes fully divorced. If he wishes, he can return to her what he took from her, and she remains his wife, and he may do so. I said: It has been narrated that she does not become fully divorced until the divorce follows her. He said: That is not the case if it is a khal'. I said: She becomes fully divorced? He said: Yes. The reason in this narration, likewise, is what we previously mentioned: interpreting it as being based on taqiyya (dissimulation). And his saying 'That is not the case if it is a khal'' means in their view. And the meaning is not that it is not a khal' in our view. And that which reveals what we said regarding the exit of that from the realm of taqiyya.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa from Ibn Abi Umayr from Sulayman ibn Khalid said: I said: What do you think if he divorces her after she has paid khul' (compensation for divorce), is it valid upon her? He said: Why would he divorce her, when khul' has sufficed for him? And if the matter were in our hands, we would not validate a divorce.

Muhammad ibn Yahya narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from Muhammad ibn al-Fudayl, from Abu al-Subah al-Kinani, who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: When the woman initiates the mutual divorce (khula') with her husband, she is one of the parties initiating, and he is a suitor from among the suitors.

Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Faddal, from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan, from Muhammad ibn Abdillah, from Ali ibn Hadid, from some of our companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), and from Zurarah and Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) He said: Al-mubarāh (divorce by mutual agreement) is a final divorce, and there is no revocation (raj'ah) in any of that. And Zurarah said: It does not occur except in the same state as the place of divorce, either when pure (from menses) or pregnant, with witnesses.

From him, from Amr ibn Uthman, from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from Ali ibn Ri'ab, from Humran, who said: I heard Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) saying: 'Al-mubar'ah (separation of the marital bond) becomes clear from that moment without a formal divorce, and there is no inheritance between them, because the 'ismah (bond of marriage) has separated from them at the moment that condition occurred from her and from the husband.'

From him, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Hakim, from Jamil ibn Darradj, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Al-Mubar'ah (mutual separation/divorce) becomes clear (final) without being followed by a third divorce. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: We have presented these narrations as they were reported, but the practice is not upon their apparent meaning, because Al-Mubar'ah does not effect separation without a divorce. Rather, it affects a type of divorce in which it becomes a final separation (Ba'in) where the husband does not have the right of return. This is the opinion of all the jurists of our companions, both early and late, and we know no disagreement among them in that. The explanation for these narrations is that we carry them upon Taqiyyah (dissimulation), because they are consistent with the opinion of the general public (Sunni scholars), but we do not act upon it.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Abu Ali al-Ash'ari, from al-Hasan ibn Ali, from al-Abbas ibn Amir, from Dawud ibn al-Husayn, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: And the mothers breastfeed their children. He (the Imam) said: As long as the child is in the period of breastfeeding, he is equally shared between the parents. When he is weaned, the father has more right to him than the mother. If the father dies, the mother has more right to him than the agnates (male relatives). If the father finds someone to breastfeed him for four dirhams, and the mother says 'I will not breastfeed him except for five dirhams,' then he has the right to take him from her, unless it is better for him and more gentle for him to leave him with his mother.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Ali ibn Muhammad al-Qassani, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from al-Munqari, from the one he mentioned, who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) was asked about a man who divorces his wife while they have a child, which of them is more entitled to the child? He said: The wife is more entitled to the child as long as she has not married. The meaning in this report is one of two things: one of them is that she is more entitled if she accepts the same wage that others take for the nursing and upbringing of the child, which indicates that.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from al-Husayn ibn Muhammad from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad from al-Hasan ibn Ali al-Washsha' from Fadl Abu al-Abbas who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): Is the man more entitled to his child or the woman? He said: No, but the man. However, if the woman says to her husband (the one who divorced her): I will breastfeed my son for the same amount you would pay whoever else you find to breastfeed him, then she is more entitled to him.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from Muhammad ibn al-Fudayl, from Abu al-Subah al-Kinani, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: When a man divorces his wife while she is pregnant, he provides for her until she gives birth to her child. If she nurses him, he gives her her wage, and he does not disadvantage her, unless he finds someone who is cheaper in wage than her. If she accepts that wage, then she is more entitled to her son until she weans him. The other view is that we interpret it as the father being a slave; for if he is so, then the mother is more entitled to her child than he is.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Mahbub, from Dawud al-Raqqi, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a free woman who married a slave and he fathered children with her. He (the Imam) said: 'I have more right to them than you, if you marry.' Then he said: 'The slave does not have the right to take the children from her, and if she marries until he is freed, she has more right to the children than he does, as long as he is a slave. But when he is freed, he has more right to them than she does.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ibn Faddal from Ibn Bukayr from Ubayd Allah al-Halabi said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): A woman gave birth from zina (unlawful sexual intercourse); should I take her as a wet-nurse? He said: Do not have her wet-nurse, nor her daughter.

From him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from al-'Umariyyi, from Ali ibn Ja'far, from his brother Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about a woman who gave birth from adultery (zina), is it permissible for her milk to be used for wet-nursing? He said: No, it is not permissible, nor is the milk of her daughter who was born from adultery.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from a number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from Hammad ibn 'Uthman, from Isحاق ibn 'Ammar, who said: I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about a slave boy of mine who jumped upon a female slave of mine and impregnated her, so she gave birth, and we needed her milk. I had declared permissible for them what they had done. Is the milk good (pure)? He said: Yes.

From him, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hisham ibn Salim and Jamil ibn Darraj and Sa'd ibn Abi Khalaf, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding a woman who has a servant (nursemaid) who has committed fornication, and her milk is needed; he said: Tell her to have the servant purify herself so that the milk becomes pure.

Ali ibn Ibrahim narrated from his father, from Hammad, from Hariz, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: The milk of the Jewess, the Christian, and the Magian is more pleasing to me than the milk of the child of fornication. And he did not see any harm with the child of fornication if the master of the slave girl who committed fornication with the slave girl is considered free (i.e., not a slave). Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Tusi said: The explanation in these narrations is that the emancipation of the master of the promiscuous slave girl only affects the 'sweetening' (acceptability) of the milk, not that the ugly act of fornication itself becomes good and permissible, because that act has already occurred and no subsequent event changes it. Its effect is only what we said regarding the sweetening of the milk, and nothing else.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Hisham ibn Salim from Ammar al-Sabati who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) was asked about a man who has a young wife who menstruates once every two or three months. How should her husband divorce her? He said: Her case is severe. She is divorced with a single Sunnah divorce, on a day of purity, without sexual intercourse, with witnesses. Then she is left alone until she menstruates three times. Whenever she has her period, her waiting period is completed. I said to him: If a year passes and she does not menstrrate three times in it, he said: He waits for her for three months after the year, then her waiting period is completed. I said to him: If she dies or her husband dies, he said: Whichever of them dies, the survivor inherits him/her within the period between them and fifteen months.

From him (Al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl) from Ibn Mahbub from Malik ibn Atiyyah from Sawrah ibn Kulaib, who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) was asked about a man who divorced his wife with a single revocable divorce while she was in a state of purity, without sexual intercourse, with witnesses, the divorce of the Sunnah. She was one who menstruates. Three months passed and she did not menstruate except for one period, then her menstruation ceased, so another three months passed and she did not know what had stopped her menstruation. He (peace be upon him) said: If she is a young woman with regular menstruation, and she does not menstruate in three months except for one period, then her menstruation ceases and she does not know what stopped it, then she waits (for the waiting period) for nine months from the day he divorced her. Then she observes her waiting period after that for three months, then she may marry if she wishes. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: This report should be acted upon because she is cleared of pregnancy by nine months, which is the maximum duration of pregnancy, so it is known that she is not pregnant. Then she observes her waiting period after that, which is three months. And we interpret the first report as a case of supererogatory precaution, that she observes the waiting period until fifteen months.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Ali ibn al-Hakam from 'Illan from Muhammad ibn Muslim from one of the Imams (peace be upon him) who said: Regarding the woman who menstruates once every three months, or in a year, or in seven months, and the istihadah (continuous bleeding) woman, and the one who has not yet reached puberty, and the one who menstruates once and then stops once, and the one who does not hope for children, and the one whose menstruation has ceased but claims she has not despaired (of it returning), and the one who sees the white discharge from menstruation which is not regular, he mentioned that the waiting period ('iddah) for all of these is three months.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Hammad ibn Isa from Shu'ayb from Abu Basir from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) that he said: Regarding the woman whose husband divorces her while she is menstruating, with one menstruation every three months, he said: If three months pass, her waiting period is complete; one menstruation is counted for each month. The resolution between these two narrations is that she only counts three months if she passes them without seeing blood at all, for she is considered pure. But if she sees blood before the completion of three months, even by one day, her waiting period is by menstruations (al-aqra'), even if that extends to fifteen months, according to what we have previously stated, and that which indicates this.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Abu Maryam from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) from the man How does he divorce his wife while she is menstruating, having one period in every three months? He said: He divorces her with one divorce at the beginning of the month. So when three months have passed from the day he divorced her, she is definitively divorced from him, and he is one of the suitors.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Fadhal, from Ibn Bukayr, from Zurara, from one of the Imams (peace be upon them), said: Whichever of the two conditions occurs first, her waiting period (iddah) is completed. If three months pass and she does not see blood in them, her waiting period is completed. And if three menstrual periods pass, her waiting period is completed.

From him, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Jamil ibn Darraj, from Zurara, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: There are two matters; whichever comes first causes the doubtful divorced woman to be considered divorced. She doubts her menstruation: if three white months pass through her without blood in them, she is divorced by them. And if three menstruations pass through her, with no three months between the two menstruations, she is divorced by the menstruation. Ibn Abi Umayr said, Jamil said: The explanation of this is: if three months pass through her minus one day, then she menstruates, then three months pass through her minus one day, then she menstruates, then three months pass through her and she menstruates, then this woman considers herself bound by the menstruations in this manner and does not consider herself bound by the months. And if three white months pass through her and she does not menstruate in them, then she is divorced.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from Muhammad ibn al-Fudayl, from Abu al-Subah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about the woman who menstruates once every three months; how does she count her waiting period? He said: She waits for the duration of her usual menstrual period during times of regularity, so let her count three menstrual periods, then she may marry if she wishes. The meaning in this report is that we interpret it as referring to a woman with istihadah (irregular bleeding); for in her state of istihadah she acts according to her habit during times of regularity and counts the menstrual periods during her days.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Yazid ibn Ishaq al-Sha'ir, from Harun ibn Hamzah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), concerning a woman who was divorced and had reached an advanced age, who experienced one period of menstruation, then her menstruation ceased. He said: She observes the waiting period by that one menstruation and two following months, for she has become menopausal (lost hope of menstruation). Therefore, the correct interpretation of this report is to restrict it to a woman who had become menopausal after experiencing one period of menstruation; for after that menstruation passes, she observes the waiting period of two months, in accordance with what the first report contained.

And as for what Ali ibn Ibrahim narrated from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about the saying of Allah, the Exalted: 'If you are in doubt' [2:228] — what is the doubt (ribah)? He said: That which exceeds one month is considered doubt. So she should observe a waiting period of three months, and refrain from menstruation. And whatever occurred in the month, if she did not exceed three periods of menstruation, her waiting period is three periods. The explanation of this narration is that if the blood (menstruation) is delayed from her usual pattern by less than a month, that is not due to the doubt of pregnancy, but perhaps due to an ailment. So she should observe the waiting period by menstruation, however much it reaches. If the blood is delayed from her by a month or more, it is permissible that it be for pregnancy or for other reasons, thus establishing doubt. So she should observe three months, provided she does not see blood in them. If she sees blood before the completion of the three months, her ruling is as we mentioned in the earlier narrations, equally.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from al-Husayn ibn Muhammad from al-Mu'alla ibn Muhammad from al-Washsha' said: I asked Abu al-Hasan al-Rida (peace be upon him) about a man who manumits his slave conditionally (mudabbar), and he is in good health, then later the master needs money; is it permissible for him to sell him? He said: Yes, if he needs to that.

Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Abu Ayyub from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about a man who had manumitted his slave partially (dabbara), then he needed the money for his price. He said: The slave is his. If he wishes, he sells him; if he wishes, he frees him completely; if he wishes, he keeps him until he dies. When the master dies, the slave becomes free from one-third of his estate.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Yaqtin from his brother al-Husayn from Ali ibn Yaqtin who said: I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about the sale of the mudabbir (a slave manumitted upon the master's death). He said: If the master gave permission for it, there is no harm in it. And if there was a debt upon the master of the slave, and he manumitted him to escape the debt, his manumission is not valid. And if he manumitted him while healthy, the creditor has no claim against him, and his manumission proceeds.

Al-Hus-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Safwan from Isḥāq ibn ʿAmmār said: I said to Abū Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him): A man frees his slave by manumission from the back (i.e., upon his death), then he needs the slave's price (to pay the master or for other purposes). He said: He sells him. I said: But if he is wealthy regarding the price? He said: If the slave is pleased.

From him (al-Layth) from Ibn Abi Umayr from Jamil who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the Mudabbir (a slave manumitted upon death), is he sold? He said: If his owner needs his price (money), [then yes]. And he said: If the slave consents, there is no harm.

From him, from Safwan and Fadala, from al-Ala' ibn Muhammad, who said: I said to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him): A man manumitted his slave conditionally (mudabbarr), then he [the master] needed the money. He said: When he needs the money, it is for him to sell [the slave] if he wishes. And if he frees him, that [the value] is from the third.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Safwan, from al-'Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from one of the Imams (peace be upon him), regarding: A man who frees his male slave or female slave manumission from behind (upon his death), then he needs the value of the slave, should he sell him? He (peace be upon him) said: No, unless he stipulates upon the one to whom he sells him that he frees him upon his death.
From him, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), like that. Like that.

From him, from Fadalah, from Aban, from Abu Maryam, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: He was asked about a man who frees his female slave by manumission from the back (i.e., upon his death or at a specified time); may he have sexual relations with her if he wishes, or marry her, or sell her service during her life? He said: Yes, whatever he wishes he may do.

From him, from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from 'Asim, from Abu Basir, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the male and female slave who are freed upon the master's death (mudabbars). He said: It is for their master to manumit them by writing a manumission contract (kitabah) if he wishes, and he is not permitted to sell them, unless the slave wishes to sell himself for the duration of his life, and he has the right to take his wealth if he has wealth.

From him, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from Ali (peace be upon him) who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who freed his female slave by manumission from the back (i.e., upon his death) during his lifetime. He said: If he wishes to sell her, he sells her service (bondage) for the duration of his life. So when he dies, the female slave is freed. And if she bears children, they are in her position (i.e., they are also freed upon his death).

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Ibrahim ibn Hashim, from al-Nawfali, from al-Sakuni, from Ja'far, from his father, from Ali (peace be upon them), who said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) sold the service of the Mudabbir (a slave manumitted upon the master's death) but did not sell his neck (full ownership). The way to reconcile between these narrations and the narrations that included the sale of the Mudabbir in all cases is that we say: If the master wishes to sell the neck (full ownership) of the slave, he needs to annul his Tadbir (manumission upon death), just as when he makes a will and then wishes to change it, he needs to annul his will, because it is in the position of a will. So if he annuls the Tadbir, it is permissible for him to sell the Mudabbir in all cases. And if he does not wish to annul his Tadbir and prefers to leave it in its state, it is permissible for him to sell its service for the duration of its life and stipulate with the buyer. And when the one who was Tadbir-ed dies, he becomes free. And that which indicates this distinction is... And that which indicates this distinction is...

Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Abu Ayyub from Aban ibn Taghlib said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who manumitted his female slave conditionally (dabbartu), then married her to another man, and she bore children from him. Then her husband died and left children from her. He said: 'Her children are like her status.' So when the one who manumitted her mother dies, they are free. I said to him: 'Is it permissible for the one who manumitted her mother to revoke the manumission if he needs to?' He said: 'Yes.' I said: 'What if you see that her mother dies after the husband has died, and her children from the free husband remain? Is it permissible for her master to sell her children and reclaim the manumission regarding them?' He said: 'No. He only has the right to reclaim the manumission regarding her mother if he needs to and she consents to that.'

From him, from Ali ibn Abi Hamzah, from Abu Basir, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Mudabbir (a slave manumitted upon his master's death) is a slave, and his master has the right to revoke the manumission; if he wishes, he may sell him, if he wishes, he may gift him, and if he wishes, he may marry him off. And if his master leaves him in the state of Mudabbir and no incident occurs in him until the master dies, the Mudabbir becomes free when the master dies. He is in the position of a man who made a will, then changed his mind later and altered it before his death; if he left it and did not alter it until he died, it is executed.

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the Mudabbir (a slave manumitted upon the master's death), so he said: 'He is in the position of the will (wasiyyah); he returns (to full freedom) in whatever he chooses from it.'

Muhammad ibn Yahya narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Faddal, from Ibn Bukayr, from Zurara, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about the Mudabbir (a slave manumitted upon the owner's death), is he from the one-third [of the estate]? He said: Yes. And the testator has the right to return [revoke or alter] in his will, whether he be in health or in sickness.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Abu Ja'far, from his father, from Wahb, from Ja'far, from his father, that Ali (peace be upon him) said: The mudabbarr (slave manumitted upon payment of a fixed sum) is not sold except from his own self. This report carries two meanings: one is that he is not sold on behalf of others, but rather it is preferable that he be sold from his own self, just as the mukatab is sold in the same manner; if he desires that, then that is considered recommended, because the earlier reports are general regarding the permissibility of selling him to whomever one wishes. The other meaning is that only the self of the mudabbarr is sold, and his children are not sold; and when he returns in his manumission (by paying the rest of the price), his children do not return in their manumission, according to what was detailed earlier in the narration of Aban ibn Ghutfan. And the mudabbarr and his children are counted from the third (of the estate for bequests); if their price exceeds one-third, they are asked to pay the remainder for the heir.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Yazid ibn Ishaq Sha'ir, who raised it to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about a female slave manumitted from behind (from one side of her master's ownership) by her master. He said: Whatever she bears, they are in her position, and they are from his third. If they are more than the third, they are made to bear the deficiency. And the manumission (kitabah) is for whatever she bears during her manumission period; they are in her position. If she dies, then upon them is what remains of her debt, if they wish. So when they pay it, they are manumitted.

From him, from Abu Ja'far, from Abu al-Jawza', from al-Husayn ibn 'Alwan, from 'Amr ibn Khalid, from Zayd ibn 'Ali, from his fathers, from Ali (peace be upon him) who said: The Mudabbir (slave manumitted upon death) is from the third (of the estate), and what he commits (of debts/damages) and the Mukatab (slave who pays for manumission in installments) and the Umm al-Walad (mother of the child) is borne by the master, so the master is liable for their liabilities.

Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Barqi, from al-Nuflī, from al-Sakkūnī, from Ja'far, from his father, from Ali (peace be upon him), that a man came to him and said to him: I have vowed to slaughter my son at the Station of Abraham, if I do such and such. So I did it. Ali (peace be upon him) said: Slaughter a fat sheep, and give its meat in charity to the poor.

Ibrahim ibn Mahziyar from al-Hasan from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad from Aban ibn Uthman from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Abdillah said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who swore to slaughter his son, so he said: 'That is from the steps of Satan.' He said: 'It does not contradict the first report, because the first report is based on a type of preference (istihbab), not obligation (farḍ) or compulsion (ijbar).'

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Isḥaq ibn 'Ammar, from Abu Ibrahim, (peace be upon him) said: I said to him (peace be upon him): A man was obligated by the duty of Islam (to perform Hajj), and he intended to perform Hajj. He was told: 'Marry, then perform Hajj.' He said: 'If I marry before I perform Hajj, my slave is freed.' So he married before performing Hajj. He said: 'His slave was freed.' I said: 'He did not intend the face of Allah (Exalted) by freeing him.' He said: 'It is a vow in obedience to Allah, and Hajj is more deserving than marriage, and more obligatory upon him than marriage.' I said: 'Indeed, Hajj is voluntary (nafl).' He said: 'And even if it is voluntary, it is obedience to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. He has freed his slave.'

And as for what Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Abu Ali ibn Rashid, who said: I said to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), the second Imam: Indeed, a woman from our people had a child who fell ill, and she said: 'O God, if You relieve His illness, then so-and-so is my slave girl, free, and the slave girl does not know [which is better], so whichever is superior, free her, or spend her price in the way of piety.' He said: 'It is not permissible except [the freeing of] her [the slave girl].' The explanation in this narration and the first narration is that we interpret both as meaning: if that [freeing] is in the manner of a vow, then fulfilling it is obligatory, provided that it is not a pure freeing conditional upon a specific condition.

Al-Saffar from Ibrahim ibn Hashim from Abd al-Rahman ibn Hammam from Ibrahim ibn Abd al-Hamid from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) said: Abbad ibn Abdillah al-Basri asked him about a man who made a vow to God to walk to His Sacred House, so he walked half the way, or less, or more. He said: He looks at what he spent from that point onward and gives it in charity.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Ibn Abi 'Umayr from Hammad from Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Halab (Al-Halabi) from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Any man who makes a vow to walk to the House of Allah (the Sacred Kaaba) and then becomes unable to walk, let him ride and sacrifice a camel, when Allah knows effort from him.

From him, from Safwan, from Ishaq ibn 'Ammar, from 'Anbasah ibn Mus'ab, who said: I made a vow for one of my sons that if Allah healed him, I would perform Hajj on foot. So I walked until I reached the 'Aqabah (pass), then I complained (of weakness), so I rode. Then I found ease, so I walked. I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about that. He said: 'I like that if you are financially capable, you slaughter a cow.' I said: 'With me is the cost of a cow, and if I wished to slaughter, I would, but I have a debt.' He said: 'I like that if you are financially capable, you slaughter a cow.' I said: 'Is it something obligatory that I do?' He said: 'No. Whoever dedicates something to Allah and reaches his utmost capacity, there is no obligation upon him.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Rifa'ah and Hafs, said: We asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who vowed to walk to the House of God on foot. He said: Let him walk, but when he becomes weary, let him ride.

Abu Ali al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn al-Jabbar, from al-Saffan, from al-'Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from one of the Imams (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about a man who made it a vow upon himself to walk to the House of God, but he was unable to do so; he said: 'He performs Hajj riding.' Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: 'There is no contradiction between these narrations, because that which is obligatory upon one who vows to walk to the Sacred House of God is to fulfill it if he is able to do so and has the capacity, to the extent that he should stand on his feet in the passage.' If he is unable to do so and cannot walk, it is permissible for him to ride, provided that he drives along with him a camel or a cow. If he is unable to do that [drive an animal], then let him ride and there is no penalty upon him.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Abu Ali al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn al-Jabbar and Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, all from Safwan, from Ibn Mukkan, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding the expiation of an oath: one feeds ten poor people, for each poor person a mudd of wheat or a mudd of fine flour and a handful, or their clothing, for each person two garments, or freeing a slave, and he has the choice among the three; whichever he does. If he cannot afford any of the three, then fasting for three days.

Al-Husayn ibn Said from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad from Ali ibn Abi Hamzah from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: I asked him about the expiation for an oath. He said: Freeing a slave, or clothing, and the clothing is two garments, or feeding ten poor people. Whichever of these he does, it suffices for him. If he cannot find [the means], then fasting three consecutive days, and feeding ten poor people, a modd each.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Ibn Abi Najran from Asim ibn Humayd from Muhammad ibn Qays, who said: Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: Allah the Exalted said to His Prophet (peace be upon him): 'O Prophet, why do you prohibit what Allah has made permissible to you, seeking the pleasure of your wives? And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.' Allah has prescribed for you the expiation for your oaths. So he made it an oath and expiated it, the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him). I said: 'With what did he expiate?' He said: 'He fed ten poor people, for each poor person a mudd.' We said: 'And whoever finds clothing?' He said: 'A garment that covers his private parts.'

From him, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Nasr and al-Hajjāl, from Thal'abah ibn Maymūn, from Ma'mar ibn 'Uthmān, who said: I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about whom the clothing is obligatory in the expiation of the oath. He said: A garment that covers his 'awrah (private parts).

Ibn Mahbub from Abu Ayyub from Abu Basir said: I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about the average food you provide for your family. He said: 'That which you rely on to feed your dependents from the average of that.' I said: 'And what is the average of that?' He said: 'Vinegar, oil, dates, and bread, with which you satisfy them once.' I said: 'Their clothing?' He said: 'One garment.' So there is no contradiction between these reports and the earlier reports, because the obligation of clothing is determined according to the person's state. Whoever is able to afford two garments, that is upon him. And whoever cannot afford more than one, then one suffices him. And whoever is unable to do that either, then fasting is upon him. And if he is unable to fast either, let him seek forgiveness from Allah, and there is no [further] obligation upon him, as indicated by that.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from Abi Jumaylah, from Abi Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Regarding the expiation of an oath: freeing a slave, or feeding ten poor people from the average of what you feed your family, or clothing them. The average is bread and oil, and its best is meat and bread. The charity is a measure (mudd) for each poor person, and the clothing is two garments. And for one who cannot find [the means], upon him is fasting, for the saying of Allah, the Exalted: So whoever cannot find [the means] must fast for three days.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ibn Faddal from Ibn Bukayr from Zurara from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about something of the expiation of an oath. He said, 'He fasts for three days.' I said, 'If he is weak from fasting and unable to do so,' he said, 'He gives charity to ten poor people.' I said, 'If he is unable to do that,' he said, 'Then let him seek forgiveness from Allah, the Exalted, and not repeat [the oath].'

Yunus ibn Abd al-Rahman from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) said: I asked him about a man who is obligated to feed ten poor people for expiation: should he give to the young and the old equally, and to the women and the men equally, or should he prefer the old over the young and the men over the women? He said: They are all equal. And he completes the number if he cannot find [enough] from the Muslims and their dependents, to complete the count that is obligatory for the weak, from those who do not stand [in line/wait].

Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ghiyas, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: It is not permissible to feed a single child in the expiation of an oath, but two children with one adult is permissible, and this does not contradict the first report, because the impermissibility of feeding a child applies only if he is alone; as for when he is mixed with adults, there is no objection to that.

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: 'From the best of what you feed your families,' he said: It is as it happens, that in the house there is one who eats more than a mud, and from them there is one who eats less than a mud. And if you wish, you provide them with a side dish (idam). The lowest side dish is salt, the middle is oil, and the highest is meat.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from al-Nawfali, from al-Sakuni, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) said: If you find in the expiation only one man or two men, then repeat [the payment] upon them until you complete ten. Give them [their share] today, then give them [their share] tomorrow.

Al-Husayn ibn Said from Safwan ibn Yahya from Ishaq ibn 'Ammar who said: I asked Abu Ibrahim (peace be upon him) about feeding ten poor people or feeding sixty poor people: is that combined for one person to whom it is given? He said: No, but a person gives to one person as Allah, the Exalted, said. I said: So should the man give it to his relatives if they are needy? He said: Yes. I said: So should he give it to the weak from those outside the Wilayah? He said: Yes, and those of the Wilayah are more beloved to me. So it does not contradict the first report, because repetition is permissible only when the person does not find the number of men upon whom feeding is obligatory; then it is permissible for him to repeat it upon them. But if he finds them, it is appropriate that he gives to each one of them until he completes the number.

Al-Saffar from Ali ibn Muhammad al-Qashani, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad al-Isfahani, from Sulayman ibn Dawud al-Minqari, from Hafs ibn Ghiyath, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the expiation of a vow, so he said: The expiation of a vow is the expiation of an oath. And whoever vowed to sacrifice a she-camel, upon him is a camel which he should adorn and shear and stop with at Arafat. And whoever vowed to sacrifice a male camel, he may slaughter it wherever he wishes.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Isma'il, from Hafsh, from 'Umar al-Bayy' al-Sabiri, from his father, from Abu Basir, from one of the Imams (peace be upon them), who said: Whoever makes a vow to Allah and binds himself with an oath to Him in a matter of obedience to Allah, and then breaks it, then upon him is the freeing of a slave, or fasting for two consecutive months, or feeding sixty poor people.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad al-Kukabi, from al-Umari al-Bufi, from Ali ibn Ja'far, from his brother Musa ibn Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about a man who made a vow to God in something permissible (non-disobedience), what is upon him if he does not fulfill his vow? He said: He frees a slave, or gives charity, or fasts for two consecutive months.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Abu al-Jawza', from al-Husayn ibn 'Alwan, 'Amr ibn Khalid, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: The vow is of two types: that which is for Allah and that which is for other than Allah; its expiation is the expiation of an oath.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad, from al-Sanadi ibn Muhammad, from al-Saffan al-Jammal, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I said to him: 'My father and mother be sacrificed for you, I have made it incumbent upon myself to walk to the House of God.' He said: 'Expiate your oath, for you have only made an oath upon yourself, and what you made for God, fulfill it.'
Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from Jamil ibn Salih, from Abu al-Hasan Musa (peace be upon him), that he said: Whoever is unable to fulfill a vow he has made, its expiation is the expiation of an oath.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: If you say 'It is upon me for Allah,' its expiation is the expiation of an oath.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Abu Abdillah, from Muhammad ibn Abdillah ibn Mihran, from Ali ibn Ja'far, from his brother Musa ibn Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about a man who dedicates to the Ka'bah such and such, what is upon him if he is unable to provide what he dedicated? He (AS) said: If he made it a vow and does not own it, there is nothing upon him. And if it is from what he owns, such as a slave boy or girl or similar, he sells it and buys perfume with its price and perfumes the Ka'bah with it. And if it is an animal, there is nothing upon him. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: The discussion regarding these narrations is like the discussion regarding the narrations we presented earlier concerning the expiation of an oath. And that depends on the state of the man. Thus it is in the expiation of the vow, because whoever is able to free a slave, or feed sixty poor people, or fast two consecutive months, does whichever he wishes. And when he is unable to do that, the expiation of the oath is upon him. If he is unable to do that as well, then forgiveness is upon him and there is nothing else.

Asim ibn Humayd, from Abu Basir, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: Whoever is unable to perform the expiation that is obligatory upon him, whether it is freeing a slave, fasting, or giving charity, in the case of an oath, a vow, or killing, or any other matter requiring expiation, then seeking forgiveness is sufficient as expiation for him, except for the oath of Dhihar (linguistic divorce), for if he cannot find what to expiate with, it becomes prohibited for him to have sexual intercourse with her, and they are separated, unless the wife agrees that he remains with her without having sexual intercourse with her.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali from his father from Safwan ibn Yahya from Isḥaq ibn 'Ammar from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) that Regardingẓ-ẓihār, if its owner is unable to pay the expiation, let him seek forgiveness of his Lord, then intend not to return [to intercourse] before he consummates [the marriage], then let him consummate, and that will suffice for him from the expiation. When he finds the means to pay what he expiates with, on any of the days, let him pay it. And if he gives charity by feeding himself and his dependents, that suffices for him if he is needy. And if he does not find that, let him seek forgiveness of Allah his Lord and intend not to return; that suffices for him, and by Allah, it is an expiation. So the first report does not contradict the second, because the first report only addressed the prohibition of intercourse before the expiation after seeking forgiveness, if he did not intend that whenever he is able he will pay it. And the second report addressed the permissibility of that when he is determined to pay the expiation whenever he is able to do so, and that runs in the manner of a debt upon him, and there is no contradiction between them.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Al-Hasan from Ali ibn al-Nu'man from Mu'awiya ibn Wahb said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the Mu'adhar (one who practices Dhikr al-Zihar), and he said: Upon him is the freeing of a slave, or fasting for two consecutive months, or feeding sixty poor people. And the slave is valid if he was born in Islam.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from 'Uthman ibn 'Isa from Sama'ah who said: I asked him about a man who said to his wife, 'You are upon me like the back of my mother.' He said: The freeing of a slave, or feeding sixty poor people, or fasting two consecutive months. As for what these two reports contained regarding the wording or the phrase used for choice, the way to handle it is to assume sequential order, based on the indication of the first reports that are consistent with the apparent meaning of the Quran. And we have cited in our Great Book what relates to that in full detail, and what we have mentioned is sufficient, if God wills.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from 'Uthman ibn 'Isa from Sama'ah from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: Do not eat the jarith, nor the marmaahi, nor the taifi, nor the tihal, because it is the house of blood and a morsel of the devil.

From him, from Muhammad ibn Khalid, from Abu al-Jahm, from Rifā'ah, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the Girrith, and he said: 'By Allah, I have never seen it, but we found it in the book of Ali (peace be upon him) as forbidden (haram).'

From him, from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from 'Asim, from Abu Basir, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about what is disliked from fish, so he said: As for in the Book of Ali (peace be upon him), then it forbids the Jarith.

From him, from Safwan, from Mansur ibn Hazim, from Samurah, from Abu Sa'id, who said: The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) rode out on the she-camel of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family), so we went out with him walking until we reached the place of the fish sellers. He gathered them and then said: 'Do you know for what reason I have gathered you?' They said: 'No.' He said: 'Do not buy the Jirris, nor the Marmahi, nor the Tafi that floats on the water, and do not sell it.'

From him, from Ibn Faddal, from more than one of our companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The jarri, the marmahi, and the tafi are forbidden in the book of Ali (peace be upon him).
Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Safwan from Ibn Muskhan from Muhammad al-Halabi said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: Nothing from the fish is disliked (makruh) except the Jari.

From him, from Fudayla, from Aban, from Hariz, from Hakim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: Nothing from fish is disliked except the Jirith (a type of fish, often identified as the sturgeon or a specific species with a hard shell). The correct approach in these two narrations and what follows their pattern is that it is not disliked with the dislike of prohibition (karahat al-tahrim) except for the Jari (a type of fish, often identified as the sturgeon or similar), although it is disliked with the dislike of recommendation/preference (karahat al-nadb) and preference. And what we have previously presented from the narrations, even if some of them contained the wording of prohibition (tahrim), such as the hadith of Ibn Fudayl and others, it is to be understood according to this type of prohibition that we have previously established and which is indicated by that.

From him, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Najran, from Asim ibn Humayd, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the jarri (a type of fish), the marmaahi (a type of fish), the zammir (a type of fish), and fish that have no skin/scale, asking: Is it forbidden? Say, 'I do not find in that which has been revealed to me anything forbidden to one who eats it.' He said, so I recited it until I finished. He said: 'The forbidden is only that which Allah and His Messenger have forbidden in His Book. But they used to dislike certain things, so we dislike them.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad, from al-Hasan ibn Ali, from Abu al-Hasan al-Rida (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about a man who freed his female slave while she was pregnant. He said: If he knew of the female slave's pregnancy, then what is in her womb is like her (free); and if he did not know, then what is in her womb is a slave.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from a number of our companions from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Uthman ibn Isa al-Kilabi from Abu al-Hasan al-Awwal (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a woman who manumitted her slave girl, and the slave girl gave birth to a valuable female child, so the woman did not know whether the born child was manumitted or not. He said to me: 'When was the pregnancy with the manumitted woman? Before she was manumitted or after she was manumitted?' I said: 'I do not know, but answer me for both cases.' He said: 'If the woman manumitted while she was pregnant and did not specify what was in her womb, then the slave girl is manumitted and the child is a slave. And if the pregnancy occurred only after the manumission, then the child is manumitted in the manumission of his mother, and this does not contradict the first report, because we interpret his statement in this report:

Al-Husayn ibn Said from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad ibn Uthman from Al-Halabi said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about fish that are found floating on the water or that the sea casts up dead, so he said: Do not eat it.

From him, from Amr ibn Uthman, from al-Mufaddal ibn Salih, from Zayd al-Shahham, who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) was asked about fish found floating on the water, which the sea casts up dead: 'Do I eat it?' He said: 'No.'

From him, from Fadala, from al-Qasim ibn Burayd, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: Do not eat what the water cast out of the fish, and what the water dried up from it.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from 'Abd Allah ibn Bah'r from a man from Zurarah, who said: I asked: 'The fish leaps from the water and falls onto the bank, and wriggles until it dies.' He said: 'Eat all of it.' The meaning in this report is that we interpret it as: when it came out of the water, he caught it while it was alive, then it died; its eating is permissible. But if it died before he caught it, eating it would not be permissible. This indicates that.

Muhammad ibn Yahya narrated from al-'Umariyy ibn Ali, from Ali ibn Ja'far, from his brother Musa ibn Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about a fish that remained in the water and then fell onto the dry land and died. Is it permissible to eat it? He said: If you take it before it dies, then it dies, you may eat it. And if it dies before you take it, do not eat it.

Muhammad ibn Yahya narrated from Abdullah ibn Muhammad from Ali ibn al-Hakam from Aban from Salama, Abu Hafs, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) that Ali (peace be upon him) used to say: Regarding the catching of fish: when you catch it while it is wriggling, beating with its hand (fin), moving its tail, and blinking its eye, then its slaughter is valid.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Fadala, from al-Qasim ibn Burayd, from Ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), in a man who set up a net in the water, then returned to his house and left it standing; he came to it later and found fish had fallen into it and died. He said: 'His hand did not act [directly], so there is no objection to eating what fell into it.'

From him, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad ibn Uthman, from al-Halabi, who said: I asked him about a pen made of reeds that is placed in the water for fish, so the fish enter it and some of them die in it. He said: There is no harm with it. Indeed, that pen was made only to catch fish in it. The way to reconcile these two narrations is to assume that if what died in the water is not distinguished from what did not die in it, and it is taken out, it is permissible to eat all of it. But with distinction, it is not permissible in any case that indicates that.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Ali ibn al-Nu'man, from Ibn Muskhan, from Abd al-Rahman, who said: I instructed a man to ask Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) on my behalf about a man who caught fish while they were alive, then took them out after some of them had died. He said: 'That which died, do not eat it, for it died in what contains its life, and this report does not contradict this.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Harun ibn Muslim, from Mas'adah ibn Sadqah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I heard my father saying: When the owner of the net strikes with the net, whatever it catches in it, whether living or dead, is permissible, except that which has no shell. And the floating fish is not to be eaten, because the meaning in this report is what we said in the earlier reports: it is the same whether the dead one is distinguished from the living one, in which case it is permissible for him to eat all of them; but if they are distinguished, then it is not permissible, according to what we have previously presented.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad from Al-Halabi said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the catch of fish, even if not named (specifically), and he said: There is no harm. And I asked him about the catch of the Magians (Zoroastrians), 'Do I eat the fish?' He said: I would not eat it until I look at it.

From him, from Hammad, from Hariz, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a Magian who catches fish, is it permissible to eat from it? He said: 'I would not eat it until I see it.' Hammad said, meaning: until I hear him reciting the name of God (Tasmi'). Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: What Hammad mentioned in his interpretation of the hadith is not correct, for we have clarified in the first narration that reciting the name of God is not required in catching fish, and this adds further clarification.

From him, from Fadalah, from al-Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from one of the Imams (peace be upon him), like that, he said: And I asked him about catching fish, and he did not specify [a particular type], he said: There is no objection.

From him, from Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from Al-Mu'alla ibn Muhammad, from Al-Wasshash, from Abdillah ibn Sinan, who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) say: 'There is no harm with the fish that the Magian catches.'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Uthman, from Sama'ah, from Abu Basir, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the fishing of the Magians when they strike with the net and do not recite a name, or the Jews and do not recite a name. He said: There is no objection. Indeed, the fishing of fish is merely catching them.

From him, from al-Nadr, from Hisham ibn Salim, from Sulayman ibn Khallid, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the fish that the Magians catch, so he said: Indeed, Ali (peace be upon him) used to say: Fish and locusts are pure.

From him, from Ibn Faddal, from Yunus ibn Ya'qub, from Abu Marim, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'What do you say about what the Magians catch of fish?' He said, 'Ali (peace be upon him) used to say: Fish and locusts are [considered] slaughtered.'

From him, from Al-Hasan ibn Ali al-Wassash, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: 'There is no objection to the Kawamikhi of the Magians, and there is no objection to their catching of fish.' The approach in these narrations is to interpret them as meaning: 'There is no objection to the catching of fish by the Magians if a person takes it from them while it is alive before it dies.' Their word is not accepted regarding the removal of the fish from the water while it is alive, because they are not trusted regarding that, which indicates that.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Fadala from Aban from 'Isa ibn 'Abdullah who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the hunting of the Magians, so he said: There is no harm if they give it to you alive, and the fish as well; otherwise, do not accept their testimony unless you witness it yourself.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from a number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Shummun, from Abdullah ibn al-Rahman, from Mis'mam, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) forbade going to the birds at night, and he said: 'Indeed, the night is a security/protection for them.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr said: I asked al-Rida (peace be upon him) about the flight of birds at night in their nests, and he said: There is no harm in that.
Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa narrated from Ali ibn Ahmad ibn Ashyam, from Safwan, from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him), like it.

Al-Saffar narrated from Muhammad ibn 'Isa ibn 'Ubayd from Yunus ibn 'Abd al-Rahman from Abu al-Hasan al-Rida (peace be upon him) who said: I said, 'May I be your ransom, what do you say regarding hunting birds in their burrows and wild animals in their habitats at night, for people dislike that?' He said, 'There is no harm in that.' The approach in these narrations is to interpret them as permitting and removing prohibition, and the first two narrations are interpreted as indicating a type of dislike (karahah) short of prohibition (hazr).

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Abu Yahya al-Wasiti who said: He was asked about the speckled crow, so he said: 'It is not eaten.' He said: 'And who permitted you to eat the black one?'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from al-'Amarkki ibn Ali, from Ali ibn Ja'far, from his brother Musa ibn Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about the speckled crow and the black one, is its eating permissible? He said: The eating of anything from the crows, whether speckled or not, is not permissible.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Fadala from Aban ibn Uthman from Zurara from one of the Imams (peace be upon him) that he said: The eating of the crow is not forbidden; rather, the forbidden is only what God has forbidden in His Book, but the souls shy away from much of it out of aversion.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Ibrahim ibn Ishaq, from Ali ibn Muhammad, from al-Hasan ibn Dawud al-Raqqi, who said: We were sitting with Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) when a man passed by with a slaughtered 'khattaf' (a type of bird) in his hand. Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) jumped at him and took it from his hand, then rolled it on the ground. He then said: 'Did your scholar command you to do this, or your jurist?' Indeed, my father informed me from my grandfather that the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) forbade the killing of six: the bee, the ant, the frog, the locust, the hoopoe, and the khattaf.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Fadhal from Amr ibn Sa'id from Musaddiq ibn Sadaqah from 'Ammar ibn Musa from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) from the man who catches a kite in the desert or hunts it, does he eat it? He (peace be upon him) said: 'It is among what is eaten.' And regarding the hare, is it eaten? He said: 'No, it is forbidden.' The meaning of his saying (peace be upon him) 'It is among what is eaten' is that we should interpret it as expressing wonder at that, rather than informing about its permissibility. And this runs in the manner of one of us when he sees a person eating something that the souls (people) loathe, [saying] 'This is something eaten,' and he only intends to mock it, not to inform about its permissibility.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Ibn Abi 'Umayr from 'Umar ibn Udhaynah from Muhammad ibn Muslim and others from both of them, both said: Regarding the dog, when a man sends it and calls out (the name of God), they said: If it catches it and you find its throat still fresh (alive), then slaughter it; and if you find it has already killed it and eaten from it, then eat what remains.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa narrated from Muhassan ibn Ahmad from Yunus ibn Ya'qub who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who sent his hunting dog, and the dog caught the prey and it had been killed (by the dog). He said: 'Eat it, even if the dog ate from it.'

From him, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Saif ibn Umayrah, from Aban ibn Taghlib, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, who said: I heard Salman saying: Eat from what the dog held, even if it ate two-thirds of it.

From him, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Saif, from Mansur ibn Hazim, from Salim al-Ashall, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the game hunted by a trained dog that had eaten from its catch, and he said: 'Eat from it.'
