Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from al-Husayn ibn Muhammad from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad from al-Hasan ibn Ali from Aban ibn 'Uthman from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi 'Abdillah, who said: I asked Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who sent his hunting dog, and it caught game, and the dog ate from it; should I eat from its surplus? He said: Eat whatever the dog killed, if you named it (God), and if you were forgetful, then eat from it as well, and eat its surplus.

From him, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Musa ibn Bakr, from Zurara, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) that he said: Regarding the hunting of the dog: if he sends it and says 'Bismillah', he should eat from what it holds back, and if it kills and if it eats, then eat what remains.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad from al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Halab from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) that he was asked about the hunting of the falcon and the dog; if it hunts and kills its prey and eats from it, do we eat from its surplus or not? He said: As for what the bird kills, do not eat it unless you slaughter it (recite the name of Allah); and as for what the dog kills and you have mentioned Allah's name upon it, then eat it even if it eats from it.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad from Mu'awiya ibn Wahb from Abu Sa'id al-Makari said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the dog that is sent out for hunting, and it says the name of God, then it kills and eats from the prey; he said: 'Eat, even if it eats from it.'

From him, from Fadala, from Abd Allah ibn Bukayr, from Salim al-Ashall, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the dog that catches game for you and has eaten from it, so he said: There is no harm; it has eaten, and it is halal for you.

From him, from Safwan, from Ibn Muskhan, from Muhammad al-Halabi, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the dog that hunts and eats from its catch; should we eat its remainder? He said: Yes.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from 'Uthman ibn 'Isa from Sama'ah ibn Mihran said: I asked him about what the trained hunting dog catches for you, and this is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: 'What you have taught of the hunting beasts, teaching them from what Allah has taught you, so eat of what they catch for you and mention the name of Allah over it.' He said: There is no harm in you eating from what the dog catches, provided the dog has not eaten from it. If the dog eats from it before you catch it, then do not eat from it. I also asked him about the catch of the cheetah (fahd) when it is trained for hunting. He said: If you catch it alive, slaughter it and eat it; if it kills it, do not eat from it.

From him, from Fadala ibn Ayyub, from Rifa'a ibn Musa, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the dog when it kills [prey], so he said, 'Eat.' I said, 'Do I eat from it?' He said, 'If it eats from it, it does not withhold [the rest] from you; it only withholds from itself.' The meaning in these two reports is that we interpret them in one of two ways: one is that we interpret them as meaning that if the dog is accustomed to eating what it hunts, then what remains of it is not eaten, and its remainder is only eaten if that is unusual and rare for it. The other meaning is that we interpret them as a form of precautionary piety (taqiyyah), because among the jurists is one who says that and argues that 'it withheld from itself, not from you' indicates that.

Al-Husayn ibn Said from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd from Hisham ibn Salim from Sulayman ibn Khalid said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the dog of the Magians: if a Muslim man takes it and names it when he releases it, does he eat from what it catches? He said: Yes, because it is trained (to hunt) and the name of Allah (Exalted and Mighty) is mentioned over it.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa narrated from Ali ibn al-Hakam from Saif ibn Amirah from Mansur ibn Hazim from Abd al-Rahman ibn Sayyabah who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): If I borrow a Magian's dog to hunt with it, is it permissible? He said: Do not eat from its catch unless a Muslim has taught it. This does not contradict the first report, because the meaning of this report is that if the Muslim has not taught it and does not mention God's name when sending it, it is not permissible to eat what it catches. But if he teaches it and mentions God's name, there is no harm according to what the first report contained, and that which indicates this.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from al-Nawfali, from al-Sakuni, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The dog of the Magians (Zoroastrians), you do not eat its game unless the Muslim takes it, teaches it, and sends it; and likewise the falcon, and the dogs of the People of the Covenant, and their falcons are permissible for Muslims to eat their game.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Hariz, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), that he disliked the hunting of the falcon except for that whose slaughter was completed.

From him, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from Aban ibn Uthman, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Abdillah, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who sent his falcon, which caught prey, and he ate from it; do we eat from its surplus? He said: Whatever the falcon killed, do not eat from it unless you slaughter it.

From him, from al-Qasim, from Aban, from Abu al-Abbas, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about the hunting of the falcon and the hawk, so he said: Do not eat what the falcon and the hawk kill, and do not eat what the birds of prey kill.

From him, from Uthman ibn Isa, from Sama'ah, who said: I asked him about the hunting of falcons and hawks and the birds that hunt, and he said: This is not in the Quran, except that you catch it alive and slaughter it; and if it kills (the prey), do not eat until you slaughter it.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa narrated from Ali ibn Mahziyar who said: Abdullah ibn Khalid ibn Nasr al-Mada'ini wrote to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him): 'I ask you, may I be your ransom, regarding the falcon (bazi) when it catches its prey and has been named over it, then it kills the prey; is it permissible to eat it?' He (peace be upon him) wrote with his own hand and seal: 'If you named it, you eat it.' And Ali ibn Mahziyar said: 'I read it.'

From him, from Muhammad ibn Isma'il ibn Bazee', from Ali ibn al-Nu'man, from Abu Maryam al-Asvari, who said: I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about the falcon and the hawk among the birds of prey, are they [permissible]? He said: Yes, in the status of dogs.

From him, from al-Baraqi, from Sa'd ibn Sa'd, from Zakariyya ibn Adam, who said: I asked al-Rida (peace be upon him) about the prey of the falcon and the hawk when they kill their prey, and a man looks at it. He said: 'Eat from it, even if it has eaten something from it as well.' I asked him three times, and each time he said the same. The reason for interpreting these narrations is that we should attribute them to taqiyya (dissimulation), which we have previously mentioned, because the rulers of the time considered it permissible, and their jurists issued fatwas regarding its permissibility. Thus, the narrations came in agreement with them, as did other narrations of a similar nature, and that which indicates this...

Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Ali ibn Ri'ab from Abu Ubaydah al-Hadda' said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): What do you say about the falcon, the hawk, and the eagle? He said: If you catch its slaughter (by cutting the throat), then eat from it, and if you do not catch its slaughter, then do not eat.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Mufaddal ibn Salih, from Aban ibn Ghutfan, who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: 'My father used to give a fatwa in the time of the Banu Umayya that whatever the falcon and the hawk kill is permissible (halal), and he would be cautious of them (the Umayyads). And I am not cautious of them, and it is forbidden (haram) whatever it kills.'

From him, from Safwan, from Ibn Muskān, from al-Ḥalabī, who said: Abū ʿAbdillāh (peace be upon him) said: My father used to give legal rulings, and we used to give legal rulings while we were fearful regarding the hunting of hawks and falcons. But now, we are not fearful. And we do not permit their hunting unless their slaughter (death by bleeding) is achieved. And indeed it is in the Book of Allah, Exalted and Glorified, that Allah, Exalted and Glorified, said: 'What you have taught of the hunting beasts, making them train.'

From him, from Al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Fadhal, from Al-Mufaddal ibn Salih, from Layth al-Muradi, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the falcon and the hawk, and about their prey, so he said: 'Eat whatever they catch, provided you find it alive (have reached its state of slaughter), and the final moment of slaughter is when the eye twitches, the leg kicks, and the tail moves.' He also said: 'The falcon and the hawk are not mentioned in the Quran.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Muhammad ibn Abdillah ibn Hilal, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a female slave who had been manumitted in part (mudabbarah) and had run away (abqa) from her master for years, then she returned after her master had died, bringing with her many children and possessions. Two witnesses testified that her master had indeed manumitted her in his lifetime before she ran away. He (peace be upon him) said: 'I hold that she and all that is with her belong to the heirs.' I said: 'Should she not be manumitted from one-third of her master's estate?' He said: 'No, because she ran away while disobedient to Allah and to her master, and the act of running away (abqa) nullified the manumission (tadbir).'

Al-Husayn ibn Said from Ali ibn al-Nu'man from Ya'qub ibn Shu'ayb said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who has a servant girl, and he says: 'She is for so-and-so to serve him as long as he lives, and when he dies, she is free.' The slave girl runs away (abiq) before the man dies, by five or six years. Then his heirs find her. Is it for them to use her after she has run away? He said: No. When the man dies, she has become free, so it does not contradict the first report, because the aspect of it is that the manumission (tadbir) had been attached to the time for which she was to serve him. Wherever she ran away, it prevented the man who was granted that authority over her, and that does not invalidate the manumission. And in the first report, the manumission was attached to the death of the master, so wherever her running away prevented her master from having authority over her, that invalidated that manumission. And that which confirms the first report.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Hisham ibn Salim, from Abu Hamzah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Do not eat the meat of the Jalalah, and if its sweat touches you, wash it off.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from a number of our companions from Sahl ibn Ziyad from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Shammun from Abd Allah ibn Abd al-Rahman from Mis'mam from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) said: The fat camel (al-jallalah) — its meat is not to be eaten and its milk is not to be drunk until it has been fed [on clean fodder] for forty days. And the fat cow — its meat is not to be eaten and its milk is not to be drunk until it has been fed for forty days. And the fat sheep — its meat is not to be eaten and its milk is not to be drunk until it has been fed for five days. And the fat duck — its meat is not to be eaten until it has been tied [confined] for five days. And the chicken [for] three days.

From him, from Ali, from his father, from al-Nawaffali, from al-Sakuni, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) said: The meat of the jalalah chicken is not to be eaten until it is tied up (confined) for three days, and the jalalah duck for five days, and the jalalah sheep for ten days, and the jalalah cow for twenty days, and the jalalah camel for forty days.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Barqi, from Sa'd ibn Sa'd, from Abu al-Hasan al-Rida (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about eating the meat of chickens from the Daskar (a place or type of enclosure), while they are not prevented from anything that passes by the excrement, leaving it for them, and eating their eggs. He said: 'There is no harm in it.' This report does not contradict what we have previously presented from other reports, because in that report it is not stated that they become 'Jallalah' (animals whose meat is disliked due to diet), but rather that they pass by excrement and are not prevented from anything. All of this does not necessitate that they are Jallalah. And even if the report explicitly stated that they are Jallalah, it would be permissible for us to say that his statement 'There is no harm in it' implies that they are purified (istibra') for three days, as we have previously established, because we did not say that the meat of Jallalah is forbidden in all cases. And it has been narrated that the condition for istibra' is that if she does not mix her food with anything other than excrement, then if she does mix it, there is no harm in eating her meat. That clarifies it.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from some of his companions, from Ali ibn Hassan, from Ali ibn Uqbah, from Musa ibn Uqayl, from some of our companions, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) In a sheep that drank urine, then was slaughtered, he said: What is in its stomach should be washed out, then there is no harm with it. And likewise, if it ate excrement, as long as it is not a 'Jallalah', and the Jallalah is that which that [excrement/urine] is its food.
Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from al-Khashshab from Ali ibn Asbat, from one who narrated in al-Jalalat: There is no harm in eating them if they are mixed.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Musa ibn Umar from Ja'far ibn Bashir from Dawud ibn Kathir al-Raqi who said: I wrote to Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) asking him about the meat of the Bakhit (a type of camel) and its milk, so he said: 'There is no harm with it, and this report does not contradict this news.'

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Bakr ibn Salih, from Sulayman al-Ja'fari, from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) who said: I heard him say: 'I do not eat the meat of the Bukhay (a type of fish), and I do not command anyone to eat it.' In a long hadith, because his saying 'I do not eat it' is a report of his abstaining from eating it, and his saying 'I do not command' merely negates that it is something commanded. And if it were so, eating it would be obligatory, and that is not the saying of anyone. And in the report it is not stated that it is forbidden or not permissible, so it does not contradict the first report. On the basis that the prohibition of the meat of the Bukhay was something Abu al-Khattab (may God curse him) and his companions said, so it is permissible that Sulayman al-Ja'fari heard some of his companions say that and attribute it to him, so he narrated it from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) believing in his truthfulness and good belief in him, which indicates that.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from al-Hasan ibn Ali, from Dawud ibn Kathir al-Raqqi, who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'May I be your ransom, indeed a man from the companions of Abu al-Khattab forbade me from eating the bukhth (a type of turtle/tortoise) and from eating the musarral pigeon.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'There is no harm in riding the bukhth, drinking its milk, eating its meat, and eating the musarral pigeon.'

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa narrated from Ali ibn al-Hakam from Saif ibn Amirah from Abu Bakr al-Hadrami from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) that he said: That which is not slaughtered with iron is not to be eaten.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from several of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from Uthman ibn Isa, from Sama'ah, who said: I asked him about slaughtering (al-dhaka), so he said: One does not slaughter except with a sharp blade. The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) forbade that.

From him, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Umar ibn Udhaynah, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about the slaughtered animal using the flax-fiber rope and the reed-stick, so he said: There is no valid slaughter except with iron. From him, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammam, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about the slaughter using wood, reed, and stone. He said, then Ali (peace be upon him) said: Slaughter is not valid except with iron.

Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Zayd al-Shahham said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who did not have a knife at hand, should he slaughter with a reed? He said: Slaughter with stone, with bone, with reed, and with wood, if it is not iron, when it cuts the windpipe and the blood comes out, there is no objection.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, who said: I asked Abu Ibrahim (peace be upon him) about the marwa (a type of knife/cutting tool), the qasabah (a bone or hard stick), and the wood; is it permissible to slaughter with them if they do not find a knife? He said: If they sever the windpipe and gullet, there is no objection.

Muhammad ibn Yahya narrated from Abdullah ibn Muhammad from Ali ibn al-Hakam from Aban from Muhammad ibn Muslim who said: Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said regarding slaughtering with something other than iron: If you are compelled to do so, and you do not find iron, then slaughter it with a stone. The meaning in these narrations is that we restrict it to the state of compulsion in which one is unable to find iron. As for when iron is available, slaughtering is not permissible in any case except with it.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Fadala, from Abu al-Maghra', from Sama'a, from Abu Ibrahim (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about the slaughtered meat of the Jew and the Christian, so he said: 'Do not approach it.'

From him, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Qutaybah al-A'sha, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the sacrifices of the Jews and the Christians, so he said: 'The sacrifice (dhabīḥah) is a name, and one cannot be trusted regarding the name except the Muslim.'

From him, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from al-Husayn ibn al-Mundhir, who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): We compete with these Kurds in the pastures of the sheep, and they are merely fire-worshippers and the like of that. So the share falls [to us], they slaughter it, and we sell it. He said: I do not like that you do that with your wealth. The slaughtered animal is merely a name, and one cannot be confident regarding the name except [if it is] a Muslim.

From him, from Ali ibn al-Nu'man, from Ibn Muskhan, from Qutaiba, who said: A man asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) while I was with him, saying: 'Sheep are sent out, and among them is the Jew and the Christian. If an illness strikes them and they are slaughtered, do we eat their slaughtered meat?' He said to him: 'Do not include its price in your wealth, and do not eat it, for it is merely the name, and one cannot be certain of it except from a Muslim.' The man said to him: 'God has made the good things permissible for you, and the food of those who were given the Book is permissible for you, and their food is permissible for you.' He said: 'My father used to say: It is only for small livestock and similar things.'

From him, from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the sacrifices of the Christian Arabs, whether they are permissible to eat? He said: Ali (peace be upon him) used to prohibit eating their sacrifices and their game. He said: A Jew or a Christian should not slaughter your Udhiyah (sacrificial animal).

From him, from Hammad ibn Isa, from al-Husayn ibn al-Mukhtar, from al-Hasan ibn Abdillah, who said: Al-Mu'alla ibn Khunays and Ibn Abi Ya'fur traveled together. One of them ate the slaughtered meat of the Jew and the Christian, while the other refused to eat it. They met at the presence of Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) and informed him. He asked, 'Which of you refused?' He said, 'I.' He said, 'Well done.'

From him, from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from 'Asim ibn Humayd, from Abu Basir, who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: A Jew or a Christian or a Magian should not slaughter your Udhiyah (sacrificial animal), and if it is a woman, let her slaughter for herself.

From him, from Fudayla, from Aban, from Salama, Abu Hafs, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), from his father, from the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family), that Ali (peace be upon him) said: The Jews and the Christians do not slaughter your sacrificial animals, and none but a Muslim may slaughter them.

From al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from Ali, from Abu Basir, who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to me: Do not eat from the slaughtered meat of the Magians. And he said: Do not eat the slaughtered meat of the Christians of Taghlib, for they are the polytheists of the Arabs.

From him, from Amr ibn Uthman, from al-Mufaddal ibn Salih, from Zayd al-Shahham, who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) was asked about the slaughtered meat of the Dhimmi (non-Muslim protected person), so he said: Do not eat it, whether it was named (with God's name) or not named.

From him, from Hanan ibn Sadeer, who said: I entered upon Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), along with my father. He said: We said to him, 'May we be your ransom, we have neighbors among the Christians, and we visit them and they slaughter for us chickens, chicks, and young sheep; should we eat them?' He said: 'Do not eat them and do not approach them, for they say over their slaughtering something that I do not like for you to eat.' So when we returned to Kufa, some of them invited us, but we refused to go. He said: 'What is the matter with you? You used to visit us, then you left off today?' We said: 'A scholar of ours forbade us, claiming that you say something regarding your slaughtering that he does not like for us to eat.' He said: 'Who is that scholar?' By Allah, the One who created them knows better, and by Allah, we indeed say with the name of the Messiah (Jesus).

From him, from Yusuf ibn Aqil, from Muhammad ibn Qays, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) said: Do not eat the slaughtered meat of the Arab Christians, for they are not People of the Book.

From him, from Hammad ibn Isa, from al-Husayn ibn al-Mukhtar, from al-Husayn ibn Abdillah, who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): We are in the mountain and we send the shepherds to the sheep, and perhaps the sheep becomes sick or injured, so they slaughter it and we eat it. He said: It is merely a slaughtered animal, so it is not considered safe to eat unless it is slaughtered by a Muslim.

From him, from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from Shu'ayb al-Aqarqufi, who said: I was with Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), and with us was Abu Basir and some people from the Mountains, asking him about the sacrifices of the People of the Book. He said to them, 'You have heard what Allah, the Exalted, said in His Book.' They said to him, 'We would like you to inform us [explicitly].' He said, 'Do not eat them.'

From him, from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr, from al-Husayn al-Ahmasi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: A man said to him: 'May God improve you. We have a butcher neighbor, and he brings a Jew to slaughter for him, so the Jews buy from him.' He said: 'Do not eat his slaughtered meat, nor buy from him.'

From him, from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Faddal, from his father, from Abu al-Maghra' Humayd ibn al-Muthanna, from Sama'ah, from al-Abd al-Salih (peace be upon him), that he asked him about the slaughtered meat of the Jew and the Christian, so he said: Do not approach it.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Ibn Abi 'Umayr from 'Umar ibn Udhaynah from Zurarah from Humran, who said: I heard Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) saying regarding the sacrifice of the Nāsibī (those who repudiate the Imams), the Jew, and the Christian: Do not eat their sacrifice until you hear them mention the name of Allah. I said: What about the Magus? He said: Yes. Did you not hear the saying of Allah, the Exalted: 'Do not eat from that upon which the name of Allah has not been mentioned'?

From him, from Fadalah ibn Ayyub, from al-Qasim ibn Yazid, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: Eat the slaughtered meat of the polytheists if they mention the name of Allah upon it while you hear it, and do not eat the slaughtered meat of the Arab Christians.

From him, from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr, from Jamil and Muhammad ibn Humran, that they asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the sacrifices of the Jews, Christians, and Magians, so he said: "Eat [them]." Some of them said, "Indeed, they do not mention [God's name]." He said, "If you are present with them and they do not mention [God's name], then do not eat [them]." And he said, "If they are absent [of your presence], then eat [them]."

From him, from Safwan, from Ibn Muskhan, from Muhammad al-Halabi, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the slaughtered meat of the People of the Book and their women, so he said: There is no harm in it.

From him, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from Jamil ibn Salih, from Abd al-Malik ibn 'Amr, who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'What do you say about the sacrifices of the Christians?' He said, 'There is no harm in them.' I said, 'But they mention the Messiah upon them.' He said, 'They only meant God by the Messiah.'

From him, from Al-Hasan, from Al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from Ali, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), from Abu Basir, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the slaughtered animal of the Jew, and he said: 'It is permissible.' I said: 'But if he mentions Al-Masih (the Messiah) [in the name of Allah]?' He said: 'Even if he mentions [Al-Masih], for indeed he only intends Allah [by it].'

From him, from Fadalah, from Saif ibn 'Amirah, from Abu Bakr al-Hadrami, from Abu al-Ward ibn Zayd, who said: I said to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him): 'Narrate a hadith to me and dictate it to me so that I may write it down.' He said: 'Where is your memory, O people of Kufa?' I said: 'So that no one may refute it back to me.' I asked: 'What do you say regarding the sacrifice of a Magian (Zoroastrian)?' He said: 'In the name of Allah, then he slaughters.' I said: 'A Muslim slaughters and does not mention (the name of Allah).' He said: 'Do not eat it.' Indeed, Allah the Exalted says: 'So eat of that (meat) upon which the name of Allah has been mentioned, and do not eat of that upon which the name of Allah has not been mentioned.'

From him, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Hariz, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) and Zurarah, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), that the two said: Regarding the slaughtered animals of the People of the Book: when you witness them and they have invoked the name of Allah, then eat their slaughtered animals; and if you do not witness them, then do not eat. And if a Muslim man comes to you and informs you that they have invoked [the name], then eat.

From him, from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from al-Qasim ibn Sulayman, from Hariz, who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) was asked about the sacrifices of the Jews, Christians, and Magians. He said: If you hear them mentioning the Name of God, or a witness for you has seen them mentioning the Name of God, then eat. But if you do not hear them, and no one who saw them testifies to you, then do not eat their sacrifice.

Al-Saffar narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Barqi, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Yunus ibn Bahman, who said: I said to Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him): A Christian relative of mine sent me as a gift roasted chickens and chicks, and prepared for me falawudhajah (a type of dish). Should I eat it? He said: There is no harm in it.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa narrated from Sa'd ibn Isma'il from his father Isma'il ibn Isa who said: I asked al-Rida (peace be upon him) about the slaughtered animals of the Jews and Christians and their food, and he said: Yes. First, among these narrations is that they do not contradict the earlier narrations because the earlier ones are more numerous. Also, among those who narrated these narrations is one who narrated what we mentioned earlier regarding the prohibition of their milk, namely Abu Basir and Muhammad ibn Muslim. And if it were safe from all of this afterwards, it would still carry two possibilities: one of which is that we apply it to the state of necessity, not the state of choice, because at the time of necessity the dead animal becomes permissible, so how much more so the slaughtered animal of one who differs from Islam, and that which indicates this.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Ahmad ibn Hamzah al-Qummi from Zakariyya ibn Adam who said: Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) said to me: 'I prohibit you from the slaughtered meat of everyone who is in opposition to the belief upon which you and your companions are, except in the time of necessity for it. And the second aspect is that these narrations came in the place of Taqiyya (dissimulation), because all those who opposed us consider its permissibility, and that which indicates that.'

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Sahl ibn Ziyad from Ahmad ibn Bashir from Ibn Abi Ghufaylah, al-Hasan ibn Ayyub, from Dawud ibn Kathir al-Raqqi, from Bashir ibn Abi Ghaylan al-Shaybani, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the sacrifices of the Jews, the Christians, and the Nasibis ( those of the Sunnis). He turned his cheek and said: 'All of them are until a day that is not.'
Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from al-Nuḍr ibn Suwayd from Zur'ah from Abū Baṣīr said: I heard Abū ʿAbdillāh (peace be upon him) saying: The slaughtered animal of the Nāṣib is not permissible.
From him, from Hammad ibn Isa, from al-Husayn ibn al-Mukhtar, from Abu Basir, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) that he said: The sacrifices (of the Haruriyyah) are not permissible.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Ahmad ibn Hamzah, from Muhammad ibn Ali, from Yunus ibn Ya'qub, from Abu Basir, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who buys meat from the market, and among his brothers there is one who slaughters and sells it, yet he deliberately buys from the 'Nassab' (those who set enmity). He said: 'What thing do you ask me to say? He eats nothing but like the dead body (jaththah), blood, and meat of the pig.' I said: 'Glory be to Allah, like the dead body, blood, and meat of the pig?' He said: 'Yes, and greater than that is with Allah.' Then he said: 'Indeed, this is in his heart against the believers, a sickness.'

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from al-Husayn ibn Saeed, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from 'Umar ibn Udhaynah, from Humran, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said: I heard him (peace be upon him) saying: Do not eat the slaughtered meat of the Nāsib (one who bears enmity to the Ahl al-Bayt) unless you hear him mentioning (the name of God).

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Al-Hasan from Yusuf ibn Aqil from Muhammad ibn Qays from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) said: The slaughtered meat of one who professes the word of Islam, fasts, and prays is lawful for you, provided he mentions the name of Allah over it. This does not contradict the earlier reports for two reasons: the first is that he who sets up war and enmity against the Family of Muhammad (peace be upon him) does not truly profess the word of Islam, but rather professes the word of disbelief, and is excluded from what the report encompasses. The second reason is that it may be attributed to the state of precautionary piety (Taqiyyah).

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from one not specified from Abu al-Maghra', and Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Ibn Abi 'Umayr from Hammad from al-Halabi from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about the sacrifice of the Murji'ah and the Haruriyyah, so he said: Eat and be content and settle down until it becomes a matter of time, and it is possible that the report is specific to the state of necessity, according to what the report included which we presented earlier in the first chapter from his saying: 'I forbid you from the sacrifice of everyone who is upon a difference from what you are upon and your companions, except in the time of necessity.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Hammad, from Hariz, who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to Zurarah and Muhammad ibn Muslim: Milk, curds, egg, hair, wool, horn, tusk, hoof, and everything that is separated from the beast or the sheep is pure (halal for use), even if you take it from it after it dies; wash it and pray in it.

Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Ali ibn Ri'ab from Zurarah from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: I asked him about the udder (infaḥah) that is taken from a dead goat. He said: There is no objection to it. I said: The milk remains in the udder of the sheep after it has died. He said: There is no objection to it. I said: And the wool, the hair, the bones, the bones of the elephant, the skin, and the eggs that are taken from the hen (after it dies). He said: All of this is permissible.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Abu Ja'far, from Wahb, from Ja'far, from his father, (peace be upon him), that Ali (peace be upon him) was asked about a sheep that died, and milk was drawn from it, so he said: Ali (peace be upon him): That is pure haram (forbidden). Therefore, this is a rare (shadh) narration, and its narrator is Wahb ibn Wahb, who is weak as we have clarified previously. And accepting the report, it can be understood as a form of taqiyya (dissimulation), because it is the belief of some of the Sunnis.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from al-Mukhtar ibn Muhammad ibn al-Mukhtar and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him), who said: I wrote to him asking about the skins of the dead animal whose meat is eaten if slaughtered, and he wrote back: 'One may not derive benefit from the dead animal's hide, sinew, and all that belongs to the sheep from the wool, hair, coarse hair, horns, and claws, and one does not exceed these, God willing.'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from 'Uthman ibn 'Isa from Sama'ah who said: I asked him about eating cheese and carrying a sword in which there is glue and tallow, so he said: There is no harm with it, as long as you do not know that it is from a dead animal.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Al-Husayn ibn Zur'arah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding the skin of a dead sheep that is tanned, milk and water are poured into it, so one drinks from it and performs ablution with it. He said: Yes. And he said: It is tanned and benefit is derived from it, and one prays in it. Al-Husayn said: And my father asked him about the udder that is in the belly of the she-camel and the goat, and it is dead, so he said: There is no harm in it.

From him, from Al-Hasan, from Zur'ah, from Samaan, who said: I asked him about the skin of the female animal that has died (maitah) which has been salted, and it is the kaimukht (tanned leather), so he granted permission regarding it, and said: 'And if you do not touch it, it is better.' The resolution between these two narrations is that we should attribute them to a form of taqiyya (dissimulation/prudence), because the skin of the maitah does not become pure through tanning (dabagh) in our view, as we have clarified in the Book of Salat.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from al-Barqi, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Hisham ibn Salim, from 'Umar ibn Hanzalah, who said: I carried the rabeebah in a small bag until I entered upon Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) and asked him about it. He said: 'All of it is permissible,' and added: 'For it has a rind/skin.' From him (al-Barqi), from Muhammad ibn Isma'il ibn Bazi', who said: 'I wrote to him asking: 'People differ regarding the rabeebah, so what do you think about it?' He wrote back: 'There is no harm in it.' From him, from Bakr ibn Muhammad and Muhammad ibn Abi 'Umayr together, from al-Fadl ibn Yunus, who said: 'Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) had breakfast at my place in Mina, with him was Muhammad ibn Zayd. They were brought sugary treats containing the rabeebah. Muhammad ibn Zayd said to him: 'This is the rabeebah.' He took a piece, dipped it in it, and then ate it.'

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Fadhal from Amr ibn Sa'id from Musaddiq ibn Sadaqa from 'Ammar ibn Musa al-Sabati from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about the Rabiya, and he said: Do not eat it, for we do not know it in fish, O 'Ammar. The meaning in this narration is that we should interpret it as a type of dislike (karahah) rather than prohibition (haram), based on the evidence of the earlier narrations and the narrations we added to this one in our Great Book.

First: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Fadala from Dawud ibn Farqad from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) said: 'Whoever eats this food, let him not approach our mosque,' meaning garlic, and he did not say it is forbidden. Second: From him, from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr from Umar ibn Udhayna from Muhammad ibn Muslim from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: I asked him about garlic, and he said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) only forbade it because of its smell, and said: 'Whoever eats this bad vegetable, let him not approach our mosque.' As for whoever eats it and does not come to the mosque, there is no harm. Third: From him, from Hammad ibn Isa from Shu'ayb from Abu Basir said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) was asked about garlic, onions, and leeks, and he said: There is no harm in eating them raw or cooked in the pot, and there is no harm in being treated with garlic, but when one of you eats that, let him not go out to the mosque.

First: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd from al-Qasim ibn Sulayman from Jarrah al-Mad'ai ni from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: The man should not drink while standing. The meaning in this report is a type of dislike (karahah) rather than prohibition (haram), which is indicated by this. Second: What Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Fadalah ibn Ayyub from Ismail ibn Abi Ziyad from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) He said: Drinking while standing is stronger for you and more sound.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Jamil ibn Darraj, from Ibn Bukayr, from Zurara, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about old wine that is made into vinegar; he said: There is no harm (in it). 2. Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Fadala ibn Ayyub, from Ibn Bukayr, from Ubayd ibn Zurara who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who takes wine and makes it into vinegar; he said: There is no harm. 3. From him, from Safwan, from Ibn Bukayr, from Ubayd ibn Zurara, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) that he said regarding a man who sold fresh grape juice, and the ruler detained it until it became wine, and its owner made it into vinegar; he said: When it changes from the name of wine, there is no harm with it.

From him, from Ibn Abi Umayr and Ali ibn Hadid, from Jamil, who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'I have dirhams owed to me by a man, and he gives me wine in payment for them.' He said: 'Take it, then spoil it.' Ali said: 'And turn it into vinegar.'

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn Isa ibn Ubayd, from Abd al-Aziz ibn al-Muhtadi, who said: I wrote to al-Rida (peace be upon him): 'I am your ransom, grape juice turns into wine, so vinegar and something that changes it are poured over it until it becomes vinegar.' He said: 'There is no objection to it.'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr from Al-Husayn al-Ahmasi from Muhammad ibn Muslim and Abu Basir and Ali from Abu Basir from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) He was asked about vinegar being added to wine, he said: 'Not except what comes from itself (i.e., natural transformation), so it does not contradict the earlier reports, because the matter is to be understood as a type of dislike, for it is preferable to leave it until it becomes vinegar naturally.'

Al-Husayn narrated from Fadala ibn Ayyub, from Ibn Bukayr, from Ubayd ibn Zurara, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who takes vinegar (khamr) and turns it into vinegar (khall). He said: There is no harm in it, provided he does not put into it that which causes it to turn back (to wine). The ruling in it is also what we mentioned in the first report, equally.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Muhammad ibn Khalid from Abdullah ibn Bukayr from Abu Basir who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about wine in which something is made until it ferments. He said: If that which is made in it is the dominant factor over what was made, then there is no harm. This report is rejected on the apparent level by consensus, because there is no disagreement that that in which wine falls becomes impure, and if it becomes impure, its use is not permissible even if it is dominant over it, and that which reveals what we mentioned.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn Musa, from al-Hasan ibn al-Mubarak, from Zakariyya ibn Adam, who said: I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about a drop of intoxicating nabidh that fell into a pot containing meat and a large amount of broth. He said: The broth should be poured out, or fed to the Ahl al-Dhimma or to dogs, and the meat should be washed and eaten. I said: And if blood fell into it? He said: The blood will be eaten by the fire, if God wills.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan, from Amr ibn Sa'id, from Musaddiq ibn Sadah, from 'Ammar al-Sabati, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about Al-Fuqqa' (a type of fermented drink), and he said: 'It is wine (khamr).'

From him, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Al-Husayn al-Qala'ansi, who said: I wrote to Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) the Predecessor, asking him about Al-Fuqqa', so he said: 'Do not approach it, for it is from the wine.'

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan from Abu Sa'id from Abu Jamil al-Basri who said: I was with Yunus ibn 'Abd al-Rahman in Baghdad, and I was walking with him in the market. The owner of the vinegar jar opened his jar, and vinegar splashed onto Yunus. I saw him become upset because of it until the sun set. I said to him, 'Why do you not pray?' He said, 'I do not wish to pray until I return home and wash this vinegar from my garment.' I said to him, 'Is this your own opinion or something you have narrated?' He said, 'Hisham ibn al-Hakam informed me that he asked Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) about vinegar, and he said, 'Do not drink it, for it is unknown wine (khamar majhul). And if it touches your garment, wash it.'

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Ya'qub ibn Yazid, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Muramim, who said: Al-Fuqqah (a type of bread) was prepared for Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) in his house. Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya said: Abu Ahmad (meaning Ibn Abi Umayr) said: And Fuqqah is not prepared if it boils. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan is the one who clarifies what Ibn Abi Umayr mentioned.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from 'Uthman ibn 'Isa said: 'Abdullah ibn Muhammad al-Razi wrote to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him): If you see fit to explain al-fuqqa' to me, for it has become ambiguous to us whether it is disliked after it boils or before it boils. So he wrote to him: Do not approach al-fuqqa' except that which does not harm its vessel, or if it is new. So he sent the letter back to him: Indeed, I wrote asking about al-fuqqa' before it boiled, and there came to me that I should drink it if it was in a new vessel or one that does not harm. And I did not know the limit of 'damage' and 'newness', and he asked that this be explained to him, and whether it is permissible to drink what is prepared in clay, glass, wood, and similar vessels. So he wrote: Al-fuqqa' is prepared in glass and in new pottery for the duration of three boilings, then do not exceed it after three boilings except in a new vessel, and wood is the same.

From him, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Hasan, from al-Husayn his brother, from his father Ali ibn Yaqtin, from Abu al-Hasan al-Madi (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about drinking al-fuqqa' (a type of beer/drink) which is made in the market and sold, and I do not know how it was made or when it was made. Is it permissible for me to drink it? He said: 'I do not like it.'

First: Ali ibn Mahziyar said: I said to him, 'Some of your mawalis have narrated from your fathers (peace be upon them) that every waqf (endowment) to a known time is obligatory upon the heirs, and every waqf to an unknown, ignorant time is invalid upon the heirs. And you are more knowledgeable about the opinion of your fathers.' So he wrote: 'It is as I said.' Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: The waqf is valid as long as it is perpetual, according to the earlier narrations in the first chapter which include the condition of the deed of waqf. And if it is not perpetual, it is not valid in any case. The meaning in this report is that his saying 'every waqf to a known time' means that if the object of the waqf is mentioned, because if he does not mention the object of the waqf in the endowment, the waqf becomes invalid. And he did not mean by 'time' the fixed term (age), and this was a convention among them. And that which indicates this is what Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar narrated, who said: I wrote to Abu Muhammad (peace be upon him) asking him about the waqf that is valid, how is it? For it has been narrated that the waqf, if it is not timed, is invalid and returned to the heirs, and if it is timed, it is valid. Then some people said: The timed one is the one who mentions in it that it is a waqf for so-and-so and his descendants, and when they perish, it is for the poor and the needy until Allah (Exalted and Mighty) inherits the earth and whoever is on it. And others said: This is timed if he mentions that it is for so-and-so and his descendants as long as they remain, and he does not mention at the end for the poor and the needy until Allah inherits the earth and whoever is on it. And that which is not timed is that he says: 'This is a waqf' and does not mention anyone. So which of these is valid and which is invalid? So he wrote: The endowments are according to what one endows, if Allah wills.

Aban narrated from Abu al-Jarud, who said: Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: A man should not buy what he has given in charity. And if he gives a dwelling in charity to a relative, if he wishes, he may live with them. And if he gives a servant in charity to a relative, the servant serves him if he wishes. As for what Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Faddal narrated from Amr ibn Uthman from Abdullah ibn al-Mughira from Talhah ibn Zayd from Abu Abdillah from his father (peace be upon him) that a man gave his house in charity while he was living in it, so he said, 'Leave it,' when he exited from it. This does not contradict the first report, because the meaning of his command to leave the house was only to validate the endowment (waqf), because we have explained that part of its validity is handing over the endowment to the one upon whom it is endowed, and the purpose was not that it was forbidden for him to be prohibited, and this does not contradict that. What Ali ibn al-Hasan narrated from Ya'qub ibn Yazid al-Katib from Ibn Abi Umayr from Abu al-Maghra from Abu Basir from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about the charity of what has not been received and not divided. He said: It is permissible, because the meaning in this report is that the charity of what has not been received is permissible, and we did not say that it is not permissible, but we said that fulfilling it is not obligatory, and its owner is free to choose in that matter.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from Muhammad ibn al-Fudayl, from Abu al-Subah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) He said: He was asked about al-sukna (residence for life) and al-'umra (endowment for life), so he said: If he made the residence for his own life, it is as he stipulated. And if he made it for him and his descendants until their line ends, they cannot sell it nor bequeath it, then the house returns to its original owner. Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad from al-Halabi from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) regarding a man who houses another man in his house and for his descendants after him: He said: It is permissible, and they cannot sell it nor bequeath it. I asked: And a man who houses a man in his house for his life? He said: That is permissible. I asked: And a man who houses a man in his house without specifying a time? He said: It is permissible, and he can evict him whenever he wishes. Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Ibn Abi Umayr from Husayn ibn Nu'aym from Abu al-Hasan Musa (peace be upon him) said: I asked him about a man who made a house a residence for a man for the days of his life, or made it for him and his descendants after him. Is it for him and his descendants as he stipulated? He said: Yes. I asked: If he needs it, does he sell it? He said: Yes. I asked: Does his sale invalidate the residence? He said: No, the sale does not invalidate the residence. Thus, I heard my father (peace be upon him) say: Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: Sale does not invalidate rent nor residence, but he sells it on the condition that the buyer does not own what he bought until the residence expires as stipulated. And so with rent. I asked: If he returns to the tenant his money and all that was incumbent upon him regarding maintenance and construction for what he rented? He said: With good will and the tenant's satisfaction with that, there is no harm. As for what al-Hasan ibn Mahbub narrated from Khalid ibn Nafi' al-Bajali from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a man who made a house a residence for a man for his life, meaning the owner of the house. Then the one for whom the residence was made died, and the one who was given the residence remained. Do you see that if the heirs wish to evict him from the house, they have that right? He said: I ask you, if the

First: Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Faddal from Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Hakim from Jamil ibn Darraj from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) from a man who gave something as a gift to his son, asking if it is permissible for him to take it back; he said: Yes, unless he is young. Second: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Isma'il from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan from Ibn Abi Umayr from Abd al-Rahman who said: I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about a man who gave charity to some of his children while they were young, in the form of a female slave; then the slave pleases him while they are young dependents; do you think he can take her or appraise her at a fair price and witness against himself for its value, or leave it all and not deal with any of it? He said: He appraises her at a fair price, accounts for its value for them against himself, and takes her. Third: As for what Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Faddal narrated from al-Abbas ibn Amir from Dawud ibn al-Husayn from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him if anyone can take back charity or a gift; he said: As for what is given as charity for God's sake, no; as for the gift and the grant, he can take it back whether he has taken possession of it or not, even if it is for a relative. Fourth: Ahmad ibn Muhammad from al-Husayn from Safwan ibn Yahya who said: I asked al-Rida (peace be upon him) about a man who had a debt from another man, so he gifted it to his son; the man mentioned the debt to him, so he said to him: There is nothing upon you regarding it in this world and the next, to please him, and he had indeed gifted it to one of his sons; he said: Yes, he gives it to him then revokes it and makes it a gift to this one; the meaning in these two narrations is that we interpret them as: if the children are adults, it is permissible for him to take back the gift; and we only prevented taking back what he gives to the young ones among them. Fifth: As for what Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Ibn Abi Nasr from Hammad from al-Mu'alla ibn Khunays who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) if anyone can take back charity or a gift; he said: As for what is given as charity for God's sake, no; as for the gift and the grant, he can take it back whether he has taken possession of them or not, even if it is for a relative; the meaning in this narration is what we said in the first two narrations, equally.

From him, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'The example of the one who returns his charity is like the one who returns his vomit.'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Fadala from Aban from Abu Marim said: When a man gives charity or a gift, whether the recipient takes possession of it or does not take possession, whether it is known or unknown, it is valid.
From him, from Fudaylah, from Aban, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Sayyabah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), like it.

Yunus ibn Abd al-Rahman from Abu al-Mi'za from Abu Basir said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: A gift (hiba) is valid whether it has been taken possession of or not, whether it has been divided or not. And for honey (nahln), that is not valid until it is taken possession of. The people intended that [distinction] and thus erred. The meaning in these narrations is a type of preference (istihbab) rather than obligation (wujub). Furthermore, the latter report included a distinction between honey and a gift, and we have clarified that there is no difference between them. It is permissible that it emerged as a form of precautionary piety (taqiyyah), because it is the view of some of the Sunni Muslims. And what we mentioned is for clarification.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from Ali ibn Ri'ab, from Zurarah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Charity (Sadaqah) is that which is given for the sake of God. In the time of the Messenger of God (peace be upon him), people would give gifts (Nihlah) and bestow gifts (Hibah), and it is not fitting for one who gives something to God, Exalted and Majestic, to take it back. He said: And whatever was not given to God and for God's sake, then he may take it back, whether it was a gift (Nihlah) or a bestowal (Hibah), whether it was taken possession of or not. And a man does not take back what he gives to his wife, nor does a woman take back what she gives to her husband, whether it was taken possession of or not. Because God, the Exalted, says: 'And it is not permissible for you to take back from them anything you have given them.' 'But if they give up willingly to you anything of it, then take it in satisfaction and ease.' And this ruling applies to the dowry (Sadaq) and gift (Hibah).

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Isma'il from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan from Ibn Abi 'Umayr from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who has dirhams owed to him by another man, and he gifts them to him; is it for him to return to them? He said: No. The ruling in this narration is also as we said in the previous narrations, equally. And it is also possible that it is to be understood as referring to preference (istihbab).

Abu Ali al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn al-Jabbar, from Safwan, from Mansur ibn Hazim, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who bequeathed to one of his heirs that he had a debt due from him (the deceased). He said: If the deceased was in a state of illness, then give to the one to whom he bequeathed.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from 'Uthman ibn 'Isa from Sama'ah who said: I asked him about one who confesses to the heirs for a debt upon himself while he is ill. He said: It is permissible upon him what he confesses to, if it is small.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ibn Mahbub from Hisham ibn Salim from Isma'il ibn Jabr said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who confessed to one of his heirs a debt upon himself while he was ill. He said: It is valid for him if he confesses to it for less than one-third.

Ibn Mahbub from Abu Waddad said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a sick man who confessed at the time of death to an heir that he owed him a debt. He said: That is permissible. I said: And if he bequeathed something to an heir? He said: It is permissible.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Ali ibn al-Nu'man, from Ibn Muskhan, from al-'Ala', the seller of Sabir, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a woman who deposited wealth with a man. When death approached her, she said to him, 'The wealth that I gave you is for So-and-so.' The woman died, and her heirs came to the man and said, 'There was wealth belonging to our companion which we do not see except with you; swear to us that there is nothing with you.' He would swear to them. He (the Imam) said to them, 'If the woman was trustworthy in your eyes, then swear to them; and if she was suspected (of owing more), then do not swear, and leave the matter as it was. Indeed, she is entitled to one-third of the wealth.'

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Bunan ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Abdullah ibn al-Mughira, from al-Sakuni, from Ja'far, from his father, from Ali (peace be upon him), that he used to reject the bequest (nahlah) in the will. And whatever he acknowledged at the time of his death without proof or clear evidence, he rejected it. The meaning of this report is that we interpret it as: if the one acknowledging is suspected by the heirs, his acknowledgment is not accepted unless there is evidence. If no evidence stands, what he acknowledged is valid from his one-third share. This has been clarified by him (peace be upon him) in the narration of al-Halabi, Mansur ibn Hazim, and Isma'il ibn Jabir, whose mention was preceded. As for if he was healthy (not near death), what he acknowledged is from the principal of the wealth, like other debts, and that which reveals what we mentioned.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Jabbar who said: I wrote to al-Askari (peace be upon him): A woman made a will to a man and acknowledged to him a debt of eight thousand dirhams, and likewise whatever household goods she had of wool, hair, similar items, gold, and copper, and all that she had she acknowledged to the executor, and she witnessed her will, and she instructed that two pilgrimages be performed on her behalf from this estate, and a slave-girl be given to her for four hundred dirhams. The woman died and left a husband, so we did not know how to proceed from this and the matter became confused upon us. A scribe mentioned that the woman consulted him, so she asked him to write for her what is valid for this will. He said: It is not valid unless you leave her with your acknowledgment of the debt to him by the testimony of witnesses, and you command him after that to execute what you instruct him to do. So he wrote to him the will on this basis, and she acknowledged to the executor this debt. What is your opinion, may Allah preserve your honor, regarding the jurists before you about this, and inform us of that so that we may act upon it, if Allah wills. He wrote in his hand: If the debt is sound, well-known, and understood, then the debt is deducted from the principal of the estate, if Allah wills. And if the debt is not true, then what she willed from her third is executed, whether it suffices or does not suffice.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Harun ibn Muslim, from Ibn Sa'dan, from Mas'adah ibn Sadah, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father (peace be upon him), who said: Ali (peace be upon him) said: 'There is no bequest for an heir, and no acknowledgment of debt.' He means: if the sick person acknowledges a debt to one of the heirs, it is not valid for him. The way to understand this report is to carry it on taqiyyah (dissimulation), because it includes 'no bequest for an heir and no acknowledgment of debt.' And we have explained that his acknowledgment to the heirs is valid. And we will explain later that he may bequeath to those other than the heirs if there is something that needs mentioning, although we have fully covered this in our Great Book, so whoever wishes to stop at it, let him stop there. And it is possible that what is meant by the report is that there is no acknowledgment of the debt in what exceeds one-third if it is suspect, because we have explained that this is not permissible if the one acknowledging is not trustworthy and acceptable, and that it remains valid in the one-third and below.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Ibn Abi Umayr from Jamil said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who accused a group of men of adultery. He said: If they bring him together [in one session], he is given one hadd punishment. And if they bring him separately [in different sessions], a hadd punishment is given to each one individually.
From him, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Najran, from Muhammad ibn Humran, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), like it. Like it.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Al-Hasan from Zur'ah from Sama'ah from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) ruled in the case of a man who accused a group of people collectively, so he flogged him with one limit (hadd). The explanation in this report is one of two things: One is that we interpret it according to the detail contained in the first report, that only one limit was obligatory upon him if they came to him together, but if they came separately, it would be obligatory upon him for each person a limit according to the complete report. The second explanation is that we interpret it as: if he accused them with one word, he is obligated one limit, but if he accused them with different words, he is obligated for each person a limit, which indicates that.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Fadala, from Aban, from Al-Hasan al-Attar, who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): A man slandered a group of people all together, so he said with one word. I said: Yes. He said: He receives one hadd (flogging). And if he distinguished between them in the slander, a hadd is inflicted on each one of them.

From him, from Ibn Mahbub, from Abu al-Hasan al-Shami, from Burayd, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), in the case of a man who accuses all the people with a single word, he said to him: If he does not name them specifically, then only one hadd (fixed punishment) is upon him; and if he names them, then upon him is a hadd for each man.

Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Mu'awiya ibn Wahb from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: I said to him, 'I manumitted a slave-girl for some orphans of ours, and stipulated upon her that if she became unable (to pay), she would return to slavery, and I would be free of what I had taken from her.' He said, 'Your stipulation is valid.' And it will be said to you, 'Indeed, Ali (peace be upon him) used to say: The manumitted slave is freed proportionate to what he pays of his manumission contract.' I said, 'That was only Ali's (peace be upon him) opinion before the stipulation was made; when people made stipulations, they had their own stipulation.' I said to him, 'What is the definition of inability (ajz)?' He said, 'Indeed, our judges say that the inability of the manumitted slave is that he delays the installment (najm) to the next installment until a year passes over him.' I said, 'What do you say?' He said, 'No, and no concession: he does not have the right to delay an installment beyond its due time if that is part of his stipulation.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Mu'awiya ibn Wahb, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a female slave who entered into a contract of manumission (mukatabah) and paid two-thirds of its value, and it had been stipulated upon her that if she became unable to pay, she would return to slavery. We are free from what we took from her, so two installments have converged upon her. He (peace be upon him) said: She is returned [to slavery], and they are content with what they took from her, and she does not have the right to delay the installment after its due date for one month except with their permission.

Al-Husayn ibn Said from al-Nadr from al-Qasim ibn Sulayman from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Indeed, Ali (peace be upon him) would make easy for the muqatib (slave seeking manumission by installment), for they did not stipulate that if he became unable [to pay], he would remain a slave. And Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'Their stipulation holds.' And he said: 'The muqatib is waited for for three periods (of payment). If he becomes unable, he is returned to slavery.' The solution in these narrations is one of two things: one is that they came in agreement with the general public (Ahl al-Sunnah) and according to what they narrate from Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him), for they narrate from him that he said: 'When the muqatib pays something, he is freed from it in proportion to what he paid,' and they do not distinguish between whether the condition is fulfilled or not. And his son (peace be upon him) clarified this in the narration of Mu'awiya ibn Wahb, which we presented at the beginning of the chapter. The other solution is that it is to be understood as recommended (istihbab), for whoever waits for the muqatib for a year, or two years, or three years, or delays a period to another period, has much merit and abundant reward in that, even if it is not obligatory upon him.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Ibn Abi 'Umayr from Hammad from Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Halab (Al-Halabi) from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) regarding the Muqatib. He pays part of his manumission debt, so he said: 'The people used not to stipulate [conditions], but today they do stipulate, and the Muslims are bound by their conditions. If he stipulated upon him that if he becomes unable [to pay], he returns [to slavery], and if he did not stipulate upon him, he does not return.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: When a slave strikes a free man, he is flogged with eighty (strikes). And he said: This is from the rights of the people.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad from 'Uthman ibn 'Ibn 'Isa from Sama'ah who said: I asked him about the slave who falsely accuses a free man. He said: He receives eighty [lashes]. I said: And if he commits fornication? He said: He is flogged fifty [lashes].

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa narrated from Muhammad ibn Isma'il from Muhammad ibn al-Fudayl from Abu al-Subah from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a slave who accused a free man of adultery, and he said: 'Upon him is eighty [lashes].'

Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ibn Mahbub from Ali ibn al-Hakam from Musa ibn Bakr from Zurara from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) in a freed slave woman was slandered by a male slave, he said: He is flogged with eighty [lashes] because he is only flogged for her right.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid from Uthman ibn Isa from Sama'ah who said: The mukatib (slave who has agreed to pay a fixed sum for his freedom) is lashed if he commits zina, in proportion to the amount of his manumission price that has been paid off. If he accuses a muhsan (free, chaste woman), then upon him is to be lashed eighty [lashes], whether he is free or a slave.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Saif ibn 'Umayrah from Abu Bakr al-Hadrami who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a slave who slandered a free man. He said: 'He is flogged with eighty [strikes]. This is from the rights of the Muslims.' Then he said: 'As for what is from the rights of Allah, the Exalted, then he is struck with half the punishment.' I said: 'What is that which is from the rights of Allah?' He said: 'When he commits adultery or drinks wine, this is from the rights in which half the punishment is struck.'

Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from al-Saffan, from al-Hariz, from al-Bukayr, from one of the Imams (peace be upon him), that he said: Whoever accuses a Muslim of zina (or false testimony), he is to be given eighty stripes, whether he is a Jew, a Christian, or a slave.

From him, from Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from Saif ibn 'Amirah, from Ibn Bukayr, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the lash (hudud) of a slave who threw accusations (at a free man). He said: 'He is lashed with eighty.' This is from the rights of people. As for what is from the rights of God, then he is lashed with half the punishment. I said: 'Which one is the one in which half the punishment is applied?' He said: 'When he commits zina (unlawful sexual intercourse) or drinks wine, this is from the rights of God in which half the punishment is applied.'

Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn, from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from al-Qasim ibn Sulayman, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the slave who accuses the free man, how many lashes is he given? He said: Forty. And he said: If he commits a lewd act, then upon him is half the punishment. This is a strange report (khabar shadh) contrary to the apparent meaning of the Quran and the many reports we have presented, and its ruling is that it is not acted upon and is not countered with similar reports. As for its contradiction of the apparent meaning of the Quran, then indeed Allah, the Exalted, said: 'And those who accuse chaste women... then flog them eighty lashes and do not accept their testimony ever,' and that is general for every accuser, whether free or slave. As for His saying: 'If they commit a lewd act, then upon them is half of what is upon the free women,' that is specific to the fornicator as we have clarified from the reports, for their contradiction is not permissible.

And as for what Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Hammad from Hariz from Muhammad ibn Muslim from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) regarding the slave who falsely accuses a free man, he said: He is flogged with a full hadd, except for one or two lashes. This report implies that he meant by 'false accusation' that which does not reach the level of qadhf (full legal accusation), for that does not obligate the complete hadd, but rather ta'zir is obligatory upon him. And that which reveals what we mentioned is that Muhammad ibn Muslim, the narrator of this hadith, has narrated the opposite of this, in agreement with the reports we presented earlier.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Ibn Abi Umayr, from al-'Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from one of the Imams (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about a slave who falsely accuses a free man, he said: He is flogged with the prescribed punishment.

And as for what Yunus narrated from Sama'ah, he said: I asked him about the slave who falsely accuses the free man, and he said: Upon him is fifty lashes. The ruling in this is also what we mentioned in the first report, because Sama'ah has narrated that the hadd punishment of eighty is obligatory upon him, and we have previously presented this narration from him.

And as for what Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Al-Nadr from Al-Qasim ibn Sulayman, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the slave who accuses the free man, how many lashes is he given? He said: Forty. Thus we have explained the reasoning in this narration in the report of Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub, so there is no need to repeat it, and it adds to what we mentioned as clarification.

Yunus ibn 'Abd al-Rahman from Ibn Muskhan from Abu Basir said: He said: The punishment for the Jew, the Christian, and the slave for drinking wine and for slander is the same. And the People of the Covenant were settled upon the condition that they drink it in their houses.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd from 'Asim ibn Humayd from Muhammad ibn Qays from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) ruled regarding a slave who calls a free man his father (other than his actual father): He said, 'I see that his skin should be stripped (exposed for flogging).' And he said regarding a man who was called (by another) to be his father: 'Present your proof, and I will enable you against him.' So when he brought the proof, he said, 'Indeed, his mother was a slave-girl.' He said, 'There is no full hadd punishment upon you for his cursing, just as he cursed you, or pardon him.' What this report contains from his saying 'I see that his skin should be exposed' implies that he may have meant that his skin should be exposed so that the hadd punishment is carried out upon him. And it implies that the meaning is if his mother was a slave-girl and he attributed her to zina (fornication), then the full hadd is not obligatory upon him, but ta'zir (discretionary punishment) is obligatory upon him. And there is in the hadith something that weakens reliance upon it, which is that Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) said to him, 'Curse him as he cursed you.' And it is not permissible for him (peace be upon him) to order cursing, because cursing is ugly (improper), and he only has the right to carry out the hadd upon him, either the full one or ta'zir.

Yunus narrated from Ishaq ibn 'Ammar from Abu Basir who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said regarding a man who said to his wife, 'I did not find you a virgin (or having discharge):' He said, 'He is struck (with a light beating).' I said, 'If he repeated it,' he said, 'He is struck, for he is likely to stop.'

Yunus narrated from Zurarah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), regarding a man who said to his wife, 'I have not been given the virginity token.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'There is no penalty upon him, because the virginity token can be lost through intercourse other than the primary act.' Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: His statement 'There is no penalty upon him' means there is no complete fixed punishment (hadd), although there is discretionary punishment (ta'zir) upon him according to what the first report contained.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Ibn Mahbub from Hammad from Ziyad ibn Sulayman from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) regarding a man who said to his wife after he had entered with her: 'I did not find you a virgin.' He said: 'There is no hadd (fixed punishment) upon him.'

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from al-Husayn ibn Saeed, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: When a man says to his wife, 'I did not find you a virgin,' and he has no proof, he is flogged with the ta'zir punishment, and he is kept apart from her; this does not contradict the earlier reports, because the meaning of his statement 'he is flogged with the punishment' refers to the discretionary punishment (ta'zir), and he did not mean a complete (fixed) punishment, as indicated by the preceding reports.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Al-Hasan from Zur'ah from Sama'ah said: I asked him about a man who accuses another man of false testimony (qadhf), then the accuser pardons him, then he wants to flog him after his repentance. He said: He does not have that right after the pardon.

Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Abu Ayyub from Sama'ah who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who accuses another man of adultery, and the accused pardons him and makes himself free from that (li'n) penalty, then afterwards it occurs to him that he should bring him forward so that a limit (hadd) is inflicted upon him. He (AS) said: There is no limit for him after the pardon.

Yunus ibn Abd al-Rahman from al-Ala' from Muhammad ibn Muslim said: I asked him about a man who accuses his wife [of zina], he said: She is flogged. I said: What do you think if she pardons him? He said: No, and not [even] for the sake of honor. The meaning in this report is that we interpret it as: when she refers the matter to the Imam or the judge, she has no right of pardon after that. And we have detailed this in our Great Book, and that which indicates this.

Sahl ibn Ziyad from Ibn Mahbub from Durays al-Kunasi from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: The divine limits (hudud) are not pardoned except by the Imam. As for what is the right of the people, there is no harm in pardoning it without the Imam.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Mahbub, from al-Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him: 'A man has committed a wrong against me; should I pardon him or refer him to the ruler?' He said: 'It is your right. If you pardon him, it is good; and if you refer him to the Imam, you are merely seeking your right. And how can you refer him to the Imam?'

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Ibrahim, from al-Nawfali, from al-Sakuni, from Ja'far, from his father, that Ali (peace be upon him) said: Whoever acknowledges a child and then repudiates him, he is given the flogging (for paternity dispute) and is compelled to provide for the child.

Muhammad ibn Yahya narrated from Muhammad ibn Ahmad, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from al-Ala', from al-Fudayl, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked: A man repudiates his child, yet he has acknowledged him. He said: If the child is from a free woman, he is lashed with fifty lashes, the penalty of a male slave; and if the child is from a female slave, there is no penalty upon him. The meaning in this report is that we should assume it is a mistake by the narrator, because the first report is consistent with the apparent meaning of the Quran and the reports we have presented in the first chapter, and this report is anomalous, so it is not objected against what we said with a similar one.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd from al-Qasim ibn Sulayman from Abu Maryam al-Ansari said: I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about the boy who has not reached puberty; if a man accuses him (of zina), is he flogged?
