This does not contradict the first hadith, because in that hadith it is not stated that he is not subject to any punishment (hadd), and the first hadith is detailed, so it is more appropriate to follow it.

Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Abu Jamilah from Aban ibn Taghlib from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: For the lower lip is six thousand, and for the upper lip four thousand, because the lower one holds the water (saliva).
And Zarif ibn Nasih narrated in his book, like that.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Al-Hasan from Zur'ah from Sama'ah said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: The upper and lower lips are equal in the blood money (diyah), so they do not contradict the first two reports, because it is possible that the intended meaning of the equality between them is in the obligation of the diyah, not in its amount; thus, they are equal in that a diyah is obligatory for each one of them, even if they differ in amount.
And Ahmad ibn Abi Abdillah narrated from Uthman ibn Isa from Sama'ah who said: I asked him about the teeth, so he said: They are equal in the blood money (diyah).

And Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from al-Ala' ibn al-Fudayl, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) that he said: The teeth and the molars are equal; [the diyah for each is] one-tenth.

And what Al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Fadhl narrated from Zarif from Ali ibn Abi Hamzah from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Regarding the tooth, there are five from the camels, its minimum and maximum, and it is half of one-tenth of the blood money. Therefore, the correct approach in these narrations is to interpret them as referring to the front teeth rather than the back teeth, because they are the ones equal in the obligation of blood money, five hundred for each one, according to what was detailed in the first narration. And it is appropriate to build the general upon the specific, as we have clarified in other places. And if the intended meaning were not what we said, the blood money would increase beyond the complete blood money if five hundred were obligated for every tooth, because all of them are twenty-eight teeth, and that is what everyone accepts.

Al-Nawfali from al-Sakawni from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) said: The teeth are thirty-one. In each socket (gum cavity) there are three molars and one-fifth of a camel [as blood money]. Therefore, the way to handle this narration is to attribute it to taqiyya (dissimulation), because it agrees with the opinion of some of the Sunnis, but we do not act upon it.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Ibn Mahbub from Abdullah ibn Sinan from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: If a tooth is struck, it is waited upon for a year; if it falls out, the striker is fined five hundred dirhams; and if it does not fall out but turns black, he is fined two-thirds of its blood money (diya).

Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ali ibn al-Hakam and others from Aban from some of his companions from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) used to say: 'When the incisor tooth turns black, the blood money (diyah) is established for it.' Therefore, the meaning in this narration is that we should interpret it according to the distinction we mentioned in the first narration, which is that two-thirds of the blood money is due for it, rather than the complete blood money.

Sahl ibn Ziyad from Ibn Mahbub from Ali ibn Ri'ab from al-Fudayl ibn Yasar said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the forearm when it is struck and the ulna (zen) breaks from it. He said: If the palm dries out and all the fingers of the hand become paralyzed, then in it is two-thirds of the blood money of the hand. And if some of the fingers become paralyzed and some remain, then in each paralyzed finger is two-thirds of its blood money. He said: And the same ruling applies to the leg and the foot when the fingers of the foot become paralyzed.

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding the finger, ten dinars of blood money (diyah) if it is severed from its root or paralyzed. He said: And I asked him about the fingers, are they equal in blood money? He said: Yes. He said: And I asked him about the teeth, he said: Their blood money is equal. The meaning in this report is that we interpret it as: if what paralyzes it is done to the finger, it becomes entitled to two-thirds of its blood money, and if it is severed after that, there is one-third of the blood money in it, so it becomes a complete blood money for it, and that does not contradict the detail contained in the first report.

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: I asked him about the fingers: Are they equal in the blood money (diyah)? He said: Yes.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ibn Mahbub from Abdullah ibn Sinan from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The fingers of the two hands and the two feet are equal in blood money (diyah); for each finger, ten camels, and for the nail, five dinars.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Al-Hasan from Zur'ah from Sama'ah said: I asked him about the fingers, is there a preference for some of them over others regarding the blood money? He said: They are equal in the blood money.

From him, from al-Qasim, from Ali, from Abu Basir, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Regarding the fingers, for each finger is ten camels. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: These narrations are agreed upon, not differing. And Zarif ibn Nasih has narrated in his narration that the fingers are equal except for the thumb, for it has a separate blood money, and it is that it has one-third of the hand's blood money, and two-thirds of the blood money between the four fingers equally. And we have cited his narration in its form in our book, Al-Kabir. And it is permissible to reconcile these narrations with this distinction. As for what the narration of Abu Basir and Abdillah ibn Sinan included, that in each finger is ten camels, it is permissible that it be from the speech of the narrator, namely that when he heard that the fingers are equal in blood money, he interpreted it as ten camels for each finger, and he did not know that this ruling is specific to the four fingers. And we said this so that the action may be based on all the narrations without discarding any of them.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Ibn Abi 'Umayr from Hammad from Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan (Al-Halabi) from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: When a man is struck on his head and his tongue becomes heavy, the letters of the alphabet are presented to him; whatever he fails to articulate clearly from the speech, the blood money is due as qisas (compensation) for that.

From him, from Al-Hasan, from Zur'ah, from Sama'ah The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) ruled in the case of a man who struck a slave boy on the head, causing part of his tongue to be lost; he could articulate some speech but not all. He was asked to recite the 'Mujam' (a reference text, likely for pronunciation/diction), so the Commander of the Faithful divided the blood money upon him: whatever he could articulate clearly, he was exempted from paying for it, and whatever he could not articulate clearly, he was held liable for it.

From him, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: So when a man is struck on the head and his tongue becomes heavy (stiff), the letters of the alphabet are presented to him. Whatever he fails to articulate clearly from them, he pays compensation for that portion of the alphabet. The original blood money is established upon the entire alphabet, then he is given [deducted] according to what he failed to articulate from them, and they are thirty-six letters.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Sulayman ibn Khalid from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) in a man who struck another man on the head, causing his tongue to become heavy (impaired), [the ruling is] that all the letters of the alphabet are presented to him, then he is given his blood money according to the letter he failed to articulate.

Al-Nawfali, from al-Sakawni, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) was brought a man who had been struck, so part of his speech was lost and part remained. He set his blood-money (diyah) according to the letters of the alphabet (al-mu'jam). Then he said: 'Speak the alphabet; whatever is missing from his speech is calculated accordingly.' The alphabet consists of twenty-eight letters, so he made twenty-eight parts; whatever is missing from that is calculated accordingly.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya and al-Saffar, both, from al-Ubaydi, from Uthman ibn Isa, from Sama'ah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I said to him: A man struck a slave boy with a blow and severed part of his tongue, so he articulated some letters but not others. He said: He reads the 'Mujam' (the numerical table of letters); whatever he articulated is deducted from the blood money, and whatever he did not articulate is charged to the blood money. I said: How is it? He said: According to the calculation of the Mujam: Alif has a diyah of one, Ba of two, Jim of three, Dal of four, Ha of five, Waw of six, Zay of seven, Ha of eight, Ta of nine, Ya of ten, Kaf of twenty, Lam of thirty, Mim of forty, Nun of fifty, Sin of sixty, Ain of seventy, Fa of eighty, Sad of ninety, Qaf of one hundred, Ra of two hundred, Shin of three hundred, Ta of four hundred, and every letter added after this from the letters of Abatath has a value of one hundred dirhams. Whatever this report contains regarding the detailed diyah of the letters, it is permissible that it is from the speech of some of the narrators, in that they heard him say 'that is distributed among the letters of the Mujam,' so they assumed it was according to the familiar numerical calculation of those letters, and the intention was not that. Rather, the meaning was that it is divided among all the letters in equal parts, each letter being a portion of the total, as al-Sikuni detailed in his narration and others. And if the matter were according to what this narration contains, the letters would not complete the full diyah, because that amount does not reach the complete diyah if calculated in dirhams, and if calculated in dinars, the diyah would double, and all of that is invalid. Therefore, it is appropriate that practice follows the previously mentioned reports, God willing.

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from al-Hasan ibn Musa, from Muhammad ibn al-Subbakh, from some of our companions, who said: Al-Rabi' came to Abu Ja'far al-Mansur while he was caliphal and performing tawaf. He said: 'O Commander of the Faithful, so-and-so, your mawla, died yesterday, and so-and-so cut off his head after his death.' He said: 'He became furious and angry.' He said to Ibn Shubrumah, Ibn Abi Layla, and a number of judges and jurists: 'What do you say about this?' Each one said: 'We have nothing regarding this.' He said: 'So he kept repeating the question, saying: 'Should I kill him or not?' They said: 'We have nothing regarding this, but a man has just arrived. If anyone has an answer, it is with him, and he is Ja'far ibn Muhammad, and he has entered al-Mas'a.' He said to al-Rabi': 'Go to him and tell him: 'If we did not know of your preoccupation with what you are in, we would have asked you to come to us, but answer us regarding such and such.' Al-Rabi' came to him while he was on al-Marwah and conveyed the message to him. Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'You see the preoccupation I am in, and the jurists and scholars are with you, so ask them.' He said to him: 'I have asked them, and they had nothing regarding it.' He sent him back to him and said: 'I ask you for what you did not answer us with, for the people have nothing regarding this.' Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to him: 'Until I finish what I am in.' When he finished, he sat on the side of al-Masjid al-Haram and said to al-Rabi': 'Go and tell him: 'Upon him is one hundred dinars.' He said: 'And he conveyed that to him, and they said to him: 'Ask him how it became upon him one hundred dinars.' Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'In the nutfah (drop), twenty dinars; in the 'alaqah (clot), twenty; in the mudghah (chewed lump), twenty dinars; in the 'adam (bones), twenty dinars; and in the lahm (flesh), twenty dinars.' Then We developed him into another creation, and this is he who is dead, in the same status as before the soul was blown into him in his mother's womb as a fetus.' He said: 'So he returned to them and informed them of the answer, and they were pleased with that.' He said: 'And they said: 'Return to him and ask him: 'To whom are the dinars? Are they for his heirs or not?' Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'His heirs have nothing in it. This is someth

Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr, from Jamil, from more than one of our companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: severing the head of the dead is more severe than severing the head of the living.

And Ibn Abi 'Umayr and Safwan narrated from their men, he said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'God forbid that a good opinion be not held of the believer; and your breaking of his bones, whether alive or dead, is the same.'

Muhammad ibn Abi Umair narrated from Mis'm Kirdin who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who broke the bone of a dead body. He said: 'Its sanctity as a dead body is greater than its sanctity while alive, so there is no contradiction between these narrations and the first narration, because nothing in them indicates that its sanctity as a dead body is like its sanctity while alive regarding the obligation of the complete blood-money upon the one who severs its head. It is permissible that what is meant by that is the liability for punishment regarding that, just as he deserves it if he did it to a living one.'

And as for what Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub narrated from Ya'qub ibn Yazid from Yahya ibn al-Mubarik from Abdullah ibn Jabala from Abu Jamilyah and Isḥaq ibn 'Ammar from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked: 'If a dead person's head is cut off, what is due?' He said: 'The blood money (diyah) is due.' I asked: 'Then who takes its blood money?' He said: 'The Imam.' This is for Allah. And if his right hand or something from his limbs is cut off, the arsh (compensation) is for the Imam.'

From him, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Abi Najran and Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Abd Allah ibn Maskan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding a man who cut off the head of a dead body, he said: The blood money is due, because its sanctity when dead is like its sanctity when alive.

Al-Husayn ibn Said from Ibn Sinan, from one who informed him, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about a man who cut off the head of a dead man. He said: Upon him is the blood money (diyah), for his sanctity when dead is like his sanctity when alive.

Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Muhammad ibn Hafsh from al-Husayn ibn Khalid, and it was narrated by Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from Muhammad ibn Ashyam from al-Husayn ibn Khalid, who said: I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) and said, 'We have narrated a hadith from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) that I would like to hear from you.' He said, 'What is it?' I said, 'It reached me that he said regarding a man who cut off the head of a dead man: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) said, 'Indeed, Allah has made sacred the body of a deceased Muslim what He made sacred from him while alive. So whoever does to the dead man what would constitute violation of the life of the living, upon him is the blood money.' He said, 'Abu Abdillah was truthful. Thus the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) said.' I said, 'If one cuts off the head of a dead man, or splits his belly, or does to him an act that constitutes violation of the life of the living, is the penalty upon him the full blood money of a soul?' He said, 'No.' Then he pointed to me with his little finger and said, 'This one has no blood money.' I said, 'Yes.' He said, 'Do you consider it the blood money of a soul?' I said, 'No.' He said, 'You are truthful.' I said to him, 'What is the blood money of this if his head is cut off while he is dead?' He said, 'Its blood money is the blood money of the fetus in its mother's womb before the soul is breathed into it, and that is one hundred dinars.' I remained silent and was pleased with his answer. He said, 'Why do you not exhaust your inquiry?' I said, 'I do not have more to ask than what you have answered, unless there is something I do not know.' He said, 'The blood money of the fetus, when its mother is struck and it falls from her womb before the soul is breathed into it, is one hundred dinars, and it belongs to its heirs. And indeed, the blood money of this one (the dead man whose head is cut off) if his head is cut off or his belly split, is not for his heirs; rather, it is for him alone, distinct from the heirs.' I said, 'What is the difference between the two?' He said, 'The fetus is anticipated, and its benefit is hoped for, whereas this one has passed and his benefit has gone. So when he is mutilated after his death, his blood money becomes due to him specifically because of that mutilation, not for others. It

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Ibn Abi 'Umayr from Hafs ibn Suqah from Ibn Bukayr from Zurarah who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'What is that thing in which there is no vow?' He said: 'Whatever you have benefit in for religion or worldliness, there is no sin upon you if you do not fulfill it.'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Hammad ibn Isa from Ali ibn Abi Hamzah said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who made it incumbent upon himself to walk to the House of Allah (the Sacred Kaaba), and all his slaves were free; when he went out with his aunt to Mecca, he did not hire a mount for her nor did he accompany her. He said: 'It is not sufficient; he must hire a mount for her and go out with her.'

Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from more than one of our companions, from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding a man who has a concubine, and his wife annoys him and is jealous of her, so he says to her, 'She is a charity (gift) upon you.' He (the Imam) said: If he dedicated her to Allah and mentioned Allah's name, he is not permitted to have sexual relations with her. And if he did not mention Allah's name, she remains his concubine, and he does with her as he pleases. The correct interpretation of this report is that we construe it in one of two ways: First, that it is obligatory for him to fulfill it if he made it a valid vow (nadhr), and there is no religious or worldly benefit for him in breaking it; and it is permissible for him to break it only if he derives benefit and advantage from it, as we stated regarding oaths. The second way is that we construe it as recommended (mustahabb).

And as for what Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Abu Abdillah al-Razi, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from al-Hasan ibn Ali, from Abu al-Hassan (peace be upon him), who said: I said to him: 'I have a female slave who has no place with me (i.e., I do not desire her), and she is worth the price, except that I had sworn an oath regarding her, saying: 'It is upon me to God that I will never sell her.' And I have a need for her price to reduce expenses.' He said: 'It is for you according to your word.' We mentioned this report in the Chapter on Categories of Oaths in the narration of al-Saffar because he narrated it with the wording of 'oath' (yamin), and we repeated it here because it contains the wording of 'vow' (nadhru). The meaning within it is the meaning we mentioned: that it is to be understood either as recommended (istihbab) or as removing suitability in selling her both religiously and mundanely, and the two matters stand on equal footing, as we said there.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from 'Uthman ibn 'Isa from Sama'ah who said: I asked him about a man who placed upon himself oaths that he would walk to the Kaaba, or give charity, or a vow, or a sacrifice, if he spoke to his father or his mother or his brother or a relative, or severed a kinship tie, or committed a sin, or an act that is not suitable for him to do. He said: There is no oath in the disobedience of Allah. Rather, the obligatory oath is that which befits its owner to fulfill, which he has made for Allah in gratitude, if He healed him from his illness, or saved him from something he fears, or returned his wealth to him, or brought him back from his journey. For Allah, upon him, such and such is gratitude. This is obligatory upon its owner, and it befits him to fulfill it.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Jabbar, from Abu Jamilyah, from Amr ibn Hurayth, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him, said: I asked him about a man who said: If he spoke to a relative of his, then upon him is the journey to the House of God, and all that he owns in the way of God, and he is free from the religion of Muhammad (peace be upon him and his family). He said: He should fast for three days, and give charity to ten poor people. The approach in this narration is to interpret it as recommended (mustahabb), or that he makes that as gratitude to God by opposing His disobedience, rather than it being an expiation (kaffarah), in contrast to a vow, and this is confirmed.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Ibn Abi 'Umayr from Hammad from Al-Halabi from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) that he said: Regarding a man who swore an oath not to speak to a relative of his, he said: It is not binding, so let him speak to the one he swore upon. And he said: Every oath not intended for the face of Allah is not binding, in divorce or otherwise.

From him, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Ali ibn Abi Hamzah, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who made it upon himself to walk to the Sacred House of God, and for every slave he owned to be free if he went out with his aunt to Mecca, and he did not hire a mount for her nor did he accompany her. He said: 'It is not valid; he should hire a mount for her and he should go out with her.'

When God created the Intellect, He made it speak. Then He said to it: 'Come forward!' and it came forward. Then He said to it: 'Turn back!' and it turned back. Then He said: 'By My Might and My Majesty! I have not created any creature more beloved to Me than you, nor have I perfected you except in those whom I love. Indeed, it is you whom I command, and you whom I forbid, and you whom I punish, and you whom I reward.'

Ali ibn Muhammad, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Amr ibn Uthman, from Mufaddal ibn Salih, from Sa'd ibn Tarif, from al-Asbagh ibn Nubata, from Ali (peace be upon him), who said: Jibraeel descended upon Adam (peace be upon him) and said: 'O Adam! I have been commanded to give you a choice of one from three, so choose it and leave the other two.' Adam said to him: 'O Jibraeel! And what are the three?' He said: 'The intellect, modesty, and religion.' Adam said: 'I have chosen the intellect.' So Jibraeel said to modesty and religion: 'Depart and leave him.' But they said: 'O Jibraeel! We have been commanded to remain with the intellect wherever it may be.' He said: 'Then that is your affair,' and he ascended.

I said to him: What is the intellect ('aql)? He said: That by which the All-beneficent is worshipped and the Gardens are attained. He (the narrator) said: I said: Then that which was in Muawiya? So he said: That is the heinous cunning, that is the devilry — and it resembles the intellect but is not the intellect.
I heard al-Ridha (peace be upon him) saying: 'A friend of every person is his intellect, and his enemy is his ignorance.'

I said to Abu Al-Hassan (peace be upon him): 'Indeed among us there is a group of people who have love [for the Ahlul Bayt], but they do not have that firm resolve — they profess this declaration [of al-Wilayah].' So he (peace be upon him) said: 'Those are not among those whom Allah has admonished. Rather Allah said: "Therefore take a lesson, O you who have vision." [Quran 59:2]

Ahmad ibn Idris, from Muhammad ibn Hassan, from Abu Muhammad al-Razi, from Sayf ibn Amira, from Ishaq ibn Ammar who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'Whoever is an intellectual (rational person), there will be religion for him; and whoever has religion will enter Paradise.'

A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Yaqtin, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Abu al-Jarud, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: Indeed, God will hold the servants strictly accountable in the Reckoning on the Day of Resurrection according to the measure of the intellect He gave them in this world.

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about so-and-so — his worship, his religiosity, and his virtue. So he said: 'How is his intellect?' I said: 'I do not know.' So he said: 'Indeed, the reward is according to the measure of the intellect.' Indeed, a man from the Children of Israel was worshipping God on an island from the islands of the sea — green, fresh, abundant in trees, and with flowing water. And indeed an angel from the angels passed by him and said: O my Lord! Show me the reward of this servant of Yours. So God the Exalted showed him that, and the angel considered it little. So God the Exalted revealed to him to accompany him. So the angel came to him in the form of a human being and said to him: Who are you? He said: I am a worshipping man; news of your place and your worship in this location has reached me, so I came to you to worship God with you. He was with him that day. When morning came, the angel said to him: Your place is truly scenic and is suitable for nothing but worship. So the worshipper said to him: There is indeed a defect in this place of ours. He said: What is it? He said: There is no animal for our Lord. If He had a donkey, we would graze it in this spot, for this pasture is being wasted. That angel said to him: And does your Lord not have a donkey? He said: If He had a donkey, such pasture as this would not be wasted. So God revealed to the angel: I reward him only according to the measure of his intellect.

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from al-Nawfali, from al-Sakuni, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'When the news of a man's good state reaches you, then look at the goodness of his intellect, for truly he will be recompensed according to his intellect.'

Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ibn Mahbub from Abdullah ibn Sinan who said: I mentioned to Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) a man afflicted with obsessive doubts regarding wudu and salat, and I said, 'He is an intelligent man.' So Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) said: 'And what intellect does he have, while he is obeying Shaytan?' So I said to him, 'And how is he obeying Shaytan?' So he said: 'Ask him about this that comes to him — from which thing is it? For he will tell you: it is from the acts of Shaytan.'

The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said: God has not distributed among His servants anything more superior than the intellect. Thus, the sleep of the intelligent person is superior to the vigil of the ignorant, and the staying of the intelligent person is superior to the going out of the ignorant; and God never sent a Prophet or a Messenger until He had perfected the intellect for him, and his intellect was superior to the entirety of his community's intellects. And whatever the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) conceals within himself is superior to the striving of the strivers; and a servant does not fulfill the obligations of God until he comprehends them with intellect; and all the worshippers would not reach, in the merit of their worship, what the intelligent person reaches. And the people of intellect, they are those possessing understanding of whom God the Exalted said: 'And none will take heed except those possessing understanding.'

Ali ibn Muhammad, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, raising it (marfu'), said: The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) said: The intellect is a concealing veil, and virtue is a manifest beauty; therefore conceal the defects of your character with your virtue, and fight your vain desires with your intellect — cordiality will become submissive to you and love will manifest for you.

I was in the presence of Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), and with him was a group of his followers, and the mention of intellect and ignorance came up. So Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'Recognise the intellect and its army, and the ignorance and its army, and you will be rightly guided.' Sama'a said: 'So I said: May I be sacrificed for you! We do not recognise anything except what you have taught us.' So Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'Indeed, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, created the intellect, and it was the first creation from among the spiritual beings, from the right side of the Throne, from His Light. So He said to it: "Turn away!" So it turned away. Then He said to it: "Come forward!" So it came forward. So Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: "I have created you as a magnificent creation, and I have honoured you above all of My creation."' He said: Then He created ignorance from the bitter, dark ocean. So He said to it: "Turn away!" So it turned away. Then He said to it: "Come forward!" But it did not come forward. So He said to it: "You have been arrogant." So He cursed it. Then He made seventy-five armies for the intellect. So when ignorance saw what Allah had honoured the intellect with and what He had granted it, it harboured enmity towards it. So ignorance said: "O Lord! This is a creation like me. You created it and honoured it and strengthened it, and I am its opposite, and I have no power against it. So grant me an army like what You granted it." So He said: "Yes, but if you disobey after this, I shall expel you and your army from My mercy." It said: "I am satisfied." Then He granted it seventy-five armies. So from what He gave the intellect from among the seventy-five soldiers: Goodness — and it is the minister of the intellect — and He made its opposite evil — and it is the minister of ignorance. Faith and its opposite is disbelief. Affirmation and its opposite is denial. Hope and its opposite is despair. Justice and its opposite is injustice. Contentment and its opposite is displeasure. Gratitude and its opposite is ingratitude. Aspiration and its opposite is hopelessness. Reliance [on God] and its opposite is greed. Compassion and its opposite is cruelty. Mercy and its opposite is anger. Knowledge and its opposite is ignorance. Understanding and its opposite is foolishness. Chastity and its opposite is shamelessness. Ascetic

A group of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Faddal, from some of our companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) never spoke to the servants with the full depth of his intellect at all. And he said: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said: Indeed we, the community of Prophets, have been commanded to speak to people according to the level of their intellects.

Ali ibn Muhammad, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from al-Nawfali, from al-Sakuni, from Ja'far, from his father (peace be upon him) who said: The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) said: 'Verily, the hearts of the ignorant are agitated by greed, held hostage by vain desires, and ensnared by deceptions.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad al-Ash'ari, from Ubaydullah al-Dihqan, from Durust, from Ibrahim ibn Abd al-Hamid, who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'The most perfect of the people in intellect is the best of them in morals.'

Ali, from his father, from Abu Hashim al-Ja'fari who said: We were in the presence of al-Ridha (peace be upon him) and we were discussing the intellect and good manners. So he said: 'O Abu Hashim! The intellect is a gift from God, and good manners is an effort and burden. So whoever strives to develop good manners will have ability over it; but whoever pretends to have intellect will only increase in ignorance by doing so.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Yahya ibn al-Mubarak, from Abdullah ibn Jabala, from Is'haq ibn Ammar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I said to him, 'May I be sacrificed for you! I have a neighbour who is frequent in salat, frequent in charity, and frequent in hajj — there is nothing wrong with him.' So he said, 'O Is'haq, how is his intellect?' I said to him, 'May I be sacrificed for you — he has no intellect.' So he said, '(His deeds) will not be elevated for him because of that.'

Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Sayyari, from Abu Ya'qub al-Baghdadi, who said: Ibn al-Sikkit said to Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him): 'Why did God send Moses son of Imran (peace be upon him) with the staff, the white hand, and means pertaining to magic; and sent Jesus with means pertaining to medicine; and sent Muhammad (peace be upon him and his family) and upon all the prophets with speech and eloquent discourse?' So Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) said: 'When God sent Moses (peace be upon him), magic was predominant among the people of his era. So he came to them from God with that which was beyond their power to produce anything like it, and by which he invalidated their magic and established the proof against them.' And God sent Jesus (peace be upon him) at a time when chronic diseases had appeared and the people were in need of medicine. So he came to them from God with that which they had nothing comparable to — with which he revived the dead for them, cured those born blind and the lepers by God's permission, and established the proof against them. And God sent Muhammad (peace be upon him and his family) at a time when eloquent discourse and speech were predominant among the people of his era — and I believe he said: 'and poetry' — so he came to them from God, from His admonitions and His wisdom, with what invalidated their speech and established the proof against them. He said: Then Ibn al-Sikkit said, 'By God, I have never seen anyone like you! So what is the proof upon mankind today?' He said: Then he (peace be upon him) said: 'The intellect — by which the one who speaks truthfully on behalf of God is known and thus believed, and the one who lies on behalf of God is known and thus disbelieved.' He said: Then Ibn al-Sikkit said, 'This, by God, is the answer!'

Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad, from al-Washa', from al-Muthanna al-Hannat, from Qutayba al-A'sha, from Ibn Abi Ya'fur, from a freed slave of the Banu Shayban clan, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: When our Qa'im rises, God will place His hand upon the heads of the servants, so He gathers their intellects through it, and their understanding becomes complete through him.

Ali ibn Muhammad, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Muhammad ibn Sulayman, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Proof of God upon the servants is the Prophet, and the Proof between the servants and God is the intellect.

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: The pillar of man is the intellect, and from the intellect come insightfulness, understanding, memorization, and knowledge; and through the intellect he becomes complete — it is his guide, his insight, and the key to his affairs. So when the support of his intellect is from the light, he would be a scholar, a memorizer, oft-remembering of God, discerning, and understanding. Thus he would know how, and why, and where; and he would recognize who counseled him sincerely and who deceived him. So when he recognizes that, he recognizes its course, its connections and its disconnections, and he dedicates the oneness of God sincerely and the acknowledgement of obedience. So when he does that, he would be a recoverer of what was missed and would anticipate what is coming; he knows what he is in, and for what reason he is here, and from where it comes to him, and toward what he is heading — and all of that is from the support of the intellect.
Ali ibn Muhammad, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ismail ibn Mihran, from some of his men, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The intellect is the guide of the believer.
The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'O Ali! There is no poverty more intense than ignorance, and there is no wealth more assisting than the intellect.'

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ibn Abi Najran, from al-Ala ibn Razin, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said: When God created the intellect, He said to it: 'Come forward!' So it came forward. Then He said to it: 'Turn back!' So it turned back. Then He said: 'By My Might and My Majesty! I have not created a creation better than you. To you I command, and to you I forbid, and to you I give reward, and to you I give punishment.'

A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Haytham ibn Abi Masruq al-Nahdi, from al-Husayn ibn Khalid, from Ishaq ibn Ammar who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'A man — I come to him and speak to him with some of my speech, and he understands all of it; and among them is one whom I come to and speak to him with the full speech, and he receives all of my speech completely, then returns it back to me just as I had spoken to him; and among them is one whom I come to and speak to him, and he says, "Repeat it to me".' So he said: 'O Ishaq! And do you not know why this is so?' I said: 'No.' He said: 'The one to whom you speak with part of your speech and he understands all of it — that is one whose seed was kneaded with his intellect. As for the one to whom you speak and he receives your speech completely then answers you based on your speech — that is the one in whom his intellect was superimposed in the womb of his mother. And as for the one to whom you speak with the speech and he says, "Repeat it to me" — that is the one in whom his intellect was superimposed after he had grown old, so he says to you, "Repeat it to me".'

A number of our companions narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from someone who raised it, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'Whenever you see a man abundant in salat and abundant in fasting, do not boast of him until you look at how (good) his intellect is.'

Some of our companions, raising it (the chain), from Mufaddal ibn Umar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: O Mufaddal! He will not succeed who has no intellect, and he has no intellect who does not know. Soon he who understands will be distinguished, and he who is clement will be victorious. Knowledge is a shield, truthfulness is honour, ignorance is disgrace, understanding is glory, generosity is success, and good morals are a cause of affection. The knowledgeable one of his time will not be assailed by confusions. Prudence is to expect the worst of conjectures. Between a person and wisdom, a scholar is a blessing; and the ignorant is wretched between the two. God is the protector of the one who truly knows Him, and the enemy of the one who pretends to know Him. The wise one is forgiving and the ignorant one is treacherous. If you wish to be honoured, be gentle; and if you wish to be humiliated, be harsh. He whose origin is noble has a soft heart, and he whose nature is harsh has a hard liver. He who is excessive will be entangled, and he who fears the consequences will refrain from plunging recklessly into what he does not know. He who rushes into a matter without knowledge will mutilate his own nose (pride). He who does not know will not understand, he who does not understand will not be safe, he who is not safe will not be honoured, he who is not honoured will be devoured, he who is devoured is most blameworthy, and he who is such is more deserving of regret.

The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) said: Whoever has firmly established in him a characteristic from the characteristics of goodness, I shall be tolerant of him on account of it and forgive the absence of whatever else besides it. But I shall not forgive the absence of intellect nor of religion. Because the separation from religion is the separation from security, and there is no enjoyment of life alongside fear; and the loss of intellect is the loss of life, and such a person can only be compared to the dead.

Ali ibn Ibrahim ibn Hashim, from Musa ibn Ibrahim al-Muharabi, from al-Hasan ibn Musa, from Musa ibn Abdullah, from Maymun ibn Ali, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) said: 'A person's self-admiration is an indication of the weakness of his intellect.'

Abu Abdillah al-'Asimi, from Ali ibn al-Hasan, from Ali ibn Asbat, from al-Hasan ibn al-Jahm, from Abu al-Hasan al-Ridha (peace be upon him), who said: Our companions were mentioned in his presence, and the intellect was (also) mentioned. So he (peace be upon him) said: 'No regard is given to the people of the religion from those who have no intellect.' I said: 'May I be your ransom! Indeed among those who profess this matter (al-Wilayah), there is a group who are not found faulty in our view, yet they do not possess those intellects.' So he said: 'These are not among those whom God addressed. Indeed, God created the intellect and said to it: Come forward! So it came forward. And said to it: Turn back! So it turned back. Then He said: By My might and My majesty! I have not created anything better than you, nor more beloved to Me than you. Through you I take (hold accountable), and through you I give (reward).'

Ali ibn Muhammad, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from his father, from some of our companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: 'There is nothing between faith and disbelief except a deficiency of intellect.' It was asked: 'And how is that so, O son of the Messenger of God?' He said: 'Indeed, the servant directs his desire toward a created being, whereas if he had made his intention sincere for God, He would have given him what he desires in a time quicker than that.'

A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ubaydullah al-Dihqan, from Ahmad ibn Umar al-Halabi, from Yahya ibn Imran, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) used to say: 'Through the intellect, the profundity of wisdom is extracted; and through wisdom, the profundity of the intellect is extracted; and through excellence in governance, righteous conduct comes about.' He said: And he used to say: 'Reflection is the life of the discerning heart, just as the wayfarer walks in darkness with light, through excellence in extrication and the minimizing of hesitation.'

A number of our companions, from Abdullah al-Bazzaz, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Hammad, from al-Hasan ibn Ammar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), in a lengthy hadith: Indeed, the first of all matters, its beginning, its strength, and its flourishing — without which nothing is of benefit — is the intellect, which God made an adornment for His creation and a light for them. So it is by the intellect that the servants recognized their Creator; that they are created beings, that He is the Regulator over them and they are the regulated ones, that He is the Eternal and they are the perishable. They reasoned by their intellects upon what they saw of His creation: His heavens and His earth, His sun and His moon, His night and His day — and that for Him and for them there is a Creator and a Regulator who has never ceased and will never cease. And they recognized by it the good from the ugly, that darkness lies in ignorance and that light lies in knowledge. So this is what the intellect indicated to them. It was said to him: 'Can the servants then suffice themselves with the intellect alone, without anything else?' He said: 'The rational person, by the guidance of his intellect — which God made his straightener, his adornment, and his guidance — knows that God is the Truth and that He is his Lord. And he knows that for his Creator there is that which He loves and that which He dislikes, that there is obedience to Him and disobedience. Yet he does not find that his intellect alone can guide him to the specifics of all that. He knows that he cannot reach God except through knowledge and its seeking, and that he will not benefit from his intellect if he does not attain that through his knowledge. Thus it is obligatory upon the rational person to seek knowledge and the discipline without which there is no foundation.'

Ali ibn Muhammad, from some of his companions, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from Humran and Safwan ibn Mihran al-Jammal — they both said: We heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: 'There is no wealth more enriching than the intellect, nor a poverty more abasing than stupidity, nor any backing in a matter greater than consultation in it.'
The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'Seeking knowledge is an obligation upon every Muslim. Indeed, Allah loves the seekers of knowledge.'
Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Muhammad ibn Abdullah, from Isa ibn Abdullah al-Umari, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: Seeking knowledge is an obligation.

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yunus ibn Abd al-Rahman, from some of his companions who said: Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) was asked: 'Do the people have the leeway to abandon asking about what they are in need of?' So he said: 'No.'

Ali ibn Muhammad and others, from Sahl ibn Ziyad and Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, altogether from Ibn Mahbub, from Hisham ibn Salim, from Abu Hamza, from Abu Is'haq al-Sabi'i, from one who narrated to him, who said: I heard the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) saying: 'O people! Know that the perfection of the religion is seeking knowledge and acting upon it. Indeed, seeking knowledge is more obligatory upon you than seeking wealth. Wealth is apportioned and guaranteed for you; a Just One has apportioned it among you and guaranteed it and will fulfill it for you. But knowledge is treasured with its rightful possessors, and you have been commanded to seek it from them — so seek it.'

Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) said: The Messenger of Allah (blessings of Allah be upon him and his family) said: 'Seeking knowledge is an obligation.' And in another hadith, he said: Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) said: The Messenger of Allah (blessings of Allah be upon him and his family) said: 'Seeking knowledge is an obligation upon every Muslim. Indeed, Allah loves the seekers of knowledge.'

I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: 'Acquire deep understanding in the religion, for indeed whoever among you does not acquire deep understanding in the religion is a Bedouin.' Indeed, Allah says in His Book: 'that they may acquire deep understanding in religion, and that they may warn their people when they return to them, so that they may be cautious.'

Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from Al-Qasim ibn al-Rabi', from Mufaddal ibn Umar who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: It is upon you to acquire deep understanding (tafaqquh) in the religion of God, and do not become like Bedouins. For indeed, whoever does not acquire deep understanding in the religion of God — God will not look at him on the Day of Resurrection, and will not purify any deed of his.
I would even wish that the heads of my companions were struck with whips until they acquire religious understanding.

Ali ibn Muhammad, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from one who reported it, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: A man said to him, 'May I be your ransom! A man who has recognized this matter (al-Wilayah) has confined himself to his house and does not introduce himself to anyone among his brethren.' He (the narrator) said: He (the Imam) then replied, 'How will this one gain deep understanding in his religion?'

Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Muhammad ibn Ismail ibn Bazi', from Mansur ibn Hazim, from Talha ibn Zayd, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I read in the Book of Ali (peace be upon him): Indeed, God did not take a covenant upon the ignorant ones to seek knowledge until He first took a covenant upon the scholars to impart knowledge to the ignorant ones — because knowledge existed before ignorance.

A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Barqi, from his father, from Abdullah ibn al-Mughira and Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Talha ibn Zayd, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) regarding this verse: 'And do not turn your cheek away from people [in contempt]' He said: 'Let the people be equal with you in knowledge.'

And by this chain, from his father, from Ahmad ibn al-Nadr, from Amr ibn Shimr, from Jabir, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: The zakat of knowledge is that you teach it to the servants of God.

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn Isa ibn Ubayd, from Yunus ibn Abd al-Rahman, from the one who mentioned it, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: 'Isa ibn Maryam (peace be upon him) arose to address the Children of Israel, and he said: "O Children of Israel! Do not speak words of wisdom to the ignorant, for you would be doing injustice to those words; and do not withhold wisdom from those who deserve it, for you would be doing injustice to them."'

Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad and Abdullah, two sons of Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Sayf ibn Amira, from Mufaddal ibn Yazid who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to me: 'I forbid you from two characteristics in which lies the destruction of men. I forbid you from worshipping God through falsehood and from issuing fatwas to people about what you do not know.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn Isa ibn Ubayd, from Yunus ibn Abd al-Rahman, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to me: Beware of two traits, for in these two were destroyed those who were destroyed: beware of issuing fatwas to the people based on your own opinion, or following as religion that which you do not know.

Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from Ali ibn Ri'ab, from Abu Ubayda al-Hadhdha', from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: Whoever issues a fatwa to the people without knowledge and without guidance — the angels of mercy and the angels of punishment curse him, and the burden of those who acted upon his fatwa is attached to him.

A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from al-Hasan ibn Ali al-Washsha', from Aban al-Ahmar, from Ziyad ibn Abi Raja', from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said: What you know, say it; and what you do not know, say: God knows best. Indeed, a man snatches a verse from the Quran and falls because of it farther than the distance between the sky and the earth.

Muhammad ibn Ismail, from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Rabi'i ibn Abdallah, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: It is proper for the scholar, when asked about something he does not know, to say: God knows best. And it is not proper for one who is not a scholar to say that.

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Hariz ibn Abdullah, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: When the man from among you is asked about what he does not know, let him say, 'I don't know', and he should not say, 'God knows best', for that would cast a doubt in the heart of his companion. And when the questioned one says, 'I don't know', the questioner cannot accuse him.

Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn Asbat, from Ja'far ibn Sama'a, from more than one person, from Aban, from Zurara ibn A'yan who said: I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him): 'What is the right of Allah upon the servants?' He said: 'That they should say what they know, and refrain from speaking about what they do not know.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Yunus ibn Abd al-Rahman, from Abu Yaqub Is'haq ibn Abdillah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: 'Indeed, God has singled out His servants with two verses from His Book: that they should not speak until they know, and that they should not reject what they do not know. And He — Mighty and Majestic — said: [7:169] Was not a covenant taken from them in the Book that they would not say anything about God except the truth? And He said: [10:39] But they denied that of which they had no encompassing knowledge, and whose interpretation had not yet come to them.'

Ibn Shubrama said: 'I do not recall a hadith I heard from Ja'far ibn Muhammad (peace be upon him) except that it almost pierces my heart. He said: My father narrated to me, from my grandfather, from the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family).' Ibn Shubrama said: 'And I swear by God, his father did not lie about his grandfather, nor did his grandfather lie about the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family).' He said: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said: Whoever acts by analogies (qiyas) has been destroyed and has caused destruction, and whoever issues fatwas to the people without knowledge, while he does not know the abrogating verse from the abrogated, and the decisive from the allegorical, has been destroyed and has caused destruction.

A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from his father, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Talha ibn Zayd, who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: 'The one who acts without insight is like the traveller upon a road other than the right one — the speed of his travel increases him nothing but distance.'

Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Ibn Muskan, from Husayn al-Sayqal, who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: 'God does not accept a deed except with understanding, and there is no understanding except with a deed. So whoever has understanding, the understanding guides him toward the deed; and whoever does not act, has no understanding. Indeed! Faith — part of it is from another part.'

From him, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Faddal, from the one who reported it, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: Whoever acts without knowledge, what he corrupts will be more than what he corrects.

Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Umar ibn Udhaynahh, from Aban ibn Abi Ayyash, from Sulaym ibn Qays al-Hilali who said: I heard the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) narrating from the Prophet (may God's blessings be upon him and his family) that he said in a speech of his: The scholars are two (types of) men — a scholar who acts upon his knowledge, and this one is saved; and a scholar who neglects his knowledge, and this one is destroyed. The inhabitants of the Fire will surely be harmed by the stench of the scholar who neglected his knowledge. And the one with the most intense remorse and anguish among the inhabitants of the Fire will be a man who invited a servant toward God, and he answered him and accepted from him, and so he obeyed God, and God admitted him into Paradise — but admitted the inviter into the Fire because of his abandoning his knowledge, his following of personal desires, and prolonged worldly ambitions. As for following personal desires, it blocks one from the Truth; and prolonged worldly ambitions cause one to forget the Hereafter.

Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Isma'il ibn Jabir, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Knowledge is coupled to deed. So the one who knows, acts; and the one who acts, knows. And knowledge calls out to deed — so if it responds, well and good; otherwise, knowledge departs from him.

A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from Ali ibn Muhammad al-Qasani, from the one who mentioned it, from Abdullah ibn al-Qasim al-Ja'fari, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Indeed the scholar, when he does not act according to his knowledge, his admonition slides off hearts just as rain slides off smooth rock.

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from al-Minqari, from Ali ibn Hashim ibn al-Barid, from his father, who said: A man came to Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon him) and asked him about certain matters, and he answered. Then the man returned to ask about similar matters. So Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon him) said: It is written in the Injil (Gospel): 'Do not seek knowledge of what you do not know while you have not yet acted upon what you already know, for indeed knowledge, when not acted upon, does not increase its owner except in disbelief, and does not increase him from God except in remoteness.'

Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from al-Mufaddal ibn Umar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I said to him, 'By what is the rescued one recognised?' He said: 'The one whose deed corresponds to his word — for him the testimony is affirmed. And the one whose deed does not correspond to his word — that (faith) is merely entrusted (temporary).'

A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from his father, raising it (mursal), he said: The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) said in a speech of his which he delivered as a sermon upon the pulpit: O you people! When you know, then act according to what you have known so that you may be guided. Indeed, the scholar who acts contrary to his knowledge is like the confused ignorant one who has not awakened from his ignorance. Nay, I have indeed considered that the argument against him is greater, and the regret is more prolonged for this scholar who has stripped himself away from his knowledge, compared to this bewildered ignorant one who is confused in his own ignorance — and both of them are confused, perishing. Do not be suspicious lest you become doubtful, and do not doubt lest you fall into disbelief; do not grant yourselves concessions lest you become lax, and do not be lax with the Truth lest you incur loss. It is part of the Truth that you acquire religious understanding, and it is part of understanding that you not be deceived. Truly, the most sincere among you to himself is the most obedient to his Lord, and the most treacherous among you to himself is the most disobedient to his Lord. Whoever obeys God will be secure and receive glad tidings, and whoever disobeys God will be disappointed and will regret.

A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from his father, from someone he mentioned, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla, from his father who said: I heard Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) saying: 'When you hear knowledge, apply it, and let your hearts be expansive. For when knowledge becomes abundant in the heart of a man who cannot bear it, Satan gains power over him. So when Satan disputes with you, confront him with what you know; for the plot of Satan has always been weak.' So I said: 'And what is it that we should know?' He said: 'Dispute with him using whatever of the power of God, Mighty and Majestic, has become manifest to you.'

Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, and Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father, all from Hammad ibn Isa, from Umar ibn Udhaina, from Aban ibn Abi Ayyash, from Sulaym ibn Qays who said: I heard the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) saying: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'Two greedy ones are never satiated — a seeker of the world and a seeker of knowledge. So whoever confines himself from the world to what God has made permissible for him is saved, and whoever takes it through other than its permissible means is destroyed, unless he repents or retracts. And whoever takes knowledge from its rightful people and acts according to his knowledge is saved, and whoever seeks the world by it — then it is his share.'

Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad ibn Amir, from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad, from Al-Hasan ibn Ali al-Washsha', from Ahmad ibn A'idh, from Abu Khadijah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: Whoever seeks hadith for the benefit of this world, there will be no share for him in the Hereafter; and whoever seeks it for the goodness of the Hereafter, God will give him the goodness of this world and the Hereafter.

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad al-Asbahani, from al-Minqari, from Hafs ibn Ghiyath, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Whoever seeks hadith for the benefit of this world, there will be no share for him in the Hereafter.

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from al-Qasim ibn al-Minqari, from Hafs ibn Ghiyath, from Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) who said: 'Whenever you see the scholar in love with his worldly life, then suspect him regarding your religion, for every lover of a thing guards what he loves.' And he (blessings of Allah be upon him) said: 'Allah revealed to Dawud (peace be upon him): "Do not place between Me and yourself a scholar who is infatuated with the world, lest he block you from the path of My love — for they are bandits on the road to My servants who are devoted seekers. The least of what I shall do to them is that I will remove the sweetness of My intimate discourse from their hearts."'

Ali, from his father, from al-Nawfali, from al-Sakuni, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Messenger of God (may God bless him and his family) said: 'The jurists are the trustees of the Messengers, as long as they do not enter into worldly affairs.' It was said: 'O Messenger of God, what is their entering into worldly affairs?' He said: 'Following the ruling authority. So when they do that, beware of them regarding your religion.'

Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, from Hammad ibn 'Isa, from Rib'i ibn 'Abdillah, from one who narrated to him, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: Whoever seeks knowledge in order to boast before the scholars by it, or to dispute with the foolish by it, or to turn the faces of people toward him by it — let him take his seat in the Fire. Verily, leadership is not fitting except for its rightful people.

Ali ibn Ibrahim ibn Hashim, from his father, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from al-Minqari, from Hafs ibn Ghiyath, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: 'O Hafs! He would forgive seventy sins of the ignorant one before He forgives one sin of the scholar.'
Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'Isa ibn Maryam — may peace be upon our Prophet and his family and upon him — said: 'Woe to the evil scholars! How the Fire blazes upon them!'

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, and Muhammad ibn Ismail, from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, altogether from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Jameel ibn Darraj, who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: 'When the soul reaches here' — and he pointed with his hand to his throat — 'there would be no repentance for the scholar.' Then he recited: 'Indeed, repentance with God is only for those who do evil in ignorance.'

Muhammad b. Yahya, from Ahmad b. Muhammad b. Isa, from al-Husayn b. Saeed, from al-Nadr b. Suwayd, from Yahya al-Halabi, from Abu Saeed al-Mukari, from Abu Baseer — from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) regarding the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: 'So they shall be flung into it, they and the erring ones' [26:94] He (peace be upon him) said: 'They are a group who described justice with their tongues, then they opposed it by going to something else.'
The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) used to say: 'Rest your souls with the splendid wisdom, for indeed they grow weary just as bodies grow weary.'

Abu Basir said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) used to say: O seeker of knowledge! Knowledge is possessed of many virtues. Its head is humility, its eye is freedom from envy, its ear is understanding, its tongue is truthfulness, its memory is investigation, its heart is good intention, its intellect is the recognition of things and matters, its hand is mercy, its foot is visiting the scholars, its aspiration is safety, its wisdom is piety, its resting place is salvation, its guide is well-being, its mount is loyalty, its weapon is gentleness of speech, its sword is contentment, its bow is diplomatic tact, its army is dialogue with scholars, its wealth is proper conduct, its treasure is abstaining from sins, its provision is good deeds, its water is cordiality, its indicator is divine guidance, and its companion is love for the righteous.

Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from Hammad ibn Uthman, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'Excellent is the vizier of faith — knowledge; and excellent is the vizier of knowledge — forbearance; and excellent is the vizier of forbearance — gentleness; and excellent is the vizier of gentleness — patience.'

A man came to the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) and said: 'O Messenger of God, what is knowledge?' He said: 'Silence.' He said: 'Then what?' He said: 'Intent listening.' He said: 'Then what?' He said: 'Memorisation.' He said: 'Then what?' He said: 'Acting upon it.' He said: 'Then what, O Messenger of God?' He said: 'Propagating it.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim raised it (as marfu') to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: The seekers of knowledge are three — recognize them by their persons and their descriptions: a type who seeks it for ignorance and disputation, a type who seeks it for domination and deception, and a type who seeks it for understanding and intellect. The one seeking it for ignorance and disputation is harmful and argumentative, exposing himself to speech in the assemblies of men by discussing knowledge while claiming the attribute of forbearance; he has clothed himself in humility while stripping himself of piety. May God crush his nose and cut off his chest. The one seeking it for domination and deception is possessed of cunning and flattery — he dominates over those who resemble him, yet humbles himself before the wealthy beneath him. So he devours their worldly sweets while destroying his religion. May God blind his reputation and cut off his trace from the legacies of the scholars. The one seeking it for understanding and intellect is possessed of grief, sorrow, and sleepless vigils — he has wrapped his cloak and stands the night in its darkness; he works and fears, trembling, supplicating, compassionate, attentive to his affairs, knowing the people of his time, wary even of his most trusted brethren. So may God strengthen his foundations and grant him security on the Day of Resurrection. And it was narrated to me by Muhammad ibn Mahmud Abu Abdillah al-Qazwini, from a number of our companions, among them Ja'far ibn Muhammad al-Sayqal in Qazwin, from Ahmad ibn Isa al-Alawi, from Abbad ibn Suhayb al-Basri, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him).

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Talha ibn Zayd, who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: The reporters of the Book are many, but its due carers are few; and how many a seeker of advice from the hadith is yet treacherous toward the Book. The scholars are grieved by the neglect of due care, while the ignorant are grieved by the preservation of narrations. Thus one shepherd tends its life, and another shepherd tends its destruction. At that point the two shepherds diverge and the two groups part ways.

Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad al-Ash'ari, from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Jumhur, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Najran, from the one who mentioned it, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Whoever memorizes forty hadiths from our hadiths, God will resurrect him on the Day of Resurrection as a scholar and a jurist.

A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from his father, from whoever mentioned it, from Zayd al-Shahham, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) regarding the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: 'Then let the human being look at his food.' I said: 'What is his food?' He said: 'His knowledge which he is taking — from whom he is taking it.'

Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from 'Ali ibn al-Nu'man, from 'Abdullah ibn Muskan, from Dawud ibn Farqad, from Abu Sa'id al-Zuhri, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: Pausing at the doubtful matter is better than storming into destruction; and your refraining from narrating a hadith you have not fully verified is better than your narrating a hadith you have not mastered.

He presented to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) some of the sermons of his father; until when he reached a passage in it, he said to him: 'Stop, and be silent.' Then Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'There is no leeway for you regarding what comes upon you from what you do not know, except to refrain from it, to verify carefully, and to refer it back to the Imams of Guidance, until they guide you in it toward the right path, and they dispel from you the blindness in it, and they make the truth known to you in it.' God the Exalted said: 'So ask the People of the Reminder if you do not know' [16:43].

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from al-Minqari, from Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna who said: I heard Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) saying: 'I found the knowledge of all people in four things: the first is that you recognize your Lord; the second is that you recognize what He has done with you; the third is that you recognize what He intends from you; and the fourth is that you recognize what would remove you from your religion.'

I said to Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him), 'What is the right of God upon His creation?' So he said: 'That they say what they know, and that they refrain from what they do not know.' So when they do that, they have indeed fulfilled God's right.

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ibn Sinan, from Muhammad ibn Marwan al-Ijli, from Ali ibn Hanzala, who said: 'I heard Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) saying: 'Recognise the statuses of the people upon a measurement of their reporting from us (Our Ahadeeth)'.

Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) said in one of his sermons: 'O people! Know that he is not possessed of intellect who becomes agitated by false words spoken about him, nor is he possessed of wisdom who is pleased with the eulogies of the ignorant directed at him. The people are the offspring of what they excel in, and the worth of every person is what he excels in. Therefore, speak about knowledge — your worth will become manifest.'

Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad, from al-Washsha', from Aban ibn Uthman, from Abdullah ibn Sulayman, who said: I heard Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) speaking, while in his presence was a man from the people of al-Basra called Uthman the Blind, who was saying: 'Al-Hasan al-Basri alleges that those who conceal knowledge will harm the inhabitants of the Fire by the odor of their bellies.' So Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: 'Then the Believer of the people of Pharaoh has perished! Knowledge has not ceased to be concealed since God sent Noah (peace be upon him). So let al-Hasan go right and left — by God, knowledge will not be found except here.'

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) [about] the saying of God, Majestic is His laudation: 'Those who listen intently to the Word, then follow the best of it' [39:18]. He said: It is the man who hears the hadith, then narrates it just as he heard it — he neither adds to it nor reduces from it.

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'I hear a hadith from you, and sometimes I add to it and sometimes reduce from it.' He said: 'If you are intending to preserve its meanings, then there is no problem.'

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'I hear the speech from you and I want to narrate it exactly as I heard it from you, but it does not come (exactly).' He said: 'Do you do that deliberately?' I said: 'No.' So he said: 'Do you intend (to preserve) the meanings?' I said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Then there is no problem.'

And from him, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from al-Husayn ibn Said, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn Abi Hamza, from Abu Baseer, who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'The hadith I hear from you — can I narrate it as being from your father? Or if I hear it from your father, can I narrate it as being from you?' He said: 'It is the same, except that your narrating it as being from my father is more beloved to me.' And Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to Jamil: 'Whatever you hear from me, narrate it as being from my father.'

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): Groups of people come to me and want to hear your hadiths from me, and I become wearied and am not able (to continue). He said: Then read to them one hadith from its beginning, one hadith from its middle, and one hadith from its end.

From him, by his chain, from Ahmad ibn Umar al-Hallal who said: I said to Abu al-Hasan al-Rida (peace be upon him): 'A man from our companions gives me a book but does not say to me, "Narrate it from me." Is it permissible for me to narrate it from him?' He (the narrator) said: So he (the Imam) said: 'When you know that the book belongs to him, then narrate it from him.'

Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) said: 'Whenever you narrate a hadith, attribute it to the one who narrated it to you. For if it was true, it is to your credit; and if it was a lie, it is upon him.'

Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Abdillah, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Abu Ayyub al-Madani, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Husayn al-Ahmasi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The heart relies upon the written (words).
I heard Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: 'Write down (our narrations), for indeed you will not preserve (them) until you write (them) down.'

Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from al-Hasan ibn 'Ali ibn Faddal, from Ibn Bukayr, from 'Ubayd ibn Zurara, who said: Abu Abd Allah (peace be upon him) said: 'Guard your books carefully, for you will soon have need of them.'

Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) said to me: 'Write and transmit your knowledge among your brethren. If you die, then bequeath your books to your sons. For there will come upon the people a time of commotion (harj) in which they will find no comfort except in their books.'

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'Beware of the originating lie!' It was said to him: 'And what is the originating lie?' He said: 'That a man narrates a hadith to you, and you leave him and report it from the one from whom he had narrated it.'

Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from Jamil ibn Darraj, who said: Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) said: 'Express our hadith clearly, for we are an eloquent people.'

Ali ibn Muhammad, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, from Hisham ibn Salim and Hammad ibn Uthman and others — they said: We heard Abu Abdullah (AS) saying: My hadith is the hadith of my father, and the hadith of my father is the hadith of my grandfather, and the hadith of my grandfather is the hadith of al-Husayn (AS), and the hadith of al-Husayn is the hadith of al-Hasan (AS), and the hadith of al-Hasan is the hadith of Amir al-Mu'minin (AS), and the hadith of Amir al-Mu'minin is the hadith of the Messenger of God (SAWW), and the hadith of the Messenger of God is the word of God, Mighty and Majestic.

A group of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Abi Khalid Shaynula, who said: I said to Abu Ja'far the Second (عليه السلام): 'May I be made your ransom! Indeed our elders narrated from Abu Ja'far and Abu Abd Allah (عليه السلام), and the taqiyyah was intense, so they concealed their books and did not narrate from them. When they died, the books came to us.' So he (عليه السلام) said: 'Narrate from them, for indeed they are true.'

A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from Abdullah ibn Yahya, from Ibn Muskan, from Abu Basir, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I said to him (about the verse): 'They have taken their rabbis and their monks as lords besides God' [9:31]. So he said: By God, they did not call them to worship themselves, and even if they had called them, they would not have responded. But they permitted for them what was forbidden, and forbade upon them what was permissible, and thus they worshipped them from an aspect they were not aware of.

Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) said to me: 'O Muhammad! Are you more intense in taqlid, or the Murjiites?' He said: I said, 'We are in taqlid and they are in taqlid.' So he said: 'I did not ask you about this.' So there was no answer with me beyond the first answer. Then Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) said: 'Indeed, the Murjiites established a man whose obedience was not obligatory, and they followed him in taqlid. And you have established a man whose obedience is obligatory, and then you did not follow him in taqlid. Therefore they are more intense in taqlid than you.'

Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, from Hammad ibn 'Isa, from Rib'i ibn 'Abdillah, from Abu Basir, from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) regarding the words of God, Majestic and Mighty: 'They took their rabbis and their monks as lords besides God' [9:31] so he said: 'By God! They (the people) neither fasted for them (the religious leaders) nor prayed to them. But rather they (the leaders) permitted for them what was forbidden, and they forbade to them what was permissible — so they (the people) followed them.'

Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad al-Ash'ari, from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad, from al-Hasan ibn Ali al-Washa', and a number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Faddal, all together from Asim ibn Humayd, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said: The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) addressed the people and said: 'O people! Indeed, the beginning of the occurrence of seditions is desires that are followed, and rulings that are innovated, in which the Book of God is opposed, and men take command over men therein. For if falsehood were pure, it would not be hidden from one with intelligence. And if truth were pure, there would be no disagreement.
