But a bunch is taken from this and a bunch from that, and they are mixed together and come at once — and therein Satan takes hold of his allies, while those who have previously received the good decree from God are saved.

The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'When innovations appear in my community, the scholar should manifest his knowledge. So whoever does not do so, upon him be the curse of God.'

And by this chain, from Muhammad ibn Jumhur, who raised it (traced it back to the Prophet), he said: Whoever comes to one who has introduced an innovation and glorifies him, he is indeed working toward the demolition of Islam.

The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'God refuses repentance for the one who practices innovation (bid'ah).' It was said: 'O Messenger of God, how is that so?' He said: 'Indeed his heart has been made to drink of its love.'

Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from Mu'awiya ibn Wahb who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'Indeed, for every innovation (bid'a) that occurs after me, by which faith (iman) is intended to be undermined, there is a guardian from the people of my household appointed for it — he defends (faith) against it, speaking by inspiration from God, declaring the Truth and illuminating it, and repelling the plots of the schemers, speaking on behalf of the weak ones. Therefore take heed, O people of insight, and rely upon God.'

Muhammad ibn Yahya, from some of his companions; and Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Harun ibn Muslim, from Mas'ada ibn Sadaqa, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him); and Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Mahbub, who raised it (marfu') from Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him), that he said: Indeed, among the most hateful of creatures to God, Mighty and Majestic, are two men. A man whom God has left to himself — he is biased away from the straight course, enamored of the speech of innovation (bid'ah); he has become engrossed in fasting and prayer, yet he is a trial for those who are tempted by him; straying from the guidance of those who came before him; leading astray those who follow him in his lifetime and after his death; bearing the sins of others and pledged by his own sin. And a man who has gathered up ignorance among the ignorant of the people, submerged in the darknesses of strife; people resembling scholars have named him a scholar, yet he has not been sound in it even for a single complete day. He rose early and accumulated much of what little of it is better than much — until when he had drunk his fill from stagnant water and stored up from that which has no benefit, he sat among the people as a judge, guaranteeing to clarify what had become confused for others. If he opposes a judge who preceded him, he cannot be secure that his ruling will not be overturned by one who comes after him, just as he did to the one before him. And if one of the ambiguous, intractable matters descends upon him, he concocts stuffing for it from his own opinion and then issues a definitive ruling on it. So he is, in his wearing of obscurities, like the web of a spider — he does not know whether he has hit the mark or erred. He does not reckon that there is knowledge in anything he has denied, nor does he see that behind what he has reached there is a school of thought. If he compares something to something, he does not doubt his own view. And if a matter becomes obscure to him, he conceals it because he knows of his own ignorance, lest it be said of him that he does not know; then he becomes bold and passes judgment. So he is a key to darknesses, a rider upon obscurities, a blunderer through ignorances. He does not excuse himself from what he does not know so that he might be saved, nor does he bite into knowledge with a cutting molar so that he might p

I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: 'The companions of analogies sought knowledge through analogies, but the analogies only increased them in distance from the truth, and indeed the religion of God cannot be attained through analogies.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father, and Muhammad ibn Ismail from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, raising it, from Abu Ja'far and Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: Every innovation is a straying, and every straying, its way is to the Fire.

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Muhammad ibn Hakim who said: I said to Abu al-Hasan Musa (peace be upon him), 'May I be your sacrifice! You granted us understanding in the religion, and God made us needless of [other] people through you, to the extent that a group from us would be in a gathering and a man would not even ask his companion [about a matter], for the question and its answer would both be present with him — due to what God has favored upon us through you. However, sometimes a matter comes to us about which nothing has come from you nor from your forefathers. So we look to the best of what is present with us and the most compatible of things with what has come to us from you, and we take by it.' He said: 'Far be it! Far be it! By God, whoever perished, perished by that, O Ibn Hakim!' He then said: 'May God curse Abu Hanifa! He used to say, "Ali said, and I say."' Muhammad ibn Hakim said to Hisham ibn al-Hakam: 'By God! I only intended that he grant me permission regarding qiyas (analogical reasoning).'

Muhammad ibn Abi Abdillah narrates, raising the chain from Yunus ibn Abd al-Rahman, who said: I said to Abu al-Hasan al-Awwal (peace be upon him): 'By what do I establish the tawhid of God?' So he said: 'O Yunus! Do not become an innovator. Whoever views (religion) by his own opinion perishes, and whoever abandons the People of the Household of his Prophet (may God bless him and his family) goes astray, and whoever abandons the Book of God and the words of His Prophet commits kufr.'

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'Things come to us that we neither recognize in the Book of God nor in the Sunnah; so shall we apply our reasoning in them?' So he (peace be upon him) said: 'No. Know that if you are correct, you will not be rewarded, and if you err, you would have lied against God, Mighty and Majestic.'

A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Umar ibn Aban al-Kalbi, from Abd al-Raheem al-Qasir, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'Every innovation is a straying, and every straying is in the Fire.'

ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā ibn ʿUbayd, from Yūnus ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from Samāʿah ibn Mihrān, from Abū al-Ḥasan Mūsā عليه السلام, who said: I said, “May Allah keep you well! We gather together and discuss what is with us. Nothing is brought to us except that we have something written regarding it, and that is from what Allah has bestowed upon us through you. Then a small matter comes to us for which we have nothing, so some of us look to others, while we have something resembling it, and we make analogy according to what seems best of it.” So he said, “What have you to do with analogy? Those before you were only destroyed by analogy.” Then he said, “When there comes to you that which you know, then speak by it; and if there comes to you that which you do not know, then—” and he gestured with his hand toward his mouth. Then he said, “May Allah curse Abū Ḥanīfah. He used to say: ‘ʿAlī said, and I say; and the Companions said, and I say.’” Then he said, “Did you use to sit with him?” I said, “No, but this is his speech.” Then I said, “May Allah keep you well! Did the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله bring the people what would suffice them in his time?” He said, “Yes, and what they would need until the Day of Judgment.” I said, “So has anything of that been lost?” He said, “No, it is with its أهل.”

From him, from Muhammad, from Yunus, from Aban, from Abu Shaybah, who said: I heard Abū ʿAbdillāh (عليه السلام) saying: The knowledge of Ibn Shubrumah is astray in comparison with al-Jāmiʿah, dictated by the Messenger of Allah (صلى الله عليه وآله) and written by ʿAlī (عليه السلام) with his own hand. Indeed, al-Jāmiʿah has left no room for anyone's speech; in it is the knowledge of the halal (permissible) and the haram (forbidden). Indeed, the companions of qiyās sought knowledge through analogy, but they increased in nothing from the truth except distance. Indeed, the religion of Allah cannot be attained through qiyās.

Muhammad ibn Ismail, from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, from Aban ibn Taghlub, from Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him), who said: The Sunnah cannot be analogized. Do you not see that a woman makes up her fasts but does not make up her prayers? O Aban! The Sunnah, when analogized, obliterates the Religion.

A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Uthman ibn Isa, who said: I asked Abu al-Hassan Musa (peace be upon him) about qiyas (analogical reasoning), so he said: 'What have you to do with qiyas? Indeed, God will not be asked how He made things permissible or how He made things forbidden.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Harun ibn Muslim, from Mas'ada ibn Sadaqa, who said: 'Ja'far (AS) narrated to me from his father (AS) that Ali (blessings of God be upon him) said: 'Whoever sets himself up for analogy (qiyas) will not cease to be in confusion throughout his lifetime; and whoever makes a religion of God based on personal opinion (ra'y) will not cease to be in a state of drowning throughout his lifetime.' He said: And Abu Ja'far (AS) said: 'Whoever issues fatwas to the people by his own opinion has thereby made a religion of God with what he does not know; and whoever makes a religion of God with what he does not know has opposed God, making permissible and forbidding that which he does not know.'

Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Yaqtin, from Al-Husayn ibn Mayyah, from his father, from Abu Abd Allah (peace be upon him), who said: Indeed, Iblees analogised himself with Adam (peace be upon him), so he said: "You created me from fire and You created him from clay." And had he compared the essence from which God created Adam (peace be upon him) with the fire, that would have been more light and radiance than the fire.

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn Isa ibn Ubayd, from Yunus, from Hariz, from Zurara who said: I asked Abu Abdallah (peace be upon him) about the halal and the haram. So he (peace be upon him) said: 'The halal of Muhammad (peace be upon him and his family) is halal forever until the Day of Judgment, and his haram is haram forever until the Day of Judgment. There will be nothing else, nor will anything else come.' And he said: 'Ali (peace be upon him) said: No one introduces a bid'a (religious innovation) except that a sunnah is abandoned by it.'

Abu Hanifa came to Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him). He (AS) said to him: 'O Abu Hanifa! It has reached me that you practice qiyas.' He said: 'Yes.' He (AS) said: 'Do not practice qiyas, for indeed the first to use analogy was Iblis, when he said:' 'You created me from fire, and You created him from clay.' So he analogised between fire and clay. Had he compared the luminous nature (nuriyya) of Adam with the luminous nature of fire, he would have recognised the superiority between the two lights and the purity of one over the other.

Ali, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yunus, from Qutayba, who said: A man asked Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) a question, and he (peace be upon him) answered him regarding it. The man then said, 'What is your opinion if it were such and such — what would the ruling be regarding it?' He (peace be upon him) said to him: 'Enough! Whatever I have answered you regarding it is from the Messenger of God (may God bless him and his family). We have nothing to do with ra'y ("what is your opinion?") regarding anything.'

A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from his father in a mursal (disconnected) chain, said: Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: 'Do not take a confidant from besides Allah, for then you would not be believers. Indeed, every means, and lineage, and kinship, and confidant, and innovation, and doubtful matter is severed, except what the Quran has affirmed.'

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan and Ali ibn Muhammad, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ubaydullah ibn Abdullah al-Dihqan, from Durust al-Wasiti, from Ibrahim ibn Abd al-Hamid, from Abu al-Hasan Musa (peace be upon him) who said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) entered the mosque, and there was a group who had encircled a man. So he said: 'What is this?' It was said: 'An Allama (great scholar).' He said: 'And what is an Allama?' They said to him: 'The most knowledgeable of the people regarding the lineages of the Arabs, their battles, the days of the Jahiliyya, and Arab poetry.' So the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'That is a knowledge which neither harms the one who is ignorant of it, nor benefits the one who knows it.' Then the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'Indeed, knowledge is only of three types: a decisive verse (from the Quran), or a just obligation, or an established Sunnah — and whatever is besides these is superfluous.'

Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Muhammad ibn Khalid, from Abu al-Bakhtari, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: The scholars are the inheritors of the Prophets, and that is because the Prophets did not leave dirhams or dinars as inheritance, but rather they bequeathed narrations from their narrations. So whoever takes something from them has indeed taken an abundant share. Therefore, look carefully at this knowledge of yours — from whom you take it — for among us, the People of the Household, in every generation there are just ones who repel from it the distortions of the exaggerators, the false attributions of the falsifiers, and the misinterpretations of the ignorant.

Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad, from Al-Hasan ibn Ali al-Washsha', from Hammad ibn Uthman, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Whenever Allah intends good for a servant, He grants him understanding in the Religion.

Muhammad ibn Ismail, from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Rib'i ibn Abdillah, from a man, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: Perfection — all of perfection — is deep understanding of the religion, patience in the face of calamity, and the wise regulation of one's livelihood.
The scholars are trustees, the pious are fortresses, and the successors are chiefs. And in another narration: The scholars are beacons, the pious are fortresses, and the successors are chiefs.

Ahmad ibn Idris, from Muhammad ibn Hassan, from Idris ibn al-Hasan, from Abu Ishaq al-Kindi, from Bashir al-Dahhan who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'There is no goodness in one from our companions who does not acquire religious understanding. O Bashir! Verily, when the man from among them does not suffice himself with his jurisprudence, he becomes needful of them (others). And when he becomes needful of them, they lead him into the gate of their misguidance while he does not even realize it.'

Ali ibn Muhammad, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from al-Nawfali, from al-Sakuni, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), from his forefathers, who said: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'There is no goodness in life except for two men — a scholar who is obeyed, or an attentive listener.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, and Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Sayf ibn Amira, from Abu Hamza, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: A scholar from whose knowledge people benefit is superior to seventy thousand worshippers.

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): A man who is a narrator/transmitter of your hadiths, disseminating them among the people and fastening them into their hearts and the hearts of your Shia — and there is perhaps a worshipper from your Shia who does not have this narration — which of the two is superior? He said: The narrator of our hadiths who fastens the hearts of our Shia with it is superior to a thousand worshippers.

Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ali ibn Hadid, from Murazim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Indeed, Allah, Blessed and Exalted, has revealed in the Quran a clarification of everything, to the extent that, by God, Allah has not left out anything which the servants would be in need of, such that no servant is able to say, 'If only this (matter) had been revealed in the Quran,' except that Allah has already revealed it therein.

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yunus, from Husayn ibn al-Mundhir, from Umar ibn Qays, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: I heard him saying: 'Verily, Allah, Blessed and Exalted, did not leave anything which the community would need except that He revealed it in His Book and explained it to His Messenger (may the blessings of Allah be upon him and his family), and He made a limit for every thing, and He placed upon it an indication pointing to it, and He made a penalty upon whoever transgresses that limit.'

Ali, from Muhammad, from Yunus, from Aban, from Sulayman ibn Harun who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: 'Allah has not created anything permissible nor anything forbidden except that there is a limit for it, like the boundary of a house. Whatever falls on the road side belongs to the road, and whatever falls on the house side belongs to the house — even the compensation for a scratch, and what is beyond it, and the lash, and half a lash.'
Ali, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yunus, from Hammad, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I heard him saying: 'There is nothing except that in it there is a Book or a Sunnah.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yunus, from Hammad, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, from Abu al-Jarud, who said: Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: 'Whenever I narrate something to you, ask me (to show you) where it is in the Book of God.' Then he said in one of his discourses: 'The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) forbade idle talk — the "it was said" and "he said" — and the waste of wealth, and excessive questioning.' So it was said to him: 'O son of the Messenger of God, where is this in the Book of God?' He said: 'Indeed God, Mighty and Majestic, says: [4:114] There is no good in most of their secret counsels except for one who enjoins charity, or good conduct, or reconciliation between people. And He says: [4:5] Do not give the foolish your wealth which God has made a means of support for you. And He says: [5:101] Do not ask about things which, if disclosed to you, would trouble you.'

Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Faddal, from Tha'laba ibn Maymun, from one who narrated to him, from al-Mu'alla ibn Khunays who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'There is no matter regarding which two (people) differ except that it has an origin in the Book of God, Mighty and Majestic — but the intellects of men do not reach it.'

Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) said: O people! Verily Allah, Blessed and Exalted, sent the Messenger (peace be upon him and his family) to you and revealed the Book to him with the Truth, while you were illiterate regarding the Book and the One Who revealed it, and regarding the Messenger and the One Who sent him — at a time of a gap in messengership, and a prolonged slumber among the nations, and a spreading of ignorance, and the prevalence of strife, and the breaking of solemn covenants, and blindness from the Truth, and oppression by tyrants, and the obliteration of religion, and the blazing of wars — at a time of yellowing of the orchards of the gardens of this world, and the drying of their branches, and the scattering of their leaves, and despair from their fruits, and the drying up of their waters. The banners of guidance had decayed and the banners of destruction had appeared. The world was scowling in the faces of its inhabitants, gloomy and turning away without facing. Its fruit was strife, its food was carrion, its slogan was fear, and its garment was the sword — you were torn apart entirely. It had blinded the eyes of its inhabitants and darkened their days. They had severed their family ties, shed each other's blood, and buried alive their female infants among their own children. Comfort and the welfare of low worldly life passed them by. They neither hoped for reward from God nor feared, by God, His punishment. Their living were blind and filthy, and their dead were in the Fire in utter despair. Then he (the Messenger) came to them with a copy of what was in the former Scriptures, and a confirmation of what was before him, and a detailed explanation of the permissible from the doubtful of the forbidden. That is the Quran. So try to make it speak, but it will never speak to you. I will inform you about it: in it is knowledge of what has passed and knowledge of what is to come until the Day of Judgment, and a ruling for what is between you, and an explanation of that about which you have come to dispute. So if you were to ask me about it, I would teach you.

Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, from Ibn Faddal, from Hammad ibn Uthman, from Abd al-A'la ibn A'yan who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: 'I was born from the lineage of the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family), and I know the Book of God; in it is the beginning of creation and what shall come to pass until the Day of Resurrection, and in it is the news of the heavens and the news of the earth and the news of Paradise and the news of the Fire and the news of what has been and the news of what shall come to pass. I know all that just as I look upon my own palm. Indeed God says: in it is a clear exposition of every thing. [16:89]

A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ali ibn al-Nu'man, from Ismail ibn Jabir, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Book of God — in it is the news of what was before you, and information of what is to be after you, and the arbitration of what is between you, and we know it (all).

A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from Isma'il ibn Mihran, from Sayf ibn 'Amira, from Abu al-Maghra', from Sama'a, from Abu al-Hassan Musa (AS), who said: I said to him (AS), 'Is everything in the Book of God and the Sunnah of His Prophet (SAWW), or do you (Imams) also give opinions about it?' He (AS) said, 'Rather, everything is in the Book of God and the Sunnah of His Prophet (SAWW).'

ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm ibn Hāshim, from his father, from Ḥammād ibn ʿĪsā, from Ibrāhīm ibn ʿUmar al-Yamānī, from Abān ibn Abī ʿAyyāsh, from Sulaym ibn Qays al-Hilālī, who said: I said to Amīr al-Muʾminīn عليه السلام: “I heard from Salmān, al-Miqdād, and Abū Dharr something of the tafsir of the Qur'an and hadith from the Prophet of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله that differs from what is in the hands of the people. Then I heard from you confirmation of what I heard from them, and I saw in the hands of the people many things from the tafsir of the Qur'an and from hadith from the Prophet of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله in which you oppose them, and you claim that all of that is false. So do you see that the people deliberately lie against the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله and interpret the Qur'an according to their own opinions?” He said: Then he turned toward me and said: “You have asked, so understand the answer. In the hands of the people there is truth and falsehood, truthfulness and lying, abrogating and abrogated, general and specific, decisive and ambiguous, retention and delusion. Lies were indeed attributed to the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله in his own lifetime, until he stood as an orator and said: ‘O people, liars against me have become many; so whoever deliberately lies against me, let him take his seat in the Fire.’ Then lies were attributed to him after him as well, and hadith only came to you from four types, with no fifth among them.” And Allah had informed him about the hypocrites with what He informed him, and described them with what He described them. So He, Mighty and Majestic, said: “And when you see them, their bodies please you, and if they speak, you listen to their speech.” “One is a hypocritical man who outwardly shows iman, feigning Islam. He feels no sin and no restraint in deliberately lying against the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله. Had the people known that he was a lying hypocrite, they would not have accepted from him nor believed him. But they said: ‘This man accompanied the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله, saw him, and heard from him,’ so they took from him while not knowing his condition. They remained after him and drew near to the Imams of misguidance and the callers to the Fire through false testimony, lying, and slander. So those leaders appointed them over affairs and placed them over the necks of the pe

A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Uthman ibn Isa, from Abu Ayyub al-Khazzaz, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I said to him: 'What is the matter with people who narrate from so-and-so and so-and-so, from the Messenger of God (may God's blessings be upon him and his family), and they are not accused of lying, yet something contrary to it comes from you?' He said: 'Indeed, the hadith is abrogated just as the Quran is abrogated.'

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'What is the matter with me that I ask you a question and you answer me with one answer, then someone other than me comes to you, and you answer him with a different answer about the same question?' So he said: 'We answer people according to increase and decrease (of their capacity).' He said: I said: 'Then inform me about the companions of the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) — did they narrate truthfully from Muhammad (peace be upon him and his family) or did they lie?' He said: 'Rather, they were truthful.' I said: 'Then what is the matter with them that they differed?' So he said: 'Do you not know that a man would come to the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) and ask him a question, and he would answer him regarding it with an answer, then he would answer him after that with what abrogated that answer — and so the narrations abrogated one another?'

Ali ibn Muhammad, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ibn Mahbub, from Ali ibn Ri'ab, from Abu Ubayda, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: He (the Imam) said to me: 'O Ziyad! What would you say if we were to issue a fatwa to a man from those who follow our authority, with something from taqiyya?' He (Abu Ubayda) said: I said to him (the Imam): 'You are more knowing, may I be sacrificed for you.' He (the Imam) said: 'If he acts upon it, it is better for him and of greater reward.' And in another report: 'If he acts upon it, he will be rewarded; and if he abandons it, by God, he sins.'

Ahmad ibn Idris, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, from al-Hasan ibn Ali, from Tha'laba ibn Maymun, from Zurara ibn A'yan, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a question, and he answered me. Then a man came and asked him the same question, and he answered him differently from how he had answered me. Then another man came and he answered him differently from how he had answered me and how he had answered my companion. When the two men left, I said: 'O son of the Messenger of God! Two men from the people of Iraq, from your Shia, came asking, and you answered each of the two with something other than what you answered his companion.' He said: 'O Zurara! This is better for us and more lasting for us and for you. And if you all were to gather upon one matter, the people would confirm your words against us, and it would be less for our survival and yours.' He (the narrator) said: Then I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'Your Shia — if you were to command them onto spears or into fire, they would march forward, yet they come out from your presence differing.' He said: So he answered me with the like of his father's answer.

Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Nasr al-Khath'ami who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: 'Whoever recognises that we do not say except the truth, let him be content with what he knows from us. And if he hears from us something contrary to what he knows, let him know that it is a defence from us on his behalf.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Uthman ibn Isa and al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, both together, from Sama'a, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a man upon whom two men from the people of his religion disagree regarding a matter — both of them narrate it — one of them commanding him to follow it and the other forbidding him from it. How should he deal with it? So he said: He should defer it until he meets someone who will inform him, for he is in a leeway until he meets him. And in another narration: 'Whichever of the two you take, from the door of submission, it is permissible for you.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Uthman ibn Isa, from al-Husayn ibn al-Mukhtar, from some of our companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: 'What is your view — if I were to narrate a hadith to you this year, then you came to me next year and I narrated something contrary to it, which of the two would you take?' He said: I said, 'I would take the later one.' So he said to me: 'May God have mercy on you.'

And from him, from his father, from Ismail ibn Marrar, from Yunus, from Dawood ibn Farqad, from al-Mualla ibn Khunays who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): When there comes a hadith from your first ones and a hadith from your last ones, by which of the two should we act? So he said: Adhere to it until there reaches you from the living one; then if there does reach you from the living one, take his words. He (the narrator) said: Then Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: We, by God, do not lead you into anything except what is within your capacity. And in another report: Take the most recent.

Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Dawood ibn al-Husayn, from Umar ibn Hanzalah, who said: I asked Aba Abdillah عليه السلام about two men from our companions between whom there was a dispute concerning a debt or an inheritance, so they sought judgment from the ruler and from the judges. Is that permissible? He عليه السلام said: Whoever seeks judgment from them in a matter of right or falsehood has only sought judgment from the tyrannical authority, and whatever is judged for him, he only takes as illicit gain, even if it is an established right, because he took it by the judgment of the tyrannical authority, while Allah has commanded that it be disbelieved in. Allah, the Exalted, said: “They desire to seek judgment from the tyrannical authority, though they were commanded to disbelieve in it.” I said: So what should the two of them do? He عليه السلام said: They should look to one among you who has narrated our hadith, examined our halal and our haram, and recognized our rulings; then let them be satisfied with him as an arbiter, for I have appointed him as a ruler over you. So if he judges by our judgment and it is not accepted from him, then the judgment of Allah has been taken lightly, and us has been rejected; and the one who rejects us rejects Allah, and he is on the verge of shirk with Allah. I said: Then if each man chose one man from our companions, and they were both satisfied that the two should examine their right, but they differed in what they judged, and both differed regarding your hadith? He عليه السلام said: The ruling is what is judged by the one who is more just, more learned in fiqh, more truthful in hadith, and more scrupulous; and no attention is to be given to what the other rules. He said: I said: If both of them are just and approved by our companions, and neither of them is preferred over the other? He عليه السلام said: Then one should look at what in their narrations from us concerning that matter is agreed upon by your companions; then it is to be taken from our ruling, and the anomalous report that is not well known among your companions is to be left, for that which is agreed upon has no doubt in it. Matters are only of three kinds: a matter whose right guidance is clear, so it is followed; a matter whose error is clear, so it is avoided; and a difficult matter whos

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from al-Nawfali, from al-Sakuni, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'Upon every truth there is a reality, and upon every correct thing there is a light. So whatever is in accordance with the Book of God, take it; and whatever contradicts the Book of God, leave it.'

And Husayn ibn Abi al-'Ala' narrated to me that he was present with Ibn Abi Ya'fur in this gathering. He said: I asked Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the discrepancy in hadiths — some narrated by those we trust and some by those we do not trust. He said: 'Whenever a hadith comes to you and you find a witness for it from the Book of God or from the words of the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family), [accept it]. Otherwise, the one who brought it to you is the closest to it [and bears its responsibility].'

A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from his father, from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from Yahya al-Halabi, from Ayyub ibn al-Hurr who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: 'Everything is to be referred back to the Book and the Sunnah, and every hadith that is not in accordance with the Book of God is mere ornamentation (falsehood).'

Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ibn Faddal, from Ali ibn Uqba, from Ayyub ibn Rashid, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Whatever from the hadith does not accord with the Quran is mere decoration (zukhruf).

Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hisham ibn al-Hakam and others, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Prophet (may Allah's blessings be upon him and his family) delivered a sermon at Mina and said: 'O people! Whatever comes to you from me that accords with the Book of Allah, I said it; and whatever comes to you opposing the Book of Allah, I did not say it.'
He said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: Whoever opposes the Book of God and the sunnah of Muhammad (peace be upon him and his family) has indeed disbelieved.
Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon him) said: 'The most superior of the deeds in the Presence of God is what is performed by (following) the Sunnah, even though it may be little.'

A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from Ismail ibn Mihran, from Abu Sa'id al-Qammat and Salih ibn Sa'id, from Aban ibn Taghlub, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) — that he was asked a question and he answered regarding it. Then the man said: 'The jurists do not say this!' So he said: 'O woe unto you! Have you ever seen a jurist at all? Verily, the jurist who is truly a jurist is the one ascetic in this world, desirous of the Hereafter, and holding fast to the Sunnah of the Prophet (may God's blessings be upon him and his family).'

A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from his father, from Abu Ismail Ibrahim ibn Is'haq al-Azdi, from Abu Uthman al-Abdi, from Ja'far, from his forefathers, from the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) who said: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said: There is no speech except with a deed, and there is neither speech nor deed except with an intention, and there is neither speech nor deed nor intention except with attaining the Sunnah.

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ahmad ibn al-Nadr, from Amr ibn Shimr, from Jabir, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said: There is no one except that he has vigour and slackening. So whoever's slackening leads him to the sunnah has been guided, and whoever's slackening leads him to an innovation has deviated.

Ali ibn Muhammad, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Barqi, from Ali ibn Hassan; and Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Salamah ibn al-Khattab, from Ali ibn Hassan, from Musa ibn Bakr, from Zurarah ibn A'yan, from Abu Ja'far عليه السلام, who said: Everyone who exceeds the sunnah (prophetic tradition) is to be returned to the sunnah (prophetic tradition).

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from al-Nawfali, from al-Sakuni, from Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him), from his forefathers (peace be upon them), who said: Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) said: 'The sunnah is of two (types): a sunnah pertaining to an obligation — adherence to it is guidance and its abandonment is going astray; and a sunnah pertaining to other than an obligation — adherence to it is a merit and its abandonment for [something] other is a sin.'

Ali ibn Muhammad, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, and Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa — all together from Ibn Mahbub, from Abu Usama, from Hisham ibn Salim, from Abu Hamza, from Abu Ishaq al-Sabi'i, from the one who narrated to him among those who are trusted — he said: I heard the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) saying: 'Verily, the people, after the Messenger of God (may God's blessings be upon him and his family), divided into three [groups]. They divided to: a scholar upon guidance from God, whom God had made self-sufficient with what he knew, from the knowledge of others; and an ignorant one claiming to have knowledge — with no knowledge for him — being self-conceited by what he possesses, while the world had tempted him, and he tempted others; and a student learning from a scholar upon the way of guidance from God and salvation. Then, those who claimed (falsely) perished, and those who fabricated (lies) were lost.'

Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad al-Ash'ari, from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad, from Al-Hasan ibn Ali al-Washa', from Ahmad ibn 'A'idh, from Abu Khadija Salim ibn Mukram, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: 'The people are three: a scholar, a student, and scum (the worthless).'

Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Abdullah ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from al-Ala ibn Razin, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Hamza al-Thumali who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to me: 'Become a scholar, or a student (of knowledge), or love the people of knowledge, but do not become a fourth (type), so you would be destroyed by their hatred.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yunus, from Jamil, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I heard him saying: 'The people come to be of three types: a scholar, a student, and scum. So we are the scholars, and our Shia are the students, and the rest of the people are scum.'

The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said: Whoever travels a path seeking knowledge therein, God will cause him to travel a path to Paradise. The angels lay down their wings for the seeker of knowledge out of pleasure with him. Those in the heavens and those in the earth — even the fish in the sea — seek forgiveness for the seeker of knowledge. The merit of the scholar over the worshipper is like the merit of the moon over all other stars on the night of the full moon. The scholars are the inheritors of the Prophets — the Prophets left no dinar or dirham as inheritance; rather, they bequeathed knowledge. So whoever takes from it has taken an abundant share.

Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from Jamil ibn Salih, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: Verily the one from among you who teaches knowledge shall receive a reward equal to the reward of the student, and he shall have merit over him. Therefore, learn knowledge from the bearers of knowledge, and teach it to your brothers just as the scholars have taught it to you.

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Barqi, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Ali ibn Abi Hamza, from Abu Baseer who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: 'Whoever teaches a good thing, for him is a reward like that of the one who acts upon it.' I said: 'What if he (in turn) teaches it to others — does that (reward) flow for him?' He said: 'If he were to teach it to all of the people, it would still flow for him.' I said: 'What if he has died?' He said: 'And even if he has died.'

And by this chain, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Hamid, from al-Ala' ibn Razin, from Abu Ubayda al-Hadhdha', from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: Whoever teaches a subject of guidance, for him is the like of the reward of whoever acts upon it, and nothing will be reduced from their rewards; and whoever teaches a subject of misguidance, upon him shall be the like of the burdens of whoever acts upon it, and nothing will be reduced from their burdens.

Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Sa'd, raising it (mursal), from Abu Hamza, from Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon him), who said: Had the people known what is in seeking knowledge, they would seek it even if it were by spilling their lifeblood and diving into the ocean depths. Indeed, Allah, Blessed and Exalted, revealed to Daniel: The most detestable of My servants to Me is the ignorant one who takes lightly the rights of the people of knowledge, the one who neglects following them; and that the most beloved of My servants to Me is the pious one, the seeker of abundant reward, the one who stays close to scholars, who follows the forbearing ones, and who accepts from the wise.

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from Sulayman ibn Dawud al-Minqari, from Hafs ibn Ghiyath who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to me: 'Whoever learns knowledge and acts by it and teaches for God's sake will be called magnificent in the kingdom of the heavens, and it will be said: He learned for God, and he acted for God, and he taught for God.'

Muhammad ibn Yahya al-'Attar, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from Mu'awiya ibn Wahb who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: Seek knowledge and adorn yourselves along with it with forbearance and dignity, and be humble toward those you teach knowledge to, and be humble toward those from whom you sought knowledge, and do not become tyrannical scholars such that your falsehoods obliterate your truth.

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yunus, from Hammad ibn Uthman, from al-Harith ibn al-Mughira al-Nasri, from Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) regarding the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: 'but rather the ones from His servants who fear Allah are the scholars' [35:28] He (peace be upon him) said: 'By "the scholars" it means those whose actions ratify their words; and whoever whose actions do not ratify his words, then he is not a scholar.'

The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) said: 'Shall I not inform you of the true jurisprudent (faqih)? The true jurisprudent is one who does not cause the people to despair of God's mercy, does not make them feel secure from God's punishment, does not grant them license to commit acts of disobedience to God, and does not abandon the Quran out of a desire for something other than it.' Indeed, there is no goodness in knowledge that has no understanding in it. Indeed, there is no goodness in recitation that has no reflection in it. Indeed, there is no goodness in worship that has no contemplation in it. And in another narration (he said): 'Indeed, there is no goodness in knowledge without understanding. Indeed, there is no goodness in recitation without reflection. Indeed, there is no goodness in worship without jurisprudential understanding. Indeed, there is no goodness in a ritual without piety in it.'

Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn 'Isa, and Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan al-Naysaburi, all from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Abu al-Hasan al-Rida (AS), who said: Verily, among the signs of fiqh (deep religious understanding) are forbearance and silence.

Ahmad ibn Abdillah, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Barqi, from some of his companions, raising it (marfu'), said: The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) said: Foolishness and arrogance cannot exist in the heart of a scholar.

And by this chain, from Muhammad ibn Khalid, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, who raised it (mursal), saying: Isa ibn Maryam (peace be upon him) said: 'O group of disciples! I have a need from you — fulfil it for me.' They said: 'Your need is fulfilled, O Spirit of God!' So he arose and washed their feet. They said: 'We were more deserving of this (washing your feet), O Spirit of God!' So he said: 'Indeed the most deserving of people for service is the scholar. I have only humbled myself like this so that you may be humble after me among people, as I have been humble toward you.' Then Isa (peace be upon him) said: 'Wisdom is cultivated through humility, not through arrogance, and likewise it is in the plain that crops grow, not on the mountain.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ali ibn Ma'bad, from the one who mentioned it, from Muawiya ibn Wahb, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: Amir al-Momineen (peace be upon him) used to say: O seeker of knowledge! Indeed, the (true) scholar has three signs: knowledge, forbearance, and silence; and the pretentious one has three signs: he disputes with those above him through disobedience, he oppresses those below him through domination, and he supports the oppressors.

A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from Uthman ibn Isa, from Abu Ayyub al-Khazzaz, from Sulayman ibn Khalid, from Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him), who said: There is no one dying from among the believers whose death is more beloved to Iblis than the death of a faqih.

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from some of his companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: When a believing jurist (faqih) dies, a breach occurs in Islam -- a breach that nothing can fill.

Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Mahbub, from Ali ibn Abi Hamza who said: I heard Abu al-Hasan Musa ibn Ja'far (peace be upon him) saying: When a believer dies, the angels weep over him, and the spots of the earth upon which he used to worship God, and the gates of the heaven through which his deeds used to ascend, and a breach is rent in Islam — a breach that nothing can fill — because the believing jurists (fuqaha') are the fortresses of Islam, like the fortified wall that a city has for its defense.
There is no one among the believers whose death is more beloved to Iblis than the death of a jurist (faqih).

Ali ibn Muhammad, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ali ibn Asbat, from his paternal uncle Yaqub ibn Salim, from Dawud ibn Farqad, who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: My father used to say: Indeed, God—Mighty and Majestic—does not withdraw knowledge after having sent it down; rather, the scholar dies and takes with him what he knows, and then the crude ignorant ones succeed them, going astray and leading others astray. And there is no good in anything that has no root.

Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon him) used to say: What consoles my soul regarding the swiftness of death and killing among us is the saying of God: 'Do they not see that We come to the earth reducing it from its sides?' And it is the departure of the scholars.

Luqman said to his son: 'O my son! Choose the gatherings according to your own discernment. If you see a group mentioning Allah, Majestic and Mighty, then sit with them. If you happen to be knowledgeable, your knowledge will benefit you, and if you happen to be ignorant, they will teach you, and perhaps Allah will shade them with His mercy and cover you along with them. And when you see a group who are not mentioning Allah, do not sit with them. If you happen to be knowledgeable, your knowledge will not benefit you, and if you happen to be ignorant, they will increase you in ignorance, and perhaps Allah will inflict them with His punishment and cover you along with them.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, and Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa — all from Ibn Mahbub, from Durust ibn Abi Mansur, from Ibrahim ibn Abd al-Hamid, from Abu al-Hasan Musa ibn Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said: A discussion with the scholar upon the rubbish dump is better than a discussion with the ignorant upon the carpets.

A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Barqi, from Sharif ibn Sabiq, from al-Fadl ibn Abi Qurra, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Messenger of God (may God's blessings be upon him and his family) said: The disciples said to Isa, 'O Spirit of God! Whom should we sit with?' He said: 'One whose sight reminds you of God, and whose speech increases your knowledge, and whose deeds make you desirous of the Hereafter.'

Muhammad ibn Ismail, from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Mansur ibn Hazim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Messenger of God (may God's blessings be upon him and his family) said: 'Gatherings of the people of religion are a nobility of this world and the Hereafter.'
I heard Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) saying: 'A sitting that I sit in with one I trust is more strengthening for my soul than working for a year.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from some of our companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a person with smallpox who was afflicted with major ritual impurity (janaba), so they washed him (with full ghusl), and he died. He (the Imam) said: 'They killed him. Why did they not ask? For indeed, the cure for incompetence is asking.'

Muhammad b. Yahya, from Ahmad b. Muhammad b. Isa, from Hammad b. Isa, from Hariz, from Zurara and Muhammad b. Muslim and Buray al-Ijali who said: Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) said to Humran b. A'yan regarding something he had asked him: 'Indeed, the people are destroyed because they do not ask.'

He (peace be upon him) said: 'Indeed, this knowledge has a lock upon it, and its key is asking [questions].' Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from al-Nawfali, from al-Sakuni, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) — similar to it.

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn Isa ibn Ubayd, from Yunus ibn Abd al-Rahman, from Abu Ja'far al-Ahwal, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The people have no leeway (for not doing so) until they ask, gain religious understanding, and recognize their Imam, and they have the capacity to take with what he says, even if it is under dissimulation (taqiyyah).

Ali, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yunus, from the one who mentioned it, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Messenger of God (may God bless him and his family) said: 'Fie to a man who does not devote himself during every Friday to the matter of his religion — so that he revisits it and asks about his religion.' And in another report: '(Fie is) to every Muslim.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'Verily God, Mighty and Majestic, says: The mutual discussion of knowledge among My servants is from what revives the dead hearts, when they end up in it toward My command.'

Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Abu al-Jarud, who said: I heard Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) saying: 'May God have mercy on a servant who revives knowledge.' He said: I asked, 'And what is its revival?' He said: 'That he discusses it with the people of religion and the people of piety.'

Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Abdullah ibn Muhammad al-Hajjal, from some of his companions, who raised it (marfū'), saying: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'Discuss among yourselves, meet one another, and narrate hadith; for indeed hadith is a polishing for the hearts. The hearts rust just as swords rust, and their polishing is hadith.'

A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from his father, from Fazalah ibn Ayyub, from Umar ibn Aban, from Mansur al-Sayqal who said: I heard Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) saying: The mutual discussion of knowledge is a study (dirasa), and study is a good prayer (salat).

Hisham ibn al-Hakam said to me: There was an atheist in Egypt who had heard certain things about Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him). So he went out to Medina in order to debate with him, but did not find him there. He was told that the Imam had gone out to Mecca. So he went out to Mecca, and we were with Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) during the tawaf. His (the atheist's) name was Abd al-Malik and his kunya was Abu Abdillah. He struck his own shoulder against the shoulder of Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him). So Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to him: 'What is your name?' He said: 'My name is Abd al-Malik.' He asked: 'And what is your kunya?' He said: 'My kunya is Abu Abdillah.' So Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to him: 'Then who is this king whose slave you are? Is he from the kings of the earth or from the kings of the sky? And inform me about your son — is he the slave of the god of the sky or the slave of the god of the earth? Say whatever you like, you will be refuted either way.' Hisham ibn al-Hakam said: I said to the atheist: 'Are you not going to respond to him?' He (the narrator) said that the atheist found fault with my words. Then Abu Abdillah said: 'When we are done with the tawaf, come to us.' So when Abu Abdillah finished, the atheist came to him and sat in his presence, and we were gathered around him. So Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to the atheist: 'Do you know that the earth has an underneath and an above?' He said: 'Yes.' He asked: 'Have you entered its underneath?' He said: 'No.' He asked: 'Then what would make you know what is beneath it?' He said: 'I don't know, except that I suppose there is nothing beneath it.' So Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'Conjecture is helplessness regarding that of which you are not certain.' Then Abu Abdillah said: 'Have you ascended to the sky?' He said: 'No.' He asked: 'Do you know what is in it?' He said: 'No.' He said: 'How strange your case is! You have not reached the east and not reached the west and not descended into the earth and not ascended to the sky, and not passed through there to know what is beyond them — yet you deny what is in them. Would a rational person deny what he does not know?' The atheist said: 'No one has spoken to me like this before you.' So Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'So you are in doubt about this — perhaps He exists and perhaps He does

Ahmad ibn Muhassin al-Maysami said: I was in the presence of Abu Mansur al-Mutatabbib (the physician), and he said: A man from my companions informed me, saying: I, Ibn Abi al-Awja', and Abdullah ibn al-Muqaffa' were in the Sacred Mosque. Ibn al-Muqaffa' said: Do you see these people? — and he gestured with his hand toward the place of circumambulation (tawaf). None among them deserves the name of humanity except that seated elder — meaning Abu Abd Allah Ja'far ibn Muhammad (peace be upon him). As for the rest, they are rabble and beasts. Ibn Abi al-Awja' said to him: How did you grant this name to this elder but not to these others? He said: Because I have seen in him what I did not see in them. Ibn Abi al-Awja' said to him: There is no way around testing what you have said about him, from him. He said, and Ibn al-Muqaffa' said to him: Do not do it, for I fear he will corrupt what is in your possession. He said: That is not your real view — rather you fear your opinion of him will weaken in my eyes after you placed him in the station you described. Ibn al-Muqaffa' said: Since you imagine this of me, then go to him, and guard yourself as much as you can against slipping, and do not let your reins turn toward indulgence lest it deliver you into fetters — and put him to the test, whatever turns out for you or against you. He said: So Ibn Abi al-Awja' arose, while I and Ibn al-Muqaffa' remained seated. When Ibn Abi al-Awja' returned to us he said: Woe to you, O Ibn al-Muqaffa'! This is not a human being! And if there is in the world a spiritual being who takes on a body when he wills, manifestly, and becomes spirit again when he wills, invisibly — then he is this one! He said to him: And how is that? He said: I sat with him. When no one was left with him but me, he addressed me first and said: If the matter is as these say — meaning the people of the circumambulation — and it is as they say, then they are saved and you are ruined. And if the matter is as you say, and it is not as you say, then you and they are equal. I said to him: May God have mercy on you — and what do we say and what do they say? My position and theirs is not but one! He said: How can your position and theirs be the same, when they say they have resurrection, reward, and punishment — and they profess that in the heaven there is a god that in the heaven there is a god and that it is inhabited

Muhammad ibn Ja'far al-Asadi narrated to me, from Muhammad ibn Isma'il al-Barmaki al-Razi, from al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan ibn Burd al-Dinawari, from Muhammad ibn Ali, from Muhammad ibn Abdullah al-Khurasani, the servant of al-Ridha (peace be upon him), who said: A man from the zanaqiqa (atheists) came to Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) while a group was in his presence. Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) said: 'O man! What is your view -- if the claim were your claim, and reality were not as you say it is, would we and you not be equal, with what we have prayed, fasted, paid zakat, and acknowledged causing us no harm?' The man fell silent. Then Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) said: 'And if the claim were our claim -- and it is our claim -- would you not be ruined while we are saved?' The man said: 'May God have mercy on you! Make me find how He is and where He is.' He said: 'Woe to you! What you have set upon is wrong. He is the One who gave place to where without a where, and gave manner to how without a how. He cannot be known through how-ness, nor through where-ness, nor can He be grasped by any sense, nor compared to anything.' The man said: 'Then He is nothing, since He cannot be grasped by any sense from among the senses.' Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) said: 'Woe to you! When your senses were incapable of grasping Him, you denied His Lordship. Whereas we, when our senses are incapable of grasping Him, become even more certain that He is our Lord -- unlike anything among things.' The man said: 'Then tell me -- when did He begin to exist?' Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) said: 'Tell me when He did not exist, and I will tell you when He began.' The man said: 'Then what is the proof of Him?' Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) said: 'When I look at my body, and am unable to increase or decrease it in its breadth and length, or to repel harm from it and draw benefit to it, I know that this structure has a Builder. So I affirm Him -- together with what I observe of the orbiting of the celestial sphere by His power, the forming of clouds, the routing of winds, the course of the sun and moon and stars, and other than that from the wondrous, evident signs. I know that for all this there is a Determiner and a Creator.'

'Abdullah al-Daysani asked Hisham ibn al-Hakam, saying to him, "Do you have a Lord?" He said, "Yes." He said, "Is He Powerful?" He said, "Yes, Powerful, Compelling." He said, "Is He able to enter the whole world into an egg, without the egg growing larger and without the world becoming smaller?" Hisham said, "Give me respite." So he said to him, "I give you one year's respite." Then he went away from him. So Hisham rode to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) and sought permission to see him, and he granted it. He said to him, 'O son of the Messenger of God! Abdullah al-Daysani came to me with a question for which there is no reliance in answering except upon God and upon you.' So Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to him, 'What did he ask you about?' He said, 'He said to me such and such.' So Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said, 'O Hisham! How many are your senses?' He said, 'Five.' He said, 'Which is the smallest of them?' He said, 'The eye (the pupil).' He said, 'And how large is the pupil?' He said, 'Like a lentil seed, or smaller than it.' So he said to him, 'O Hisham, look in front of you and above you, and tell me what you see.' He said, 'I see sky and earth, houses and palaces, open plains and mountains and rivers.' So Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to him, 'Verily, the One who was able to bring all that you see into a lentil seed or something smaller than it is able to bring the entire world into an egg — without the world becoming smaller and without the egg growing larger.' So Hisham fell upon him and kissed his hands, his head and his feet, and said, 'This is enough for me, O son of the Messenger of God,' and he departed to his home. The next morning al-Daysani came to him and said, 'O Hisham! I came to you just to greet you, not to demand the answer.' So Hisham said to him, 'If you came to demand it, then here is the answer.' So al-Daysani went out from him until he came to the door of Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), sought permission, and it was granted. When he sat down, he said to him, 'O Ja'far ibn Muhammad! Guide me to my object of worship.' So Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to him, 'What is your name?' He then went out and did not tell him his name. His companions said to him, 'Why did you not tell him your name?' He said, 'If I had said to him Abdullah, he would have asked: who is this one whose slave you are?' So they sa

The hadith of the atheist (zindiq) who came to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), and it was from the words of Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'Your statement that there are two (gods) cannot be free from the possibility that they are both eternal and powerful, or both weak, or one is powerful and the other weak. If they were both powerful, why does not each one of the two repel its companion and be alone in governance? And if you claim that one is powerful and the other weak, then it is proven that He is One — as we say — due to the manifest incapacity of the second. If you say they are two, it cannot be free from their being in total agreement from every aspect or in total disagreement from every aspect. When we see creation ordered, the celestial sphere moving, governance unified, and night and day, sun and moon — the soundness of the order and governance, and the harmony of affairs all point to the Regulator being One. Then it would be necessary for you, if you claim two, that there be a gap between them so that they may be two. So that gap itself becomes a third eternal entity alongside them, and three would be required of you. If you claim three, the same would apply as with two, until there is a gap between them, making them five, and then you would end up in the numbering at what has no end in its multitude.' Hisham said: It was part of the atheist's questioning that he said, 'So what is the proof of Him?' Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'The existence of effects proves that there is a Maker who made them. Do you not see that when you look at a well-constructed building you know it has a builder, even if you have not seen the builder or witnessed its construction?' He said, 'So what is He?' He said: 'A thing unlike all things. I return with my words to establishing a meaning: He is a thing in the true reality of thing-ness, except that He has no body, no form, cannot be felt, cannot be touched, and cannot be perceived by the five senses. Imaginations cannot grasp Him, the ages do not diminish Him, and time does not change Him.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub said, a number of our companions narrated to me, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Barqi, from his father, from Ali ibn al-Nu'man, from Ibn Muskan, from Dawud ibn Farqad, from Abu Sa'id al-Zuhri, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: It suffices for those possessing understanding — the creation of the Subduing Lord, the Kingdom of the Compelling Lord, the Majesty of the Manifest Lord, the Light of the Dazzling Lord, the proof of the Truthful Lord, what He caused the tongues of the servants to speak with, what He sent the Messengers with, and what He revealed to the servants — as evidence for the Lord.

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from al-Abbas ibn Ma'ruf, from Ibn Abi Najran, from Hammad ibn Uthman, from Abd al-Rahim ibn Atik al-Qasir who said: I wrote via the hands of Abd al-Malik ibn A'yan to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), that a group of people in Iraq are describing God with a form/image and with lines/outlines. So if you see fit — may God make me a ransom for you — write to me the correct doctrine of tawhid. So he wrote to me: 'You asked — may God have mercy on you — about tawhid and what has prevailed in your vicinity. Exalted is God, Who has nothing like Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing, exalted above what the describers describe — those who liken God to His creation, the fabricators of lies against God.' So know — may God have mercy on you — that the correct doctrine regarding tawhid is what the Quran has revealed of the attributes of God, Majestic and Mighty. So negate from God the Exalted all nullification and anthropomorphism: neither negate nor liken — He is God, the Established, the Existent. Exalted is God above what the describers describe, and do not transgress the Quran lest you go astray after the clarification.

Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Ibrahim ibn Abd al-Hamid, from Abu Hamza who said: Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon him) said to me: 'O Abu Hamza! Indeed, God cannot be described by limitation. Our Lord is too great to be described, so how can one who cannot be limited be described by limitation? Visions cannot comprehend Him, while He comprehends all visions, and He is al-Latif (the Subtle), al-Khabir (the All-Aware).'

Muhammad ibn Abi Abdillah, from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan, from Bakr ibn Salih, from al-Hasan ibn Sa'id, from Ibrahim ibn Muhammad al-Khazzaz and Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, who said: We entered upon Abu al-Hasan al-Rida (peace be upon him) and we told him that Muhammad (peace be upon him and his family) had seen his Lord in the form of a well-proportioned young man of approximately thirty years of age. And we said that Hisham ibn Salim, Sahib al-Taq, and al-Maysami say that He is hollow to the navel and the rest is Samad (not hollow). So he fell prostrating to God, then said: 'Glory be to You! They have not recognised You, nor have they declared Your Oneness; it is for this reason that they have described You (in such terms). Glory be to You! Had they truly recognised You, they would have described You with what You have described Yourself. Glory be to You! How could their souls incline them to liken You to others?! O God! I do not describe You except with what You have described Yourself, nor do I liken You to Your creation. You are worthy of every good; so do not place me among the wrongdoing people.' Then he turned towards us and said: 'Whatever you can imagine as a thing, conceive of God as other than it.' Then he said: 'We, the family of Muhammad, are the middle path — the extremist cannot reach us, nor can the follower outpace us. O Muhammad! Indeed the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family), when he looked at the Majesty of his Lord, was in the likeness of a well-proportioned young man of approximately thirty years of age. O Muhammad! My Lord, Mighty and Majestic, is far too exalted to be in the description of created beings.' He (the narrator) said: I said, 'May I be your ransom! Whose legs were in greenness?' He said: 'That was Muhammad. When he looked at his Lord with his heart, He placed him in a light like the light of the Veils, until what was within the Veils became clear to him. The light of God — part of it is green, part of it is red, part of it is white, and part of it is other than that. O Muhammad! Whatever the Book (Quran) and the Sunnah testify for Him, we are the speakers of it.'

Harun ibn al-Jahm informed me, from Abu Hamza, from Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon him), who said: If the inhabitants of the heaven and earth were to gather together to describe Allah by His magnificence, they would not be able to.

I wrote to the man (peace be upon him) that those before us from your followers have differed regarding tawhid — some of them say 'a body' and some of them say 'a form'. So he (peace be upon him) wrote in his own handwriting: Glorified is the One Who cannot be limited, nor can He be described. There is nothing like unto Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing — or he said: the All-Seeing.

Sahl, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn Hakim who said: Abu al-Hasan Musa ibn Ja'far (peace be upon him) wrote to my father: Indeed, God is too Exalted, too Majestic, and too Magnificent for the full reality of His description to be reached. So describe Him by what He has described Himself with, and refrain from whatever is besides that.

Sahl, from al-Sindy ibn al-Rabi', from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hafs, brother of Murazim, from al-Mufaddal who said: I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about something from the Attributes (of God). So he said: Do not exceed what is in the Quran.

I wrote to him (peace be upon him) that the ones before us are differing regarding tawhid. He said: So he (peace be upon him) wrote: 'Glory be to the One Who cannot be limited nor described. There is nothing like Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing.'

I wrote to the man (peace be upon him) that those among us have disagreed concerning the Divine Unity (Tawhid) — among them is one who says 'He is a body,' and among them is one who says 'He is a form/image.' So he wrote back to me: Glorified is the One Who cannot be limited, nor described, nor can anything resemble Him, and there is nothing like unto Him — and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing.

Sahl said: I wrote to Abu Muhammad (peace be upon him) in the year two hundred and fifty-five: 'My chief! Our companions have differed regarding tawhid — from them is one who says He is a body, and from them is one who says He is an image. So if you see fit, O my chief, to teach me from that what I may stand upon and not exceed — if you do so, it would be a prolonged favour upon your servant.' So he signed in his own handwriting (peace be upon him): You asked about tawhid, and this matter is removed from you all. God is One, Unique — He did not beget and was not begotten, and there is no match for Him whatsoever. He is the Creator and is not created. He, Blessed and Exalted, creates whatever He wills of bodies and other than that, and He is not a body; and He forms images of whatever He wills, and He is not an image. Majestic is His praise and holy are His names — [too exalted] for there to be a resemblance of Him. He is He — not other than He. There is nothing like Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing. [Quran 42:11]

I heard Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) saying: 'Indeed, God cannot be described. And how can He be described, when He has already said in His Book: "And they do not appreciate God with the appreciation that is due to Him" [Quran 6:91] Thus, He cannot be described with any estimation except that He would be greater than that.'

ʿAlī ibn Muḥammad, from Sahl ibn Ziyād, and from another, from Muḥammad ibn Sulaymān, from ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from ʿAbdullāh ibn Sinān, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: Indeed, Allah is Great and Exalted. The servants are not able to describe Him, nor do they attain the reality of His greatness. Visions do not comprehend Him, while He comprehends visions, and He is the Subtle, the All-Aware. And He is not described by 'how', nor by 'where', nor by location. How could I describe Him by 'how', when He is the One who originated the 'how' until it came to be 'how'? Thus 'how' came to be known only through what He originated for us of 'how'. Or how could I describe Him by 'where', when He is the One who originated the 'where' until it came to be 'where'? Thus 'where' came to be known only through what He originated for us of 'where'. Or how could I describe Him by location, when He is the One who originated location until it came to be location? Thus location came to be known only through what He originated for us of location. So Allah, Blessed and Exalted, is within every place and outside every thing. Visions do not comprehend Him, while He comprehends visions. There is no god except Him, the Most High, the Magnificent, and He is the Subtle, the All-Aware.

I said to Abu Abd Allah (peace be upon him): 'I heard Hisham ibn al-Hakam narrating from you that God is a body, self-sufficient and luminous, whose recognition is a necessity, which He grants to whomever He wills among His creation.' So he (peace be upon him) said: 'Glory be to the One Whom no one knows how He is, except He Himself. There is nothing like unto Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing. He cannot be limited, nor felt, nor touched, nor do the visions comprehend Him, nor the senses, nor can He be encompassed by anything — no body, no image, no lines, no boundaries.'

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Hamza ibn Muhammad, who said: I wrote to Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) asking him about the body and the image. So he wrote back: Glorified is the One like Whom there is nothing — neither a body nor an image. And it was also narrated by Muhammad ibn Abi Abdillah, except that he did not name the man.

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Muhammad ibn Ismail ibn Bazi', from Muhammad ibn Zayd who said: I came to al-Rida (peace be upon him) to ask him about tawhid. So he dictated to me: 'Praise be to Allah, Originator of things by their bringing into existence and their Initiator — by His power and His wisdom — not from anything, so that creation would be invalidated, nor for a cause, so that initiation would not be sound. He created what He willed, however He willed, uniquely so, to manifest His wisdom and the reality of His Lordship. Intellects cannot comprehend Him, imaginations cannot reach Him, sights cannot perceive Him, no measure can encompass Him. Expression falls short before Him, sights are dulled before Him, and the applications of attributes go astray in Him. He is veiled without a veil that veils, hidden without a covering that conceals, known without being seen, described without form, and characterized without body. There is no god but Allah, the Great, the Most High.'

Muhammad ibn Abi Abdillah, from whoever mentioned it, from Ali ibn al-Abbas, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from Muhammad ibn Hakim, who said: I described to Abu Ibrahim (peace be upon him) the words of Hisham ibn Salim al-Jawaliqi, and I related to him the words of Hisham ibn al-Hakam that He (God) is a body. So he said: Verily, God the Exalted — nothing resembles Him. What greater obscenity or turpitude exists than the words of one who describes the Creator of all things as having a body, or an image, or a creature-like nature, or a limitation, or body parts? Exalted is God above that, a great elevation.

Ali ibn Muhammad, raising it (with a gap in the chain), from Muhammad ibn al-Faraj al-Rukhkhaji, who said: I wrote to Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) asking him about what Hisham ibn al-Hakam said regarding [Allah's] body (jism), and what Hisham ibn Salim said regarding [Allah's] image (sura). So he wrote: 'Leave from yourself the confusion of the confused ones, and seek refuge with God from Satan. The correct saying is not what the two Hishams have spoken.'

Muhammad ibn Abi Abdillah, from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan, from Bakr ibn Salih, from al-Hasan ibn Sa'id, from Abdallah ibn al-Mughira, from Muhammad ibn Ziyad, who said: I heard Yunus ibn Zabyan saying: I entered upon Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) and said to him: Hisham ibn al-Hakam is making a grave statement — though I shall summarize some of it for you. He alleges that God is a body, because things are of two kinds: a body, and the action of a body. Therefore it is impermissible that the Maker could be [understood] in the sense of an action, and it is permissible that He could be [understood] in the sense of an actor. So Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: Woe to him! Does he not know that a body is limited and finite, and an image is limited and finite? So when it admits of limitation, it admits of increase and decrease. And when it admits of increase and decrease, it would be a creation. He said: I asked, 'So what should I say?' He said: 'Neither a body nor an image. He is the One who gives body to bodies and form to forms. He cannot be divided, cannot have an end-point, cannot increase, and cannot decrease. Had it been as they say, there would be no difference between the Creator and the created, nor between the Originator and the originated. But He is the Originator — there is a difference between the One who gave it a body, gave it a form, and originated it. For nothing resembles Him, nor does He resemble anything.'

Muhammad ibn Abi Abdillah, from Muhammad ibn Ismail, from Ali ibn al-Abbas, from al-Hasan ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Himmani who said: I said to Abu al-Hasan Musa ibn Ja'far (peace be upon him): 'Hisham ibn al-Hakam has alleged that God is a body; there is nothing resembling Him — All-knowing, Hearing, Seeing, Powerful, a Speaker, and articulate — and that Speech, Power, and Knowledge flow as one flow, none of them being created.' So he said: 'May God destroy him! Does he not know that the body is limited, and speech is other than the speaker? I seek refuge in God and disavow before God this statement. There is neither body, nor image, nor limitation, and everything besides Him is created. Things come into being only by His Will and His Decree, without speech, without hesitation in Himself, and without articulation by a tongue.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yunus, from Muhammad ibn Hakim, who said: I described to Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) the words of Hisham al-Jawaliqi and what he was saying regarding the fully-grown youth, and I described to him the words of Hisham ibn al-Hakam. So he said: 'Indeed, nothing resembles God.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn Khalid al-Tayalisi, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Ibn Muskan, from Abu Baseer who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: 'God, Mighty and Majestic, has always been our Lord; and Knowledge is His very Essence with no object of knowledge, and Hearing is His very Essence with no object of hearing, and Sight is His very Essence with no object of sight, and Power is His very Essence with no object of power.
