So if it is pierced, its wergild is a quarter of the wergild of its breaking, being ten Dinars’.

And the blood money (diyah) of the shoulder, when the shoulder bone is broken, is one-fifth of the blood money of the hand, which is one hundred dinars. So if there is a crack in the shoulder, its blood money is four-fifths of the blood money for its breaking, which is eighty dinars. So if it is exposed, its blood money is one-quarter of the blood money for its breaking, which is twenty-five dinars. So if the bones are displaced from it, its blood money is one hundred and seventy-five dinars: of which one hundred dinars is for its complete breaking, and fifty dinars for the displacement of its bones, and twenty-five dinars for its exposure. So if it is pierced, its blood money is one-quarter of the blood money for its breaking, which is twenty-five dinars. So if it is bruised and becomes defective, its blood money is one-third of the blood money of the soul, which is three hundred and thirty-three dinars and one-third of a dinar. So if it is disjointed, its blood money is thirty dinars.

And regarding the arm, when it breaks, so it is bandaged upon and there is no fault, so its wergild is a fifth of the wergild of the hand, being one hundred Dinars; and wergild for its exposure is a quarter of the wergild of its breaking, being twenty-five Dinars; and wergild for the displacement of its bone is half the wergild of its breaking, being fifty Dinars; and wergild of its being pierced is a quarter of the wergild of its breaking, being twenty-five Dinars.

And regarding the elbow: if it breaks and is set without a defect or flaw, its wergild is one hundred dinars, and that is one-fifth of the wergild of the hand. If it cracks, its wergild is four-fifths of its breaking, being eighty dinars. If the bones are displaced from it, its wergild is one hundred and seventy-five dinars: one hundred for the breaking, fifty for the displacement of the bones, and twenty-five for the exposure. If it was pierced, its wergild is one-quarter of the wergild of its breaking, being twenty-five dinars. If the elbow is bruised and becomes defective, its wergild is one-third of the wergild of the soul, being three hundred and thirty-three dinars and one-third of a dinar. If it was disjointed, its wergild is thirty dinars.

And regarding the forearm, if it breaks and is then set without a defect or flaw, its blood-money is one-third of the blood-money of the soul, being three hundred and thirty-three dinars and one-third of a dinar. So if one of the two bones of the forearm breaks, its blood-money is one-fifth of the blood-money of the hand, being one hundred dinars. So if both bones of the forearm break, its blood-money is one-fifth of the blood-money of the hand, being one hundred dinars. And regarding the break of one of the two radius/ulna bones, it is fifty dinars, and regarding both of them is one hundred dinars. So if one of the two bones cracks, regarding it is four-fifths of the blood-money of one of the two bones of the forearm, being forty dinars; and the blood-money for its exposure is a quarter of the blood-money of its break, being twenty-five dinars; and the blood-money of the displacement of its bones is a quarter of the blood-money of its break, being twenty-five dinars; and the blood-money of its piercing is half the blood-money of its exposure, being twelve dinars and half a dinar; and the blood-money of its being jabbed is fifty dinars. So if there is in it a wound that does not heal, its blood-money is one-third of the blood-money of the forearm, being thirty-three dinars and one-third of a dinar, and that is one-third of the blood-money of that which is in it.

And the wergild (blood money) for the wrist, when it is bruised so that it is bandaged upon and there is no fault or defect, is one-third of the wergild of the hand, being one hundred and sixty-six Dinars, and one-third of a Dinar.

And regarding the palm: if it breaks and is set without deformity or defect, its wergild is one-fifth of the wergild of the hand, being one hundred Dinars; and if the palm is disjointed, its wergild is one-third of the wergild of the hand, being one hundred and sixty-six Dinars and two-thirds of a Dinar; and regarding its exposure, it is a quarter of the wergild of its breaking, being twenty-five Dinars; and the wergild for the displacement of its bones is fifty Dinars, being half the wergild for its breaking; and regarding its piercing, if it is not sealed up, it is one-fifth of the wergild of the hand, being one hundred Dinars. So if it was pierced (and sealed), its wergild is a quarter of the wergild of its breaking, being twenty-five Dinars. And regarding the wergild of the fingers and the bones which are in the palm: so regarding the thumb when it is cut off, it is one-third of the wergild of the hand, being one hundred and sixty-six Dinars and two-thirds of a Dinar; and the wergild of the bone of the thumb which is in the palm, if set without deformity or defect, is one-fifth of the wergild of the thumb, being thirty-three Dinars and one-third of a Dinar, when its setting is even and firm; and the wergild of its cracking is twenty-six Dinars and two-thirds of a Dinar; and the wergild for its exposure is eight Dinars and one-third of a Dinar; and the wergild of the displacement of its bone is sixteen Dinars and two-thirds of a Dinar; and the wergild for its piercing is eight Dinars and one-third of a Dinar, being half the wergild of the displacement of its bones. And the wergild of its exposure is half the wergild of its displacement, being eight Dinars and one-third of a Dinar; and the wergild of it being disjointed is ten Dinars; and the wergild of the second joint from the top of the thumb, if it breaks and is set without deformity or defect, is sixteen Dinars and two-thirds of a Dinar; and the wergild of the exposure, if it is in it, is four Dinars and one-sixth of a Dinar; and the wergild of its cracking is thirteen Dinars and one-third of a Dinar; and the wergild of the displacement of its bones is five Dinars. So whatever is cut from it, it is by its accounting.

And regarding the fingers, for every finger is a sixth of the wergild of the hand, being eighty-three Dinars and one-third of a Dinar; and wergild for the bones of the fingers of the palm beside the thumb, is a wergild of all bones being twenty Dinars and one-third of a Dinar; and wergild of every exposure regarding each of the bone from the four bones is four Dinars and one-sixth of a Dinar; and wergild of displacement of every bone from these is eight Dinars and one-third of a Dinar; and wergild of breaking of every joint from the four fingers which emerge from the palm is sixteen Dinars and one-third of a Dinar; and regarding a crack in each bone from these is thirteen Dinars and one-third of a Dinar. So if there was a sore in the palm which does not get cured, so its wergild is thirty-three Dinars and one-third of a Dinar; and regarding the displacement of its bone is eight Dinars and one-third of a Dinar; and regarding the exposure is four Dinars and one-sixth of a Dinar; and regarding a piercing is four Dinars and one-sixth of a Dinar; and regarding a disjointing is five Dinars; and wergild of the middle joint from the four fingers, when it is cut, so its wergild is fifty-five Dinars and one-third of a Dinar; and regarding the breaking of one (finger) is ten Dinars and one-third of a Dinar; and regarding its cracking is eight Dinars and half a Dinar; and regarding exposure are two Dinars and one-third of a Dinar; and regarding the displacement of its bone is five Dinars and one-third of a Dinar; and regarding a piercing are two Dinars and one-third of a Dinar; and regarding is disjointing is three Dinars and two-thirds of a Dinar; and regarding the upper joint from the four fingers, when it is cut, is twenty-seven Dinars and a half, and one-quarter, and half of a tenth of a Dinar; and regarding breaking it is five Dinars and four-fifth of a Dinar; and regarding its cracking is four Dinars and a fifth of a Dinar; and regarding its exposure are two Dinars and one-third of a Dinar; and regarding displacement of its bone is five Dinars and one-third of a Dinar; and regarding its piercing are two Dinars and one-third of a Dinar; and regarding its disjointing is three Dinars and one-third of a Dinar; and regarding a nail of each finger from these, is five Dinars; And regarding the palm when it breaks, so it is bandaged upon and there is no fault, so its werg

Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Kazzaz, from Ghayath ibn Ibrahim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding the extra finger: if it is cut off, its compensation is one-third of the wergild of the healthy (finger).

And by the first chain, he said: And regarding the chest, when it is bruised so both of its sides are bent, its wergild is five hundred Dinars; and the wergild of one side when it is bent is two hundred and fifty Dinars; and when the chest and the two shoulders are bent, its wergild is one thousand Dinars; and if one of the sides of the chest and one of the shoulders are bent, its wergild is five hundred Dinars; and the wergild of the exposure of the chest is twenty-five Dinars; and the wergild of the exposure of the shoulders and the back is twenty-five Dinars; and if the man gets twisted from that, not being able to turn around, its wergild is five hundred Dinars. So if the spine breaks, and it is bandaged and there is no flaw, its wergild is one hundred Dinars; and if there remains a flaw, its wergild is one thousand Dinars; and regarding the nipple of the breast of the man, the wergild is one hundred and twenty-five Dinars.

And regarding the ribs, those that are adjacent to the heart: if a rib from them breaks, its wergild is twenty-five dinars; and regarding its fracture (crack), twelve dinars and a half; and the wergild of the displacement of its bone is seven dinars and a half; and its exposure is one-quarter of its breaking, and its piercing is like that; and regarding the ribs from what follows the two upper arms, the wergild of each rib is ten dinars when it breaks; and the wergild of its fracture is seven dinars; and the wergild of the displacement of its bone is five dinars; and the exposure of each rib from them is one-quarter of the wergild of its breaking, being two dinars and a half. So if a rib from it were pierced, its wergild is two dinars and a half; and regarding the fatal injury (al-jaa'ifah), it is one-third of the wergild of the soul, three hundred and thirty-three dinars and one-third of a dinar. So if it penetrates from both sides, by an arrow or a jab, its wergild is four hundred and thirty-three dinars and one-third of a dinar.

And regarding the hip: if it breaks and is set without a defect or flaw, its compensation is one-fifth of the wergild of the leg, which is one hundred dinars. And if the hip is fractured, its compensation is one hundred and sixty dinars, which is four-fifths of the wergild of its breaking. If it is exposed, its compensation is one-quarter of the wergild of its breaking, which is fifty dinars. And the compensation for the displacement of its bones is one hundred and seventy-five dinars: from this, one hundred dinars is for its break, fifty dinars for the displacement of its bones, and twenty-five dinars for its exposure. And the compensation for its disjointing is thirty dinars. So if it is bruised and becomes defective, its compensation is three hundred and thirty-three dinars and one-third of a dinar.

And regarding the thigh, if it breaks and is set without a flaw or defect, its compensation is one-fifth of the wergild of the leg, being two hundred dinars. If it has a flaw, its compensation is three hundred and thirty-three dinars and one-third of a dinar, and that is one-third of the wergild of the soul. And the compensation for a fracture of the thigh is four-fifths of the compensation of its breaking, being one hundred and sixty dinars. If it was a wound that does not heal, its compensation is one-third of the compensation of its breaking, being sixty-six dinars and two-thirds of a dinar. And the compensation for its exposure is a quarter of the compensation of its breaking, being fifty dinars. And the compensation for the displacement of its bones is half the compensation of its breaking, being one hundred dinars. And the compensation for its piercing is a quarter of the compensation of its breaking, being one hundred and sixty dinars.

And regarding the knee, if it breaks and is set without a defect or flaw, its compensation is one-fifth of the wergild of the leg, being two hundred Dinars. So if it is fractured, its compensation is four-fifths of the wergild of its breaking, being one hundred and sixty Dinars; and the compensation for its exposure is one-quarter of the wergild of its breaking, being fifty Dinars; and the compensation for the displacement of its bones is one hundred and seventy-five Dinars, from which the compensation for its breaking is one hundred Dinars, and regarding the displacement of its bone is fifty Dinars, and regarding its exposure is twenty-five Dinars; and regarding bruising in it which does not heal, is thirty-three Dinars and one-third of a Dinar; and regarding its piercing is one-quarter of the wergild of its breaking, being fifty Dinars; and the compensation for its bruising is one-quarter of the wergild of its breaking, being fifty Dinars. So if it is bruised and becomes defective, regarding it is one-third of the wergild of the soul, being three hundred and thirty-three Dinars and one-third of a Dinar. So if it was disjointed, regarding it is three parts from the break, being thirty Dinars.

And regarding the leg, when it breaks and is set without defect or flaw, its compensation is one-fifth of the wergild of the leg, being two hundred Dinars; and the compensation for its fracture (crack) is four-fifths of the compensation for its breaking, being one hundred and sixty Dinars; and regarding its exposure is one-quarter of the compensation for its breaking, being fifty Dinars; and regarding its piercing is half the compensation for its exposure, being twenty-five Dinars; and regarding the displacement of its bones is one-quarter of the compensation for its breaking, being fifty Dinars; and regarding its penetration is one-quarter of the compensation for its breaking, being fifty Dinars; and regarding a wound in it that does not heal is thirty-three Dinars and one-third of a Dinar. So if the leg becomes defective, its compensation is one-third of the wergild of the soul, being three hundred and thirty-three Dinars and one-third of a Dinar.

And regarding the heel, when it is bruised and bandaged without a fracture or defect, [the compensation is] one-third of the wergild of the leg, being three hundred and thirty-three dinars and one-third of a dinar.

And regarding the foot, when it breaks and is set without deformity or defect, is one-fifth of the wergild of the leg, being two hundred Dinars; and the wergild of its exposure is one-quarter of the wergild of its breaking, being fifty Dinars; and regarding the displacement of its bones is one hundred Dinars, half the wergild of breaking it; and regarding a piercing in it which does not close, is one-fifth of the wergild of the leg, being two hundred Dinars; and regarding a bruising in it is one-quarter of the wergild of its breaking, being fifty Dinars.

That which is in the foot and the big toe: The wergild of the big toe is one-third of the wergild of the leg, being three hundred and thirty-three dinars and one-third of a dinar; and the wergild of the breaking of the bone of the big toe which is adjacent to the foot is one-fifth of the wergild of the big toe, being sixty-six dinars and two-thirds of a dinar; and regarding the displacement of its bone is twenty-six dinars and two-thirds of a dinar; and regarding its fracture is twenty-six dinars and two-thirds of a dinar; and regarding its fracture is twenty-six dinars and two-thirds of a dinar; and regarding its exposure is eighty dinars and one-third of a dinar; and regarding its piercing is eighty dinars and one-third of a dinar; and regarding its disjointing is ten dinars; And the wergild of the upper joint of the big toe, and it is the second one in which is the nail, is sixteen dinars and two-thirds of a dinar; and regarding its exposure is four dinars and one-sixth; and regarding the displacement of its bone is eight dinars and one-third of a dinar; and regarding its piercing is four dinars and one-sixth; and regarding its fracture is thirteen dinars and one-third of a dinar; and regarding its disjointing is five dinars; and regarding its nail is thirty dinars, and that is because it is one-third of the wergild of the leg; And the wergild of the toes: The wergild of each toe from it is one-sixth of the wergild of the leg, being three and eighty dinars and one-third of a dinar; and the wergild of the bones of the four toes besides the big toe: The wergild of each bone from them is sixteen dinars and two-thirds of a dinar; and the wergild of the exposure of the bone of each toe from them is four dinars and one-sixth of a dinar; and the wergild of the displacement of a bone of each of the bones from them is eight dinars and one-third of a dinar; and the wergild of its fracture is thirteen dinars and two-thirds of a dinar; and the wergild of the piercing of each bone from them is four dinars and one-sixth of a dinar; and the wergild of a wound that does not heal in the foot is three and thirty dinars and one-third of a dinar; and the wergild of the breaking of each joint from the four toes which are adjacent to the foot is sixteen dinars and one-third of a dinar; and the wergild of its fracture is thirteen dinars and one-third of a dinar; and the wergild

A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Shamoun, from Abdullah ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Asamm, from Misma', from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) ruled regarding the nail when it is ripped out and does not grow back, and comes out black and spoiled, [the blood money is] ten dinars. So if it comes out white, [the blood money is] five dinars. He returned to the first chain and said: And he ruled regarding the exposure of the toes [or fingers], [it is] one-third of the blood money of the finger. So if a man is struck and both his testicles are turned inside out, his blood money is four hundred dinars. So if he is straddled [or crippled in walking] and cannot walk except with a slight walk that is not beneficial to him, his blood money is four-fifths of the blood money of the soul, being eight hundred dinars. So if the back becomes hunched from it, then at that point his blood money is complete, being one thousand dinars. And the swearing oaths regarding everything from that are six people, according to whatever his blood money reaches. And the blood money of the rupture, if it is above the pubic area, is one-tenth of the blood money of the soul, being one hundred dinars. So if it is in the pubic area and it pierces the membrane, so there occurs a swelling in one of the testicles, its blood money is two hundred dinars, being one-fifth of the [complete] blood money.

And by this chain, from Amir Al-Momineen (peace be upon him) who said: He made the wergild of the foetus one hundred Dinars, and made the man's semen up to the stage it becomes a foetus into five segments. So if it is a foetus before the spirit enters it, it is one hundred Dinars. And that is because Allah, Mighty and Majestic, created man from an extract, which is the seed. So this is one segment. Then a clot, so it is two segments. Then a lump, so it is three segments. Then bones, so it is four segments. Then it is clothed with flesh, so at that time the foetus is complete, and its five segments are complete, being one hundred Dinars. And the one hundred Dinars are five segments: so for the seed is one-fifth of the hundred, twenty Dinars; and for the clot is two-fifths of the hundred, forty Dinars; and for the lump is three-fifths of the hundred, sixty Dinars; and for the bones is four-fifths of the hundred, eighty Dinars. So when the flesh covers it, it becomes one hundred Dinars complete. So when another creation prevails in it, which is the spirit, then at that time it is a soul, and its wergild is one thousand Dinars complete if it is a male; and if it is a female, it is five hundred Dinars. And if a woman is killed while pregnant, and the foetus is complete and has not miscarried, and it is not known whether it is male or female, and it is not known whether it died after her or before her, then its wergild is two halves: half the wergild of the male and half the wergild of the female. And the wergild of the woman is complete after that, and that is six segments from the foetus. And he (peace be upon him) issued a verdict regarding the semen of the man which flows out from his bride, so the water is isolated from her, and that is not returned, being half of the fifth of the hundred, ten Dinars; and when it is poured from her, it is twenty Dinars. And he judged regarding the wergild of the injuries of the foetus from the accounting of the hundred, based on what it is, from the injury of the male and the female, the man and the woman complete. And he made for it in retaliation for its injury and its blood money according to the measure of its wergild, which is one hundred Dinars.

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yunus or someone else, from Ibn Muskan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: The wergild (blood money) of the foetus is five parts: one-fifth for the nutfah (seed/drop) is twenty dinars; and for the alaqah (clot) two-fifths is forty dinars; and for the mudghah (lump of flesh) three-fifths is sixty dinars; and for the 'idham (bones) four-fifths is eighty dinars. So when the foetus is complete, its wergild is one hundred dinars. So when the spirit is breathed into it, its wergild is one thousand dinars or ten thousand dirhams if it is a male; and if it is a female, then five hundred dinars. And if the woman is killed while she is pregnant, and it is not known whether her child was a male or a female, then the wergild of the child is two halves: half the wergild of the male and half the wergild of the female; and her wergild is complete.

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Aban, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Muhammad ibn Abi Hamza, from Dawud ibn Farqad, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: A woman came and sought redress against a Bedouin who had terrified her, causing her to miscarry a fetus. The Bedouin said, 'I did not shout loudly, nor was I fully conscious (of the impact), and the like of it is excused.' The Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) said, 'Be silent! The compensation for your shouting is upon you: a slave or a slave-girl.'

Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Ali ibn Abi Hamza, from Abu Baseer, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: If a man strikes the belly of a pregnant woman, and she miscarries what is in her belly as a stillborn, then upon him is the fine of a male or female slave, which he must pay to her.

Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad and Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father, both together, from Ibn Mahboub from Nu'aym ibn Ibrahim from Abu Sayyar from Abu Abdillah (Allah) (peace be upon him) Regarding a man who killed the foetus of a slave-girl belonging to others, which was in her womb, he (peace be upon him) said: If it died in her womb after he had struck her, then upon him is half of a tenth of the value of its mother; and if he struck her and she miscarried it alive and then it died, then upon him is a tenth of the value of its mother.

Ibn Mahboub, from Ali ibn Ri'ab, from Abu Ubayda, from Abu Ja'da, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) Regarding a woman who drank medicine while pregnant to abort her child, so she miscarried. He said: If it was bone with flesh grown upon it, and its hearing and sight had been pierced, then upon her is its wergild, to be submitted to its father. He said: And if it was a foetus, a clot or a lump, then upon her is forty Dinars or a ghurrah, to be submitted to its father. I said: So she does not inherit from her child from its wergild? He said: No, because she killed it.

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Al-Nawfali, from Al-Sakuni, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: Rasool-Allah (peace be upon him and his family) judged regarding the foetus of Al-Hilaliya when she was pelted by a rock, so she miscarried what was in her belly, a compensation of a (male) servant, or a (female) servant.

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umeyr, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, from a man, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: I said to him, 'When a man strikes a woman and she drops the seed,' he said, 'Upon him is twenty Dinars. So if it was a clot, then upon him is forty Dinars; and if it was a lump, then upon him is sixty Dinars; and if it was bones, then upon him is the wergild.'

Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Muhammad ibn Ismail, from Salih ibn Uqba, from Suleyman ibn Salih, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding the seed (nutfah) is twenty dinars, and regarding the clot (alaqah) is forty dinars, and regarding the lump (mudghah) is sixty dinars, and regarding the bones (azam) is eighty dinars. So when the flesh covers it, it is a hundred dinars. Then it is its wergild (diyah) until it commences (breathing/crying). So when it commences, the wergild is complete.

Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ibn Mahboub, from Abu Ayyub al-Khazzaz, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about the man who strikes the woman, so she drops the nutfah (seed/embryo). He (peace be upon him) said: 'Upon him is twenty dinars.' I said: 'He hits her and she drops the 'alaqah (clot)?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Upon him is forty dinars.' I said: 'So he hits her and she drops the mudghah (lump of flesh)?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Upon him is sixty dinars.' I said: 'So he hits her and she drops it, and bones have formed upon it?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Upon him is the complete diyyah (blood money), and by this Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) judged.' I said: 'So what is the description of the creation of the nutfah by which it is recognized?' He said: 'The nutfah is white, like thick phlegm. It remains in the womb. When forty days pass over it, then it becomes an 'alaqah (clot).' I said: 'So what is the description of the creation of the 'alaqah by which it is recognized?' He said: 'It is a clot like the clot of coagulated blood, solidified. It remains in the womb after its conversion from the nutfah for forty days, then it becomes a mudghah (lump of flesh).' I said: 'So what is the description of the mudghah and its creation by which it is recognized?' He said: 'It is a lump of red flesh in which are green veins, entangled. Then it becomes bones.' I said: 'So what is the description of its creation when it is bones?' He said: 'When it is bones, the hearing and sight are formed for it, and its limbs are arranged. So when it is like that, then regarding it is the complete diyyah.'

Salih ibn 'Uqba from Yunus al-Shaybani who said: I said to Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him), 'If a drop of blood comes out in the seed?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'The drop is a tenth of the seed, regarding it is twenty-two Dinars.' I said, 'So if it drops two drops?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Twenty-four Dinars.' He said. I said, 'So if it drops three?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Twenty-six Dinars.' I said, 'So four?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Twenty-eight Dinars; and regarding five is thirty Dinars; and whatever increases upon the half, so it is based upon the accounting of that until it becomes a clot. So when it becomes a clot, so with regards to it is forty (Dinars).' So Abu Shibl asked him (peace be upon him), and Abu Shibl informed us saying, 'Yunus was present and Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) informed him with the wergilds.' I said, 'So if the seed comes out submerged in the blood?' So he (peace be upon him) said to me: 'So it has clotted, if it was clear blood. Therefore with regards to it is forty Dinars; and if it was black blood, so there is nothing upon it except for the reprimanding, because whatever was from clear blood, so that is for the child, and whatever was from the black blood, so that is from the inside.' Abu Shibl said, 'So if the clot is such that there happen to be in it resembling the veins from the flesh?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Forty-two and the one-tenth.' I said, 'So if the tenth is forty-four?' So he (peace be upon him) said: 'No! But rather, it is a tenth of the lump, because its one-tenth has gone. So whatever is increased, it increased until it reaches the sixty.' I said, 'So what is your view regarding the lump with nodes resembling the dry bones?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'So that is the bone. It is like that in the beginning, what is the beginning of (the formation of) the bones, by five months. Therefore, with regards to it is forty Dinars. So if it is additional, so it increases by four, four, until it is completed at eighty.' I said, 'And similar to that when the bones attain flesh?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'It is like that.' I said, 'So when she is punched (in the belly) and the child is dropped, and it is not known whether it was alive, or not?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Far be it! O Abu Shibl, when five months elapse, so the life has come into it, and the wergild is Obligated.'

Salih ibn 'Uqba from Yunus al-Shaybani who said: I and Abu Shibl were present with Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), so I asked him about these questions regarding the diyyat (blood money). Then Abu Shibl asked, and he was more intense in his questioning, so I left him until he exhausted (the Imam's answers).

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umeyr, from Jameel ibn Darraj, from Ubayd ibn Zurara, who said: I said to Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him), 'The ghurrah (blood money for a fetus) is valued at eight dinars, and it is valued at ten dinars?' So he (peace be upon him) said: 'It is fifty.'

A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from Uthman ibn Isa, from Sama'ah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about a man who struck his daughter while she was pregnant, so she miscarried a dead foetus. The husband of the woman complained against him. The woman said to her husband, 'If there is a wergild (blood money) for this foetus, and I have inheritance rights in it, then my inheritance from it is for my father.' He said: 'It is permissible for her father whatever she gifts him.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Mahboub, from Abdullah ibn Ghalib, from his father, from Saeed ibn al-Musayyab, who said: I asked Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon him) about a man who struck a pregnant woman with his leg, so she dropped what was in her belly as dead. He (peace be upon him) said: 'If it was a nutfah (seed/embryo), then upon him is twenty dinars.' I said, 'So what is the limit of the nutfah?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'It is that which, when it falls into the womb and settles in it for forty days.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'And if she dropped it and it was an 'alaqah (clot), then upon him is forty dinars.' I said, 'So what is the limit of the 'alaqah?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'It is that which, when it falls into the womb and settles in it for eighty days.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'And if she dropped it and it was a mudghah (lump of flesh), then upon him is sixty dinars.' I said, 'So what is the limit of the mudghah?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'It is that which, when it falls into the womb and settles in it for one hundred and twenty days.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'And if she dropped it and it was a nasamah (formed person) with bones and flesh, distinguished limbs, and the spirit of intellect had been blown into it, then upon him is a complete diyah (blood money).' I said to him, 'What do you think if it transforms in her belly to a state, would it be with a spirit or without a spirit?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'With a spirit, other than the old life which is transferred in the loins of men and the wombs of women. And if it were not that there was a spirit in it other than the life, it would not have transformed from one state to another in the womb, and there would not have been a diyah upon the one who kills it while it is in that state.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Mahboub, from Is'haq ibn Ammar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: The commencement of the foetus increases and decreases, but its value is forty Dinars.

Deliberate killing is every [act] in which the striking was intended, so upon him is retaliation (qisas); and rather, the erroneous [killing] is that he intends the thing but hits another. And he said: When he confesses against himself with the killing, he is killed, even if there is no proof against him. .

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: The deliberate act is everything whereby one intends something and strikes it with an iron implement, or with a stone, or with a stick, or with a punch — all of this is deliberate. And the erroneous act is when one intends something but strikes something else.

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Safwan — and Abu Ali al-Ash'ari from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, from Safwan — all together from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to me: 'Does Yahya ibn Sa'id differ from your judges?' I said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Bring me something in which they disagreed.' I said: 'Two youths fought each other in an open space; one of them bit his companion. So the bitten one deliberately picked up a stone and struck with it the head of his companion who had bitten him, splitting it open. He then became afflicted with tetanus and died. That matter was brought before Yahya ibn Sa'id, and he ordered qisas. This was deemed grave by Ibn Abi Layla and Ibn Shubruma, and there was much discussion about it, and they said: This is but an error. So Isa ibn Ali paid the blood money from his own wealth.' He then said: 'Those with us do indeed impose qisas for a deliberate blow; rather, the error is when one intends something but strikes something else.'

They both said: We asked him about a man who struck a man with a stick and did not stop until he died. Should he be handed over to the guardian of the slain one so that he may kill him? He said: Yes, and he should not be left to abuse him with it, but rather the sword should be used upon him.

A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from Dawud ibn al-Husayn, from Abu al-Abbas, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him). He said: I asked him about the error (killing) in which there is blood money and expiation — is it that one intends to strike a man but does not intend to kill him? He said: Yes. I said: (What about one who) shot at a sheep but hit a human being? He said: That is the error in which there is no doubt — upon him is the blood money and the expiation.

Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from Musa ibn Bakr, from Abd Salih (peace be upon him), regarding a man who struck a man with a stick, and he did not raise the stick until he died. He said: He shall be handed over to the guardians of the slain, but he shall not be left to derive pleasure from it; rather, he shall be executed upon him with the sword.

Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Ali ibn Abi Hamza, from Abu Basir, who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'If a man were to strike a man with pottery, or with a brick, or with a plank of wood, and he died, it would be a deliberate (killing).'
The deliberate (killing) is in which he strikes with the weapon or the stick and does not desist from it until he kills; and the error is in which he does not intend it.

If a man strikes a man with a stick or with a rock, and he dies from a single blow before he speaks, then it is quasi-intentional killing (shubh al-'amd), and the blood money (diya) is upon the killer. And if he pounces upon him and hits him incessantly with the stick or with rocks until he kills him, then it is deliberate intentional killing ('amd) for which he shall be killed (in retaliation). And if he strikes him with a single blow, and he speaks (after), then remains alive for a day or more than a day, then dies — then it is quasi-intentional killing.

Humayd ibn Ziyad, from Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Sama'ah, and Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, all together from Ahmad ibn Al-Hasan Al-Mithammi, from Aban ibn Uthman, from Abu Al-Abbas, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I said to him, 'I threw something at a man, the like of which does not kill (but he dies)?' He said: 'This is erroneous (killing).' Then he picked up a small pebble and threw it. I said, 'I threw it at a sheep but it hit a man?' He said: 'This is the error in which there is no doubt, and the deliberate is that which he strikes with something, the like of which could kill.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from al-Husayn ibn Musa, from Muhammad ibn al-Subah, from one of our companions, who said: Al-Rabi' came to Abu Ja'far al-Mansur while he was performing the circumambulation (al-Tawaf). He said to him, 'O Commander of the Faithful, so-and-so, your mawla, died last night, and so-and-so cut off his head after his death.' He became furious and angry. He said to Ibn Shubrumah, Ibn Abi Layla, and a number of judges and jurists with him, 'What do you say about this?' Each of them said, 'We have nothing regarding this.' He kept repeating the question regarding this, saying, 'Shall I kill him or not?' They said, 'We have nothing regarding this.' He said, 'One of them said to him, 'A man has arrived at this moment; if anyone has something regarding this, the answer is with him, and he is Ja'far ibn Muhammad, and he has entered into al-Mas'a.' So he said to al-Rabi', 'Go to him and say to him, 'Had we not known of your preoccupation with what you are in, we would have asked you to come to us, but answer us regarding such and such.' He said, 'So al-Rabi' came to him while he was at al-Marwa, and he delivered the message to him. Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to him, 'You see the preoccupation I am in, and the jurists and scholars are before you, so ask them.' He said to him, 'I have asked them, and there was nothing with them regarding it.' He said, 'So he returned him to him and said, 'I ask you, do not answer us regarding it, for the people have nothing regarding this.' Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to him, 'Until I finish from what I am in.' He said, 'So when he finished, he came and sat by the side of the Sacred Mosque. He said to al-Rabi', 'Go and say to him, 'Upon him is one hundred dinars.' He said, 'So he delivered that to him. They said to him, 'Ask him how it became one hundred dinars upon him.' Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said, 'In the nutfah (seed/drop) is twenty, and in the 'alaqah (clot) is twenty, and in the mudghah (lump) is twenty, and in the 'izam (bones) is twenty, and in the lahm (flesh) is twenty. Then We developed it into another creation, and this is a dead person in the status of what it was before the soul was blown into it in the belly of its mother, a fetus.' He said, 'So he returned to him and informed him of the answer. They were amazed by that and said, 'Return to him and ask him about

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umeyr, from Jameel, from one of our companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), that he said: Cutting the head of the deceased is harsher (more severe) than cutting the head of the living.

Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from the one who informed him, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I said, 'A man cuts off the head of a deceased person.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'The sanctity of the deceased is like the sanctity of the living.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Muhammad ibn Hafs, from Al-Husayn ibn Khalid, who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) was asked about a man who cut off the head of a dead man, so he (peace be upon him) said: 'Indeed, Allah (Exalted and Majestic) sanctified the dead from it just as He sanctified the living from it. So whoever does with the dead an act that would be a violation of the living soul if done to the living, upon him is the blood money (diyah).' So I asked Abu Al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about that, so he (peace be upon him) said: 'Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) spoke truthfully. Thus spoke the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family).' I said: 'So whoever cuts off the head of a dead man, or pierces his belly, or does with him what constitutes a violation of the living soul, is upon him the complete blood money of the soul?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'No, but its blood money is the blood money of the foetus in the belly of its mother, before the spirit is breathed into it, and that is one hundred dinars, and it is for its inheritors, while the blood money of this one (the dead man) is for him, not for the inheritors.' I said: 'So what is the difference between the two?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'The foetus is a matter of the future, its benefit is hoped for, and this one has passed and its benefit has gone. So when he is mutilated after his death, his blood money becomes for the mutilation for him, not for someone else. It is used to perform Hajj on his behalf, and the doors of goodness and righteousness are opened with it, from charity or other than it.' I said: 'So if a man intends to dig a grave for him in order to wash him in the grave, and the man shovels from what he digs, and the shovel in his hand touches his belly so it pierces it, so what is upon him?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'When it is like that, so it is a mistake (accidental), and its expiation is the freeing of a neck, or fasting for two consecutive months, or charity upon sixty poor people, a Mudd for each poor person, by the Mudd of the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family).'

A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from Uthman ibn Isa, from Sama'ah who said: I asked him (peace be upon him) about the man who digs a well in his house or in his land. He said: As for what he digs in his own property, there is no liability upon him; and as for what he digs in the road or in what he does not own, he is liable for whatever falls into it.

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yunus, from Zurara, from Sama'ah, similar to it. Ali, from his father, from Ibn Abu Umeyr, from Hammad, from Al-Halby, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him). He said: I asked him about the thing which is placed on the road, so the animal passes by, so it panics and fells its rider. So he said: Everything which harms the Muslims on the road, so its owner is responsible for what (harm) it causes.

Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Nu'man, from Abu al-Subbah al-Kinanī, who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'Whoever causes harm with something from the roads of the Muslims, he is responsible for it.'

Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Mahboub, from Abu Ayoub, from Sama'ah who said: I asked Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) about the man who digs a well in his house or in his property. He (peace be upon him) said: 'Whatever he dug in his house or in his property, there is no liability upon him, and whatever he dug in the road or in other than his property, he is liable for whatever falls into it.'

A number of our companions, from Sahl bin Ziyad, from Ibn Abi Nasr, from Dawud bin Sirhan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding a man who carried provisions on his head, and they struck a person so he died, or something broke from him. He (peace be upon him) said: 'He is responsible (liable for compensation).'

Sahl and Ibn Abi Najran, both together, from Ibn Abi Nasr, from Musanna al-Hannat, from Zurara, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: If a man were to dig a well in his house, then a man enters and falls into it, there is nothing upon him, and no responsibility (guarantee), but he should cover it.

Ibn Abi Najran, from Musanna Al-Hannat, from Zurara, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I said to him, 'A man dug a well in land that was not his own, and a man passed by it and fell into it.' He said, 'Upon him is the liability (damages), because everyone who digs in what is not his own property, upon him is the liability.

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Al-Nawfali, from Al-Sakuni, from Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'Whoever extracts a water spout, or a toilet (enclosure), or fixes a peg, or fastens an animal, or digs a well in the road of the Muslims, and something is damaged, then he is responsible for it.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yunus, from a man, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), that he said: The cattle of the livestock: its owner is not liable for any compensation as long as they are left free to roam.

Yunus narrated from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from al-Ala' ibn al-Fudayl, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), that he was asked about a man who travels on a road of the Muslims upon his animal, so it hits with its leg. So he (peace be upon him) said: 'There is no liability upon him for what it hits with its leg, and there is liability upon him for what it hits with its hand, and when it stops, then upon him is what it hits with its hand and its leg, and if he is driving it, then upon him is what it hits with its hand and its leg as well.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umeyr, from Hammad, from Al-Halby, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), that he was asked About a man who passes on a road from the roads of the Muslims, so his animal hits a person with its leg. He (peace be upon him) said: There is no liability upon him for what it hit with its leg, but there is liability upon him for what it hit with its hand, because its leg is behind him if he is riding, and if he was guiding it, then he controls its hand by the Permission of Allah, placing it wherever he wishes. He said: And he was asked about a camel that was in heat, so it went out from the house and killed a man. So the brother of the man came and struck the stallion with the sword and slew it. He (peace be upon him) said: The owner of the camel is responsible for the blood money, and he takes the price of his camel. And about a man who causes a man to flee, so he slays him, and his animal slays another man. He (peace be upon him) said: He is responsible for whatever was from something.

A number of our companions, from Sahl bin Ziyad and Muhammad bin Yahya, from Ahmad bin Muhammad, all together from Ibn Mahboub, from Ibn Raib, from Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) Regarding a man who carried his slave upon an animal, so it trampled a man. He (peace be upon him) said: 'The fine is upon his master'.

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from a Sheikh from the people of Kufa, from one of our companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him, saying, 'May I be sacrificed for you! A man entered the house of a man, and a dog leaped upon him in the house and injured him.' So he (peace be upon him) said: 'If he was invited, then upon the people of the house is the compensation for the scratch; and if he was notching (injury); and if he was not invited, so he entered (of his own accord), then there is nothing upon them.'

From him, from Abdul Rahman ibn Abi Najran, from Sabbah the Shoemaker, from a man, from Sa'd ibn Tareef the Shoemaker, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: A man came to the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) and said, 'The bull of so-and-so killed my donkey.' The Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) said to him, 'Go to Abu Bakr and ask him.' So he went to him and asked him, and he said, 'There is no qawd (blood money/compensation) upon the animals.' So he returned to the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) and informed him of what Abu Bakr had said. The Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) said to him, 'Go to Umar and ask him.' So he went to him and asked him, and he said the same as what Abu Bakr had said. So he returned to the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) and informed him. The Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) said to him, 'Go to Ali (peace be upon him) and ask him.' So he went to him and asked him, and Ali (peace be upon him) said, 'If the bull was the one who entered upon your donkey in its resting place until it killed it, then its owner is liable (dhamin); and if it was the donkey that entered upon the bull in its resting place, then there is no liability upon its owner.' He said, 'So he returned to the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) and informed him. The Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) said, 'Praise be to Allah Who made from the People of my Household one who judges by the judgment of the Prophets.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yunus, from Ubaydullah al-Halabi, from a man, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) sent Ali (peace be upon him) to Yemen. A horse of a man from the people of Yemen escaped, and it passed galloping by a man, and kicked him with its foot, so it killed him. So the guardians of the killed man went to the owner and seized him, and brought him to Ali (peace be upon him). So the owner of the horse established the evidence in the presence of Ali (peace be upon him) that his horse had escaped from his house and kicked the man. So Ali (peace be upon him) invalidated the blood money (diyah) for their companion. So the guardians of the killed man came from Yemen to the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family), and they said, 'O Messenger of Allah! Ali (peace be upon him) has been unjust to us and invalidated our companion.' So the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said, 'Ali (peace be upon him) is not unjust, and he was not created for injustice. Verily, the Wilayah is for Ali (peace be upon him) after me, and the judgment is his judgment, and the word is his word. And none would repudiate his Wilayah, and his word, and his judgment except an infidel; and none would be pleased with his Wilayah, and his word, and his judgment except a believer.' So when the Yemenis heard the word of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) regarding Ali (peace be upon him), they said, 'O Messenger of Allah! We are pleased with the judgment of Ali (peace be upon him) and his word.' So the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said, 'It is your repentance from what you had said.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umeyr, from Hammad, from Al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: He said: 'Any man who startles another man from a wall, or dislodges him from his animal, so he falls and dies, then he is liable for his blood money; and if he breaks something, then he is liable for the blood money of whatever is broken from him.'

A number of our companions, from Sahl bin Ziyad and Muhammad bin Yahya, from Ahmad bin Muhammad, all together from Ibn Mahboub, from Ibn Raib, from a man, from Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him). Regarding a man who carried his slave upon an animal, so it trampled (someone). So he (peace be upon him) said: 'The fine is upon his master'.

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Fazzal, from Yunus ibn Yaqoub, from Abu Maryam, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said: Amir Al-Momineen (peace be upon him) judged regarding the owner of the animal that he is responsible for whatever it tramples with its foreleg and hind leg, and whatever it kicks with its hind leg; so there is no responsibility upon him except if a human being strikes it.

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Al-Nawfaly, from Al-Sakuni, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) judged regarding a man who entered the house of a people without their permission, so their dog injured him. He (peace be upon him) said: 'There is no liability upon them, and if he had entered with their permission, they would have been liable.'

From him, from his father, from Al-Nawfali, from Al-Sakuni, from Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) that he assigned liability to the guide, the driver, and the rider, so he said: Whatever the foot hits, it is upon the driver, and whatever the hand hits, it is upon the guide and the rider.

Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad and Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, both together, from Ibn Mahboub, from Abdullah ibn Sinan and Abdullah ibn Bukayr, both together, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) ruled regarding a man who was found killed, and it was not known who killed him. He (peace be upon him) said: 'If it was known and he had guardians seeking his blood money, they would be given his blood money from the treasury of the Muslims, and the blood of a Muslim man would not be invalidated, because his inheritance is for the Imam (peace be upon him). Thus, his blood money is upon the Imam, and they pray over him and bury him.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'And he ruled regarding a man who was crushed by the people on Friday in the throng of the people, so he died, that his blood money is from the treasury of the Muslims.'

Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Mahboub, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Sawwar, from Al-Hasan, who said: Indeed, when Ali (peace be upon him) defeated Talha and Al-Zubayr, the people came back in defeat, so they passed by a pregnant woman on the road. She panicked from them, so she cast out what was in her belly alive. It was restless until it died, then its mother died after it. So Ali (peace be upon him) and his companions passed by her, and she was lying there with her child on the road. He asked them about her matter, so they said to him, 'She was pregnant, so she panicked when she saw the fighting and the defeat.' He said, 'So he asked them, which of the two died before its companion?' So they said, 'Her son died before her.' He said, 'So he called for her husband, the father of the deceased boy, so he made him inherit two-thirds of the wergild from his son, and he made the mother inherit one-third of the wergild.' Then he made the husband inherit from his deceased wife half of the one-third of the wergild which she had inherited from her deceased son, and he made the relatives of the deceased inherit the remainder. He said, 'Then he made the husband inherit also from the wergild of the deceased wife, half the wergild, and it was two thousand and five hundred dirhams, and that is because there was no child for her except the one she cast out when she panicked.' He said, 'And he paid all of that from the treasury of Basra.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Fazzal, from Yunus ibn Yaqoub, from Abu Maryam, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: Amir Al-Momineen (peace be upon him) judged that whatever erroneous judgement is made regarding blood (diyah) or cutting (amputation), it is upon the public treasury of the Muslims.

A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Shamoun, from Abdullah ibn Abd al-Rahman, from Misma', from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), that Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) said: Whoever dies in the throng of the people on the day of Friday, or the day of Arafaat, or upon a bridge, not knowing who killed him, so his wergild is from the public treasury.

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Mahbfrom his father, from Ibn Mahboub, from Abu Ayoub, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said: The people thronged on the day of Friday during the emirate of Ali (peace be upon him) at Al-Kufa, so a man was killed, and his wergild was paid to his family from the public treasury of the Muslims.

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from al-Nawfali, from al-Sakuni, from al-Sakuni, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) said: 'In al-ha'ishat (sudden attacks/commotion), there is no diyyah (blood money) paid by the 'aqilah (kin group) and no qisas (retaliation). Al-ha'ishat is the sudden commotion that occurs by night and day, in which a man is struck (wounded) or a corpse falls, and it is not known who killed him and wounded him.' And Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said, in another hadith, narrating it up to Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him): 'So its diyyah is paid from the bayt al-mal (public treasury).'

Ali, from his father, from one of his companions, from Aasim ibn Humayd, from Muhammad ibn Qays, who said: I heard Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) saying: If a man is killed in a town, or near a town, and no evidence is found against the people of that town that he was killed in their presence, then there is no liability upon them.

Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Aban, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), that he said: Regarding a man who was sitting with a group of people and he died while with them, or a man was found among a tribe, or at the door of a people's house, and it was claimed against them (that they were responsible for his death), he said: 'There is nothing upon them, and his blood is not invalidated (i.e., no blood money is due).'

Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Ali ibn Abi Hamza, from Abu Baseer, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: If a corpse is found in a wilderness area, its blood money (diyah) is paid from the public treasury, for the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) used to say: 'The blood of a Muslim man shall not be invalidated.'

A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from Uthman ibn Isa, from Sama'ah ibn Mihran, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about a man who was found killed in a town, or between two towns. So he said: 'Measure what is between the two; whichever of the two is nearer, it is held responsible (for his blood/diyah).'
Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umeyr, from Hammad, from Al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Similar to it

Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn Hadeed and Ibn Abi Umeyr, from Jameel ibn Darraj, from one of his companions, he raised it to Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him). Regarding a man who was killed and had two guardians, so one of them forgave and the other refused to forgive. He (peace be upon him) said: 'If the one who did not forgive wants to kill, he kills, and returns half the blood-money to the guardians of the killed one for the retaliation from it.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, and Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, all together, from Ibn Mahboub, from Abu Wallad al-Hannat, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who was killed and for him were a mother, a father, and a son. So the son said, 'I want to kill my father's killer.' And the father said, 'I forgive.' And the mother said, 'I want to take the wergild.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'So let the son give the mother of the killed one one-sixth of the wergild, and give to the inheritors of the killer one-sixth of the wergild as the right of the father who forgave, and let him kill him.'

Ibn Mahboub, from Abu Wallad, who said: I asked Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) about a man who was killed and had young and adult children. I asked: What is your view if the adult children forgive? He said: He would not be killed, and the forgiveness of the adult children is valid regarding their shares. So when the young ones grow up, it is for them to claim their shares from the blood money.

Ibn Mahboub, from Ali ibn Ri'ab, from Zurara, who said: I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about a man who was killed, and he had a brother in the House of Migration (who had migrated) and a brother in the House of the Bedouins (who had not migrated). I said: 'Do you see, if the emigrant forgives and the Bedouin wants to kill, is that for him?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'It is not for the Bedouin that he kills an emigrant until he emigrates.' I said: 'And if the emigrant forgives, then his forgiveness is valid.' I said: 'So is there for the Bedouin anything from the inheritance?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'As for the inheritance, he has his share from the wergild (blood money) of his brother, if it is taken.'

Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Kufi, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad al-Nahdi, from Muhammad ibn al-Walid, from Aban, from Abu al-Abbas, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: There is neither forgiveness nor retaliation for the women.

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Fazzal, from Yunus ibn Yaqoub, from Abu Maryam, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: Amir Al-Momineen (peace be upon him) judged regarding the one with a share who forgave, so his forgiveness is allowed; and he judged regarding four brothers, one of them forgave, he said: 'He would be given the wergild, and from the remaining ones, (the wergild) would be raised from them by the share of the one who forgave'.

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ali ibn Hadeed, from Jameel ibn Darraj, from Zurara, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), regarding two men killed a man deliberately, and for him were two guardians, so one of the guardians forgave. So he said: 'When one of the guardians forgives both of them, the killing would be staved off from them, and the wergild would be dropped from both of them by the measurement of the share of the one who forgave, and they would pay the remainder from their wealth to the one who did not forgive.' And he said: 'Forgiveness of every one with a share is allowed.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad ibn Uthman, from Al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about the Words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: 'So whoever gives it in charity, it is an expiation for him.' He said: 'It expiates from his sins to the extent of what he forgives.' And I asked him about the Words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: 'But if any remission is made to any one by his (aggrieved) brother, then prosecution (for the blood wit) should be made according to usage, and payment should be made to him in a good manner.' He said: 'It is befitting for the one who has the right that he should not constrain his brother when he has reconciled with him upon the wergild, and it is befitting for the one upon whom is the right that he should not delay his brother when he has the ability to give what he owes, and he should pay it to him in a good manner.' He said: 'And I asked him about the Words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: 'So whoever exceeds the limit after this, he shall have a painful punishment.' He said: 'He is the man who accepts the wergild, or forgives, or reconciles, then exceeds, so he kills. Thus, for him is a painful punishment, just as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, Says.'

Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Ali ibn Abi Hamza, from Abu Baseer, who said: I asked Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) about the Words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: 'So whoever gives it in charity, it is an expiation for him.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'It expiates from him of his sins by the measure of whatever he forgives from injuries or other than it.' He said: 'And I asked him about the Words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: 'So whoever forgives a brother of his, let there be a pursuit according to what is just, and let payment be made to him in a good manner.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'He is the man who accepts the blood money (diyah). It is befitting for the seeker that he should be kind to him, so he does not constrain him, and it is befitting for the sought that he should pay to him in a good manner and not delay it when he is able.'

A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from Abu Jameela, from Al-Halby, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding the Words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: 'So whoever exceeds the limit after this, he shall have a painful Punishment.' A man asked: 'Does he forgive, or take the wergild, then injure his companion (the killer), or kill him, so for him is a painful Punishment?'

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from Abdul Kareem, from Sama'ah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding the Words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: 'So whoever is forgiven something by his brother, then follow it with good conduct and pay it with kindness.' What is that thing? He said: It is the man who accepts the wergild (blood money). So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, commanded the man who has the right to follow it with good conduct and not make it difficult for him, and commanded the one upon whom the right lies to pay it with kindness when he is financially solvent. I said, 'What is your view of His Words, Mighty and Majestic: 'So whoever exceeds the limit after this, then for him is a painful punishment'?' He said: 'It is the man who accepts the wergild or reconciles, then comes after that and tortures or kills, so Allah has promised him a painful punishment.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, and Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, all together from Ibn Mahboub, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj who said: I heard Ibn Abi Layla saying: 'The blood money (diya) in the pre-Islamic period was one hundred camels, and the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) confirmed this. Then he prescribed for the owners of cattle two hundred cows, and for the owners of sheep a thousand mature sheep, and for the owners of gold a thousand dinars, and for the owners of silver ten thousand dirhams, and for the cloth merchants of Yemen one hundred garments.' Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj said: So I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about what Ibn Abi Layla had narrated, and he said: 'Ali (peace be upon him) used to say: The diya is one thousand dinars, and the value of a dinar is ten dirhams, and ten thousand dirhams for the people of the cities; and upon the Bedouin people the diya is one hundred camels; and for the people of the fertile lands two hundred cows or a thousand sheep.'

Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Ali ibn Abi Hamza, from Abu Basir who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: The blood money for the erroneous (killing) when the man did not intend it is: one hundred camels, or ten thousand (dirhams) of silver, or one thousand sheep. And he said: The aggravated blood money (mughallazha) which resembles deliberate killing but is not intentional is higher than the blood money for erroneous killing by the age-categories of camels: thirty-three hiqqah (four-year-old she-camels), thirty-three jadha'ah (five-year-old she-camels), and thirty-four thaniyyah (six-year-old she-camels), all fit for mating with the stallion. He said: And I asked him about the blood money, and he said: The blood money of a Muslim is ten thousand (dirhams) of silver, or one thousand mithqals of gold, or one thousand sheep according to their ages in three (equal) parts, and one hundred camels according to their ages, and two hundred cows.

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from some of his companions, from Abdullah ibn Sinan who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) said regarding the erroneous killing resembling the deliberate — namely killing with a whip, a stick, or rocks — that the wergild for that is made severe. It is one hundred camels, among which are forty pregnant she-camels (khalifa) ranging from a thaniyya (six-year-old) to a bazil of its year (nine-year-old), and thirty hiqqas (four-year-old she-camels), and thirty bint labuns (three-year-old she-camels). And for the purely erroneous (killing), there should be thirty hiqqas, and thirty bint labuns, and twenty bint makhaz (two-year-old she-camels), and twenty male ibnu labuns (three-year-old male camels). And the value of each camel in silver is one hundred and twenty dirhams, or ten dinars; and from sheep, the value of each old she-camel (nab) from the camels is twenty sheep.

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Jamil ibn Darraj, regarding the blood money (diya), he said: 'A thousand dinars, or ten thousand dirhams; and from the owners of garments, garments are taken; and from the owners of camels, camels are taken; and from the owners of sheep, sheep; and from the owners of cattle, cattle.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Jamil and Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The blood money (diya) is ten thousand dirhams or one thousand dinars. Jamil said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: The blood money (diya) is one hundred camels.
I asked Abu Abd Allah (peace be upon him) about a man who is killed during the Sacred Month — what is his diyah? He said: 'A diyah and one-third.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yunus, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from al-A'la ibn al-Fudayl, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), that he said: Regarding the accidental killing, (the diyya is) one hundred camels, or one thousand sheep, or ten thousand dirhams, or one thousand dinars. If (it is paid in) camels, then twenty-five Ibnat Makhad (one-year-old she-camels), and twenty-five Ibnat Labun (two-year-old she-camels), and twenty-five Hiqqah (three-year-old she-camels), and twenty-five Jadha'ah (four-year-old she-camels). And the aggravated blood money for the erroneous (killing) which resembles the deliberate — that is, one who strikes with a stone or a stick, one strike or two, not intending to kill him — then it is in thirds: thirty-three Hiqqah, and thirty-three Jadha'ah, and thirty-four Thaniyyah (five-year-old she-camels), all of them being pregnant and capable of bearing the stallion. And if (it is paid in) sheep, then a thousand rams. And (as for) the deliberate (killing), it is retaliation (qisas) or (according to) the satisfaction of the guardian of the slain.

Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn Hadid and Ibn Abi Umayr together, from Jamil ibn Darraj, from Muhammad ibn Muslim and Zurara and others besides these two, from one of the two (peace be upon them both) regarding the wergild. He said: 'It is one hundred camels, and there are neither dinars in it, nor dirhams, nor anything other than that.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yunus, from some of our companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Whoever kills a believer deliberately, he is subject to retaliation, unless the guardians of the killed one agree to accept the diya (blood money), or they mutually agree on more than the diya or less than the diya. If they do this among themselves, it is permissible, but if they retract, retaliation is applied. And he said: The diya is ten thousand dirhams, or one thousand dinars, or one hundred camels.

Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, and Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father, both together from Ibn Mahboub, from Abu Wallad, from Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) who said: Ali (peace be upon him) was saying: 'The wergild of the erroneous (killing) is to be paid off within three years, and the wergild of the deliberate (killing) is to be paid off within one year.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umeyr, from Hammad, from Al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about the compurgation (sworn oaths), how it was? So he said: 'It is truth, and it is written with us. And had it not been for that, the people would have killed each other, then nothing would remain. But rather, the compurgation is a salvation for the people.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yunus, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, who said: I asked Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) about the compurgation (sworn oaths), was a Sunnah established regarding it? He said, 'Yes.' Two men from the Ansar went out to gather fruit, then they separated, and one of the two was found dead. His companion said to the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family), 'The Jews killed our companion.' The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said, 'Make the Jews swear an oath.' They said, 'O Messenger of Allah! How can we make the Jews swear upon our brother, while they are an infidel people?' He (peace be upon him and his family) said, 'So you all swear an oath.' They said, 'How can we swear upon what we do not know and did not witness?' He (peace be upon him and his family) said, 'So the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) paid his blood money from himself.' I said, 'How did the compurgation come to be?' He (peace be upon him and his family) said, 'Indeed, it is the truth, and had it not been for that, people would have killed one another. And indeed, the compurgation is a safeguard by which people are protected.'

From him, from Abdullah ibn Muskam, from Suleyman ibn Khalid, who said: I asked Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) about the compurgation (sworn endorsements), has the Sunnah flowed regarding it? He said, so he mentioned a hadith similar to the one of Ibn Sinan, and said in his hadith: 'It is the truth, and it is written with us.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Umar ibn Udhaynah, from Bureyd ibn Muawiya, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about the compurgation (sworn endorsements), so he said: 'For all rights, the burden of proof is upon the claimant, and the oath is upon the defendant, except specifically regarding blood (murder)' For the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) was in Khaybar when the Helpers missed a man from among them, so they found him killed. So the Helpers said, 'So-and-so the Jew killed our companion.' So the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said to the seekers: 'Establish two just men from others, I shall retaliate by its entirety. So if you do not find two witnesses, then establish compurgation of fifty men, I shall retaliate by its entirety.' So they said, 'O Messenger of Allah! There are no two witnesses with us from others, and we hate that we swear upon what we have not seen.' So the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) paid the blood money from himself, and said: 'Rather, the blood of the Muslims is saved by the compurgation, so that when the immoral, mischievous one sees an opportunity from his enemy, he restrains himself in fear of the compurgation that he himself would be killed by it, so he refrains from killing him. Or else the defendant would swear an oath of compurgation of fifty men,

Abu Ali Al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn al-Jabbar, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Ibn Bukayr, from Abu Baseer, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: Indeed, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, judged regarding your blood (lives) with a ruling different from what He judged regarding your wealth. He judged regarding your wealth that the burden of proof is upon the claimant and the oath is upon the defendant; and He judged regarding your blood that the burden of proof is upon the one against whom it is claimed and the oath is upon the one who claims, so that the blood of a Muslim is not lost.

Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Ali ibn Abi Hamza, from Abu Baseer, who said: I asked Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) about al-qasamah (compurgation), where did its beginning come from? He (peace be upon him) said: It was from the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family). When it was after the conquest of Khaybar, a man from the Ansar was left behind from his companions, so they returned seeking him and found him covered in his blood, killed. So the Ansar came to the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) and said: O Messenger of Allah, the Jews have killed our companion. He (peace be upon him) said: Let fifty men from you swear that they killed him. They said: O Messenger of Allah, how can we swear upon what we have not seen? He (peace be upon him) said: Then let the Jews swear. They said: O Messenger of Allah, who would believe the Jews? He (peace be upon him) said: I will then pay your companion's blood money. So I said to him: How is the ruling? He (peace be upon him) said: Indeed, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, ruled regarding blood what He did not rule regarding anything from the rights of people, due to His honoring of blood. If a man were to claim upon a man ten thousand dirhams, or less than that, or more, the oath would not be for the claimant, and the oath would be upon the defendant. So when the man claims upon the people with blood that they killed him, the oath is for the claimant of the blood before the defendant. Thus, it is upon the claimant to bring fifty men who swear that so-and-so killed so-and-so, and he is handed over to them, the one against whom the oath was taken. If they wish, they may pardon him; and if they wish, they may kill him; and if they wish, they may accept the blood money. And if they do not swear, then it is upon those against whom it was claimed that fifty of them swear: We did not kill him, nor did we know his killer. If they do that, the people of the town in which he was found among them pay his blood money; and if he was in a wilderness land, his blood money is paid from the public treasury. Indeed, the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) says: The blood of a Muslim man shall not be invalidated.

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Fazzal and Muhammad ibn Isa, all from Al-Reza (peace be upon him), and a number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Al-Hasan ibn Zareef, from his father Zareef ibn Nasih, from Abdullah ibn Ayoub, from Abu Amr al-Mutatabbib, who said: I presented to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) what Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) had issued verdicts regarding the blood money (diyat). Among what he issued verdicts on, he issued a verdict regarding the body and made it six obligations: the self, the sight, the hearing, the speech, the deficiency of the voice from croaking and hoarseness, and the paralysis of the two hands and the two legs. Then he made for each of these a compurgation (qasamah) according to the amount the blood money reached. He made for the self in case of deliberate killing fifty men, and for the self in case of accidental killing twenty-five men. And for whatever of the injuries reached a blood money of one thousand dinars, he made six persons. And whatever was less than that, it is by calculation from six persons. And the compurgation is for the self, the hearing, the sight, the intellect, the voice from croaking and hoarseness, and the deficiency of the two hands and the two legs; so it is from the six parts of the man.
