The right of the offering (hady) is that you desire God through it, and do not desire His creation through it; you desire through it only to be exposed to God's mercy and the deliverance of your spirit on the day you encounter Him.

As for the right of the possessor of authority (sultan), is that you know that you have been made a trial for him, and that he is being tested through you by the authority God has given him over you. And it is upon you not to expose yourself to his displeasure, thereby casting yourself by your own hands into destruction, and becoming his partner in the evil that comes to you from him.

And as for the right of the one who trains you through knowledge, magnifying him, respecting his sessions, listening well to him, and attending to him with devotion. You should not raise your voice toward him. You should never answer anyone who asks him about something, in order that he may be the one who answers. You should not speak to anyone in his session nor speak ill of anyone with him. If anyone ever speaks ill of him in your presence, you should defend him. You should conceal his faults and make manifest his virtues. You should not sit with him in enmity or show hostility toward him in friendship. If you do all of this, God's angels will give witness for you that you went straight to him and learned his knowledge for God's sake, not for the sake of the people.

And as for the right of your master/owner through property, it is that you obey him and do not disobey him, except in what displeases God, Exalted and Mighty, for there is no obedience to a creature in the disobedience of the Creator.

As for the rights of your subjects through authority, it is that you should know that they have become your subjects due to their weakness and your strength. Hence it is incumbent upon you to act with justice toward them and to be like a compassionate father toward them. You should forgive them their ignorance and not hurry them to punishment, and you should thank God, the Mighty and Majestic, for the power over them which He has given you.

And as for the right of your subjects through knowledge, is that you should know that God, the Mighty and Majestic, made you a caretaker over them only through the knowledge He has given you and His storehouses which He has opened up to you. If you do well in teaching the people, not treating them roughly or annoying them, then God will increase His bounty toward you. But if you withhold your knowledge from people or treat them roughly when they seek knowledge from you, then it will be God's right to deprive you of knowledge and its splendour and to make you fall from your place in people's hearts.

And as for the right of the wife, it is that you know that God, the Mighty and Majestic, made her for you a repose and a comfort; so you should know that this is a favour from God upon you, and thus honour her and treat her gently. And although your right upon her is more incumbent, she has a right upon you that you show her mercy because she is your prisoner, and you feed her and clothe her. And if she is ignorant, you should pardon her.

As for the right of your slave (mamluk), is that you should know that he is the creature of your Lord, the son of your father and mother, and your flesh and blood. You own him, but you did not make him; God made him. You did not create any one of his limbs, nor do you provide him with his sustenance; on the contrary, God gives you the sufficiency for that. Then He subjugated him to you, entrusted him to you, and deposited him with you so that you may be safeguarded by the good you give to him. So act well toward him, just as God has acted well toward you. If you dislike him, replace him, but do not torment a creature of God. And there is no strength save in God.

As for the right of your mother, that you know that she carried you where no one carries anyone, she gave you of the fruit of her heart that which no one gives to anyone, and she protected you with all her limbs. She did not mind going hungry while feeding you, being thirsty while giving you drink, being naked while clothing you, being in the sun while shading you, and forsaking sleep for your sake. She protected you from heat and cold, so that you might belong to her. Indeed, you cannot fulfill her gratitude except with the help and success of God.

And as for the right of your father, it is that you know that he is your root, and that without him you would not have been. So whatever you see in yourself that pleases you, know that your father is the root of the blessing upon you in it, and praise God and thank Him to the extent of that, and there is no strength except with God.

As for the right of your child, know that he is from you and is ascribed to you in the immediate affairs of this world, both for his good and his evil. And you are questioned about what was entrusted to you regarding him: good upbringing, guiding him to his Lord, and assisting him in obeying Him. So act in his affairs as one who knows he will be rewarded for doing good to him and punished for doing evil to him.

As for the right of your master (mawla) who has favoured you, is that you know that he has spent his property for you and brought you out of the abasement and estrangement of bondage to the exaltation and comfort of freedom. He has freed you from the captivity of possession and loosened the bonds of slavehood from you. He has brought you out of prison, given you ownership of yourself, and given you leisure to worship your Lord. and that he is the closest of God's creatures to you in your life and your death and that aiding him with your life and what he needs from you is incumbent upon you. And there is no strength save in God.

As for the right of your slave whom you have favoured [by freeing him], is that you know that God, the Mighty and Majestic, made your freeing him a means of access to Him and a veil against the Fire, and that your immediate reward is to inherit from him, if he does not have any maternal relatives, as a compensation for the property you have spent for him, and your ultimate reward is the Garden.

As for the right of the one who does a kindly act toward you, is that you thank him and mention his kindness; you spread good words about him, and you sincerely supplicate for him between you and God Almighty. For if you do that, you have thanked him secretly and openly. Then, if you are able to repay him one day, you repay him.

And as for the right of the mu'adhdhin, it is that you know that he is reminding you of your Lord, calling you to your good fortune, and helping you to accomplish what God has made obligatory upon you, so thank him for that just as you thank one who does good to you.

The right of your imam in your ritual prayer is that you know that he has taken on the role of mediator between you and your Lord, may He be exalted, and he speaks for you while you do not speak for him, and he supplicates for you while you do not supplicate for him, and he spares you the terror of standing before God, may He be exalted. If there is any deficiency, it is his alone and not yours; but if it is complete, you are his partner, and he has no superiority over you. So protect yourself through him, and protect your prayer through his prayer, and thank him to the measure of that.

And as for the right of your sitting companion, it is that you treat him mildly, show fairness toward him while vying with him in discourse, and do not stand up from sitting with him without his permission. But it is permissible for him who sits with you to leave without asking your permission. You should forget his slips and remember his good qualities, and you should tell nothing about him but good.

As for the right of your neighbour, is that you guard him when he is absent, honour him when he is present, and aid him when he is wronged. You do not pursue anything of his that is shameful; if you know of any evil from him, you conceal it. If you know that he will accept your counsel, you counsel him in that which is between him and you. You do not forsake him in difficulty, you release him from his stumble, you forgive his sin, and you associate with him generously. And there is no strength save in God.

As for the right of the companion is that you accompany him with bounty and fairness, honour him as he honours you, and do not let him be the first to act with generosity; if he is the first, you repay him. You wish for him as he wishes for you, and you restrain him from any act of disobedience he might attempt. Be a mercy for him, not a chastisement. And there is no strength save in God.

And as for the right of the partner, if he is absent, suffice him [in his affairs], and if he is present, show regard for him. Do not make a decision without his decision, and do not act on your own opinion without consulting him. Guard his property for him, and do not betray him in that which is difficult or of little importance of his affairs, for God's hand is above the hands of the two partners as long as they do not betray each other. And there is no strength save in God.

As for the right of your property, is that you take it only from what is lawful, and spend it only in what is proper, and do not prefer above yourself those who will not praise you. Act with it in obedience to your Lord and do not be miserly with it, lest you fall back into regret and remorse while suffering the ill consequence. And there is no strength save in God.
As for the right of your creditor who demands his due: if you are wealthy, pay him back; and if you are in straitened circumstances, satisfy him with good words and send him away with gentleness.
The right of the associate (khalit) is that you neither mislead him, nor act dishonestly toward him, nor deceive him, and you fear God in his affair.

The right of the adversary who has a claim against you is that, if what he claims against you is true, you give witness to it against yourself, and you do not wrong him and you give him his full due. If what he claims against you is false, you act with kindness toward him and you show nothing in his affair other than kindness; you do not displease your Lord in his affair. And there is no strength save in God.
The right of the one who seeks advice (mustashir) is that, if you know he has a good opinion, you advise him to follow it, and if you do not know, you direct him to someone who does.

The right of the counselor is that you act gently toward him and give ear to him. If he presents you with the right course, you praise God, but if he does not agree with you, you show compassion toward him and make no accusations against him; you consider him to have made a mistake, and you do not take him to task for that, unless he should be deserving of accusation. Then attach no more importance to his affair. And there is no strength save in God.

The right of the elder is that you show him reverence because of his age, and honor him because he entered Islam before you, and refrain from confronting him in a dispute, and do not precede him in a path, nor go ahead of him, and do not consider him foolish; and if he acts foolishly toward you, you bear with him and honor him because of the right of Islam and its sanctity.
The right of the younger one is compassion toward him through teaching him, pardoning him, covering his faults, kindness toward him, and helping him.
The right of the petitioner (sa'il) is to give him according to the measure of his need.
The right of the one from whom you ask is that if he gives, you accept from him with gratitude and recognition of his bounty, and if he withholds, you accept his excuse.
The right of him through whom God makes you happy is that you first praise God, then you thank him.

The right of him who does evil to you is that you pardon him. But if you know that your pardon will harm him, you defend yourself. God says, 'Whosoever defends himself after he has been wronged - against them there is no way.'

The right of the people of your creed is harbouring safety for them, compassion toward them, kindness toward their evildoer, treating them with friendliness, seeking their well-being, thanking their good-doer, and keeping harm away from them. You should love for them what you love for yourself and dislike for them what you dislike for yourself. Their old men stand in the place of your father, their youths in the place of your brothers, their old women in the place of your mother, and their young ones in the place of your children.
The right of the people under the protection [of Islam] (dhimma) is that you accept from them what God has accepted from them and you do no wrong to them as long as they fulfil God's covenant.

Said Sheikh Abu Ja'far al-Tusi — student of the one described — in al-Fihrist: Among the theologians of the Imamiyya. The leadership of the Imamiyya in his time culminated in him. He was preeminent in knowledge and the craft of kalam. He was a faqih of the highest rank in it, of excellent sagacity, precise in intelligence, and quick with answers. And he said in his Rijal, in the section of those who did not narrate from them, peace be upon them: Eminent, trustworthy.

Al-Sharif Abu Ya'la al-Ja'fari (may God have mercy on him) — the successor of the described Sheikh, his student who sat in his place after him, and his son-in-law — said: The Sheikh would not sleep at night except for a brief doze, then he would rise to pray, or to read and study, or to teach, or to recite the Quran.

And al-Najashi, may God have mercy on him, said in his Rijal: 'Our sheikh and teacher, may God be pleased with him — his excellence is more renowned than can be described in fiqh, kalam, hadith narration, trustworthiness, and knowledge.'

Ibn al-Nadim said in al-Fihrist: '(Abu Abdallah — in our era the leadership of the Shia theologians has come to rest with him; he is foremost in the craft of kalam according to the school of his companions, of subtle perception and sharp-mindedness — I observed him and found him to be brilliant...)' He also said in another place: '(In our time, the leadership of his companions from the Imami Shia has come to rest with him — in fiqh, kalam, and the transmitted traditions...)'

Al-Khatib al-Baghdadi stated in his history ('the sheikh of the Rafida...') — and so on to the end of his remarks, in which he bore down unfairly against the Sheikh — we deem ourselves too dignified to transmit it, for it reveals his own foolishness. And this nonsense of his is not at all strange coming from him, once we know that — as Ibn Taghri Birdi said about him in al-Nujum al-Zahira, being one of those who recognized al-Khatib's stupidity, stubbornness, and ill judgment — ('that he would attack the prominent ascetic scholars with words that cast them out of Islam, by means of that malicious tongue'). For this reason we have omitted the rest of his words; for he attacked the Sheikh with criticism of incomparable foolishness and unparalleled impudence. Sufficient for him from all of that is the ill repute and infamy he has earned, and sufficient for our Sheikh — whose biography we are recording — is the fine account that is spoken of him and the shining pages of his works that history has immortalized with pride.

Al-Dhahabi said in his Mizan, vol. 3, p. 129: Abu Abd Allah ibn al-Mu'allim the Rafidi, surnamed Sheikh al-Mufid — he has many compilations; he died in the year 413, and he was possessed of greatness and grandeur in the Buyid state. And he also said (p. 131): Sheikh al-Mufid, the scholar of the Rafida — Abu Abd Allah ibn al-Mu'allim, possessor of compilations... numbering two hundred works... He wielded great power by virtue of 'Adud al-Dawla. Eighty thousand Rafidis escorted his funeral. He died in the year 413.

Abu Hayyan al-Tawhidi said in Al-Imta' wa al-Mu'anasa, vol. 1, p. 141: "As for Ibn al-Mu'allim, he is eloquent of tongue and skilled in dialectical disputation, patient against his opponent, resourceful in stratagems, discreet in secrets, and beautiful in public conduct."

Ibn al-Athir said in his al-Kamil, vol. 9, p. 113; Abu al-Fida' in his Tarikh, vol. 2, p. 154; and Ibn al-Wardi in his Tarikh, vol. 1, p. 339, in the events of the year 413: (And in it, Abu 'Abd Allah ibn al-Mu'allim, the jurist of the Imamiyyah, passed away, and [there was] the elegy of al-Murtada.)

And al-Imad al-Hanbali said in Shadharat al-Dhahab, Vol. 3, p. 199: al-Mufid, Abu Abdallah Muhammad ibn Muhammad ibn al-Nu'man al-Baghdadi al-Karkhi, also known as Ibn al-Mu'allim — the scholar of the Shia, the imam of the Rafidah, and the author of numerous compilations.

Ibn Abi Tayy al-Halabi said in the History of the Imamiyya: (He is a sheikh from among the sheikhs of the Sufis, the tongue of the Imamiyya, the chief of kalam, fiqh, and dialectics. He used to debate the adherents of every creed while holding great standing in the Buyid state. He was generous in charitable donations, great in humility, abundant in salat and sawm, and excellent in dress.)

Al-Yafi'i said in Mir'at al-Jinan, vol. 3, p. 28: (The scholar of the Shia and the Imam of al-Rafida — possessor of many compositions, their Sheikh known as al-Mufid and also as Ibn al-Mu'allim, proficient in kalam, jadal, and fiqh; and he used to debate the people of every creed, with great majesty in the Buyid state...)

Ibn Kathir al-Shami states in Al-Bidaya wa'l-Nihaya, vol. 12, p. 15: (He was) the Sheikh of the Imami Rafidis, their author, and the defender of their hawzah. He enjoyed prestige among the regional rulers (muluk al-atraf), on account of the inclination of many people of that era toward Shi'ism. His scholarly gathering was attended by large numbers of scholars from all sects. Among his students were al-Sharif al-Radi and al-Murtada; and the one who eulogized him — meaning al-Murtada — did so with a qasida (elegy) after his death.

Ibn Hajar said in Lisan al-Mizan, vol. 5, p. 368: (Scholar of the Rafida, author of heretical works — being two hundred compositions in which he criticized the Salaf; he wielded great power due to 'Adud al-Dawla; eighty thousand Rafidis accompanied his funeral procession; he died in the year 413) Then he mentioned the saying of al-Khatib: (He was greatly given to asceticism, reverence, and devotion to knowledge; a group of scholars graduated through his tutelage, and he excelled in the Imami doctrinal school to the point that it was said: 'he has a favor upon every Imam'; his father was a teacher in Wasit and he was born there; he was killed in 'Ukbara; and it is said that 'Adud al-Dawla would visit him at his home and would visit him when he was ill)

And Ayatullah al-Allama al-Hilli said in al-Khulasa: '... Among the most eminent of the scholars of the Shia, their chief and their teacher. Every one who came after him benefited from him. His excellence in fiqh, kalam, and hadith transmission is more famous than can be described. The most trustworthy and the most knowledgeable among the people of his time. The leadership of the Imamiyya in his time culminated in him. He had an excellent mind, sharp discernment, and was always ready with an answer...'

Ibn Dawud said in his Rijal — a manuscript — (The Sheikh of the Imami theologians and jurists; their leadership in knowledge in his time culminated with him; a faqih of fine thought, subtle in intelligence, prompt in response; and his stature is greater than what any praise can express — he has nearly two hundred authored works.)

Ibn al-Jawzi states in Al-Muntazam (vol. 8, p. 11): [He is] the Sheikh of the Imamiyya and their scholar; he authored works according to their school of thought, and among his students was al-Murtada. Ibn al-Mu'allim had a scholarly debate session at his home — in Darb Rabah — which all scholars attended. He had standing with the regional princes by virtue of their inclination toward his school of thought.

Al-Shahid al-Thani said, having written in some of his notes in his own handwriting: The Master, the Imam, the Blessed, the Most Learned, the Most Excellent, the Most God-fearing, the Most Scrupulous — Abu Abdallah Muhammad ibn Muhammad ibn al-Nu'man al-Mufid — may Allah sanctify his soul and purify his grave.

'Alam al-Huda Muhammad ibn al-Fayd al-Kashani states in Nadd al-Idah (p. 315), after mentioning his complete lineage going back to Ya'rub ibn Qahtan, he said: (Abu Abdillah, known as Ibn al-Mu'allim — the chief of the mutakallimun of the Imamiyya and their fuqaha'; the scholarly leadership of their community ended with him in his era in knowledge and jurisprudence (fiqh). He has close to two hundred works.)

And al-Naraqi said in Shu'ab al-Maqal: Sheikh al-Ta'ifa and their leader and their teacher — he possesses illustrious noble virtues, overflowing glories, and manifold excellences… He was the most trustworthy of the people of his era and the most learned among them; the leadership of the Imamiyya devolved upon him in his time.
Al-Zarkali said in al-A'lam, p. 969: ...a great critical scholar to whom the leadership of the Imamiyya came in his time, prolific in writings on usul, kalam, and fiqh...

And Sh. Sami said in Kamus al-A'lam — Turkish — p. 668, the translation of which is: (Abu Abdillah Muhammad ibn Muhammad ibn al-Nu'man al-Baghdadi is among the most celebrated scholars; his honorific title is al-Shaykh al-Mufid. He enjoyed standing and esteem among the Buyid dynasty; 'Adud al-Dawla used to visit him in his home. He has numerous works; he is an ascetic, a devout worshipper, and head of the Shia in Baghdad.)

And Ayatullah Sayyid Bahr al-Ulum said in his Rijali Fawa'id: The Sheikh of the eminent Sheikhs and head of the leaders of the community, the opener of the doors of research through the establishment of proofs, and the crusher — through the eloquent outpourings of his articulate elucidation — of the arguments of the misguided sects, In him were gathered the noble qualities of excellence; to him ended the leadership of all; and all agreed upon his knowledge, his virtue, his fiqh, his uprightness ('adala), his reliability (thiqa), and his grandeur. He was — may Allah be pleased with him — of abundant virtues and plentiful noble merits, sharp of thought, subtle in discernment, ready with answers, ample in transmission, and an expert in rijal (narrator biography), historical reports, and poetry. He was the most reliable of the people of his era in hadith and the most knowledgeable of them in fiqh and kalam; and every scholar who came after him benefited from him…

And said the Seal of the Hadith Scholars, Sheikh al-Nuri, in the Conclusion of al-Mustadrak: 'The Sheikh of the great Sheikhs and the Proof of the noble guiding Proofs, the Reviver of the Sharia and the Obliterator of vile Innovation, the Inspired one of Truth and its Guide, the Beacon of Religion and its Path, the possessor of the well-known Mahdawi tawqi'at upon which the consensus of the Imamiyya has been transmitted, and the one exclusively distinguished by the distinctions and sublime virtues therein, and besides these the manifest karamat, lofty spiritual stations, and numerous, dazzling, and splendid disputations...'
He is Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn ʿAlī ibn al-Hasan al-Tusi, the epithet deriving from Tus, one of the cities of Khorasan.
He is called by the kunya of Abu Ja'far and is titled Shaykh al-Ta'ifa and al-Shaykh without qualification.
He was born in the month of Ramadan in the year 385 [AH].
He came to Baghdad from Khorasan in the year [408 AH], and he was twenty-three years old.

He attended [the sessions of] Sheikh al-Mufid for approximately five years and remained devoted to him until he passed away — may God have mercy on him — three nights having elapsed from the month of Ramadan, in the year 413.

After the death of his teacher al-Mufid, he became exclusively devoted to al-Sayyid al-Murtada for thirteen years, until al-Sayyid [may God have mercy on him] passed away five days before the end of the month of Rabi' al-Awwal, in the year 436 AH.
Al-Sayyid al-Murtada allocated twelve dinars for him every month, from which he managed his livelihood.
The number of his teachers reached more than fifty persons from the notables of both groups.
He became independent in prominence and religious leadership after the death of his teacher al-Murtada, may his secret be sanctified.
The number of his students reached three hundred mujtahids from the Shia (al-Khāṣṣa), and from the Sunni (al-ʿĀmma) their number cannot be counted.

The Abbasid Caliph [al-Qa'im bi-Amrillah, Abdullah ibn al-Qadir billah Ahmad] granted him the Chair of Discourse and Instruction (kursi al-kalam wal-ifada), and this was something they would permit at that time only for the singular, peerless scholar of the age (wahid al-'asr).

His existence weighed heavily upon his adversaries among the people, so they began inciting against him until he was denounced to the Abbasid Caliph [al-Qadir Billah Ahmad]. When [the Caliph] summoned him and questioned him about their denunciation and what they had charged him with, the Sheikh answered him in a manner that the Caliph accepted from him; so [the Caliph] elevated his standing, took revenge upon the informant, and humiliated him.

The enemies of the Sheikh did not cease in their persistent transgression; they used to exploit the masses to incite against him, until they burned his house, his books, and whatever he possessed of the chair of kalam (theology) and teaching.
He remained in Baghdad for twelve years after the death of his teacher al-Sayyid, independently assuming the leadership, then departed from it after that.

He descended to the holy Najaf in the year [448] and he is the first who established the Hawza Ilmiyya there; to him belongs the credit for its establishment. May God preserve it from evils and afflictions.

He (may his secret be sanctified) was the Shaykh of the Imamiyya, their foremost representative, and chief of the sect. Of great rank, great station, trustworthy, reliable, truthful, knowledgeable in hadith, rijal, fiqh, usul, kalam, adab, and all virtues — all of which are attributed to him. He authored works in every field of Islamic science, and he is the refiner of creedal positions in usul and furu', the one who combined the perfections of the soul in knowledge and action.
The number of his works whose names we have identified amounts to more than fifty books in various branches of Islam.
He passed away on the night of Monday, the 22nd of Muharram al-Haram, in the year 460 AH, at the age of seventy-five years.
He was buried in his house, which was converted into a mosque after him according to his will, and his grave today is a well-built shrine visited for blessings in the noble Najaf.

He left behind a son named al-Hasan, known by the kunya Abu Ali and nicknamed al-Mufid al-Thani (the Second Mufid), among the most renowned scholars. He succeeded his father in teaching and issuing legal opinions (fatawa). He passed away in the year 515 AH, and he left behind great works.

Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad informed me, from his father, from Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allāh, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā, from ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥakam, from Sayf ibn ʿAmīrah, from Abī Bakr, who said: I asked Abā Jaʿfar عليه السلام, “What should I do when I become junub?” He said, “Wash your hands and your private part, perform wudu (ablution) as for salat (prayer), then perform ghusl (ritual bath).”

And al-Shaykh—may Allah, Exalted is He, strengthen him—informed me, saying: Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad informed me from his father, from Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from ʿUthmān ibn ʿĪsā, from Samāʿah, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about the Friday ghusl, and he said: “It is obligatory in travel and residence, except that a concession was given to women while traveling due to scarcity of water.” And he said: “The ghusl of janābah is obligatory; the ghusl of the menstruating woman when she becomes pure is obligatory; the ghusl of istiḥāḍah is obligatory if she uses cotton and the blood passes through the cotton, then she must perform ghusl for every two prayers, and for Fajr there is a ghusl. If the blood does not pass through the cotton, then she must perform ghusl once each day and wudu (ablution) for every salat (prayer). The ghusl of the woman in nifās is obligatory; the ghusl of the newborn is obligatory; the ghusl of the dead is obligatory; the ghusl of the one who has washed a dead person is obligatory; the ghusl of the muḥrim is obligatory; the ghusl of the Day of ʿArafah is obligatory; the ghusl for ziyārah is obligatory except in case of illness; the ghusl for entering the House is obligatory; the ghusl for entering the sanctuary is recommended, that one should not enter it except with ghusl; the ghusl of mubāhalah is obligatory; the ghusl for seeking rain is obligatory; the ghusl of the first night of the month of Ramaḍān is recommended; the ghusl of the twenty-first night is sunnah (prophetic tradition); the ghusl of the twenty-third night is sunnah (prophetic tradition), one should not abandon it, because Laylat al-Qadr is hoped for in one of them; the ghusl of the Day of al-Fiṭr and the ghusl of the Day of al-Aḍḥā are sunnah (prophetic tradition), I do not like their being abandoned; and the ghusl of istikhārah is recommended.” So this hadith includes, by the apparent wording, the obligation of the six ghusls mentioned earlier. No one may say that you cannot cite this report as evidence because it includes mention of the obligation of ghusls regarding which you have agreed that they are not obligatory. For if we were left with the apparent wording of the report, we would say that all these ghusls are obligatory; however, reports clarifying these ghusls and that t

And al-Shaykh, may Allah the Exalted support him, informed me from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Ahmad ibn Idris, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yunus, from some of his men, from Abu Abdillah عليه السلام, who said: "Ghusl is in seventeen situations; among them, three are obligatory." So I said: "May I be your ransom, which of them are obligatory?" He said: "The ghusl of janabah, the ghusl of one who has washed a deceased person, and the ghusl for ihram." As for his statement, "and the ghusl for ihram," although according to us it is not obligatory, its meaning is that its reward is the reward of an obligatory ghusl.

And al-Shaykh, may Allah Most High support him, informed me from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan ibn Aban, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from al-Qasim ibn 'Urwah, from 'Abd al-Hamid, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far عليه السلام, who said: The ghusl (ritual bath) for janabah, and the ghusl of Friday, the two 'Ids, the Day of 'Arafah, three nights in the month of Ramadan, when you enter the Haram, when you intend to enter the Mosque of the Messenger صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم, and for the one who has washed the deceased.

And with this chain of transmission, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from Ṣafwān, from Ibn Muskān, from Muḥammad al-Ḥalabī, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: Perform ghusl on the day of al-Aḍḥā, al-Fiṭr, and Friday, and when you have washed a dead person. But do not perform ghusl from touching him when you have placed him in the grave, nor when you have carried him.

Aḥmad ibn ʿAbdūn informed me, from ʿAlī ibn Muḥammad ibn al-Zubayr, from ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥasan ibn Faḍḍāl, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Zurārah, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī al-Ḥalabī, from Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said: "The ghusl of janabah and of hayd is one." He said: And I asked Abā ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام about the menstruating woman: is there upon her a ghusl like the ghusl of the junub? He said: "Yes."

With this chain of narration, from ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥasan ibn Faḍḍāl, from ʿAlī ibn Asbāṭ, from his uncle Yaʿqūb ibn Sālim al-Aḥmar, from Abī Baṣīr, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: I asked him: “Is ghusl (ritual bath) upon her like the ghusl of the junub?” He said: “Yes” — meaning the menstruating woman.

And the Shaykh, may Allah the Exalted support him, informed me from Abū al-Qāsim Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb, from Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn Abī Naṣr, from Muthannā al-Ḥannāṭ, from al-Ḥasan al-Ṣayqal, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: “The menstruating woman performs ghusl with nine ratls of water.” Although the apparent wording of this report is the wording of a statement, what is intended by it is a command, since it is impossible that what is intended by it be mere information; for if information had been intended, it would have been false. And this is like His, the Exalted’s, saying: “And whoever enters it shall be safe.” Its meaning is only: Grant him safety.

With this chain of transmission, from Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, from Hammad ibn 'Isa and Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Mu'awiyah ibn 'Ammar, from Abu 'Abdillah عليه السلام, who said: The woman with istihadah observes her menstrual days, so she does not perform salat (prayer) during them, and her husband does not approach her. When her days have passed and she sees that the blood pierces the cotton, she performs ghusl (ritual bath) for Zuhr and 'Asr, delaying this one and hastening that one, and for Maghrib and the later 'Isha' one ghusl, delaying this one and hastening that one; and she performs ghusl for Subh, stuffs herself with cotton, and binds herself tightly, and does not bend, and she presses her thighs together in the masjid while the rest of her body is outside. Her husband does not approach her during the days of her menstrual period. But if the blood does not pierce the cotton, she performs wudu (ablution), enters the masjid, and performs every salat (prayer) with wudu (ablution); and this one, her husband may approach her except during the days of her hayd.

And the Shaykh, may Allah the Exalted support him, informed me through this chain of transmission, from Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from 'Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from 'Umar ibn Udhaynah, from al-Fudayl ibn Yasar and Zurarah, from one of them both, peace be upon them, who said: The woman in nifas refrains from salat (prayer) for the days of her menstrual periods during which she used to remain, then she performs ghusl (ritual bath) and acts as the mustahadah acts.

Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb narrated from ʿAlī ibn al-Sindī, from Ḥammād ibn ʿĪsā, from Ḥarīz, from Zurārah, from one of them, peace be upon them, who said: "If you perform ghusl after the rising of dawn, that ghusl suffices for janabah, Jumuʿah, ʿArafah, Naḥr, slaughtering, and ziyārah. So when duties owed to Allah come together upon you, a single ghusl suffices for them on your behalf." He said: Then he said, "Likewise, for the woman, a single ghusl suffices for her janabah, her iḥrām, her Jumuʿah, her ghusl from her menstruation, and her ʿĪd." And the report narrated by Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allāh, from ʿAlī ibn Khālid, from Muḥammad ibn al-Walīd, from Ḥammād ibn ʿUthmān, from Muʿāwiyah ibn ʿAmmār, from Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said: I heard him saying: "There is no ghusl upon the woman in nifās during travel." What is meant is only that ghusl is not upon her when she is unable to use water, either because of scarcity of water, fear of cold, or her need for it for drinking; it was not meant that no ghusl is upon her in every circumstance.

Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan al-Ṣaffār narrated from Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā, from al-Qāsim ibn al-Ṣayqal, who said: I wrote to him: May I be made your ransom, did Amīr al-Muʾminīn, may the prayers of Allah be upon him, perform ghusl when he washed the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him and his family, at the time of his death? So he answered him: “The Prophet, peace be upon him and his family, is pure and purified, but Amīr al-Muʾminīn عليه السلام did perform it, and the sunnah (prophetic tradition) has proceeded accordingly.”

With this chain of transmission, from Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb, from Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd and Muḥammad ibn Khālid, from al-Naḍr ibn Suwayd, from Ibn Miskān, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about the ghusl (ritual bath) of the deceased, so he said: “Wash him with water and lotus leaves, then after that wash him a second washing with water and camphor and dharīrah, if it is available, and wash him the third time with plain water.” I said: Three washings for his entire body? He said: “Yes.” I said: Should there be a garment upon him when he is washed? He said: “If you are able, let a shirt be upon him, and wash him from underneath it.” And he said: “I like that the one who washes the deceased should wrap a cloth around his hand while washing him.”

With this chain of transmission, from Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb, from ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from Ḥammād ibn ʿĪsā, from Ḥarīz, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: “Whoever washes a dead person, let him perform ghusl.” He said: “And if he touches him while he is still warm, then no ghusl is upon him; but when he has become cold and then he touches him, let him perform ghusl.” I said: “Then what about one who places him into the grave?” He said: “There is no ghusl upon him; he is only touching the clothes.”

With this chain of transmission, from Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb, from a number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyād, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn Abī Naṣr, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Sinān, from Abū ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said: The one who has washed the deceased performs ghusl. If a person kisses the deceased after his death while he is still warm, then there is no ghusl upon him. But if he touches him and kisses him after he has become cold, then ghusl is obligatory upon him. There is no harm in touching him after the ghusl and kissing him. So what these reports contain of the wording of command regarding ghusl from touching the deceased and washing the dead indicates obligation, because a command by its apparent meaning entails obligation, and one does not depart from obligation to recommendation except with evidence.

As for what Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan al-Ṣaffār narrated from Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Najrān, from a man who narrated to him, who said: I asked Abū al-Ḥasan عليه السلام about three persons who were on a journey: one of them was in janābah, the second was dead, and the third was without wudu (ablution). The time of salat (prayer) arrived, and they had with them only enough water for one of them. Who should take the water and perform ghusl with it, and what should they do? He said: "The person in janābah should perform ghusl, the deceased should be buried, and the one who requires wudu (ablution) should perform tayammum, because ghusl for janābah is an obligation, washing the dead is sunnah (prophetic tradition), and tayammum is permissible for the other." What this hadith contains, namely that washing the dead is sunnah (prophetic tradition), does not conflict with what we have stated, for several reasons. One of them is that this report is mursal, because Ibn Abī Najrān said, "from a man," and did not name him, and it is possible that he was neither trusted nor reliable. Then even if it were authentic, the intent in attributing this ghusl to the sunnah (prophetic tradition) would be that its obligation became known through the sunnah (prophetic tradition), because the Qur'an does not indicate the obligation of washing the dead; rather, we only came to know it through the sunnah (prophetic tradition). We have previously cited the narration of Yūnus from some of his companions, from Abū ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, that he said: "Among the ghusls, three are obligatory." Then he mentioned among them washing the dead, and we have already discussed this report earlier.

And among what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā narrated, from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from al-Ḥasan al-Tiflīsī, who said: I asked Abā al-Ḥasan عليه السلام about a dead person and a junub who came together, while with them there was only enough water for one of them. Which of the two should be given the ghusl? He said: “When a sunnah and an obligation come together, the obligation is begun with first.”

From him, from al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Naḍr al-Armanī, who said: I asked Abā al-Ḥasan al-Riḍā عليه السلام: A group are on a journey, and one of them dies, while among them is a person in janābah, and they have only a small amount of water, enough for only one of the two. Which of them should be given precedence? He said: “The junub performs ghusl, and the dead person is left, because this is an obligation and that is a sunnah.” So the interpretation concerning these two reports is the same as what we presented regarding the first report. And it has also been narrated: “When the dead person and the junub are together, the dead person is given ghusl and the junub performs tayammum.”

I said: A deceased person and a person in janabah come together in one place where there is no water except an amount sufficient for only one of them. Which of the two has more right that the water be assigned to him? He said: “The junub performs tayammum, and the deceased is washed with water.” From his father, from al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan ibn Aban, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from Ibn Sinan, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: “Ghusl is for janabah, the day of Jumu'ah, the day of al-Fitr, the day of al-Adha, the day of 'Arafah at the sun’s decline, for one who has washed a deceased person, when one enters into ihram, upon entering Makkah and al-Madinah, upon entering the Ka'bah, the ghusl of ziyarah, and the three nights of the month of Ramadan.”

And al-Shaykh—may Allah, the Exalted, support him—informed me, from Abū al-Qāsim Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb, from ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Mughīrah, from Abū al-Ḥasan al-Riḍā عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about the ghusl on Friday, and he said: “It is obligatory upon every male and female, whether slave or free.”

And with this chain of transmission, from Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb, from ʿAlī ibn Muḥammad, from Sahl ibn Ziyād and Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from Ibn Abī Naṣr, from Muḥammad ibn ʿUbayd Allāh, who said: I asked al-Riḍā عليه السلام about the ghusl of Friday, and he said: “It is obligatory upon every male and female, whether slave or free.”

With this chain of transmission, from Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb, from a number of our companions, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from ʿAlī ibn Sayf, from his father Sayf ibn ʿUmayrah, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Khālid, who said: I asked Abā al-Ḥasan al-Awwal عليه السلام: How did the ghusl of Friday become obligatory? He said: “Indeed, Allah, the Exalted, completed the obligatory salat by means of the supererogatory salat, and He completed the obligatory fasting by means of the supererogatory fasting, and He completed the wudu (ablution) of the supererogatory by means of the Friday ghusl, for whatever there may be in that of forgetfulness, deficiency in performance, or shortcoming.”

And al-Shaykh, may Allah Most High support him, informed me from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from his father, from Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā, from ʿAlī ibn Yaqṭīn, who said: I asked Abā al-Ḥasan عليه السلام about women: is ghusl of Friday upon them? He said: “Yes.” So if someone says: how do you use these reports as evidence while they imply that ghusl of Friday is obligatory, whereas according to you it is a sunnah (prophetic tradition), not an obligation? We say: what these reports contain of the wording of obligation is intended to mean that it is more appropriate for a person to do it. A thing may be called obligatory when doing it is more fitting, and what indicates this interpretation is that what is intended is not the obligation that it is never permissible to leave under any circumstance.

What al-Shaykh—may Allah the Exalted support him—informed me of, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from al-Hasan ibn 'Ali ibn Yaqtin, from his brother al-Husayn, from 'Ali ibn Yaqtin, who said: I asked Aba al-Hasan عليه السلام about ghusl (ritual bath) on Friday, al-Adha, and al-Fitr. He said: "It is a sunnah (prophetic tradition), and it is not obligatory."

And al-Shaykh, may Allah Most High support him, informed me from Abū al-Qāsim Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from his father, from Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allāh, from Yaʿqūb ibn Yazīd, from Muḥammad ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from ʿUmar ibn Udhaynah, from Zurārah, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about the ghusl of Friday, and he said: “It is a sunnah (prophetic tradition) in travel and residence, except when the traveler fears the cold for himself.”

And with this chain of transmission, from Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from al-Qāsim, from ʿAlī, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام about the ghusl of the two ʿIds: Is it obligatory? He said, “It is a sunnah.” I said: Then [what about] Friday? He said, “It is a sunnah.” So this report indicates that what the hadith of ʿUthmān ibn ʿĪsā from Samāʿah contains regarding the mention of the obligation of the ghusl of the two ʿIds, what is intended by it is what we have mentioned concerning the emphasis of the sunnah.

As for what was narrated by Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Mahbub, from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan ibn 'Ali, from 'Amr ibn Sa'id, from Musaddiq ibn Sadaqah, from 'Ammar al-Sabati, who said: I asked Aba 'Abdillah عليه السلام about a man who forgets the ghusl on Friday until he has prayed. He said: “If it is still within the time, then he must perform ghusl and repeat the prayer; and if the time has passed, then his prayer has been valid.” So this report is to be understood as recommendation, and likewise what has been narrated concerning making up the ghusl of Friday on the following day, and performing it earlier on Thursday if missing it is feared—the proper understanding in it is recommendation, as we have explained. (299) 31. What we have mentioned was narrated by Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Sahl, from his father, who said: I asked Aba al-Hasan عليه السلام about a man who leaves the ghusl of Friday out of forgetfulness or otherwise. He said: “If he was forgetful, then his prayer is complete; and if he was deliberate, then ghusl is more beloved to me, and if he has done so, then let him seek Allah’s forgiveness and not return to it.”

Al-Saffar, from Ya'qub ibn Yazid, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Ja'far ibn 'Uthman, from Sama'ah ibn Mihran, from Abi 'Abdillah عليه السلام: concerning A man who does not perform ghusl on Friday at the beginning of the day—he said: “He should make it up at the end of the day, and if he is not able, then let him make it up on Saturday.”

Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb, from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn, from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Faḍḍāl, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Bukayr, from Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a man who missed the ghusl on Friday. He said: “He performs ghusl in the time between that and the night; and if he misses it, he performs ghusl on Saturday.” Then he said, may Allah the Exalted support him: the ghusl of iḥrām for hajj is also a sunnah (prophetic tradition), without disagreement; and likewise, the ghusl of iḥrām for ʿumrah is a sunnah. The evidence for that is what we have cited from the report from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from al-Naḍr, from Ibn Sinān, from Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, from his statement: “and when he enters into iḥrām.” Since iḥrām may be for hajj and for ʿumrah, it is established that the sunnah in both of them is ghusl. Then he said: the ghusl of the Day of al-Fiṭr and the ghusl of the Day of al-Aḍḥā are sunnah. The mentioned report indicates it, in that he said: “and the Day of al-Fiṭr and the Day of al-Aḍḥā.” Then he said: the ghusl of the Day of al-Ghadīr is sunnah. And we shall mention later, when mentioning the salat (prayer) of the Day of al-Ghadīr, that which indicates that ghusl on this day is recommended and encouraged; and upon it also is the consensus of the rightful sect, not differing concerning that. Then he said, may Allah the Exalted support him: the ghusl of the Day of ʿArafah is sunnah. So the hadith which we narrated from ʿUthmān ibn ʿĪsā, from Samāʿah, includes mention of the ghusl of the Day of ʿArafah. Then he said, may Allah the Exalted support him: the ghusl of the first night of the month of Ramaḍān, and the ghusl of the middle night of it, and the ghusl of the night of the seventeenth of it, and the nineteenth night, and the twenty-first night, and the twenty-third night, are an emphasized sunnah. The report from ʿUthmān ibn ʿĪsā, from Samāʿah, includes mention of these ghusls, as does likewise the report narrated by al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from al-Naḍr, from Ibn Sinān, from Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام; and that also indicates it.

What the Shaykh, may Allah support him, informed me of, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan ibn Aban, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Hammad, from Hariz, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from one of the two عليهما السلام, who said: Ghusl is in seventeen occasions. The night of the seventeenth of the month of Ramadan, and it is the night of "the two groups met." and the night of the nineteenth, in which the delegation of the year is written; and the night of the twenty-first, which is the night in which the awsiya' of the Prophets were struck, and in it 'Isa ibn Maryam عليه السلام was raised and Musa عليه السلام was taken; and the night of the twenty-third, in which Laylat al-Qadr is hoped for; and the two days of the two 'Ids; and when you enter the two sanctuaries; and the day you enter ihram; and the day of visitation; and the day you enter the House; and the Day of Tarwiyah; and the Day of 'Arafah; and when you wash a dead person or shroud him or touch him after he has become cold; and the day of Friday. The ghusl of janabah is obligatory, and the ghusl for the eclipse, when the entire disc is obscured, then perform ghusl. Then he said, may Allah Most High support him: And the ghusl of the night of al-Fitr is sunnah. And that which indicates it.

What the Shaykh, may Allah Most High support him, informed me of, from Abū al-Qāsim Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb, from Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from al-Qāsim ibn Yaḥyā, from his grandfather al-Ḥasan ibn Rāshid, who said: I said to Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام: People say that forgiveness descends upon the one who fasts the month of Ramadan on Laylat al-Qadr. So he said: “O Ḥasan, the worker is only given his wage upon completing his work, and likewise the servant.” I said: Then what should we do in it? He said: “When the sun sets, perform ghusl, and when you have prayed the three rakʿahs, raise your hand and say...” The rest of the hadith. The Shaykh, may Allah Most High support him, said: The ghusl for entering the city of the Messenger صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم to perform an obligatory act therein or a recommended one is sunnah (recommended); the ghusl for entering Makkah for the like of that is sunnah; the ghusl for visiting the grave of the Prophet صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم is sunnah; the ghusl for visiting the graves of the Imams عليهم السلام is sunnah; the ghusl for entering the Kaʿbah is sunnah; the ghusl for entering al-Masjid al-Ḥarām is sunnah; and the ghusl of mubāhalah is sunnah. These ghusls have already been mentioned in the hadith of ʿUthmān ibn ʿĪsā from Samāʿah, and some of them in the hadith of Muḥammad ibn Muslim mentioned earlier, and in those two there is sufficiency from citing other than them, if Allah Most High wills. The Shaykh, may Allah Most High support him, said: The ghusl of repentance from major sins is sunnah.

It is narrated from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام that a man came to him and said: I have neighbors who have slave-girls who sing and play the lute, and sometimes I enter the privy and prolong my sitting there in order to listen to them. He عليه السلام said to him, “Do not do that.” The man said, “By Allah, it is not something that I go to with my feet; rather, it is only hearing that I hear with my ears.” Al-Ṣādiq عليه السلام said, “By Allah, have you not heard Allah saying: “Indeed, the hearing, the sight, and the heart — all of those will be questioned about.” The man said, “It is as though I had never heard this verse from the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, neither from an Arab nor a non-Arab. No doubt, I have abandoned it, and I seek Allah’s forgiveness, Exalted is He.” Then al-Ṣādiq عليه السلام said to him, “Rise and perform ghusl, and pray as much as appears fit to you, for you had been persisting in a grave matter. How evil your state would have been had you died upon that! Seek Allah’s forgiveness, and ask Him for tawbah from everything that He dislikes, for He dislikes nothing but what is vile; and leave the vile for its people, for every thing has its people.” Then he mentioned the ghusl for al-istisqāʾ, and its mention has already passed in the hadith of ʿUthmān ibn ʿĪsā from Samāʿah. Then after it he mentioned the ghusl for the salat of al-istikharah and the ghusl for the salat of needs, and this indicates that.

What the Shaykh, may Allah Most High support him, informed me of, from Abū al-Qāsim Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb, from ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from Aḥmad ibn Abī ʿAbd Allāh, from Ziyād al-Qandī, from ʿAbd al-Raḥīm al-Qaṣīr, who said: I entered upon Abū ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام and said to him: May I be made your ransom, I have devised a supplication. He said: “Leave me aside from your devising. When some matter befalls you, then seek refuge with the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم, and perform two rakʿahs, offering them as a gift to the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم.” I said: How should I do it? He said: “You perform ghusl and pray two rakʿahs.” And he mentioned the hadith to its end. Then Abū ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام said: “I guarantee before Allah that you will not depart from your place until your need is fulfilled.”

With this chain of transmission, from Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb, from Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from ʿAlī ibn Dhuwayl, from Muqātil ibn Muqātil, who said: I said to al-Riḍā عليه السلام: “May I be your ransom, teach me a supplication for the fulfillment of needs.” He said: “When you have an important need to Allah, the Exalted, then perform ghusl and wear your cleanest clothes.” And he mentioned the hadith.

And al-Shaykh, may Allah the Exalted support him, informed me from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan ibn Aban, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Fadalah, from Mu'awiyah ibn Wahb, from Zurarah, from Abi 'Abdillah عليه السلام, concerning a matter which the seeker asks from his Lord. He said: "He gives charity during his day to sixty needy persons, for each needy person one sa' according to the sa' of the Prophet صلى الله عليه وآله. Then when night comes, he performs ghusl in the second third of the night, and he wears the humblest of what he wears." And he mentioned the hadith until he said: "Then when he raises his head in the second sajdah, he performs istikharah of Allah one hundred times, saying..." and he mentioned the supplication. Then he said, may Allah the Exalted support him: The ghusl of the night of the middle of Sha'ban is sunnah (recommended prophetic practice).

Al-Husayn ibn Ahmad al-Maliki narrated to us; he said: Ahmad ibn Hilal al-Abarta'i narrated to us; he said: Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr narrated to us, from Hammad ibn Uthman, from Abi Basir, from Abi Abdillah عليه السلام, who said: "Fast in Sha'ban and perform ghusl on the night of its middle, "that is a lightening from your Lord." "Then he said: And the ghusl of the one making up the salat of the eclipse, due to having deliberately abandoned it, is sunnah (prophetic tradition). This indicates that."

41—What al-Shaykh, may Allah Most High support him, informed me of, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from his father, from al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Ḥasan ibn Abān, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from Ḥammād, from Ḥarīz, from one who informed him, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: “If the moon is eclipsed and the man wakes up but does not perform salat (prayer), then he must perform ghusl (ritual bath) the next day and make up the salat. But if he did not wake up and did not know of the eclipse of the moon, then nothing is upon him except making up the prayer, without ghusl.” And al-Shaykh, may Allah Most High support him, said: The ghusl of the newborn at the time of his birth is a sunnah (prophetic tradition). Its mention has already preceded in the hadith of ʿUthmān ibn ʿĪsā from Samāʿah.

That is indicated by what the Shaykh—may Allah Most High support him—informed me of, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from 'Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Dawud ibn al-Nu'man, who said: I asked Aba 'Abd Allah عليه السلام about tayammum, He said: “'Ammar was affected by janabah, so he rolled about as an animal rolls about. Then the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم said to him, while mocking him: ‘O 'Ammar, you rolled about as an animal rolls about.’” So we said to him: Then how is tayammum? He placed his two hands upon the ground, then raised them, and wiped his face and his hands a little above the wrists.

And al-Shaykh, may Allah the Exalted support him, informed me from Abū al-Qāsim Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb, from ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from Ḥammād ibn ʿĪsā, from some of our companions, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام: That he was asked about tayammum, so he recited this verse: "As for the male thief and the female thief, cut their hands." And he said: "So wash your faces and your hands up to the elbows." And he said: "And wipe over your two palms from the place of the cutting." And he said: "And your Lord is never forgetful."

And with this chain of transmission, from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn, from Ṣafwān, from al-Kāhilī, who said: I asked him about tayammum. He said: He struck the mat with his hand, then wiped his face with it, then wiped his two palms, one of them over the back of the other.

And al-Shaykh, may Allah Most High support him, informed me from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Bukayr, from Zurarah, who said: I asked Aba Ja'far عليه السلام about tayammum, so he struck the earth with his two hands, then raised them and shook them off, then wiped with them his forehead and his two palms once. As for the report which al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from 'Uthman, from سماعة, who said: I asked him, 'How is tayammum?' So he placed his hand upon the earth and wiped with it his face and his forearms up to the elbows. He only intended by that the ruling, not the act itself, because when he wipes the outer side of the palm, it is as though he had washed his forearms in wudu (ablution). Thus, by wiping the two palms in tayammum, there is obtained for him the ruling corresponding to washing the two forearms in wudu (ablution), and this indicates that he did not intend the actual wiping of the forearms.

What al-Shaykh, may Allah the Exalted support him, informed us of, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Fadalah ibn Ayyub, from Hammad ibn 'Uthman, from Zurarah, who said: I heard Aba Ja'far عليه السلام saying: And he mentioned tayammum and what 'Ammar did. So Abu Ja'far عليه السلام placed his two palms upon the earth, then wiped his face and his two hands, and he did not wipe the forearms with anything. Then he said, may Allah the Exalted support him: If his state of hadath is from defecation, he performs istibra' with three pure stones that have not previously been used in removing najasah. He takes one stone from them and wipes the place with it and throws it away, then takes the second stone and wipes the place with it and throws it away, then wipes with the third, following the places of visible najasah and removing it with the stones. It is not permissible for him to purify himself with one stone alone. Then he performs tayammum as we have described: striking the dust with the inner sides of his two palms, wiping his face and the outer sides of his two hands; and by that the ruling of najasah has departed from him, as we have stated before. So all of this, its explanation has already passed in what preceded, and this also confirms it.

What the Shaykh—may Allah the Exalted support him—informed me of, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Safwan ibn Yahya, Fadalah ibn Ayyub, and al-Hasan ibn 'Ali ibn Faddal, from 'Abd Allah ibn Bukayr, from Zurarah, from Abi Ja'far عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about wiping with stones, and he said: “Al-Husayn ibn 'Ali عليه السلام used to wipe with three stones.”

With this chain of transmission, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from Ḥammād, from Ḥarīz, from Zurārah, from Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said: There is no salat except with taharah, and for istinja', three stones suffice you; upon that the sunnah (prophetic tradition) of the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم has proceeded. But as for urine, then it must necessarily be washed.
And with this chain of transmission, from Hammad, from Hariz, from Zurarah, who said: He would cleanse himself from urine three times, and from feces with clods and cloths.

Al-Shaykh, may Allah the Exalted support him, informed me from Abū al-Qāsim Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from his father, from Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allāh, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from some of our companions, who raised it to Abū ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said: “The sunnah (prophetic tradition) in al-istinjāʾ is with three unused stones, and it is followed by water.” Then he said, may Allah the Exalted support him: If the person in a state of ritual impurity due to janābah wishes purification, he performs istibrāʾ before tayammum in the manner we explained previously. Then he strikes the earth with the inner sides of his two palms once and wipes his face with them from the hairline to the tip of his nose. Then he strikes the earth with them a second time and wipes with the left one the back of his right hand, and with the right one the back of his left hand. The ruling of janābah has thereby departed from him, and salat (prayer) has become lawful for him. This is indicated by it.

What al-Shaykh, may Allah the Exalted support him, informed me of, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from his father, from al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Ḥasan ibn Abān, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from Ibn Sinān, from Ibn Muskān, from Layth al-Murādī, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, concerning tayammum. He said: "You strike the earth with your two palms twice, then shake them off, and wipe your face and your forearms with them."

And the Shaykh, may Allah the Exalted support him, informed me from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Isma'il ibn Hammam al-Kindi, from al-Rida عليه السلام, who said: Tayammum is one strike for the face and one strike for the two palms.

And al-Shaykh, may Allah the Exalted support him, informed me from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan ibn Aban, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from al-'Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from one of the two, peace be upon them, who said: I asked him about tayammum, and he said: “Twice, twice for the face and the hands.”

And with this chain of transmission, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from Ḥammād, from Ḥarīz, from Zurārah, from Abī Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said: I said to him, 'How is tayammum?' He said, 'It is one striking for wudu (ablution) and ghusl (ritual bath) from janabah. You strike with your hand twice, then shake them off once: once for the face and once for the hands. And whenever you find water, then ghusl is upon you if you were junub, and wudu (ablution) if you were not junub.'

With this chain of transmission, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Ibn Udhaynah, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about tayammum. So he struck the ground with his two palms, then wiped his face with them. Then he struck the ground with his left hand and wiped with it from his elbow to the fingertips, once over its outer side and once over its inner side. Then he struck the ground with his right hand, then did with his left as he had done with his right. Then he said: “This is tayammum for that in which ghusl is required. And in wudu (ablution), the face and the two hands up to the elbows [are included], and what there had been wiping over is omitted: the head and the two feet are not subjected to tayammum with earth.” As for what this hadith contains, that he wiped from the elbow to the fingertips, once over its outer side and once over its inner side, its meaning is what has previously been mentioned in the interpretation of the report of Samāʿah which ʿUthmān ibn ʿĪsā narrated from him: that what is intended by it is the ruling, not the act itself. It is as though he said: he wiped over the back of his palm, and thereby attained the ruling of one who washed his hand from the elbow, its outer and inner sides. This does not invalidate what we have held. If someone says: The first two reports—one of them from Abū Baṣīr Layth al-Murādī from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, and the second from Ismāʿīl ibn Hammām al-Kindī from al-Riḍā عليه السلام—together with the report narrated by Ṣafwān ibn Yaḥyā from al-ʿAlāʾ from Muḥammad ibn Muslim from one of them both عليهما السلام, do not outwardly indicate that the two strikes or the two times are specifically for ghusl of janābah rather than for wudu (ablution). So from where do you say that it is restricted to the ruling of janābah? Why did you not say, as others have held, that the obligation in wudu (ablution) also is two times? It is said to him: When many reports are established indicating that the obligation in tayammum is once, once, then these reports came containing two strikes, we interpret what contains the ruling of once as referring to wudu (ablution), and what contains the ruling of twice as referring to ghusl of janābah, so that the reports do not contradict one another. Moreover, we have already cited two reports that explain these reports: one of them f

What the Shaykh — may Allah, the Exalted, support him — informed me of, from Abū al-Qāsim Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb, from ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, and ʿAlī ibn Muḥammad, from Sahl ibn Ziyād, all together from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn Abī Naṣr, from Ibn Bukayr, from Zurārah, who said: I asked Abā Jaʿfar عليه السلام about tayammum, so he struck the ground with his right hand, then raised it and shook it off, then wiped with it his forehead and his two palms once.

The Shaykh, may Allah the Exalted support him, informed me from Abū al-Qāsim Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from his father, from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan al-Ṣaffār, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from Ṣafwān, from ʿAmr ibn Abī al-Miqdām, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام. That he described tayammum: he struck the ground with his two hands, then raised them and shook them off, then wiped over his forehead and his two palms once.

And with this chain of transmission, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from al-Qāsim ibn ʿUrwah, from Ibn Bukayr, from Zurārah, from Abī Jaʿfar عليه السلام, concerning tayammum. He said: “You strike the earth with your two palms, then shake them off, and wipe your face and your two hands.” Then al-Shaykh, may Allah the Exalted support him, said: Likewise, the menstruating woman, the woman in post-partum bleeding, and the woman with istiḥāḍah do this in place of ghusl when they do not find water or when its use would harm them.

So al-Shaykh—may Allah the Exalted support him—informed me, from Abū al-Qāsim Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb, from Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from ʿUthmān ibn ʿĪsā, from Ibn Miskān, from Abī Baṣīr, who said: I asked him about a man who was on a journey and had water with him, but forgot it, so he performed tayammum and prayed, then remembered that he had water with him before the time had ended. He said: “He must perform wudu (ablution) and repeat the salat (prayer).” He said: And I asked him whether the tayammum of the menstruating woman and the junub is the same when they do not find water. He said: “Yes.”

Al-Shaykh, may Allah the Exalted support him, informed me from Abū al-Qāsim Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from his father, from Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allāh, from Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Faḍḍāl, from ʿAmr ibn Saʿīd, from Muṣaddiq ibn Ṣadaqah, from ʿAmmār ibn Mūsā al-Sābāṭī, from Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about tayammum in place of wudu (ablution), janābah, and menstruation for women—are they the same? He said: “Yes.” Then he said, may Allah the Exalted support him: The one who enters a state of ritual impurity through sleep, fainting, and al-mirrah performs tayammum as we mentioned in the chapter of one rendered muḥdith by urine and feces, and by that enters into salat (prayer). If these things are among what nullifies taharah (ritual purity), and the one whose taharah is nullified is required to perform tayammum according to what we have mentioned, then there is no difference between his taharah being nullified by one of these things or by urine and feces, according to what we have mentioned concerning the obligation of tayammum upon him. Then he said, may Allah the Exalted support him: Whenever one of those whom we have mentioned finds water after having lacked it, or becomes able to use it, he purifies himself with it according to what he had missed: if it was wudu (ablution), then wudu; and if it was ghusl (ritual bath), then ghusl. The difference between tayammum as a substitute for ghusl and tayammum as a substitute for wudu is what we have explained: that the muḥdith whose purification is required by ghusl, if he is unable to perform it, does tayammum with two strikes, one of them for his face and the second for the back of his hands; while the muḥdith whose purification is required by wudu does tayammum with one strike for his face and his hands. Its explanation has already passed in full, and in it there is sufficiency, if Allah the Exalted wills. Then he said, may Allah the Exalted support him: If water is not found for washing the deceased, the Muslim gives him tayammum just as the living person who is incapacitated by chronic illness is given tayammum when he needs tayammum from his janābah: he strikes with his two hands on the earth and wipes with them his face from the hairline of his head to the tip of his nose, then strikes with them another strike and wipes with them the back of his hands. Then he himself performs tayammum for

Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb, from Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā, from al-ʿAmrakī ibn ʿAlī, from ʿAlī ibn Jaʿfar, from his brother Mūsā ibn Jaʿfar عليهما السلام, who said: I asked him about a man: is it proper for him to insert medicine [into himself] and then perform salat (prayer) while it is still with him? Does it invalidate the wudu (ablution)? He said, “It does not invalidate the wudu (ablution), but he should not perform salat (prayer) until he expels it.”

From him, from Muḥammad ibn Ismāʿīl, from al-Faḍl ibn Shādhān, from Ṣafwān ibn Yaḥyā, from Ibn Miskān, from Muḥammad al-Ḥalabī, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about a man who is in a state of taharah, then takes from his nails or his hair: should he repeat the wudu (ablution)? He said: “No, but he should wipe his head and his nails with water.” He said: I said: They claim that wudu (ablution) is required for it. So he said: “If they dispute with you, then do not dispute with them; say: this is the sunnah (prophetic tradition).”

A man trims some of his hair with his teeth; should he wipe it with water before he performs salat (prayer)? He said: “There is no harm; that only applies in the case of iron.” Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan said: What the first report contains, that he should wipe the place with water, is to be understood as recommendation rather than obligation. That is indicated by the following. (1012) 4. What Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allāh narrated from Ayyūb ibn Nūḥ, from Ṣafwān ibn Yaḥyā, from Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Aʿraj, who said: I said to Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام: I clip my nails, trim my moustache, and shave my head—must I perform ghusl (ritual bath)? He said: “No, there is no ghusl upon you.” I said: Then should I perform wudu (ablution)? He said: “No, there is no wudu upon you.” I said: Then should I wipe water over my nails? He said: “No; it is pure, and there is no wiping required of you.”

Al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from Ḥammād ibn ʿĪsā, from Ḥarīz, from Zurārah, who said: I said to Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام: A man trims his nails, cuts his moustache, and takes from the hair of his beard and his head—does that invalidate his wudu (ablution)? He said: O Zurārah, all of this is sunnah (prophetic tradition), and wudu (ablution) is an obligation. Nothing from the sunnah (prophetic tradition) invalidates the obligation, and indeed that surely increases him in purification.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Fadalah and Muhammad ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Mu'awiyah ibn 'Ammar, who said: I asked Aba 'Abdillah عليه السلام about a man who fiddles with his private part during the obligatory salat (prayer). He said: “There is no harm in it.”

From him, from his brother al-Ḥasan, from Zur‘ah, from Samā‘ah, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdِ اللَّهِ عليه السلام about a man who touches his penis, or his private part, or lower than that, while he is standing performing salat (prayer): should he repeat his wudu (ablution)? He said: “There is no harm in that; it is only a part of his body.”

From him, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from ʿUmar ibn Udhaynah, from Zurārah, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: Nothing makes wudu (ablution) obligatory except feces, or urine, or a passing of wind whose sound you hear, or a silent breaking of wind whose smell you perceive.

From him, from Faḍālah ibn Ayyūb, from Muʿāwiyah ibn ʿAmmār, who said: Abū ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام said: “Indeed, al-Shayṭān blows into the rear of the human being until it is imagined to him that wind has come out from him; and nothing invalidates his wudu (ablution) except wind that he hears or whose smell he finds.”

Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah, from al-Hasan ibn 'Ali, from Ahmad ibn Hilal, from Muhammad ibn al-Walid, from Aban ibn 'Uthman, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi 'Abd Allah, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said: I said to him: I feel wind in my belly until I think that it has come out. So he said, “There is no wudu (ablution) upon you until you hear the sound or find the wind.” Then he said, “Indeed, Iblis comes and sits between the buttocks of a man and breaks wind in order to make him doubt.”

Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb, from ʿAlī ibn al-Sindī, from Ṣafwān, who said: A man asked Abā al-Ḥasan عليه السلام while I was present, and he said: “I have a wound in my anus. I perform wudu (ablution), then do istinjāʾ, then after that I find moisture and yellowness coming out from the anus, so I repeat the wudu (ablution).” He said: “Have you cleansed it thoroughly?” He said: “Yes.” He said: “No; rather, sprinkle it with water, and do not repeat the wudu (ablution).”

From him, from Abū ʿAbdillāh al-Rāzī, from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Abī Ḥamzah, from Sayf ibn ʿUmayrah, from ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar, the client of the Anṣār: that he asked Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about a man—whether it is permissible for him to shake hands with a Magian. So he said: "No." Then he asked him, "Should he perform wudu (ablution) if he shakes hands with them?" He said, "Yes. Indeed, shaking hands with them invalidates the wudu (ablution)." Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan said: This report is to be understood as referring to the washing of the hand, and that may be called wudu, as we have explained, because when a Muslim shakes hands with a kāfir, washing his hand becomes obligatory upon him, as we have explained.

Hariz narrated from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام that he said: If a man has urine and blood dripping from him while he is in salat (prayer), he should take a pouch and place cotton in it, then attach it to himself and put his private organ into it, then pray. He should combine the two salats of Zuhr and 'Asr, delaying Zuhr and bringing 'Asr forward, with one adhan and two iqamahs; and he should delay Maghrib and bring 'Isha' forward, with one adhan and two iqamahs; and he should do that in the morning prayer as well.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Hanan ibn Sudayr, who said: I heard a man ask Aba 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, and he said: “At times I urinate and cannot access water, and that becomes difficult for me.” So he عليه السلام said: “When you urinate and wipe yourself, then wipe your male organ with your saliva. Then if you find something, say: this is from that.”

From him, from Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Faḍḍāl, from ʿAmr ibn Saʿīd, from Muṣaddiq ibn Ṣadaqah, from ʿAmmār ibn Mūsā, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: He was asked about a man who performs wudu (ablution) and then touches the inner part of his anus. He said: “He has invalidated his wudu (ablution). And if he touches the inner part of his urethra, then he must repeat the wudu (ablution). And if he is in the salat (prayer), he cuts off the salat (prayer), performs wudu (ablution), and repeats the salat (prayer). And if he opens his urethra, he repeats the wudu (ablution) and repeats the salat (prayer).”

Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī al-Washshāʾ, who said: I heard Abā al-Ḥasan عليه السلام say: Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام used to say, concerning a man who inserts his hand into his nose and blood reaches his five fingers: He said, “He should clean it, and he does not repeat the wudu (ablution).”

Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Mahbub, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Safwan, from al-'Ala', from Muhammad, from one of the two of them, peace be upon them, who said: I asked him about a man who has sores that keep bleeding continuously: how should he perform salat (prayer)? He said: "He performs salat (prayer), even if the bloods are flowing."

From him, from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn, from ʿUthmān ibn ʿĪsā, from Abī Hilāl, who said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام: “Do nosebleeding, vomiting, and plucking the armpit hair invalidate wudu (ablution)?” He said: “What will you do with this? This is the saying of al-Mughīrah ibn Saʿīd—may Allah curse al-Mughīrah. It is sufficient for you, regarding nosebleeding and vomiting, that you wash it off and do not repeat the wudu (ablution).”

And from him, from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn, from ʿUthmān ibn ʿĪsā, from Samāʿah, who said: I asked him about a man afflicted by dripping from his private part, whether blood or something else. He said: “Let him make a pouch, perform wudu (ablution), and pray, for that is only an affliction with which he has been tried. He should not repeat [the prayer] except due to the hadath from which wudu (ablution) is performed.”

From him, from ʿAlī ibn Khālid, from Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan, from ʿAmr ibn Saʿīd, from Muṣaddiq ibn Ṣadaqah, from ʿAmmār al-Sābāṭī, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said: I asked him about a boil that appears on a man and then bursts while he is in salat (prayer).
