Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub, from al-Abbas, from Abdullah ibn al-Mughira, from Isma'il ibn 'Abbad, from Khirash, from some of our companions, from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I said to him, 'May I be your ransom, indeed these opponents of ours say: When the sky is completely overcast or darkened so that we do not recognize the direction of the sky, we and you are equal in ijtihad (deduction).' He said, 'It is not as they say. If that is the case, let him pray facing four directions.'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Isma'il ibn 'Abbad, from Khirash, from some of our companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): like it. As for what indicates that seeking (carefully) is sufficient in case of necessity, what he narrated:

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Hammad from Hariz from Zurara said: Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: "Determination (of direction) is sufficient always if the direction of the Qibla is not known."

And from him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Uthman ibn Isa, from Sama'ah, who said: I asked him about praying at night and during the day when the sun, the moon, and the stars are not visible. He said, 'Exert your opinion and direct yourself to the Qiblah with all your ability.'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from al-Hasan from Zur'ah from Sama'ah said: I asked him about prayer by night and by day when the sun, the moon, and the stars are not visible. He said, 'Exert your opinion and face the Qiblah with all your ability.' And it is not for anyone to say, 'Why have we interpreted these narrations as applying to the state of necessity rather than the state of choice? And is it not permissible to seek direction at every time when the Qiblah becomes obscured?' Because if we did not interpret these narrations as applying to the state of necessity, there would be no meaning for what we presented from the two narrations that one prays towards four directions. For according to the apparent meaning of these hadiths, seeking direction is sufficient, and one does not need in any case to pray towards four directions, so their content would be nullified entirely. And if we interpret these narrations as applying to the state of necessity and those two hadiths as applying to the state of choice, we would have reconciled them in a way that there is no contradiction between them. And that which indicates what we said, that the meaning of these narrations is the state of necessity rather than the state of choice.

Al-Tatari narrated from Muhammad ibn Ziyad from Hammad from Amr ibn Yahya who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who prayed facing a direction other than the Qibla, then the Qibla became clear to him, and the time for another prayer had already entered. He said: 'He must repeat it before he prays this one whose time has entered.'

And from him, from Muhammad ibn Ziyad, from Hammad ibn 'Uthman, from Ma'mar ibn Yahya, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who prayed facing a direction other than the Qibla, then the Qibla became clear to him, and the time for another prayer had entered. He said: 'He should pray the missed one before praying this one whose time has entered, unless he fears missing the one whose time has entered.' If the meaning intended by those hadiths were not the state of compulsion, then there would be no sense in requiring re-prayer after the time has passed, according to what these two reports contain, because their apparent meaning dictates that whenever he strives for the Qibla and prays, then the time passes, his prayer is sufficient. Al-Shaykh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: And whoever misses the Qibla or is heedless of it, then recognizes that while the time remains, he must re-pray. If he recognizes it after the time has passed, there is no re-prayer upon him for what has passed, unless he prayed facing away from the Qibla, in which case it becomes obligatory upon him at that time to re-pr the prayer, whether the time remains or has passed.

Ali ibn Mahziyar from Fadalah ibn Ayyub from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Abdillah from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "When you pray while facing away from the Qibla, and it becomes clear to you that you prayed while facing away from the Qibla, and you are within the time [of that prayer], then repeat [the prayer]; and if the time has passed for you, then do not repeat."

And from him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hisham ibn Salim, from Sulayman ibn Khalid, who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): A man is in the wilderness of the earth on a cloudy day, so he prays facing a direction other than the Qibla. Then morning comes and he realizes that he prayed facing a direction other than the Qibla. What should he do? He (peace be upon him) said: 'If it is still within the prayer time, let him repeat his prayer; and if the time has passed, his effort (ijtihad) is sufficient for him.'
Al-Tatarī narrated from Muḥammad ibn Abī Ḥamzah from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Miskān from Sulaymān ibn Khālid from Abū ʿAbd Allāh (peace be upon him) Like it.

And from him, from Muhammad ibn Ziyad, from Aban ibn Uthman, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Abdillah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: "When you pray and you are facing away from the Qibla, and it becomes clear to you that you are facing away from the Qibla, and you are within the time [of the prayer], then repeat [the prayer]; and if the time has passed for you, then do not repeat."

Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from Ya'qub ibn Yaqteen said: I asked a virtuous man about a man who prayed on a cloudy day not facing the qibla, then the sun rose while he was still within the prayer time. Should he repeat the prayer if he had prayed not facing the qibla, even if he had exerted himself to determine the qibla? Will his prayer suffice? He said: 'He repeats it if it was within the time; and if the time has passed, there is no repetition for him.'

From him, from Ahmad, from al-Husayn, from Fudaylah, from Aban, from Zurarah, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: When you pray facing a direction other than the Qiblah, and it becomes clear to you before morning that you prayed facing a direction other than the Qiblah, then repeat your prayer.

From him, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from al-Hajjaj, from Thalabah ibn Maymun, from Mu'awiyyah ibn 'Ammar, from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I asked: A man stands in prayer, then looks after he has finished and sees that he has deviated from the Qibla to the right or left. He (peace be upon him) said: 'His prayer is valid, and whatever is between the East and the West is a Qibla.' Ahmad ibn al-Hasan ibn 'Ali, from 'Amr ibn Sa'id, from Musaddiq ibn Sadaqah, from 'Ammar ibn Musa al-Sabati, from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him): Regarding a man who prayed facing away from the Qibla, and he knew while still in prayer before finishing it: He (peace be upon him) said: 'If he was facing somewhere between the East and the West, let him turn his face to the Qibla when he knows [the direction]. And if he was facing the back of the Qibla, let him cut off [the prayer], then turn his face to the Qibla, then commence the prayer anew.' Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, said: I wrote to 'Abdullah ibn Sinan (peace be upon him): A man prays on a cloudy day in an open field of land and does not know the Qibla, so he prays until when he finishes his prayer the sun appears, and he finds he has prayed facing away from the Qibla. Should he consider his prayer valid or repeat it? He wrote: 'He repeats it, as long as the time has not passed. Did he not know that Allah says, and His word is true: "So wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah."'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from Muhammad ibn 'Isa ibn 'Ubayd from Yunus from Aban ibn 'Uthman from Isma'il al-Ju'fi said: I heard Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) saying: 'The Adhan and the Iqamah are thirty-five letters,' so he counted that with his hand one by one: 'The Adhan is eighteen letters and the Iqamah is seventeen letters.'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from al-Nadr from 'Abdullah ibn Sinan said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the Adhan, so he said: 'You say - Allahu Akbar, Allahu Akbar. Ashhadu an la ilaha illa Allah, Ashhadu an la ilaha illa Allah. Ashhadu anna Muhammadan Rasul Allah, Ashhadu anna Muhammadan Rasul Allah. Hayya 'ala al-salah, Hayya 'ala al-salah. Hayya 'ala al-falah, Hayya 'ala al-falah. Hayya 'ala khayr al-'amal, Hayya 'ala khayr al-'amal. Allahu Akbar, Allahu Akbar. La ilaha illa Allah, La ilaha illa Allah.'

Muhammad ibn al-Habbar narrated from Ali ibn al-Sindi, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Ibn Udhaynah, from Zurarah and al-Fadl ibn Yasar, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said: When the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) was taken on the Night Journey and reached the Bait al-Ma'mur, the time for prayer arrived. Gabriel (peace be upon him) called the Adhan and then the Iqamah. The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) stepped forward, and the angels and prophets formed rows behind him. We asked him, 'How did he call the Adhan?' He said: 'Allah is the Greatest, Allah is the Greatest. I bear witness that there is no god but Allah. I bear witness that there is no god but Allah. I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah. I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah. Come to prayer, come to prayer. Come to success, come to success. Come to the best of deeds, come to the best of deeds. Allah is the Greatest, Allah is the Greatest. There is no god but Allah, there is no god but Allah.' The Iqamah is the same as the Adhan, except that in it, 'Qad qamat al-salah' (Prayer has risen) is said twice, placed between 'Come to the best of deeds' and 'Allah is the Greatest, Allah is the Greatest'. The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) ordered Bilal to call the Adhan with this format, and he continued to do so until Allah took (passed away) His Messenger (peace be upon him and his family).

From him, from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan, from Fadala, from Saif ibn 'Amira, from Abu Bakr al-Hadrami, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) and Kulaib al-Asadi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): that he narrated to them the Adhan, so he said: "Allah is the Greatest, Allah is the Greatest, Allah is the Greatest, Allah is the Greatest. I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, I bear witness that there is no god but Allah. I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah. Come to prayer, come to prayer. Come to success, come to success. Come to the best of deeds, come to the best of deeds. Allah is the Greatest, Allah is the Greatest. There is no god but Allah, there is no god but Allah." And the Iqamah is likewise.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Fadala from Hammad ibn 'Uthman from Isḥāq ibn 'Ammār from al-Mu'alla ibn Khunays, who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) giving the Adhan, so he said: 'Allahu Akbar, Allahu Akbar, Allahu Akbar, Allahu Akbar. Ashhadu an la ilaha illa Allah, Ashhadu an la ilaha illa Allah. Ashhadu anna Muhammadan Rasul Allah, Ashhadu anna Muhammadan Rasul Allah. Hayya 'ala al-salat, Hayya 'ala al-salat. Hayya 'ala al-falah, Hayya 'ala al-falah.' Until he finished the Adhan, and he said at the end: 'Allahu Akbar, Allahu Akbar. La ilaha illa Allah, La ilaha illa Allah.' As for the first two hadiths, although they included the mention of 'Allahu Akbar' twice at the beginning of the Adhan, it is permissible that he restricted himself to that because he intended to convey to the questioner the manner of pronouncing it, and it was known to him that restricting oneself to it without the four times is not sufficient. And that which reveals what we mentioned, that it is not permissible to restrict oneself to twice with choice, is what he narrated:

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, from Hammad ibn Isa, from 'Isa, from Zurarah, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: "O Zurarah, you begin the Adhan with four Takbirs, and conclude it with two Takbirs and two Tahliqs."

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Fadalah from Mu'awiya ibn Wahb from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "The Adhan is recited twice, twice, and the Iqamah is recited once, once." And what Sa'd narrated - from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Safwan ibn Yahya from Abdillah ibn Sinan from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "The Iqamah is once, once, except for his saying 'Allahu Akbar, Allahu Akbar', for indeed it is twice." This is attributed to the state of Taqiyya (dissimulation) or in times of haste, rather than the state of choice, and that which clarifies what we mentioned.

Sa'd ibn Abdullah narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Fadalah ibn Ayyub, from al-'Ala' ibn Razin, from Abu 'Ubaydah al-Hadda', who said: I saw Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) saying 'Allahu Akbar' one by one in the Adhan. I said to him, 'Why do you say 'Allahu Akbar' one by one?' He said, 'There is no harm in it if you are in a hurry.'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Ibn Abi Najran from Safwan ibn Mihran al-Jammal, who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: 'The Adhan is recited twice, twice, and the Iqamah is recited twice, twice.'

And from him, from Fadala, from Husayn ibn 'Uthman, from Ibn Muskan, from Yazid mawla al-Hakam, from whoever narrated to him, from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I heard him (peace be upon him) say: 'To establish the call to prayer (iqamah) in pairs is more beloved to me than to call the adhan and establish the iqamah individually (one by one).'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from al-Qasim ibn 'Urwah from Burayd ibn Mu'awiya from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: The Adhan is shortened during travel just as the prayer is shortened; the Adhan is called out one by one, and the Iqamah is called out one by one.

Sa'd narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Ja'far ibn Bashir, from Nu'man al-Razi, who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: 'One call to prayer (iqamah) suffices for you in place of the second call during travel.'

Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahb Mahbub from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan from al-Husayn from Hammad ibn Isa from Shu'ayb ibn Ya'qub from Abu Basir from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "The call (nidā') and the response (tathwīb) in the Iqamah are from the Sunnah." And what he narrated - he also from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan from al-Husayn from Fadalah from al-'Ala' from Muhammad ibn Muslim from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: "My father used to call in his house 'As-salatu khayrun min an-nawm' (Prayer is better than sleep), and if you responded to that, there would be no harm in it." And whatever is similar to these two hadiths that includes mention of these phrases, they are attributed to Taqiyyah (dissimulation/prudence) because the sect agrees on abandoning action upon them, and it is also indicated by what is narrated:

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Fadalah and Hammam ibn Isa from Mu'awiya ibn Wahb, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the Tathwib (the recitation of specific supplications or verses) that occurs between the Adhan and the Iqamah, so he said, 'We do not know it.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ibn Mahbub from Ali ibn Abi Hamzah from Abu Basir from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "If a mu'adhdhin repeats the Shahadah, and the 'Hayya 'ala al-Salah' or 'Hayya 'ala al-Falah' twice, three times, or more than that, when he is an Imam who wishes to gather the people to assemble them, there is no harm in it." Al-Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: So when he finishes his Adhan as we explained, he should sit after it with a light sit until he says: 'When he intends to establish the Iqamah.'

Al-Husayn ibn Said from Ibn Abi Umayr from Umar ibn Udhaynah from Al-Hasan ibn Shihab from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "There is a necessity for sitting between the Adhan and the Iqamah."

And from him (Al-Shaykh) from Sulayman ibn Ja'far al-Ajdafi, who said: I heard him (peace be upon him) say: "Separate between the Adhan (call to prayer) and the Iqamah (second call) by sitting or by praying two Rak'ahs."
And from him, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, who said: "Sitting between the Adhan and the Iqamah is [recommended] in all prayers, if there is no prayer performed before the Iqamah."

Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Yusuf from Saif ibn 'Amirah from some of our companions from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "Between every two Adhans there is a sitting period, except for Maghrib, for between them there is only a breath." And it has been narrated that he sits between them in Maghrib, and we have mentioned it later in the Additions.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from al-Husayn ibn Muhammad from 'Abdullah ibn 'Amir from 'Ali ibn Mahziyar from al-Husayn ibn Rashid from Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Yaqtin, he raised it to them, saying: The man says when he finishes the Adhan and sits: 'O God, make my heart pure and my sustenance abundant, and make for me a resting place and abode near the grave of the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family).'

Sa'd ibn Abdillah narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Muhammad ibn 'Isa ibn 'Ubayd, from Sa'dan ibn Muslim, from Ishaq al-Jariri, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: He (peace be upon him) said: 'Whoever sits between the call to prayer (adhan) of the Maghrib prayer and the call to establish the prayer (iqamah), it is like shedding his blood in the cause of Allah.' The Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: And when he intends to say the iqamah, let him recite it until the end of the chapter. Its explanation has already passed with sufficient detail, if Allah wills. And what he mentioned regarding the melodious recitation of the adhan and the rapid recitation of the iqamah, explanation and confirmation of it has also passed in what was narrated:

Al-Husayn ibn Said from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Al-Hasan ibn al-Sarri, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "The Adhan is recited with slow, melodious chanting, and the Iqamah is recited with rapid, brisk recitation."

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father and Muhammad ibn Isma'il from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, all from Hammad from Hariz from Zurara from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: If you forget a prayer or pray it without ablution, and there are missed prayers upon you, begin with the first of them, call the Adhan for it, and call the Iqamah, then pray it, then pray what follows it with an Iqamah, an Iqamah for each prayer. He said, and Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: And if you have prayed Dhuhr and the morning prayer (Fajr) has been missed by you, and you remember it, pray it at whatever hour you remember it, even after Asr, and whenever you remember a missed prayer, you pray it. And he said: If you forget Dhuhr until you pray Asr, and you remember it while you are in prayer or after finishing it, intend it as the first (Dhuhr), then pray Asr, for it is the four rak'ahs that you have prayed in place of the four (of Dhuhr). And if you remember that you did not pray the first (Dhuhr) while you are in the prayer of Asr, and you have prayed two rak'ahs from it, then pray the remaining two rak'ahs, stand up and pray Asr. And if you remember that you did not pray Asr until the time of Maghrib entered, and you do not fear missing it (Asr), then pray Asr, then pray Maghrib. And if you have already prayed Maghrib, stand up and pray Asr. And if you have prayed two rak'ahs from Maghrib, then you remember Asr, intend Asr, then give Salam, then pray Maghrib. And if you have prayed the final Isha, and you forgot Maghrib, stand up and pray Maghrib. And if you remember it (Maghrib) and you have prayed two rak'ahs from the final Isha, or you are standing in the third (rak'ah), intend Maghrib, then give Salam, then stand up and pray the final Isha. And if you have forgotten the final Isha until you have prayed Fajr, then pray the final Isha. And if you remember it while you are in one rak'ah or in the second of the morning (Fajr), intend Isha, then stand up and pray the morning (Fajr), call the Adhan and Iqamah. And if Maghrib and Isha have both been missed by you, begin with them before you pray the morning (Fajr), begin with Maghrib then Isha. And if you fear that the morning (Fajr) will be missed if you begin with them (Maghrib and Isha), then begin with Maghrib, then with the morning (Fajr), then pray Isha. And if you fear that the prayer of the mornin

And from him (Al-Hilli) from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Ibn Abi Umayr from Ibn Udhaynah from Zurarah from Ja'far from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) that he was asked: About a man who prayed without ablution, or forgot a prayer that he did not perform, or slept through it, so he said: 'He must make it up whenever he remembers it, whether in the night or day. When the time for the current prayer enters and he has not completed what has passed, he should make up the prayer whose time has not yet passed, as it is more deserving, so let him make it up. When he has made it up, let him pray what has passed from what is gone, and he should not offer a voluntary rak'ah until he has completed all the obligatory prayer.'

Three - Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub from al-Abbas from Abdullah ibn al-Mughira from Hariz from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who prayed the prayers while in a state of major ritual impurity (junub) for one day, two days, and three days. Then he mentioned after that, he said: 'He purifies himself, gives the adhan, and calls the iqamah for the first one, then prays and calls the iqamah after that for each prayer, so he prays without adhan until he fulfills his prayer.'. Al-Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: And whoever misses the Friday prayer, he prays it as four (rak'ahs). That is indicated by what he narrated:

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Ibn Abi 'Umayr from Hammad ibn 'Uthman from al-Halabi who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about one who did not catch the sermon on Friday. He said, 'He prays two rak'ahs. And if the prayer missed him and he did not catch it, let him pray four.' And he said, 'If you catch the Imam before he bows in the final rak'ah, you have caught the prayer. And if you catch him after he has bowed, it is Dhuhr (four rak'ahs).'

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Yusuf ibn al-Harith from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Arzmī from his father Abd al-Rahman from Ja'far from his father from Jabir from Ali (peace be upon him) who said: "Whoever catches the Imam on Friday while he is reciting the Tashahhud, let him pray four rak'ahs; and whoever catches one rak'ah, let him add another to it, making it audible." And that which was narrated - Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Fadalah and al-Nadr from Ibn Sinan from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "Friday prayer is not valid except for one who catches both sermons." So it is interpreted to mean that he does not attain the reward of one who catches both sermons, without it being obligatory upon him to repeat four rak'ahs. Do you not see what was narrated - Al-Husayn from Fadalah from Hammad from al-Fadl ibn Abd al-Malik who said Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: "Whoever catches one rak'ah has caught Friday." So it is explicitly stated in this report that whoever catches one rak'ah has caught Friday; so if the meaning of the first report was not what we mentioned, they would contradict each other, and this is invalid. And that is because the time for prayer entered before we went out." The Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: "And if the traveler forgets a prayer and remembers it after its time has passed while he is resident, he prays it with reduction (qasar)."

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Hammad from Hariz from Zurarah, who said: I said to him, 'A man missed a prayer from the travel prayer and remembered it during residence.' He said, 'He should make up what he missed as it was missed. If it was the travel prayer, he performs it during residence like it [shortened]. And if it was the residence prayer, he should make up the residence prayer during travel.'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd from Musa ibn Bakr from Zurara from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him): He was asked about a man whose prayer time entered while he was traveling, so he delayed the prayer until he arrived home, intending to pray it when he reached his family, but forgot to pray it upon arrival until the time had passed. He said: 'He prays it two rak'ahs as the prayer of the traveler, because the time entered while he was a traveler, and it was incumbent upon him to pray at that time.'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Safwan ibn Yahya from al-'Is ibn al-Qasim said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man for whom the time of prayer arrives while traveling, and then he enters his house before praying it. He said: 'He prays it as four [rak'at].' And he said: 'He continues to shorten [the prayer] until he enters his house.' For this narration is understood to mean that if he enters [his house] and the time is still remaining, full prayer is obligatory upon him. As for after the time has passed, he is not obligated to make up the prayer except according to what was missed by him. And likewise, if he sets out for travel and the time is still remaining, shortening is obligatory upon him. And that which indicates this is what he narrated:

Al-Husayn ibn Said from Safwan ibn Yahya and Fadala ibn Ayyub from al-Ala' ibn Razin from Muhammad ibn Muslim from one of them (peace be upon them both) Regarding a man who arrives from the absence (ghaybah) and the time for prayer enters upon him, he said: 'If he does not fear that the time will expire, let him enter (the house) and complete (the prayer); and if he fears that the time will expire before he enters, let him pray and shorten (it).' So it was inferred from this news that whoever does not fear missing the time by delaying the prayer until he enters the house, he delays it until he performs it completely; for if missing the time were not considered in this matter, there would be no meaning in restricting the completion to this state. Al-Sheikh (may God have mercy on him) said: And the traveler should not lead the resident, nor the resident lead the traveler. The preferable and best is that the traveler does not pray behind the resident, nor the resident behind the traveler. If they do that, they leave the preference, but their prayer is valid. And whenever the traveler prays behind the resident, he prays two rak'ahs and departs. And when the traveler prays with the people, he prays two rak'ahs with them, then he appoints someone to complete the prayer for them, and he (the traveler) departs. And that which indicates what we mentioned is what they narrated.

Sa'd ibn Abdillah narrated from Abu Ja'far, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from Dawud ibn al-Husayn, from Abu al-Abbas al-Fadl ibn Abd al-Malik, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The resident should not lead the traveler in prayer, nor should the traveler lead the resident. If one is tested by one of these situations (i.e., leading the other), and the traveler leads a group of residents, he should complete two rak'ahs, then say the taslim (salutation), then take the hand of one of them and place him in front to lead them. And if the traveler prays behind a group of residents, he should complete his prayer as two rak'ahs, then say the taslim. And if he prays with them for Dhuhr, he should consider the first two as Dhuhr and the last two as Asr. And from him (Sa'd), from al-Hasan ibn al-Husayn al-Lu'lu'i, from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Fadhal, from Abu al-Mi'ya Humayd ibn al-Muthanna, from Imran, from Muhammad ibn Ali: He asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who is traveling when he joins the prayer with those who are resident. He said: 'He should complete his prayer (as two rak'ahs), then say the taslim, and consider the last two (rak'ahs) as a single unit of lightness (subhah).'.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad ibn 'Uthman said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the traveler praying behind the resident. He said, 'He prays two rak'ahs and proceeds wherever he wishes.'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Fadalah ibn Ayyub, from Husayn ibn 'Uthman, from 'Abdullah ibn Muskhan, from Abi Basir, who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'The traveler does not pray behind the resident; if he prains, he should dismiss himself (complete his prayer) in two rak'ahs.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad, from al-Wassha', from Aban ibn 'Uthman, from 'Umar ibn Yazid, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): Regarding the traveler who prays behind the Imam and catches two rak'ahs of the prayer, does that suffice for him? He said, 'Yes.'

Sa'd ibn 'Abdillah from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from al-'Abbas ibn Ma'ruf from Safwan ibn Yahya from 'Abdullah ibn Muskān and Muhammad ibn al-Nu'man al-Aḥwal from Abū 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "When a traveler joins a group of residents in their prayer, if it is the first prayer (Dhuhr), he should make the obligatory prayer in the first two rak'ahs; and if it is 'Asr, he should make the first two rak'ahs voluntary (nafl) and the last two obligatory." The jurisprudence of this hadith is that he said 'if it is Dhuhr' because whenever he does that, it is permissible for him to make the last two rak'ahs the prayer of 'Asr. And if it is the prayer of 'Asr, he only makes the last two rak'ahs his prayer because it is disliked to pray after the 'Asr prayer except in the manner of Qada (making up). And whoever prays as we mentioned, nothing remains upon him, and he counts it among the voluntary prayers. Al-Shaykh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: "And the one who performs tayammum does not lead those who perform wudu, and the one who performs wudu does not lead those who perform tayammum." This issue is like the first one in that it is preferable that the one who performs tayammum does not lead those who perform wudu. And if he does that, it does not invalidate his prayer, but he has left the more preferable option. As for that which indicates the dislike of that, it is what we narrated:

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Abbad ibn Shuayb said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) say: 'The one performing tayammum does not lead the prayer of a congregation that is performing wudu.' (362) 23 And - Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Bunan ibn Muhammad from his father from Ibn al-Mughira from al-Sakuni from Ja'far from his father (peace be upon them both) who said: 'The one performing tayammum does not lead those performing wu in prayer, nor does the one with palsy lead the healthy.' If it is said: 'The apparent meaning of these two narrations is that it is not permissible for the one performing tayammum to lead those performing wu in any way, so why did you interpret it as disliked (karamah) rather than forbidden (haram)?' We said: 'We did so only because many other narrations have come indicating the permissibility of this, so we needed to reconcile between them. Among those is what he narrated:'

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Hamid, from Abu Jamilah, from Abu Usamah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): Regarding a man who is in a state of major ritual impurity (junub) and has no water with him, while he is the Imam of the people, he said: 'Yes, he performs dry ablution (tayammum) and leads them in prayer.' And from it, what was narrated: Sa'd ibn Abdillah from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Fadalah ibn Ayyub, from Abdillah ibn Bukayr, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who became junub, then performed tayammum, and led us in prayer while we were in a state of purity (having performed wudu/ghusl), and he said: 'There is no harm in it.' And from him, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr, from Muhammad ibn Humran and Jamil ibn Darraj, who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): An Imam of a people was affected by major impurity during travel, and he did not have with him enough water for ghusl. Should some of them perform wudu and pray behind him? He said: 'No, but the junub should perform tayammum and pray behind them, for indeed Allah, Exalted and Majestic, made the earth a purifier.' And from him, from Abu Ja'far, from his father, from Abdillah ibn al-Mughirah, from Abdillah ibn Bukayr, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I said to him: A man led a people in prayer while he was junub and had performed tayammum, while they were in a state of purity, and he said: 'There is no harm in it.' The Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: And the missed prayer is made up with adhan and iqamah if the person missed that. We have already presented what indicates this, and what increases its clarification is what he narrated:

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ali from Amr ibn Sa'id from Musaddiq ibn Sadah from 'Ammar al-Sabati from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: He was asked about a man who repeats the prayer, does he repeat the Adhan and the Iqamah? He said, 'Yes.' Al-Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: And the missed voluntary prayers (Nawafil) are made up at any time, provided it is not the time of a obligatory prayer (Fard), or at the rising of the sun, or at its setting. And it is disliked to make up voluntary prayers when the sun turns yellow (before sunset) until it sets. What has preceded previously contains a full explanation of what indicates this, and what increases that clarity is what he narrated:

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from Muhammad ibn Isa ibn Ubayd from Yunus ibn Abd al-Rahman from Ibn Muskhan from Abu Basir from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "Prayer during travel is two rak'ahs; there is nothing before them or after them except for Maghrib, for after it are four rak'ahs; do not leave them in residence or in travel. And there is no making up for you the prayer of the day, and pray the prayer of the night and make it up." The Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: And one who completes (the prayer) in travel out of forgetfulness, he repeats it if the time remains, and if the time has passed, there is no repetition upon him. And whoever intentionally completes in travel after the one who has the right of argument (the Imam) upon him being in shortening, that does not suffice him and repetition becomes obligatory upon him.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from Safwan from al-'Is ibn al-Qasim said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who prayed while traveling and completed the prayer. He said: 'If it was within the time, let him repeat it; and if the time has passed, then no (he does not need to repeat).'

Saad narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from Ali ibn al-Nu'man from Suwayd al-Qalla' from Abu Ayyub from Abu Basir from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a man who forgets and prays four rak'at during travel. He said: 'If he remembered on that day, he should repeat [the prayer]; but if he did not remember until that day passed, there is no need for him to repeat [it].' Thus, this report is interpreted as indicating a type of recommended act (istihbab), while the first case [remembering on the same day] is interpreted as indicating obligation (wujub).

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Hammad ibn Isa said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) asked about prayer on a ship, and he said: 'If you are able to go out to the Qibla (the deck/open area), then go out; and if you cannot, then pray standing; and if you cannot, then pray sitting, and seek the Qibla.'

Al-Husayn ibn Said from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad al-Jawhari from Ibn Abi Hamzah from Ali ibn Ibrahim, who said: I asked him about prayer on a ship. He said: 'He prays while sitting if he is unable to stand on the ship, and he does not pray on the ship while he is able to [pray] on the shore.' And he said: 'He prays on the ship, turning his face towards the Qibla, then he prays however the ship turns.'

And from him, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Abu Ayyub, who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): We were tested and were on a ship, and we spent the night and could not find a place to exit. He said: 'The companions of the ship do not pray our day as long as we hope to exit.' Then he said: 'Indeed my father used to say: That is the prayer of Noah (peace be upon him). Do you not accept that you pray the prayer of Noah?' I said: Yes, may I be your ransom. He said: 'Do not be distressed, for Noah had prayed on the ship.' I said: Standing or sitting? He said: 'Rather, standing.' I said: For I sometimes face the Qibla and the ship turns. He said: 'Determine the Qibla to the best of your ability.'

And from him, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Ibn Muskān, from Sulayman ibn Khālid, who said: I asked him about prayer on a ship. He said: 'He prays standing, and if he cannot stand, he should sit and pray while facing the Qiblah. If the ship turns, he should turn with the Qiblah if he is able to do so; and if he is not able to do so, he should remain in his place and strive to determine the Qiblah.' And he said: 'He prays the voluntary prayer facing the front of the ship, and he is facing the Qiblah when he says the Takbir, then it does not harm him wherever the ship turns.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from Yazid ibn Ishaq from Harun ibn Hamzah al-Ghanawi from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about prayer on a ship. He said, 'If it is heavily laden and when you stand in it it does not move, then pray standing. And if it is light and tilts, then pray sitting.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad from al-Halabi, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the Prayer of Fear. He said: 'The Imam stands up, and a group of his companions comes and stands behind him, while another group faces the enemy. The Imam prays one rak'ah with them, then stands up and they stand with him, remaining standing, and they pray the second rak'ah. Then some of them greet each other with salam, then they depart and stand in the place of their companions, and the others come and stand behind the Imam. The Imam prays the second rak'ah with them, then the Imam sits, and they stand up and pray another rak'ah. Then he greets them with salam, and they depart with a single salam.' He said: 'And in the Maghrib prayer it is the same: The Imam stands up, and a group comes and stands behind him, so he prays with them. Then he stands up and they stand up, and the Imam remains standing, and they pray the two rak'ahs, and they recite the tashahhud, and some of them greet each other with salam. Then they depart and stand in the place of their companions, and the others come and stand in the place of their companions behind the Imam. He prays one rak'ah with them, in which he recites. Then he sits and recites the tashahhud, and stands up, and they stand with him, and he prays another rak'ah with them. Then he sits, and they stand up and pray another rak'ah. Then he greets them with salam.'

And from him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Abdullah ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Aban, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Abdullah, from Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) who said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) led his companions in the Prayer of Fear during the Battle of Dhat al-Riqa. He divided his companions into two groups: one group remained facing the enemy, and the other remained behind him. He said 'Allahu Akbar' and they said it; he recited and they listened; he bowed and they bowed; he prostrated and they prostrated. Then the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) remained standing, and they completed one rak'ah for themselves. Then some of them greeted the others with peace. Then they went to their companions, remained facing the enemy, and their companions came and stood behind the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family). He prayed one rak'ah with them, then sat for the Tashahhud and greeted them with peace. They stood up and completed one rak'ah for themselves, and some of them greeted the others with peace.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Fudaylah from Hammad from Abu Basir said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: 'If you are in a land of fear and you fear a thief or a beast, then pray the obligatory prayer while you are on your mount.' And from him, from Fudaylah, from Aban, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Abdillah, said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the man who fears from a beast or a thief, how does he pray? He said: 'He says Takbir and gestures with his head.'

Saad narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn Hadid, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Najran and al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Hariz ibn Abdillah, from Zurarah, who said: Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: 'One who fears robbers and wild beasts prays the prayer of al-Muwaqafah by gesture while on his mount.' I said: 'Do I understand that if the one praying is not in a state of wudu, what should he do when he cannot dismount?' He said: 'He performs tayammum from the felt of his saddle or his mount or from the saddle-ring of his mount, for there is dust in it, and he prays and makes the prostration lower than the bowing, and he does not turn his body towards the Qibla, but wherever his mount turns, provided that he faces the Qibla with the first Takbir when he sets out.'

Al-Husayn ibn Said from Ibn Abi Umayr from Umar ibn Udhaynah from Zurarah and Fudayl and Muhammad ibn Muslim from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: Regarding the Prayer of Fear during skirmishing, close combat, and the clash of fighting, then every person among them prays by nodding (gesturing) wherever their face is. And when it is the continuous fighting and close engagement and the clash of battle, then the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) on the night of Siffin, which is the night of Harir, did not pray with them the Dhuhr, Asr, Maghrib, and Isha prayers at the time of each prayer except by Takbir, Tahleel, Tasbih, Tamjid, and Du'a. So that was their prayer, and he did not order them to repeat the prayer. And from him, from Al-Hasan, from Zur'ah, from Sama'ah, who said: I asked him about the Prayer of Battle, and he said: 'When they meet and fight, then the prayer at that time is by Takbir (saying Allahu Akbar). And when they are standing, then the prayer is by nodding (gesturing).'

Saad narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad ibn Uthman, from Ubaydullah ibn Ali al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The prayer of Zaf (marching forward) while on the back is a nod of the head with a Takbir; Al-Musayafah is a Takbir with a nod; Al-Mutaradah is a nod; each man prays facing his own direction. And from him, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Abdillah ibn al-Mughirah and Ayub ibn Nuh, from Abdillah ibn al-Mughirah, who said: Some of our companions narrated to me from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The minimum that suffices in the measure of Al-Musayafah regarding the Takbir is two Takbirs for each prayer, except for the Maghrib prayer, for it has three.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Ahmad ibn Hilal, from Ibn Muskān, from Abū Baṣīr, who said: Abū ʿAbdillāh (peace be upon him) said: "Whoever is in a place where he cannot reach the ground, let him bow with a gesture."

Sa'd ibn 'Abdullah narrated from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan ibn 'Ali ibn Fadhal from 'Amr ibn Sa'id from Musaddiq ibn Sadah from 'Ammar ibn Musa from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a man who gestures (with his head) in the obligatory and voluntary prayers if he cannot find something to prostrate upon and has no place to prostrate in, so he said: 'If it is thus, let him gesture throughout the entire prayer.'

And with this chain of narration, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), he said: I asked him about a man who is struck by rain while he is in a place where he cannot prostrate due to mud, nor does he find a dry spot. He said: 'He begins the prayer; when he bows, let him bow as he bows when he prays [normally]. And when he raises his head from bowing, let him indicate the prostration with a nod while he is standing. He continues to do that until he finishes the prayer, and he recites the Tashahhud while standing, and he gives the Taslim [salutation].' Al-Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: And if he is prevented by Ribat [standing guard in a fortress or border] and similar conditions, he prays according to his ability.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from a number of our companions from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid from his father from Zur'ah from Samaan, who said: I asked him about the captive whom the polytheists capture, and prayer time approaches, but the one who captured him prevents him from praying. He said: 'He gestures with a nod.' The Sheikh (may God have mercy on him) said: 'And the sick person prays standing while having the ability, up to his saying, and it is disliked.'

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ali from Amr ibn Sa'id from Musaddiq ibn Sadah from 'Ammar from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The sick person, if he cannot pray sitting, prays as he is able: either he turns [his body] and indicates with gestures. And he said: 'He turns as a man turns in his grave, and sleeps on his right side, then indicates with the prayer. If he cannot sleep on his right side, then as he is able is permissible for him, and he faces the Qiblah with his face, then indicates with the prayer with gestures.'

Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Abdullah ibn al-Qasim from Amr ibn Uthman from Muhammad ibn Ibrahim from whoever narrated to him from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The sick person prays standing; if he cannot do that, he prays sitting; if he cannot do that, he prays lying on his back. He says Takbir then recites. When he intends to bow (Ruku'), he closes his eyes, then glorifies (Allah); when he has glorified, he opens his eyes, and the opening of his eyes is the raising of his head from Ruku'. When he intends to prostrate (Sujud), he closes his eyes, then glorifies; when he has glorified, he opens his eyes, and the opening of his eyes is the raising of his head from Sujud. Then he recites the Tashahhud and turns for Salam.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali from his father from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Abu Hamzah from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) Regarding the saying of Allah, Exalted and Mighty: 'Those who remember Allah while standing,' he said: 'The healthy person prays standing and sitting.' The sick person prays sitting, and 'upon their sides' refers to the one who is weaker than the sick person who prays sitting.' The Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: 'And it is disliked for him to place his forehead on a prayer mat held by another or on a hand-mirror (mirwah).'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Fadala from Husayn from Sama'a from Abu Basir said: I asked him about the sick person: does the woman hold something for him to prostrate upon? He said, 'No, unless he is in need and has no one else, and there is nothing forbidden by Allah except that He has made it permissible for one who is in need of it.' And from him (Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id) from Ibn Abi Umayr from Umar ibn Udhayna from Zurara from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) He said: I asked him about the sick person. He said, 'He prostrates on the ground, or on a hand-fan, or on a miswak stick. Raising it is better than gesturing. Those who disliked prostrating on the hand-fan did so because of the idols that were worshipped besides Allah, and we have never worshipped anything other than Allah. So prostrate on the hand-fan, or on a miswak, or on a stick.'

And from him, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Umar ibn Udhaynah, from one who informed him, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him): that he was asked, 'What is the limit of the illness that compels its owner [to pray sitting], and the illness that causes its owner to leave the prayer while standing?' He said, 'Rather, the person is perceptive of himself.' He said, 'That is to him; he knows himself best.' And from him, from Fadalah ibn Ayyub, from Jamil and Ibn Abi Umayr, from Jamil who said: 'I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)' 'What is the limit of the illness that causes its owner to pray sitting?' He said, 'Indeed, a man may be sick and wounded, but he knows himself best; when he is strong, let him stand.'

Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Saif, from Bakkar, who said: My father asked him (meaning Abu Abdillah, peace be upon him), while I was listening: 'What is the limit of the illness that permits leaving the fast?' He said, 'When he is unable to eat the pre-dawn meal (suhoor).'

Al-Saffar from Muhammad ibn Isa from Sulayman ibn Haf al-Marwazi said: The Faqih (peace be upon him) said: 'The sick person only prays sitting when he reaches a state in which he is unable to walk the distance equivalent to his prayer until he finishes standing.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Hammad, from Hariz, from Zurarah, who said: I said to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him): A man emerged from a ship naked, or his clothes were stripped from him, and he found nothing to pray in. He said: 'He prays by nodding (i'ma'). And if it is a woman, she places her hand over her private part, and if it is a man, he places his hand over his private part. Then they sit and nod by way of nodding, and they do not bow (ruku') nor prostrate (sajdah). When what is behind them is exposed, their prayer is by nodding with their heads.' He said: 'And if they are in water or a deep sea, they do not prostrate upon it, and the facing (tawajjuh) is excused from them; they nod in that regard. Their raising [of the head] is facing, and their lowering [of the head] is [also] facing.'

Sa'd narrated from Abu Ja'far, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a group of people who prayed in congregation while they were naked (without upper garments). He said: 'The Imam should advance on his knees, and he prays with them sitting, while he himself is sitting.'

Three: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Ayub ibn Nuh, from some of our companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The naked one who has no garment, if he finds a pit, enters it and prostrates in it and bows. And what he mentioned after that regarding the manner of the funeral prayer for the deceased when he is naked indicates this, as narrated:

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from Marwan ibn Muslim, from Ammar al-Sabati, who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): What do you say about a group of people who were traveling and walking on the shore of the sea, when they found a dead man naked whom the sea had cast up? They were naked, having only an izār (loincloth) or a ridā’ (garment) on them. How do they pray over him while they are naked, with no surplus garment to shroud him with? He (peace be upon him) said: 'A grave is dug for him, and he is placed in his grave (lahd). A brick is placed over his private part, so he is covered by the brick and the stone. Then the funeral prayer is prayed over him, and then he is buried.' I said: So the funeral prayer is not prayed over him after he is buried? He said: 'The funeral prayer is not prayed over the dead after he is buried, nor is it prayed over him while he is naked until his private part is covered.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Muhammad ibn Khalid from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd from Yahya al-Halabi from 'Amr ibn Hurayth said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: "Pray two rak'ahs and seek guidance from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. By Allah, no Muslim seeks guidance from Allah except that Allah guides him for it definitively."

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from 'Uthman ibn 'Isa from 'Amr ibn Shimir from Jabir from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon them both) used to, when intending a matter of Hajj or Umrah or trade or purchase or manumission, purify himself, then pray two rak'ahs of Istikhara, reciting in them Surah al-Hashr and Surah ar-Rahman, then reciting the two Mu'awwidhat and 'Qul Huwa Allahu Ahad'. Then he would say: 'O Allah, if such and such is good for me in my religion and my world and my Hereafter and in the immediate and delayed aspects of my affair, then facilitate it for me in the best of ways. O Allah, if such and such is bad for me in my religion and my world and my Hereafter and in the immediate and delayed aspects of my affair, then turn it away from me in the best of ways. My Lord, make me firm upon my guidance even if I dislike that or my soul rejects it.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ibn Faddal said: Al-Hasan ibn al-Jahm asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) regarding Ibn Asbat, saying to him: 'What do you think regarding him?' Ibn Asbat was present, and we were all traveling by sea or by land to Egypt. He informed him about the news of the land route. He (peace be upon him) said, 'Go to the mosque at a time other than that of a compulsory prayer, pray two rak'ahs, and seek guidance from Allah a hundred times. Then see what comes to your heart and act upon it.' Al-Hasan said to him, 'The land route is more preferable to me.' He said, 'And to me as well.'

And from him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn Hadeed, from Murazim, who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: "When one of you desires something, let him pray two rak'ahs, and praise Allah, and extol Him, then send blessings upon Muhammad and his Family, and say: 'O Allah, if this matter is good for me in my religion and my worldly life, then facilitate it for me and decree it for me; and if it is otherwise, then turn it away from me.' So I asked him about what I should recite in them, and he said: "Recite in them whatever you wish, and if you wish, you may recite 'Qul Huwa Allahu Ahad' and 'Qul Ya Ayyuha al-Kafirun'".

And from him, from Ali ibn Muhammad, from Sahl ibn Ziyad and Muhammad ibn Isa, from Amr ibn Ibrahim, from Khalaf ibn Hammad, from Ishaq ibn Ammar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I said to him, 'Sometimes I intend a matter and two inclinations arise in me, one commanding me and the other forbidding me.' He said, 'If you are in such a state, then pray two rak'ahs and seek God's guidance (istikhara) a hundred times and one time. Then see which of the two matters is more decisive for you and do it, for the good is in it, if God wills. And let your istikhara be in health/soundness, for perhaps a man is chosen for the cutting of his hand, the death of his child, and the loss of his wealth.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from more than one, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Basri, from al-Qasim ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Hashimi, from Harun ibn Harizah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: When you desire a matter, take six pieces of paper and write on three of them: 'In the name of Allah, the Merciful, the Compassionate. A choice from Allah, the Mighty, the Wise. For So-and-so ibn So-and-so, do it.' And on the other three: 'In the name of Allah, the Merciful, the Compassionate. A choice from Allah, the Mighty, the Wise. For So-and-so ibn So-and-so, do not do it.' Then place them beneath your prayer mat. When you finish, prostrate and say one hundred times: 'I seek Allah's choice through His mercy, a choice in well-being.' Then sit upright and say: 'O Allah, choose for me in all my affairs with ease from You and well-being.' Then strike with your hand towards the papers, mix them, and draw out one. If three consecutive ones are 'do it', then do that matter which you intend. And if three consecutive ones are 'do not do it', then do not do it. And if one is 'do it' and the other is 'do not do it', then draw out from the papers up to five, and look at the majority, and act according to it, and leave the sixth, for you do not need it.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Umar ibn Udhaynah, from Zurarah, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'What do people narrate, that prayer in congregation is superior to the prayer of a man alone by twenty-five prayers?' He said, 'They are truthful.' I said, 'When two men are in congregation?' He said, 'Yes, and the man stands to the right of the Imam.'

Hammad from Hariz from Zurarah and al-Fudayl said: We said to him, Is prayer in congregation obligatory? He said, 'The prayers are obligatory, but the gathering [congregation] is not obligatory in all prayers; rather, it is a sunnah. Whoever leaves it out of preference for it and for the congregation of the believers without an excuse, has no prayer [for him].'

Three [narrators] - Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father and Muhammad ibn Isma'il from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, all from Hammad ibn Isa from Hariz from Zurarah, who said: I was sitting with Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) one day when a man came to him and entered. He said to him, 'May I be your ransom, I am a man whose mosque is with my people. If I do not pray with them, they will speak ill of me and say such and such.' He said, 'If you say that, indeed Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) said: Whoever hears the call to prayer and does not respond to it without an excuse, he has no prayer.' The man left, and he said to him, 'Do not leave praying with them, and behind every Imam.' When he left, I said to him, 'May I be your ransom, your saying to this man when he asked you seemed heavy upon me, if they are not believers?' He smiled (peace be upon him) and said, 'I do not see you except here, O Zurarah. What excuse do you want that is greater than the fact that he is prayed behind?' Then he said, 'O Zurarah, what do you think?' I said, 'Pray in your mosques and pray with your Imams.'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from an-Nadr ibn Suwayd from 'Abdullah ibn Sinan from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "Prayer in congregation surpasses every individual prayer by twenty-four degrees, making it twenty-five prayers." And from him, from an-Nadr from 'Abdullah ibn Sinan from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I heard him saying: "The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) prayed Fajr, then turned his face to his companions and asked about some people, naming them by name, saying, 'Did they attend the prayer?' They said, 'No, O Messenger of God.' He said, 'Are they absent?' They said, 'No.' He said, 'Indeed, there is no prayer more burdensome for the hypocrites than this prayer and the 'Isha prayer. If they knew what merit is in them, they would come to them even if they had to crawl.'

Sa'd narrated from Abu Ja'far, from al-Abbas ibn Ma'ruf, from Ali ibn Mahziyar, from Muhammad ibn al-Hamid, from Muhammad ibn 'Umara, who said: I sent to Abu al-Hasan al-Rida (peace be upon him) asking him about a man: is his prayer of the obligatory prayer alone in the mosque of Kufa better, or his prayer in congregation better? He said, 'Prayer in congregation is better.'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Bistam from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: A man said to him, 'May I be your ransom, does a man embrace his brother?' He said, 'Yes. Indeed, the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) was informed on the day Khaybar was conquered that Ja'far had arrived. He said, 'By Allah, I do not know which of the two I am more joyful about: Ja'far's arrival or the conquest of Khaybar.' He said, 'Then Ja'far did not delay before arriving.' He said, 'The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) rose and embraced him and kissed what was between his eyes.' The man said to him, 'The four rak'ahs that I have heard the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) commanded Ja'far (peace be upon him) to pray.' He said, 'When he arrived, peace be upon him, he said to him,

And from him, from Ya'qub ibn Yazid, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Yahya ibn 'Imran, from Dharih, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: "If you wish, pray the Salat al-Tasbih at night; and if you wish, [pray it] during the day; and if you wish, [pray it] while traveling; and if you wish, make it part of your voluntary prayers; and if you wish, make it from the makeup of a missed prayer." And in the narration of Ibrahim ibn 'Abd al-Hamid, from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him): "It is recited in the first [rak'ah] 'When the earth is shaken', in the second 'By the runners [horses]', in the third 'When the help of Allah comes', and in the fourth 'Say: He is Allah, One'" I said, 'What is its reward?' He said, 'If there were upon him as many sins as the sand of 'Araj, Allah would forgive him.' Then he looked at me and said, 'That is specifically for you and your companions.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Muhassin ibn Ahmad from Aban said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: 'Whoever is in a hurry and prays the Salat of Ja'far exclusively, then completes the tasbih while going about his needs.'

And from him (Al-Shaykh) from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Abdullah ibn al-Qasim, he narrated from one who narrated to him from Abu Sa'id al-Mad'ini, who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to me: 'Shall I teach you something you should say in the Salat of Ja'far?' I said: 'Yes.' He said: 'When you are in the final prostration of the four rak'at, say, after you have finished your tasbih (glorification):' Glory be to He who wore honor and dignity, glory be to He who girded Himself with glory and honored with it, glory be to Him to whom glorification is due, glory be to He whose knowledge encompasses all things, glory be to the Possessor of bounty and blessings, glory be to the Possessor of power and command. O God, I ask You by the knots of honor from Your Throne, and the utmost of mercy from Your Book, and Your Greatest Name, and Your perfect words which were completed in truth and justice, Send blessings upon Muhammad and his family, and do for me so-and-so.'

And from him, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ali ibn Asbat, from al-Hakam ibn Miskin, from Isḥāq ibn ʿAmmār, who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'For the one who prays the Prayer of Jaʿfar, is recorded for him in reward the like of what the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said to Jaʿfar.' He said: 'Yes, by Allah.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from a number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Barqi, from Sa'dan, from Abdillah ibn Sinan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Whoever prays four rak'ahs, reciting 'Qul Huwa Allahu Ahad' fifty times in each rak'ah, will not depart [from this world] and there is no sin between him and Allah.

And from him, from Ali ibn Muhammad, through his chain, from some of them (peace be upon them): Regarding the saying of Allah, Exalted and Mighty: 'Indeed, the night prayer is more effective in contact [with God] and more suitable for speech [of Quran],' he said: 'It is two rak'ahs after the Maghrib prayer,' you recite in the first rak'ah - Al-Fatiha and ten verses from the beginning of Al-Baqarah, and the Verse of Al-Sukhr (dominion), from His saying: 'And your god is one God. There is no deity [worthy of worship] except Him, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and earth and the alternation of the night and the day are signs for those of understanding' - until His saying: 'For a people who use reason.' And fifteen times 'Say: He is Allah, [who is] One.' And in the second rak'ah, Al-Fatiha, the Verse of the Throne (Ayat al-Kursi), and the end of Al-Baqarah from His saying: 'To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth' - until you conclude the surah, and fifteen times 'Say: He is Allah, [who is] One.' Then supplicate after this with whatever you wish.' He said: 'And whoever is consistent with it, Allah will record for him, for every prayer, six hundred thousand Hajj [rewards].'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad ibn 'Uthman and Hashim ibn Salim, from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) would say Takbir (glorify God) over some people five times, and over other people four times. And if he said Takbir over a man four times, he was accused, meaning of hypocrisy.

And from him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn Abi Hamzah, from Abi Basir, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) pronounced the takbir (prayer of the deceased) over Hamzah seventy times, and Ali (peace be upon him) pronounced the takbir over Sahl ibn Hunayf twenty-five times. He said: 'He pronounced the takbir in groups of five; whenever the people caught up with him, they would say, O Commander of the Faithful, we have not caught up with the prayer over Sahl, so he would lay him down and pronounce five takbirs over him, until he reached his grave, doing this five times. The Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: And there is no prayer (of the deceased) among the Family of Muhammad for one who does not comprehend the prayer.

And from him, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Zurara, who said: I saw a son of Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) during the life of Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who was called 'Abdullah al-Fayim', who had grown up. I said to him, 'O boy, who is the one beside you, a master to them?' He said, 'This is my master.' The master said to him, teasing him, 'I am not a master to you.' He said, 'That is worse for you,' and he thrust his spear into the boy's funeral shroud, so he died. He was taken out in a basket to al-Baqi', and Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) came out wearing a yellow silk tunic, a yellow silk turban, and a yellow silk edge. He walked towards al-Baqi', leaning on me, while the people consoled him on the death of his grandson. When he reached al-Baqi', Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) stepped forward and prayed over him, saying 'Allahu Akbar' four times over him. Then he ordered that he be buried. Then he took my hands, moved aside with me, and said, 'Indeed, prayer was not performed over children. Rather, the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) would order them to be buried behind, behind, and not pray over them. And I prayed over him on account of the people of the city, lest they say,

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa narrated from Musa ibn al-Qasim al-Bajali from Ali ibn Ja'far from his brother Musa ibn Ja'far (peace be upon them both) who said: I asked him about a child: is the funeral prayer performed for him if he dies at the age of five years? He said: 'When he understands the prayer, the funeral prayer is performed for him.'

Ibn Abi Umayr from Abdullah ibn Sinan from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Prayer is not performed over the newborn who has not yet cried out, nor is he validly inherited, nor is blood money (diyah) paid for him from either ransom or other sources. But if he cries out, then pray over him and inherit him. Thus, this report is to be understood as indicating a type of preferability (istihbab) or precautionary piety (taqiyyah), so that it does not contradict what we have previously established, and it adds clarification to what we have mentioned.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan, from 'Amr ibn Sa'id, from Musaddiq ibn Sadah, from 'Ammar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): that he was asked about the newborn whose writing has not yet been done upon him, is prayer offered for him? He said: "No, rather prayer is offered for the man and the woman only when the writing has been done upon them." Al-Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: And whoever catches one takbirah for the deceased or two, he completes it.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Safwan ibn Yahya from 'Isa ibn al-Qasim who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the man who catches up with the funeral prayer with one Takbir; he said, 'He completes what remains.'

Saad narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from al-Nadr ibn Shu'ayb, from Khalid ibn Mad al-Qalanisi, from a man, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: I heard him say: Regarding the man who catches up with the Imam in the funeral prayer, [catching] one or two takbirs, he said: 'He completes the takbirs while walking with them. If he does not catch the takbir, he says takbir at the grave. If he catches them and they have already buried [the deceased], he says takbir over the grave.'

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from his father, from Abdullah ibn al-Mughira, from Abdullah ibn Muskhan, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: "When a man catches the first Takbirah and the two Takbiratayn of the Salat al-Mayyit (prayer over the deceased), he must make up what remains, consecutively."

From him, from Al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Fadhal, from Abu Jamilah, from Zayd al-Shahham, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the funeral prayer (Salat al-Janazah) if a man missed one of the takbirs, or two, or three, he said: 'He should takbir for what he missed.'

Sa'd ibn 'Abdillah from al-Hasan ibn Musa al-Khashshab from Ghiyath ibn Kalub from Isma'il ibn 'Ammar from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) from his father (peace be upon him) that Ali (peace be upon him) used to say: "The missed Takbirat of the funeral prayers are not made up." The meaning in this narration is that they are not made up in the manner in which they were originally begun, with a pause between them for supplication; rather, they are made up consecutively, as al-Halabi detailed in his preceding narration. The Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: "And there is no objection to praying over the grave for a day and a night; if it exceeds a day and a night, the prayer is not valid."

Saad narrated from Ya'qub ibn Yazid, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hisham ibn Salim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: "There is no harm in a man praying over the deceased after he has been buried." And from him, from Abu Ja'far, from his father, from Abdillah ibn al-Mughirah, from Abdillah ibn Muskhan, from Malik, the freedman of al-Jahm, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: "If the prayer over the deceased is missed by you until he is buried, then there is no harm in praying over him after he has been buried." And from him, from Abu Ja'far, from al-Husayn ibn Ali ibn Yusuf, from Mu'adh ibn Thabit al-Jawhari, from Amr ibn Jumay', from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: "The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) would pray over the grave if the prayer over the deceased was missed by him."

Ali ibn al-Husayn narrated from Sa'd, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from al-Husayn ibn Musa, from Ja'far ibn Isa, who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) arrived in Mecca and asked me about Abdullah ibn A'ynah. I said, 'He has died.' He said, 'He has died.' I said, 'Yes.' He said, 'Then take us to his grave so that we may pray over him.' I said, 'Yes.' Then he said, 'No, but we will pray over him here.' He raised his hands and supplicated, exerting himself in the supplication, and showed mercy to him.

Al-Saffar from Ibrahim ibn Hashim from Nu'ayn ibn Shu'ayb from Hariz from Muhammad ibn Muslim or Zurarah said: "The prayer (salat) on the deceased after he is buried is merely supplication." He said: I said, "Then regarding the Negus, the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) did not pray on him?" He said, "No, he merely supplicated for him." Al-Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: And one prays on the deceased at any time of the day and night.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Abu Ali al-Ash'ari from Muhammad ibn al-Jabbar from Safwan ibn Yahya from al-'Ala' ibn Razin from Muhammad ibn Muslim from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: Prayer is performed over the funeral at any hour, for it is not a prayer of bowing and prostration; rather, prayer is disliked at the rising of the sun and at its setting, which is when there is bowing and prostration, because it sets between the horns of Satan and rises between the horns of Satan. Al-Sheikh (may God have mercy on him) said: And there is no objection to praying over the deceased without ablution, and likewise for the one in a state of major ritual impurity (junub).

And from him, from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, and Abu Ali al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, all of them, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Abd al-Hamid ibn Sa'd, who said: I said to Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him): 'When the funeral is being carried out and I am not in a state of ablution, if I go to perform ablution, I will miss the funeral prayer. Will it suffice for me to pray over it while I am not in a state of ablution?' He said: 'It is more beloved to me that you be in a state of purity.' And this narration includes that purity is superior, and it indicates that non-purity is also permissible, and it is permissible for a person to perform dry ablution (tayammum) instead of purity if he fears missing the prayer. This was narrated.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from his brother al-Hasan from Zur'ah from Samaan, who said: I asked him about a man who a funeral procession passed by him while he was not in a state of purity. He said: 'He strikes his hands against a wall of baked brick and performs tayammum.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Humayd ibn Ziyad, from al-Hasan ibn Muhammad al-Kindi, from al-Mitham, from Aban ibn Uthman, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Abdillah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him, 'Does the menstruating woman pray over the funeral?' He said, 'Yes, and she does not stand with them; she stands alone.'

Ali (ibn al-Hakam) from his father from Hammad ibn Isa from Hariz from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the menstruating woman: does she pray behind the Imam for the funeral? He said, 'Yes, and she does not stand with them; she stands alone.'

Sa'd from Abu Ja'far from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Najran and al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Hammad from Hariz from one who informed him from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "The menstruating woman prays over the funeral [prayer] because there is no bowing or prostration in it, and the person in major ritual impurity performs dry ablution and prays over the funeral [prayer]." And from him from Abu Ja'far from Uthman from Sama'ah from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): Regarding the menstruating woman when she attends the funeral, he said: "She performs dry ablution and prays over it, and she stands alone, separate from the row [of worshippers]."

And from him, from Abu Ja'far, from his father, and al-Abbas ibn Ma'ruf, from Abdullah ibn al-Mughira, from a man, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about the menstruating woman praying over the funeral (body), so he said: 'Yes, and she does not stand with them, and the person in major ritual impurity prays over the funeral (body).' Al-Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: 'And the people most entitled to pray over the deceased are those most entitled to his inheritance, until the end of the chapter.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from some of his companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The one most deserving of the funeral prayer is the one who prays over the deceased, or he may command whomever he wishes.

And from him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn Abi Hamzah, from Abi Basir, from Abi Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him, 'When a woman dies, who is most entitled among people to pray over her?' He said, 'Her husband.' I said, 'Is the husband more entitled than the father, the son, and the brother?' He said, 'Yes, and he washes her.'

Muhsin ibn Ahmad from Aban ibn Uthman from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Abdillah said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the prayer over the woman (for funeral prayer): is the husband more entitled to perform it, or the brother? He said, 'The brother.'

Ahmad ibn Abi Abdillah narrated from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hafs ibn al-Bakhtari, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): Regarding a woman who dies while her brother and her husband are present, which of them prays over her? He said, 'Her brother has more right to pray over her.' The explanation (resolution) in these two narrations is that we attribute them to a form of precautionary concealment (taqiyyah), because they agree with the schools of the general public (Sunnis).

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Talhah ibn Zayd, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: "When the Imam attends the funeral, he is more entitled than the people to pray over it."

37 - Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Ibrahim ibn Hashim, from al-Nawfali, from al-Sakuni, from Ja'far, from his father, from his forefathers (peace be upon them), who said: The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) said: 'When a ruler from the rulers of Allah attends a funeral, he is more entitled to pray over it if the deceased's guardian appoints him; otherwise, he is a usurper.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Sahl ibn Ziyad from Isma'il ibn Mihran from Saif ibn 'Amirah from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Prayer is offered over the funeral (body) with sandals, and there is no harm with the khuff (leather sock). The second part of the Book of Prayer has concluded, and praise and grace belong to God, and upon His Prophet and his family be peace and mercy.

Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub from al-Abbas ibn Ma'ruf from Hammad ibn Isa from Hariz from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'It is necessary to wear the turban and the burda (outer garment) on the days of Eid al-Adha and Eid al-Fitr. As for Friday prayer, it suffices without a turban and burda.'
