And from him (Al-Shaykh) from Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Abu Ayyub from Al-Fudayl ibn Yasar who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: "When one of you fasts the three days of the month, let him not argue with anyone, nor act foolishly, nor hasten to oaths and swearing by Allah. And if someone acts foolishly towards him, let him bear it patiently."

And from him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Hammad ibn 'Uthman, who said: I heard Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: It is disliked to recite poetry for the fasting person, for the one in ihram, in the sanctuary (Mecca), on Friday, and to be recited at night. I asked: Even if it is true poetry? He said: Even if it is true poetry.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from al-Hasan ibn Musa from Ghiyath ibn Ibrahim from Isḥāq ibn 'Ammār from Abū 'Abdillāh (peace be upon him) who said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'Indeed, Allah disliked for me six characteristics, and I disliked them for the successors from among my offspring and their followers after me: Raffath (excessive eating/drinking or sexual intimacy) during fasting.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ahmad ibn al-Nadr al-Kazzaz, from Amr ibn Shimir, from Jabir ibn Yazid, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said to Jabir ibn Abd Allah: 'O Jabir, this is the month of Ramadan. Whoever fasts its day, prays during a portion of its night, keeps his stomach and private parts chaste, and restrains his tongue, will emerge from his sins as he emerged from the month.' Jabir said: 'O Messenger of Allah, how beautiful is this hadith!' The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'O Jabir, how severe are these conditions!'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from al-Qasim ibn 'Urwah from 'Abdullah ibn Bukayr from Zurarah from one of the Imams (peace be upon them) who said: I asked him about the nights in which it is recommended to perform the ritual bath (ghusl) during the month of Ramadan, so he said: 'The night of the nineteenth, the night of the twenty-first, and the night of the twenty-third.' And he said: 'In the night of the nineteenth, the delegation of the pilgrims is recorded, and in it every wise matter is distinguished (decided).' And the night of the twenty-first - in it Jesus (peace be upon him) was raised, and in it the successor of Moses (peace be upon him) was taken, and in it the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) was taken. And the night of the twenty-third - and it is the Night of the Juhani, and his narration is that he said to the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family): 'Indeed, my dwelling is far from the city, so order me to a night in which I may enter.' So he ordered him to the night of the twenty-third.' And we have previously mentioned in the Book of Prayer, in the chapter on the practices of the month of Ramadan, what is recommended for a person to say from supplication and recitation of the Quran, so there is no need to repeat it here, and it is sufficient, God willing.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Ibrahim ibn Umar al-Yamani, from Amr ibn Shimir, from Jabir, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family), when the crescent of the month of Ramadan appeared, would face the Qibla and raise his hands and say: 'O Allah, make it appear for us with security and faith, and safety and Islam, and encompassing health, and abundant provision, and repelling of diseases. O Allah, grant us its fasting and its night prayer, and recitation of the Quran within it. O Allah, deliver it to us and accept it from us, and grant us safety within it.'

And from him, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hasan, from Ali ibn Asbat, from al-Hakam ibn Miskeen, who said: Amr ibn Shimir narrated to us, who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him), when the crescent of the month of Ramadan appeared, would face the Qibla. And he would say: 'O Allah, present it to us with security and faith, and safety and Islam, and encompassing well-being. O Allah, grant us its fasting and its night prayer, and the recitation of the Quran within it. O Allah, deliver it to us and accept it from us, and grant us safety within it.'

And from him, from a number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ya'qub ibn Yazid, from Muhammad ibn Ibrahim al-Nawfali, from al-Husayn ibn al-Mukhtar, he raised it (to the Imam) saying: The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) said: 'When you see the new moon, do not depart (from this state/remembrance) and say: O God, I ask You for the goodness of this month, its light, its victory, its blessing, its purification, and its sustenance. And I ask You for the goodness that is in it and the goodness that is after it. And I seek refuge in You from the evil that is in it and the evil that is after it. O God, bring it to us with security, faith, safety, Islam, blessing, piety, and success for what You love and are pleased with.'

Sa'd ibn Abdillah narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Najran, from Asim ibn Humayd and al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from Asim ibn Humayd, from Abi Basir, from Abi Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about the zakat (alms-tax) of camels, and he said: 'There is no zakat in fewer than five camels. When there are five, there is one sheep, up to ten. When there are ten, there are two sheep, up to fifteen. When there are fifteen, there are three sheep, up to twenty. When there are twenty, there are four sheep, up to twenty-five. When there are twenty-five, there are five sheep. If one more is added, there is an ibn makhad (a young female camel that has entered its fourth year) up to thirty-five. If there is no ibn makhad, then a ibn labun (a young male camel that has entered its fifth year). If one more is added to thirty-five, there is an ibn labun (female) up to forty-five. If one more is added, there is a hiqqah (a three-year-old female camel) up to sixty. If one more is added, there is a jadh'ah (a four-year-old female camel) up to seventy-five. If one more is added, there are two ibn labun (females) up to ninety. If one more is added, there are two hiqqah up to one hundred and twenty. When the camels become numerous, for every fifty camels, one hiqqah is due. And a old (herim) camel is not taken, nor one with a defect (dhawt 'awar), unless the collector wishes to count the young and the old together.'

And from him, from Abu Ja'far, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: In five qilas (young camels), one sheep; and there is nothing in what is less than five. In ten, two sheep; in fifteen, three; in twenty, four; in twenty-five, five. In twenty-six, a ibnathu makhidh (one-year-old female camel) until thirty-five; if one more is added, then in it is an ibnathu labun (two-year-old female camel) until forty-four; if one more is added, then in it is a hiqqah (three-year-old female camel) until fifty; if one more is added, then in it is a jadha'ah (four-year-old female camel) until seventy-five; if one more is added, then in it are two ibnathu labun until ninety; if one more is added, then in it are two hiqqah until two hundred; when the camels become numerous, then in every fifty is a hiqqah.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father and Muhammad ibn Isma'il from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, all from Ibn Abi Umayr from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: In five qalas (young camels), one sheep; and there is nothing in less than five. In ten, two sheep; in fifteen, three sheep; in twenty, four sheep; in twenty-five, five sheep; and in twenty-six, a bint makhad (a one-year-old female camel) up to thirty. And Abd al-Rahman said: This is the difference between us and the people. Then he continued the hadith to its end according to what we presented earlier.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from al-Hasan 'an Zur'ah 'an Sama'ah said: I asked him about the pre-dawn meal (suhur) for one who intends to fast, so he said: 'As for Ramadan, then indeed there is merit in the suhur, even with a sip of water. As for voluntary fasting outside of Ramadan, then whoever wishes to take the pre-dawn meal, let him do so, and whoever does not do so, there is no harm.'

Ali ibn al-Hasan from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Yusuf from Mu'adh ibn Thabit, Abu al-Hasan, from Amr ibn Jumay', from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) from his father (peace be upon him) who said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'Eat suhoor (pre-dawn meal), even if it is just a sip of water. Indeed, may the prayers of Allah be upon those who eat suhoor.'

And from him, from Ya'qub ibn Yazid, from Muhammad ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Hafs ibn al-Bakhtari, from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: "The best of your suhoor (pre-dawn meal) is as-sawiq (barley porridge) and dates."

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from al-Nawfali, from al-Sakuni, from Ja'far, from his fathers (peace be upon them), who said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: "The pre-dawn meal (suhur) is a blessing." The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: "Let my ummah not abandon the pre-dawn meal, even if it is just a sip of water."

Ali ibn al-Hasan, from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Yusuf, from Abd al-Salam ibn Salim, from Saif ibn 'Amirah, from 'Amr ibn Shimir, from Jabir, who said: I heard Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) saying: 'The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) would break his fast on the two blacks.' I said: 'May Allah have mercy on you, and what are the two blacks?' He said: 'Dates and water, and raisins and water, and he would eat suhoor with them.'

Sa'd ibn Abdillah narrated from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) from Muhammad ibn Abdillah al-Razi from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Abi Hamzah from Rifa'ah ibn Musa from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) from his father (peace be upon him) who said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: "Cooperate in eating the pre-dawn meal (suhur) for the sake of fasting during the day, and in sleeping during the midday rest (qaylulah) for the sake of standing in prayer during the night."
Al-Husayn ibn Said from Ibn Sinan from a man from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "Breaking the fast with water washes away the sins of the heart."
And from him, from some of our companions, he elevated it from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ghiyath ibn Ibrahim from Ja'far from his father: "That Ali (peace be upon him) used to prefer to break his fast on milk."

Ali ibn al-Hasan from Muhammad and Ahmad, the sons of al-Hasan, from their father from Abdillah ibn Bukayr from some of our companions from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: It is recommended for the fasting person, if he is able to do so, to pray before breaking his fast.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from al-Nawfali, from al-Sakuni, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his fathers, peace be upon them, who said: Indeed, the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) would say when breaking his fast: 'O Allah, for You we fasted and upon Your provision we broke the fast, so accept it from us. The thirst is gone, the veins are moistened, and the reward remains.'

And from him, from al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from Ahmad ibn Ishaq, from Sa'dan, from Abi Basir, from Abi Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: You should say at the time of breaking the fast until the end of every night of the month of Ramadan: 'All praise is due to Allah who enabled us, so we fasted, and provided for us, so we broke the fast. O Allah, accept from us, help us in it, keep us safe in it, and accept it from us with ease from You and well-being. And all praise is due to Allah who discharged for us one day of the month of Ramadan.'

Ali ibn al-Hasan, from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Jahm, from Abdullah ibn Maymun al-Qaddah, from Abu Abdillah, from his father, upon them be peace, said: Qanbar, the freedman of Ali (peace be upon him), brought his breaking of the fast to him. He said: So he came with a bag containing sawiq (crushed barley flour) with a seal on it. He said: And a man said to him, O Commander of the Faithful, is this not stinginess? You seal your food. He said: So Ali (peace be upon him) smiled. He said: Then he said: And is it not so that I do not like anything to enter my stomach except something whose path I know. Then he broke the seal, took out the sawiq, put some of it in a cup, and gave it to him. He took the cup, and when he wanted to drink, he said: In the name of God, O God, for You we fasted and upon Your provision we broke the fast, so accept from us. Indeed, You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing. And what he mentioned in the book of the supplication every day and night, and the explanation of the prayers and the glorification, has already passed in full detail, so there is no reason to repeat it.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Salamah, the companion of al-Sabiri, from Abu al-Subah al-Kinanī, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "Whoever gives food to a fasting person, he will have a reward like his."

And from him, from several of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Sa'dan ibn Muslim, from Musa ibn Bakr, from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him), who said: "Breaking the fast of your fasting brother is superior to your own fasting."

And from him, from Ali ibn Mahziyar, from Harun ibn Muslim, from Mas'adah ibn Sadah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: Sadeer entered upon my father (peace be upon him) in the month of Ramadan and he said: 'O Sadeer, do you know which nights these are?' He said: 'Yes, my father, may I be your ransom, these are the nights of the month of Ramadan.' He said to him: 'What then?' He said to him: 'Can you afford to free ten slaves from the descendants of Ismail every night?' Sadeer said to him: 'My father and mother be my ransom, my wealth does not reach that.' He kept reducing the number until he reached one slave, and Sadeer kept saying 'I cannot afford that.' He said to him: 'Then can you afford to break the fast with a Muslim man every night?' He said: 'Yes, and ten.' He said to him: 'That is what I meant, O Sadeer. Your breaking the fast with your Muslim brother is equivalent to freeing one slave from the descendants of Ismail.'

Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Faddal from Muhammad ibn Hammad ibn Zayd from his father from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) from his father (peace be upon him) who said: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said: "Whoever gives food to a fasting person will have a reward equal to his, without any decrease, and the reward of the good deeds he performed with the strength of that food."

And from him, from Ja'far ibn Uthman, from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from Abu Ayyub, from Abu al-Ward, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) delivered a sermon on the last Friday of Sha'ban, praised Allah and extolled Him, and spoke some words, then said: 'The month of Ramadan has come upon you. Whoever gives food to a fasting person in it, for him is, by that, the emancipation of a slave and forgiveness of his sins in what has passed,' at the presence of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. It was said to him: 'O Messenger of Allah, not all of us can afford to give food to a fasting person.' He said: 'Indeed, Allah is Generous; He gives this reward to whoever can do nothing but give a mouthful of milk to feed a fasting person, or a drink of fresh water, or a few dates, which he cannot afford more than that.'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad ibn 'Uthman from Muhammad ibn Muslim said: I heard Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) saying: 'What the fasting person does does not harm him, if he avoids three things: food, drink, and women, and immersing himself in water.'

And from him, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Mansur ibn Yunus, from Abu Basir, who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: 'A lie breaks the wudu and breaks the fast.' I said, 'We are lost,' he said, 'Not where you think. That is the lie directed at Allah, and at His Messenger (peace be upon him and his family), and at the Imams (peace be upon them).' His saying (peace be upon him) 'breaks the wudu' means it breaks the completeness of the wudu, its reward, and the aspect for which the reward is deserved, because if he had not done it, his reward would have been greater and its ranks more abundant. And the Imam (peace be upon him) did not intend by 'breaking the wudu' that one must repeat the wudu, because we have already explained in the Book of Purification what breaks the wudu, and this is not among them.

And Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from 'Uthman ibn 'Isa from Sama'ah who said: I asked him about a man who broke his fast by eating or drinking in the month of Ramadan, so he said: 'He has broken his fast, and upon him is its making up (qada'), and he is considered fasting [in terms of obligation] but he must make up his fast and his ablution if he did so deliberately.' His saying (peace be upon him) in this report 'he makes up his ablution' is on the level of recommendation (istihbab), based on the indication of what we mentioned in the Book of Purity. And it is not obligatory upon that to make up the fast, because if we were to follow the apparent meaning of the report, we would say that making up the purity is also obligatory. But we referred it to recommendation due to the evidence we presented earlier, and that evidence is not present in making up the fast, so it remains upon its apparent meaning regarding the obligation of making up the fast for whoever did that deliberately, as opposed to forgetfulness.
Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad from al-Halabi from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "The fasting person immerses himself in water and does not rub his head."
And from him, from Hammad, from Hariz, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: The fasting person and the person in Ihram should not immerse their head completely in water.

And from him, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him), that he asked him about a man who uses enema, where the ailment requires it in the month of Ramadan. So he said: 'The fasting person is not permitted to use enema.' And that which Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Ali ibn al-Hasan from his father (1) who said: I wrote to Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) What do you say about using enema with solid substances, which a person uses while he is fasting? So he wrote (peace be upon him): 'There is no harm with the solid (substance).' So it is understood to refer to solid substances that do not rise into the cavity of the human body because they are solid and not liquid. As for enema with water, then that is not permitted, according to what we have previously stated.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from Ali ibn al-Hakam from al-'Ala' ibn Razin from Muhammad ibn Muslim from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: "The fasting person may immerse himself in water, pour water over his head, cool himself with his garment, sprinkle water with a fan, and sprinkle water with a reed mat, but he must not submerge his head completely in water."

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Husayn, from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan, from his father, from Ali ibn Ribat, from Ibn Muskhan, from Layth al-Muradi, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the fasting person who undergoes cupping and pours oil into his ear. He said, 'There is no harm, except for snuff (sua'at), for it is disliked.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from a number of our companions from Sahl ibn Ziyad from al-Rayyan ibn al-Salt from Yunus said: The fasting person in the month of Ramadan may use the siwak (tooth-stick) whenever he wishes. And if he rinses his mouth during the time of obligatory prayer and water enters his throat, there is no blame upon him and his fast is complete. But if he rinses his mouth during non-obligatory prayer time and water enters his throat, he must repeat the fast. The best for the fasting person is to not rinse his mouth. And we have explained in the Chapter of the Sunnah of the Fasting Person what the fasting person must avoid from that which breaks the fast, so there is no need for repetition. And we will explain in the following chapter what of it requires making up (qada) and expiation (kaffarah), from the total of what we have mentioned previously, if God Almighty wills.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from a number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from Abdillah ibn Sinan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding a man who deliberately broke his fast for one day in the month of Ramadan without an excuse, he said: 'He must free a slave, or fast two consecutive months, or feed sixty poor people; and if he is unable, he should give charity according to his ability.'

And from him, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, and Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, all from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Jamil ibn Darraj, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): that he was asked about a man who deliberately broke his fast for one day in the month of Ramadan, so he said: "Indeed, a man came to the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) and said, 'I am ruined, O Messenger of Allah.' He said, 'What is wrong with you?' He said, 'Hellfire, O Messenger of Allah.' He said, 'What is wrong with you?' He said, 'I had intercourse with my wife.' He said, 'Give charity and seek forgiveness from your Lord.' The man said, 'By He who has magnified your right, I did not leave in the house anything small or large.' A man from the people entered with a measure of dates containing twenty sa's, which is ten asw'uq by our sa'. The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said to him, 'Take these dates and give charity with them.' He said, 'O Messenger of Allah, with whom shall I give charity, when I have told you that I have neither little nor much in my house?' He said, 'Then take them and feed your family, and seek forgiveness from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.' He said, 'And when we returned, our companions said, 'Indeed, he began with manumission.' He said, 'Manumit, or fast, or give charity.'"

And from him, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding a man who had intercourse with his wife in the month of Ramadan and did not find what to give in charity to sixty poor people, he said: 'He gives in charity what he is able to.'

And from him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Safwan, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the man who plays with his wife in the month of Ramadan until he ejaculates. He said: 'Upon him is the expiation like that of the one who has intercourse.'

And from him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Uthman ibn Isa, from Samaan, who said: I asked him about a man who was taken [for punishment] in the month of Ramadan, having broken his fast three times, and his case was referred to the Imam three times. He said, 'He should be killed on the third [time].'

Sa'd ibn 'Abdillah from Abu Ja'far, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Fudaylah ibn Ayyub, from Aban ibn 'Uthman, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi 'Abdillah, from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a man who deliberately broke his fast for one day in the month of Ramadan. He said: 'Upon him is fifteen sa' for each poor person, a mud with the mud of the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) is better.' And from him, from Abu Ja'far, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn Abi al-Khattab, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from al-Mashriqi, from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a man who deliberately broke his fast for days in Ramadan, what is the expiation upon him? He wrote (replying): 'Whoever deliberately breaks his fast for one day in Ramadan, upon him is freeing a believing slave, and he fasts one day in place of one day.' And there is no contradiction in these narrations, because what is obligatory upon the one who breaks his fast deliberately for one day is one of the three things: freeing a slave, or feeding sixty poor people, or fasting two consecutive months. Whichever of the three he does, it suffices him. So whenever he is unable to do one of them, he fasts what he is able to do and gives charity with what he can, and this is with the varying conditions of people from weakness and strength. And it has been said that he fasts eighteen days in place of freeing the slave and feeding (the poor). That which indicates this is what he narrated:

Sa'd ibn Abd Allah from Ibrahim ibn Hashim from Isma'il ibn Marar and Abd al-Jabbar ibn Mubarak from Yunus ibn Abd al-Rahman from Abd Allah ibn Muskan from Abu Basir and Sama'ah ibn Mihran said: We asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who has upon him the fasting of two consecutive months, and he could not manage to fast, and could not manage to free a slave, and could not manage to give charity. He said: 'Let him fast eighteen days, for every ten poor people, three days.'

Saad narrated from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Fadhal from Amr ibn Sa'id al-Mad'ani from Musaddiq ibn Sadah from Ammar ibn Musa al-Sabati who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who is fasting and has intercourse with his wife, so he said, 'He performs ghusl and there is nothing upon him.' This report is understood to mean that if he had intercourse unintentionally and not deliberately, then nothing is required of him, and the state is as we described. It also carries the possibility that the intended meaning is one who does not know that this is not permissible for him in the Sharia. What indicates this is what he narrated:

Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Fadhal narrated from Muhammad ibn Ali, from Ali ibn al-Nu'man, from Abdullah ibn Muskan, from Zurarah and Abu Basir, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), they both said: We asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about a man who had relations with his wife during the month of Ramadan, and he had relations with her while he was in the state of Ihram (for Hajj or Umrah), and he did not think except that it was permissible for him. He (peace be upon him) said: 'There is no penalty upon him.'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from 'Uthman ibn 'Isa from Sama'ah who said: I asked him about a man who had intercourse with his wife in the month of Ramadan intentionally, so he said: 'Upon him is the freeing of a slave, and feeding sixty poor people, and fasting two consecutive months, and making up for that day, and how can he find like that day?' So it is possible that the meaning of the 'waw' (and) in the report is the option (to choose one of the expiations) rather than the combination (of all), because it is used for that purpose. Allah, the Exalted, said: 'So marry of them, those that are lawful to you, two or three or four.' And he meant two or three or four, and did not mean the combination (of all four at once). And it is also possible that this ruling is specific to one who had intercourse with his wife in a state where intercourse is forbidden, such as intercourse during menstruation, or in the state of Dhihar before the expiation, for if he did that, the combination of the three expiations becomes obligatory upon him, because he had intercourse in a forbidden manner in the month of Ramadan. That which indicates this interpretation is what he narrated:

Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn Babawayh, from Abd al-Wahid ibn Muhammad ibn 'Abdus al-Naysaburi, from Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Qutaybah, from Hamdan ibn Sulayman, from Abd al-Salam ibn Sahih al-Harawi, who said: I said to al-Rida (peace be upon him): 'O son of the Messenger of God, it has been narrated from your forefathers (peace be upon them) that for one who has intercourse in the month of Ramadan or breaks his fast in it, there are three expiations. And it has also been narrated from them that there is one expiation. Which of the two narrations should we follow?' He said: 'We follow both. If a man has intercourse in a prohibited manner or breaks his fast in a prohibited manner in the month of Ramadan, then upon him are three expiations: freeing a slave, fasting for two consecutive months, and feeding sixty poor people, and making up that day. And if he had intercourse in a permissible manner or broke his fast in a permissible manner, then upon him is one expiation. And if he was forgetful, then there is nothing upon him.' As for what is apart from these matters that we have enumerated, there is no expiation nor making up for any of them, because the reports that came regarding them only came as a way of dislike, and that it is preferable to avoid them. Among them is what he narrated:

Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Fadhal narrated from Muhammad ibn Abdillah from Abdillah ibn Sinan from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: It is disliked for the fasting person to immerse himself in water.

Sa'd ibn Abdillah narrated from Imran ibn Musa, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Abdillah ibn Jabalah, from Ishaq ibn Ammar, who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'If a fasting man deliberately immerses himself in water, is he required to make up that day?' He said: 'He is not required to make it up, nor does he need to repeat it.' As for the ruling of the junubi (one in major ritual impurity) at night, the Sheikh (may God have mercy on him) has mentioned that whoever becomes junubi and sleeps with the intention of performing ghusl before dawn, and sleep continues until the sun rises, he is not required to make up the day nor does he pay expiation; rather, he performs ghusl and fasts. If he wakes up, then sleeps a second time with the intention of performing ghusl before dawn, and sleep continues until sunrise, he is required to make up the day but not pay expiation. If he sleeps a third time, he is required to make up the day and pay expiation. As for that which indicates the first case, it is what he narrated:

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa narrated from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Najran, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Isa ibn al-Qasim, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who became junub in the month of Ramadan at the beginning of the night, so he delayed the bath until dawn rose. He said: 'He completes his fast and there is no qada (make-up) upon him.' And from him, from al-Nufayli, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Sulayman ibn Abi Zaynab, who said: I wrote to Abu al-Hasan Musa ibn Ja'far (peace be upon them both), asking him about a man who became junub in the month of Ramadan from the beginning of the night, so he delayed the bath until dawn rose. He (peace be upon him) wrote to me in his own handwriting: 'I know it, just like one who is coincidentally delayed, he bathes from his junub state and completes his fast and there is nothing upon him.'

And from him from Sa'd ibn Isma'il from his father from Isma'il ibn Isa who said: I asked al-Rida (peace be upon him) about a man who incurred major ritual impurity (janabah) during the month of Ramadan and slept until morning; what is upon him? He said: 'This does not harm him and he does not break his fast, for my father (peace be upon him) said: 'Aishah said: Indeed the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) became junub from intercourse, not from wet dream.' He said: 'He does not break his fast and it does not matter to him.' And a man who incurred major ritual impurity and remained sleeping until morning; what is obligatory upon him? He said: 'Nothing is upon him; he performs ghusl.' And a man who incurred major ritual impurity in the last part of the night and rose to perform ghusl but did not find water, so he went to seek it or sent someone to bring it, and it was difficult for him until morning; what should he do? He said: 'He performs ghusl when it comes to him, then he prays.' And as for that which indicates the second category, it is what he narrated:

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from 'Uthman ibn 'Isa from Sama'ah ibn Mihran said: I asked him about a man who incurred janabah (major ritual impurity) during the night in Ramadan, then slept having known about it, and did not wake up until Fajr reached him. He said: 'He must complete his fast and make up one other day.' I said: 'If that is the case for the man while he is making up Ramadan?' He said: 'Let him eat on that day and make it up, for it is not like Ramadan in any of the months.'

And from him, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Mansur ibn Hazim, from Abdullah ibn Abi Ya'fur, who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): A man becomes ritually impure (junub) during the month of Ramadan, then he wakes up, then he sleeps until morning (Fajr). He said: 'He completes his fast and makes up one other day. And if he did not wake up until morning, his day is complete and it is valid for him.'

And from him (al-Hasan ibn Mahbub) from Fadala from al-'Ala' from Muhammad ibn Muslim from one of the Imams (peace be upon them both) who said: I asked him about a man who experiences major ritual impurity (janabah) during Ramadan, then sleeps before performing the ritual bath (ghusl). He said: 'He completes his fast and makes up that day, unless he wakes up before the dawn (fajr) rises. If he waits for water to be heated or drawn, and the dawn rises, then he does not make up that day.'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Hammad ibn Isa and Fadala ibn Ayyub from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): A man becomes junub (in a state of major ritual impurity) from the beginning of the night, then sleeps until morning in the month of Ramadan. He said: 'There is no penalty upon him.' I said: But he woke up, then slept until morning. He said: 'Let him fast that day as a penalty (qada').' As for that which indicates the third category, what he narrated...

Al-Husayn ibn Said from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr from Ibrahim ibn Abd al-Hamid from Abi Basir from Abi Abdillah (peace be upon him): In a man who became junub during the night of Ramadan, then deliberately omitted the ritual bath until dawn. He said: 'He must free a slave, or fast two consecutive months, or feed sixty poor people.' He said, and he said: 'He is worthy that I do not think he will ever catch up [with the missed obligation].'

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar from Muhammad ibn Isa, who said: He narrated to me Sulayman ibn Haf al-Marwazi from the Jurist (peace be upon him) He said: 'When a man becomes junub (in a state of major ritual impurity) during the night of Ramadan and does not perform ghusl until dawn, he must fast two consecutive months along with fasting that day, and he does not gain the merit of that day.'

And from him, from Ibrahim ibn Hashim, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Hammad, from Ibrahim ibn Abd al-Hamid, from some of his freedmen, who said: I asked him about the nocturnal emission of the fasting person. He said: 'If he emits semen during the day in the month of Ramadan, he should not sleep until he performs ghusl. And if he becomes junub at night in the month of Ramadan, he is not allowed to sleep for a moment until he performs ghusl. So whoever becomes junub in the month of Ramadan and sleeps until morning, upon him is freeing a slave or feeding sixty poor people, and making up that day, and he completes his fasting, and it will never catch up to him (i.e., it does not count as the obligatory fast for that day).'

Sa'd ibn Abdillah from Abu Ja'far from Sa'd ibn Isma'il ibn Isa from his father who said: I asked al-Rida (peace be upon him) about a man who had janabah in the month of Ramadan and slept intentionally until morning. What is upon him? He said: 'This does not harm him, nor does it break his fast, and it does not matter, for my father (peace be upon him) said: 'Aisha said: Indeed the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) became junub from intercourse, not from wet dream.' There is nothing in this report that contradicts what we mentioned, because his saying 'a man who had janabah in the month of Ramadan and slept intentionally until morning' does not indicate that he intentionally left the ghusl; rather he said 'slept intentionally until morning', so he attributed the intentionality to the sleeping. There would only be doubt if he said 'intentionally left the ghusl', and it is permissible that he intentionally slept at the beginning of the night and remained sleeping until morning, at which time the kaffarah would not be obligatory upon him, and that is what he also narrated.

Saad narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn and Muhammad ibn Ali, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from Hammad ibn Uthman, from Habib al-Kha'thami, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) would pray the night prayer in the month of Ramadan, then he would become junub, then he would deliberately delay the ritual bath until dawn rises. It is not established in it that he deliberately delayed the bath without an excuse; it is permissible that he only delayed the bath due to an excuse, either for fetching the water or for warming it in the cold, or due to an incidental reason, because when one of these excuses occurs, delaying the bath is permissible and neither making up the prayer nor expiation is required. And we have clarified previously what indicates this meaning, so there is no basis for repeating it. And regarding the one who rinses his mouth and the one who inhales water, we have clarified their ruling: if it is for prayer, there is nothing upon him regarding what enters his throat from it; but if it is for other than prayer, and it enters his throat, then he must make up the prayer and expiation is required of him. And this is also indicated by what he narrated.

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar from Muhammad ibn Isa said: He narrated to me Sulayman ibn Haf al-Marwazi said: I heard him saying: "When the fasting person rinses his mouth in the month of Ramadan, or inhales deliberately, or smells a strong scent, or sweeps a house and dust enters his nose or throat, then upon him is the fasting of two consecutive months, for that is considered breaking the fast for him like eating, drinking, and intercourse." As for snuff (su'oot), there is not in any of the narrations that it necessitates the expiation (kaffarah) for the one who takes it, but it came as a place of dislike (karahiya), and we have clarified that, and what is narrated adds to its clarification:

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar narrated from Ibrahim ibn Hashim, from Barraqah al-Asbahani, from Ghiyath ibn Ibrahim, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father (peace be upon him), who said: "There is no harm with kohl (eye makeup) for the fasting person, and sniffing snuff (sua'oot) is disliked for the fasting person."

And from him, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Muhammad ibn Ali al-Khazzaz, from Ghiyath ibn Ibrahim, from Ja'far, from his father, from Ali (peace be upon him) That he disliked the use of snuff (snufling) for the fasting person.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from a number of our companions from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ibn Mahbub from Hisham ibn Salim from Burayd al-Ajli said: Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) was asked about a man against whom witnesses testified that he broke his fast for three days in the month of Ramadan. He said: 'He is asked: Is there sin upon you for your breaking of the fast in the month of Ramadan?' If he says 'No', then it is upon the Imam to kill him. And if he says 'Yes', then it is upon the Imam to severely beat him.'

And from him, from Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Bundar, from Ibrahim ibn Ishaq al-Ahmar, from Abdullah ibn Hammad, from al-Mufaddal ibn Umar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding a man who had intercourse with his wife while he was fasting and she was fasting, he said: 'If he compelled her, then upon him is two expiations; and if she consented to him, then upon him is one expiation and upon her is one expiation; and if he compelled her, then upon him is the striking of fifty lashes, half the hadd; and if she consented to him, then he is struck with twenty-five lashes and she is struck with twenty-five lashes.'

Al-Husayn ibn Said from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad ibn 'Uthman from Al-Halabi from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about an elderly man who is weak and unable to fast during the month of Ramadan, so he said: 'He should give charity in the form of feeding one poor person for each day as a substitute.'

And from him (al-Hasan ibn al-Faraj) from Fadala from al-'Ala' from Muhammad ibn Muslim from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) Regarding the saying of Allah, Exalted and Mighty: 'And upon those who are able [to fast, but with hardship] - a ransom [as substitute] of feeding a poor person [every day],' he said: 'The old man and the one afflicted with thirst.' And regarding His saying, Exalted: 'And whoever is not able to do so, then the feeding of sixty poor people,' he said: 'From illness or thirst.'

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa narrated from Ali ibn al-Hakam from Abd al-Malik ibn Utbah al-Hashimi who said: I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about the elderly man and the elderly woman who are weak and unable to fast in the month of Ramadan. He said: 'She gives charity for each day with a mudd of wheat.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from al-'Ala' ibn Razin from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I heard Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) saying: 'The elderly man and the one suffering from chronic thirst have no blame upon them if they break their fast in the month of Ramadan, and each of them must give charity every day with a mudd of food, and there is no make-up (qada) required for them. If they are unable [to give charity], then there is nothing required of them.'

And this hadith was narrated - Sa'd ibn Abdillah from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn Abi al-Khattab, who said: We were narrated by Ja'far ibn Bashir and Muhammad ibn Abdillah ibn Hilal from 'Ala' ibn Razin from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) : (3) and he mentioned the hadith, except that he said: 'And each of them gives charity every day with two mudds of food.' And this report is not contradictory to the hadiths that included giving one mudd of food or feeding a poor person, because this ruling varies according to the varying conditions of the obligated ones. So whoever is able to feed two mudds is obliged to do so, and whoever is only able to feed one mudd does that, and whoever cannot manage any of it bears no burden, according to what we have previously stated. And to add clarification to this is what was narrated:

Sa'd ibn Abdillah narrated from Imran ibn Musa and Ali ibn Khalid from Harun from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Yahya ibn al-Mubarak from Abdillah ibn Junadab from Sama'ah ibn Mihran from Abi Basir from Abi Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him: 'An elderly man who is unable to fast,' he said: 'Some of his children should fast on his behalf.' I said: 'If he has no children?' He said: 'Then the nearest of his relatives.' I said: 'If he has no relatives?' He said: 'He should give charity with a mud of food for each day. If he has nothing, then there is no obligation upon him.'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Fudaylah ibn Ayyub from Dawud ibn Farqad from his father who said: Hafs al-A'war wrote to me: 'Ask Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about three issues.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'What are they?' He said: 'One who misses fasting three days in a month.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Due to illness or old age or thirst?' He said: 'Explain to me one by one.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'If it is due to illness, then when he recovers, let him make up for it; and if it is due to old age or thirst, then for each day, one mudd [of food].'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ibn Mahbub from al-Alla' ibn Razin from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I heard Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) saying: 'The pregnant woman who is near her delivery and the nursing mother with little milk, there is no blame upon them if they break the fast in the month of Ramadan because they cannot endure the fast. Upon them is that each of them must give charity, one mudd of food for every day she breaks the fast, and upon them is the making up of every day she broke, which she makes up later.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ahmad ibn Idris from Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn al-Husayn from Amr ibn Sa'id from Musaddiq ibn Sadah from 'Ammar ibn Musa al-Sabati from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding the man who is struck by thirst to the point of fearing for his life, he said: 'He drinks enough to maintain his vitality, and does not drink until he is fully satisfied.'

And from him, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Isma'il ibn Marar, from Yunus, from Mufaddal ibn 'Amr, who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'We have young men and girls who are unable to fast due to the severity of the thirst that afflicts them.' He said: 'Let them drink the amount by which their souls are satisfied and which they fear [from causing harm/exhaustion].' The Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: 'And none of those we mentioned may have marital relations, unless a great need drives them to do so.' That is indicated by what he narrated:

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Muhammad ibn Abi al-Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "When a man travels during the month of Ramadan, he should not approach his wives during the day in Ramadan, for that is forbidden for him."

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ibn Mahbub from Ibn Sinan said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who travels in the month of Ramadan and has a female servant with him, and he is permitted to have intercourse with her during the day. He said, 'Glory be to Allah, does this man not know the sanctity of the month of Ramadan? Indeed, he has a long night (to make up for it).' I said, 'Is it not permissible for him to eat, drink, and shorten (the prayer)?' He said, 'Indeed, Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, granted the traveler permission to break the fast and shorten (the prayer) as a mercy and alleviation for the place of fatigue, exhaustion, and hardship of travel, and He did not grant him permission for intercourse with women while traveling during the day in the month of Ramadan. He obligated him to make up the fast, and did not obligate him to complete the prayer when he returns from his travel.' Then he said, 'And the Sunnah is not to be measured (by the minimum ruling), and indeed, when I travel in the month of Ramadan, I do not eat except the basic sustenance (qut) and I do not drink except until I am fully satisfied (riyy).'

And from him, from Ali ibn Muhammad, from Ibrahim ibn Ishaq al-Ahmar, from Abdullah ibn Hammad, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, who said: I asked him about a man who has intercourse with his female slave during the day in Ramadan while traveling. He said: 'Does this man not know the right of the month of Ramadan? Indeed, for him at night is a long swim.'

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa from Muhammad ibn Sahil from his father who said: I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about a man who had relations with his wife during the month of Ramadan while he was traveling, and he said, 'There is no harm (in it).'

And from him (Al-Shaykh) from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad ibn Uthman from Umar ibn Yazeed who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who travels in the month of Ramadan, is it permissible for him to have intercourse with women? He said, 'Yes.'

Sa'd ibn Abdillah narrated from Muhammad ibn Isa ibn Ubayd from Uthman ibn Isa from Hariz from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who returns from a journey after Asr prayer in the month of Ramadan, and he has intercourse with his wife when she has become pure from her menses. Is it permissible for him to have intercourse with her? He said, 'There is no harm (in it).'

Three narrations: Hariz from Muhammad ibn Muslim from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him): Regarding the man who is unconscious for days, he said, 'He does not make up anything of his prayer.' Four: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya from Muhammad ibn al-Jabbar from Ali ibn Mahziyar, who said: I asked him about the one who is unconscious for a day or more, whether he makes up what missed of the prayer or not, so he wrote (in reply), peace be upon him: 'He does not make up the fast, nor does he make up the prayer.'
Ibn Abi Umayr from Hafs ibn al-Bakhtari from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "The one who is unconscious (faints) makes up his prayer for three days."
Hafs narrated from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The person who faints (loses consciousness) makes up what was missed from him.
Hafs narrated from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: He makes up the prayer of one day.
Hafs narrated from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: He pays back the prayer in which he regained consciousness.

Ibn Abi Umayr from Rifah from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about the one who is unconscious for a month: what does he make up of the prayer? He said: 'He makes up all of it, for the matter of prayer is severe/difficult.'

Al-Hasan narrated from Zur'ah from Samaanah who said: I asked him about the patient who loses consciousness. He said: 'If it is less than three days, there is no making up (of prayer) upon him. And if he loses consciousness for three days, then he is obligated to make up the prayers for those days.'

Al-Nadr narrated from Abdullah ibn Sinan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: "Whatever of your prayers you missed due to a period of unconsciousness, make it up when you regain consciousness."

Safwan narrated from al-Ala' from Muhammad ibn Muslim from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a man who loses consciousness and then regains it. He said: 'He makes up what he missed, and gives the adhan for the first prayer and calls the iqamah for the remainder.'

Hariz narrated from Abu Basir who said: I said to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him): A man who was unconscious for a month, does he make up anything from his prayers? He said: 'He makes up three days from it.' Thus, the approach in these narrations is to interpret them as recommended (mustahabb), because what is obligatory upon the one who was unconscious is to pray the prayer for which the time has passed when he regained consciousness. As for what is beyond that, it is recommended to make it up. And that which clarifies what we said is what he narrated:

Hammad narrated from Abu Kahmas, who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) He was asked about the person who faints (loses consciousness): does he make up what he missed of the prayer? He said, 'As for me, my children, and my family, we do that.'

Ibrahim ibn Hashim from more than one from Mansur ibn Hazim from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): that he asked him about the one who is unconscious for a month or forty nights, and he said. He said, 'If you wish, I will inform you of what I command myself and my children to do: that you make up whatever missed you.'

Ibrahim ibn Hashim narrated from Abdullah ibn al-Mughirah from Abdullah ibn Sinan from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "Whatever God has overpowered him with, there is no [blame or obligation] upon its owner."

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad from al-Halabi from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): that he was asked about a man who converted to Islam in the middle of the month of Ramadan. What is upon him regarding fasting? He said, 'He is not upon him except what he converted in it.'

And from him (Al-Shaykh) from Saffan ibn Yahya, from Al-'Is ibn Al-Qasim, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a group of people who embraced Islam in the month of Ramadan, and some days of it had already passed. Is it upon them to make up (fast) the days that passed, or just the day on which they embraced Islam? He said: 'There is no making up (fasting) upon them, nor (do they fast) the day on which they embraced Islam, unless they had embraced Islam before the rising of dawn (Al-Fajr).'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from Harun ibn Muslim from Mas'adah ibn Sadah from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) from his fathers (peace be upon them) that Ali (peace be upon him) used to say: Regarding a man who converted to Islam in the middle of the month of Ramadan, indeed he is not obligated except for what he faces (i.e., the remainder of the month).

Sa'd ibn Abdillah narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn Abi al-Khattab from Uthman ibn Isa from Sama'ah ibn Mihran, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man upon whom the month of Ramadan entered while he was ill and unable to fast, and he died in the month of Ramadan or in the month of Shawwal. He said: 'There is no fasting upon him, nor is there any making up (qada) for him.' I said: 'And a woman in postpartum bleeding, upon whom the month of Ramadan entered and she was unable to fast, and she died in the month of Ramadan or in Shawwal?' He said: 'Making up is not done for her.'

And from him, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Hamid, from Saif ibn 'Amirah, from Mansur ibn Hazim, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the sick person in the month of Ramadan who does not recover until he dies; he said: 'His fasts are not made up for him.' And about the menstruating woman who dies in the month of Ramadan; he said: 'Her fasts are not made up for her.' The explanation in these hadiths is that making up the fasts for the deceased is only obligatory if he had recovered from his illness and neglected making up what was missed of his prayer and fasting; then it becomes obligatory upon his guardian to make it up for him. But if he died while in that illness, it is not obligatory upon anyone to make it up for him. And that which indicates what we mentioned is what he narrated:

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Zarif ibn Nasih, from Abu Maryam, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: If a man fasts for part of the month of Ramadan and remains ill until he dies, there is no obligation upon him [to make up the fasts]. And if he recovered [from illness] then became ill again until he died, and he had wealth, charity is given on his behalf; and if he had no wealth, his heir gives charity on his behalf.

And in the narration of Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from al-Husayn ibn Muhammad from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad from al-Wassha' from Aban ibn Uthman from Abu Maryam Like that, except that he said: 'His guardian fasted on his behalf.'

And from him, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Abu Basir, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about a woman who fell ill in Ramadan and died in the month of Shawwal, and she instructed me to make up the fasts on her behalf. He said: 'Did she recover from her illness?' I said: 'No, she died while still ill.' He said: 'The fasts are not made up on her behalf, for Allah did not make it obligatory upon her.' I said: 'But I wish to make up the fasts on her behalf, and she instructed me to do so.' He said: 'How can you make up something that Allah did not make obligatory upon her? If you wish to fast for your own sake, then fast.'

And also what he narrated - Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from Ali ibn al-Hakam from al-'Ala' ibn Razin from Muhammad ibn Muslim from one of the Imams (peace be upon them) who said: I asked him about a man whom the month of Ramadan overtook while he was ill, and he died before recovering. He said: 'There is nothing upon him, but it is compensated on behalf of the one who recovers then dies before compensating.'

And also what Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Faddal narrated from Muhammad and Ahmad, the sons of al-Hasan, from their father, from Abdullah ibn Bukayr, from some of our companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): Regarding a man who dies in the month of Ramadan, he said: 'It is not incumbent upon his guardian to make up for him what remained of the month. And if he became ill and did not fast Ramadan, then remained ill until Ramadan passed while he was still ill, then died in that illness, it is not incumbent upon his guardian to make up the fasting for him. But if he became ill, did not fast the month of Ramadan, then recovered, then did not make it up, then became ill and died, then it is incumbent upon his guardian to make it up for him, because he had recovered but did not make it up, and it became obligatory upon him.' As for what is missed by the deceased from fasting due to travel, making it up is obligatory upon him in all cases.

Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Faddal from Muhammad ibn al-Rabii from Saif ibn 'Amirah from Mansur ibn Hazim from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding a man who travels in the month of Ramadan and then dies, he said: 'Fasts are made up on his behalf. And if a woman who had her menses in Ramadan dies, no fasts are made up on her behalf. And if a patient in Ramadan does not recover until he dies, no fasts are made up on his behalf.'

And from him, from Ali ibn Asbat, from 'Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding a woman who fell ill in the month of Ramadan, or had her menses, or traveled, and then died before Ramadan ended: Is the fast made up on her behalf? He said: 'As for menstruation and illness, no; and as for travel, yes.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from a number of our companions from Sahl ibn Ziyad from al-Hasan ibn Ali al-Washsha' from Abu al-Hasan al-Rida (peace be upon him) who said: I heard him (peace be upon him) saying: 'If a man dies while he is obligated to fast two consecutive months due to an illness, he must give charity for the first month and make up for the second.' And whoever misses something from the month of Ramadan due to illness and does not make it up until another Ramadan arrives, if he was not cured in between, he should fast the second (Ramadan) and give charity for the first, and there is no make-up obligation upon him. And if he was cured in between but did not make up what he missed, and he intends to make it up, he should fast the current (Ramadan) and make up for the first. And if he left it negligently, the make-up and the expiation for the first become obligatory upon him, and he must fast the one whose time has arrived. And that which indicates this is what we narrated:

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Ibn Abi 'Umayr from Hammad ibn Isa from Hariz from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I asked them (peace be upon them) about a man who became ill and did not fast until another month of Ramadan reached him. They said: 'If he had recovered and then delayed before the next fasting reached him, he should fast the one he reached and give charity for each day with a mudd of food for a poor person, and he must make up the missed days. But if he remained ill until another month of Ramadan reached him, he should fast the one he reached and give charity for the first [year] for each day a mudd for a poor person, and there is no making up [the fasts] upon him.'

And from him, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr and Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Jamil, from Zurarah, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him): Regarding a man falls ill and Ramadan overtakes him, and he is excused from fasting while he is ill, until another Ramadan overtakes him. He said: 'He gives charity for the first [year], and fasts the second. If he recovers in between and does not fast until another Ramadan overtakes him, he fasts both [years] and gives charity for the first [year].'

And from him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from Muhammad ibn al-Fudayl and al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Muhammad ibn al-Fudayl, from Abu al-Subah al-Kinanī, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who owed a portion of fasting from the month of Ramadan, then the next Ramadan caught him (before he paid it off). He said: 'If he was healthy in between, but did not pay it off until the next Ramadan caught him, then he must fast and feed one poor person for each day. And if he was sick in between until the next Ramadan caught him, then there is no obligation upon him except fasting, if he is healthy. But if the illness persisted upon him, then he must feed one poor person for each day.'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad from 'Ali from Abu Basir from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "If a man falls ill from one Ramadan to the next, then recovers, then for every day he broke the fast, the ransom is food, and it is a mudd for each poor person." He said, "And likewise in the expiation of the oath and the expiation of the zihar, a mudd, a mudd." And if he recovered in between the two Ramadans, then he is only required to make up the fasting. But if he neglected it while he was recovered, then upon him is the charity and the fasting together, for every day a mudd, when he finishes that Ramadan."

And that which was narrated is: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from 'Uthman ibn 'Isa from Sama'ah who said: I asked him about a man who was caught by Ramadan while he still had a previous Ramadan upon him which he had not fasted. He said: 'He gives charity in place of each day of the Ramadan that was upon him with a mudd of food, and let him fast this one that he caught. When he breaks his fast (in this current Ramadan), let him fast the Ramadan that was upon him. For indeed I was ill, and three Ramadans passed over me and I did not recover in them, then I caught a Ramadan, so I gave charity in place of each day of what had passed with a mudd of food, then Allah healed me and I fasted them.' So there is in it nothing that contradicts what we mentioned, that whenever the illness persists upon him, charity is obligatory upon him alone without retribution (qada), because in the report it is not stated that he did not recover between them, but rather he said 'three Ramadans passed over me and I did not recover in them, then I caught a Ramadan', and this implies that he did not recover in the Ramadans themselves, not between them. And if it did not bear except that he did not recover between them, then his action would be for him, and the combination of retribution and expiation would be considered recommended. And that which reveals what we mentioned is what he narrated:

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Fadala from 'Abdullah ibn Sinan from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "Whoever breaks his fast for part of Ramadan due to an excuse, then encounters another Ramadan while he is ill, let him give charity with a mud for each day. As for me, I fasted and gave charity." Do you not see that he (peace be upon him) only commanded those who missed Ramadan with charity, without making up the fast, and he attributed both making up the fast and giving charity to himself? If it were not for the way of recommendation (istihbab), he would not have singled himself out for that, but rather he would have generalized it to whoever shared with him in that, according to what he attributed to himself. And the report that he narrated:

Sa'd ibn Abdillah narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from 'Abbad ibn Sulayman, from Sa'd ibn Sa'd, from a man, from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about a man who becomes ill during the month of Ramadan, then recovers afterwards, but delays making up the missed days for a year, or less than that, or more. What is incumbent upon him in that case? He said: 'I like for him to hasten the fasting. If he delays it, there is nothing upon him (in terms of compensation).' Indeed, this is also based on what we mentioned previously, that whenever he delays it without being negligent, and intends to fast, there is nothing upon him from the charity (kaffarah), and only making up the days is incumbent upon him, according to what the Quran encompasses. Allah, the Exalted, said: 'The month of Ramadan in which the Quran was revealed, a guidance for the people and clear proofs of guidance and the criterion. So whoever witnesses the month, let him fast it; and whoever is ill or on a journey - then an equal number of other days.' So He made it obligatory upon whoever witnesses the month of Ramadan to fast it, and upon whoever is traveling or ill to fast an equal number of other days. And this is not contradictory to what we said first, and praise is to Allah alone.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from al-Qasim, from Ali, from Abu Basir, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a woman who began the day fasting in Ramadan, and when the day rose (midday), she became menstruating. He said, 'She breaks her fast.' And I asked him about a woman who saw (signs of) purity at the beginning of the day. He said, 'She prays (Dhuhr and Asr) and completes her day (fast) and makes up (the fast) later.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from 'Uthman ibn 'Isa from Sama'ah said: I asked him about a traveler who arrived at his family before the sun's declination (midday), and he had already eaten. He said: 'It is not appropriate for him to eat anything that day, nor to have intercourse during the month of Ramadan, if he has a wife.'

And from him, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yunus, who said: Regarding the traveler who enters his home in the month of Ramadan, having eaten before entering, he said: 'He refrains from eating for the remainder of his day, and upon him is making up the fast.' And he said: 'Regarding the traveler who enters his home while in a state of major ritual impurity before midday, and he has not eaten, he must complete his fast and there is no making up required of him.' This means if his impurity was from a nocturnal emission.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Fadalah ibn Ayyub from Al-Husayn ibn Uthman from Sama'ah from Abu Basir said: I asked him about the man who arrives from travel during the month of Ramadan, so he said: 'If he arrives before the sun's decline, he must fast that day and count it [towards his obligation].'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from a number of our companions from Sahl ibn Ziyad from Ahmad ibn Muhammad who said: I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about a man who arrived from a journey during the month of Ramadan and had not tasted anything before midday (zawal). He said, 'He fasts.' These two reports indicate that whenever he had not eaten anything and arrived before midday, it is obligatory upon him to fast that day. And that which indicates that when the dawn rises and he is outside the town, he has the choice, is what has been narrated:

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Ibn Abi 'Umayr from Rifa'ah ibn Musa, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who arrives in the month of Ramadan from travel until he sees that he will enter his home in the forenoon or mid-morning. He said: 'When the dawn breaks and he is outside (not yet entered), he has the choice: if he wishes, he fasts, and if he wishes, he breaks his fast.'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from an-Nadr ibn Suwayd from 'Asim ibn Humayd from Muhammad ibn Muslim said: I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about a man who arrived from travel during the month of Ramadan, and his family enters [the state of fasting] when dawn breaks or when the day rises. He said: 'If dawn breaks while he is still outside [not yet with his family], he is at choice: if he wishes, he fasts, and if he wishes, he breaks his fast.'

And from him, from Ali, from his father, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from a man, from Sama'ah, who said: I asked him: What is the limit of the illness that requires its owner to break the fast, just as it is required for him when traveling? He said: 'He is entrusted with it and it is delegated to him; so if he finds weakness, let him break the fast, and if he finds strength, let him fast it. The illness is whatever it is.'

And from him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya and others, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad, from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan, from Amr ibn Sa'id, from Musaddiq ibn Sadah, from 'Ammar al-Sabati, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding a man who finds in his head a pain from severe headache, is it permissible for him to break the fast? He said: 'When he is afflicted with a severe headache, and when he has a severe fever, and when his eye is inflamed with severe inflammation, then it has become permissible for him to break the fast.'

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar from Muhammad ibn Isa from Sulayman ibn Hafsh al-Marwazi said: The Jurist (peace be upon him) said: 'The sick person only prays sitting if he reaches a state in which he cannot walk the distance equivalent to the duration of his prayer while standing until he finishes.' And whoever is in a state of illness that necessitates breaking the fast, and he strives to fast, it does not suffice for him, and he must make up for it. This is indicated by the saying of the Exalted: 'And whoever is sick or on a journey, then an equal number of other days.' Thus, He obligated upon the sick person, by the apparent meaning of the wording, an equal number of other days.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya from Muhammad ibn Abdillah ibn Hilal from Uqbah ibn Khalid from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): Regarding a man who fasted Ramadan while he was ill. He (peace be upon him) said: 'He completes his fast and does not repeat it; it suffices for him.' This is not contradictory to what we mentioned, because this ill person may be such that his fast sufficed for him because he fasted and exerted himself in a state in which the fast did not harm him, and he had not yet reached the degree that made breaking the fast obligatory.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the fasting person who pours oil into his ear, he said, 'There is no harm in it.'

And from him, from Abu Ali al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Hammad ibn Uthman, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about the fasting person who suffers from an ear ailment and pours medicine into it; he said, 'There is no harm in it.'

And from him, from a number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Sulaym al-Farra', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about the fasting person who applies kohl (eye medicine). He said, 'There is no harm with it; it is not food nor drink.'

Al-Husayn ibn Said from Safwan from Al-Husayn ibn Abi Ghundar from Ibn Abi Ya'fur said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the use of kohl (eye makeup) for the fasting person, so he said: 'There is no harm with it, for it is not food that is eaten.'
And from him (Al-Shaykh) from Ibn Abi Umayr from Abd al-Hamid ibn Abi al-Alla' from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "There is no harm with the kohl (eye medicine) for the fasting person."

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Al-Hasan ibn Ali said: I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about the fasting person if his eye aches, does he apply kohl with radish or similar things, or is it permissible for him to do so? He said, 'He does not apply kohl.'

And from him, from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad ibn 'Uthman, from al-Halabi, from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him): that he was asked about a man who applies kohl while fasting, so he said: "No, for I fear that its head [of the kohl] will enter [the throat]." These two reports and what follows their pattern refer to the kohl that contains musk or something with a sharp scent that enters the throat, for that is disliked. As for what is not like that, there is no harm in it. And that which indicates what we mentioned is what he narrated:

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from 'Uthman ibn 'Isa from Sama'ah who said: I asked him about kohl (eye makeup/drops) for the fasting person, so he said: 'If it is kohl and there is no musk in it and it has no taste in the throat, then there is no harm with it.'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Fudaylah ibn Ayyub from al-Ala' from Muhammad ibn Muslim from one of the Imams (peace be upon them both): that he was asked about the woman who applies kohl (eye makeup) while she is fasting, so he said: "If it is not kohl that you find a taste of in her throat, then there is no harm." And we said that kohl is disliked if it contains musk, without that being forbidden, because of what was narrated:

Sa'd ibn 'Abdullah from al-Hasan ibn 'Ali from 'Abdullah ibn al-Mughira from Abu Dawud al-Mustarriq and from Safwan ibn Yahya from al-Husayn ibn Abi Ghundar, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'I apply kohl containing musk while I am fasting.' He said, 'There is no harm in it.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Yahya from Ali ibn al-Hakam from al-Husayn ibn Abi al-'Ala' said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about cupping for the fasting person, so he said, 'Yes, if he does not fear weakness.'

And from him (Al-Hadith) from Ali ibn al-Nu'man from Sa'id al-A'raj who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the fasting person who undergoes cupping, so he said: 'There is no harm, unless he fears weakness in his own self.'

And from him (Al-Haytham ibn Adi) from Hammad ibn Isa from Abdullah ibn Maymun from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) from his father (peace be upon him) who said: Three things do not break the fast of the fasting person: vomiting, seminal emission, and cupping. And he (peace be upon him) did not see any harm in using kohl (eye medicine) for the fasting person. And indeed, the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) underwent cupping while he was fasting.

And that which was narrated is: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Hammad from Abdillah ibn al-Mughira from Abdillah ibn Sinan from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "There is no harm in the fasting person undergoing cupping, except in Ramadan, for I dislike that he endanger himself, unless he fears for his life. And indeed, when we intend, if we seek cupping in Ramadan, we perform it at night." So it is not contradictory to what we mentioned, because he only disliked cupping in Ramadan - and attached it to the state of necessity when the person fears weakness. As for one who does not fear weakness, then there is no harm in it in any case.

And from him, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from Ali, from Abu Basir and Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, all of them from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: "The fasting person may use the siwak (tooth-stick) at any time of the day he wishes."

And from him (Al-Hassan) from Safwan from Ibn Muskan from Al-Halabi who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): Does the fasting person use siwak (tooth-stick) with water and a moist stick, tasting it? He said: 'There is no harm in it.'

Ali ibn al-Hasan narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Abu al-Jarud, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about the use of the siwak (tooth-stick) for the fasting person. He said: 'He may use it at any hour he wishes, from the beginning of the day until its end.'

And from him (Al-Shaykh) from Ali ibn Asbat from Ala' ibn Razin from Muhammad ibn Muslim who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the fasting person: at what time of the day does he use the siwak? He said, 'Whenever he wishes.' And reports have been narrated regarding the dislike of using the siwak with fresh (wet) wood.

Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Fadhl narrated from Ali ibn Asbat from Ula'a al-Qalla' from Muhammad ibn Muslim from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The fasting person may use the siwak (tooth-stick) at any time of the day he wishes, and he should not use it with a fresh (green) twig. He may rinse his mouth, pour water over his head, cool himself with his garment, sprinkle the fan, and sprinkle the buriyah (a type of cloth or mat) beneath him, and he should not immerse his head completely in water.

And from him, from Ayoub ibn Nuh, from Abdullah ibn al-Mughirah, from Sa'd ibn Abi Khalaf, who said: Abu Basir narrated to me from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "The fasting person should not use siwak (tooth-stick) with a fresh (moist) twig."

And Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Ali ibn Ibrahim from Abdullah ibn al-Mughira from Abdullah ibn Sinan from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) that he disliked for the fasting person to use a siwak (tooth-stick) that is wet, and he said: 'It does not harm if he moistens his siwak with water then shakes it off so that no moisture remains in it.' Thus, the dislike in these narrations is directed only at one who cannot control himself, so he spits out the moisture of the stick that accumulates in his mouth; as for one who can control himself, there is no harm in using it in any case.

And Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar narrated from Ibrahim ibn Hashim from Musa ibn Abi al-Hasan al-Razi from Abu al-Hasan al-Rida (peace be upon him) who said: Some of his companions asked him about using the siwak (tooth-stick) during the month of Ramadan. He said, 'It is permissible.' Some of them said, 'Indeed, the moisture of the siwak enters the stomach (jawf).' He said, 'What do you say about the wet siwak, whose moisture enters the throat?' He said, 'The water used for rinsing the mouth (madhmadha) is wetter than the wet siwak.' If a speaker says, 'There is no choice but to use water for rinsing the mouth because of the Sunnah,' then there is no choice but to use the siwak because of the Sunnah that Gabriel (peace be upon him) brought to the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family). As for what he mentioned (may God have mercy on him) regarding the ruling of snuffing (su'oot) and enema (huqna), it has already passed in what was mentioned before, so there is no basis for repeating it. And the woman does not sit in the water.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya and others from Muhammad ibn Ahmad from al-Sayyari from Muhammad ibn Ali al-Hamadani from Hanan ibn Sadir who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the fasting person who dips his head in water (for cooling), so he said: 'There is no harm, but he should not submerge his head completely.
