The Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: 'And shaving is not sufficient for the completely shorn one except shaving, and for whoever is not completely shorn, trimming is sufficient, and shaving is superior. That is indicated by what he narrated:'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from a number of our companions from Sahl ibn Ziyad from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ali ibn Abi Hamzah from Abu Basir from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "Upon the person who is performing Qiran (or Tamattu') [the Sa'ri], it is obligatory to shave his head completely and not merely trim [the hair]; indeed, trimming is [sufficient] for the one who performed the Hajj of Islam."

And Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from Aban ibn Uthman from Bakr ibn Khalid from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "For the young boy (who has not reached puberty), it is not permissible to trim (shorten the hair), but he must shave (the head)." As for that which indicates that for whoever performs the Hajj of Islam, trimming (shortening the hair) is sufficient, the first report is the evidence, and to add clarification to that is what has been narrated:

Al-Husayn ibn Said from Ibn Abi Umayr from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "It is appropriate for the al-sarurah [unshaven pilgrim] to shave [his head], and if he has already performed Hajj, then if he wishes he may trim [shorten] and if he wishes he may shave [completely]." He said, "And when he has let his hair grow long or trimmed it, then shaving is obligatory upon him and trimming is not sufficient for him." And that which indicates that shaving is superior in all cases is what has been narrated:

Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from Abd al-Rahman from Hammad from Hariz from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said on the day of Al-Hudaybiyyah: 'O Allah, forgive those who shaved [their heads],' twice. It was said: 'And those who trimmed [their heads]?' O Messenger of Allah. He said: 'And those who trimmed.'

And from him (Al-Shaykh) from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad from Al-Halabi from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) sought forgiveness for the shavers three times. I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about Al-Tafath (shaving), and he said: 'It is shaving and what is on the skin of the human being.' And we have clarified in what preceded of the book that whoever shortens his hair or mats it, shortening is not sufficient for him and shaving is obligatory upon him. And whoever restricts himself to shortening, a sheep's blood (fine) is incumbent upon him, so there is no basis for repeating it here. And for the woman, shortening by the amount of the fingernail is sufficient, he narrated.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa narrated from Ibn Abi Umayr, from some of our companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The woman shortens her hair for her Umrah by the amount of a finger-joint. And it is from the Sunnah that he begins at the forehead from the right horn and shaves up to the two bones.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa narrated from al-Hasan ibn Muslim, from some of the Imams (peace be upon them), who said: When he intended to shorten his hair for the Umrah, the barber intended to take from the sides of the head, so he said to him, 'Begin with the forehead,' and so he began with it.

And Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from Safwan, from Mu'awiya, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: He commanded the barber to place the comb on his right horn (temple), then commanded him to shave, and he himself named (recited). "O God, grant me for every hair a light on the Day of Resurrection."

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ghiyath ibn Ibrahim from Ja'far from his fathers from Ali (peace be upon him) who said: «The Sunnah in shaving (the head) is that it should reach the two bones (of the head). And whoever has no hair on his head, let him pass the razor over his head, and that is sufficient for him.» It was narrated.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Muhammad ibn Ahmad from Muhammad ibn Isa from Yasin al-Darir from Hariz from Zurarah That a man from the people of Khurasan came as a pilgrim and he was bald (shaved his head) and did not know how to say the Talbiyah, so Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) was asked about him. He ordered that the Talbiyah be said on his behalf and that a comb be passed over his head, for that suffices for him. And whoever shaves his head, then everything that was prohibited for him becomes permissible, except for women and perfume, unless he performs the Ziyarah. So when he performs Ziyarah and Sa'i, everything becomes permissible for him except women, until he performs the Tawaf al-Nisa'. So when he performs the Tawaf al-Nisa', he has made permissible from everything that was prohibited for him. What indicates that is what he narrated:

Musa ibn al-Qasim from Muhammad from Sayf from Mansur ibn Hazim said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who threw [the pebbles at the Jamarat] and shaved [his head], does he eat something containing yellow bile (or impurity)? He said: 'No, until he performs Tawaf around the House and Sa'i between Safa and Marwah. Then everything is permissible for him except women, until he performs another Tawaf around the House. Then the women are permissible for him.'

And from him, from Abd al-Rahman, from Ala', who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): I performed Tamattu', slaughtered the sacrifice, and shaved my head; should I apply henna to my head? He said: 'Yes, provided you do not touch any perfume.' I said: Should I wear the qamis (shirt)? He said: 'Yes, if you wish.' I said: Should I cover my head? He said: 'Yes.'

And from him, from Muhammad ibn 'Umar, from Muhammad ibn 'Uthafir, from 'Umar ibn Yazid, from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: "Know that when you shave your head, everything becomes permissible for you except women and perfume."

And that which was narrated is: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Abu Ali al-Ash'ari from Muhammad ibn al-Jabbar from Safwan ibn Yahya from Sa'id ibn Yasar who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the Mutamatti' (one who performs Hajj al-Tamattu') when he shaves his head, if he applies henna to it? He said: 'Yes, henna, and it is permissible for him [to wear] clothes and perfume and everything except women.' He repeated it to me twice or three times. I said: And I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about it, and he said: 'Yes, henna, and clothes, and perfume, and everything except women.' So it does not contradict what we mentioned, because in the apparent meaning of this report it is not stated that when he shaves his head, these things become permissible for him even if he has not performed Tawaf. Rather, it is possible that he meant: whenever he shaves and performs the Tawaf of Hajj and Sa'i, then these things become permissible for him, even if he does not mention it in the wording, due to his knowledge that the addressee is aware of that, or as a reference to other reports. And we have previously presented the first report in detail, so ruling with it upon this report is more preferable, because this is general/summary and that is detailed, and ruling with the detailed upon the general is more preferable. And that which was narrated:

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Abu Ali al-Ash'ari from Muhammad ibn al-Jabbar from Safwan from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj who said: A child was born to Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) in Mina, so he sent to us on the Day of Sacrifice (Eid al-Adha) khabeez (sweet flatbread) with saffron, and we had already shaved (our heads). Abd al-Rahman said: So I ate, but al-Kahili and Murazm refrained from eating it, and they said: 'We have not yet visited the Kaaba (performed Umrah/Hajj rites).' So Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) heard our words and said to Musadif, who was the messenger who brought it to us, 'What were they talking about?' He said: 'Abd al-Rahman ate, and the other two refused, saying: We have not yet visited the Kaaba.' He said: 'Abd al-Rahman was correct.' Then he said: 'Do you not remember when it was brought to us on a day like this, and I ate from it, and my brother Abd Allah refused to eat from it?' So when my father came, he urged him against me, and he said: 'O my father, indeed Musa ate khabeez with saffron and had not yet visited (the Kaaba).' So my father (peace be upon him) said: 'He is more learned in jurisprudence than you. Have you not shaved your heads?'

And what Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Fadalah from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Ibn 'Abbas was asked: 'Did the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) use perfume before visiting the House (Kaaba)?' He said: 'I saw the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) applying musk to his head before visiting the House.' Therefore, in these two reports, it is not established that the permissibility of using perfume applies only upon completion of shaving the head before the visit, for the Mutamatti' or for the Hajj who is not a Mutamatti'. And if that is not explicit in the two reports, we interpret them as applying to the Hajj who is not a Mutamatti', because it is permissible for him to use everything upon shaving his head, except women (i.e., prohibition of marrying women), only. And the use of perfume is not permissible for the Mutamatti' along with that, unlike the others. And that which indicates this is what he narrated:

Musa ibn al-Qasim from Abd al-Rahman from Muhammad ibn Humran said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the pilgrim on the Day of Sacrifice: what is permissible for him? He said, 'Everything except women.' And about the Mutamatti' (one performing Tamattu' Hajj): what is permissible for him on the Day of Sacrifice? He said, 'Everything except women and perfume.' As for wearing clothes and covering the head, there is no objection to both after shaving the head and before the Tawaf (Visitation). The mention of this has already passed, and to add further clarification, he narrated:

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Safwan and Fadalah from al-Ala' said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'I shaved my head and sacrificed (the animal) while I was in the state of Tamattu'. Can I anoint my head with henna?' He said: 'Yes, provided you do not touch any of the perfume.' I said: 'And I wear the qamis (seamless garment) and cover my head (with the qamis)?' He said: 'Yes.' I said: 'Before I perform Tawaf around the House?' He said: 'Yes.'

And as for what was narrated - Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Hammad ibn Isa from Hariz from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who performed Umrat al-Tamattu', then stood at Arafat and stood at Al-Mash'ar, and threw the Jamarah, and sacrificed, and shaved [his head]. Should he cover his head? He said, 'No, until he performs Tawaf with the House, and [Tawaf] with As-Safa and Al-Marwah.' It was said to him, 'And if he did [shave before Tawaf]?' He said, 'I do not see any blame upon him.'

And from him from Safwan from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar from Idris al-Qummi who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'Indeed, a freedman of ours performed Tamattu' (pilgratitude with Umrah then Hajj), and when he shaved his head, he put on clothes before visiting the House (Kaaba).' He said: 'What a bad thing he did.' I said: 'Is there any blame upon him?' He said: 'No.' I said: 'For I saw Ibn Abi Sammak running between Safa and Marwah, wearing two socks, a qaba' (tunic), and a belt.' He said: 'What a bad thing he did.' I said: 'Is there any blame upon him?' He said: 'No.' The explanation in these two narrations is that they came at the place of recommendation and preference, not prohibition and obligation, because it is recommended that the pilgrim does not return to the rulings of those who are free from restrictions except after completing all his rituals, so that his heart does not become occupied with performing what is obligatory upon him, and if he did it, there is no blame upon him. And that which indicates that they came on the path of recommendation is what has been narrated:

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Safwan from Mansur ibn Hazim from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) that he said: Regarding a man who was performing Tamattu' (Hajj), he stood at Arafat and Al-Mash'ar, sacrificed his animal, and shaved his head. He said: 'He should not cover his head until he performs Tawaf with the House and Sa'i between As-Safa and Al-Marwah, for my father (peace be upon him) disliked that and forbade it.' We said: 'If he did it?' He said: 'I do not see anything upon him, but if he did not do it, it was more beloved to me.' And when the Mu'tamatti' performs the Hajj visitation, everything is permissible for him except women, and we have clarified that, so there is no basis for repeating it. And what he narrated: -(840) 33 - Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Muhammad ibn Isma'il said: I wrote to Abu al-Hasan al-Rida (peace be upon him): 'Is it permissible for the Muhrim al-Mutamatti' to touch perfume before performing Tawaf al-Nisa?' He said: 'No.' So the ruling is what we mentioned previously, that it came as a recommendation (Istihbab) and leaving distraction by non-rituals, and that he should not use what is permissible for those who are released (from Ihram) except after completing all the rituals.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father and Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from al-Fadl, from Safwan, and Ibn Abi Umayr, from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: Cast [the pebbles] each day at the time of the sun's decline, and say as you said when you cast the Jamarat al-Aqaba. Begin with the first Jamarah, cast it from its left side, from the bottom of the stream, and say as you said on the Day of Sacrifice. Then stand to the left of the path, face the Qiblah, praise Allah, extol Him, and send blessings upon the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family). Then advance slightly, supplicate, and ask Him to accept [your worship] from you. Then advance again and do the same for the second, and act as you did with the first. Stand and supplicate to Allah as you supplicated. Then proceed to the third, and upon you is calmness and dignity, and do not stand at it.

And from him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Safwan, from Ya'qub ibn Shu'ayb, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the Jamars (pillars of stone), so he said: 'Stand at the two Jamars and do not stand at Jamarat al-Aqabah.' I said: 'Is this from the Sunnah?' He said: 'Yes.' I said: 'What should I say when I throw?' He said: 'Say Allahu Akbar with each pebble.'
Musa ibn al-Qasim from Abd al-Rahman from Safwan ibn Mihran said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: 'The throwing of the Jamarat is between the sunrise and its sunset.'
And from him, from Muhammad, from Saif, from Mansur ibn Hazim, who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: 'The throwing of the Jamarat is between the sunrise and the sunset.'

And from him, from Abd al-Rahman, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Hariz, from Zurarah and Ibn Udhaynah: from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) that he said to Al-Hakam ibn Uthaybah: He asked, 'What is the limit of throwing the Jamarat?' Al-Hakam said, 'At the decline of the sun.' Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said, 'O Hakam, tell me, if there were two of them, and one said to his companion, 'Guard our belongings for us until we return,' would he miss the throwing? By God, [he would not], as long as it is between sunrise and sunset.' And whoever misses throwing the Jamarat until sunset, he should not throw them at night, but delay the throwing until the next day, and throw what he missed and what is obligatory upon him for that day, distinguishing between them by an hour. Narrated.

Musa ibn al-Qasim from Abd al-Rahman from Abd Allah ibn Sinan said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who departed from Jumu'ah until he reached Mina, and a hindrance occurred to him so he did not throw [the pebbles] until the sun set. He said: 'He should throw when he rises in the morning twice: once for what was missed by him, and the second for the day on which he rises in it. And he should distinguish between the two, so that one of them is in the early morning, and it is for yesterday, and the other is at the time of the sun's decline.'

And from him (Al-Shaykh) from Al-Lu'lu'i, Hasan ibn Husayn, from Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from Ali ibn Ri'ab, from Burayd Al-Ajli, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who forgot to throw the pebbles at the middle pillar on the second day. He said: 'Let him throw it on the third day for what missed him and for what is obligatory upon him on his day.' I said: 'And if he does not remember except on the day of departure (Yawm al-Nafar)?' He said: 'Let him throw it and there is nothing upon him.' (Note: The text continues with a separate ruling regarding the sick, fearful, shepherds, and slaves being permitted to throw at night, which is included in the body as it is part of the same narrational context in this specific text segment). And permission has been granted for the sick, the fearful, the shepherds, and the slaves to throw (the pebbles) at night. (He) narrated.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Abdillah ibn Sinan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "There is no harm if the one fearing [danger or difficulty] throws [the pebbles] at night, offers the sacrifice at night, and departs [from Mina] at night."

Saad narrated from Abu Ja'far, from al-Abbas ibn Ma'ruf, from Ali ibn Mahziyar, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Zur'ah, from Sama'ah ibn Mihran, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "Permission has been granted for the servant, the fearful one, and the shepherd to throw [the pebbles] at night."

And from him, from Musa ibn al-Hasan, from Ahmad ibn Hilal, from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr, from Ali ibn 'Atiyyah, who said: We departed from Al-Muzdalifah at night, I and Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik al-Kufi, and Hisham was anxious. We arrived at Jamarat al-Aqabah at the rising of Fajr. Hisham said to me, 'What have we innovated in our Hajj? We are still in this state.' Then we met Abu al-Hasan Musa (peace be upon him), who had already thrown the pebbles at the Jamarat and had departed. Hisham's heart was comforted. If he forgot to throw the pebbles at the Jamarat until he reached Mecca, he should return and throw them.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Fadala ibn Ayyub from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'What do you say about a woman who did not know to throw the Jamarat until she returned to Mecca?' He said, 'Let her return and throw the Jamarat as she was throwing them, and the man is the same.' And if she did not remember until she had left Mecca, then there is nothing upon her. Narrated.

Musa ibn al-Qasim from al-Nakha'i from Ibn Abi Umayr from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who forgot to throw the pebbles at the Jamarat. He said, 'He returns and throws them.' I said, 'And if he forgot them until he arrived in Mecca?' He said, 'He returns and throws them separately, placing an hour between each two throws.' I said, 'And if he forgot or was unaware until the time passed and he departed?' He said, 'He is not obliged to repeat them.' His saying (peace be upon him) 'He is not obliged to repeat them' means he is not obliged to repeat them in this year, although it is obligatory for him to repeat it in the following year, either by himself if he is able, or by ordering someone to act on his behalf. And this is because the days of throwing are the days of Tashriq; so if they pass for him, nothing is obligatory upon him except in the coming year during similar days.

Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from Muhammad ibn 'Umar ibn Yazid, from Muhammad ibn 'Uthafir, from 'Umar ibn Yazid, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "Whoever neglects throwing the Jamarat or some of them until the days of Tashreeq have passed, he must throw them the following year. If he does not perform Hajj, his Wali (guardian) should throw on his behalf. If he has no Wali, he should seek help from a Muslim man to throw on his behalf, for the throwing of the Jamarat occurs only during the days of Tashreeq." And it has been narrated that whoever deliberately leaves throwing the Jamarat, women are not permissible to him, and he must perform Hajj the following year. This was narrated.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Ya'qub ibn Yazid, from Yahya ibn al-Mubarik, from Abdillah ibn Jabalah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "Whoever deliberately leaves throwing the pebbles at the Jamarat, women do not become permissible to him, and he must perform Hajj again next year." And the order (of throwing) is obligatory in the throwing; it is required that he begin with the Jamarat al-Uzma, then the middle one, then Jamarat al-Aqabah. Whenever he deviates from any of them or throws them upside down (out of order), it is obligatory upon him to repeat (the throwing). He narrated.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from a number of our companions from Sahl ibn Ziyad and Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ibn Mahbub from Ibn Ri'ab from Mis'mam from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding a man who forgot to throw the pebbles on the second day, so he started with Jamarat al-Aqabah, then al-Wusta, then al-Ula, he said: 'He delays what he threw, so he throws the middle Jamarah, then Jamarat al-Aqabah.'

And from him, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Muawiya ibn Ayyar and Hammad ibn Isa, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding a man who threw the Jamarat (pillars) in a disordered manner: He said, 'He must repeat for the Middle one and the Jamarat al-Aqaba.' If he had thrown from the first Jamarah less than four pebbles and completed the last two Jamarat, he must repeat for all three Jamarat. And if he had thrown four from the first, he should complete that and not repeat for the last two. And likewise, if he had thrown three from the second, he must repeat for it and for the third. And if he had thrown four for both of them and thrown seven for the third, he should complete them and not repeat for the third. Narrated.

Musa ibn al-Qasim from Abbas from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) regarding: A man who threw the first Jamarah with three stones, the second with seven, and the third with seven. He said: 'He must repeat and throw all of them with seven [stones each].' I said: 'If he threw the first with four, the second with three, and the third with seven?' He said: 'He throws the first Jamarah with three, the second with seven, and throws the Jamarat al-Aqabah with seven.' I said: 'If he threw the first with four, the second with four, and the third with seven?' He said: 'He repeats and throws the first with three and the second with three, and does not repeat for the third.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from a number of our companions from Sahl ibn Ziyad from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Abd al-Karim ibn Amr from Abd al-A'la from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him: 'A man threw the Jamarah with six pebbles, and one fell among the pebbles.' He said: 'He should return it, if he wishes, immediately, or if he wishes, the next day when he intends to throw, and he should not take from the pebbles of the Jamarat.' And I asked him about a man who threw the Jamarah of al-Aqabah with six pebbles, and one fell into the carrying case. He said: 'He should return it.' And whoever knows that one pebble is missing but does not know from which of the Jamarat it is missing, let him throw one pebble at each of the Jamarat.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father and Muhammad ibn Isma'il from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan from Safwan from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) that he said: Regarding a man who took twenty-one pebbles and threw them, then added one more, and did not know which of them was missing, he said: 'He should return and throw each one with a pebble.' If a pebble falls from a man and he does not know which of them it is, he said: 'He should take a pebble from under his feet and throw it.' He said: 'And if you throw a pebble and it lands in a saddle-pack, return it to its place. If it hits a person or a camel, then lands on the Jamarat, it suffices for you.' And there is no harm in a person throwing while riding, although walking is superior.
Sa'd ibn Abdillah narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa: that he saw Abu Ja'far al-Thani (peace be upon him) throw the Jamarat while riding. He threw the Jamarat while riding.

And from him, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from some of our companions, from one of them, peace be upon him. Regarding the throwing of the Jamarat (stones), 'that the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) threw the Jamarat while riding his mount.'

And from him, from Abu Ja'far, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Najran, that he saw Abu al-Hasan the Second (peace be upon him) throwing the Jamarat while he was riding, until he threw all of them. He saw Abu al-Hasan the Second (peace be upon him) throwing the Jamarat while he was riding, until he threw all of them.

And from him, from Abu Ja'far, from al-Abbas, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Najran, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who threw the Jamarat (stones) while he was riding, and he said, 'There is no harm in it.' And that which indicates that walking in it is superior is what he narrated.

Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from Ali ibn Ja'far, from his brother, from his father, from their ancestors, peace be upon them, who said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) used to throw the Jamarat while walking.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd from 'Asim from 'Anbasah ibn Mus'abb said: I saw Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) in Mina walking and riding. I told myself that I would ask him when I entered upon him, but he initiated the conversation with me, saying: 'Indeed, 'Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon them both) used to leave his house on foot when he threw the Jamarat. My house today is more spacious than his house, so I ride until I reach his house.' Then when I reached his house, I walked until I threw the Jamarat. And there is no objection if the Jamarat is thrown on behalf of the sick, the one with a full stomach (or indigestion), the unconscious, the child, and those similar to them.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Ibn Abi Umayr from Mu'awiya and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The broken [stone] and the flat [stone] are thrown on their behalf. He said: "And the children are thrown on their behalf."

And from him, from Abu Ali al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, from Safwan, from Isḥāq ibn ʿAmmār, who said: I asked Abā Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him) about the sick person for whom the Jamarāt are thrown, and he said, 'Yes, he is carried to the Jamarah and it is thrown on his behalf.'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Fadalah ibn Ayyub from Rifa'ah ibn Musa from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a man who fainted (or lost consciousness), so he said: 'The pebbles are thrown on his behalf.'

And from him, from Abdullah ibn Bahri, from Dawud ibn Ali al-Ya'qubi, who said: I asked Abu al-Hasan Musa (peace be upon him) about the sick person who is unable to throw the jamarat, so he said: 'It is thrown on his behalf.'

Ali ibn Mahziyar from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from one who narrated to him from Yahya ibn Sa'id from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a woman who fell from the mount and was injured, and could not manage the throwing of the Jamarat. He said: 'She is thrown for, and the unborn child is thrown for.'

Musa ibn al-Qasim from Abdullah from Ishaq ibn 'Ammar from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about the sick person for whom the Jamarat are thrown. He said: 'He is carried to the Jamarat and the stones are thrown on his behalf.' I said: 'But he is unable to do that.' He said: 'He is left in his home and the stones are thrown on his behalf.' I said: 'And the incapacitated sick person, is circumambulation performed on his behalf?' He said: 'No, but he is circumambulated (carried around).' And the Takbir after fifteen prayers in Mina is an emphasized Sunnah, and in the other cities after ten prayers. What indicates this is what he narrated:

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Hammad ibn Isa from Hariz from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the saying of Allah, Exalted and Mighty: 'And remember Allah during fixed days.' He said: 'The Takbir (saying Allahu Akbar) is during the Days of Tashreeq for the Dhuhr prayer from the Day of Naḥr (10th Dhu al-Hijjah) until the Fajr prayer of the third day, and in the cities (Amṣār) there are ten prayers. When the people depart with the first departure, the people of the cities and whoever stayed in Mina and prayed Dhuhr and Asr there should keep silent (not recite the extra Takbir).'

Hammad narrated from Hariz from Zurara who said: I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about the Takbir in the days of Tashriq after the prayer, so he said: 'The Takbir is in Mina after fifteen prayers, and in the other regions after ten prayers. And the first Takbir is after the Dhuhr prayer on the Day of Nahr (Sacrifice), in which you say: Allahu Akbar, Allahu Akbar, Allahu Akbar, La ilaha illa Allah, wa Allahu Akbar, Allahu Akbar, wa lillahi al-hamd. Allahu Akbar upon what He guided us, Allahu Akbar upon what He provided us from the beasts of grazing livestock. And the Takbir is made in the other regions after ten prayers because when the people depart in the first departure, the people of the regions refrain from the Takbir, and the people of Mina continue to Takbir as long as they are in Mina until the final departure.'

Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from Ibrahim, from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Takbir of the Days of Tashriq is from the Dhuhr prayer - from the Day of Sacrifice until the Fajr prayer of the Days of Tashriq, if you stay in Mina; and if you leave Mina, there is no Takbir upon you. And the Takbir is: 'Allahu Akbar, Allahu Akbar, La ilaha illa Allah, wa Allahu Akbar, Allahu Akbar, wa lillah al-hamd. Allahu Akbar 'ala ma hadana, wa Allahu Akbar 'ala ma razaqana min bahimati al-an'am, wa al-hamd lillah 'ala ma ablanah.'

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Faddal from Amr ibn Sa'id from Musaddiq ibn Sadah from Ammar ibn Musa from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Takbir is obligatory at the end of every obligatory or voluntary prayer during the days of Tashriq. His saying (peace be upon him) 'The Takbir is obligatory' means that he intended the emphasis of the Sunnah. And we have explained in other places that this is called obligatory, even if it is not a duty for which one incurs punishment by leaving it. This clarifies what we mentioned, what he narrated:

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan, from Amr ibn Sa'id, from Musaddiq ibn Sadah, from Ammar ibn Musa, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a man who forgets to say the Takbir during the Days of Tashriq. He said: 'If he forgets until he rises from his place, there is no penalty upon him.' As for the voluntary prayer, there is no Takbir after it; that is indicated by what he narrated.

Sa'd ibn 'Abdullah from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from Safwan ibn Yahya from Dawud ibn Farqad said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'The Takbir is in every obligatory prayer, and there is no Takbir in the voluntary prayers during the days of Tashriq.' And the rationale in the first narration is to remove the prohibition for whoever said Takbir after the voluntary prayers, because a person is not prohibited from saying Takbir in all circumstances, so how much more so after the voluntary prayers.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Abu Ali al-Ash'ari from Muhammad ibn al-Jabbar from Safwan ibn Yahya from Dharih al-Muharibi from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "Whoever dies and has not performed the Hajj of Islam, and was not prevented from doing so by a burdensome debt, or an illness that makes Hajj unendurable, or a ruler who prevents him, then let him die a Jew or a Christian."

And from him, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Najran, from Abi Jamiilah, from Zayd al-Shahham, who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'The merchant delays Hajj.' He said, 'He has no excuse; if he dies, he has left a pillar of the pillars of Islam.'

And from him, from Humayd ibn al-Ziyad, from al-Hasan ibn Sama'ah, from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan al-Mithamī, from Aban ibn 'Uthman, from Abū Bāsir, who said: I heard Abū 'Abdillāh (peace be upon him) saying: 'Whoever dies while he is healthy and wealthy (able to afford the journey) and has not performed Hajj, he is among those of whom Allāh, Exalted and Mighty, said: "And We will gather him on the Day of Resurrection blind."' I said: 'Blind?' He said: 'Yes, indeed Allāh, Exalted and Mighty, made him blind from the path of truth.'

Musa ibn al-Qasim from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who has wealth and has never performed Hajj. He said, "He is among those of whom Allah the Exalted said, 'And We will gather him on the Day of Resurrection blind.'" He said, I said, "Glory be to Allah, blind?" He said, "Allah made him blind from the path of Paradise."

And from him, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from Al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: "When a man has the capacity for that with which he performs Hajj, then he dismisses it from himself, and he has no excuse that justifies him, then he has left a ruling from the rulings of Islam."

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father and Muhammad ibn Isma'il from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan from Safwan from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: If you intend to depart [from Mina] on one of the two days, you are not permitted to depart until the sun passes its zenith. If you delay until the last of the days of Tashriq, which is the final day of departure, there is no blame upon you regarding which hour you depart and throw [the pebbles], before or after the zenith. When you depart and reach al-Hasba', which is al-Batha', if you wish to stay for a short while, then indeed Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'My father (peace be upon him) used to stay there, then mount and enter Mecca without sleeping in it.'

And from him, from several of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Dawud ibn al-Nu'man, from Abu Ayyub, who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): We wish to hasten the departure, and it was the Night of Departure when I asked him, so at what time should we depart? He said to me, 'As for the second day, do not depart until the sun sets, and it was the Night of Departure.' As for the third day, when the sun has brightened (risen fully), then depart in accordance with the Book of Allah, for indeed Allah, Exalted and Glorious, says: So whoever hastens [his departure] in two days - there is no blame upon him; and whoever delays - there is no blame upon him. If he had remained silent [and only mentioned hastening], no one would remain but those who hasten, but he said, 'And whoever delays - there is no blame upon him.'

And that which was narrated: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya from al-Abbas from Mansur from Ali ibn Asbat from Sulayman ibn Abi Zaynab from Hariz from Zurara from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: "There is no harm if a man departs (from Mina) in the first departure before the sun passes its zenith." This is applicable in a state of necessity; as for doing so by choice, then it is not permissible according to what we have mentioned. And whoever stays overnight on the second day until the sun sets, it is not permissible for him to depart to the third day, nor is it permissible for him to depart at night. He narrated.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali from his father from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad from al-Halabi from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "Whoever hurries in the two days, let him not depart until the sun sets; and if evening overtakes him, he stays overnight and does not depart."

And from him, from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, from Safwan, from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: "When you depart in the first departure, if you wish to stay in Mecca, you may spend the night there, and there is no harm in that." He said, and he said, "When the night comes after the first departure, if you spent the night in Mina, it is not permissible for you to leave it until you have reached the morning."

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ibn Mahbub from Muhammad ibn al-Mustanir from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "Whoever has intercourse with his wife while in his state of ihram, he is not permitted to depart (from Mina) in the first departure."

And Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated from Ya'qub ibn Yazid, from Yahya ibn al-Mubarik, from Abdullah ibn Jabala, from Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Sayrafi, from Hammad ibn 'Uthman, from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding the saying of Allah, Exalted and Mighty: 'So whoever hastens [his departure] within two days - there is no blame upon him' ... 'for whoever feared' the game, meaning during his ihram. 'If he catches it, he is not permitted to depart in the first departure.' And it is upon the Imam to depart before midday in the final departure, so that he may pray Dhuhr in Mecca. Narrated.
Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Ali from his father from Ibn Abi Umayr from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Imam prays Dhuhr on the day of al-Nafar in Mecca.

And from him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Abdullah ibn Ja'far, from Ayub ibn Nuh, who said: I wrote to him that our companions had differed regarding us, so some of them said: 'The departure (Nafar) on the last day (13th of Dhul-Hijjah) after midday (Zawal) is superior,' and some of them said: 'Before midday.' So he (peace be upon him) wrote: 'Do you not know that the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) prayed Dhuhr and Asr in Mecca, so that could not have been except when they had already departed before midday?' And whoever wishes to stay in Mina after the departure, let him stay without difficulty.

Sa'd ibn Abdillah narrated from Muhammad ibn Ahmad, from Ali ibn Isma'il, from Safwan, from Abdillah ibn Muskhan, from Al-Husayn ibn Ali al-Sari, who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): What do you think about staying in Mina after the people depart? He said: 'If he has completed his ritual duties, let him stay as long as he wishes and go wherever he wishes.' And when a person departs from Mina, if he wishes, he returns to Mecca and stays there; he may do so. And if he wishes, he returns to his residence without entering Mecca; that is permissible for him. Narrated.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from a number of our companions from Sahl ibn Ziyad from Mansur ibn al-Abbas from Ali ibn Asbat from Sulayman ibn Abi Zaynab from Isḥaq ibn 'Ammar from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: My father used to say: 'If I had a path to my house from Mina, I would not enter Mecca.'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr from Jamil ibn Darraj from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "There is no objection if a man departs (from Mina) in the first departure, then stays in Meah."

Musa ibn al-Qasim from Ibrahim from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Pray in the Masjid al-Khayf, which is the Masjid of Mina. And the Masjid of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) during his time was near the minaret that is in the middle of the Masjid, and its proximity to the Qibla was about thirty cubits, and to the right and left and behind it about that much. If you are able to make your place of prayer in it, then do so, for indeed a thousand prophets prayed in it.
Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad from 'Ali from Abi Basir from Abi 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "Pray six rak'at in the mosque of Mina at the base of the Sa'wah."

Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from Ibrahim, from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: When you depart [from Mina] and reach al-Hasbah, which is al-Batha', and you wish to stay for a short while, then indeed Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'Indeed my father (peace be upon him) used to stay there, then depart and enter Mecca without sleeping in it.' And he said: 'Indeed the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) only stayed there where he sent Aisha with her brother Abd al-Rahman to al-Tan'im, so she performed 'Umrah due to the reason that had befallen her, so she circled the Ka'bah, then performed Sa'i, then returned, and he departed on that same day.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from a number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Abi Abdillah, from Amr ibn Uthman, from Ali ibn Khalid (who narrated from the one who told him), from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: He used to say: 'The one who enters the Ka'bah enters with Allah being pleased with him, and he exits free of sins.'

And from him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad, from Ya'qub ibn Yazid, from Ibn Fadhal, from Ibn al-Qaddah, from Ja'far, from his father (peace be upon them both), who said: I asked him about entering the Ka'bah. He said: 'Entering it is entering into the mercy of Allah, and exiting from it is exiting from sins. He is protected for the remainder of his life, and forgiven for what preceded of his sins.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Numan, from Sa'id al-A'raj, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The pilgrim must enter the House before departing; so when you enter it, enter with calmness and dignity, then go to each of its corners. Then say: 'O Allah, indeed You said, and whoever enters it is secure, so make me secure from Your punishment on the Day of Resurrection.' And pray between the two pillars that are adjacent to the door, upon the red marble. If the people are many, face each corner from your standing position where you prayed, and supplicate to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and ask Him.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Safwan from Hammad ibn 'Uthman said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about entering the House, so he said: 'As for the Sarrur, he enters it, and as for whoever has performed Hajj, he does not.'

Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Isma'il ibn Hammam said: Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) said: "The Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) entered the Ka'bah and prayed in its four corners, two rak'ahs in each corner."

And from him (Al-Shaykh) from Ibn Faddal from Yunus who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'When I enter the Ka'bah, what should I do?' He said, 'Take hold of the door rings when you enter the Ka'bah, then proceed until you reach the two pillars, and pray on the red marble. Then when you exit the House and descend the stairs, pray two rak'ahs to your right.'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Fadalah from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar said: I saw the Servant (peace be upon him) enter the Ka'bah and pray two rak'ahs upon the red marble. Then he stood and faced the wall between the Yemeni corner and the Western corner, raised his hand against it, pressed it against it, and supplicated. Then he moved to the Yemeni corner, pressed against it, and supplicated. Then he went to the Western corner, then exited.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Safwan from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar concerning the supplication for the child, he said: "Pour a bucket of Zamzam water, then enter the House. When you stand at the door of the House, take hold of the door ring, then say: 'O Allah, indeed the House is Your House and the servant is Your servant, and You have said, "And whoever enters it is secure," so secure me from Your punishment and save me from Your wrath.' Then enter the House and pray two rak'ahs on the red marble." Then proceed to the pillar opposite the Stone, and press your chest against it, then say: 'O One, O Noble, O Near, O Distant, O Mighty, O Wise: "Do not leave me solitary, and You are the best of inheritors." "Grant me from Yourself a good offspring, indeed You are the Hearer of supplication."' Then circle the pillar, pressing your back and stomach against it, and supplicate with this supplication; if Allah wills something, it will be.' And it is not permissible for a person to pray the obligatory prayer in the Ka'bah when choosing, but it is permissible in case of necessity and fear of missing the time. Narrated. 11 - Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Fadalah from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) He said: "The obligatory prayer is not prayed in the Ka'bah, for the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) did not enter the Ka'bah during a pilgrimage or a visitation, but he entered it during the Conquest - the Conquest of Mecca - and prayed two rak'ahs between the two pillars, with him was Usamah ibn Zayd."

And from him, from Safwan and Fadalah, from al-Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from one of the Imams (peace be upon them both), who said: “The obligatory prayer is not valid inside the Kaaba.” And as for when one fears missing the prayer, there is no harm in praying it inside the Kaaba. Narrated.

Al-Husayn ibn Said from Al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Fadhal from Yunus ibn Ya'qub said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): The obligatory prayer arrived while I was in the Ka'ah; should I pray in it? He said, 'Pray.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd from Ibn Muskān who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) while he was exiting the Ka'bah, and he was saying 'Allahu Akbar, Allahu Akbar,' saying it three times. Then he said, 'O Allah, do not exhaust my afflictions, nor let our enemies rejoice in us, for You are the One who causes harm and confers benefit.' Then he descended and prayed beside the stairs, placing the stairs to his left, facing the Ka'bah, with no one between him and it. Then he went out to his house.

And from him, from Ibrahim ibn Abi Mahmud, who said: I saw Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) bid farewell to the House (Kaaba). When he intended to exit from the door of the mosque, he prostrated, then stood up, faced the Kaaba, and said: 'O Allah, I am returning upon the basis that there is no god but You.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from a number of our companions from Ahmad ibn Muhammad and Abu Ali al-Ash'ari from al-Hasan ibn Ali al-Kufi from Ali ibn Mahziyar, who said: I saw Abu Ja'far (the second Imam, peace be upon him) in the year 215 AH bidding farewell to the House (Ka'bah) after the sun had risen. He circumambulated the House, touching the Yemeni Corner in every lap. When he was on the seventh lap, he touched it, then touched the Stone, wiped his hand with it, then wiped his face with his hand. Then he went to the Maqam (Station of Abraham) and prayed two rak'ahs behind it. He went out to the rear of the Ka'bah to the Multazam, held the House fast, uncovered his shirt from his belly, then stood there for a long time supplicating. Then he went out through the door of the Hanateen and set off. And I saw him in the year 219 AH bidding farewell to the House at night, touching the Yemeni Corner and the Black Stone in every lap. When he was on the seventh lap, he held the House fast at the rear of the Ka'bah, near the Yemeni Corner and above the elongated Stone. He uncovered his shirt from his belly. Then he went to the Black Stone, kissed it, and wiped it. He went out to the Maqam and prayed behind it, then departed and did not return to the House. His standing at the Multazam was equal to the time it took some of our companions to circumambulate seven laps, and others eight laps. And whoever forgot the Farewell Tawaf, or was occupied from it, then departed, there is no blame upon him.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ali from one of the Imams, upon them be peace Regarding a man who did not bid farewell to the House (Kaaba), he said: 'There is no harm with him if he had an excuse or was forgetful.'

Sa'd ibn 'Abdullah from Muhammad ibn Isma'il from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr from Hisham ibn Salim who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about one who forgot the visitation of the House until he returned to his family, so he said: 'It does not harm him if he has fulfilled his rituals.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from al-Husayn ibn Muhammad from Muhammad ibn Ahmad al-Nahdi from Ya'qub ibn Yazid from Abdillah ibn Jabalah from Qutham ibn Ka'b who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'You are accustomed to performing Hajj.' I said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Then let your final farewell with the House be that you place your hand on the door and say: 'The poor man is at your door, so give charity to him with Paradise.' And when he intends to leave Mecca, let him buy dates with a dirham and give them in charity, and let that be expiation for what entered upon him.' He narrated.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad from al-Halabi from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar and Hafsh ibn al-Bakhtari from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "It is appropriate for the pilgrim, when he has completed his ritual duties and intends to depart, to purchase dates with a dirham and give them in charity, so that it serves as expiation for any minor defects that entered upon him during his Hajj, such as shaving [hair] or the falling of lice, or similar matters."

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father and Muhammad ibn Isma'il from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan from Ibn Abi Umayr and Safwan ibn Yahya from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "Part of the perfection of Hajj and 'Umrah is that you enter into the state of Ihram from the Miqat (stations of entering Ihram) that the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) designated. Do not pass them unless you are in the state of Ihram. For he designated for the people of Iraq, and at that time there was no Iraq [as a specific region], the Belly of al-'Aqiq from the side of the people of Iraq. And he designated for the people of Yemen, Yalamlam. And he designated for the people of Ta'if, Qarn al-Manazil. And he designated for the people of the Maghreb (West), al-Juhfa, which is Mahya'ah. And he designated for the people of Medina, Dhu al-Hulayfah. And whoever's dwelling is behind these Miqat stations, from the side facing Mecca, then his Miqat is his dwelling."

And from him, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who forgot to enter the state of Ihram until he entered the Haram (sanctuary). He said: 'He must go out to the Miqat of the people of his land. If he fears that the Hajj will be missed, he enters Ihram from his place. And if he is able to go out from the Haram, let him go out, then let him enter Ihram.'

And from him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from Muhammad ibn al-Fudayl, from Abu al-Subah al-Kinanī, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who was unaware of entering the state of Ihram until he entered the Haram (sanctuary), what should he do? He said, 'He exits the Haram, then enters Ihram for Hajj.' All these narrations indicate the obligation of Ihram, because the first report included a prohibition on crossing the Miqat (boundary) without Ihram, and the remaining reports indicate that whoever crosses it must return to the Miqat of his people if he is able to do so; if he is not able, he enters Ihram from where he is. If its obligation and emphasis as a duty were not established, this strictness would not have been applied, and its omission would have been permissible in all cases. As for that which indicates the obligation of Talbiyah, it is what he narrated:

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Ibn Abi 'Umayr and Muhammad ibn Isma'il from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan from Safwan and Ibn Abi 'Umayr, all from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Talbiyah is: 'Here I am, O Allah, here I am. Here I am, You have no partner, here I am. Indeed praise and grace are Yours and the dominion, You have no partner.' Then he mentioned the hadith until he said: 'And know that the four Talbiyahs which are at the beginning of the report are obligatory, and they are Tawhid (divine unity), and by it the Messengers proclaimed, and increase in Dhi al-Maaraj, for indeed the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) used to increase in it.' And we have cited this report in its form previously, and as for Tawaf, we have also clarified its obligation in what preceded, and that the Mufrid is required to perform two Tawafs and one Sa'i between al-Safa and al-Marwah, and likewise the Qarin and the Mutamatti' are required to perform three Tawafs and two Sa'is between al-Safa and al-Marwah, and there is sufficiency in it, if Allah wills, and that is also confirmed by what was narrated:

Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from Jamil, from some of our companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: A man prays the two rak'ahs of the obligatory Tawaf behind the Maqam (Station of Abraham) reciting 'Qul Huwa Allahu Ahad' and 'Qul Ya Ayyuha al-Kafirun'.

And from him (Al-Shaykh) from Saffan ibn Yahya, from one who narrated to him, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): Like it. And he said: 'It is not permissible for him to pray the two rak'ahs of the obligatory Tawaf except behind the Maqam, due to the saying of Allah, Exalted and Glorious: And take you the station of Ibrahim as a place of Salat (prayer).' So if you pray them in any other place, then upon you is the re-prayer of the Salat.'

And from him (Al-Hadith) from Safwan ibn Yahya and others from Muawiya ibn 'Ammar from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: You supplicate with this supplication after the two rak'ahs of the obligatory Tawaf, saying after the Tashahhud, So all these narrations explicitly state that Tawaf is obligatory. As for its quantity and how it applies to each type of pilgrim, we have explained it in what preceded, so there is no need to repeat it. As for the Tawaf of the women, it is also obligatory, and we have explained it in what preceded, and what is narrated adds to its clarification:

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from a number of our companions from Sahl ibn Ziyad from Ahmad ibn Muhammad who said: Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) said regarding the saying of Allah, Exalted and Mighty: 'And let them circumambulate the Ancient House' (1). He said: 'The obligatory circumambulation is the circumambulation of the women.'

And from him, from al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad, from some of our companions, from Hammad ibn 'Uthman, from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding the saying of Allah, Exalted and Mighty: 'And let them fulfill their vows and let them circumambulate the Ancient House,' he said, 'The circumambulation of the women.' And the two rak'ahs of the circumambulation are also obligatory, as evidence for that is what he narrated:

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Ibn Abi Umayr from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I said to him: A man forgot the stoning (of the pillars) until he arrived in Mecca. He said: 'He returns and stones them, separating between each two throws by an hour.' I said: If he missed that and departed (from Mina), he said: 'There is no penalty upon him.' I said: And a man forgot the Sa'i (walking) between As-Safa and Al-Marwah. He said: 'He repeats the Sa'i.' I said: If he missed that until he departed, he said: 'He returns and repeats the Sa'i. Indeed, this is not like the stoning of the pillars, for indeed the stoning is a Sunnah and the Sa'i between As-Safa and Al-Marwah is a Fard (obligatory duty).' And we have also clarified in what preceded that standing at 'Arafat and Al-Mash'ar is obligatory, except that we do not exclude in this place what confirms what we have presented, and that which indicates that standing at 'Arafah is obligatory is what he narrated:

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Ali ibn Abi Hamzah, from Abi Basir, from Abi Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "When you stand at Arafat, draw near to the hills." [And the hills are the mountains.] "For the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) said, 'Those who stand at Arak have no Hajj.'" [Meaning those who stand at the Arak (low ground).]

And from him, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said during the standing (at Arafat): 'Ascend from the bottom of Batin Urnah.' And he said: 'Indeed, the people of Al-Arak have no Hajj.' The basis of inference from these two reports is that the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) invalidated the Hajj of anyone who left the boundary of Arafat, even if he was standing. Had the standing in it not been obligatory, he would not have invalidated the Hajj of one who stood outside its boundary; rather, he would have permitted him to not stand at all. As for what was narrated:

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Ya'qub ibn Yazid, from Ibn Faddal, from some of our companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: "Standing at al-Mash'ar is an obligation (fard), and standing at 'Arafah is a sunnah." What we mentioned is not contradicted, because the meaning of this report is that its obligation was known from the side of the Sunnah, not from the explicit text of the Quran. And whatever its obligation is known from the side of the Sunnah, it is permissible to be called by the name of 'Sunnah', and we have explained this in other places. But it is not so for standing at al-Mash'ar, because its obligation is known from the explicit text of the Quran. Allah, the Exalted, said: "So when you have departed from 'Arafat, remember Allah at al-Mash'ar al-Haram." So He made it obligatory upon us to remember Him at al-Mash'ar al-Haram, and there was no command in the explicit text of the Quran regarding standing at 'Arafat; therefore, for that reason, it was attributed to the Sunnah. As for that which indicates that standing at al-Mash'ar al-Haram is an obligation, it is the Verse and the preceding report as well, which is His saying: "Standing at al-Mash'ar is an obligation." And to add clarity to that is what was narrated:

Musa ibn al-Qasim from al-Nakha'i from Safwan ibn Yahya from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "Whoever departs from 'Arafat to Muna, let him return and come to Jamarat (Jum'ah) and stand there, even if he finds that the people have already departed from Jum'ah."

And Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Faddal, from Yunus ibn Ya'qub, who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): A man departed from Arafat and passed by Al-Mash'ar but did not stop until he reached Mina, then he threw the Jamarah, and he did not know until the day rose. He (peace be upon him) said: 'He returns to Al-Mash'ar and stands, then returns and throws the Jamarah.' And the Hady (sacrificial animal) is obligatory upon the Mutamatti'. Allah the Exalted said: 'So whoever performs Hajj and 'Umrah together, he should bring whatever is easy of the Hady. And whoever cannot find [or afford it], then a fast of three days during Hajj and seven when he returns [to his home].' (2)

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Muhammad ibn Sinan from Ibn Muskhan from Sa'id al-A'raj who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'Whoever performs Tamattu' during the months of Hajj and then stays in Mecca until Hajj arrives, upon him is a sheep; and whoever performs Tamattu' in other than the months of Hajj and then stays (as a neighbor/resident) until Hajj arrives, there is no blood (sacrifice) upon him. It is an individual Hajj, and the sacrifice (Al-Adha) is upon the people of the cities (Amsar).' The Sheikh (may God have mercy on him) said: And whoever entered Mecca on the Day of Tarwiyah, up to his saying: 'And whoever arrived at Arafat'. For the explanation of that has already passed previously, so there is no need to repeat it, because there is sufficiency in that location. The Sheikh (may God have mercy on him) said: And whoever arrived at Arafat before the rising of the dawn on the Day of Sacrifice, he has caught it; and if he did not arrive until the dawn rose, he has missed it. And if he arrived at Al-Mash'ar Al-Haram before the rising of the sun on the Day of Sacrifice, he has caught the Hajj; so if he did not arrive until the sun rose, he has missed the Hajj.

Musa ibn al-Qasim from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad from al-Halabi said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who arrives after the people have departed from Arafat. He said: 'If he has respite until he reaches Arafat from its night, then stands at it, then departs and catches the people at al-Mash'ar before they depart, his Hajj is not complete until he reaches Arafat. And if he arrives and Arafat has been missed for him, let him stand at al-Mash'ar al-Haram, for indeed Allah the Exalted has excused His servant, and his Hajj is complete if he catches al-Mash'ar al-Haram before the sunrise and before the people depart. If he does not catch al-Mash'ar al-Haram, then Hajj has been missed for him, so let him make it a separate Umrah, and upon him is Hajj next year.'

And from him, from Muhammad ibn Sahl, from his father, from Idris ibn Abdillah, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who reached the people at Jamarat (the stoning site) and feared that if he went to Arafat, the people would depart from Jamarat before he reached it. He (AS) said: 'If he expects that the people will be at Jamarat before sunrise, let him go to Arafat. But if he fears that he will not reach Jamarat, let him stand at Jamarat, then depart with the people, and his Hajj will be complete.' And these two narrations indicate the obligation of standing at Arafat, and that with ability it is necessary. And whoever leaves it while the situation is as we described, his Hajj is not valid. As for with compulsion/necessity, there is no harm if the person does not stand at Arafat and restricts himself to standing at Al-Mash'ar, according to what the two narrations contain. And to clarify that further is what he narrated:

Musa ibn al-Qasim from Safwan ibn Yahya from Muawiya ibn 'Ammar from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) was traveling, and there was an old man who said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what do you say about a man who catches the Imam at Jam' (the gathering place before Arafat)?' He said to him: 'If he thinks that he will go to Arafat and stand there for a little while, then catch Jam' before the sunrise, let him go to it. And if he thinks that he will not reach it until the people depart from Jam', then let him not go to it, for his Hajj is complete.'

And from him (Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id) from Muhammad ibn Sinan who said: I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about the one whom a person reaches, [meaning the standing at Arafah], so he has reached Hajj. He said: 'If he arrives at Jam' (Muzdalifah) while the people are at Al-Mash'ar Al-Haram before the sunrise, he has reached Hajj and his Umrah is not valid. And if he reaches Jam' after the sunrise, it is a separate Umrah and he has not performed Hajj. So if he wishes to stay in Mecca, he stays; and if he wishes to return to his family, he returns, and Hajj is still incumbent upon him.' And it has previously passed in these narrations that whoever reaches Al-Mash'ar after the sunrise has missed Hajj, and this is also confirmed by what he narrated:

Musa ibn al-Qasim from Muhammad ibn Sahl from his father from Isḥāq ibn ʿAbd Allāh said: I asked Abū al-Ḥasan (peace be upon him) about a man who entered Mecca performing Tamattuʾ (or Qirān/Ifrād contextually implying missing the standing) for Hajj, and feared that the two standings (Mawqifān) would be missed by him. He said: 'He has his day until the sunrise of the Day of Nahr (10th Dhu al-Hijjah). When the sun rises, he has no Hajj.' I said: 'What should he do with his Ihram?' He said: 'He should go to Mecca and perform Tawaf around the House and Saʿy between Ṣafā and Marwah.' I said to him: 'When he does that, what does he do after?' He said: 'If he wishes, he stays in Mecca; and if he wishes, he returns to the people at Minā and is not one of them in anything (i.e., not bound by their specific rituals). If he wishes, he returns to his family, and Hajj is incumbent upon him next year.'

And from him (Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id) from Muhammad ibn Fudayl who said: I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about the limit/time by which if a man reaches it, he has attained the Hajj. He said: 'If he arrives at Jam' while the people are at al-Mash'ar before the sunrise, he has attained the Hajj and his Umrah is not separate. But if he does not arrive at Jam' until the sun has risen, then it is a separate Umrah and he has no Hajj. If he wishes, he may stay, and if he wishes, he may return, and Hajj is incumbent upon him next year.'

And as for what Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Ibn Abi Umayr from Jamil ibn Darraj from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "Whoever reaches the Mash'ar al-Haram on the Day of Nahar before the sun's decline has completed the Hajj."

And what Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar narrated from Abdullah ibn Amir, from Ibn Abi Najran, from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr, from Abdullah ibn al-Mughira, who said: A man came to us in Mina and said, 'I did not catch up with the people at both stations together.' Abdullah ibn al-Mughira said to him, 'Then your Hajj is not valid.' He asked Ismail ibn 'Ammar, but he did not answer him. So Ismail entered upon Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) and asked him about that. He said to him, 'If he catches up with Muzdalifah and stands at it before the sun sets on the Day of Nahr (sacrifice), then he has caught up with the Hajj.' These two reports carry two possible meanings: one is that whoever catches up with Muzdalifah before the sun sets has caught up with the excellence and reward of Hajj, without it being meant that whoever catches it has had the obligation of the Hajj of Islam removed from him. It also carries the possibility that this ruling is specific to whoever caught up with Arafat then came to al-Mash'ar before the sun's decline, for he has caught up with the Hajj because whoever is in this state has caught up with one of the two stations at its proper time, and his Hajj is complete. And that which indicates this is what was narrated:

Musa ibn al-Qasim from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Ali ibn Ri'ab from al-Hasan al-Attar from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "When the pilgrim reaches Arafat before the rising of dawn, then turns back from Arafat and does not catch the people at Jamarat, and finds that they have already proceeded (to Mina), then he should stand for a short while at al-Mash'ar al-Haram and join the people at Mina, and there is no penalty upon him." And whoever misses standing at al-Mash'ar, his Hajj is not valid under any circumstance, as indicated by what has been narrated:

Sa'd ibn 'Abdullah from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from al-'Abbas ibn Ma'ruf from Ibn Abi 'Umayr from Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Khas'ami from some of his companions from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding the one who was ignorant and did not stand at al-Muzdalifah and did not spend the night there until he went to Mina, he said: 'He returns.' I said: 'Indeed, that has been missed by him.' He said: 'There is no harm in it.'

And what Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Ibn Abi Umayr from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) that he said: Regarding a man who did not stand at Al-Muzdalifah and did not spend the night there until he went to Mina, he said: 'Did he not see the people? They did not hasten to Mina when they entered it.' I said: 'Indeed, he was ignorant of that.' He said: 'He should return.' I said: 'Indeed, that has already passed him.' He said: 'There is no harm.' The explanation in these two narrations, although their origin is Muhammad ibn Yahya Al-Khas'ami, and that he narrates it once from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) without an intermediary and once with an intermediary, is that whoever has stood at Al-Muzdalifah for a short time, that has sufficed him. And what is meant by his saying 'he did not stand at Al-Muzdalifah' is the complete standing, which when a person performs it, it is more perfect and superior, and when he does not stand in that manner, it is less in reward, although it does not invalidate the Hajj, because the short standing suffices there in case of necessity. And that which indicates this is what he narrated:

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Muhammad ibn Sinan from Ibn Muskān from Abū Baṣīr said: I said to Abū 'Abdillāh (peace be upon him), 'May I be your ransom, indeed these two companions of mine were ignorant that they did not stand at al-Muzdalifah.' He said, 'They return to their place and stand at al-Mash'ar for an hour.' I said, 'Indeed no one informed them, until it was the day when the people had departed.' He lowered his head for a moment, then said, 'Did they not pray the morning prayer at al-Muzdalifah?' I said, 'Yes.' He said, 'Did they not make qunut in their prayer?' I said, 'Yes.' He said, 'Their Hajj is complete.' Then he said, 'Al-Mash'ar is part of al-Muzdalifah, and al-Muzdalifah is part of al-Mash'ar, and indeed a little supplication suffices for them.'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Hammad ibn 'Uthman, from Muhammad ibn Hakim, who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): May Allah improve you. The non-Arab man and the weak woman are with the Bedouin camel-herder. When he sends them forth from 'Arafat, he passes them by as they are to Muna without dismounting them for a collective stay. He said: 'Is it not that they have prayed there, so it suffices them?' I said: 'And if they did not pray there?' He said: 'Then they remembered Allah there. If they had remembered Allah there, it suffices them.' And whoever deliberately leaves standing at Al-Mash'ar, upon him is a camel (as expiation). That was narrated.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from a number of our companions from Sahl ibn Ziyad from Ibn Mahbub from Ibn Ri'ab from Hariz from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "Whoever departs from Arafat with the people and does not stay with them at Jumu'ah and proceeds to Muzdalifah deliberately or lightly, then upon him is a camel." And whoever misses the Hajj, let him make it an Umrah, and upon him is the Hajj next year; what he narrated indicates that:

Musa ibn al-Qasim from Muhammad ibn Sinan said: I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about the one whom a person catches, then he has caught the Hajj. He said: 'If he arrives at Jam' while the people are at al-Mash'ar al-Haram before the sunrise, then he has caught the Hajj and his Umrah is not valid. And if he catches Jam' after the sunrise, it is a separate Umrah and he has no Hajj. If he wishes to stay in Mecca, he stays; and if he wishes to return to his family, he returns, and Hajj is incumbent upon him next year.'

And from him, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Muawiya ibn 'Ammar, from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: "Whoever catches the 'Jam' (combined Hajj and 'Umrah), has indeed caught Hajj." He said, and Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: "Any pilgrim who is bringing the offering (saiqin lil-hady), or performing Hajj al-Mufrid, or performing Hajj al-Tamattu' (with 'Umrah) — if he arrives and Hajj has passed for him, let him make it an 'Umrah, and Hajj is due from him next year."

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Safwan from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): A man came as a pilgrim but missed the Hajj and had not performed Tawaf. He said: 'He stays with the people in a state of Ihram during the days of Tashriq, without performing Umrah in them. When they end, he performs Tawaf with the House and Sa'i between As-Safa and Al-Marwah, then he exits Ihram, and Hajj is incumbent upon him for the following year; he enters Ihram from where he entered Ihram.'

And that which was narrated - Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Dawud ibn Kathir al-Raqqi, who said: I was with Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) in Mina when a man entered upon him and said, 'A group of people have arrived today who have missed the Hajj.' He said, 'We ask Allah for well-being.' Then he said, 'I see that each one of them should slaughter a sheep, shave his head, and Hajj will be obligatory upon them next year if they return to their lands; and if they stay until the days of Tashriq pass in Mecca, then they go out to some of the miqat places of the people of Mecca, enter into ihram from there, and perform Umrah, then Hajj will not be obligatory upon them next year.' So it is understood that if their Hajj was a Hajj of voluntary performance, then Hajj is not obligatory upon them next year; and it is only obligatory upon them if their Hajj was the Hajj of Islam (Fard), according to what we have previously mentioned. And no one should say, 'If it were a voluntary Hajj, he would not have said at the beginning of the report, 'Hajj is obligatory upon them next year if they return to their lands,' because we interpret this as a way of preference and excellence rather than obligation and necessity.' It is also possible that the report is specific to one who stipulated a condition during ihram, for if he stipulated, Hajj is not obligatory upon him next year; and if he did not stipulate, that is obligatory upon him in the coming year. And that which indicates this is what was narrated:

Musa ibn al-Qasim from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Ali ibn Ri'ab from Durays ibn A'yan, who said: I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about a man who set out in Tamattu' (combining Umrah and Hajj) from Umrah to Hajj, and he did not reach Mecca except on the Day of Nahri (8th of Dhu al-Hijjah). He said: 'He remains in his state of Ihram and cuts off the Talbiyah when he enters Mecca, then he performs Tawaf and Sa'i between al-Safa and al-Marwah, shaves his head, and returns to his family if he wishes.' And he said: 'This is for the one who made a condition upon his Lord when he entered into Ihram. If he did not make the condition, then upon him is Hajj next year.' And whoever attends the rituals while intoxicated, there is no Hajj for him. Narrated.

Muhammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā, from Muhammad ibn ʿĪsā, from Abū ʿAlī ibn Rāshid, who said: I wrote to him asking about a man in iḥram who became intoxicated, and performed the rituals while drunk. Does his ḥajj become complete despite his intoxication? He wrote back in peace: 'His ḥajj does not become complete.'

Musa ibn al-Qasim from Hammad ibn Isa al-Juhani from Ibrahim ibn Umar al-Yamani from Sa'd al-Iskaf said: I heard Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) saying: 'Indeed, when the pilgrim takes his travel gear, every step he takes is recorded by Allah as ten good deeds, erases ten bad deeds, and raises him ten degrees, until he finishes his gear. When his mount stands firm, every time it lifts a hoof or places it, Allah records for him the like of that, until he completes his pilgrimage rites. When he completes his rites, Allah forgives him for the remainder of Dhu al-Hijjah, Muharram, Safar, and the month of Rabi' al-Awwal. When four months have passed, he mixes with the people.'

And from him, from Safwan and Ibn Abi Umayr, from Muawiya ibn Ammar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), from his father, from his forefathers (peace be upon them): That the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) was met by a Bedouin who said to him: 'O Messenger of Allah, I set out intending to perform Hajj, but I was prevented, and I am a man of means. Order me to do with my wealth what will bring me the same reward as the pilgrim.' He said: 'The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) turned to him and said to him: "Look at Abu Qubays [the mountain near Mecca]. If Abu Qubays were gold for you, red gold, and you spent it in the way of Allah, you would not reach with it what the pilgrim reaches."' Then he said: 'Indeed, when the pilgrim prepares his gear, he raises nothing and places nothing except that Allah writes for him ten good deeds, erases ten bad deeds, and raises him ten degrees. When he mounts his camel, he lifts not a hoof nor places it except that Allah writes for him the like of that. When he circumambulates the House, he goes forth from his sins. When he runs between Safa and Marwa, he goes forth from his sins. When he stands at Arafat, he goes forth from his sins. When he stands at Al-Mash'ar Al-Haram, he goes forth from his sins. When he throws the pebbles at the Jamarat, he goes forth from his sins.' He said: 'So the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) enumerated so many and so many stations; whenever the pilgrim stands at them, he goes forth from his sins.' Then he said: 'How can you reach what the pilgrim reaches?' Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'And sins are not written against him for four months, and good deeds are written for him, unless he commits a major sin.'

And from him, from Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from Ali ibn Ri'ab, from Muhammad ibn Qays, who said: I heard Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) saying, while he was narrating to the people in Mecca, so he said: "Indeed, a man from the Ansar came to the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) asking him, so the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said to him: 'If you wish, ask, and if you wish, I will inform you of what you came to ask me about.' He said: 'Inform me, O Messenger of Allah.' He said: 'You came to ask me about your reward in your Hajj and Umrah. Indeed, for you, when you set out for the path of Hajj, then mounted your mount, then said "Bismillah" and "Alhamdulillah", then your mount proceeded, placing no hoof and raising no hoof, except that a good deed was recorded for you and a bad deed was erased from you.
