From him, from Al-Hasan ibn Ali (peace be upon him), who said: I asked Abu Al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about a man who bought a barren land from another man for one hundred kurrs of wheat, on the condition that he give him from the land. He said, 'It is forbidden.' I said, 'May I be your ransom, for I buy the land with a known measure of wheat and barley from each other.' He said, 'There is no objection to that.'

Ahmad ibn Muhammad from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from al-'Ala' from Muhammad ibn Muslim from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about purchasing the land of the People of the Covenant (Ahl al-Dhimma). He said, 'There is no harm with it, so it will be, as that is in their station, he pays as they pay.' And a man from the people of the Nile asked him about a piece of land he had purchased at the mouth of the Nile from the people of the land, who said, 'It is their land,' and the people of al-Ustan (1) said, 'It is from our land.' He said, 'Do not buy it except with the consent of its people.'

Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Sama'ah, from more than one, from Aban ibn Uthman, from Isma'il ibn al-Fadl al-Hashimi, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who rented land from the land of the Ahl al-Dhimma (people of the covenant) from the khaj (land tax), and its people were reluctant, and the Sultan only accepted it because of their inability to manage it or despite their ability. He said: 'If the owners are unable to manage it, you may take it, unless they cause you harm. And if you give them something and their souls are pleased with you, then take it.' He said: And I asked him about a man who bought land from the khaj land, building in it or not, except that some people from the Ahl al-Dhimma settled in it. Is he entitled to take the rent of the houses from them if they pay the jizyah of their heads? He said: 'Make a condition with them, and whatever he takes after the condition is halal.' And Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar wrote to Abu Muhammad al-Hasan ibn Ali (peace be upon him): About a man who bought a house from a man in his courtyard with all its rights, and above it is another house. Does the upper house enter into the rights of the lower house or not? So he (peace be upon him) wrote: 'He has only what he bought by its name and location, if God wills.'

He wrote to him: Regarding a man who bought a room or a dwelling in a house with all its rights, and above it are other rooms and another dwelling; does the upper room and the upper dwelling belong to the rights of this lower room and the lower dwelling that he bought, or not? He (peace be upon him) wrote: 'He has nothing of that except the right that he bought, if God wills.' He wrote to him: Regarding a man who said to two men: 'Bear witness that all this house, located in such and such a place, with all its boundaries, belongs to so-and-so son of so-and-so, and all his belongings in the house.' The testimony does not identify what the belongings are. He (peace be upon him) wrote: 'It is valid if the purchase encompasses all of that, if God wills.' He wrote to him: Regarding a man who owned a plot of land, and it was time for him to depart for Mecca, and the village was several stages from his home, and he did not have enough time to stay to define the boundaries of his land. He defined the four boundaries of the village and said to the witnesses: 'Bear witness that I have sold to so-and-so (meaning the buyer) the entire village, of which one boundary, the second, the third, and the fourth are from it.' He only owned a plot of land in this village. Is this valid for the buyer, even though he only owns part of this village, yet he acknowledged to him the whole? He (peace be upon him) wrote: 'The sale of what is not owned is not valid, and the purchase from the seller is established upon what he owns.' He wrote to him: Regarding a man whom another man asked to bear witness that he had sold a farm from another man, which is a plot of land, and he did not define the boundaries at the time he asked him to witness, and said: 'When they come to you with the boundaries, bear witness with them.' Is this valid for him, or is it not valid for him to bear witness? He (peace be upon him) wrote: 'Yes, it is valid, and praise be to God.' He wrote to him: Is it valid for him to bear witness regarding the boundaries if another group from the people of the village comes to bear witness for him that the boundaries of this farm that the man sold are these? Is it valid for this witness, whom he asked to witness regarding the farm and did not specify the boundaries, to bear witness regarding the boundaries by the statement of these people who knew this farm and testified for hi

Ali ibn Ibrahim narrated from his father, from al-Nawfali, from al-Sakuni, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: The Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'Whoever plants a tree or digs a barren valley that no one has preceded him to, or revives dead land, it is his by decree of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and His Messenger.'

From him, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Muhammad ibn Humran, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I heard Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) saying: 'Any people who revive a portion of the land and develop it, they are more entitled to it, and it belongs to them.'

Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Mu'awiya ibn Wahb said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: "Whoever comes to a barren, ruined land, extracts its water, irrigates its rivers, and develops it, then charity (khums/zakat) is upon him in it. If it was land belonging to a man before him, who was absent from it, left it, and ruined it, then later he came and claimed it, then the land belongs to Allah (Exalted and Mighty) and to the one who developed it."

Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Hisham ibn Salim from Abu Khalid al-Kabuli from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: We found in the book of Ali (peace be upon him): "Indeed, the earth belongs to Allah, and He bequeaths it to whom He wills of His servants; and the [good] end is for the righteous." I and my family, who were bequeathed the earth, and we are the righteous, and the entire earth is for us. So whoever revives a piece of land from among the Muslims, let him cultivate it and let him pay its land tax (kharaj) to the Imam from my family. And he has what he consumed from it. And if he left it and ruined it, and a man from the Muslims took it after him, cultivated it, and revived it, then he is more entitled to it than the one who left it. Let him pay its land tax to the Imam from my family. And he has what he consumed until the Rising One (al-Qa'im), peace be upon him, from my family appears with the sword. He will gather it, prevent [others from taking it], and expel them from it, just as the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) gathered it and prevented [others from taking it]. Except what was in the hands of our Shia, for he will grant them tenure over what was in their hands and leave the land in their hands."

Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from Dhubyan from Musa ibn Uqayl from Dawud ibn al-Husayn from Umar ibn Hanzalah from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): In a man sold a piece of land on the condition that it contained ten ajribah (units of land). The buyer purchased it from him with its boundaries, paid the price, and the sale was concluded, and they parted. When he measured the land, he found it to be only five ajribah. He (peace be upon him) said: 'If he wishes, he may reclaim his money and take back the land. If he wishes, he may return the land and keep all his money. Unless there are also lands of his adjacent to that land, in which case he should compensate him (the buyer) for the adjacent land, and the sale becomes binding upon him, and he must fulfill the sale in its entirety. If he has no other land in that place besides the one he sold, then if the buyer wishes, he may take the land and reclaim the surplus of his money, and if he wishes, he may return the land and take all the money.'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from an-Nadr from 'Abdullah ibn Sinan from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about staying with the people of the kharam (tax-paying locals), and he said, 'Three days.' This was narrated from the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family).
From him, from Fadalah, from Aban, from Muhammad, who said: I asked him about lodging with the people of the kharaj (land tax), so he said: 'They are lodged with them for three days.'

From him, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad and Fadalah ibn Ayyub, from Aban, from Isma'il ibn al-Fadl, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the corvée (sukhrat) in the villages and what is taken from the soldiers and laborers when they settle in the villages. He said: 'It is stipulated for them; whatever is stipulated for them of dirhams, corvée, and other than that is permissible for you. And you are not allowed to take anything from them until you negotiate with them, even if it is as certain as it is, that whoever settles in that land or village, that is taken from him.' He said: And I asked him about a man who built houses or a house in his own land next to a neighbor, and the people of his neighbor's house moved to him. Is it for him to turn them away while they are unwilling? He said: 'They are free; they settle where they wish and move where they wish.'

From him, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from Aban, from Isma'il ibn al-Fadl, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the land of Khraj (land tax): if a man buys land from it, builds on it or does not build, and people from the Ahl al-Dhimma (non-Muslims under protection) settle in it, is it permissible for him to take from them the rent of the houses if they pay the Jizyah (poll tax) of their heads? He said: 'He should stipulate terms with them, and whatever he takes from them after the stipulation is halal (permissible).'

From him, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Jamil ibn Dirraj, from Ali al-Asraq, who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: 'The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) - Ali (peace be upon him) - at his death, said: 'O Ali, the farmers will not be wronged in your presence, and no extra tax will be taken on land upon which a tax has been fixed, and no corvée (forced labor/service) will be imposed on a Muslim.'' From him, from Safwan, from Ibn Muskhan, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: 'The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) used to write to his governors: 'Do not impose corvée on the Muslims, and whoever asks you for more than the fixed tax, he has transgressed, so do not give him.' And he used to write: 'I advise regarding the farmers, that they be treated well, and they are the farmers (karrun).'

Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn, from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from al-Qasim ibn Sulayman, from Jarrah al-Mad'ini, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a courtyard that contains three rooms (apartments) and has no separate entrance (hujrah), and he said: 'Permission is required for the individual rooms, not for the courtyard itself.' Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Babawayh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: He meant by this the courtyard in which the residents live by rent or residence, so for such courtyards there is no need for permission; permission is only for the individual rooms. As for the courtyard that is not for profit (commercial use), no one may enter it except with permission.

Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Sama'ah, from Abdullah ibn Jabalah, from Ishaq ibn 'Ammar, from Al-Abd al-Salih (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him: 'If a man from the people of Najran owns land and then converts to Islam, is the khums due upon him according to what the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) made a treaty with them on, or is it according to what is due upon Muslims?' He said: 'The khums is due upon him as it is due upon Muslims, for if they had converted, the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) would not have made a treaty with them.'

From him, from Muhammad ibn Abi Hamzah, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the difference between Ibn Abi Layla and Ibn Shubrumah regarding the black land (fertile land conquered by Muslims) and its owners. I said: Indeed, Ibn Abi Layla said that when they (the non-Muslim owners) embrace Islam, they become free, and the land in their possession belongs to them. As for Ibn Shubrumah, he claimed that they are slaves (or remain in a state of servitude regarding the land) and that the land in their possession does not belong to them. He (peace be upon him) said: 'Regarding the land, it is as Ibn Shubrumah said.' And he said: 'Regarding the men, it is as Ibn Abi Layla said, that when they embrace Islam, they become free.' And with this, there is a statement that I did not memorize.

34 - Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar said: I wrote to Abu Muhammad (peace be upon him). Regarding a man who bought a piece of land from another man with its four boundaries, and in it there was crops, palm trees, and other trees, but he did not mention the palm trees, nor the crops, nor the trees in his deed, and he mentioned in it that he had bought it with all its rights, both those inside it and those outside it: Do the palm trees, trees, and crops fall under the rights of the land or not? So he (peace be upon him) wrote: 'When one purchases the land with its boundaries and what is enclosed by its door, then all that is in it belongs to him, if God wills.'

Al-Saffar from Ayub ibn Nuh from Safwan ibn Yahya said: Abu Burdah ibn Rajaa' told me, saying: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'What is your view regarding the purchase of the land of the Khurasan tax?' He said: 'And who sells that, while it is the land of the Muslims?' I said: 'The one who holds it in his possession sells it.' He said: 'And what does he do with the tax of the Muslims?' Then he said: 'There is no harm. He buys his right from it, and the right of the Muslims shifts to him, and perhaps he will be stronger upon it and more enduring with their tax than he is.'

Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Abu Waddad from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) and others from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: "There is no harm in the wage of the broker and the guide; he merely buys for the people day after day for a known amount. He is like the laborer."

Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Ali ibn al-Hakam or another from Abdullah ibn Sinan, who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) was asked, and I was listening. He said to him: 'We command a man to buy for us land, a boy, a house, and a girl, and we give him a fee/commission.' He said, 'There is no harm in that.'

From him, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from some of our companions, from the companions of Al-Raqiq, who said: I bought a female slave for Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him). He handed me four dinars, but I refused. He said, 'You must take them.' So I took them. Then he said, 'Do not take [the money] from the seller.'

From him (Al-Shaykh) from Ibn Mahbub from Abdullah ibn Sinan who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) was asked, and I was listening, and he said: 'Sometimes we command a man to buy for us land, a house, a slave, and a female slave, and we give him a fee/commission.' He said, 'There is no harm in it.'

From him, from Al-Husayn ibn Yasar, from Abu Al-Hasan (peace be upon him) Regarding a man who acts as a guide/broker for houses and estates and takes a fee for it, he said: 'This is a fee, there is no harm with it.'

Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Sama'ah, from Husayn ibn Hashim and Ali ibn Ribat and Safwan ibn Yahya, from Ya'qub ibn Shu'ayb, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about a man who sells for a group of people, with the condition that his liability covers their property. He said: 'If his soul is pleased with that, I only fear that they will impose upon him more than he gains from them. But if his soul is pleased with it, there is no harm.'

From him, from these three, from Ya'qub ibn Shu'ayb, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about a man who sells goods to a group, bringing them this batch, that pair of batches, and this triple batch, with some being superior to others. Then a man comes to him and says, 'Sell them to me as a single lot.' He said, 'I do not like that.'

From him, from Muhammad ibn Ziyad, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, from al-Abd al-Salih (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about a man who says to another man, 'I will buy this food and other things from you on the condition that you set aside a profit for me in it, or set aside something for me in it, on the condition that I buy from you.' He disliked that.

From him, from Safwan, from Abdullah ibn Muskān, from Abū Baṣīr, from Abū Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said: I said to him: 'A man comes to him with their loads, and he sells them for them for a fee, and they say to him: 'Lend us dinars, for we find someone other than you who sells for us, but we give preference to you with our loads because you lend us.' He said: 'There is no harm with it. He only takes dinars like his dinars, and it is not a garment; if he wears it, it diminishes from its price, nor an animal; if he rides it, it wears out. And it is merely a kindness he does for them.'

Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from Muthanna al-Hannat, from Minhal al-Qassab, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: He said: 'Do not go out to meet (the seller) and do not buy what is brought out to be met (for sale), and do not eat from it.'

Abu Ali al-Ash'ari from Muhammad ibn al-Jabbar from Ahmad ibn al-Nadr from 'Amr ibn Shimir from 'Urwah ibn 'Abdullah from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'Let not one of you go out to the countryside to meet and buy goods before they arrive from the city, and let not those in the city sell to those in the countryside, and the Muslims are providers for one another.'
Ibn Mahbub from Abdullah ibn Yahya al-Kahili from Minhal al-Qassab said: I asked him, 'What is the limit of talliq?' He said, 'Rahwa.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, from Minhal al-Qassab, who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'Do not go out to meet (the traveler), for the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) forbade al-tallaqqi.' I asked: 'And what is the limit of al-tallaqqi?' He said: 'That which is less than a gadwah or a rawhah.' I asked: 'Then how much is the gadwah and the rawhah?' He said: 'Four farsakhs.' Ibn Abi Umayr said: 'And that which is above that is not tallaqqi.'

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Ya'qub ibn Yazid, from al-Ghiffari, from al-Qasim ibn Ishaq, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'The sign of God's pleasure with His creation is the justice of their rulers and the affordability of their prices, and the sign of God's wrath with His creation is the injustice of their rulers and the high cost of their prices.'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Fadalah ibn Ayyub, from Isma'il ibn Abi Ziyad, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), from his father (peace be upon him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: "Only a mistaken person monopolizes food."

Sahl ibn Ziyad narrated from Ja'far ibn Muhammad al-Ash'ari, from Abu al-Ala', from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'The bringer of goods is provided for, and the hoarder is cursed.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from al-Nawfali, from al-Sakuni, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: "Hukrah (monopoly/hoarding) in times of plenty is forty days, and in times of hardship and trial is three days. So whoever exceeds forty days in times of plenty, its owner is cursed, and whoever exceeds three days in times of hardship, its owner is cursed."

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Yahya narrated from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ghayath from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "Monopoly (Hukrah) is not [permitted] except in wheat, barley, dates, raisins, and ghee."

Muhammad ibn Ahmad narrated from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Hudhayfah ibn Mansur, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Food was scarce during the time of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family), so the Muslims came and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, food has become scarce, and nothing remains of it except with so-and-so, so order him to sell it.' He said, then he praised Allah and extolled Him, and then said: 'O so-and-so, indeed the Muslims have mentioned that food has become scarce except for a little with you, so bring it out and sell it as you wish, and do not withhold it.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim narrated from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: "Al-Hukrah (monopolizing a commodity) is when you buy food that is not available elsewhere in the city, so you hoard it; but if food is available in the city or other food is sold, there is no harm in seeking a premium for your goods." He said: And I asked him about oil. He said: "If it is with others (i.e., available in the market), there is no harm in holding onto it."

Abu Ali al-Ash'ari from Muhammad ibn al-Jabbar from Safwan from Abu al-Fadl al-Hannat (the cloth merchant) said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'What is your trade?' I said: 'A cloth merchant, and sometimes I arrive when there is a shortage (of goods) and sometimes when there is a glut (surplus), so I hold back (my goods).' He said: 'And what do the people say about you in this regard?' I said: 'They say I am a hoarder (muhtakir).' He said: 'Does anyone else sell it (the held goods)?' I said: 'I do not sell from a thousand parts even one part.' He said: 'There is no harm. That was only a man from Quraysh, called Hakim ibn Hizam. When food entered Medina, he would buy it all. The Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) passed by him and said: "O Hakim ibn Hizam, beware of hoarding!"'.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid from Isma'il ibn Mihran from Hammad ibn 'Uthman said: A severe shortage and famine struck the people of Medina, so much so that a wealthy man would mix wheat with barley and eat it, and as he spent the food, it was consumed. There was good food at the house of Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) which he had purchased at the beginning of the year. He said to some of his freed slaves: 'Buy barley for us and mix it with this food, or sell it, for we dislike eating well while the people eat poor quality food.'

Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Attar from Ali ibn Isma'il from Ali ibn al-Hakam from al-Jahm ibn Abi al-Jahm from Mu'ttab who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to me, while prices were rising in Medina: 'How much food do we have?' I said: 'We have enough for many months.' He said: 'Take it out and sell it.' I said: 'There is no food in Medina.' He said: 'Sell it.' He said: So when I sold it, he said: 'Buy with the people day by day.' And he said: 'O Mu'ttab, make the sustenance of my family half barley and half wheat, for Allah knows that I am able to feed them pure wheat, but I love that Allah sees me having done well in estimating/providing for the livelihood.'

Ahmad ibn Abi Abdillah narrated from Muhammad ibn Ahmad from Yunus ibn Ya'qub from Mu'ttab who said: Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) used to command us: 'When the fruit ripens, we should take it out and sell it, and buy back with the Muslims day for day.'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd from 'Abdullah ibn Sulayman from Abu 'Abdullah (peace be upon him) that he said: Regarding merchants who arrived in a land and agreed that they would not sell their goods except at whatever price they desired, he said, 'There is no objection to that.'

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Wahb, from al-Husayn ibn Abd Allah ibn Damrah, from his father, from his grandfather, from Ali ibn Abi Talib (peace be upon him), that he said: He elevated the narration to the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family). That he passed by the hoarders (al-muhtakirin) and ordered that their hoarding be removed and brought to the centers of the markets and where the eyes could see them. It was said to the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family), 'If you had fixed their prices (qawwamta 'alayhim)?' The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) became angry until the anger was evident on his face, and he said, 'I will fix their prices? No, the price (al-si'r) is to Allah; He raises it when He wills and lowers it when He wills.'

Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from al-Nadr ibn Ishaq al-Kufi from A'iz ibn Junab, who said: I heard Ja'far ibn Muhammad (peace be upon him) saying: 'Buying wheat removes poverty, and buying flour creates poverty, and buying bread is destruction.' I asked him, 'Why, may Allah preserve you?' He said, 'For one who is able but does not do it.'

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Durust, from Ibrahim, from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him), who said: "Whoever buys wheat, his wealth increases; and whoever buys flour, half of his wealth is lost; and whoever buys bread, all of his wealth is lost."

From him, from Abu Basir, from Abu al-Hasan al-Sabah al-Za'farani, from Hammad ibn Khalid, from Abd al-Karim, from Abu Ishaq, from al-Harith, from Ali (peace be upon him), who said: "Whoever sells food, mercy is removed from him."

From him, from Salamah, from Ali ibn al-Mundhir al-Zabbal, from Muhammad ibn al-Fudayl, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: When you have a dirham, buy wheat with it, for the deficiency (in weight/measure) is in the flour.

From him, from Bunan ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Ibn al-Mughira, from al-Sakuni, from Ja'far, from his father, upon them be peace, who said: Do not withhold the loan of sourdough starter and bread, for withholding it breeds poverty.

From him, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from al-Hakam ibn Maskin, from Ishaq ibn 'Ammar, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'I borrow a loaf of bread from the neighbors, so we take a large one and give a small one, or we take a small one and give a large one?' He said, 'There is no harm in it.'

From him, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Abdullah ibn Jabala, from al-Kinanī, who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'O Abu al-Subbah, buying flour (refined wheat) is humility (or modesty), buying whole wheat is dignity, and buying bread is poverty, and I seek refuge with God from poverty.'

And he (peace be upon him) said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) entered upon Aishah while she was counting/keeping track of the bread. He said: 'O Aishah, do not count the bread, lest it be counted against you.'

From him, from Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from al-Dihqan, from Durust, from Ibrahim ibn 'Abd al-Hamid, from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him), who said: A group of people came to the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) and complained to him about the rapid depletion of their food. He (peace be upon him and his family) said, 'Do you measure (precisely) or do you scoop (generously)?' They said, 'We scoop, O Messenger of Allah,' meaning the rough, unmeasured scoop. He said to them, 'Measure, for it is greater for blessing.'
From him, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from al-Husayn ibn Thuwair, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: "When famine strikes you, pay attention to raisins."

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Ali ibn Muhammad, from Ibrahim ibn Ishaq, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Hammam, from Jamil ibn Darradj, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: "When the arrows fall, the right of pre-emption is elevated."

Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Sama'ah, from Ja'far ibn Sama'ah, from Aban, from Abu al-Abbas al-Baqqaq, who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: 'Pre-emption is not valid except for a partner.'
From him, from Ja'far, from Aban, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Abdillah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I heard him say: 'Pre-emption (al-shuf'ah) is not valid except for a partner.'

Muhammad ibn Yahya narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Muhammad ibn Abdillah ibn Hilal, from Uqbah ibn Khalid, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) ruled regarding pre-emptive right (shuf'ah) among partners in lands and dwellings, and said, 'No harm and no causing harm.' And he said, 'When boundaries are marked and limits are set, there is no pre-emptive right.'

From him, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Yazid ibn Ishaq, from Harun ibn Hamzah al-Ghanawi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about pre-emption in dwellings: Is it a mandatory right for the partner, and is it offered to the neighbor, who has more right to it than others? He said, 'Pre-emption in sales, if he is a partner, he has more right to it than others at the price.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim narrated from Muhammad ibn Isa ibn Ubayd from Yunus ibn Abd al-Rahman from Abd Allah ibn Sinan from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Pre-emption (shuf'ah) is only for two partners as long as they have not divided the property; but if they become three, then none of them has pre-emption.

Yunus narrated from some of his men, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about pre-emption (al-shuf'ah): for whom is it, in what is it, and for whom is it suitable? And is there pre-emption in animals, and how is it? He said: 'Pre-emption is permissible in everything, whether animal, land, or movable property, if the item is shared by two partners exclusively. If one of them sells his share, his partner has more right to it than anyone else. And if there are more than two, there is no pre-emption for any of them.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim narrated from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Jamil ibn Darradj, from Mansur ibn Hazim, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a house containing multiple dwellings where they share one path within the courtyard. If one of them sold his house to a man, do his partners have the right of pre-emption (shuf'ah) in the path? He said: 'If the door of the house and what surrounds it faces the path, and otherwise it does not, then they have no right of pre-emption. But if he sold the path along with the house, then they have the right of pre-emption.'

Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from al-Kahili, from Mansur ibn Hazim, who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): A house was shared among a group of people who divided it, and each took a portion, built upon it, and left a courtyard between them for their passage. Then a man came and bought the share of one of them. Is that permissible for him? He said: 'Yes, but he must close his door and open a door to the road, or descend from above the house and close his door. And if the owner of the road wishes to sell it to him, they have more right to it; otherwise, it is his road, and he comes and sits at that door.'

Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Sama'a, from Muhammad ibn Ziyad, from Hisham ibn Salim, from Sulayman ibn Khalid, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: "There is no shuf'ah (pre-emption) in animals." Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: His (peace be upon him) statement 'There is no shuf'ah in animals' is to be understood as referring to the case where there is more than one partner. And we have clarified in what preceded in the narration of Yunus that there is shuf'ah in animals. And to add further clarification, he narrated:

Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Sama'a, from Muhammad ibn Ziyad and Safwan, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): A slave is owned by partners, and one of them sold his share. Then one of them said, 'I have more right to him.' Is that so? He said, 'Yes, if he is single.'

Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad from al-Halabi from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) that he said: Regarding a slave owned by partners, if one of them sells his share, the other partner says, 'I have more right to it.' Is that so? He said, 'Yes, if there is only one [other partner].' It was said to him, 'Is there shuf'ah in animals?' He said, 'No.'

Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Barqi, from al-Nawfali, from al-Sakuni, from Ja'far, from his father, from his forefathers, from Ali (peace be upon him) who said: "Pre-emption is according to the number of men." Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: This report agrees with the opinions of some of the Sunnis, but we do not adopt it. And that upon which we act is what we have previously stated, that preemption is established if the property is between two persons; but if they increase (in number), there is no preemption for one of them.

Ali ibn Ibrahim narrated from his father, from al-Nawfali, from al-Sakuni, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: He said: "There is no pre-emptive right (shuf'ah) for the Jews and the Christians." And he said: "There is no pre-emptive right except for a partner who is not a co-heir." He said: "And the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) said: 'The guardian of the orphan is in the position of his father; he takes the pre-emptive right for him if he has a desire for it.'" And he said: "There is a pre-emptive right for the absent one."

From him, from his father, from al-Nawfali, from al-Sakuni, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'There is no pre-emption in a ship, nor in a river, nor in a road.'

Ibn al-Walid from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar, from al-Haytham ibn Abi Masruq al-Nahdi, from Ali ibn Mahziyar, who said: I asked Abu Ja'far (the second Imam, peace be upon him) about a man who sought the right of pre-emption (shuf'ah) for a piece of land, and it was agreed that he would bring the money, but he did not arrive. So what should the owner of the land do if he wishes to sell it? Should he sell it or wait for the arrival of his partner, the owner of the right of pre-emption? He said: 'If he is in the city, the owner should wait with him for three days. If he comes with the money, then [the sale is valid with him]; otherwise, he should sell it and his right of pre-emption in the land is nullified. And if he requested a delay until he could bring the money from one town to another, the owner should wait for him for the duration of the man's travel to that town, plus an additional three days upon his arrival. If he meets him [with the money], then [the sale is valid with him]; otherwise, he has no right of pre-emption.'

Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Sama'a from Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Ali ibn Ri'ab from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) regarding: A man bought a house along with slaves, goods, textiles, and gems. He said: 'There is no pre-emption right for anyone in it.'

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Talhah ibn Zayd from Ja'far from his father from Ali (peace be upon him) who said: "There is no pre-emption except for a partner who is not a co-sharer." And he said, "Indeed, the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said, 'Pre-emption is not valid in the fixed punishments.'" And he said, "Pre-emption is not inherited."

Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Malik ibn 'Atiyyah from Abu Basir from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a man who married a woman in exchange for a room in his house, and he had partners in that house. He said: 'It is permissible for him and for her, and there is no pre-emption (shuf'ah) for any of the partners against her.'

Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Sama'ah, from Muhammad ibn Ziyad, from al-Kahili, from Mansur ibn Hazim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I said to him: 'A house was shared among a group of people, and they left a courtyard between them in which is their passage. Then a man came and bought the share of one of them. Is that permissible for him?' He said: 'Yes, but he must close his door and open a door to the road, or descend from above the house. If their partner wishes to sell the passage of his feet, then they have more right to it. And if he wishes, he comes until he sits on the closed door that he sold, and they cannot prevent him.'

Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ali ibn al-Hakam from Muhammad ibn Muslim from Abu Hamzah from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: I asked him about collateral and guarantee in credit sales, and he said, 'There is no objection to it.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim narrated from his father, from Isma'il ibn Marar, from Yunus, from Mu'awiya, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who gives a loan in animals and food, and pledges a pledge. He said, 'There is no harm; you secure what is from your wealth.'

Abu Ali al-Ash'ari from Muhammad ibn al-Jabbar from Safwan from Isḥāq ibn ʿAmmār said: I asked Abū Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him) about a man who has a pledge (rahn) with him but does not know whose it is among the people. He said, 'I dislike that he sell it until its owner comes.' I said, 'He does not know whose it it is among the people.' He said, 'There is either an excess or a deficiency in it.' I said, 'If there is excess or deficiency in it?' He said, 'If there is deficiency in it, it is easier for its sale; he is rewarded for what was lost from its value. And if there is excess in it, it is more severe than the current state; he sells it and keeps the excess until the owner comes.'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Safwan from Ibn Bukayr said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who pledged a pledge, then departed and could not be found; is the pledge sold? He said, 'No, until its owner comes.'

Ahmad ibn Abi Abdillah from his father from Ibn Bukayr from Ubayd ibn Zurarah from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding a man who pledged a pledge for an indefinite time, then the pledgor was absent, is there a time for which his pledge is sold? He said, 'No, until he comes.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Abdullah ibn al-Mughirah, from Ibn Sinan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) ruled regarding a man who pledged an item that had produce/yield, that its yield is accounted for the owner of the pledge from what is owed to him.

From him, from his father, from Ibn Abi Najran, from Asim ibn Humayd, from Muhammad ibn Qays, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), that the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) said: A man mortgages barren land (which bears no fruit); he cultivates it and spends from his own wealth on it. Indeed, his expenses and his labor are considered purely his own. Then he looks at the share of the land and accounts for it from the wealth with which he mortgaged the land, until he has fully recovered his capital from his wealth. When he has recovered his capital, he should return the land to its owner.

From him, from his father, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who pledged a female slave to a group of people: Is it permissible for him to have intercourse with her? He said, 'Those who took the pledge will prevent him from having intercourse with her.' I said, 'What do you think if he had power over her in private?' He said, 'Yes, I do not consider this forbidden upon him.'

Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Safwan from al-Ala' from Muhammad ibn Muslim from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) Regarding a man who pledged his female slave to a group of people: Is it permissible for him to have intercourse with her? He said, 'Those who took the pledge prevent him from having intercourse with her.' I said, 'What do you think if he is able to do so privately?' He said, 'Yes, I see no harm in that.'

From him, from Ibn Faddal, from Ibrahim ibn Uthman, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I said to him: 'There is a man who owes me dirhams, and his house is pledged as collateral; I wish to sell it.' He said: 'I seek your protection by Allah that you expel him from the shadow of his head.' And from him, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Mansur ibn Hazim, from Hisham ibn Salim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: He was asked about a man who has a debt against another man, and the latter has pledged collateral with him; should he buy the collateral from him? He said: 'Yes.'

Abu Ali al-Ash'ari from Muhammad ibn al-Jabbar from Safwan from Muhammad ibn Rabah al-Qalla' said: I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about a man whose brother died and left a chest of pledges (rhn); some of it had the owner's name on it and its pledge value was known, while for some no one knew who they belonged to or what their pledge value was. What do you think regarding that which has no known owner? He said, 'It is [distributed] like its entirety.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi: Regarding a man who pledges an item with another man, and it is damaged or lost, he said: 'He returns with his money upon him (the pledgee).'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad and Fadalah from Aban from Ubayd ibn Zur'arah said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): A man pledged two bracelets, and one of them was lost. He said: 'He reverts to what remains.' And he said regarding a man who pledged a house to him, which was burned or collapsed: 'His wealth is in the dust of the earth.'

From him, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Aban, from a man, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding a man who pledged a house to another man, and it burned down or collapsed, he said: 'His wealth (the value of the pledge) is in the dust of the earth (i.e., lost/absorbed by the debtor).' And he said regarding a man whose slave was pledged to him and became diseased (or) whose goods were pledged to him, and he did not sell the goods, nor did he take care of them, nor did he move them, so they deteriorated: 'Does his wealth decrease by that amount?' He said: 'No.'

Muhammad ibn Yahya from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from Safwan from Ibn Bukayr said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the pledge (rahn), and he said: 'If the pledge is more than the value of the debt owed by the pledgee, and it perishes, he must pay the surplus to the owner of the pledge. And if it is less than his debt, and the pledge perishes, he pays the owner the remainder of his debt. And if they are equal, there is nothing upon him.' And what Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Abu Hamzah, who said: 'I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about the saying of Ali (peace be upon him) regarding the pledge: The resolution in these two narrations is that if the pledge perishes due to negligence on the part of the pledgee, such as misplacement or otherwise, then as for if it perishes from itself or from another party, nothing is incumbent upon him, and he has recourse to the owner for the value. And that which clarifies what we mentioned is what he narrated:

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Ja'far al-Razzaz from Muhammad ibn al-Hamid from Saif ibn 'Amirah from Mansur ibn Hazim from Sulayman ibn Khalid from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: If you take a slave or an animal as a pledge (rahn) and they die, there is nothing upon you; but if the animal perishes or the boy runs away, you are liable (guarantor). The meaning here is also that the cause of their destruction or running away must be something from the side of the pledge-holder; as for if it was not due to anything from his side, then nothing is obligatory upon him, and his ruling is the same as that of death.

Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Attar narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Safwan, from Isḥaq ibn ʿAmmār, who said: I asked Abā Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him) about a man who pledges a slave, or a garment, or jewelry, or household items, and the owner of the item says to the pledgee: 'You are free to wear this garment or jewelry, so wear it and benefit from the item and use the servant.' He said: 'It is permissible for him if he gives permission and declares it permissible, and I like that he does so.' I said: 'If he pledges a house that has produce/income, whose is the produce?' He said: 'The owner of the house.' I said: 'If he pledges a bare land?' He said: 'The owner of the land should cultivate it for himself.' He said: 'This is not like that; he cultivates it for himself, so it is permissible for him as he declared it permissible for him, because he cultivates it with his own wealth and develops it.'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Fadala from Aban from a man from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: I asked him: How is the pledge (rahn) if what is in it is an animal or a beast, or gold, or silver, or goods, and a calamity strikes it, such as fire or a thief, so its wealth perishes or its goods diminish, and he has no proof of his loss? He said: 'If all his goods are gone and nothing is found for him, then there is nothing upon him. And if he says: Wealth went from my house, and he has wealth, he is not believed.'

From him, from Safwan and Fudalah, from al-Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) Regarding a man who pledged an item as collateral with his partner, and there was no clear evidence between them regarding it: The one holding the collateral claimed it was worth one thousand dirhams, while the owner of the collateral claimed it was worth one hundred. He (peace be upon him) said: 'The burden of proof is on the one holding the collateral who claims it is worth one thousand dirhams; if he has no proof, then the oath is upon the pledgor.' And he said regarding a man who pledged an item as collateral with his partner: The one holding the collateral said, 'I took it as collateral from you for such and such,' while the other said, 'It is merely a deposit with you.' He said: 'The burden of proof is on the one holding the collateral that it is such and such; if he has no proof, then the oath is upon the one who owns the collateral.'

From him, from Muhammad ibn Khalid, from Ibn Bukayr and Al-Nadr, from Al-Qasim ibn Sulayman, all from Ubayd ibn Zur'arah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding a man who pledged an item with his partner as collateral, and there was no clear evidence between them: The one holding the collateral claimed it was worth one thousand, while the owner of the collateral claimed it was worth one hundred. He (peace be upon him) said: 'The burden of proof is on the one holding the collateral who claims it is worth one thousand; if he has no proof, then the oath is upon the owner of the collateral that it is worth one hundred.'

Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Sama'ah, from more than one, from Aban, from Ibn Abi Ya'fur, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: If they differ regarding the pledge, and one says 'I pledged it for a thousand [dinars]' and the other says 'for a hundred dirhams', he says: 'The owner of the thousand is asked for proof; if he has no proof, the owner of the hundred swears an oath.' And if the pledge is less than what was pledged or more, or they differ, and one says 'It is a pledge' and the other says 'It is a deposit', he says: 'The proof is upon the owner of the deposit; if he has no proof, the owner of the pledge swears an oath.'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Safwan from Ya'qub ibn Shu'ayb said: I asked him about a man who has a debt of dates, or wheat, or pomegranates against another man, and he has land containing some of that, so he pledges it until he receives what is due to him. He said: 'He takes security from his wealth.'

Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub from Ibn Abi Nasr from Dawud ibn al-Husayn from Abu al-Abbas from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a man who pledged two slaves to another, and one of them died; would his right be in the other? He said, 'Yes.' I said, or a house that burned down; would his right be in the ashes/ground? He said, 'Yes.' Or two beasts, would his right be in one of them? He said, 'Yes.' Or goods that spoil due to the length of time they were left, or food that spoils, or a slave who contracted smallpox and went blind, or clothes that were left folded and not aired until they perished? He said, 'This is permissible to take; his right remains upon him.' And I asked him how the pledge remains with what is in it if it is an animal or beast or gold or silver or goods, and a calamity befalls it—fire or thieves—and all his property perishes, except that part, and some of his goods have perished, and he has no proof of his loss? He said, 'If all his goods are gone and nothing is found for him, then there is nothing upon him.' And he said, 'If part of his property is gone and he still has property, he is not believed [to claim total loss], and it is ruled for every pledge that has produce/yield, that its yield is calculated for the owner of the pledge from what is upon him.'

Muhammad ibn al-Hassan ibn Mahbub narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Nawfali, from al-Sakuni, from Ja'far, from his father, from Ali (peace be upon him). In a case of a pledge (rahn) where the pledgor (rahin) and the pledgee (murta-hin) differed regarding it, the pledgor said: 'It is such and such,' and the pledgee said: 'It is more than that.' Ali (peace be upon him) said: 'The pledgee is believed until he covers the value, because he is its trustee.'

From him, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Barqi, from Abdullah ibn al-Mughira, from al-Sakuni, from Ja'far, from his father, from his ancestors, from Ali (peace be upon him) who said: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'The camel (dhabh) may be ridden if it is pledged (as security), and upon the one who rides it is the burden of its maintenance (nafaqah). And the donkey (dar) may be drunk from (for its milk) if it is pledged, and upon the one who drinks from it is the burden of its maintenance.'

From him (Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub) from 'Abbad ibn Shu'ayb, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about goods in the possession of two men, one of whom says, 'I deposited it with you,' and the other says, 'It is a pledge with me.' He said: 'The word of the one who says,

Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ibn Abi Umayr from al-Husayn ibn Uthman from Isḥāq ibn ʿAmmār from Abū ʿAbdillāh (peace be upon him): In a man said to another man, 'A thousand dirhams are due from you to me.' He said, 'No, but they are a deposit (wadiʿah).' Abū ʿAbdillāh (peace be upon him) said: 'The word of the owner of the money is accepted with his oath.'

From him, from Al-Hasan, from Abu Waddad, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who takes an animal or a camel as a pledge for his money, whether he has the right to ride it. He said: 'If he feeds it, he has the right to ride it; and if the one who pledged it to him feeds it, he does not have the right to ride it.'

Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Sama'ah, from Safwan, from 'Asim ibn Humayd, from Muhammad ibn Qays, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said: "There is no pledge (rahn) unless it is taken into possession."

From him, from Ahmad ibn Abi Bishr, from Muawiya ibn Maythara, who said: I heard Abu al-Jarud ask Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) About a man who sold his house to another man, and there was a mortgage/encumbrance between him and the buyer. He stipulated: 'If you bring me my money within three years, the house is yours.' He brought him his money. The Imam said: 'He has his condition (the right to redeem).' Abu al-Jarud said to him: 'That man has acquired/kept that money within three years.' He said: 'It is his money.' And Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'What do you think if the house burned down? Whose money was it? The house belongs to the buyer.'

From him, from Muhammad ibn Ziyad, from Hisham ibn Salim, who said: Hafs al-A'war asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) while I was sitting with him, saying: 'There was a laborer for my father who worked at his mill, and he had some dirhams with us, and he had no heir.' Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'You give it to the poor.' Then he said: 'What is your opinion regarding it?' Then he repeated the question to him, and he said to him the same thing. He repeated the question to him a third time, so Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'You seek an heir for him; if you find an heir for him, [give it to him], otherwise it is like your property.' Then he said: 'What do you suppose you will do with it?' Then he said: 'You bequeath it; if a claimant comes for it, [give it to him], otherwise it is like your property.'

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Abu Abdillah, from Mansur ibn al-Abbas, from al-Husayn ibn Ali ibn Yaqtin, from Amr ibn Ibrahim, from Khalaf ibn Hammad, from Isma'il ibn Abi Qurrat, from Abi Basir, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding a man who borrowed one hundred dinars from another man and pledged jewelry to him as security for the one hundred dinars, then the borrower came to the lender and said, 'Lend me the security I pledged to you as a loan for use,' so he lent it to him, and the security perished in his possession. There is something due from the borrower to the lender in this matter. He (peace be upon him) said: 'It is upon the owner of the security (the borrower), for he is the one who pledged it and he is the one who caused its destruction, and there is no compensation for the property of this one (the lender).' And Muhammad ibn Hassan narrated from Abu 'Imran al-Armani, from Abdillah ibn al-Hakam, who said I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who went bankrupt and had a debt owed to a group of people, and with some of them was security (pledged property) and with others there was no security, then he died and his wealth was not sufficient to cover the debt. He said: 'All that he left of the securities and other property is divided among the creditors in shares.' And Muhammad ibn 'Isa ibn 'Ubayd narrated from Sulayman ibn Hafsh al-Marwazi, who said I wrote to Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) regarding a man who died with a debt and left nothing except a security in the hand of one of the creditors, and its price does not exceed more than the value of the security itself. Does he take it with its value, or is he and the other creditors partners in it? He wrote back (peace be upon him): 'All the creditors are equal in this; they distribute it among themselves in shares.' And he said: And I wrote to him regarding a man who died and had heirs, and a man came and claimed a debt from him and said that he has a security with him. He wrote back (peace be upon him): 'If he has a debt from the deceased and has no proof against him, let him take his debt from what is in his hand and return the remainder to his heirs. And whenever he acknowledges what is in his hand, it is taken from him and he is required to provide proof for his claim, and he fulfills his right after the oath. And whenever he does not produce proof and

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa from Ali ibn al-Hakam from Abu Ayyub from Muhammad ibn Muslim from Abu Hamzah from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: I asked him about the pledge (rahn) and the guarantor (kafil) in a sale on credit (bai' al-nasi'ah). He said, 'There is no objection to it.'

From him, from Al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Fadhal, from Ibrahim ibn Uthman ibn Ziyad, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I said: 'There is a man who has a debt owed to me, and his house is pledged as collateral (rahn). I wish to sell it.' He (peace be upon him) said to him: 'I advise you by Allah not to evict him from the shadow of his head (i.e., do not evict him while the debt remains unpaid).'

Ahmad ibn Muhammad and Sahl ibn Ziyad together from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr from Hammad ibn 'Uthman from Isḥaq ibn 'Ammar who said: I asked Abu al-Ḥasan (peace be upon him) about a man who deposited with another man one thousand dirhams, which were then lost. The first man said, 'It was a deposit with me,' and the other said, 'It was merely a loan from you.' He (peace be upon him) said, 'The money remains with the depositor unless he produces evidence that it was a deposit.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim narrated from his father, from Hammad, from Hariz, from Zurarah, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the deposit of gold and silver. He said, 'Everything that is a deposit and is not guaranteed (liable for loss) is not liable (for compensation if lost).'

From him, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: "The keeper of the deposit and the merchant of the goods are two trusted persons." -(791) 4 - Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar said: I wrote to Abu Muhammad (peace be upon him): A man deposited a trust with another man, who placed it in his neighbor's house, and it was lost. Is it obligatory upon him if he disobeyed his command and took it out of his possession of it? He (peace be upon him) replied: "He is liable for it, if God wills."

Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub from Ya'qub ibn Yazid from Ibn Abi Umayr from Habib al-Kha'thami from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I said to him: A man has wealth in his possession as a trust (deposit); may he take from it without the owner's permission? He said: 'He does not take unless he has 'afā' (ability to compensate/replace it).' I said: What if he finds someone to guarantee it for him, but he himself does not have 'afā', and the one who guarantees it testifies on his behalf? Will he take from it? He said: 'Yes.'

From him, from Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Shurah, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from Sulayman ibn Dawud, from Hafs ibn Ghiyath, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man from the Muslims who deposited with him a man from the thieves [some] dirhams or goods, and the thief is a Muslim; should he return it to him? He said: 'He does not return it. If he is able to return it to its owner, he does so; otherwise, it remains in his hand like a found object (luqata). He recognizes it for a year. If he finds its owner, he returns it to him; otherwise, he gives it in charity. If the owner comes after that, he is given a choice between the reward (for keeping it) and the compensation (for losing it). If he chooses the reward, it is for him; if he chooses the compensation, he pays compensation to him, and the reward is for him.'

Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from al-Barqi, from Muhammad ibn al-Qasim, from Fudayl, who said: I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about a man who deposited with a man from your mawali (clients/freemen) some wealth of his. The man upon whom the wealth is due is an Arab who is able to withhold it from him, while the depositor is a wicked, outgoing, devilish man. I did not leave out any detail, so he said to me, 'Tell him to return it to him, for he entrusted it to him with the trust of Allah.' I said, 'And what about a man who bought from a woman from some of the Abbasids some of their plots of land, and he wrote for her a deed, and she has taken the money but has not taken the deed? Should he give her the money or withhold it?' He said, 'He should withhold it from her with the strongest withholding, for she sold what she did not possess.' Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn Babawayh (may Allah be pleased with him) said: Our scholars (may Allah have mercy on them) have passed upon that the word of the depositor is accepted, and that he is trustworthy, and there is no oath upon him.

And it has been narrated that a man said to Al-Sadiq (peace be upon him): 'I entrusted a man with wealth that I had deposited with him, but he betrayed me and denied my wealth.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'The trustworthy one did not betray you, but you entrusted the betrayer.'

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Ibrahim ibn Hashim, from al-Husayn ibn Yazid al-Nawfali, from Isma'il ibn Abi Ziyad al-Sakuni, from Ja'far, from his father, from Ali (peace be upon him). Regarding a man who deposited two dinars with another man, and that man deposited one dinar with him, and one dinar was lost from them, he ruled: 'The owner of the two dinars is entitled to one dinar, and the two parties share the remaining dinar between them in two equal halves.'

Al-Husayn ibn Said from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad from Al-Halabi from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "There is no guarantee (liability for loss/damage) on the borrower of a loan for use, and the owner of the loan for use and the deposit is trustworthy."

From him, from Fadalah, from Aban, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about the loaned item (ariyyah); if a person borrows it and it perishes or is stolen, he said: 'If he is trustworthy (amin), there is no compensation (ghurm) upon him.'

From him, from al-Nadr, from 'Asim, from Muhammad ibn Qays, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) ruled regarding a man who lent a female servant, and she died in his possession, and no cause of liability was sought against her; he ruled that the lender is not liable for compensation, nor is the man liable if he rents an animal, provided he does not force it or a cause of liability is not sought against it.

From him, from al-Nadhr, from Ibn Sinan, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the loan for use (ariyyah), so he said: 'There is no liability (guarantee) on the borrower of a loan for use if it perishes, provided he was trustworthy (did not exceed the normal limits of use).'

From him, from Fudayla, from Aban, from Salama, from Abu Abdillah, from his father (peace be upon them both), who said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) came to Safwan ibn Umayya and asked him for weapons, eighty breastplates. Safwan asked him, 'As a loan (ariyyah) that is guaranteed (dhaminah), or as a seizure (ghasb)?' The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said, 'No, as a loan that is guaranteed.' Safwan said, 'Yes.'

From him, from al-Nadr, from 'Asim, from Abu Basir, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I heard him saying: 'The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) sent to Safwan ibn Umayyah and borrowed from him seventy armor coats with their straps. He said: 'Is it by force (ghasb)? O Muhammad.' The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'No, it is a loan ('ariyyah) that is guaranteed (liable for return/damage).'

From him, from Safwan, from Ibn Muskān, who said: Abū ‘Abdillāh (peace be upon him) said: “The ‘āriyyah (item lent for use) is not guaranteed [for loss/damage] unless a guarantee was stipulated for it, except for the dānīr (gold coins), for they are guaranteed even if no guarantee was stipulated for them.”

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Ibn Abi Yafur, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: The keeper of the deposit and the merchant are two trusted parties. And he said: If the item borrowed for use perishes in the possession of the borrower, he is not liable for it unless a condition was stipulated upon him.

Ali ibn Ibrahim narrated from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Jamil, from Zurarah, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'Is the borrowed item (for use) liable for loss?' He said, 'All that you borrow is liable for loss, but your liability for its loss is not required except for gold and silver, for they are liable. Unless it is stipulated that whenever it is lost, you are not liable for its loss. And likewise, all that you borrow and it is stipulated upon you is liable for you. And gold and silver are liable for you even if it is not stipulated upon you.'

Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub from Ali ibn al-Sindi from Safwan from Isḥaq ibn ʿAmmār from Abū ʿAbdillāh and Abū Ibrāhīm (peace be upon them both) said: «The loan for use (ʿāriyyah) carries no guarantee (ḍamān) on the borrower, except for what is made of gold or silver, for they are guaranteed whether stipulated or not.» And they said: «If a loan for use is borrowed without the owner's permission and it perishes, the borrower is liable.»

Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr from Jamil ibn Salih from Abd al-Malik ibn Amr from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The borrower of a loaned item is not liable for its loss, unless the owner stipulates otherwise, except for dirhams (coins), for they are liable whether the owner stipulated or not.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from al-Husayn ibn Muhammad from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad from al-Hasan ibn Ali from Aban from one who narrated to him from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding a man who borrowed a garment, then went to it and pledged it as collateral, so the owners of the goods came to their goods, and he said: 'They take their goods.'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Fadalah from Aban from Hudhayfah from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding a man who borrowed a garment, then took it and pledged it as collateral, and the owners of the item came to their item, he said: 'They take their item.'

From him, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: Regarding a man who hired a laborer and had him sit on his goods, and they were stolen, he said: 'He is considered a trustee (liable for compensation).'

From him, from Fadala, from Aban, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a man who borrows money, which is then lost or stolen; is there liability (guarantee) on the borrower? He said, 'There is no compensation/liability on him after the man has been trustworthy (in safeguarding it).'

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Harun ibn Muslim, from Mas'adah ibn Ziyad, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad (peace be upon him) who said: I heard him saying: 'There is no compensation (guarantee) upon the borrower of a loan for use if it perishes, or is stolen, or is lost, provided that the borrower is trustworthy (has exercised due diligence).'

From him, from Abu Ja'far, from his father, from Wahb, from Ja'far, from his father, peace be upon them, that Ali (peace be upon him) said: Whoever borrows a slave owned by a group of people and he causes defect/damage, he is liable (guarantor); and whoever borrows a free minor and he causes defect/damage, he is liable.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Ibn Ri'ab said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: "It is not fitting for a Muslim man to partner with the Dhimmi, nor to entrust him with merchandise, nor to deposit with him a trust, nor to reciprocate him with affection."

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from al-Nawfali, from al-Sakuni, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) That the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) disliked the partnership of the Jew, the Christian, and the Magian, 'unless it is a present trade' in which one does not absent oneself.

Five - Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Sama'ah from 'Abdullah ibn Jabalah and Ja'far and Muhammad ibn 'Abbas from 'Ala' from Muhammad ibn Muslim from one of them (peace be upon them) who said: I asked him about two men who have wealth between them, part of which is absent (not yet realized) and part is in their hands. They divided what was in their hands, and each one schemed/claimed for his share of the absent portion. One of them claimed it, and the other did not claim it. He said: 'What one of them claimed is between them; it goes with his wealth.'

From him, from Muhammad ibn Ziyad, from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about two men who have wealth between them, part of which is in their hands and part is absent from them. They divided the part that was in their hands, and each one of them managed his share of the absent part. One of them collected his share, while the other did not. He (peace be upon him) said: 'Whatever one of them collected, it is between them, according to what he spent to collect it.'

From him, from Muhammad ibn Ziyad, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about two men who had shared property, part of which was debt and part was specific assets. They divided the specific assets and the debt. The share of one of them from the debt was paid off or partially paid off, and the share of the other remained. I asked: Does he return [the value] to his partner? He said: 'Yes, as long as it does not consume his capital.'

From him, from Salih ibn Khalid and Ubays ibn Hasham, from Thabit ibn Sharih, from Dawud al-Abzari, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about a man who made a sale but did not have cash on hand, so he went to one of his partners and said, 'Settle the debt for me, and the profit will be shared between you and me.' He replied, 'If it is a profit, it is shared between them both; and if there is a loss, it is upon them both.'

From him, from Salih ibn Khalid and Ubays ibn Hasham, from Thabit ibn Sharih, from Dawud al-Abzari, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about two men who shared in wealth and profited from it, and the wealth consisted of both tangible assets and debts. One said to the other, 'Give me my principal capital, and the profit is yours, and the loss is upon you.' He said, 'There is no harm if they stipulate it; but if the stipulation contradicts the Book of Allah, it is returned to the Book of Allah.'

From him, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Ishaq ibn 'Ammar, who said: I said to the Virtuous One (peace be upon him): A man points out a commodity to another man and says, 'Buy it, and half of it is mine.' The man buys it and pays from his wealth. He (Imam al-Sadiq, peace be upon him) said: 'He has half the profit.' I said: 'If the price is reduced, will he be affected by the reduction?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'He bears the reduction just as he took from the profit.'

From him, from Wahb, from Abu Basir, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding a man who partners with another man in a commodity, and one indicates it to the other: he said, 'If there is profit, it is for him; and if there is a loss, it is upon him.'

He narrated from Ibn Ribat, from Mansur ibn Hazim, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about two men, for each of whom there is food with the other's companion, and one does not know how much he has on the other, nor does the other know how much he has on the first. He said: 'Each of them says to his companion: 'For you is what is with you, and for me is what is with me,' and they both agreed to that.' He said: 'There is no harm if they agree to that and their souls are pleased with it.'

Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Sama'ah, from Wahb, from Abi Basir, from Abi Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding a man who gives another man money for mudarabah (profit-sharing partnership) and prohibits him from taking it to another land, but he disobeys him, he said: 'He is liable (for loss) to him, and the profit is shared between them, if he violates his condition and disobeys him.'

Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Aban and Yahya, from Abu al-Maghra', from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "The capital which is worked with as a mudarabah (profit-sharing partnership) belongs to the investor from the profit, and he is not liable for any loss except if he contradicts the order of the capital owner."

Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Sama'ah, from Abdullah ibn Jabalah, from Ishaq ibn 'Ammar, from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about the capital of mudarabah (profit-sharing partnership). He said: 'The profit is shared between them, and the loss is borne by the capital.'

From him, from Safwan, from Asim ibn Humayd, from Muhammad ibn Qays, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: Ali (peace be upon him) ruled regarding a merchant who traded with capital and stipulated half the profit: 'There is no guarantee/liability on the Mudarib (worker).' And he also said: 'Whoever guarantees the profit for his Mudarib, he is entitled only to the principal capital and he gets nothing from the profit.'

Ahmad ibn Isha narrated from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from al-Kahili, from Abu al-Hasan Musa (peace be upon him): Regarding a man who gave a man wealth as a mudarabah (profit-sharing partnership), and designated for him a specific portion of the profit. The mudarib (partner managing the trade) purchased goods and placed them in the capital. He said: 'Upon the mudarib is [liable for] the loss [in value] to the extent of the profit designated for him.' This does not contradict the earlier reports, because this report is understood to be when the wealth is a partnership between them, in which case the profit and loss are shared between them. The term 'mudarabah' was applied to it metaphorically, or because the wealth was entirely from his side, even if he made some of it a debt upon himself to validate the partnership. And that which clarifies what we mentioned is what he narrated:

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa from al-Hasan ibn al-Jahm from Thal'abah from Abd al-Malik ibn Utbah said: I asked some of these, meaning Abu Yusuf and Abu Hanifa, and I said: 'I constantly hand over money as muḍārabah (profit-sharing partnership) to a man, and he says: It has been lost or gone.' He said: 'Then hand over most of it to him as a loan (qarḍ), and the remainder as muḍārabah.' I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about that, and he said: 'It is permissible.'

From him, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Abd al-Malik ibn Utbah al-Hashimi, who said: I asked Abu al-Hasan Musa (peace be upon him): Is it permissible for the owner of wealth, when he wishes to secure his own capital, to make a portion of it a partnership so that it becomes more secure for him in his wealth? He said, 'There is no harm in it.'

From him, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Abd al-Malik ibn Utbah, from Abu al-Hasan Musa (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about a man to whom I give money, saying to him: 'When I give you the money, which is fifty thousand, ten thousand dirhams of this money are a loan upon you, and the remainder remains with me; buy for me whatever you see fit with it.' I asked: 'Is this arrangement sound? Is it more preferable to you, or should I hire him for the money for a known wage?' He said: 'There is no objection to it.'

From him, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Aban and Yahya, from Abu al-Maghra', from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding a man who gives a man money and says to him, 'Go to such and such land and do not exceed it; buy from it.' He (the Imam) said: 'If he exceeds it and the money is lost, he is liable (guarantor); if he buys something and it is placed (in storage/possession), it is upon him; and if he profits, it is between them (shared).'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Safwan, from al-Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from one of the Imams (peace be upon them both), who said: I asked him about a man who gives money as muḍārabah (profit-sharing partnership) and commands that it not be taken out, but he takes it out. He said: 'He guarantees the capital, and the profit is shared between them.'

From him, from Muhammad ibn al-Fudayl, from al-Kinanī, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about al-mudarabah (partnership), where a man is given money to take to a specific land, and he was instructed not to take it to another land; but he disobeyed and took it to a different land, and the money was lost. He said: 'He is liable (for the loss). If it survives and yields profit, then the profit is shared between them.'

From him, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from Al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding a man who gives another man money for mudarabah (profit-sharing partnership), and he deviates from what was stipulated for him, he said: 'He is liable (for loss), and the profit is shared between them.'

From him, from al-Nadr, from 'Asim, from Muhammad ibn Qays, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said: The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) said: "Whoever invests capital and stipulates half the profit, there is no guarantee (of loss) upon him." And he said: "Whoever provides capital to a merchant, he is entitled only to his principal capital and has no share in the profit."

From him, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from Aban, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Abdillah, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who has capital in a mudarabah (profit-sharing partnership) partnership, and his profit decreases, so he fears that [the capital owner] will take [his share of profit], so he increases [the profit given to] his partner beyond the condition that was between them. And he does this out of fear that [his share] will be taken from him. He said, 'There is no harm with it.'

From him, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Muhammad ibn Qays, who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): A man gave a thousand dirhams to another man as a mudarabah (profit-sharing partnership), and he [the agent] bought a slave for him, while he [the agent] did not know [the value]. He [the Imam] said: 'It is appraised; if it exceeds by one dirham, he is freed, and he is given leeway in the man's wealth [to cover the difference].'

From him, from Muhammad ibn Khalid, from Abdullah ibn al-Mughira, from Mansur ibn Hazim, from Bakr ibn Habib, who said: I said to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him): A man gave the wealth of an orphan for mudarabah (profit-sharing partnership). He said: 'If there is profit, it is for the orphan; and if there is a loss, the one who gave [the capital] is the guarantor.'

From him (Al-Shaykh), from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from Al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), that he said: Regarding the capital in which you engage in mudarabah (profit-sharing partnership), you are entitled to a share of the profit, and you bear no loss from the capital unless you violate the condition of the owner of the capital. Indeed, Al-Abbas was wealthy and would give men capital to work on as mudarabah, stipulating that they not settle in the bottom of a valley and not buy 'Dha Kabad' (a ratbah' (fresh dates with the kernel). If you violate anything of what I have commanded you, then you are liable/guarantor for the capital.

From him, from Fadalah, from Rifah ibn Musa, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: The investor (mudarib) says to his partner (sahib al-mal): 'If you cause him harm or consume his capital, then you are liable (guarantor) for him.' He (the Imam) said: 'He is liable for him if he violates his condition.'

Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Sama'ah, from Muhammad ibn Ziyad, from Abdullah ibn Yahya al-Kahili, from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him), who said: I said: A man asked me to ask you about a man who gave him capital for mudarabah (profit-sharing partnership), to buy for him whatever he sees fit. He said: 'Buy a female slave who will be with you. The female slave belongs to the owner of the capital; if there is a minor defect in her, it is upon the mudarib (agent), and if there is profit, it is for the mudarib.'
