From him, from Fudayla, from Aban, from Zurara, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon them both) would not return a slave girl who was not pregnant if he had intercourse with her; he would deduct from her price an amount equal to her defect. He (peace be upon him) narrated from a man who bought a slave girl, not knowing she was pregnant, and then had intercourse with her; he said: He returns her to the one from whom he bought her, and returns to him half of the tenth of her value as compensation for his marriage (intercourse) with her. And Ali (peace be upon him) said: She is not returned if her owner has intercourse with her, and an amount equal to her defect is deducted from her price if there is a defect in her.

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Jamil ibn Salih, from Abd al-Malik ibn 'Amr, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: "The one who is not pregnant is not returned [to the seller] if her husband has had intercourse with her, and he is entitled to the compensation for her defect; but the pregnant one is returned, and with her half of one-tenth of her value is returned."

Al-Husayn ibn Said from Ibn Abi Umayr from Jamil from Abd al-Malik ibn Amr from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): In the man who buys a female slave while she is pregnant and then has intercourse with her, he said: 'He returns her and returns one-tenth of her price if she is pregnant.'

From him, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from Aban ibn Uthman, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Abdillah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a man who buys a female slave, has sexual intercourse with her, and then finds her to be pregnant. He said: 'He returns her, and returns with her something (a portion of the price).'

From him, from Fudaylah, from Aban, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) Regarding a man who buys a pregnant slave-girl, then has intercourse with her while he is unaware (of her pregnancy), he said: 'He returns her and clothes her.'

Abu al-Maghra' from Fudayl, the freedman of Muhammad ibn Rashid, said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who sold a pregnant slave girl while he was unaware of her pregnancy, and the buyer married her. He said: 'He returns her and returns half of the tenth of her value.'

Ahmad ibn Muhammad from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Ibn Abi 'Umayr from some of our companions from Sa'id ibn Yasar from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Regarding a man who sold a pregnant slave girl while he was unaware of her pregnancy, and the buyer married her, he said: 'He returns her and returns half of one-tenth of her value.' Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: There is no contradiction between these narrations, because that which is incumbent upon the one who consummates marriage with the slave girl while she is pregnant, and then wishes to return her, is to return with her half of one-tenth of her price. This is what was contained in the hadith of Ibn Sinan, 'Abd al-Malik ibn 'Amr, Muhammad ibn Rashid, and Sa'id ibn Yasar. As for the narration of 'Abd al-Malik ibn 'Amr which al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated, stating that it is incumbent upon him one-tenth of her value, it is possible that it was a mistake by the transcriber, that 'half' was dropped and 'one-tenth of the value' remained. For we have cited the narration from him, agreeing with the other narrations, regarding the obligation of half of one-tenth of the value, in what was narrated by 'Ali ibn Ibrahim. And if this narration were precise, it would be permissible to interpret it as referring to the one who consummates marriage with the slave girl while knowing that she is pregnant; in that case, one-tenth of her value is incumbent upon him as a penalty. However, half of one-tenth is incumbent only if he did not know of her pregnancy, consummated marriage with her, and then learned of the pregnancy. As for the report of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi 'Abdillah, and his saying that he returns with her 'something', it is not impossible that by 'something' he meant half of one-tenth of her value, because that is possible for him and for others. And when the amount is clarified in another report, this report should be interpreted according to it. As for the report narrated by Muhammad ibn Muslim, from his saying 'he returns her and clothes her', it is not impossible that he meant to clothe her with clothing equal in value to half of one-tenth of her price. And there is no contradiction between the narrations on this interpretation, in any case.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa from Abu Hammam said: I heard al-Rida (peace be upon him) saying: 'The slave is returned due to defects of the year, namely insanity, leprosy, and vitiligo. So when you buy a slave and find in him any of these characteristics, between you and the holder of Dhul-Hijjah (i.e., within the year), then return him to his owner.' Muhammad ibn Ali asked him, 'What if he ran away (abqa)?' He said, 'He is not returned unless he produces evidence that he ran away while in his possession.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn Asbat, from Abu al-Hasan al-Rida (peace be upon him), who said: I heard him (peace be upon him) saying: 'The option of return (khiyar) in animals is three days for the buyer, and in non-animals it is that they separate, and 'ahdath al-sanah' (sudden defects) are returned after one year.' I asked: 'And what are 'ahdath al-sanah'?' He said: 'Madness, leprosy, vitiligo, and qaran (a specific defect). So whoever buys and these defects occur in it, the ruling is that he returns it to its owner until the completion of the year from the day he bought it.'

Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub from Muhammad ibn al-Hamid from Muhammad ibn Ali said: I heard al-Rida (peace be upon him) saying: 'The slave is returned due to defects occurring within the year, from insanity, leprosy, vitiligo, and cataracts.' I said, 'And how is it returned from defects occurring within the year?' He said, 'This is the beginning of the year,' meaning Muharram. 'So when you buy a slave, if one of these characteristics occurs in him between you and Dhu al-Hijjah, you return him to his owner.'

Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Abu Abdillah al-Farra', from Hariz, from Zurarah, who said: I said to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him): 'We buy a female slave from the market, bear children by her, then a man comes and establishes proof that she was his slave, had not been sold, nor given as a gift.' He said: 'He should return his female slave to him and compensate him for what he benefited from.' He said: 'It seems his meaning is the value of the child.'

Sahl ibn Ziyad from Ibn Faddal from Abu al-Hasan al-Rida (peace be upon him) said: The female slave is returned (from the purchase) due to four traits: madness, leprosy, vitiligo, hunchback, and kyphosis, because they are in the chest, causing the back to enter and the chest to protrude.

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Isma'il ibn Marar, from Yunus: In a man who bought a slave girl on the condition that she was a virgin, but did not find her to be a virgin, he (peace be upon him) said: 'The excess of the value is returned to him, if it is known that he is truthful.'

Ahmad ibn Muhammad from al-Husayn from Zur'ah from Sama'ah said: I asked him about a man who sold a female slave on the condition that she was a virgin, but he did not find her to be so. He said: 'She is not returned to him, nor is anything obligatory upon him, because she may have lost her virginity due to an illness or an ailment that affected her.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Jamil ibn Darraj, from some of our companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): Regarding a man who bought a female slave and she bore him a child, and it was found that the female slave had been stolen. He said: 'The owner takes the female slave, and the man takes his child by paying her value.'

Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Malik ibn 'Atiyyah from Dawud ibn Farqad said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who bought a mature slave-girl, and she did not menstruate at his place until six months had passed for her, and there was no pregnancy in her. He said: 'If girls like her do menstruate, and it was not due to old age, then this is a defect, and she is returned because of it.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from al-Husayn ibn Muhammad from al-Sayyari, who said: It was narrated from Ibn Abi Layla. A man brought his adversary to him and said, 'This man sold me this slave girl, but when I uncovered her, I did not find hair on her pubic area, and he claimed she never had any.' Ibn Abi Layla said to him, 'People use tricks in this matter to escape liability; what did you dislike?' He said, 'O Judge, if it is a defect, rule for me on that.' He said, 'Wait until I come out to you, for I feel discomfort in my stomach.' Then he entered and exited through another door and went to Muhammad ibn Muslim al-Thaqafi, and said, 'What do you narrate from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) regarding a woman who does not have hair on her pubic area; is that considered a defect?' Muhammad ibn Muslim said to him, 'As for this explicitly, I do not know it, but Abu Ja'far narrated to me from his father from his forefathers (peace be upon them) from the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) that he said: "Whatever is part of the original creation, if it increases or decreases, it is a defect."' Ibn Abi Layla said, 'That is sufficient for me,' then he returned to the people and ruled in their favor regarding the defect.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr from Jamil ibn Darraj from Muyassir said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): A man buys a skin of oil and finds dregs (sediment) in it. He said: 'If he is someone who knows that dregs are usually in the oil, he does not have the right to return it; and if he does not know, he has the right to return it.'

From him, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Hamzah, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a man who bought a house that had an addition from the road. He said, 'If that was included in what he bought, there is no harm.'

Al-Saffar from Muhammad ibn Isa from Ja'far ibn Isa said: I wrote to Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him), 'May I be your ransom, goods are sold, and the caller calls out on them. When he calls out on them, he is free from every defect in them. When the buyer buys it and is satisfied with it, and only the payment of the price remains, perhaps he becomes indifferent (to it). When he becomes indifferent to it, he claims defects in it and that he did not know of them. So the caller says to him, 'I have freed myself from them.' And the buyer says to him, 'I did not hear the freeing from them.' Is he believed so that the price is not obligatory upon him, or is he not believed so that the price is obligatory upon him?' He (peace be upon him) wrote back, 'The price is obligatory upon him.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father, from al-Nawfali, from al-Sakuni, from Ja'far, from his father, upon them be peace: 'That Ali (peace be upon him) ruled in the case of' a man who bought from another man a skin containing ghee, which had been hoarded as a single unit, and found in it butter. He disputed with him and went to Ali (peace be upon him). Ali (peace be upon him) said to him, 'For you is the amount of ghee corresponding to the measure of the butter.' The man said to him, 'I sold it to you as a hoarded unit.' Ali (peace be upon him) said to him, 'You bought ghee from him, and did not buy butter from him.'

Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan, from Amr ibn Sa'id, from Musaddiq ibn Sadah, from Ammar ibn Musa, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about the vineyard (or fruit-bearing land), when is its sale permissible? He said: 'When it sets (the fruit) and becomes 'Uqud'. And 'Uqud' is the name of Al-Hisrm in the Nabataean (Syriac) language.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad al-Jawhari from Ali ibn Abi Hamzah who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who bought a garden containing date palms and trees, some of which had borne fruit and some of which had not. He said: 'There is no objection if it contains what has borne fruit.' He said: And I asked him about a man who bought a garden containing date palms that contained nothing but green unripe dates. He said: 'No, until they become ready (yazhwu).' I said: 'And what is the readiness (al-zahw)?' He said: 'Until they change color (yatalawwan).'

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid from 'Uthman ibn 'Isa from Sama'ah who said: I asked him about the sale of fruit, whether its purchase is valid before its sprouts emerge, so he said, 'No, unless he buys other things along with it, fresh or vegetables, so he says: I buy from you this fresh produce and this palm tree and this tree for such and such an amount. If the fruit does not emerge, the buyer's principal capital is in the fresh produce and the vegetables.'

Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Sama'ah, from more than one, from Aban, from Isma'il ibn al-Fadl, said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the sale of fruit before it is ripe, so he said: 'If in that land there is a sale of it with produce that has ripened, then the sale of all of it is permissible.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from Safwan from Ya'qub ibn Shu'ayb said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: "When a wall-enclosed garden contains different types of fruits, and some of them ripen, there is no objection to selling all of them."

From him, from Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad, from Al-Hasan ibn Ali al-Wassash, who said: I asked Al-Rida (peace be upon him): 'Is it permissible to sell the palm trees when they have borne fruit?' He said: 'It is not permissible to sell them until they become ripe (yazhwa).' I said: 'And what is ripening (al-zahw)? May I be your ransom.' He said: 'They turn red and yellow, and similar to that.'

From him, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) was asked about buying palm trees, vineyards, and fruits for three or four years. He said, 'There is no harm in it. He means: if it does not produce in this year, it will produce in the next. And if you buy it for one year, do not buy it until it matures. And if you buy it for three years before it matures, there is no harm.' And he was asked about a man who buys named fruit from a land, and that entire land perishes. He said, 'They disputed that matter before the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family). They would keep mentioning it, and when he saw that they did not cease the dispute, he forbade them from that sale until the fruit matures, but he did not forbid it completely; he did so because of their dispute.'

From him, from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Rib'i, who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'I have date palms in Basra, so I will sell them and name the price, and reserve the kur (a specific measure/quantity) of dates or more.' He said, 'There is no objection.' I said, 'May I be your ransom, do we sell the pre-harvest dates (sine)?' He said, 'There is no objection.' I said, 'May I be your ransom, indeed that is significant with us.' He said, 'As for if you say that, indeed the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) permitted that, but they imposed restrictions upon it. So he (peace be upon him) said,

Ahmad ibn Muhammad from al-Hajjaj from Thal'abah ibn Zayd from Burayd said: I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about the fresh dates (ruthab) being sold in two or three portions (qita'), he said, 'There is no harm in it.' He said, So I increased my questioning about similar matters, and he would say, 'There is no harm in it.' So I said, 'May Allah rectify you, indeed those among us are corrupting this entirely for us.' He said, 'I think they heard the hadith of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) regarding the palms.' Then a man interposed between me and him, so he fell silent. So I commanded Muhammad ibn Muslim to ask Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about the saying of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) regarding the palms. Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said, 'The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) went out and heard a noise/clamor, so he said, "What is this?"' It was said, "The people are trading in the palms," so the palms were held back (not sold) this year.' So he (peace be upon him and his family) said, "When they do that, do not buy the palms until something appears in them and is not yet prohibited (by drying out)."'

Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from 'Uthman ibn 'Isa from Sama'ah who said: I asked him about the leaves of the tree, is the purchase of three 'kharatat' or four 'kharatat' valid? He said: 'When you see the leaves on a tree, buy whatever you wish from the 'kharat'.'

Sahl ibn Ziyad from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr from Muawiya ibn Maythara said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about selling the palm trees for two years. He said, 'There is no harm in it.' I said, 'And the rutbah (fresh dates), we sell this portion, and so and so portion after it.' He said, 'There is no harm in it.' Then he said, 'My father used to sell the henna in such and such batches.'

Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Sama'a, from more than one, from Aban ibn Uthman, from Yahya ibn Abi al-Ala', who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'Whoever sells a palm tree that has been pollinated, the fruit belongs to the seller, unless the buyer stipulates otherwise; the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) ruled according to that.'

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa narrated from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ghiyath ibn Ibrahim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) said: 'Whoever sells a palm tree that has fruited, its fruit belongs to the seller, unless the buyer stipulates otherwise.' Then he said: 'Indeed, Ali (peace be upon him) said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) ruled according to that.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from Muhammad ibn Abdillah ibn Hilal from Uqbah ibn Khalid from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) ruled that the fruit of the palm tree belongs to the one who pollinates it, unless the buyer stipulates otherwise.

Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Khalid ibn Jarir from Abu al-Rabii al-Shami said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) used to say: 'When an orchard containing date palms and trees is sold for one year, it should not be sold until its fruit ripens. And when it is sold for two or three years, there is no harm in selling it after there is some greenery in it.'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Safwan and Ali ibn al-Nu'man from Ya'qub ibn Shu'ayb said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the purchase of palm trees, and he said: 'My father (peace be upon him) disliked the purchase of palm trees before the fruit of the year emerges, but for two or three years he would say: "If it does not bear fruit in this year, it will bear fruit in the next year."' Ya'qub said: And I asked him about a man who buys palm trees and fruit before they emerge, purchasing for two years, or three years, or four. He said: 'There is no harm. Only the purchase of one year before the fruit emerges is disliked, out of fear of defect until it becomes clear.'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd from Hisham ibn Salim and Ali ibn al-Nu'man from Ibn Mukkan, all from Sulayman ibn Khalid, who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'Do not buy the palm trees for one year until they bear fruit, even if they are bearing fruit, and if you wish to buy them for two years, then do so.'

From him, from Uthman ibn Isa, from Sama'ah, from Abu Basir, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), that he said: "Do not buy the palm trees for one year until they bear fruit, and if you wish to buy them for two years, then do so." Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: The basis for this is that it is more precautionary that the fruit is not bought for one year except after its goodness becomes apparent. If it is bought, it is not bought except with something else accompanying it. If it loses value, the principal capital remains in what is left. And whenever it is bought otherwise, the sale is not invalid, but the doer has done what is disliked. And this was made explicit in the narrations we presented earlier, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), including the hadith of al-Halabi, that the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) forbade it in order to cut off the disputes occurring between the companions, and he did not forbid it strictly. And Thalabah ibn Zayd mentioned this and added that he forbade them in that specific year alone, not the other years. And in the hadith of Ya'qub ibn Shu'ayb, that his father (peace be upon him) disliked it and did not say that he forbade it strictly. And in this manner, there is no contradiction between the narrations.

Al-Husayn ibn Said from Safwan ibn Yahya from Ibn Muskhan from Muhammad al-Halabi from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a man who buys fruit, then sells it before he takes possession of it. He said: 'There is no harm in it; if he finds profit, let him sell it.'

From him, from Safwan and Fadalah, from al-Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from one of the Imams (peace be upon them both), that he said: Regarding a man who bought fruit, then sold it before he took possession of it, he said: 'There is no harm (in it).'

From him, from Ali ibn al-Nu'man and Safwan ibn Yahya, from Ya'qub ibn Shu'ayb, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), saying: 'I give a man twenty dinars for his fruit, and I say to him: When your fruit stands (matures), it is mine for that price; if I please, I take it, and if I dislike, I leave it.' He said: 'Can you not give it to him without stipulating anything?' I said: 'May I be your ransom, he does not specify anything; God knows that intention.' He said: 'It is not valid if that is his intention.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim narrated from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said regarding a man who said to another: 'Sell me the fruit of your palm tree, this one in it, for two qafizs of dates, or less or more, specifying whatever he wishes,' and he sold it: 'There is no objection to it.' He also said: 'Dates and unripe dates (busr) from a single palm tree are permissible (in sale), but if old dates and unripe dates are mixed, it is not valid, and raisins and grapes are the same.'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Abu Dawud from some of our companions from Muhammad ibn Marwan said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'I pass by fruit (on the tree) and eat from it.' He said, 'Eat, but do not carry (take away).' I said, 'May I be your ransom, indeed the merchants have bought it and paid their money.' He said, 'They bought what is not theirs.'

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: I wrote to him (peace be upon him) regarding a man who sold a garden of his that contained trees and a vineyard, and he excepted one tree from it. Is he entitled to a passage to the garden to reach the location of the tree he excepted? And how much of the surrounding land belongs to this excepted tree: is it according to the spread of its branches, or according to the spot where it is growing? So he (peace be upon him) wrote: 'He has that according to what he sold and kept, so he does not exceed the right in that, if God wills.'

Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Sama'ah, from Muhammad ibn Abi Yunus, from Yazid ibn Ishaq, from Harun ibn Hamzah al-Ghanawi, who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): A man buys palm trees to cut them for their trunks, but leaves them standing, and the palms bear fruit. He said: 'The fruit is for him, unless the owner of the land watered it and tended to it.'

From him, from Salih ibn Khallad and Ubays ibn Hasham, from Thabit, from Abdullah ibn Abi Ya'fur, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about a village that has outlying farms, date palms, crops, gardens, and orchards; I buy its produce. He said, 'There is no objection.'

From him, from Ja'far, from Dawud ibn Sirhan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: "The sale of dry dates for fresh dates is not valid, for fresh dates are moist and dry dates are dry; so when the fresh dates dry out, they lose weight."

From him, from Ubays ibn Hisham, from Thabit ibn Sharih, from Dawud al-Abzari, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I heard him say: 'It is not permissible to sell dates (tamar) with fresh dates (rutab); the dates are dry and the fresh dates are moist.'

From him, from Ubays ibn Hisham, from Thabit ibn Sharih, from Dawud al-Abzari, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: "It is not valid that you lend a fruit (crop) and take a better one from it in another land, other than what you lent from it."

From him, from Abdullah ibn Jabala, from Ali ibn Abi Hamza, from Abi Basir, from Abi Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: He was asked about palm trees and dates, when a man buys them for one year before they bear fruit. He said: 'No, until they bear fruit and their fruit is safe from defects. When they bear fruit, buy them for four years, if you wish, in addition to that year, or more than that, or less.'

From him, from Abdullah ibn Jabalah, from Ali ibn al-Harith, from Bakkar, from Muhammad ibn Shurayh, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who bought the fruit of a palm tree for two or three years, and there was no other palm tree in the land [of the transaction]. He said: 'It is not valid except for one year, and he should not buy it until its validity becomes clear.' He said: 'And it reached me that he said: Regarding the fruit of trees, there is no harm in buying it if its fruit has become valid.' It was said to him: 'And what is the validity of its fruit?' He said: 'When it sets [forms] after the falling of its blossom.'

From him, from Al-Hasan ibn Hisham, from Ya'qub ibn Shu'ayb, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about two men who have date palms between them, and one says to the other: 'Choose either that you take these date palms for such and such a specified measure, and give me half of that measure, whether it increases or decreases; or that I take them for that, and return [the value] to you.' He said, 'There is no objection to that.'

From him (Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad) from Ibn Ribat from Abu al-Subbah al-Kinanī who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: 'A man had a debt of fifteen wasqs of dates owed to him by another man, and the debtor had a date palm grove. The creditor said to him, "Take what is in my palm grove in exchange for your dates," but the debtor refused to accept. So the creditor went to the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) and said, "O Messenger of Allah, so-and-so owes me fifteen wasqs of dates; ask him to take what is in my palm grove in exchange for his dates." The Prophet sent to him and said, "O so-and-so, take what is in his palm grove in exchange for your dates." He said, "O Messenger of Allah, it will not be sufficient (in quality/quantity)," and he refused to do so. The Messenger of Allah said to the owner of the palm grove, "Cut your palm trees." So he cut them, and he weighed out for him fifteen wasqs.' So some of our companions informed me from Ibn Ribat, and I do not know except that I heard it from him, that Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'When Rabī'ah al-Ra'yī heard this from the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family), he said, "This is riba (usury)." I said, "I bear witness by Allah that he is among the liars." He said, "He was truthful."'

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Fadhal, from Amr ibn Sa'id, from Musaddiq ibn Sadah, from 'Ammar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) He was asked about fruit, when is its sale permissible? He said: 'If there is abundant fruit in one place, and some of it has been fed to the birds (or ripened), then the sale of all the fruit becomes permissible. If it is of one kind, its sale is not permissible until it is fed. If there are different kinds, nothing from it is sold until each kind is fed individually, then those kinds are sold.'

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Yaqteen, from his brother al-Husayn ibn Ali ibn Yaqteen, from Ali ibn Yaqteen, who said: I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about a man who passes by fruit from crops, palm trees, vineyards, trees, and places of grazing, and other such fruits: Is it permissible for him to take something from it and eat without the permission of the owner? And what is his status if the owner of the fruit forbids him, or the guardian commands him (to stop) and he does not? And what is the limit that allows him to take from it? He (peace be upon him) said: 'It is not permissible for him to take anything from it.' Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: His (peace be upon him) statement 'It is not permissible for him to take anything from it' is to be understood as referring to what he carries with him (for storage/transport). As for what he eats on the spot from the fruit, it is permissible, and we have clarified that. And to add further clarification to this, what has been narrated is:

Al-Husayn ibn Said from Ibn Abi Umayr from some of our companions from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a man who passes by date palms, grain ears, and fruit, and whether it is permissible for him to eat from them without the owner's permission, whether out of necessity or not. He said, 'There is no harm.'

Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Abu Dawud, from some of our companions, from Muhammad ibn Marwan, who said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'I pass by a date-palm and eat from it.' He said, 'Eat, but do not carry (take away).' I said, 'May I be your ransom, the merchants have bought it and paid its price.' He said, 'They bought what is not theirs.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from al-Husayn ibn Muhammad from al-Mu'alla from al-Washsha' said: I asked Abu al-Hasan al-Rida (peace be upon him) about a man who emancipates his slave while he is in good condition, then later needs money; is it permissible for him to sell the slave? He said, 'Yes, if he needs to do so.'

Ali ibn Ibrahim narrated from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Muawiya ibn Ayyar, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about Al-Tadbir (manumission of a slave), so he said: 'It is in the position of a will/testament; the master may revert [to keeping the slave] in whatever he wishes from it.'

From him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Faddal, from Ibn Bukayr, from Zurarah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about the Mudabbir (a slave manumitted upon the owner's death), is he from the one-third [of the estate]? He said, 'Yes, and the testator has the right to return [revoke or modify] in his will, whether he bequeathed in health or in sickness.'

Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Abu Ayyub from Aban ibn Taghlib said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who manumitted his female slave conditionally (tabeer), then married her to another man, and she bore children from him. Then her husband died and left children from her. He (peace be upon him) said: 'Her children are like her status; so when the one who manumitted her dies, they become free.' I said to him: 'Is it permissible for the one who manumitted her mother to return her to conditional manumption if he needs to?' He said: 'Yes.' I said: 'What if you see that if their mother dies after the husband has died, and her children from the free husband remain? Is it permissible for her master to sell her children and return them to conditional manumption?' He said: 'No. He only has the right to return her to conditional manumption if he needs to and she agrees to that.'

And from him, from Ali ibn Abi Hamzah, from Abu Basir, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: "The Mudabbir (a slave manumitted upon the owner's death) is a slave, and his master may revoke the manumission if he wishes: he may sell him, or if he wishes, give him away as a gift, or if he wishes, marry him off." He (the Imam) said: "And if his master leaves him in the state of Mudabbir and does not introduce a change in him until the master dies, then the Mudabbir is free when the master dies. And from the third (of the estate), it is only like a man who made a will, then changed his mind later and altered it before his death; and if he left it and did not alter it until he died, it is taken according to it."

And from him, from Abu Ayyub, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about a man who manumitted his slave by deed (dabbara) and then needed the money for its price. He said, and he said: 'He is his slave; if he wishes, he can sell him; and if he wishes, he can free him; and if he wishes, he can keep him until he dies. So when the master dies, the slave is freed from one-third of his estate.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Isma'il ibn Marar, from Yunus Regarding the Mudabbir (male slave manumitted upon owner's death) and the Mudabbarah (female slave manumitted upon owner's death): They are sold; their owner sells them during his lifetime. When he dies, they have become free, because manumission upon death is a promise (wa'd), not a mandatory obligation (wajib). Therefore, when he dies, the Mudabbir is from his third (of the estate) which he leaves, and her freedom is permissible for her master who manumitted her, and for the buyer if he bought her, her purchase is permissible before his death.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Ibrahim ibn Hashim, from al-Nawfali, from al-Sakuni, from Ja'far, from his father, from Ali (peace be upon him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) sold the service of the Mudabbir, but did not sell his neck (freedom).

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad, from al-Hasan ibn Ali, from Abu al-Hasan al-Rida (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about a man who manumitted his female slave while she was pregnant. He said: 'If he knew of the pregnancy, what is in her womb is like her [in status], and if he did not know, what is in her womb is a slave [not manumitted].'

And from him, from several of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Uthman ibn Isa al-Kilabi, from Abu al-Hasan (the first) (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about a woman who manumitted her slave girl on condition of manumission (tadbir), and the slave girl gave birth to a valuable female child. The woman did not know whether the born child was also manumitted on condition (mudabbarah) or not. He said to me, 'When was the pregnancy with the manumitted one? Before she manumitted her, or after she manumitted her?' I said, 'I do not know, but answer me for both cases.' He said, 'If the woman manumitted her while she was pregnant and did not specify what was in her womb, then the slave girl is manumitted on condition, and the child is a slave. But if the pregnancy occurred only after the manumission, then the child is manumitted on condition along with the manumission of its mother.'

Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Ibn Ri'ab from Burayd ibn Mu'awiya said: I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about a man who freed his slave conditionally upon his death (mudabbir), who was a wealthy merchant. The freed slave bought a female slave, and then the freed slave died before his master. He said, and he (the Imam) said: 'I see that all the wealth or possessions left by the mudabbir belong to the one who freed him. And I see that the mother of his child (umm walad) belongs to the one who freed him. And I see that her children are also mudabbarun, in the manner of their father. So when the one who freed their father dies, they become free.'

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from Wahb ibn Hafth from Abu Basir who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who emancipated his slave while he had a debt, fleeing from the debt. He said: 'There is no emancipation for him, and if he emancipated him while in good health and soundness, there is no claim for the creditor against him.'

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa narrated from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Yaqteen from his brother al-Husayn from Ali ibn Yaqteen who said: I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about the sale of the mudabbir (a slave manumitted upon the owner's death). He said: 'If the owner gave permission for it, there is no harm in it. And if there was a debt upon the master of the slave, and he manumitted him to escape the debt, there is no manumission for him. And if he manumitted him while in health and soundness, the creditor has no claim against him, and his manumission proceeds.'

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from Yazid Sha'ir from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a female slave manumitted via 'tadbir' (manumission upon the master's death) by her master. He said: 'Whatever she bears, they are in her position, and they are from one-third of his estate. If they are more than one-third, they will be accommodated regarding the reduction. And the manumission contract (mukatabah) applies to whatever she bears during her mukatabah period, so they are in her position. If she dies, then upon them is what remains of her debt, if they wish; so when they pay it, they are freed.'

And from him, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from al-Washsha', who said: I asked al-Rida (peace be upon him) about a man who manumitted his female slave while she was pregnant, and he said: 'If he knew of the pregnancy of the female slave, then what is in her womb is like her [in terms of manumption], and if he did not know, then what is in her womb is a slave [not yet manumitted].'

From him, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Abi Hamzah, from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him), who said: I said to him, 'My father passed away and left two slave-girls whom he had manumitted conditionally (dabbara), and I am among those who testify to their manumission, and he has a large debt. What is your opinion?' He said, 'May Allah be pleased with your father and raise him with Muhammad (peace be upon him and his family). Paying off his debt is better for him, if Allah wills.'

From him, from Abu Ja'far, from Abu al-Jawza', from al-Husayn ibn 'Ulwān, from 'Amr ibn Khālid, from Zayd ibn 'Alī, from his fathers, from 'Alī (peace be upon him) who said: "The one manumitted on the master's death (mudabbad) is from the one-third [of the estate], and whatever debt he incurs, and the one who enters into a contract of manumission (mukatib), and the mother of the child (umm al-walad), then the master is liable for their debts."

From him, from Abu Ja'far, from his father, from Wahb, from Ja'far, from his father, peace be upon them, that Ali (peace be upon him) said: The Mudabbir (slave manumitted upon owner's death) is not sold except from his own self (i.e., using his own money).

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Safwan from Ishaq ibn 'Ammar said: I said to Abu Ibrahim (peace be upon him): A man frees his slave by manumission upon his death (tadbir), then he needs the price of the slave. He said: 'He sells him.' I said: 'And if he is wealthy regarding the price?' He said: 'If the slave agrees.'

And from him (Al-Shaykh) from Ibn Abi Umayr from Jamil who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the Mudabbir (a slave manumitted upon the owner's death), is he sold? He said, 'If his owner needs his price (to pay debts or for other needs).' And he said, 'If the slave consents, there is no harm.'

From him, from Safwan and Fadalah, from al-Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I said to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him): A man manumits his slave conditionally (mudabbir), then later needs the money (to buy him back or use the value). He said: 'If he needs the money, it is for him; he may sell (the slave) if he wishes, or he may free (him) completely, and that is from the third (part of the value/ownership).'. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: What these narrations include regarding the permissibility of selling the mudabbir is actually the permissibility of selling his service/labor, not the neck (full ownership), because we have clarified that as long as he is mudabbir, the owner possesses only his service for the duration of his life. And if he does not possess anything else from him, then selling anything other than that is not valid from him. And we will also cite later what confirms this. As for what the preceding narrations included regarding that conditional manumption is like a will, and a person may retract his will, the meaning in it is that the owner may annul the conditional manumption, just as he may annul the will. So whenever he annuls it, the mudabbir returns to being a pure slave, at which point it is permissible for him to sell his neck (full ownership), just as it is permissible for him to sell the others among his slaves. And whenever he does not annul the conditional manumption and wishes to sell him, it is not permissible for him to sell except the service, according to what we have presented. And that which adds clarification to this is what he narrated:

And from him, from Fadala, from Aban, from Abu Maryam, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: He was asked about a man who frees his female slave by manumission upon death (tadbir): does he have the right to have sexual relations with her if he wishes, or to marry her, or to sell her service during his lifetime? He said: 'Yes, he may do whichever he wishes.'

And from him (Al-Hassan ibn Ma'shah) from An-Nadr ibn Suwayd from 'Asim from Abu Basir who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the male and female slave who are manumitted upon the master's death (tadbir). He said: 'It is for his master to manumipate them by writing a deed of manumission (mukatabah) if he wishes, and it is not for him to sell them unless the slave wishes to sell himself for the duration of his life, and it is for him to take their wealth if they have wealth.'

And from him (Al-Hassan ibn Ma'shah) from Al-Qasim ibn Muhammad from Ali (peace be upon him) who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who freed his female slave by manumission upon his death (tadbir) during his lifetime. He said: 'If he wishes to sell her, he sells her service during his lifetime. When he dies, the female slave is freed. And if she bears children, they are in her position (free upon his death).'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from Muhammad ibn Abdillah ibn Hilal from Muhammad ibn Muslim from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a female slave who had been manumitted upon death (mudabbarah) and had run away (abqa) from her master for years, then she returned after her master had died, bringing with her many children and possessions. Two witnesses testified that her master had indeed manumitted her upon death while he was alive, before she ran away. He said: 'I see that she and all that is with her belongs to the heirs.' I said: 'Will she not be manumitted from one-third of her master's estate?' He said: 'No, for she ran away while disobedient to Allah, Exalted and Majestic, and to her master, and the running away (ibaq) annulled the manumission (tadbir).'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Ali ibn al-Nu'man from Ya'qub ibn Shu'ayb said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who has a female servant, and he says: 'She is for so-and-so to serve him as long as he lives, and when he dies, she is free.' The servant escapes before the man dies by five or six years, then his heirs find her. Is it for them to employ her after she has escaped? He said: 'No, when the man dies, she has become free.' Because the meaning in this report is that the manumission (tadbir) was suspended upon the death of the man for whom she was designated to serve. Where she escaped, it prevented the man (while alive) from exercising authority over her, and that does not invalidate the manumission. The first case was that the manumission was suspended upon the death of the master; where she escaped, her escaping prevented her master from exercising authority over her, and that invalidated the manumission. There is no contradiction between the two reports, and the first report adds clarification to what was narrated.

Al-Bazofari from Ahmad ibn Idris, from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Abdillah ibn al-Mughira, from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Fadhal, from al-'Ala' ibn Razin, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) In the case of a man who manumitted conditionally (dabbara) a slave of his, and the slave ran away (abaq) and went to a people and married among them, and he did not inform them that he was a slave, and children were born to him and he acquired wealth, and the master who had manumitted him died. Then the heirs of the deceased who had manumitted the slave came and sought the slave. He was asked: What do you think? He said: 'The slave and his children belong to the heirs of the deceased.' I said: 'Has he not already been manumitted conditionally?' He replied: 'When he ran away, it invalidated his manumission, and he returned to slavery.'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Fadala from Aban from Abd al-Rahman said: I asked him about a man who said to his slave: 'If an event befalls me, he is free, and upon the man is the freeing of a neck as expiation for an oath or for dhihar.' Is it permissible for him to emancipate the slave whom he designated for emancipation if an event befalls him, in the expiation of that oath? He said: 'It is not permissible for the one who designated that for him.'

Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Mu'awiya ibn Wahb from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I said to him, 'I manumitted a slave-girl belonging to our orphans, and stipulated with her that if she became unable (to pay), she would be returned to slavery, and I would be free of what I took from you.' He said, 'Your condition is valid. And it will be said to you that Ali (peace be upon him) used to say, "The manumitted slave is freed in proportion to what he has paid of his manumission contract." So say, "That was only from the saying of Ali (peace be upon him) before the people made stipulations; when the people made stipulations, their condition became valid."' I said to him, 'What is the definition of inability?' He said, 'Our judges say: If the manumitted slave is unable to delay the installment (najm) until the next installment, until a year passes over it.' I said, 'And what do you say?' He said, 'No, and no honor; he is not allowed to delay an installment beyond its appointed time if that is part of his condition.'

And from him, from Umar ibn Yazid, from Burayd al-Ajli, who said: I asked him about a man who manumitted his slave by installments (mukatab) for one thousand dirhams, and did not stipulate at the time of the contract that if he became unable to pay, he would return to slavery. And the mukatab paid his master five hundred dirhams, then the mukatab died, leaving wealth, and leaving a mature son. He said: 'Half of whatever the mukatab left is for his master who contracted with him, and the remaining half is for the son of the mukatab. Because the mukatab died, and half of him was free and half of him was a slave to the one who contracted with him. So the son of the mukatab is in the same state as his father: half of him is free and half of him is a slave to the one who contracted with his father. If he pays to the one who contracted with his father what remained on his father, then he is free, and there is no claim of anyone among the people upon him.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Safwan from al-'Ala' ibn Razin from Muhammad ibn Muslim from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: Indeed, the mukatab (slave who has agreed to pay a fixed sum for his freedom) is freed in proportion to what he pays, unless his masters stipulate that if he is unable to pay, he is returned to slavery, so the condition holds for them.

And from him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Mu'awiya ibn Wahb, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a female slave who entered into a contract of manumission (mukatabah) and had paid two-thirds of the agreed amount, and it had been stipulated upon her that if she became unable to pay, she would return to slavery. We were in a state of freedom regarding what we had taken from her, and two installments (najm) had become due upon her. He said: 'She is returned [to slavery], and it is pleasing to them [the master] regarding what they had taken from her.' And he said: 'She does not have the right to delay the installment after its due date by one month, except with their permission.'

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from al-Hasan ibn Musa al-Khashshab from Ghiyath ibn Kalhub from Isḥaq ibn 'Ammar from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) from his father that 'Ali (peace be upon him) used to say: "When the mukatab (slave with a contract of manumission) becomes unable [to pay], his contract is not revoked back into slavery, but he is given a year or two; if he fulfills his contract, [he is freed], otherwise he is returned to slavery." And if he had not done it, he would not have deserved punishment, nor would he have been transgressing regarding an obligation for which leaving it incurs sin; and that which clarifies also what we mentioned, that when the condition is fulfilled, he has the right to be returned to slavery, is what he narrated:

Al-Husayn ibn Said from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad from Al-Halabi from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): In the mukatab (slave who has contracted for manumission for a specified sum) who pays part of his manumission money, he said: 'Indeed, the people used not to stipulate [a condition of return if unable to pay], but today they do stipulate. And Muslims are upon their conditions. So if he stipulated upon him that if he became unable [to pay], he would return [to slavery], and if he did not stipulate upon him, he would not return.' And regarding the saying of Allah, Exalted and Mighty: 'So write for them if you know in them any good' (1), he said: 'Write for them if you know they have wealth.'

Ibn Mahbub from Ali ibn Abi Hamzah from Abu Basir from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: The mukatab (slave who has contracted for manumission upon paying a sum) is not permitted to have emancipation, nor gift, nor marriage, nor testimony, nor pilgrimage, until he pays all that is upon him. If his master stipulated that if he were unable to pay one installment, he would be returned to slavery.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Amr ibn Uthman, from al-Husayn ibn Khalid, from al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) who said: He was asked about a man who manumitted his slave girl through mukatabah (agreement to pay a sum for freedom). The slave girl said, 'Whatever portion of my mukatabah I have paid, I am free in proportion to that.' He said to her, 'Yes.' Then she paid part of her mukatabah, and her master had intercourse with her after that. He said: 'If he forced her to do so, he is flogged with a number of lashes corresponding to the portion she had paid, and the flogging is deferred for him corresponding to the portion remaining for her to pay. And if she followed his lead (consented), she is his partner in the flogging; she is flogged just as he is flogged.'

Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Malik ibn 'Atiyyah from Sulayman ibn Khalid from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a man who had a slave father, and the father's wife was a mukatabah (slave woman contracted for manumission) who had paid part of what was due to her. The son of the slave said to her, 'Would you like me to assist you in your manumission contract until you pay what is due to you, on the condition that you do not have the option to choose to stay with your master if you acquire your own freedom?' She said, 'Yes.' So he gave her the manumission contract on the condition that she would not have the option afterwards. He (the Imam) said, 'She does not have the option; Muslims are bound by their conditions.'

From him, from Malik, from Abu Basir, who said: I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about a man who freed half of his female slave, and then he contracted a manumission agreement (kitabah) with her for the remaining half after that. He said, so he should stipulate upon her that if she is unable to pay the installments (nujum), then she returns to slavery in respect of half of her body. He said, 'If he wishes, he may have service from her one day and she serves one day, if he does not contract kitabah with her.' I said, 'Is she permitted to marry in that state?' He said, 'No, until she pays all that is upon her from the half of her body.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from al-Nawfali from al-Sakuni from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) that the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) said: In the case of a female slave who is contracted for manumission (mukattabah), and her master has sexual relations with her, causing her to become pregnant, he said: 'He returns to her the dowry of her like (i.e., comparable value), and strives to pay her valuation. If she is unable to pay, she is considered one of the mothers of children (ummahat al-awlad).'

From him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from al-'Ala' ibn al-Fudayl, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding the saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: 'So write for them if you know within them any good and give them from the wealth of Allah which He has given you.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'You reduce for him from the installments (stipulated amounts) that you had not intended to reduce from them, and you do not increase beyond what is in your mind (your estimation of his ability to pay).' I asked: 'How much?' He said: 'Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) reduced for his slave one thousand from six thousand.'

Al-Husayn ibn Said from Abu Ahmad from 'Amr, the master of al-Karabis, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding a man who manumitted his slave on condition that the inheritance would be his, he raised that matter to Ali (peace be upon him), who annulled his condition and said, 'The condition of God is prior to your condition.'

From him, from Safwan, from Ibn Muskān, from al-Ḥalabī, from Abū ʿAbdillāh (peace be upon him) Regarding the saying of Allah, Exalted and Mighty: 'Write for them if you know in them any good.' He said: 'If you know for them religion and wealth.'

And from him, from Yusuf ibn Aqil, from Muhammad ibn Qays, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said: If the enslaved person entering into a contract of manumission (mukatab) stipulates upon his master that there is no right of patronage (walayah) for anyone upon him if he pays the money, and the one who contracted with him acknowledges this, then there is no right of patronage for anyone upon him. And if the master stipulates the patronage of the mukatab, and the one who was contracted with (the master) acknowledges it, then the patronage belongs to him.

And from him, from Safwan, from Al-As and Hammad, from Hariz, all of them, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from one of the two (Imams), upon them be peace, who said: I asked him about the saying of Allah, Exalted and Mighty: 'And give them from the wealth of Allah which He has given you.' And give them from the wealth of Allah which He has given you. He said: 'That which you intend to manumit him for. Do not say: I will manumit him for five thousand and leave a thousand for him, but rather look to that which you intended for him and give it to him from it.'

And from him, from al-Nadhr, from 'Asim ibn Humayd, from Muhammad ibn Qays, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said: The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) issued a ruling regarding a female slave who had entered into a contract of manumission (mukatabah), who died after having paid most of what was due to her, and who had given birth to a child during her period of manumission. He ruled regarding her child: 'One half of him is freed, corresponding to what was freed from her, and the other half remains in servitude, corresponding to what remained in servitude from her.'

And from him (Al-Hurr al-Amili) from Ibn Abi Umayr from Jamil ibn Darraj from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding a mukatab (a slave who has agreed to pay a specific sum for his freedom) who dies after having paid part of his manumission contract, and he has a son from a concubine, and he left wealth, he (the Imam) said: 'His son pays the remainder of his manumission, and he is freed, and he inherits what remains (of the wealth).'

And from him (Al-Hassan ibn Muhammad) from Ali ibn al-Nu'man from Abu al-Subbah from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding the mukatab (slave who has contracted for manumission for a specified sum), if he pays half of his manumission money and the half remains upon him, then he calls his masters to the remainder of his manumission and says: 'Take what remains as a single payment.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'They take what remains, then he is freed.' And he said regarding the mukatab who pays part of his manumission money, then dies, leaving a son and wealth greater than what he owes from his manumission: 'He pays his masters what remains of his manumission, and what remains is for his son.'
And from him (Al-Saduq), from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from Al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Like these two questions.

From him, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Ibn Sinan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): Regarding A mukatab (slave who has agreed to pay a sum for his freedom) dies having paid part of his manumission price, and he has a son by a concubine. He said: 'If it was stipulated that if he became unable [to pay], he would remain a slave, then his son returns as a slave, and the concubine [remains]. And if it was not stipulated, his son pays what remains of the manumission price, and inherits what remains.'

And from him (Al-Shaykh) from Ibn Abi Umayr and Fadala from Jamil ibn Darraj, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a mukatab (a slave who has contracted to pay a sum for his freedom) who pays part of his manumission contract, then dies, leaving a son from his own concubine. He said: 'If it was stipulated that if he became unable to pay, he would return to slavery, then his son returns as a slave along with the concubine. And if it was not stipulated, his son becomes free, and he returns the remainder of the manumission sum to the master, and his son inherits whatever remains.'

And from him (Al-Hadith) from Ibn Abi Umayr from Jamil from Mihran who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the mukatab (a slave who has contracted to pay a sum for his freedom) who dies and leaves children. He said: 'If it was stipulated upon him (the father) that his children would remain slaves, then his children are slaves. And if it was not stipulated upon him, his children will strive to free their father, and they will be freed if they pay (the debt).'

And from him, from Fadala, from Aban, from one who informed him, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding a man who owned a slave who had wealth, and the slave asked his master for mukatabah (contract of manumission), is it permissible for the master to stipulate that he does not contract with him except at a high price? He said, 'Yes.'

From him, from Al-Hasan, from Zur'ah, from Samaan, who said: I asked him about a slave whom his master manumits by installments (mukatabah), while the master knows that the slave has neither little nor much wealth. He (peace be upon him) said: 'He manumits him, even if the slave asks the people [for money], and his lack of wealth does not prevent the manumitation, for indeed Allah provides for the servants one from another, and the benefactor is assisted [by Allah].'

Al-Bazawfari from Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Malik from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn Abi al-Khattab from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Malik ibn 'Atiyyah who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) was asked about a mukatab (a slave who has contracted to pay a sum for his freedom) who died without paying off his contract, leaving wealth and a son. Who inherits him? He said: "If his master, at the time of contracting, stipulated that if he were unable to pay the installments, he would return to slavery, and he had indeed become unable to pay the installments, then whatever wealth he left belongs to the master, and his son returns to slavery. If his son was free after him, or if the master had contracted with him and his son together, [the ruling differs]. And if he did not stipulate that for him, then his son is free and pays on behalf of his father whatever remained of what his father left. The son has no share [of the estate] until he pays what is due upon him. And if his father left nothing, then there is nothing upon the son." Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: His saying (peace be upon him) 'and if his father left nothing, then there is nothing upon the son' is to be understood as meaning that the son is not liable for more than what remained due on his father, because we have clarified in the preceding narration, which Jamil narrated from Mihran, that if he had no wealth, his son would strive to pay what remained due on the father, and then he would become free after that.

Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad from al-Halabi from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: In the case of a mukatab who pays half of his manumission contract and the half remains upon him, so he calls his masters and says: 'Take what remains as a single payment,' he said: 'They take what remains and he is freed.'

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya from al-Hasan ibn Musa al-Khashshab from Ghiyath ibn Kalub from Isḥaq ibn 'Ammar from Ja'far from his father (peace be upon them both) A mukatab (a slave who has contracted to pay a sum for his freedom) came to Ali (peace be upon him) and said: 'My master contracted with me and stipulated installments (nujum) to be paid each year. I brought him the entire money in one lump sum, and asked him to accept it all at once and validate my freedom, but he refused. Ali (peace be upon him) called him and said: 'He is truthful.' Then Ali (peace be upon him) asked him: 'Why do you not accept the money and validate his freedom?' He said: 'I only accept the installments that I stipulated, so that I may be exposed to inheriting him [if he dies before the full amount is paid].' Ali (peace be upon him) said: 'You are more entitled to your stipulation.' Because the first report only included permitting the taking of his money from the installments in one lump sum, and did not include that it is obligatory for him to accept his money before the time, and the latter report included that he has the right to refuse accepting it and to demand it according to what he stipulated for him, and there is no contradiction between them in any case.

Al-Bazofari from Ahmad ibn Idris from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Najran from Asim ibn Humayd from Muhammad ibn Qays from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) ruled regarding a muqatib (a slave who has contracted for his manumission) who died and left wealth, saying: 'His wealth is divided according to the portion of it that was freed for his heirs, and what was not freed is accounted for his masters who contracted with him; it is their wealth.' The manner [of this ruling] is such that all the narrations are safe from contradiction.

And from him, from Ahmad ibn Idris, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Najran, from Asim ibn Humayd, from Muhammad ibn Qays, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said: The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) ruled regarding a mukatab (a slave who has contracted manumission for a specified sum) who had a free woman under him; she bequeathed to him upon her death. He said: 'The bequest of the wife to her husband is not valid, because he is a mukatab who has not yet been freed and does not inherit.' So he ruled that he inherits according to the portion of him that has been freed, and his bequest to him is valid according to the portion of him that has been freed. And he ruled regarding a mukatab who had paid a quarter of what was due to him, and he was bequeathed to; so he validated for him a quarter of the bequest. And he ruled regarding a free man who bequeathed to his mukatabah (female slave under contract), and she had paid a sixth of what was due to her; so he validated for her according to the portion of her that had been freed. And he ruled regarding the bequest of a mukatab who had paid part of what he was contracted to pay, that it is validated from his bequest according to the portion of him that has been freed.

Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Ali ibn Ri'ab from Abu Basir from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: The mukatab (slave who has contracted for manumission upon paying a sum) is not permitted to have his manumission, nor a gift, nor marriage, until he pays what is upon him. If his master stipulated to him, and he was unable, then he returns to slavery. However, he may buy and sell. And if a debt fell upon him in trade, it is upon his master to pay his debt, because he is his slave.

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Abu Ishaq, from some of our companions, from Al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) who said: He was asked about a mukatab (a slave who has contracted to pay a sum for his freedom) who became unable to pay the remainder, having already paid part of it. He said: 'The remainder is paid on his behalf from the wealth of zakat (alms-tax).' Indeed, Allah, the Exalted, says in His Book: 'And for the freeing of slaves.'

From him, from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Fadhal, from Amr ibn Sa'id, from Musaddiq ibn Sadah, from Ammar ibn Musa, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding a mukatabah (manumission contract) between two partners, where one of them frees his share: How should the servant act? He said: 'She serves the other [partner] one day and serves herself one day.' I said: 'If she dies and leaves wealth?' He said: 'The wealth is split in half between the one who freed [his share] and the one who retained [his share].'

From him, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad, from al-Amriki, from Ali ibn Ja'far, from his brother Musa ibn Ja'far (peace be upon them both), who said: I asked him about a man who manumitted his slave by contract (mukatabah), and after making the contract he said to him: 'Give me a portion of the price, and I will expedite your manumission in place of the contract.' He asked: Is that permissible? He replied: 'If it is a gift (hiba), there is no harm; but if he said: 'Reduce [the price] for me, and I will expedite [your manumission],' then it is not valid.'

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa from Ali ibn al-Hakam from Abu al-Mi'za from al-Halabi said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: "In the case of a mukatab (a slave who has contracted for his manumission), he is given the hadd (flogging) to the extent of what has been freed from him." I asked: "Do you see if half of him is freed, does his testimony become valid in divorce?" He said: "If there is with him a man and a woman, his testimony is valid."

Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Mahbub, from Umar ibn Yazid, from Burayd al-Ajli, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said: I asked him about a man who manumitted his slave by contract (mukatabah) for one thousand dirhams, and did not stipulate at the time of contract that if he were unable to pay the full amount, he would return to slavery. The mukatab paid his master five hundred dirhams, then the mukatab died, leaving wealth and a mature son. He said: 'Half of whatever the mukatab left is for the master who contracted with him, and the remaining half is for the son of the mukatab, because he died half free and half slave. When he pays the one who contracted with his father what remained on his father, he is free, with no claim of anyone from the people upon him.'

From him, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad al-A'lawi, from Ali ibn Ja'far, from his brother Musa ibn Ja'far (peace be upon them both), who said: I asked him about the mukatab (a slave who has contracted a manumission deed), whether the fitrah of Ramadan is upon him or upon the one who contracted with him, or whether his testimony is valid? He said: 'The fitrah is upon him, and his testimony is not valid.'

Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Bunan ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Ibn al-Mughira, from al-Sakuni, from Ja'far, from his father, from Ali (peace be upon him) who said: "The Umm al-Walad fulfills the expiation for Dhihar."

From him, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Ghayath ibn Ibrahim, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father (peace be upon him), who said: The blind man is not excused regarding the neck (in prostration), and he is excused for what is from him like the one missing a limb, the lame, and the one-eyed; and the seated man is not excused.

From him, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from his men, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'Every emancipation is valid for the newborn, except in the case of the blood-guilt expiation, for indeed Allah the Exalted says, "So free a believing slave" (32:18), meaning one who has reached puberty. And in the case of Dhihar, a child born in Islam is sufficient. And in the expiation of the oath, a garment that covers his private parts is sufficient,' and he said, 'Two garments.'

From him, from some of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Dawud ibn Farqad, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding the expiation for the first part of the month, he said: He should give charity with one dinar; and for the middle part, with half a dinar; and for the last part, with a quarter of a dinar. I asked: And if he does not have what to expiate with, he said: Let him give charity to one poor person; or else, let him seek forgiveness from Allah and not return [to the act], for indeed seeking forgiveness is repentance and expiation for whoever does not find the means to give any of the expiations.

Asim ibn Humayd narrated from Abu Basir from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "Whoever is unable to perform the expiation that falls upon him, whether by fasting, freeing a slave, or giving charity, in the case of an oath, a vow, or killing, or any other matter requiring expiation, then seeking forgiveness is sufficient as an expiation for him, except for the oath of Dhihar (linguistic divorce), for if he cannot find what to expiate with, it becomes forbidden for him to have sexual intercourse with her, and they are separated, unless the woman consents that he remain with her without having sexual intercourse."

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali from his father from Safwan ibn Yahya from Isḥaq ibn 'Ammar from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) He (peace be upon him) said: 'If the owner of Dhihar is unable to pay the expiation, let him seek forgiveness from his Lord and intend not to return [to the act] before he consummates [the marriage], then let him consummate, and that will suffice for him in place of the expiation. When he finds the means to pay what expiates it, on any of the days, let him pay it. And if he gives charity from his hand, or feeds himself and his family, that will suffice for him if he is needy. And if he does not find that, let him seek forgiveness from his Lord and intend not to return; that is sufficient for him, and God is the Expiator.'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from 'Uthman ibn 'Isa from Sama'ah from Abu Basir said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: 'A man came to the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) and said: O Messenger of God, I have performed Dhihar with my wife. He said: 'Free a slave.' He said: 'I do not have one.' He said: 'Then fast two consecutive months.' He said: 'I cannot.' He said: 'Then feed sixty poor people.' He said: 'I do not have.' He said: 'Then the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said: I will give charity on your behalf.' So he gave him the cost of feeding sixty poor people and said: 'Go and give this in charity.' He said: 'By the One who sent you with the truth, what is between her two labia is more in need than I and my family.' He said: 'Go and eat and feed your family.' Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: These three narrations are consistent and not contradictory, because the first narration which said: 'If he is unable to perform the expiation, forgiveness does not suffice for it, and it only suffices for what is other than Dhihar, and it is forbidden for him to have intercourse with her,' does not contradict the final narration in which the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said to him: 'Eat and feed your family,' after he had given charity on his behalf, for two reasons: one is that it is permissible that when the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) gave charity on his behalf, the expiation fell from him, then he (peace be upon him) treated him in the manner of the weak among people by saying to him: 'Eat, you and your family,' because he saw their need for that. And the second is that he may have permitted this for him on the condition that whenever he is able to perform the expiation, he will give it, according to what the second narration contained which was narrated by Ishaq ibn 'Ammar, and there is no contradiction between them in any case.

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from 'Uthman ibn 'Isa from Sama'ah who said: I asked him about a man who said to his wife, 'You are upon me like the back of my mother.' He said, 'Upon him is the freeing of a slave, or feeding sixty poor people, or fasting two consecutive months.' Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: What this hadith and the preceding hadith of Mu'awiya ibn Wahb contained regarding the wording of choice in the expiation is diverted from its apparent meaning because we have clarified that the expiation of Dhihar is sequential as mentioned in the Book of Divorce. It is not impossible that it was used metaphorically, and the intended meaning is that if one cannot find/perform each of the expiations individually, the obligation transfers to the next. On this basis, there is no contradiction between the narrations.
Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Ibn Abi Umayr from Rifah from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: "The Muzahhir, if he fasts for a month and then falls ill, counts his fasting [towards his kaffarah]."

Yunus ibn Abd al-Rahman from Abd Allah ibn Sinan who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'The expiation of blood, if a man kills a believer intentionally, is that he must make himself available to their heirs; if they kill him, he has fulfilled what is upon him, provided he is remorseful for what he did and determined to avoid returning to it. And if they pardon him, he must free a slave, fast for two consecutive months, and feed sixty poor people, and be remorseful for what he did, be determined to avoid returning to it, and seek Allah's forgiveness forever as long as he lives. And if he kills by mistake, he pays their blood money and then frees a slave; if he cannot find one, he fasts for two consecutive months; if he cannot do that, he feeds sixty poor people, a modd each. And likewise, if the blood money of the slain is given to him, the expiation is incumbent upon him between himself and his Lord.'

From him, from Uthman ibn Isa, from Sama'ah, who said: I asked him about one who deliberately kills a believer, is there for him repentance? He said: 'He does not receive forgiveness until he pays his blood money (diyah) to his family, frees a slave, fasts for two consecutive months, seeks forgiveness of Allah, repents to Him, and supplicates humbly; for indeed I hope that forgiveness will be granted to him if he does that.' I said: 'And if he has no wealth to pay his blood money?' He said: 'He asks the Muslims until he pays his blood money to his family.'

From him, from Al-Hasan, from Al-Qasim, from Aban, from Ismail Al-Ju'fi, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him, 'If a man kills another man intentionally,' he said, 'He must perform three expiations: freeing a slave, fasting for two consecutive months, and feeding sixty poor people.' And he said, 'Ali ibn Al-Husayn (peace be upon them both) issued a fatwa to the same effect.'

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Abdillah ibn al-Mughirah, from the one who narrated to him, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding a man who slept through the 'Isha prayer and did not rise until after the middle of the night, he said: 'He prays it and becomes a fasting person in the morning.'

Al-Husayn ibn Said from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad from Al-Halabi from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) that he said: Regarding a man who killed his slave, he said: 'I like that he frees a slave, fasts for two consecutive months, and feeds sixty poor people, and then repentance follows after that.'

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar narrated from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Fadhal, from his father, from Abu al-Mi'za Humayd ibn al-Muthanna, from Mu'alla Abu Uthman, from al-Mu'alla and Abu Basir, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), that they heard him say: "Whoever kills his slave intentionally, upon him is to free a neck, or to fast for two consecutive months, or to feed sixty poor people."

From him, from Ibrahim ibn Hashim, from al-Nawfali, from al-Sakuni, from Ja'far, from his father, from Ali (peace be upon him), who said: "The blind slave, the one with a missing limb (amputee), and the insane person are valid for expiations (kaffarat), because the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) freed them."

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr from Abdillah ibn Sinan from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) Regarding a man who had intercourse with his wife in the month of Ramadan and could not find what to give in charity to sixty poor people, he said: 'He gives in charity according to his ability.'

From him, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from al-'Ala' ibn Razin, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) Regarding the saying of Allah, Exalted and Mighty: 'So whoever cannot find [one] or cannot afford it, then the expiation is feeding sixty poor people.' He said: 'From illness or thirst.' The book of Vows, Oaths, and Expiations is completed. And to Allah belongs success, and upon Him is reliance.
